text:
Nearly half a million dollars in regional environmental grants were awarded on Thursday to three organizations working to manage the impact of climate change, pollution and sea level rise on Martha’s Vineyard.

Cong. Bill Keating joined Peter Wharton, chair of the Martha’s Vineyard Commission, and Thomas Ardito, director of the Southeast New England Watershed Grant Program, to award $249,990 to the commission to implement a permeable reactive barrier to continue to improve water quality in Lagoon Pond, $242,000 to The Trustees of Reservations for salt marsh and barrier beach restoration on Chappaquiddick, and an additional $6,000 to The Great Pond Foundation to purchase water quality monitoring equipment.

“We’re leveraging science, technology, environmental expertise and we’re empowering the local communities to do what they know their needs are,” said Mr. Keating. “That’s what’s great about this program.”

The grants were awarded via the Environmental Protection Agency’s Southeast New England Program to empower the Vineyard community by funding projects that aid climate resiliency efforts around the Island.

“Nature is healing itself with watershed protection, with marshlands,” said Mr. Keating. “All we’re doing is aiding and literally channeling this, as is the case on Chappaquiddick, channeling nature so that it’s healing itself, and in the nitrogen issue, which is fascinating.”

A permeable reactive barrier was first installed at Lagoon Pond in 2020. According to Dr. Jessica Thomas, a professor of mathematics and physics at Roger Williams University, areas that have installed similar permeable barriers have seen 99 per cent reduction in harmful bioavailable nitrogen release.

“Permeable reactive barriers are an innovative technology for dealing with nitrogen,” said Ms. Thomas. “This is a technique that we can use to try to address that and it’s a natural technique.”

Nitrogen is a common ecological issue facing coastal communities and is most often released into the groundwater via nearby septic systems. Permeable reactive barriers are designed to function as a passive on-site method for groundwater treatment using seed oils to absorb excess nitrogen.

“We inject vegetable oil into the groundwater to intercept [nitrogen molecules] and that vegetable oil will create an environment for the natural microbes to take a bioavailable nitrogen, which is our problem nitrogen, and change it into nitrogen gas, which can off-gas right into the atmosphere and is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere,” said Ms. Thomas.

Following a brief discussion, those in attendance were invited to join Alejandra Narvaez, the coastal project manager at The Trustees of Reservations, on a tour of the salt marshes situated on Chappaquiddick. There, Ms. Narvaez discussed the history of salt marshes on the Island and how The Trustees plan to bolster areas that are highly susceptible to sea level rise.

According to Ms. Narvaez, models suggest that by 2070 the Dike Bridge, which grants access to various Chappaquiddick beaches via over-sand vehicles, will be submerged during daily tidal fluctuations.

“That’s why we’re intervening now,” she said during the tour. “We’re maintaining the natural vegetation to keep up with sea level rise.”

The process to protect salt marshes and barrier beaches involves a combination of efforts that include ditch remediation, which can take anywhere from three to five years, said Ms. Narvaez, and reconnecting channels via runnelling to reach an equilibrium and maintain natural tidal flow.

Typically, runnels are dug approximately seven inches into a salt marsh and are constructed in a ‘V’ shape to allow for natural reshaping as sea levels continue to rise.

“We want a light touch restoration,” said Ms. Narvaez. “We are basically remediating or healing these ditches.”

text:
Mercedes-AMG unveiled the all-electric Mercedes-AMG GT SUV on Saturday, October 17, 2026, the first full-size SUV the Affalterbach division has developed entirely in-house. The flagship GT 63 SUV uses three axial flux motors for a peak 1,153 horsepower and reaches 60 mph in an estimated 2.4 seconds.

The 2028 model arrives at US dealerships in summer 2027 as a GT 63, GT 55 and GT 53. Mercedes has not announced US pricing. It is the production version of the electric performance SUV EVXL first covered as a winter-testing prototype in December 2024.

The AMG GT 4-Door Coupe that launched the same platform in May peaks at 600 kW on a DC fast charger. The GT 63 and GT 55 SUV peak at 710 kW.

The GT 63 SUV’s 128 kWh Battery Pushes DC Charging to 710 kW

The SUV out-charges the 4-Door because the GT 63 and GT 55 get a larger pack: 128 kWh usable across 22 modules, against 106 kWh and 18 modules in the GT 53 SUV and the 4-Door. Mercedes rates the bigger pack at 710 kW, the smaller at 600 kW.

Mercedes quotes 10 to 80 percent in 12 minutes at the 710 kW peak, and 282 miles (454 kilometers) of WLTP range added in as little as 10 minutes. On a 400 kW station, the same session takes 16 minutes. Mercedes-Benz USA’s launch release labels its charging rates and times preliminary, with no certified values yet.

The 800-volt pack uses tall, narrow cylindrical cells bathed directly in non-conductive oil, the cooling approach Mercedes credits for both the charging rate and repeatable power. It switches to 400-volt mode at older stations, and Mercedes lists NACS among the five DC plug standards it supports.

The GT 63 SUV's six round taillights and active roof spoiler. Photo credit: Mercedes-Benz

The 1,153-HP GT 63 SUV Weighs 5,941 Pounds and Has No EPA Rating

Peak output for the GT 63 SUV is 1,153 hp and 1,475 lb-ft, with 711 hp available continuously and a 63-second boost window. The 2.4-second 0 to 60 mph time uses a 1-foot rollout; without it, Mercedes estimates 2.6 seconds. Top speed is limited to 168 mph.

That output puts the GT 63 SUV just ahead of the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric, which makes 1,139 hp on launch control and charges at up to 400 kW.

The DIN curb weight is 2,695 kilograms, or 5,941 pounds. Mercedes quotes 385 to 435 miles (620 to 700 kilometers) of WLTP range. The US release carries no EPA estimate.

The GT 55 SUV uses the same three motors and pack at 805 hp. The GT 53 SUV swaps in two synchronous motors and the 106 kWh pack for 536 hp. Storage runs to 21.4 cubic feet (606 liters) in the trunk and 2.8 cubic feet (79 liters) in the frunk.

AMGFORCE Sport+ Plays a Recorded V8 and Shakes the Seat

The AMGFORCE Sport+ drive program plays a recorded V8 in the GT 63 and GT 55 SUV, or a six-cylinder in the GT 53, and pairs it with simulated gear changes, paddle shifting and seat vibration. Mercedes says it built the sound from over 100 measurements taken with 16 microphones.

Inside, the 10.2-inch driver display and 14-inch center screen form one unit, and a second 14-inch screen is optional for the passenger. Rotary dials on the center console adjust throttle response, handling balance and traction control on the GT 63, and are optional on the GT 55.

The Mercedes-AMG GT SUV cockpit. Photo credit: Mercedes-Benz

The reference cars for the sound included the AMG GT R, and a slider lets the driver turn the effect down to “Silent.” Porsche added simulated gears to the 2027 Taycan in June, a feature its own development driver had publicly dismissed. Stefan Weckbach, who runs Mercedes-AMG, summed up the SUV’s pitch as “SUV by shape. GT by nature.”

EVXL’s Take

The 710 kW peak makes the headline, but I’d pay for the bigger pack behind it. Mercedes says a 400 kW charger takes the GT 63 SUV from 10 to 80 percent in 16 minutes. Porsche quotes a little under 16 minutes for the Cayenne Electric’s 113 kWh pack, so on the same charger the Mercedes refills 128 kWh of usable capacity in about the time the Porsche needs for a smaller battery. That gap holds whether or not a 710 kW station ever shows up on your route. The release doesn’t say what the SUV pulls from a Tesla Supercharger, where the Cayenne tops out at 200 kW. I’d want that number from Mercedes before calling this the faster road-trip SUV.

Source: Mercedes-Benz USA

text:
SALT LAKE CITY — Fervo Energy announced a 396 megawatt power purchase agreement with Google on Sept. 1 — enabling southwestern Utah's Cape Station geothermal plant development, coming online in 2028.

But Fervo's geothermal giant comes with a catch: None of the energy is going to Utahns ... yet.

California got there first

Most of Cape Station's early capacity is contracted under long-term agreements to California power providers, such as Southern California Edison, Clean Power Alliance and Desert Community Energy.

California utilities purchased these initial blocks because the state's regulation explicitly mandates the procurement of "clean firm" renewable energy.

Google is purchasing the almost 400 megawatts of power which, the company hopes, will eventually power a data center on Utah soil.

The agreement also includes an option for Google to scale up its purchase by an additional 600 megawatts, reaching nearly 1 gigawatt by June 2030 — about the same amount of power Utah's Huntington coal plant can generate at any given moment.

Google and Fervo also signed a broader 3 gigawatt non-binding framework agreement to evaluate future data center power arrangements across Fervo's pipeline.

"This agreement reinforces that EGS (enhanced geothermal systems) is ready to power the next generation of computing infrastructure," said Tim Latimer, CEO and co-founder of Fervo Energy, in a press release. "As demand for reliable electricity grows, customers like Google need energy resources that can be deployed at scale, operate around the clock, and deliver where power is needed."

Overall, Fervo predicts Cape Station will be able to deliver 4.3 gigawatts of power at peak — and the rest of the potential power lies unclaimed. The leftover 3.4 gigawatts (after Google and California contracts are fulfilled) is equivalent to running three full-scale legacy coal plants at maximum output.

And Fervo is actively advertising them.

The state's dominant power provider may not be far behind. Pacificorp, which operates as Rocky Mountain Power in Utah, stated in the 2027 Integrated Resource Plan Public Input Meeting Oct. 14 that at the prices stated by Fervo with federal tax credits included, it anticipates geothermal "would be economic" and its model "would select proxy geothermal over other proxy resource options like gas."

Even without tax credits, PacifiCorp said Fervo's pricing "would still make proxy geothermal competitive with proxy gas."

Though no purchase agreement has been signed yet, PacifiCorp's statement signals Utah ratepayers could eventually benefit from the technology being built in their backyard.

Utah's energy appeal

"It checks all the boxes," said Mitchell, referring to Fervo's next-gen technology.

For the "old style" of geothermal generation, Mitchell said it required three things: the heat in the Earth, cracks in the rocks or crust, and a way to harvest the heat out of the Earth — usually water.

"And so you need the cracks to push the water through to harvest the heat, and then that brings the heat to the surface, and then that turns a turbine and creates energy," he explained.

"And that's why geothermal exists in a few spots — and it's great where it exists — but it's not everywhere," Mitchell added.

Utah is third in the nation in installed geothermal capacity, though it only makes up about 3.2%. California and Nevada hold over 90% of the nation's capacity.

But the technology being used differs significantly among the three states.

Nevada and California's geothermal plants are largely conventional — the "old style" Mitchell described. The states are home to geysers and lakes, where the hot fluid necessary for this technique is easy to find.

Though the state may be behind, many emerging Utah projects — like Fervo — use "enhanced" geothermal techniques: drilling deep into hot rock, fracturing it, and circulating water through to build an artificial reservoir.

The federal push

In places like Utah, the ground's permeability is a motivating factor. Other nearby states have similar benefits, leaving geothermal developers looking west to develop the technology.

"Utah already is a model for other states for developing geothermal energy," Mitchell said. "We have a relatively good permitting environment here, and we're seeing geothermal companies work very closely with the Bureau of Land Management offices ..."

Federal agencies — such as BLM — have started to promote geothermal-focused policies.

In August, the bureau authorized the drilling of up to 10 geothermal temperature-gradient holes in Iron County — shallow, lower-cost test wells used to measure how quickly temperatures increase before jumping into expensive, massive wells.

The U.S. Department of Energy is also funding Utah FORGE — an enhanced geothermal research site in Beaver County. Operated by the University of Utah, researchers are testing new techniques to create geothermal energy in other parts of the U.S. where no natural hot water exists.

Utah's opening

"Hopefully, we'll have very, very little water consumption also. We'll have zero air emissions, no air quality impacts, no carbon emissions. It's also dispatchable like natural gas," Mitchell said. "We want our data centers to be investing in the right technologies that are going to be viable for long periods of time."

Mitchell argues that in a world of increasing demand for power, geothermal is a dispatchable, clean energy that can be built quickly.

"What this really means is that we have a pathway for reducing the emissions and water consumption of our energy system into the future," he said.

With 3.4 gigawatts of Cape Station's potential still unclaimed — and California and Google already proving the demand — the question is whether Utah will stake a claim on the clean energy being built in its own backyard.

"At the prices stated by Fervo with tax credits included, PacifiCorp anticipates proxy geothermal would be economic and the model would select proxy geothermal over other proxy resource options like gas. Without tax credits, PacifiCorp anticipates the prices stated by Fervo would still make proxy geothermal competitive with proxy gas in the IRP model."

"For the 2027 IRP, PacifiCorp is planning to model a single proxy near-field enhanced geothermal system (NF EGS) binary resource option limited to 500 MW selectable in both Oregon and Utah for the entirety of the study horizon, first eligible in 2030. The costs for the proxy geothermal resource option would be based on Fervo's cost estimates, beginning with an overnight capital cost of $5,500 per kilowatt in 2030 and declining to $3,000 per kilowatt by 2036."

Crucially, PacifiCorp agreed to update its 2027 IRP model to incorporate Fervo's cost curve—starting at $5,500/kW in 2030 and scaling down to $3,000/kW by 2036, complete with federal tax credits

title: Which Is the Most Underestimated Climate Threat in the US? - Gizmodo
authors: Ellyn Lapointe, Webb Wright, Passant Rabie
description:
All of this got me wondering, which climate threat is the U.S. most underestimating?
To me, climate threats mean both climate hazards and their broader societal impacts.
Climate threats are shaped by weather and climate events occurring and what lies in the places where extreme events happen and people’s ability to respond and recover.
If you talk to most climate scientists, they will say that the biggest underappreciated near-term climate risk is extreme precipitation events.
My fear is not a specific climate threat per se.
text:
With each fraction of a degree Earth’s temperature rises, so does the threat of extreme weather. In the United States, climate change is exacerbating disasters that endanger the public and cost the nation hundreds of billions of dollars per year. Despite this, federal support for climate change mitigation and adaptation, as well as disaster preparedness and response, has crumbled under President Trump.

His energy agenda has sought to destroy renewable energy growth and inject new life into the nation’s fossil fuel industry. In February, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) rescinded the legal basis for greenhouse gas regulation in the United States. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) lost over 17% of its staff in 2025 alone, and the administration also withheld billions of dollars meant to help states protect residents, their homes, and the critical infrastructure they depend on from natural disasters.

I could go on. As the risks mount and the resources for addressing them disappear, knowing where the biggest gaps in preparedness lie becomes all the more important. The urgency of this situation was laid bare this summer—the hottest on record for the United States—during which communities struggled to cope with life-threatening heat waves, rampant wildfires, powerful storms, and flash flooding.

All of this got me wondering, which climate threat is the U.S. most underestimating? I posed this question to multiple experts, and while it’s clear that the federal government has hampered the nation’s ability to weather all kinds of climate-driven disasters, they pointed to several threats that may be particularly underappreciated.

Andra Garner

An assistant professor in the Department of Environmental Science at Rowan University. Garner’s research focuses on the impacts of climate change on natural hazards, including the effects of sea-level rise on tsunamis and the evolving characteristics of tropical cyclones and storm surge in a warming world.

The short, blunt answer to this question is, “all of them.” Otherwise, we’d be doing much more to help our communities become more resilient in the face of climate-driven hazards. The U.S. would be working harder to assume a leadership role on the international stage in the effort to address climate change and to find a way to curb emissions.

We would also be doing all that we could to eliminate one of the biggest barriers to climate action: funding from the fossil fuel industry that supports politicians and lobbyists to act in ways that prevent meaningful legislation that would otherwise help regulate the polluters that are driving this crisis.

But, if I had to identify a particular type of climate-driven threat that is commonly underestimated, I’d again say that the answer is not any single type of event, but rather what the climate community calls “compound hazards,” climate-driven hazards that happen either concurrently or in close succession to one another.

Consider the recent, powerful nor’easter that impacted the U.S. northeast, bringing strong winds, rainfall, and storm surge from Virginia to Maine. Climate-driven coastal flood impacts were certainly felt during this storm, but coastal defenses (including recently replenished beaches and dunes in many parts of New Jersey and Delaware) prevented complete devastation.

However, many of these defenses were also heavily compromised, as erosion ate away at beaches and dunes. So, should another coastal storm occur in the coming months, many of these communities will be unprotected, potentially facing far worse impacts and more costly damages.

Or consider hurricanes, which produce hazards like storm surge, rainfall, and exceptionally strong winds—all made worse in a warming climate. Similarly, heat waves are becoming more intense and lasting longer, with overnight lows that offer little relief, especially in humid regions.

Protocols exist to prepare for an approaching hurricane, or to help keep residents safe during heat waves. But how do we prepare for and help a community that experiences a hurricane landfall, immediately followed by an extreme heat wave, when electricity might be out for millions?

In a world where climate hazards are continuing to become more extreme, these types of compound hazards present a unique threat that remains difficult to address and requires more attention.

Deepti Singh

An associate professor in the School of the Environment at Washington State University Vancouver, where she leads the Climate Extremes and Impacts lab. Singh’s research aims to advance the physical understanding of climate extremes and their interactions that result in compound hazards, as well as their sources of predictability in the Earth system.

It’s hard to name a single threat the U.S. is underestimating. To me, climate threats mean both climate hazards and their broader societal impacts. Climate threats are shaped by weather and climate events occurring and what lies in the places where extreme events happen and people’s ability to respond and recover. I think we’re underestimating the extreme events themselves and their toll on society, particularly on health and the economy.

Heat is a big one. It is among the deadliest climate extremes globally and in the U.S., despite being reasonably well-understood and highly predictable, which enables timely early warnings. The ecological and human health impacts are very likely underestimated.

Colder places are unprepared, as we saw from the acute and devastating impacts of the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat wave, which killed an estimated 1,400 people and a billion marine animals in the region. Meanwhile, places like Florida, Arizona, and Louisiana experience chronic heat—exposure to dangerous heat that seriously affects health, but whose impacts are not as immediate or visible. Many of these places don’t have early warning systems for heat, and images of people frolicking in water fountains or rivers often used in reporting don’t motivate people to take it as seriously as death and destruction from, say, a hurricane.

Wildfires are another. Increasing heat and drought severity are fueling increasing wildfire activity across the West. Fires threaten infrastructure and ecosystems while producing smoke that is really harmful to human health near to and far beyond the burn areas. Fires also leave landscapes vulnerable for years, if not decades, and they are hard to anticipate.

We can forecast high fire weather conditions, but not precisely when and where fires will ignite, whether from human activity or lightning, or how quickly they will spread, especially with the long lead times needed to prepare. The 2020 fire season was a preview—large fires burned across California, Oregon, and Washington, and smoke blanketed the entire country. That risk will continue, and we are not adequately planning for it.

The impacts of these events are also underestimated. Billion-dollar weather disasters are increasing rapidly, with 21 already since the start of 2026. The human and ecological impacts unfold over months.

Most importantly, there is limited data for tracking these impacts in the most vulnerable communities, including low-income communities, communities of color, and indigenous communities that lack monitoring infrastructure and resources. Our models to anticipate future risks are only as good as the data underlying them. So, threats to the communities most at risk are also the ones we are less likely to anticipate and be prepared for.

Finally, communities are now facing compounding threats—multiple extremes happening at once or back-to-back disasters that hit communities while they are still recovering from a previous disaster. Our emergency resources are limited and are being depleted (for example, recent FEMA cuts), just as increasing extreme events are pushing communities beyond the boundaries of what they can manage.

Jesse Keenan

The Favrot II Associate Professor of Sustainable Real Estate and Favrot II Associate Professor of Sustainable Real Estate and Urban Planning, Director of the Center on Climate Change and Urbanism, and Director of the Climate Change Science and Practice Minor Program at Tulane University. Keenan’s research focuses on the intersection of climate change mitigation and adaptation in the built environment, including aspects of design, engineering, regulation, planning, and financing.

Climate impacts come in all shapes and sizes, from highly disruptive extreme events to not-so-obvious chronic nuisances. In recent years, my colleagues and I have investigated a simple research question: To what extent is there an alignment between people’s actual risk exposure to climate impacts and their perception of those risks?

In the first paper from this research, published in Nature Communications, we evaluated the alignment between heat risk and people’s worry about extreme heat. Our research showed significant misalignments in the Pacific Northwest and in Appalachia. This means that these areas have a fair amount of risk exposure, yet people do not seem to be too concerned.

This presents a real problem if communities and local governments delay making heat-related adaptation investments because it is incorrectly viewed as an otherwise low-risk problem. Conversely, in places whose climate is already pretty hot, such as Texas, the alignment between risk and exposure is pretty robust. All across the country, people’s historical experience, existing risk exposure, and way of life have a lot do with how people evaluate and perceive their risk.

But, existing research about people’s perception of risks tends to focus on known and likely risks. If you talk to most climate scientists, they will say that the biggest underappreciated near-term climate risk is extreme precipitation events. When it rains, it can really pour. However, there is category of risks called low-probability high-impact events that most people are grossly unaware of. In fact, if they knew more about these events, they would probably be more concerned with how we prepare for them.

One event that keeps me up at night is associated with a scenario where we have an extreme heat wave that contributes to the collapse of the grid. Without power, people roast alive. With rapidly increasing loads from data centers in urban areas, we are facing a compound risk scenario that—in a place like Phoenix—could easily lead to more causalities and deaths than all American terrorist attacks and combat casualties this century—combined.

Brad Udall

A senior water and climate research scientist/scholar at Colorado State University’s Colorado Water Center. Udall’s expertise includes climate change, hydrology, and related policy issues of the American West.

My fear is not a specific climate threat per se. It is, instead, that humans are failing to meaningfully reduce greenhouse gas emissions, let alone get to net zero emissions by mid-century.

Despite 30 plus years of scientific outcry pleading for emissions reductions, we have yet to see an emissions peak, we don’t have the technologies nor are we making the investments to reach net zero, and the world is backsliding everywhere into new decades-long committed emissions.

In the absence of significant efforts to curtail emissions, every potential threat is a worry. Only by reducing emissions will we reduce our overall risk from all threats. Arguing about which individual threat is worse is the wrong focus given our inability to deal with the root cause of the problem.

Recent work by Carbon Brief suggests that, under current policies, global warming of 5.4 degrees F (3 degrees C) by 2100 has a 75% chance of occurring, and 7.2 degrees F (4 degrees C) of warming by 2150 occurs 25% of the time.

In a rational world, a 5.4-degree F (3-degree C) rise should be completely unacceptable and 7.2 degrees F (4 degrees C) unthinkable, yet there is little discussion about these outcomes. Furthermore, the failure of the press and the scientific community to explain potential post-2100 emissions and warming trajectories has been a grave mistake. In addition, two recent studies show that since about 2015, the rate of warming has approximately doubled, heightening the long-term danger of destabilizing temperature increases.

Capitalism, acceptable standards for consumer behavior, and our governance institutions are all major problems. We allow fossil fuel producers to sell a planet-wrecking product without any consideration of the costs of that product despite having cost-effective green alternatives available in many cases (for example, carbon-free electricity and vehicles). We are taught that freedom means being able to consume anything we want, no matter the climate consequences of those actions. And our democracies, under threat from authoritarians who almost universally oppose meaningful climate action, seem unable to rise to the occasion.

It doesn’t have to be this way. We have the knowledge and many of the technologies to avoid the worst. A meaningful carbon tax would make capitalism our friend, instead of our enemy. We need to use our substantial collective wealth to protect us from what should be completely unacceptable risks, not sleepwalk into irreversible, dire outcomes.

text:
DETROIT (AP) — A group of environmental organizations sued the Trump administration on Oct. 2 over its recent relaxation of key vehicle fuel economy rules, a decision that the group says will make vehicles less efficient, contribute to more pollution and increase gas consumption.

On Sept. 28, the Trump administration lowered Corporate Average Fuel Economy, or CAFE, standards that set out how far new vehicles need to travel on a gallon of gasoline.

The announcement was made as the Trump administration negotiated with Iran over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

About a fifth of the world’s oil passes through the strait on a typical day, and the fight over its control has sent energy prices soaring across the globe.

The environmental groups filed the petition for review in the U.S. Court of Appeals against Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Jonathan Morrison, the administrator of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which sets the rules.

“We’re taking the Trump administration to court for this reckless rollback that prioritizes Big Oil and automaker profits over American families,” Katherine Garcia, director of Sierra Club’s Clean Transportation for All program, said in a statement.

“It is unlawful for Trump to turn back the clock on fuel-efficient cars, forcing drivers to waste more money on gas and communities to breathe toxic air.”

The Center for Biological Diversity, the Conservation Law Foundation, the Environmental Defense Fund and Public Citizen, along with the Sierra Club, filed the suit.

The Transportation Department and NHTSA lowered the standards to an industry fleetwide average of roughly 34.9 miles per gallon for passenger cars and light trucks in the 2031 model year, down from a projected 50.4 miles per gallon under rules set by the Biden administration.

The administration said the change would provide Americans more vehicle choice and encourage consumers to buy newer, safer vehicles.

Experts say reducing fuel economy requirements in vehicles does not necessarily lower their cost, nor would it automatically translate to new vehicle sales.

Duffy said the new rule also cuts the “illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn’t want.”

There has never been a mandate that manufacturers sell EVs or Americans buy them; the rules and other cleaner vehicle standards incentivized automakers to sell a mix of electric, hybrid electric and increasingly-efficient gasoline-powered vehicles.

When reached for comment, a DOT spokesperson referred to statements made by Duffy: “This administration understands the freedom of every American family starts with affordable cars. That’s why our new standards will make that dream more achievable by letting auto manufacturers produce the cars that fit families’ needs at a lower price.”

Auto companies and industry groups broadly welcomed the change, saying the rules under the Biden administration were too stringent and did not benefit consumers.

But environmental organizations decried the changes.

“With gas prices at historic highs, Trump picked the worst possible time to roll back federal mileage standards,” David Pettit, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity’s Climate Law Institute, said in a statement.

“Oil companies will profit from less efficient cars, but drivers will take a hit to their wallets and our kids will breathe dirtier air. We’ll all pay the price for more tailpipe pollutants spewing everywhere from playgrounds to wild places. We’re asking the courts to put a stop to this callous giveaway to Big Oil and Big Auto.”

Gas prices have hovered around $4.50 and diesel has hit unprecedented heights in recent weeks, according to AAA.

The DOT said that the rule would cut yearly oil consumption in 2050 by about 1.3 billion barrels as compared with yearly oil consumption in 2024, but NHTSA had estimated the 2024 standards would have saved 14 billion gallons of gasoline from being burned by that year.

Fuel economy requirements have been in place since the 1970s energy crisis and over time have led to improved average efficiency in vehicles.

President Donald Trump has made a number of moves to undercut cleaner vehicles in the United States.

These include eliminating electric vehicle tax credits, scrapping vehicle emissions standards, repealing the fines for automakers who don’t meet mileage rules and attempting to block the nation’s EV charging buildout.

text:
A coalition of 17 groups that want the Montana Public Service Commission to consider the effects of climate change in its decisions is taking its case to court.

Earthjustice and Western Environmental Law Center filed a complaint Thursday against the Public Service Commission.

It asks the Missoula County District Court to find the PSC has a constitutional obligation to account for climate risks in its decisions.

“Climate change poses an urgent threat to Montana and its people,” the complaint said.

It said the Public Service Commission can allow utilities to keep investing in fossil fuels or encourage them to pursue “cleaner and ultimately less costly alternatives.”

But it said the PSC has “refused to recognize and regularly disregards” the costs of climate, such as smoke that hurts asthmatic children, floods that destroy homes, and anglers who can’t fish.

The groups include healthcare providers, youth organizations and clean energy and climate advocates.

Amy Cilimburg, with lead plaintiff Climate Smart Missoula, said the PSC’s failure to regulate with climate in mind affects the health of Montanans and their ability to afford power.

“When the PSC fails to consider climate change in its decisions, Montanans bear the high costs and risks that come with fossil-fuel electricity, as well as the unaffordable and unconstitutional effects of a changing climate,” Cilimburg said in a statement.

In February 2024, more than 40 organizations and businesses asked the PSC to address its “obligations to consider climate impacts,” but the PSC denied the request in September 2025 and again last month.

The PSC regulates monopoly utilities and is made up of five elected commissioners, all of whom are currently Republican.

The complaint asks the court to vacate the PSC’s decisions and find the commission has a constitutional responsibility to consider climate as part of the state’s obligation to “maintain and improve a clean and healthful environment.”

The PSC could not be reached for comment Thursday afternoon.

When the commission voted to deny the petition by the groups in 2025, its legal counsel said the PSC is an administrative agency, so it didn’t have the authority to do what the groups wanted — to declare the constitution requires the PSC to consider the adverse impacts of climate change.

Then-chief-legal-counsel Lucas Hamilton also said the constitutional right to a clean and healthful environment appears along other rights the PSC must consider, such as to pursue life’s basic necessities — including water service.

In a news release about the lawsuit, the groups said the PSC took nearly two-and-a-half years to make a decision on their petition but never addressed its substance.

In the meantime, the PSC was making “consequential decisions,” they said.

They pointed to the PSC’s decision to approve “NorthWestern Energy’s request to charge customers for the high construction and operation costs for the Yellowstone County Generating Station.”

In December 2024, the Montana Supreme Court affirmed the constitutional right to a clean and healthful environment includes “a stable climate system” in the historic Held vs. State of Montana decision.

In a statement, Sarah Lundquist, executive director of Families for a Livable Climate, said youth fought for their constitutional rights in the Held case and have been advocating “for climate justice” ever since.

Families for a Livable Climate is part of the lawsuit.

“Now it’s our turn,” Lundquist said. “The Public Service Commission has enormous influence over Montana’s energy future, and we must ensure climate change is at the center of its decisions. It is our responsibility as adults to protect the future our kids deserve.”

Groups filing lawsuit

Earthjustice and Western Environmental Law Center represent Climate Smart Missoula, Citizens for Clean Energy, Earthworks, Families for a Livable Climate, Forward Montana, Helena Hunters and Anglers, Helena Interfaith Climate Advocates, Montana Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, Montana Environmental Information Center, Montana Health and Climate, Montana Public Interest Research Group, Montana Renewable Energy Association, NW Energy Coalition, Park County Environmental Council, Renewable Northwest, Sierra Club Montana Chapter, and 350 Montana in the lawsuit.

title: Why does it take 60 countries to build a single car? - Dagens.com
description:
From raw lithium mined in Chile to microchips stamped in Taiwan, it takes a massive, fragile supply chain spanning dozens of countries to build a single modern vehicle.
A single car might be designed in Munich, assembled in South Carolina, wired with electronics from Taiwan, and powered by a battery cell forged in China.
Stellantis—the conglomerate behind Jeep, Dodge, and Peugeot—explicitly notes that its direct supply chain spans more than 60 different countries.
The electric battery bottleneck The transition to electric vehicles has made this international web even more complex, largely due to the intense geographical concentration of battery manufacturing.
But the obvious downside to relying on 60 different countries for a single product is extreme vulnerability.
text:
The badge on your car’s grille is a marketing illusion. From raw lithium mined in Chile to microchips stamped in Taiwan, it takes a massive, fragile supply chain spanning dozens of countries to build a single modern vehicle.

When you buy a German luxury sedan, a Japanese crossover, or an American pickup truck, the badge on the grille implies a clear national origin. But that badge is a marketing sleight of hand.

According to a breakdown by Motor1, identifying the true origin of a modern vehicle is nearly impossible. A single car might be designed in Munich, assembled in South Carolina, wired with electronics from Taiwan, and powered by a battery cell forged in China. The family car is no longer a product of a single factory; it is the final output of a fragile, interconnected manufacturing web that spans the globe.

The assembly line is just the last stop

Automotive manufacturing operates on a massive tier system. Automakers rarely build their own brakes, seats, or wiring harnesses from scratch. Instead, they purchase complete sub-assemblies from Tier 1 suppliers, who in turn buy sensors, plastics, and microchips from Tier 2 and Tier 3 suppliers scattered across different continents.

The sheer scale of this logistics network is staggering. Stellantis—the conglomerate behind Jeep, Dodge, and Peugeot—explicitly notes that its direct supply chain spans more than 60 different countries.

This global dispersion completely skews the concept of domestic manufacturing. As highlighted by the 2026 Cars.com American-Made Index, a vehicle physically assembled in the United States routinely relies on engines, transmissions, and critical electronics manufactured overseas. Stamping “Made in the USA” on the door jamb often just means the final bolts were tightened there.

The electric battery bottleneck

The transition to electric vehicles has made this international web even more complex, largely due to the intense geographical concentration of battery manufacturing.

While a traditional gas engine can be cast and assembled regionally, an EV battery requires specialized minerals that cross multiple borders before they ever reach an assembly plant. Lithium is sourced heavily from Australia and Chile, cobalt is mined in the Democratic Republic of Congo, and nickel comes primarily from Indonesia.

But the true bottleneck happens during refinement and cell production. According to the International Energy Agency’s Global EV Outlook 2026, China currently accounts for roughly 70 percent of all electric car production and a staggering 80 percent of global battery-cell manufacturing. That means even if an EV is assembled in Michigan or Berlin, its core propulsion system is fundamentally tied to Chinese manufacturing.

A highly vulnerable network

Automakers utilize this sprawling global strategy to secure competitive pricing and build vehicles at an unprecedented scale. But the obvious downside to relying on 60 different countries for a single product is extreme vulnerability.

“The 'BBB' adds ~$3.5-$4 billion annually in new subsidies for the oil and gas industry, increasing federal payouts to the fossil fuel industry to $34 billion per year including existing subsidies. Over the next decade, it provides $40-$80 billion in new tax breaks and benefits for fossil fuel companies.

"$7 billion by cutting the methane fee.

But they cut incentives for rooftop solar and other energy-saving credits for everyday Americans. Which could save us billions in oil wars — I mean, you can't invade the Sun. And, by the way, renewable infrastructure is cheaper.

Meanwhile, during Line 5 reroute construction, Canadian pipeline company Enbridge has reported six spills of gas liquids, diesel, hydraulic fluid and hydrocarbons, 10 frac-outs, built an unpermitted and unapproved bypass, and breached an aquifer — without accountability. Who’s radical?

text:
Qcells announced plans to launch new versions of its residential solar panel series featuring U.S.-made aluminum frames by the end of 2026.

The updated residential product offerings, which include the company’s Q.Tron AC and Q.Peak Duo AC lines, will incorporate aluminum frames extruded, anodized, and fabricated at supplier Aluko Group’s integrated facility in Halls, Tennessee. The initiative is aimed at helping residential installers and third-party ownership TPO providers qualify for the Investment Tax Credit ITC domestic content bonus adder.

Under the Treasury Department’s domestic content guidance, solar hardware must meet specific domestic manufacturing thresholds to qualify for the 10% tax credit bonus. Qcells noted that keeping all three core stages of frame manufacturing, including extrusion, anodization, and fabrication, within the United States provides greater clarity for installers and financing partners when evaluating compliance.

The domestic frame offering comes as the statutory domestic content threshold for clean energy projects begins stepping up toward 55% for projects commencing construction in 2027.

“Through this partnership to produce modules with domestic frames, we are furthering our commitment to U.S. manufacturing, supporting clean, affordable energy and giving our customers the certainty they need to qualify projects for the domestic content bonus,” said Il Hyeong No, head of Qcells North America’s residential business.

Supply chain localized in Tennessee

Aluko Group’s manufacturing plant in Lauderdale County, Tennessee, is expected to reach full commercial production by the end of 2026. Once operational, the plant will have a planned annual capacity to manufacture enough frames to support 4 GW of solar modules.

Aluko plans to invest more than $107 million into the facility over five years, creating 285 full-time jobs. The company operates what it describes as the only facility in the U.S. performing all three major frame production steps under one roof.

“By carrying out extrusion, anodizing, and fabrication here in the United States, we are delivering a product that offers transparency and confidence at every step of the process,” said Jinwoo Park, president of Aluko Group.

The move expands Qcells’ broader domestic manufacturing push across its vertically integrated operations in Dalton and Cartersville, Georgia, where the company operates large-scale module and component assembly operations.

title: Why Britain's homes are becoming energy assets, not just places to live | LSE British Politics
authors: Alexis Papazoglou, empirical finance, corporate governance, corporate social responsibility, spans applications of accounting, Energy Policy, Environmental Policy
description:
But thanks to advances in renewable energy technology, such as solar panels, Britain’s homes are increasingly decentralising the energy system, and becoming less reliant on oil and gas price fluctuations, argues Erhan Kilincarslan.
For most of the past century, British homes had a straightforward relationship with the energy system.
In doing so, homes are evolving from passive consumers into active participants in Britain’s energy system.
Of course, rooftop solar will not solve every challenge facing Britain’s energy system.
The next stage of Britain’s energy transition may depend not only on giant infrastructure projects but also on millions of small investments made by ordinary homeowners.
text:
Recent energy crises have shown the degree to which Britain is exposed to global events. But thanks to advances in renewable energy technology, such as solar panels, Britain’s homes are increasingly decentralising the energy system, and becoming less reliant on oil and gas price fluctuations, argues Erhan Kilincarslan.

Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

For most of the past century, British homes had a straightforward relationship with the energy system. They consumed electricity generated elsewhere, paid monthly bills and had little control over either the source or the price of their energy. That relationship is beginning to change.

Across the UK, a growing number of homeowners are installing rooftop solar panels, home batteries and smart energy technologies that allow them to generate, store and manage electricity themselves. In doing so, homes are evolving from passive consumers into active participants in Britain’s energy system.

The implications extend far beyond lower electricity bills. They could change the economics of home ownership itself.

The solar panel boom

The growing interest in household solar is no coincidence. The cost of photovoltaic (PV) systems has fallen substantially over the past decade as manufacturing has expanded and the technology has become more efficient. At the same time, government policies, including zero per cent VAT on eligible residential solar installations and the Smart Export Guarantee, which allows households to receive payments for surplus electricity exported to the grid, have strengthened the financial case for investing in rooftop solar.

Recent evidence suggests that demand remains exceptionally strong. Britain recorded a record 269,000 solar installations in 2025, the highest annual total on record, with rooftop systems accounting for more than 95 per cent of new installations. At the same time, interest in home battery systems has accelerated as households seek greater control over their energy costs and reduce their dependence on the grid.

The UK government is moving forward with plans to introduce low-cost plug-in solar panels that can be installed on balconies, terraces and other small outdoor spaces.

Technology is also expanding beyond traditional rooftop systems. The UK government is moving forward with plans to introduce low-cost plug-in solar panels that can be installed on balconies, terraces and other small outdoor spaces, potentially extending the benefits of solar generation to millions of renters and flat owners who have traditionally been excluded from the market. If widely adopted, these systems could broaden access to household renewable energy and accelerate the shift towards more decentralised electricity generation.

By lowering installation costs and reducing the need for home ownership, plug-in solar could broaden participation in Britain’s energy transition in much the same way that rooftop solar transformed owner-occupied housing over the past decade. Yet the growing popularity of household solar cannot be explained by falling costs alone.

The energy crisis

The past few years have exposed how vulnerable British households remain to global energy markets. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine triggered Europe’s worst energy crisis in decades, sending wholesale gas prices to record levels and sharply increasing household energy bills across the UK. The episode served as a stark reminder that events taking place thousands of miles away can have immediate consequences for domestic finances.

More recently, renewed tensions in the Middle East have once again unsettled global oil and gas markets, highlighting the continued sensitivity of energy prices to geopolitical developments. Although Britain imports relatively little energy directly from the region, it remains exposed through interconnected international markets, where disruptions to global supply can feed through into higher wholesale prices and ultimately household energy bills.

For many homeowners, these repeated shocks have reinforced a simple lesson: generating at least some electricity at home offers not only environmental benefits but also a degree of protection against increasingly uncertain global energy markets.

This represents an important shift in thinking. Solar panels are increasingly viewed not simply as environmental investments but as financial assets capable of reducing long-term household expenditure and improving resilience against future price shocks. The transformation extends even further when battery storage enters the equation.

Rather than exporting surplus electricity during the day and buying it back in the evening, homeowners can increasingly store their own electricity for later use or combine battery systems with smart tariffs that charge when electricity is cheap and discharge when prices rise. The result is a home that no longer simply consumes electricity but increasingly generates, stores and manages its own energy.

Energy economists increasingly describe households equipped with rooftop solar and battery storage as “prosumers” because they both produce and consume electricity, reflecting a fundamental shift in the relationship between homes and the energy system. This transformation has wider implications for Britain’s electricity system.

Decentralising the energy system and transforming the home

Traditionally, electricity has been generated at large centralised power stations before being transmitted across the country through the national grid. As more households generate and store their own electricity, the energy system is becoming increasingly decentralised, with homes playing a more active role in balancing supply and demand. Millions of properties producing relatively small amounts of electricity can collectively become part of the country’s energy infrastructure, reducing pressure on the grid and improving system flexibility while supporting the wider integration of renewable energy.

As more households generate and store their own electricity, the energy system is becoming increasingly decentralised, with homes playing a more active role in balancing supply and demand.

This is not merely a theoretical possibility. In countries such as Germany and Australia, rooftop solar already accounts for a substantial share of electricity generation, demonstrating how decentralised energy production can complement conventional power generation. Britain appears to be moving steadily in the same direction as household solar and battery adoption continues to expand.

The housing market may eventually reflect this transition. Just as buyers routinely consider school catchment areas, broadband speeds or insulation standards, energy performance is becoming an increasingly important consideration for many households. Properties equipped with rooftop solar, battery storage and high energy efficiency ratings may become more attractive as buyers seek lower running costs and greater protection against future energy price volatility.

Of course, rooftop solar will not solve every challenge facing Britain’s energy system. Not every property is suitable, batteries remain expensive and large-scale investment in electricity networks, offshore wind and nuclear generation will remain essential.

But the cumulative impact of millions of household decisions should not be underestimated.

For decades, British homes have been viewed primarily as places to live and stores of wealth. Increasingly, they are becoming something else as well: energy assets capable of generating income, reducing costs and strengthening resilience against future energy shocks.

The next stage of Britain’s energy transition may depend not only on giant infrastructure projects but also on millions of small investments made by ordinary homeowners. If that trend continues, some of the country’s next generation of power stations may already be standing on suburban streets across Britain.

name: American Energy
title: Trump Tried to Defund Them, But Green Banks Keep Financing Clean Energy Projects
authors: Jeff St. John, Rachel Santarsiero, Anna Rogers, Martha Pskowski, Marianne Lavelle, Stephanie Mencimer, Sophie Hurwitz, Adam Rogers, Inae Oh, Mother Jones
description:
The report includes summaries from about 70 case studies of the work that’s been helped along by financing from green banks.
The technologies behind the projects that green banks finance aren’t risky in and of themselves, Adler said.
Green banks are also sharing technical resources to help each other lower financing costs, Adler said.
Montgomery County Green Bank in Maryland has blended financial technology support and layered financing to make home renewable-energy and energy-efficiency improvements more affordable.
But as the Green Bank 50 report highlights, many green banks operate on budgets of less than $2 million per year.
text:
This story was originally published by Canary Media and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

A community solar project built for New Orleans’ oldest historically Black Catholic order of nuns. An all-electric affordable housing complex in Salt Lake City. A program offering low-income Maryland households inexpensive loans for rooftop solar and energy efficiency.

These are just some of the recent projects financed in the US by green banks, entities that use public funds to boost lending for clean energy and climate-adaptation efforts in tough-to-finance sectors. And they’ve done it even as the Trump administration’s clawbacks of federal climate funding force them to scale down their Biden-era plans.

“We’ve continued to move capital in very challenging times,” said Dan Adler, executive director of the U.S. Green Bank 50, a coalition of 56 green banks and other organizations. To fill in the gaps, they’ve sought out financing partners ranging from commercial banks and credit unions to corporate and philanthropic funders. ​“We’re making a virtue out of a necessity,” he said.

The Green Bank 50 laid out what its members have been able to accomplish over the last two years in its inaugural impact report, released in September, which collected data from 48 green banks nationwide. Over the course of 2024 and 2025, those organizations put about $1.4 billion of their own capital, along with $11 billion in additional private capital, into more than 40,000 projects.

The report includes summaries from about 70 case studies of the work that’s been helped along by financing from green banks. Some are large-scale projects, like the $10 million community solar array being built on land owned by the Sisters of the Holy Family in New Orleans, which has committed to providing up to 350 low-income households with reduced utility bills using the solar power it will generate. Loans for that project came from the nonprofit Inclusive Prosperity Capital, the United Church of Christ Cornerstone Fund, and Pelican Community Capital, which is a Louisiana community development lender affiliated with the Baton Rouge Area Foundation.

Inclusive Prosperity Capital is among the many green banks that has had to make do without promised grants from the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund. It won $249 million from the program, which was created by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act and provided $20 billion in green bank grants and another $7 billion in Solar for All grants. The Trump administration terminated both programs last year.

“We had projects with financial commitments, training courses for developers and lenders, a predevelopment mentorship program, staff hired and trained, and more,” Inclusive Prosperity Capital CEO Kerry O’Neill said. ​“We hope recent court decisions will result in our return to this important work.”

In August, a federal judge ruled the administration’s freeze of the $20 billion to be unlawful, and this month, two separate federal judges have ruled the Solar for All termination illegal. But the administration has yet to release the funds, and is expected to appeal to the US Supreme Court.

The loss of federal funds has severely curtailed the scale of work planned by the Green Bank 50 partners. Climate United Fund, a partnership that was awarded $7 billion but had its funds frozen, has been unable to follow through on plans to finance U.S.-built electric trucks, energy-efficiency and clean energy upgrades, and loans to Native American–led clean energy projects.

The 48 green banks surveyed in the impact report have about $6.8 billion in their funding pipelines. But Adler conceded that the loss of federal funds has put some worthy projects out of reach. ​“When money is coming down from the sky at basically 0 percent [interest], you can do very interesting projects—and we’re prepared to do that again,” he said.

“But now we have to focus on tight discipline with private capital as our key partner,” he said. ​“You can’t do the higher-risk projects, so you work on what’s addressable.” The goal, he said, is to find projects that are still considered too risky or unproven for private-sector lenders, ​“but if you do it with green banks a few times, then private capital can take over.”

That’s in fact the founding principle of the green bank movement, he noted. Some of the first green banks formed in Connecticut and New York state in the 2010s have become significant drivers of private-sector lending for building energy efficiency and electrification, solar for schools and municipalities, and other categories of investment important to meeting state and local climate policies.

The technologies behind the projects that green banks finance aren’t risky in and of themselves, Adler said. But the classes of customers that green banks work with—such as affordable housing providers and solar developers working in low-income communities—can be. ​“Whether they’ve been redlined out of the traditional capital markets, or the deals are not as big as traditional lenders are motivated to engage in, we’re taking on the credit risks and the deal structure and size risks,” he explained.

Green banks have continued to find ways to reduce those risks. One method is bundling funds from multiple lenders, which reduces an individual lender’s risk. That’s how Inclusive Prosperity Capital and its partners financed the community solar project for the Sisters of the Holy Family.

It’s also how the New York City Energy Efficiency Corp., a 16-year-old green bank, supported a 396-unit, all-electric affordable housing project in Salt Lake City. The green bank worked with Utah nonprofit SustainEnergyFinance to set up a $4.5 predevelopment loan—a form of financing that can be hard to underwrite for first-time projects—so that the project’s developer could move into the next phases of construction.

Green banks are also sharing technical resources to help each other lower financing costs, Adler said. He cited the Solar and Energy Loan Fund, a Florida-based green bank that has financed nearly $80 million in home energy-efficiency, solar, and storm-hardening projects. That organization has developed a platform, now being used by 13 other green banks and similar lenders across the country, that standardizes much of the underwriting and loan-processing expertise it’s built up over the past decade, said David Graber, the green bank’s chief of staff.

“We provide the back office and the capital. Partners bring the local trust and the projects,” Graber explained. The Solar and Energy Loan Fund estimates that each lending partner on the platform avoids hundreds of thousands of dollars a year in costs it would otherwise incur running a full lending operation on its own.

Montgomery County Green Bank in Maryland has blended financial technology support and layered financing to make home renewable-energy and energy-efficiency improvements more affordable. In March 2026, the organization launched a $4 million initiative that offers households low-interest loans for rooftop solar, heat pumps, and other projects.

Qualifying homeowners can access solar loans with a subsidized interest rate of 2.99 percent for the first 15 years, with a higher rate applying afterward, said Rokas Beresniovas, the green bank’s head of partnerships and business development.

As utility bills rise, mobilizing investment for these kinds of efforts is more important than ever, Adler said. But as the Green Bank 50 report highlights, many green banks operate on budgets of less than $2 million per year.

“We could do a lot more,” he said. ​“But we’re looking at what we’re able to finance.”

title: $50M east Manatee renewable gas plant breaks ground - Business Observer
description:
A groundbreaking ceremony was held at the landfill Oct. 9 for a $50 million renewable natural gas facility.
The Environmental Protection Agency explains renewable energy monetization on its website: A credit is issued for every megawatt-hour of electricity generated and delivered to the electric grid from a renewable energy resource.
“Because the value of renewable natural gas has increased substantially, now projects have become financially viable that weren’t before,” McGinnis says.
We needed to find the right partners, and Petro Energy is bringing its renewable natural gas experience.
Mead & Hunt is designing and constructing the facility, and Manatee County is bringing an asset that was here all along.
text:
The ever-burning flame at the Lena Road Landfill in east Manatee County will be going dark about 18 months from now.

The flame is actually a flare stack that safely releases excess gas from the mounds of buried, decomposing waste, but Manatee County is moving ahead with plans to capture that gas and turn it into a commodity.

A groundbreaking ceremony was held at the landfill Oct. 9 for a $50 million renewable natural gas facility. At 3333 Lena Road, the landfill is east of Interstate 75 and south of State Road 64.

The facility is the result of a partnership between Manatee County, Johnson Controls and Nopetro Energy. The county provided the land.

Johnson and Nopetro are funding the $50 million project, with Johnson serving as the integrated developer and Nopetro serving as the owner and operator of the plant.

Charles McGinnis, a vice president for Johnson Controls, says Manatee County is guaranteed to collect at least $883,000 in annual royalties once the plant is operational, and that number could increase up to $2.1 million.

In addition to the gas itself, the plant will generate energy credits, which can also be sold.

The Environmental Protection Agency explains renewable energy monetization on its website: A credit is issued for every megawatt-hour of electricity generated and delivered to the electric grid from a renewable energy resource. Selling credits generates revenue, but the seller forfeits “the ability to make any claims about ‘using’ renewable energy.”

For local residents, the project offers better air quality because it will reduce the emissions from the biogas that’s currently being flared into the atmosphere at the Lena Road Landfill.

The plant is expected to eliminate the amount of carbon dioxide that, in comparison, would be produced by 5.3 million gallons of car gasoline each year.

“It’s environmentally great for everybody,” Manatee County Commissioner Mike Rahn says. “It helps bring dollars back into Manatee County, and we get green tax credits that will help bring down some of the costs that we have to pay at the landfill.”

He notes some county equipment at the landfill can be powered using the gas, too.

Rahn says more counties are starting to capture their biogas instead of wasting it.

According to McGinnis, the value of biogas is much higher than it’s been in previous years.

“Because the value of renewable natural gas has increased substantially, now projects have become financially viable that weren’t before,” McGinnis says. “Manatee County is one of those counties that’s at the forefront of innovation, and they saw this happening. They were already taking some of the renewable natural gas and using it themselves in their biosolids drying process.”

According to the American Biogas Council, landfills are the largest source of captured biogas in the United States, “driving record investment” in renewable natural gas production.

The “Biogas in America 2026” report states, “The nation’s 598 landfill gas capture systems provide about three-quarters of all biogas captured in the U.S. and produce 64% of the nation’s renewable natural gas.”

Additionally, developers brought 20 new landfill gas projects online in 2025. One of those projects was led by Nopetro in Vero Beach, in Indian River County.

A year later, Nopetro Energy CEO and co-founder Jorge Herrera says the operation is going so well that Indian River County has been making improvements to its landfill to produce and capture more gas.

Manatee County, company officials say, can do the same.

To simplify a complex system, Herrera says to picture straws. The straws have holes in them, and they can be stuck into the ground throughout the landfill.

More straws can collect more gas. As the organics start to decompose, the molecules get sucked into the straws and moved to the plant to be refined into usable gas

Currently, the majority of the gas produced at the landfill is being burned off into the atmosphere.

Indian River County has a population of about 174,000. Nopetro estimates that its Vero Beach plant can provide as much as 80% of the natural gas used in the county.

Herrera says Manatee County’s production will be about 20% higher, but its population is also 2.5 times that of Indian River. A ballpark estimate, he says, is the Lena Road plant could meet about a third of the county’s natural gas demands.

In 20 years, Manatee County will have the option to either extend its contract with Nopetro or take ownership of the facility. However, the latter is not likely.

“These are very complex assets,” Herrera says. “From that perspective, I don’t think I’ve witnessed across the country an example where a government has taken on the responsibility of a production plant like this because it’s so specialized. It’s basically like saying, ‘Take an oil refinery and run it.’”

Nopetro has been in business for 17 years.

“We didn’t need to become an energy company ourselves,” Commissioner George Kruse says. “We wouldn’t know what we’re doing. We needed to find the right partners, and Petro Energy is bringing its renewable natural gas experience. Johnson Controls helped develop the project and its performance strategy. Mead & Hunt is designing and constructing the facility, and Manatee County is bringing an asset that was here all along. That’s exactly what a public-private partnership is supposed to be.”

text:
The 34th Milan No-Till Field Day is scheduled for Thursday, July 23, from 8 a.m.…

Opening the eyes of middle school students to potential careers is the focus of …



Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins (left) speaks with Shyam Sankar, of Palantir, and David Friedberg, of The Production Board, during the launch of the America.gov on Sept. 29 in Washington.

U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins announced a historic $3.3 billion loan to Oglethorpe Power Corporation to help finance its Smarr Combined-Cycle electric generating facility in Monroe County, Georgia, during a visit to the construction site.

This loan is the largest ever delivered in the history of USDA Rural Development’s Rural Utilities Service and comes at a critical time for investing in U.S. energy. As stated by President Trump, the United States is experiencing a surge in electricity demand from rapid technological advancements. This project strengthens the nation’s electrical grid, and lower-cost financing will help keep electricity affordable for Georgia families.

“Historic times call for historic actions, and this tremendous investment in America’s electric power grid is evidence of President Trump’s focus on powering our nation forward,” said Secretary Brooke L. Rollins. “Great things are happening with our rural electric cooperatives nationwide, and Oglethorpe Power is one example in Georgia through this project, which will generate reliable electricity, create jobs, and bring significant investment to rural America.”



Oglethorpe Power is a generation cooperative owned by 38 electric distribution cooperatives that serve nearly 5 million people across Georgia. It supplies wholesale power through a diverse energy portfolio that includes natural gas, coal, nuclear and hydroelectric resources. Oglethorpe services 157 of Georgia’s 159 counties either in part of in total. The Tennessee Valley Authority provides service to 12 northern counties in the state.

“This historic loan will allow us to build the reliable generation Georgia families, farms and businesses need at a lower cost, helping our member cooperatives keep electricity affordable for the communities they serve,” said Annalisa Bloodworth, President and CEO of Oglethorpe Power. “We are grateful to USDA and RUS for their longstanding partnership and for providing the lower-cost financing that helps electric cooperatives make critical investments in reliable, affordable power.”

For more information on USDA Rural Development investments visit the Rural Data Gateway. The Rural Data Gateway is an online tool that strengthens USDA Rural Development partnerships with rural people, entrepreneurs, government officials and Congress by making agency investment data accessible to the public.

title: 'Clean Energy Dream Home' Shows How Ditching Gas Appliances Reduces Indoor Air Pollution
description:
During SF’s Fleet Week last week, a 18-by-8-foot mobile showroom created by Silicon Valley Clean Energy (SVCE) was set up along the Embarcadero, as KPIX reports.
According to KPIX, Governor Gavin Newsom recently signed the Clean Energy Choice Act, introduced by Assemblymember Marc Berman (D-Menlo Park).
The Clean Energy Dream Home features a range of appliances that can replace gas-powered systems, including heat pumps for heating, cooling, and hot water, an induction cooktop, and an electric fireplace.
Electric fireplaces are also a source of clean energy.
“Except this one produces no pollution.” Heat pumps were another major feature of the display.
text:
On the heels of new legislation aimed at helping Californians switch from gas to electric-powered homes, a Silicon Valley-based agency is bringing its “Clean Energy Dream Home” showroom to communities around the Bay Area.

During SF’s Fleet Week last week, a 18-by-8-foot mobile showroom created by Silicon Valley Clean Energy (SVCE) was set up along the Embarcadero, as KPIX reports. The display, powered by a Ford electric pickup truck, offers visitors a look at electric appliances designed to reduce household pollution and slash energy bills, while making homes healthier and more comfortable.

The showcase comes as California makes it easier for homeowners to ditch gas. According to KPIX, Governor Gavin Newsom recently signed the Clean Energy Choice Act, introduced by Assemblymember Marc Berman (D-Menlo Park). It requires utilities to offer financial incentives to homeowners who disconnect from gas and electrify their homes when gas service line repairs are scheduled.

“This is the all-electric home of the future,” said Nik Kaestner, senior building decarbonization coordinator for the San Francisco Environment Department, speaking to KPIX.

The Clean Energy Dream Home features a range of appliances that can replace gas-powered systems, including heat pumps for heating, cooling, and hot water, an induction cooktop, and an electric fireplace.

Kaestner demonstrated to KPIX that the induction stove, which uses electromagnets to heat cookware directly instead of burning gas, brings water to a boil considerably faster than a gas stove, keeping energy from escaping into the kitchen.

Electric fireplaces are also a source of clean energy.

“If you have an all-electric home, you may still want the comfort and warmth from a fireplace,” Kaestner said, speaking to KPIX. “Except this one produces no pollution.”

Heat pumps were another major feature of the display. The systems use electricity to transfer heat rather than generate it through combustion, allowing a single unit to heat and cool a home. Heat pump water heaters can also replace conventional gas models.

Kaestner said reducing indoor pollution is one of the central advantages of electrification.

“The most important benefit for an all-electric home is that it’s a healthier home because there is no gas combustion happening within your four walls,” he told KPIX.

Pacific Gas and Electric says customers can save an average of $714 per year by replacing gas heating systems with heat pump technology, as California moves away from new natural gas heaters, as KPIX reports.

Homeowners can also search for available rebates and incentives through Switch Is On, BayREN, and California’s home energy programs.

text:
The United States is making an unprecedented attempt to revive three shuttered nuclear plants to meet rising energy demand, including from large-scale data centers.

No commercial nuclear reactor is known to have resumed generating electricity after beginning the decommissioning process that takes one out of service, though some reactors have restarted after long outages.

The Department of Energy is lending as much as $4.4 billion to restart the Palisades Power Plant in Michigan, the Crane Clean Energy Center on Pennsylvania's Three Mile Island and the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa to restore a combined 2.25 gigawatts of electricity, which can power roughly 2 million homes and businesses. All three of the plants closed before their licenses expired, largely because the electricity they produced was considered too expensive.

Not anymore. Two of the plants have contracts with Big Tech companies that will pay a premium to get large amounts of carbon-free energy for data centers. President Donald Trump's administration is pushing hard to deploy nuclear power for artificial intelligence and manufacturing. It's also lending billions of dollars for upgrades to produce more electricity from currently operating nuclear plants.

Restarting a reactor is a fairly quick way to get a lot of electricity, and it's cheaper than building a new, large reactor, said nuclear engineering expert Todd Allen.

"There's a demand in the country for more power," he said. "You have these assets that were previously hooked up. They were previously operable, and you can relatively quickly get them generating electricity again, compared to your other possibilities. For anyone who wants zero carbon, nuclear provides that. For the Trump administration, which really wants nuclear, this fits that story also."

Restarting reactor like restoring a car

Allen compared restarting a decommissioned nuclear plant to restarting a car that sat idle for a few years. The driver still needs a valid license and all the parts need to work correctly.

"That's what they're trying to do with these nuclear plants, but it's a much bigger, complicated system," said Allen, associate dean for research at the University of Michigan's College of Engineering.

With a nuclear plant, the owner has to bring nuclear workers back and ensure their training is current, make sure everything is working and that maintenance is up to date, ensure they have enough fuel and ask regulators to restore their operating license, he added.

Allen said it's a lot to track, but it's relatively straightforward.

Expert says restarts are risky

Edwin Lyman, at the Union of Concerned Scientists, said the taxpayer money being used should go toward addressing safety risks. For example, most U.S. plants were built between 1970 and 1990 and designed to withstand natural disasters of that era, said Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at UCS. But climate change is making extreme weather events more frequent and severe.

"It's possible, if they set the right level of safety and spend the necessary funds to meet that, they could restore these plants to operable condition," he said. "That's not happening at this point."
