The battery also incorporates BMW’s Energy Master, a central control unit mounted directly on the high-voltage pack. It brings together essential power-supply and battery-management functions.

The Shenyang batteries are intended for China-built Neue Klasse models, making local battery manufacturing a key part of the company’s regional vehicle production plans.

Battery network expands across markets

BMW’s Gen6 manufacturing strategy places battery assembly close to the vehicle factories it supplies. The company says this approach supports stable supply and strengthens the resilience of its production network.

Battery assembly facilities in Woodruff, United States, and San Luis Potosí, Mexico, are also preparing to begin series production in the coming months.

All locations operate under common production, quality, and safety standards and contribute regional manufacturing and supplier expertise.

“Production in Shenyang exemplifies our global approach: We manufacture locally, efficiently and close to our markets, in line with uniform global standards and the highest quality,” Wittmann said.

Laser welding meets digital quality checks

Production starts with cell inspections before the cells are joined with cooling units to form clusters. Following laser cleaning, those clusters and the cell contact system are precision-welded together.

A specialized foaming process then bonds the components into a single mechanical unit, contributing to the battery’s safety, stability, and longevity.

Workers and production equipment complete the housing closure, sealing, and riveting before the Energy Master is installed.

Digital quality controls accompany the manufacturing process. Production data is captured and analyzed throughout assembly, while digital twins, data analytics, and AI-supported inspections help identify deviations early and maintain traceability.

title: SkillUp & TradesForce: Making Clean Energy Careers Accessible for…
description:
Today’s reality of clean energy careers is richer and more complex than most people expect.
Tech Meets Cultural Movement anchor TradesForce builds cultural movements that make clean energy careers visible, aspirational and accessible to communities that traditional hiring systems overlook.
It also requires showing up in communities, telling authentic stories and proving that clean energy jobs are for people without degrees.
Why Clean Energy Now anchor "Clean energy careers represent one of the clearest examples of where STARs can find economic mobility and job security in an AI-augmented world," says Steve Lee, CEO of SkillUp.
For clean energy careers specifically, this preview helps demystify what the work involves and builds confidence that these jobs are within reach.
text:
As they explore job listings, someone sees "Solar Installer" and imagines spending all day on a roof in the sun. What they might not know is that the job also encompasses electrical systems training, safety certifications, blueprint reading and customer consultations. And consider HVAC technician jobs; increasingly, these roles involve installing smart technology and energy-efficient systems both residentially and commercially. Today’s reality of clean energy careers is richer and more complex than most people expect. At SkillUp, we know that if individuals skilled through alternative routes (STARs) can't see themselves in these roles, we risk stalling momentum toward the sustainable energy transition.

Our data tells us something has been shifting. Since June 2025, engagement with Skilled Trades training on our platform has surged from 19% of users to 41%, more than doubling in just seven months. Solar Installer has emerged as the third most-set career goal. Among our users ages 18-24, half of all training engagement is with Skilled Trades programs. STARs are choosing hands-on careers that can't be automated and clean energy sits right at the center of that momentum.

That's one of the many reasons why we partnered with TradesForce to expand our digital catalogs to elevate these careers to our users and to support the cultural activation to connect STARs to clean energy opportunities hiding in plain sight.

Tech Meets Cultural Movement anchor

TradesForce builds cultural movements that make clean energy careers visible, aspirational and accessible to communities that traditional hiring systems overlook. SkillUp serves as the tech and career navigation partner.

"SkillUp's platform gives workers the roadmap to clean energy careers, all the way from career exploration to the actual job postings," says Jon van Gelder, Executive Director at TradesForce. "But reaching STARs who've been told these careers aren't for them requires more than technology. It also requires showing up in communities, telling authentic stories and proving that clean energy jobs are for people without degrees. That's what SkillUp and TradesForce are doing together."

Our expanded platform powers TradesForce’s efforts to bring greater career visibility to STARs with more than 2,300 training programs identified as advanced and clean energy-aligned and approximately 1,100 active clean energy job postings. Additionally, within our Clean Energy Hub, we've organized 19 aligned careers into pathways that show STARs exactly what training they need, what jobs are available and what these roles pay on average. As always, these industry-specific careers — like water treatment operator, wind turbine technician, carpenter, solar installer and more — are fully aligned with our quality standards, which include living wage requirements and regional demand signals.

TradesForce takes those digital pathways and activates them through cultural events, storytelling campaigns and community partnerships that reach workers not just online, but in-person in neighborhoods and gathering places where career decisions get made.

Why Clean Energy Now anchor

"Clean energy careers represent one of the clearest examples of where STARs can find economic mobility and job security in an AI-augmented world," says Steve Lee, CEO of SkillUp. "These are hands-on roles that require problem-solving, technical skill and human judgment. It’s the exact type of work that remains valuable as automation advances. Our partnership with TradesForce ensures STARs can both access these pathways and see themselves thriving in them."

Our data emphasizes this. STARs are gravitating toward hands-on work that can't be automated, essential infrastructure skills with long-term demand and wages that support families without degree debt. Clean energy roles deliver all of that while also offering the chance to build sustainable infrastructure that gives these jobs deeper purpose and meaning.

We've also integrated immersive exploration tools through CareerViewXR, allowing users to interact with roles like HVAC technician, electrician, carpenter, sheet metal worker, welder and construction project manager before they commit to training. For clean energy careers specifically, this preview helps demystify what the work involves and builds confidence that these jobs are within reach.

What’s Next anchor

On March 18, we will host a webinar — Opening the Door to Clean Energy Careers for Workers Without Degrees — to explore how philanthropy, workforce innovation and mission-driven technology align to build inclusive talent pipelines. Lee and van Gelder will be joined by leaders from Invest in Our Future and Clean Power Institute to discuss how partnerships create real economic mobility, why clean energy skills remain relevant as AI reshapes work and how intentional cultural activations accelerate access to opportunity.

title: US import prices rise sharply in September amid inflation pressures - ColoradoBiz
description:
WASHINGTON (Reuters) – US import prices rose more than expected in September, boosted by higher costs for energy products and other goods, further evidence of rising inflation pressures as the Middle East conflict continues.
Economists polled by Reuters had forecast import prices, excluding tariffs, to rise 0.8% after a previously reported 0.7% advance in August.
In the 12 months through September, import prices rose 8.1%, the largest gain since July 2022, after increasing 6.7% in August.
Excluding food and fuels, import prices advanced 0.7%, matching the prior month’s increase.
The so-called core import prices rose 6.2% in the 12 months through September.
text:
WASHINGTON (Reuters) – US import prices rose more than expected in September, boosted by higher costs for energy products and other goods, further evidence of rising inflation pressures as the Middle East conflict continues.

The Labor Department report on Friday followed data this week showing strong increases in consumer and producer prices last month, leaving economists convinced inflation was broadening beyond the energy sector.

The drawn-out US-Israeli war with Iran has snarled supply chains and is keeping oil prices elevated. Economists have attributed rising inflation to President Donald Trump’s policies, including import tariffs and the Middle East conflict. A Reuters/Ipsos poll also showed about 78% of Americans blamed Trump’s policies for the rising cost of living.

“Americans face an inflation threat literally on every front and everywhere they turn they have to reach in their pocketbooks and pay a little bit more for the same goods that were cheaper just a few months ago,” said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. “There was no import goods inflation before Trump 2.0 economic policies started to roll out in January 2025, but this year it is everywhere.”

Import prices jumped 1.1% last month after rebounding by a downwardly revised 0.5% in August, the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast import prices, excluding tariffs, to rise 0.8% after a previously reported 0.7% advance in August. In the 12 months through September, import prices rose 8.1%, the largest gain since July 2022, after increasing 6.7% in August.

Despite inflation heating up in September, financial markets still expected the Federal Reserve to skip a rate hike later this month and tighten monetary policy in December.

In September, the US central bank raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, speaking in Bangkok, Thailand, on Friday, gave no preview of whether he feels more interest-rate hikes will be needed, or when, in keeping with his ⁠style since taking the reins as central bank chief in May.

Stocks on Wall Street were mixed. The dollar fell against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields fell.

Imported fuel prices rebounded 4.8% last month after falling 0.2% in August. Food prices were unchanged after dropping 0.6% in August. Excluding food and fuels, import prices advanced 0.7%, matching the prior month’s increase. The so-called core import prices rose 6.2% in the 12 months through September.

Capital goods prices increased 0.9% after rising by the same margin in August, boosted by prices for computers, peripherals and semiconductors amid an AI investment boom.

The cost of imported industrial and service machinery also rose, more than offsetting a decline in the prices of scientific and medical machinery.

Acceleration in Inflation Anticipated

Prices for imported consumer goods, excluding automotives, increased 0.4%, driven by a 0.7% surge in the cost of long-lasting manufactured goods. The cost of imported automotive vehicles, parts and engines increased 0.3%.

Prices of imports from China increased 0.7%, the most since December 2021. Prices gained 3.1% in the 12 months through September. Prices of imports from Japan, the European Union, Mexico and Canada also rose.

The report also showed a 12.6% surge in import air passenger fares last month after declining in July and August.

Economists said the international airfares component that goes into the calculation of the Personal Consumption Expenditures price indexes, the inflation measures tracked by the Federal Reserve for its 2% target, was unchanged after they adjusted the data for seasonal fluctuations.

Economists’ estimates for the increase in September’s core PCE price index remained largely unchanged, in the 0.31% to 0.36% range, which could round up to 0.4%. That would translate to a 3.1% year-over-year rise. Core PCE inflation rose 0.2% in August and advanced to 3.0% year over year.

“We’re looking for inflation to accelerate in the near term but not plateau at a higher level,” said Oren Klachkin, financial markets economist at Nationwide. “That said, the risk is inflation remains higher for longer than we expect and is more difficult for the Fed to vanquish.”

While the AI investment spree is fueling inflation, it is also underpinning manufacturing. A separate Fed report showed factory production rebounded 0.3% in September, supported by businesses replenishing inventories to meet robust domestic demand. Output fell 0.2% in August. It rose 1.1% year over year in September.

But factory production lost significant momentum in the third quarter, growing at a 0.7% annualized rate after accelerating 5.6% in the April-June quarter.

Manufacturing accounts for about 9.4% of the economy. Semiconductor and related electronic component output surged 28.4% last quarter, which some economists shrugged off. Motor vehicle and parts production fell 3.0% in September and contracted 3.4% last quarter.

“While strong AI-demand has boosted business investment, much of this investment is imported, implying domestic production has not been as strong,” said Veronica Clark, an economist at Citigroup.

Outside AI-supporting industries, downside risks to production are mounting from elevated energy prices, a trade war with Canada, rising borrowing costs and fading stimulus from tax incentives. Record-high diesel prices could soon raise the cost of goods, including at the supermarket, weighing on demand.

Capacity utilization for the manufacturing sector edged up to 75.9% from 75.8% in August. It is 2.3 percentage points below its long-run average.

“This means producers may be inclined to absorb some of the increase in energy and other input costs, but clearly not all, as suggested by this week’s heated consumer and producer price reports,” said Sal Guatieri, a senior economist at BMO Capital Markets.

(Reporting By Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama and Andrea Ricci)

title: Building charging hubs for Tesla, IONNA and EVgo: Inside Osborne's work
description:
Charged: Osborne does all kinds of commercial construction, not just EV-related.
Stephen Osborne: We’ve been in the EV space for about 10 years now.
Stephen Osborne: We’ve seen more changes in the last 18 months than we saw in the prior 7 or 8 years.
Most charging equipment needs to be checked over for loose connections or software updates, annually at the minimum.
Stephen Osborne: I bet about one out of every ten projects has a nightmare situation happen.
text:
EV charging infrastructure installation is a big part of Osborne’s commercial construction business.

Over the years, Charged has interviewed execs and engineers from companies covering almost every layer of the charging stack: hardware manufacturers, software developers, security specialists, utilities, standards bodies, and of course, charge point operators (CPOs) and charging-as-a-service (CaaS) providers. However, until now we haven’t heard from a provider of one of the most important parts of the stack—a company that actually builds the charging sites.

Yes, general contractors are still required, even in this new age of vertical integration. CaaS providers offer a turnkey package to EV fleet operators, but this doesn’t mean that their own employees handle every aspect of the complex process of building and operating charging infrastructure. A CaaS provider designs infrastructure, coordinates and oversees the process of installing it, chooses quality subcontractors, provides a single point of contact to the customer, and takes responsibility if things go wrong.

Likewise, CPOs may have a high degree of vertical integration, but they don’t do everything in-house. CPOs and turnkey charging providers use contractors to handle construction, and many of them turn to Kansas-based Osborne, which has been building commercial structures since 1976. Osborne has worked for all the biggies: Electrify America, IONNA, EVgo, Tesla and more. Charged spoke with CEO Stephen Osborne.

Charged: Osborne does all kinds of commercial construction, not just EV-related. How long have you been in the EV charging field?

Stephen Osborne: We’ve been in the EV space for about 10 years now. We’ve put in something like a thousand locations in the last 10 years. We were in on a lot of the early stuff, building Tesla and Electrify America sites.

Charged: You must have seen a lot of changes in the industry.

Stephen Osborne: We’ve seen more changes in the last 18 months than we saw in the prior 7 or 8 years. It’s fascinating what’s coming. Higher charging speeds, battery backup systems. Charge port compatibility across cars, that’s been a big issue, and we’re starting to see a lot of conversions.

The efficiency of chargers is increasing. When the CPO is paying for $10,000 worth of energy, but they’re losing 20% of it in the old legacy systems, that’s money going out the door. The newer systems are reporting as much as 98% efficiency.

One of the big challenges we deal with is the amount of equipment that is put on site. In recent years the new all in-one systems have helped a lot because you can pack charging sites into much smaller locations. One charging site in Georgia had 12 chargers, but it took up almost an acre of space, because there was equipment spread all over the place. Now that same site would probably be around 2,000 square feet.

Charged: So, using all in-one chargers as opposed to a distributed system results in a smaller overall site footprint?

Stephen Osborne: Not always, but typically that helps keep a smaller footprint, so it allows people to get a lot more creative in where they put the locations. Less equipment on site is also easier to install and less costly. There’s typically less copper wire underground.

Smaller footprints can cause challenges—we still need a basic amount of space to work, have a skid loader or excavator on the site—but instead of working on an acre, I can now work on a 2,000- or 3,000-square-foot spot, and I’m not taking parking stalls away from paying customers.

Charged: Would you say the trend is towards all in-one chargers and away from distributed charging? I’ve heard a number of people telling me the opposite.

Stephen Osborne: I’m not sure I’m qualified to say it’s a trend. It’s definitely something we see a lot more of. It depends where it’s at and what the end use is.

Charged: Are most of your customers CPOs, fleets, or both?

Stephen Osborne: Both. We’ve built for Tesla, Electrify, EVgo, IONNA, Francis Energy, ABB. We’re the preferred contractor for several of them. Our company focuses on enterprise clients where we can handle large program roll-outs. If they have a hundred projects, our typical goal is to take about 30 to 50% of those.

We also have some bus charging depots that we work on. Just a couple days ago, we turned on a bus charging depot for the Transit Authority of River City [which serves the Louisville, Kentucky metro area]. We renovated their depot, made a lot of structural repairs to a hundred-year-old building. Rather than tearing it down, we were able to stabilize the building and put in ChargePoint charging systems.

Charged: That sounds like a good differentiator for your company—you do all kinds of commercial construction, which your competitors don’t necessarily do.

Stephen Osborne: That’s correct. A lot of CPOs, they’re trying to go with just the local electrician, but they still need to hire a general contractor to do the civil scope. Then when you run into a problem, it’s a pointing game of who’s to blame, change orders are flying and everybody’s upset. Our company, on the other hand, is the general contractor. We’re licensed all across the US and we stay compliant with all state and local licensing regulations. We’re not doing the rent-a-contractor thing. There’s a lot of people out there that pay a $2,000 or $3,000 fee to get a contractor’s license, which is illegal.

One thing we’re doing with IONNA right now—they’re building out convenience stores, so they hire us to do the electrical install, the site work, and our crews build out the convenience store for them at the same time. It’s more of a turnkey operation than your electrician just installing some chargers. Our differentiator is a vertically integrated one-stop shop.

Charged: Are you doing some projects where you’re building a whole new store?

Stephen Osborne: Yes, we have a few. Most of them are renovations. For example, three years ago, I was driving through Colorado with my family and we saw an old ice cream shop and some crummy EV chargers sitting there. And I thought, that would be a cool spot for an EV charging space and convenience store. About a year later, IONNA sent us a set of plans for Lyman, Colorado and it was that exact spot! It was a full gut and remodel—we put in a whole bunch of chargers and canopies.

We’re seeing a lot more amenities at charging stations. Drivers want to get out and stretch their legs, maybe use a dog park, use the restroom, grab some coffee, hop back in the car and off you go. I think that’s going to be a big trend going forward, and we’re loving it because we can do the whole thing.

Charged: Can you walk me through the steps of a typical project? Is it always the CPO that hires you, or are there some projects where perhaps a municipality or utility is taking the lead?

Stephen Osborne: That’s a good question. Generally, these companies will go to an engineering firm to do feasibility studies on the site. A lot of the big CPOs have site developers in-house that will go out and meet with the site host. Maybe it’s a store manager, maybe it’s a real estate handler. They’ll find a location that looks like it fits, then from there, they’ve got a pretty robust amount of due diligence. Can they get power there? What’s it going to cost?

We had one location several years ago, we found out there was no power in the area. The utility company would bring us a thousand feet of conduit, but it was almost a million dollars. And the customer said, “No, that location is not feasible.” But we were able to move it one parcel over and it was only $15,000 for the upgrades.

Most of the time, by the time it gets to us, all that site development is already done. We look at the plans and we might recommend modifications.

With most of our clients, we have a design feedback loop. When they try to build a charging site on the side of a cliff, we put somebody out on the location who built these before and they look at it and say, “Good idea, but if we can just move this one parking stall one aisle over, we’re going to save a ton of money.”

We have that design feedback loop with IONNA and Francis. They do a lot of that site development work, but they still call us up and say, “What do you think about this before we finalize the design?”

It’s an intelligent way of doing things to get that contractor-level design feedback. And then taking that feedback and pulling it back in is really helpful. Early stuff with leases, site development, geotechnical reports—there’s a ton of vendors out there who can provide that. There’s very few who do it all in-house.

Probably 90% of our stuff, the client has already done most of that and just hands us a set of drawings and says, “Price it and build it.” But that other 10% where we have that design feedback loop going, they’re usually change order-free jobs—the sites get built faster and it’s smooth sailing.

Charged: Do you usually procure the hardware, or do you work from what the client wants?

Stephen Osborne: On small projects or one-off projects, sometimes public entities, we’ll procure hardware, but typically the CPOs are buying tens of millions of equipment at a time and they usually procure that. A lot of them will send the equipment directly to us. Our company warehouses the equipment. We put it on a truck and send it to the site so we have just-in-time delivery. That has helped a lot with cost on these projects—we had a systemic problem for years where the equipment would not show up, or the wrong equipment would show up. Once we started centralizing that, we stopped having problems almost instantly.

Charged: Once the site is up and running, do you provide ongoing maintenance and customer support?

Stephen Osborne: Not on the equipment. Most of the CPOs have their own support network. It’s not a service we offer currently, although we will very soon, probably by the end of this year.

However, a component that nearly everyone misses is that we provide support for the physical real estate location. If somebody wants their site looking pretty, we can come in and clean it up and reseal-coat it, do all the striping work. We make sure the landscaping is set up for the spring and looking good, make sure that light poles are up and functional. It’s like the broken window theory—if a site is not being mowed or taken care of, a driver says, “Maybe I’ll go down the street to the one that looks nice.”

Charged: Reliability was a huge scandal for a long time, and I always suspected that one source of the problems was the number of companies involved in an install—CPO, contractor, hardware, software, blah, blah, blah. Are there things that can happen in the construction phase of the project that will lead to better reliability?

Stephen Osborne: Absolutely. Electronics, they’re going to fail. It’s just a matter of when and how you handle it. Do they go into a fail-safe mode where it prevents someone from being hurt? I’ve seen a lot of equipment failures. I’ve seen switchgear that catches fire. We’ve seen chargers that just stop working.

We’ve installed almost 4,000 DC fast chargers, and we’ve developed a simple quality-control checklist that has been developed with input from every single one of the CPOs we work for. We have onsite supervision, and before our project managers close the job and leave the site, they’re going through every little thing, and inevitably somebody missed something, which is why we do the checklist.

Commonly, it’s little things like not having the proper torque setting on a lug, or Megger testing the wires [using a megohmmeter to measure the insulation quality of cables] to make sure that when you pulled them through the conduit, you didn’t burn through the shielding and damage your wire.

We can fix that before we leave. And we’re there while they commission it, so if there’s a problem in commissioning, we fix it then and there. I’ve seen too many people cut corners on those things, and equipment will fail prematurely because of it. It’s unfair to the CPOs.

Charged: So the CPOs get blamed for problems that might’ve been caused by a subcontractor cutting some corners?

Stephen Osborne: Well, yes. If they have a contractor that doesn’t do what they’re supposed to, it’s not them that’s in the national news getting beat up. But at the same time, they need to be selecting good equipment and they need to spend the money to service that equipment. Most charging equipment needs to be checked over for loose connections or software updates, annually at the minimum. It’s just good maintenance practice, and that’s something we’re involved in. We go out to the sites and make sure everything’s up and running well. It starts at the parking lot stripes and the landscaping and it goes to the electronics.

Charged: I’ve been talking to companies that provide various types of portable charging, and they’re telling me that their customers don’t necessarily want portable charging so much as they want a quick install. DC-America makes a prefab charging setup on a skid. No trenching, no construction. Is that a threat to what you do, or is that something that your company also offers?

Stephen Osborne: A little of both. There are huge advantages to using the skid method as long as they’re built right. In 2021, we built a charging system for EVgo in Union Station’s parking garage in Washington, DC. We manufactured the skid system in-house—we designed it, engineered it, did the load studies, built the skid system and installed everything in 30 days. It was a very fast install—that company asked us to come back and put in a couple more.

On exterior projects there’s not necessarily a lot of time savings with the skid systems because you still have to prep the site, you still have to get some conduit in the ground. It is an option to save some time on site. If there’s a prevailing wage situation, typically the labor that’s being done in a warehouse would not fall under those prevailing wage rates, so an owner could save a little bit of money that way. It’s just very situation-dependent.

Now, when you look at the Tesla platform, it’s all big concrete skids—those things weigh about 16,000 pounds, and you have to bring in a big crane. There’s no one situation that works for all CPOs. Skids work in some scenarios. Physical, regular civil construction works in others.

Charged: Another issue I hear a lot about is utility interconnects. Delays, paperwork, hundreds of different jurisdictions with different rules. Is that something you get involved with?

Stephen Osborne: We do. We have a team of in-house utility coordinators that handles all permitting and utility connection. It’s a huge challenge, and one that is really unpredictable. Some jurisdictions may not have availability for a transformer for a year, and you’re stuck. Then another jurisdiction may say, “We’ll bring you a transformer next week and we’re not going to charge you for it.” You never know.

We’ve built good relationships with dozens of utility companies. Almost every day one of our clients will call us and ask for help with a utility, and our team’s able to push it across the line and take that burden off their back. That’s part of the service we provide.

Charged: Do you do exclusively DC fast charging sites or are there some Level 2 sites getting built?

Stephen Osborne: We’ve built a number of Level 2 sites. Not a lot though. They’re generally simpler—usually it’s a single-trade install, just an electrical contractor. There’s not as much value add on Level 2 charging, unless it’s 200 of them. DC fast involves a lot more than just electrical construction. It’s the civil construction, landscaping, design and engineering issues that have a lot of ramifications.

Charged: Before we go, tell me a horror story or two—a weird situation where you were able to solve a difficult problem for a customer.

Stephen Osborne: I bet about one out of every ten projects has a nightmare situation happen. Nine out of ten are going to go smoothly, but I do remember the ones where there were problems.

On one job in New Jersey, we found out we were two feet above an old capped landfill from 10 years ago. We started digging and we’re thinking, “This smells really bad.” Dealing with the remediation was a unique opportunity to excel because we had to find out how to deal with environmental issues. When you start adding all those extra elements, that’s where our company sets ourselves apart. We have our utility coordinators and our environmental team all in-house. We make sure that the problem stops with our company and doesn’t radiate to our client.

A lot of times it starts with missing tiny details, like perhaps not getting a geotechnical report. We had a site recently where they dug the site out and you could see water flowing. It was below the water table. A typical DC fast charging station sits on a 5,000-pound cube of concrete, and it’ll just sink right down through that kind of soil—gone! Our team was able to come up with a concrete pier solution that got us down to bedrock, stabilized the site, and everybody’s happy. When you get into a situation like that and everyone’s pointing fingers, you start to have cost impacts hit quickly and it can become really bad.

Charged: Any new products or services in the pipeline?

Stephen Osborne: The biggest thing that we’re rolling out this year is our ongoing maintenance programs. We’re offering service and maintenance every year, to make sure that our client’s sites look beautiful. If it looks beautiful, that may be the first impression somebody has of that entire brand.

title: Charged EVs | Who knew? Big Oil also sells electricity
description:
Of the six or seven behemoths collectively known as Big Oil, three—Shell, Total and BP—operate EV charging networks.
Shell Recharge claims to operate some 85,000 public charging points in several countries, including the US.
TotalEnergies boasts a network of over 60,000 charging points in Europe.
(Read our 2026 feature, How the biggest US EV charging networks got their starts for more details.)
We haven’t heard that ExxonMobil or Chevron have dabbled in the EV charging game.
text:
Would you charge your EV at a charging station owned by an oil giant? Well, lots of people do, every day. Of the six or seven behemoths collectively known as Big Oil, three—Shell, Total and BP—operate EV charging networks.

Shell Recharge claims to operate some 85,000 public charging points in several countries, including the US. TotalEnergies boasts a network of over 60,000 charging points in Europe. bp pulse operates thousands of public chargers in the US and Europe and—dig this—has a section on its web site that encourages people to buy EVs.

A few years ago, the companies were on a CPO buying spree. For example, Shell acquired Dutch charging station operator NewMotion In 2017, and the US firm Greenlots in 2019. (Read our 2026 feature, How the biggest US EV charging networks got their starts for more details.)

What could their motivation be? Did the oil giants mean to strangle the developing EV charging industry by buying up charging companies and shutting them down, or perhaps by ensuring that charging an EV costs more than fueling a legacy vehicle?

Well, if that’s what they meant to do, they haven’t accomplished it. By all accounts, the oil-owned charging stations work just fine, and pricing is comparable to that of other offerings. Furthermore, new charging stations are being installed at such a clip, and by so many different players, that it’s hard to imagine the oilers or anyone else cornering the market.

The opposite possibility—that Big Oil knows its days are numbered, and plans to phase out oil in favor of electrons—seems equally unbelievable. The last time we checked, these dinos were still planning production and exploration projects, and still lavishing billions of bucks on politicians around the world to speed the drilling.

But believe it or not, a gradual shift may be beginning. The three oil giants that are into EV charging (not coincidentally, these are the three that have European roots) are actually electric utilities as well.

A 2025 article in Medium explains that these three “energy companies” are no longer just oil producers, and argues that their involvement in the electric utility business is “not the clean-tech hype cycle we saw in 2020 [but] a disciplined, capital-driven reinvention led by profitability, not PR.”

Shell is building “an integrated power business that covers generation, trading, PPAs and retail.” Through Shell Energy, the firm supplies power directly to corporations and households. TotalEnergies aims to control 100–120 TWh of annual power generation by 2030. bp pulse was operating over 40,000 charge points in 2025, and aiming to have 100,000 by 2030. Medium reported that bp was selling some 1 TWh of power annually through its EV charging biz.

In the energy giants’ world, that’s small potatoes, but the volume could grow very quickly—and that potential provides a plausible (if paradoxical) pecuniary motivation for these multinationals to make a serious go of their EV charging ventures.

We haven’t heard that ExxonMobil or Chevron have dabbled in the EV charging game. But as Medium reports, Shell, Total and bp are “no longer fossil dinosaurs. They are hybrid utilities—with deep commodity expertise, global origination networks, and access to low-cost capital.”

name: Detroit Environment
title: Budding food scrap pickup services across the US want your coffee grounds, eggshells
description: Composting leftover coffee grounds, eggshells and carrot tops can reduce the amount of food waste that goes into landfills, producing the potent greenhouse gas methane.
text:
The U.S. economy grew at a solid 2.2% pace from April throug…

A roundup, in brief, of national and international business news.











Ricky Blanding, founder of Scrap Soils, holds composted soil made from food scraps.

Ricky Blanding, founder of Scrap Soils, picks up compostable material from the BasBlue kitchen Monday, Sept. 14, 2026, in Detroit.

Ricky Blanding, founder of Scrap Soils, collects compostable material at BasBlue kitchen, Monday, Sept. 14, 2026, in Detroit.

Ricky Blanding, founder of Scrap Soils, dumps compostable material at Sanctuary Farms in Detroit.

DETROIT – Every Monday, Ricky Blanding drives his Ford Ranger pickup truck around Detroit along a carefully planned route.

He hops in and out of the truck, grabbing buckets of food scraps from porches and restaurants, piling those scraps into bins in the truck bed and driving them to a composting site.

Blanding is the CEO of Scrap Soils, one of the many budding food waste collection services across the country helping to divert food from landfills and make composting more accessible. It’s especially important for those who can’t compost at home, who live in cities without municipal curbside pickup or who can’t get to a drop-off location.

Composting leftover coffee grounds, eggshells, carrot tops and more reduces the amount of food that goes into dumps where it produces the potent greenhouse gas methane. It also ultimately helps create healthy soil for gardeners and urban farmers.

Experts say companies like Scrap Soils are an important part of cleaning up the broader food ecosystem. Emily Cassidy, research associate at climate solutions nonprofit Project Drawdown, said composting offers the dual benefits of reducing landfill methane emissions and, once the composting process is complete, returning nutrients to soil.

“Because methane has such a big impact on the climate in a short amount of time, the more we can reduce methane, it is like pulling the emergency brake on climate change,” Cassidy said.

Beyond mitigating climate change, composting can also improve local food production, she said.

“That’s a way that we can see that we’re benefiting the environment, because we’re taking food and then replenishing the ground with those nutrients,” she said.

Blanding, a 34-year-old native Detroiter, co-launched Scrap Soils in 2020 to play a local part in solving a statewide food waste problem that mirrors what’s happening around the globe . Food waste is a huge source of methane in Michigan landfills that estimates say accounts for millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions in the state.

In Detroit, more than 70 homes and businesses are signed up for Scrap Soils’ weekly pickups. It’s an easier way to compost than making space in one’s backyard or driving to a city drop-off site. Home pickups start at $15 per month, while businesses pay $60 per month or more, depending on volume.

One of those commercial customers is The Grand Porter restaurant in a neighborhood on Detroit’s southwest side.

“We go through a lot of eggs, so mostly egg scraps, eggshells and the cardboard. We put all of our bread scraps, stale bread scraps, in here,” said Lou Hammer, the restaurant’s executive chef, pointing to a large bin with bags of food waste inside. “Some tomato tops, some avocado skins. Probably a few other things in there, too.”

“It doesn’t take any extra effort,” she said of the pickup service. “This was going to go in a bag anyway. It’s just going to go in a green bag instead.”

After completing his nine-hour, more than 100-mile weekly route, Blanding drops off the waste at Scrap Soils’ partner, Sanctuary Farms in Detroit. There, everything from apple cores to rotted pumpkins to corn husks is composted into a rich soil additive offered for sale.

“Food waste has not only become the problem,” Blanding said, “but it’s also the solution to so many issues in climate change.”

The company ultimately plans to buy a larger truck, as well as its own property and equipment for composting. It’s fundraising to meet a matching grant through the state.

That hasn’t been without challenges. As Blanding seeks to grow, he’s come up against skepticism that a small team with limited resources can make a big impact. Companies like Scrap Soils also face challenges including gaining visibility and getting people to sign up and commit.

At the same time, emphasizing what can and cannot be composted, and how to do it correctly – such as removing produce stickers before putting a peel in the bucket – is key to its success, too.

“The role of a hauler is very important, and education around composting is also very important,” Blanding said.

“Being able to continue to get more engagement and more partnership, those things go far in helping us to expand this tiny effort into something that actually can scale,” he added. This week's launch arrived after years of delays and anticipation around the new Roadster — and Tesla shares climbed in morning trading on Friday before falling amid a sell-off in companies tied to artificial intelligence.

The wait isn't completely over. Musk said production for consumers won't begin until 2028. Tesla also didn't immediately set a price tag on its latest EV.

Musk has repeatedly said that the future of driving will be autonomous — and Austin-based Tesla has focused much of its business on building out self-driving features for its vehicles and, more recently, launching its own (still limited) robotaxi business.

Kairos Lands $643M for Hermes 2 Reactor in Tennessee

Kairos Power LLC secured $643 million in combined private and government financing that will be utilized to support construction of its demonstration reactor in Tennessee. While the firm has not yet issued a formal press release, the Bloomberg wire service quoted a spokesperson from the firm about the funding.

The funding that was secured includes $368 million from investors. These investors include Google Ventures and DCVC. Also, $275 million in financing was secured from the US Energy Department. The Bloomberg report quoted Kairos CEO Mike Laufer.

According to the Bloomberg report, the bulk of the funds will support development of the Hermes 2 reactor. The funding will also support expansion of manufacturing capabilities at a plant site in New Mexico.

Another $100 million, of which $70 million is reported to be cash, was secured from Samsung C&T Corp. via a partnership that was announced last month. These funds will support Samsung’s role as the EPC for construction of Kairos reactors. Kairos Power plans to lead reactor technology, engineering, manufacturing, procurement, and construction for the nuclear island, while Samsung C&T has agreed to support selected engineering and construction activities, initially focused on power-generation systems and the balance of plant.

Samsung C&T has agreed to provide up to $100 million through a combination of direct investment and in-kind engineering services, subject to regulatory approvals, to enable the successful delivery of the Hermes 2 Demonstration Plant in Oak Ridge, TN. The investment will further strengthen Kairos Power’s financial readiness to support Hermes 2 and prepare for broader commercial deployment of KP-FHR technology.

The companies plan to collaborate on selected engineering and construction activities to strengthen technical and execution readiness, initially focused on power-generation systems and balance-of-plant scope.

This builds on a trilateral memorandum of understanding signed by Samsung C&T, Kairos Power, and Barnard Construction on 08/18/26, aimed at establishing an early framework for reliable project execution.

Hermes 2 and Commercial KP-FHR Deployment

Kairos Power received construction permits from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission for the Hermes 2 plant in December 2024 and broke ground in Oak Ridge, TN, in April 2026. Once licensed and commissioned, the grid-connected, 50 MWe reactor will demonstrate KP-FHR technology at a relevant scale to mitigate technical, licensing, manufacturing, and construction uncertainty for the full-size commercial plants that will follow it.

Kairos Power’s commercial offering is a modular, scalable, and affordable energy solution with the flexibility to meet the evolving demands of modern electricity markets. Designed for multi-unit deployment, the high-temperature reactor combines TRISO particle fuel with molten fluoride salt coolant to support efficient electricity production with robust inherent safety.

Kairos Power has made significant progress toward commercializing KP-FHR technology, leveraging the engineering, manufacturing, operational, and regulatory experience gained through its disciplined iterative development approach.

The U.S. Department of Energy is supporting the development and demonstration of Kairos Power’s technology through an Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program risk reduction award, complementing Kairos Power’s substantial private investment.

About the Kairos Hermes 2 Reactor

Hermes 2 is Kairos Power’s first deployment under its landmark deal with Google to develop an advanced reactor fleet. The plant will supply up to 50 megawatts of clean electricity to the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) grid, helping to decarbonize Google data centers in Tennessee and Alabama.

Through Kairos Power’s iterative development approach, Hermes 2 will build on lessons learned from the Hermes Low-Power Demonstration Reactor (Hermes 1), which commenced nuclear construction at the same site last year. The Hermes series will be the first fluoride salt-cooled high-temperature reactors (KP-FHRs) ever built, incorporating proven nuclear technologies that originated in Oak Ridge—including TRISO coated particle fuel and Flibe molten fluoride salt coolant—which simplify the reactor’s design, lower capital costs, and yield robust inherent safety.

Technology Class: Solid-fueled/Molten salt cooled

Reactor Type: Graphite-moderated, fluoride salt-cooled, high temperature reactor

Power Output (MWe/MWT): KP-X Demonstration Plant (50 MWe), KP-FHR Commercial Fleet (each unit will be 75 MWe)

NRC Updates AP1000 Design Certification, Streamlines Future Reactor Licensing

Updated Westinghouse AP1000 design incorporates lessons from Vogtle Units 3 and 4, extends certification to 2066

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission updated and renewed the certification of Westinghouse’s AP1000 reactor design, incorporating lessons from the construction and operation of Vogtle Units 3 and 4 (the nation’s newest nuclear reactors) into the certified design.

The action gives future applicants a standardized, field-proven AP1000 design that reflects how the reactors were actually constructed and operated. It is intended to reduce duplicative regulatory reviews, lower licensing costs and help future AP1000 projects move through the NRC’s licensing process more efficiently.

During the construction and startup of Vogtle Units 3 and 4, the NRC reviewed and approved nearly 200 license amendments. By incorporating applicable design changes and lessons learned from that experience into the renewed certification, future AP1000 applicants can reference an updated design rather than seeking separate approval for changes the NRC has already evaluated.

“The NRC’s approval of the updated AP1000 design provides the regulatory foundation for America to move from building individual reactors to deploying them at scale,” Chairman Ho K. Nieh said. “This is how safety-focused, enabling regulation reduces regulatory uncertainty and investment risk.”

The renewed certification extends the AP1000 design’s validity through 2066. Future applicants will still be required to obtain NRC approval for site-specific environmental, safety and security considerations, and this action does not authorize the siting, construction or operation of any facility.

& & &

Challenges Ahead for Westinghouse to Re-license V.C. Summer

Now that the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has updated the AP1000 Design Certification and “streamlined future licensing, it’s worth taking a look at the V.C. Summer project. The twin partially built AP1000s are likely to be the early bird users of the new NRC processes.

The NRC noted in its press statement that “applicants will still be required to obtain NRC approval for site-specific environmental, safety and security considerations, and this action does not authorize the siting, construction or operation of any facility.”

In October 2025 Brookfield, the Canadian private equity firm that holds a majority share of the ownership of Westinghouse, was selected by South Carolina utility Santee Cooper to complete two partially built Westinghouse 1,150 MW AP1000 PWR type nuclear reactors. A final investment decision is expected by the end of 2028. Once that happens work will proceed related to licensing the two reactors so that real work can take place to complete both reactors. It is expected that it will take at least four years for the first unit to come online or 2032.

In terms of regulatory status, the NRC terminated the combined licenses for the two reactors in March 2019. Santee Cooper and Brookfield may choose to submit new applications for construction and operating licenses under the NRC’s Part 50 process. The documentation from the previous COLs for both reactors should, to some extent, make life easier in terms of re-licensing the the two units.

Because the original owners agreed to legally terminate the project’s Combined Licenses (COLs) in March 2019, the project cannot simply be “restarted” under old permits. It seems logical that Westinghouse will seek to re–license the two partially built AP1000s using 10CFR52 which, unlike 10CFR50, combines the construction and operating license.

According to nuclear trade press reports, and press statements from Westinghouse, here’s an outline of some of the milestones ahead to complete the re-licensing process. These are some highlights of key items. It is not a complete list.

Application for a New Combined License (COL)

Leveraging Prior Reviews: While a completely new application is required, the NRC can work with Westinghouse and the utility to establish a tailored roadmap. The scope of the review may be streamlined by crediting and referencing the extensive safety and environmental analyses completed for the original 2012 COL, provided those baselines have not changed.

Updated Environmental Review: There is a requirement to update environmental data or submit a supplemental Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) to account for any changes to the surrounding ecosystem, water use, or local demographics since the original reviews.

Physical Site Assessments and Condition Inspections

Comprehensive Site Audits: The NRC and the EPC engineering teams must conduct exhaustive site audits to evaluate the integrity of the structures. The reactors have been sitting partially constructed, exposed to the elements, and abandoned since July 2017.

Degradation and Material Testing: Concrete, steel, rebar, and any pre-fabricated modules already installed must undergo testing to address potential issues like concrete cracking, weathering, and material degradation resulting from years of exposure.

Utility and Owner Qualifications

New Quality Assurance (QA) Program: The entity must draft and implement an entirely new QA program that meets stringent modern NRC standards to oversee the remaining construction and eventual operations.

Regulatory and Design Compliance

Design Certification Updates: The project must ensure compliance with current Westinghouse AP1000 design standards and any newly updated NRC regulations enacted since the initial abandonment.

ITAAC Implementation: The licensing process will re-establish the framework for Inspections, Tests, Analyses, and Acceptance Criteria (ITAAC), which must be systematically completed and verified by the NRC before nuclear fuel can eventually be loaded.

Bluecore Energy Secures Uranium for 10 MW Floating SMR

Bluecore Energy, a maritime nuclear energy company developing compact, water-cooled nuclear power systems, based in Long Beach, CA, announced significant progress across several critical elements of its first system, including the purchase of low-enriched uranium (LEU) from WMC, continued pre-application engagement with the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission and U.S. Coast Guard, and progress with its maritime classification pathway with the American Bureau of Shipping (ABS).

The milestones come less than three months after Bluecore Energy emerged from stealth and just weeks after the company announced $50 million innew financing just months after scoring $10 million in seed funding. Together, they represent continued progress in moving Bluecore Energy’s technology from engineering and non-fueled hardware development toward fuel fabrication, testing, validation and future deployment.

Securing Enriched Uranium Through WMC

Bluecore Energy has purchased uranium hexafluoride (UF6) enriched to 4.95% U-235 from the WMC. The material is currently held at a U.S. nuclear fuel facility outside the state of California while Bluecore Energy works on its plans for future fuel fabrication, testing and validation.

Building Safety, Regulatory and Maritime Classification Pathways in Parallel

Bluecore Energy is developing its safety, regulatory and maritime classification pathways alongside its engineering and testing program. In August, the company began pre-application engagement with a Regulatory Engagement Plan under 10CFR50 with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, presenting a conceptual overview of its design and discussing its regulatory strategy with NRC staff. The U.S. Coast Guard also participated in the meeting.

Separately, last June the NRC and Coast Guard signed an interagency memorandum of understanding (MOU) establishing a framework for coordination between the agencies on civilian maritime nuclear projects. The MOU establishes a framework to coordinate requirements and processes for the design, fabrication, construction, and operation of civilian maritime nuclear projects installed within the marine transportation system.

The MOU is important because no regulatory framework exists for siting floating nuclear power plants in U.S. harbors. This agreement may reduce paperwork and delays in areas where both agencies have jurisdiction related to floating nuclear power plants. In addition to the U.S. Coast Guard the firm must also comply with American Bureau of Shipping (ABS): Marine vessel classification, hull structural integrity, and maritime engineering safety.

Unlike conventional nuclear power plants built around permanent land-based sites, Bluecore Energy said in its press statement that it is designing its systems from the beginning for deployment on floating maritime platforms. That architecture creates flexibility in where future systems can operate. Depending on the application, regulatory requirements and site-specific safety analysis, future Bluecore Energy systems could support ports, AI data centers and coastal infrastructure from appropriate maritime locations, including potential offshore deployment.

Preliminary Details About the Reactor

The firm is developing a 10 MW PWR type reactor that will use nuclear fuel at 4.95% U-235. The firm plans to lash multiple floating barges in tethered configurations with onboard switchgear equipment branding it as the Nautilus Floating Nuclear Power Plant (FNPP).

The coolant is held under high pressure to reach operating temperatures of approximately 315°C (599°F). The primary coolant remains completely sealed within the primary loop, isolating radioactive inventory from downstream equipment. Condensation and heat rejection utilize closed-circuit cooling systems designed to interface with maritime water loops or ambient heat sinks without releasing irradiated water.

A non-nuclear, non-fuelled prototype hull and an electrically heated test pressure vessel is being built at the company’s Pier D headquarters in the Port of Long Beach to test hydrodynamic water-flow behavior, sea-motion dynamics, and thermal hydraulics.

The barges are being design to withstand harbor marine conditions, including wave action, tidal drift, seismic shocks, and collision risks via compartmentalized marine collision bulkheads and passive containment barriers.

The firm says the entire nuclear island, turbine train, containment shell, and balance of plant will be pre-integrated in a shipyard environment, bypassing standard on-site civil concrete construction.

What’s Next for Bluecore?

Kofi Asante, Blue Core Energy’s CEO, has extensive investment and business development experience, but none in the nuclear energy industry. He does not have a degree in an engineering field. The firm’s website lists five key personnel who will fill out the technical dance cards the firm needs to succeed. Here are some strategic questions about the firm’s future.

Is the firm designing the 10 MW PWR from scratch or is it considering buying a scaled-down design from a vendor liked Last Energy which has a 20 MW PWR design?

Does the firm have a fuel fabrication foundry lined up, if so, who?

What is the expected outage refueling schedule for the reactor?

Where will the firm store spent fuel right after it comes out of the reactor, and later when it has cooled off enough for dry cask storage?

Given California’s long history of politically driven hostility to all things nuclear, will the firm have to find customer out of state?

Are remote coastal communities in Canada and Alaska potential customers?

Can the barge be safely moved from Long Beach. CA, to other sites in Oregon, Washington, Canada, or Alaska?

Could the barge and the reactor be factory manufactured in South Korea and sold to customers throughout southeast Asia?

When can the firm book nonbinding MOUs with potential customers?

What is the firm’s timeline for having a licensed reactor available for customers?

Does the firm have any prospects for international customers?

& & &

ABS and DOE Collaborate on the Use of Nuclear Technology at Sea

(NucNet) Marine classification society ABS and the US Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Nuclear Energy have entered into a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to promote the use of commercial nuclear technology at sea. The work will encompass nuclear energy systems on floating platforms, nuclear-powered vessels, and the port facilities, shipyards and industrial base required for their construction and support.

Priorities include assessing concepts and feasibility for floating nuclear energy and nuclear transportation corridors. The MOU also supports a US shipbuilding sector able to construct and operate nuclear-powered assets.

“Advanced nuclear technology is moving from concept to application, and the maritime industry needs to be ready for it,” said ABS Chairman and CEO John McDonald.

Assistant Secretary for Nuclear Energy Ted Garrish said advanced nuclear technology has the potential to transform the commercial maritime industry and open new markets for American innovation. He said the partnership would “help explore how we can build on decades of experience to safely bring next-generation nuclear technologies to the maritime sector”.

The MOU follows several federal moves on commercial maritime small modular reactors (SMRs). In May the US Maritime Administration (Marad) launched an initiative to develop small SMRs for commercial shipping. In June, the Port of Long Beach agreed to create a site for trials of nuclear-powered vessels under that initiative. This was followed in August by a separate agreement between Marad and the Port of Corpus Christi to explore SMR integration, port microgrids, shoreside power and workforce development.

Global shipping depends on fossil fuels for close to 99% of its energy consumption, but the International Maritime Organization is aiming for its greenhouse gas emissions to reach net zero by around 2050.

& & &

Joint Venture Formed for a Six-Unit SMR Plant in Poland

(WNN) Poland’s SGE and ZE Pak have agreed to establish a joint venture to develop a nuclear power plant in Pątnów which will feature up to six BWRX-300 small modular reactors. The proposed plant with six of the SMRs would have a capacity of 1,800 MWe.

SGE (previously Sythos Green Energy) has a number of potential projects under way across Europe – including in Poland, where a decision in principle has already been issued for a total of 26 BWRX-300 small modular reactors (SMRs), and in the UK where a proposal for a fleet of 14 of the SMRs across three sites is being considered under the UK’s Advanced Nuclear Framework program. It is a co-investor in the standard design of GE Vernova Hitachi’s BWRX-300.

The planned SGE–ZE PAK project will repurpose an existing coal plant, which is owned by ZE PAK, who said its “participation will consist of contributing rights to land currently owned by the company to the joint venture. In subsequent years, ZE PAK will have the option to remain in the project as a minority shareholder or sell its shares in the company managing the project to SGE, thus ending its involvement in the project”.

ZE PAK said that “recent experience has shown that the construction of large-scale nuclear reactors should be a state-owned enterprise, while SMR technology can be developed by private entities such as SGE.”

The first BWRX-300 is currently under construction in Canada, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission has issued a construction permit for the first BWRX-300 reactor at the Clinch River site in Tennessee, and the SMR has also been selected for projects being developed by SaskPower in Canada, Blue Energy in the USA, and Studsvik in Sweden.

& & &

Newcleo Opens MOX fuel Development Center

(WNN) Newcleo has inaugurated its EUR10 million (USD11 million) advanced nuclear fuel engineering, testing and training center located in Chusclan, in the Gard department in southern France.

Newcleo plans to directly invest in a mixed uranium/plutonium oxide (MOX) plant to fuel its small modular lead-cooled fast reactors. The company has proposed the deployment of an advanced MOX fuel fabrication facility in France in the Aube department, near Nogent-sur-Seine, to manufacture fuel for its future European reactors.

Announced in March 2025, the FASTER (Fuel process Assembly Storage Training and Enhanced Reality) facility provides advanced engineering, prototype testing and immersive training capabilities to Newcleo’s fuel team, which comprises around 100 engineers and specialists. The facilities installed at FASTER – located near the Marcoule nuclear site – will support Newcleo’s mixed-oxide (MOX) fuel manufacturing technology.

Paris-headquartered Newcleo said the center is designed around a practical “test and learn” approach, bringing engineering and physical testing closer together.

“Concepts developed by Newcleo’s teams are translated into prototypes and test mock-ups at FASTER, tested under representative conditions and progressively refined, helping accelerate their path towards industrial deployment.”

Seven test facilities are already operational at FASTER, with further installations under development. These facilities address different stages and challenges of MOX fuel manufacturing, including powder dosing optimization, glovebox ergonomics, pellet handling, fuel pin assembly and decontamination, pellet inspection and helium filling.

Newcleo plans to fabricate MOX nuclear fuel – produced using a mixture of uranium and plutonium oxides – to power its lead-cooled fast reactors and other potential third-party off-takers. When used in fast reactors, like Newcleo’s lead-cooled fast reactor, MOX enables the multi-recycling of nuclear fuel in what is known as a “closed fuel cycle.”

This circular approach to nuclear fuel can extract more energy from the same amount of natural uranium compared with traditional once-through fuel cycles in thermal reactors, while at the same time significantly reducing the volume and radioactivity of nuclear waste.

In December 2024, Newcleo submitted its Safety Options File to the Autorité de Sûreté Nucléaire et de Radioprotection (ASNR) for its planned mixed-oxide fuel assembly facility. The ASNR’s official opinion on the submitted safety options will contribute to securing the application for authorization to construct such a facility. In July this year, ASNR published its opinion on the safety features proposed by Newcleo for its planned facility, concluding that the provisions adopted by the company for its safety approach were satisfactory at this stage.

Designed as a modular facility, the MOX plant is expected to scale its production capacity as needed. The project would represent an initial investment of EUR1.8 billion (USD2.1 billion). It could ultimately include three production lines. By 2040, an additional investment of EUR3.2 billion could enable the creation of two more lines.

Newcleo’s delivery roadmap sees the first non-nuclear precursor prototype of its lead-cooled fast neutron reactor being ready this year in Italy and the first reactor operational in France as early as 2032, while the final investment decision for the first commercial power plant is expected around 2029.

& & &

DOE Funds Next Steps for Molten Chloride Reactor

The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) has approved cost-shared funding for an accelerated final stage of the Molten Chloride Reactor Experiment (MCRE), under its Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program. The funding will support work by Southern Company, Idaho National Laboratory and CORE POWER to advance scientific understanding of molten salt reactor technology and inform future reactor development.

MCRE is designed to become the world’s first fast-spectrum molten chloride salt reactor experiment to reach criticality, marking a historic step in the development of advanced nuclear technology. The experiment is expected to generate critical data on the behavior of the fuel, reactor operation and performance, providing the scientific and engineering foundation needed to support future reactor design, licensing pathways and commercial deployment. By reducing technical risk and expanding industry understanding of fast-spectrum molten salt systems, MCRE is expected to accelerate innovation across a range of reactor developers.

Fast-spectrum molten salt reactors have the potential to transform far more than electricity generation. From powering industrial processes and producing life-saving medical isotopes to enabling future maritime propulsion and extracting additional value from used nuclear fuel, the technology could unlock a new generation of nuclear energy applications.

About the MCRE

A Molten Chloride Salt Reactor (MCSR)—often referred to as a Molten Chloride Fast Reactor (MCFR)—is an advanced category of liquid-fueled nuclear reactor that utilizes a fast neutron spectrum and molten chloride salts acting simultaneously as the fuel carrier and the primary coolant.

Fuel Salt Matrix: Typically a binary or ternary mixture of alkaline/alkaline-earth chlorides combined with actinide chlorides, most commonly Sodium Chloride and Uranium Trichloride (NaCl-UCl) or Plutonium Trichloride (NaCl-PuCl.

Core Power: 25 kWth (Experimental) to 300 kWth (MCRE)

Depending on their design and fuel-cycle configuration, future fast-spectrum molten salt reactors could use actinides recovered from spent nuclear fuels to extract more energy from existing nuclear material and reduce the volume and longevity of waste requiring final disposal.

Some configurations could also support fuel breeding and medical isotope production, as well as advances in cutting-edge chemistry and advanced materials. These are potential future capabilities; MCRE itself will not use spent fuel, demonstrate a closed fuel cycle or test a marine reactor.

Because the fuel is dissolved in liquid chloride salt, future systems could potentially recycle long-lived and minor actinides without repeatedly manufacturing new solid fuel assemblies.

Prior Coverage on this Blog

The proposed Pelindaba facility would produce enriched uranium for advanced reactors, with TerraPower identified as a future buyer.

(Business Insider Africa) A subsidiary of Quantum Leap Energy, owned by US-listed ASP Isotopes, has signed binding Heads of Agreement with the state-owned Nuclear Energy Corporation of South Africa, known as NESA..

The proposed venture would develop uranium-enrichment facilities at Necsa’s Pelindaba nuclear research site. Quantum Leap Energy would hold approximately 80%, with Necsa holding about 20%.

The agreement promotes plans for South Africa to supply a specialized fuel needed by many next-generation reactors. It does not mean that a commercial enrichment plant is operating or that Gates has announced a new investment. TerraPower has a previous MOU with ASP regarding its uranium enrichment plans.

According to ASP Isotopes’ announcement on October 15th⁠, supply agreements with TerraPower are already in place for fuel the venture expects to produce. The statement did not disclose the project’s cost, production capacity or commissioning date.

The announcement adds proposed ownership and commercial responsibilities. Quantum Leap Energy would lead operations and arrange capital, while Necsa would provide site access and nuclear safeguards and regulatory support.

Germany Launches Program to Promote Private Investment In Fusion

(NucNet) Germany has launched a fusion milestone program with federal funding of up to €2.5 billion. The program will start with funding of €500m until 2029 under the Federal Agency for Breakthrough Innovation (Sprind) on behalf of the Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, with total public spending expected to rise to €2.5 bilion as companies meet certain technical and financial milestones. The intention is to garner further private investment as companies work towards producing a commercial scale fusion demonstration plant.

The initiative will run alongside the country’s Fusion Action Plan and Fusion 2040 plan as Germany aims to become the first country to run a fusion plant – just over three years after having shut down the last reactors in its entire commercial nuclear fleet.

The director of Sprind, Rafael Laguna de la Vera, said not all the fusion companies would be successful, but through continued innovation progress would be made.

“What matters most is measurable progress, rapid learning and a willingness to consistently reallocate resources when our own results or external developments show that our assumptions were wrong. That is why we are pursuing several approaches in parallel – knowing that not all of them will ultimately succeed. Even discontinued approaches can yield valuable technologies, insights and experience.”

Target Is Operation In 2040s

In July, Germany announced it would create three national hubs to consolidate research in fusion as the country bids to have a commercial plant operating by the 2040s. One of those hubs will be at utility major RWE’s former Biblis nuclear power station in the state of Hesse, central Germany.

Others will be at Karlsruhe, home to the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, and Garching near Munich, where Proxima Fusion is building the Alpha fusion test reactor, the first fusion test plant in Germany.

Other companies are competing for funding to support the build-out of fusion. In June, Focused Energy raised $240 million in an investment round led by RWE to support the construction of a laser fusion energy plant at Biblis.

RETHINKING RGGI NJBIA has also warned state regulators of the unintended consequences of the state being a part of RGGI.
text:
By most accounts, Alpha Generation is a remarkable energy success story in New Jersey.

It is the owner and operator of the largest fleet of power plants in the state, while also the cleanest and most efficient, compromising a total of 4,000 megawatts of baseload, mid-merit and peaking power generation.

In other words, it has helped New Jersey to be ahead of the pack in its economy-wide transition from the dirtiest fuels (i.e. no more coal plants) to a cleaner energy future.

All of which is why testimony from Liam Baker, Senior Vice President of Regulatory Affairs for AlphaGen to state regulators was so concerning on Thursday.

The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection and Board of Public Utilities (BPU) held a joint hearing to discuss the price of Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) allowances.

New Jersey is a participant in RGGI, the multi-state, cap-and-invest program designed to reduce carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions from the power sector.

But as a result of RGGI policies, New Jersey ratepayers are now paying much more because of the state’s membership in the program, and the state’s air quality is worsening – all while ahead-of-the-curve companies like AlphaGen are struggling to compete.

While applauding the Sherrill administration for hosting the hearing at a time of great energy affordability challenges, the message from Baker was clear: RGGI, in its current form, is working against New Jersey on multiple fronts.

“Unfortunately, New Jersey’s ability to deliver the electricity its people need at an affordable price is directly impacted by high RGGI clearing prices,” Baker said.

“Because these costs must be included in the price of power, we are, collectively, at a significant competitive disadvantage to coal-fueled and otherwise less efficient, and higher emitting, resources in upwind states such as Pennsylvania, West Virginia and Ohio – states that are not part of RGGI.”

PEAK LEAKAGE

As Baker explained, this is a phenomenon called “leakage.”

By being a part of RGGI, New Jersey power plants must buy allowances for their CO₂ emissions. It adds to their operating costs and, subsequently, the cost to ratepayers.

The prices for those allowances have gone up exponentially since the Garden State rejoined RGGI in 2020.

Conversely, neighboring states that are not part of RGGI (like Pennsylvania, Ohio, and West Virginia) do not face the same carbon pricing requirements for their fossil-fuel or coal-fired generators.

And because electricity is dispatched across state lines based on the cheapest available cost, power demand "leaks" away from cleaner or compliant in-state generators to dirtier out-of-state plants.

Which is completely antithetical to why New Jersey is in RGGI in the first place.

“Not only does this raise costs for New Jerseyans, but it simultaneously undermines RGGI’s greenhouse gas reduction goals by incentivizing dirtier fuels in states that are not members of RGGI - and have no intention of ever joining,” Baker said.

“Consequently, our cleaner New Jersey power plants are forced to run less than the ostensibly ‘cheaper’ upwind and higher emitting power plants in those non-RGGI states.

“In causing these cleaner plants to run less and the higher emitting and less efficient plants in upwind states to run more, RGGI has inadvertently led to New Jersey suffering from millions of tons of increased pollution every year,” he added.

RETHINKING RGGI

NJBIA has also warned state regulators of the unintended consequences of the state being a part of RGGI.

The association launched a “Rethink RGGI” awareness campaign in June to promote a potential policy solution addressing the state’s current economic and environmental challenges of participating in RGGI, with auction rates now approaching $40 per ton.

Conceding the unlikely political realities of New Jersey making a clean break from RGGI, NJBIA’s solution is to eliminate the RGGI auction allowance price and replace it with a $7-per-ton allowance charge.

NJBIA Deputy Chief Government Affairs Officer Ray Cantor said this change could annually save New Jersey consumers $279 million, provide $135 million to the state for ratepayer relief or reinvestment, and also reduce carbon emissions by 5 tons.

Assemblyman Wayne D’Angelo (D-14) has also proposed similar legislation.

“Adding to New Jersey’s affordability issue for increased climate pollution is simply not a winning or sustainable formula,” Baker said.

FUTURE INVESTMENT CHALLENGES

If New Jersey stays the course in the RGGI, without changes, the issue may get worse.

Separately, the state DEP is proposing a 90% reduction in allowances from natural gas plants over the next 10 years at a time of increased energy demand.

NJBIA Deputy Chief Government Affairs Officer Ray Cantor questioned how DEP could seek such a mandate at a time of capacity shortage for New Jersey, continuing high energy demands, and no viable replacement of clean energy.

“Governor Sherrill has called for the modernization of gas plants, but no investor will upgrade their plants to stay online when RGGI makes them non-competitive with other sources and is calling for them to reduce emissions to an extent where they can no longer operate,” Cantor said.

“RGGI can’t just operate in a vacuum. It must be reevaluated, re-thought, in the context of the region, the need for capacity, the competition from non-RGGI states, and growing demand for energy.”

And as for AlphaGen’s ask of the Sherrill administration?

“That New Jersey reconsider the impacts of the very high recent clearing prices on the cost of our domestic energy supply, the impacts on consumers and, most importantly, the increases in emissions which the state bears the brunt of being downwind of the non-RGGI states,” Baker said.

“Despite these challenges, we believe there are better paths forward for New Jersey to accomplish our shared goals of protecting consumers, supporting communities and reducing GHG emissions. We are committed to being a reliable partner in this important work.”
