Local Supply Base Expands Ahead of Vehicle Assembly

The revival of Scout Motors is bringing significant direct industrial investment to South Carolina as preparations for vehicle production accelerate. Across the state's Upstate region, seven key automotive suppliers are committing over $82 million in private capital to expand their existing facilities. This localized component supply network is designed to furnish vital body, chassis, and electronic parts for the brand's upcoming electric truck and SUV lines well before full vehicle assembly officially kicks off.

Establishing a tightly integrated supply chain adjacent to the primary assembly facility represents a strategic move in modern automotive manufacturing. Sourcing heavy assemblies and subcomponents nearby drastically reduces logistics costs, minimizes vulnerability to global shipping bottlenecks, and solidifies South Carolina's growing standing as a central hub for North American electric vehicle production.

Upstate Jobs Arrive Alongside Factory and Budget Complications

The newly announced supplier expansions will directly generate more than 200 permanent manufacturing jobs across multiple South Carolina counties. These positions range from skilled assembly technicians to component engineering roles, offering competitive wages and long-term industrial employment for local workers who are eager to participate in the region's expanding clean-energy automotive ecosystem.

However, the rapid industrial expansion required to build out the brand's main assembly footprint has created real friction within adjacent communities. As land acquisition progressed for the mega-site, the company's construction footprint displaced an elderly couple who had resided on their family property for four decades. This displacement serves as a stark reminder of the human cost that often accompanies large-scale corporate development.

Beyond community challenges, financial pressures are mounting rapidly behind the scenes. Industry reports indicate that project expenditures have resulted in massive budget overruns reaching roughly one billion dollars before a single vehicle reaches consumers. To build consumer enthusiasm despite these financial strains, the company signed a major sponsorship deal, while industry insiders continue to raise concerns over potential production delays affecting the initial launch of the Terra pickup and Traveler SUV.

Early Hype Meets the Hard Realities of Assembly

Scout's expanding footprint brings tangible economic advantages to South Carolina that cannot be overlooked. Securing 200 additional supplier jobs demonstrates that real capital is flowing into the region's manufacturing sector. This influx builds an essential operational foundation that strengthens the local industrial economy and provides viable career opportunities for skilled regional labor.

Nevertheless, launching a new automotive brand remains a brutal operational challenge regardless of corporate backing. Between skyrocketing construction budgets, community resistance, and delicate supply timing, Scout faces a steep climb. To convert initial public enthusiasm into lasting market success, the automaker must quickly move past promotional activities and execute a seamless, on-time assembly rollout.

Mobility Global data reported by Nikkei show gasoline-only cars accounted for 49% of global new-car sales in the first half of 2026. Mobility Global data put that share at 73% in 2021. Gasoline-only vehicle sales fell 10% year over year to 20.25 million vehicles.

President Donald Trump continues to promote fossil-fuel production by rolling back federal vehicle-emissions rules. Since 2025, Trump's administration has ended federal clean-vehicle tax credits. Trump's administration has also eliminated federal greenhouse-gas emissions standards, reversing important policy support for electric-vehicle adoption. The United States continues to loosen constraints on fossil-fuel use. Trump met oil and gas executives at Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate in 2024. Trump asked the executives to raise $1 billion for Trump's presidential campaign in exchange for rolling back environmental regulations and dismantling Biden administration green-energy policies.

Higher gasoline prices strengthen the economic case for electrification. Tesla offers direct investment exposure to electric-vehicle adoption. Toyota Motor offers exposure to a manufacturer with a broader mix of hybrid and conventional vehicles. Ford Motor and General Motors must balance electrification investments with the profitability of existing vehicle businesses. Rivian Automotive's vehicle sales totaled $1.14 billion in Q3, up 23% annually. However, Rivian's average selling prices slipped because commercial vans and R2 deliveries accounted for a larger share of sales.

The Global X Autonomous & Electric Vehicles ETF offers exposure to autonomous and electric-vehicle technologies. The State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF tracks the energy sector, including major oil and gas producers. BYD surpassed Tesla as the world's largest electric-vehicle maker in 2025. BYD and Tesla alternate as the quarterly leader. Nio, XPeng and Li Auto also offer investment exposure to electric vehicles, although those companies currently face slowing domestic demand.

The International Energy Agency expects electric cars to account for 29% of global sales in 2026. The forecast underscores the scale of the transition and the continued role of combustion engines. Falling gasoline-car market share is not an automatic bearish signal for oil stocks or a bullish signal for every electric-vehicle maker. Investors should monitor regional powertrain sales, automaker margins and capital spending to identify businesses that can profit from the transition. Companies that can adapt to changing consumer demand may offer the strongest investment case, regardless of Washington's energy policies.

Deal to loosen the EU’s car CO₂ standards and IAA requirements a ‘historic mistake’ that puts Europe’s position in the global EV and battery race in jeopardy.

T&E has labelled the French and German government’s agreement to weaken the EU’s car CO₂ standards and IAA requirements as a ‘historic mistake’. The agreement to allow cars assembled in the EU but built with Chinese batteries to be labeled as Made-in-EU jeopardises the entire European battery supply chain, warns T&E.

Anna Krajinska, senior director at T&E, says: “Germany and France are making a historic mistake. German and French political leaders claim they are acting to save jobs, but this may well be the deal that buries Europe’s auto industry. When drivers are facing record fuel prices and Europe’s car industry is under intense pressure from the Chinese, a deal that slows down the shift to EVs is the worst possible move.”

With fuel prices at record highs and electric cars repeatedly breaking sales records, this agreement will drastically slow down the shift to electric. T&E finds that the proposed deal would curb the supply of EVs from 57% based on today’s target 57% to 43% in 2030. The recent EV progress report by T&E shows that this will jeopardise the ability of EU carmakers to compete with Chinese rivals and remain competitive in the global EV race. Crucially for consumers it will slash the availability of cheap models coming on to the market.

“Shockingly, electric cars assembled in Europe with batteries produced in China would receive a “Made-in-EU” label. This is a scandal which will cost jobs across the European battery supply chain. The car CO2 standards and the IAA are the last chance to halt the decline of Europe’s auto manufacturing. With this agreement it is impossible to see how this will be achieved,” says Anna Krajinska.

The deal suggests sourcing just 10% of battery cells in Europe in 2028–2029, rising to 20% in 2030–2031. This weakens protections for European battery manufacturing and sets ambition well below the status quo, as over 50% of cells used in electric vehicles sold in the EU were already produced in Europe in 2025. This low threshold would destroy demand certainty for European gigafactories, putting 164 GWh of capacity at risk in 2027 and 254 GWh in 2030.

“Delaying and weakening IAA requirements for Made in EU batteries and strategic components like cathodes will have catastrophic consequences on the European battery supply chain. Sourcing requirements for EU cells and cathodes are too low and come way too late. Setting such a low bar will destroy Europe’s strategic autonomy plans once and for all.” concludes Anna Krajinska.

T&E calls on members of the European Parliament and EU governments to reject any further weakening of the car CO₂ standards and to agree to effective “Made-in-Europe” measures and ambitious electrification targets for large company car fleets, which will ensure growing demand for European battery production from 2027.

John Paul Helveston, George Washington University

(THE CONVERSATION) Within three months of the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, 2026, the average price of gasoline for American drivers climbed from US$2.94 to $4.35 a gallon. If there was ever a moment for Americans to switch to electric vehicles, this was it.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

From March to May 2026, in fact, sales of hybrid electric vehicles were 18% higher than over the same months in 2025.

But sales of fully electric vehicles were 16% lower from March to May 2026 compared with the same months in 2025. Some observers took that as evidence that high gas prices alone wouldn’t push Americans toward fully electric cars, but that conclusion misses half the story.

I study car buyers and their preferences, and there is an important distinction between what consumers want and what they can actually buy. Sales reveal what cars people actually bought, but not necessarily what they actually wanted.

When the supply of some kinds of cars can’t keep up with demand, prices rise, and that’s exactly what happened for electric vehicles in 2026.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

An industry in retreat

In 2026, hybrids and all-electric vehicles faced the same jump in demand from the oil crisis. While there were plenty of hybrids available to meet that demand, the same was not true for EVs.

Hybrid production had been growing for years, led by Toyota, which sells about half of the hybrids bought in the United States. As a result, even as sales surged, hybrid inventories on dealer lots were 19% higher in March 2026 than they had been a year earlier.

However, EV production had been in retreat since the tax and spending law President Donald Trump signed in July 2025 ended federal tax credits for EVs. Buyers had been able to get up to $7,500 for new EVs and $4,000 for used ones, but that ended after Sept. 30, 2025.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Automakers responded by cutting back their EV production. General Motors laid off more than 3,400 workers at its EV and battery plants and shifted its Tennessee plant to make batteries for energy storage, not cars. Ford wrote off $19.5 billion from its EV business, ended production of the all-electric F-150 Lightning and converted a Tennessee EV plant to build gas-powered trucks.

Buyers, for their part, rushed to beat the tax credit deadline, pushing EVs to 11.3% of new vehicle sales in September 2025. But by November 2025, after the tax credits ended, their share dropped to 4.3%.

As 2026 progressed and gas prices began to rise, so did EV demand. New EV inventories declined, shrinking from about 130 days of supply in the first quarter of 2026 to 78 days by August – just two days above the supply level of gas-burning cars.

Discounts on new EV models shrank too. My analysis of online listings from marketcheck.com shows the median new EV was listed 9.8% below sticker price in February. By April, the median discount was 6.6%, and 4.7% in June. That’s a sign that dealers saw rising demand, not inventory to clear.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

A run on used electric vehicles

Before the war, prices for used electric vehicles were still drifting down in the wake of the expired used EV federal tax credit. After the war began, they climbed 13% through late June 2026. For a typical used electric vehicle, that’s about $3,500 more.

Other data sources point in the same direction. Recurrent, a company that reports on batteries and used EVs, found that the price of a used 2023 Chevrolet Bolt rose almost 20% from January to June 2026.

And inventories of used electric vehicles dropped too, with only 31 days of supply in May, 23% below the year before.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

A costly misreading

None of this means the electric vehicle market is healthy. High prices and uncertain access to charging stations are real stumbling blocks for people who are thinking about buying an EV.

But the data doesn’t support the claim that electric vehicle sales stalled in 2026 because Americans don’t want them. Rather, the sales stalled because there weren’t enough EVs available to buy – and there were plenty of hybrids as an alternative.

The distinction matters because automakers have treated a change in the policy landscape as a change in consumer demand, leading to shortages with real costs.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The average new car now sells for about $50,000 and the average new electric vehicle for about $55,000, according to Kelley Blue Book, a company that tracks car prices.

The current situation leaves drivers exposed to the volatility of oil prices with fewer alternatives. The U.S. is the world’s largest oil producer, yet a war in the Persian Gulf raised gas prices significantly in just three months. Oil trades on a global market, so American drivers pay global prices.

Seven months into the war, the pressure on drivers is still going full throttle. Oil was still above $100 a barrel in mid-October, and diesel hit a record $6.52 a gallon on Sept. 22.

Electric vehicle sales haven’t caught up. Argonne’s data show 86,000 of them sold in August, fewer than the 101,000 sold in May, while hybrid sales stayed above 216,000 a month all summer.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

A look ahead

Rather than move to increase electric vehicle supply and make them more affordable, federal policy continues to hinder the U.S. electric vehicle sector.

The fuel economy rule released Sept. 28, 2026, loosens efficiency requirements for gas-powered vehicles and in 2028 ends a system that let automakers that beat the standards – mostly EV makers – earn credits for exceeding them and sell those to automakers that fell short. That means automakers will have fewer regulatory incentives to produce EVs going forward.

Regulators say buyers will save $1,289 on the purchase price of a new gas-powered vehicle from reduced engineering and manufacturing costs to make less efficient engines. But the same analysis estimates drivers will spend about $1,600 more on gas over the life of the car, and that’s using fuel price forecasts well below today’s prices. Economists say the administration’s math does not properly account for those fuel costs.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The U.S. has also effectively shut out Chinese automakers, even though nearly three-quarters of the world’s electric cars are built in China. In 2024, Chinese car buyers could choose from over 130 EV models priced under $40,000; American buyers had just four EV models under that threshold. Beyond tariffs of more than 100% on EVs made in China, a Commerce Department rule bars cars from Chinese-linked automakers starting with model year 2027, even if they are built in the U.S. A bill pending in Congress would widen the ban, blocking Chinese investment in U.S. auto factories altogether.

As long as gas stays expensive, the gap between the electric vehicles Americans want and the electric vehicles dealers can sell them is likely to remain. Decisions such as ending the tax credit, rolling back fuel economy standards and banning Chinese technology all make it harder to build them, which means Americans will continue to have fewer affordable electric vehicles to choose from.

text:
If it seemed like Teslas and Cybertrucks were taking over Austin, you weren't imagining things.

Thousands of Tesla owners rolled into town for the X Takeover, a gathering organized around the Tesla Owners Club of Austin and its Silicon Valley counterpart. The event brought fans together at Tesla's Giga Texas factory for a celebration of the brand, its technology, and the people who drive its vehicles.

“This is a gathering to show your support of Tesla, to have community, to really just get together and enjoy each other's company,” said Matt Holm, president of the Tesla Owners Club of Austin.

The guest list included some familiar names, including Elon Musk's mother, Maye Musk, and rapper Nicki Minaj.

But for many owners, the real stars were the vehicles themselves — and the technology powering them.

Full Self-Driving takes center stage

Tesla's Full Self-Driving (FSD) technology was a major topic of conversation among owners eager to see how far the company's driver-assistance systems have come.

Holm said he uses the system daily and believes it has made a meaningful difference for his family.

“You're really driving a robot,” Holm said. He added that he purchased a Tesla for his parents, ages 85 and 83, who had difficulty driving at night.

He said the system has helped them get back behind the wheel after dark.

Tesla's Full Self-Driving system is designed to assist with driving tasks, but it still requires an attentive driver who is responsible for the vehicle.

A long wait for the Cybertruck pays off

For Harry Concepcion, the event offered a chance to see the factory where his long-awaited Cybertruck was built.

Concepcion flew in from San Jose, California, after placing his order in 2019. He finally took delivery of the electric pickup in 2024.

“I ordered a Cybertruck in 2019, took delivery of it in 2024,” he said.

At Giga Texas, Concepcion got to see the Cybertruck production line firsthand.

He said watching the manufacturing process gave him a new appreciation for the role automation plays in building the vehicles.

“I got to see the Cybertruck production line, and just seeing just how they're built — it's fascinating seeing the role that automation has played in the manufacture of these vehicles,” Concepcion said.

For some owners, it's about the car, not the CEO

Tesla's passionate fan base comes with a complicated reality: Not everyone who likes the company's vehicles is a fan of CEO Elon Musk.

Marla Smith, vice president of the North Texas Tesla Owners Club, said she can appreciate the cars while separating them from the public figure behind the company.

“So I'm loyal to the brand because I drive a Tesla and not an Elon Musk,” Smith said.

She explained that she bought her Tesla before Musk became as vocal in public as he is today.

“I separate the person from the car,” she said, adding that she considers Musk a genius but views the vehicle and its CEO separately.

Her perspective reflects a distinction some owners make between their enthusiasm for Tesla's technology and their feelings about its leadership.

More than a parking lot full of Teslas

The X Takeover was a high-profile gathering at a factory that has become central to Tesla's presence in the Austin area.

The vehicles and technology drew owners from across the country, but the event also offered something harder to measure: a sense of community among people who share an interest in electric vehicles and innovation.

For the thousands who showed up, the X Takeover was about more than Teslas and Cybertrucks. It was a chance to meet fellow owners, see how the vehicles are made, and celebrate the technology that brought them together.

title: Three Data Centers Could Undo the Millions El Paso and New Mexico Spent on their Climate Plans
description:
Twenty miles away in El Paso, construction is underway on another massive data center, this one built by Meta Platforms.
A third, larger data center project is planned less than a 30-minute drive from the Meta site, on the Fort Bliss Army post in east El Paso.
New Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva, a Democrat, represents the community of Chaparral, directly across the state line from Meta’s data center site in northeast El Paso.
Comparatively, the region spanning El Paso County and neighboring Hudspeth County released 8.4 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2019.
The Meta power plant in El Paso could release up to 1.3 million tons of climate emissions every year, according to an estimate calculated by El Paso Matters based on El Paso Electric regulatory filings and the Environmental Protection Agency’s emissions factors.
text:
Last December, New Mexico officials celebrated publication of a plan to address climate change, designed to dramatically reduce the state’s greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. A few months later, just across the state line in Texas, El Paso city officials adopted their own such plan with a similar ambition.

Each report cost millions of dollars to draft, but neither one took into account how the construction of data centers could upend climate goals in both places.

Work is underway in Doña Ana County in southern New Mexico on one of the largest data center developments in the country: Project Jupiter, built by Austin-based Oracle. Twenty miles away in El Paso, construction is underway on another massive data center, this one built by Meta Platforms.

A third, larger data center project is planned less than a 30-minute drive from the Meta site, on the Fort Bliss Army post in east El Paso.

The data centers are “going to undo a lot of the very expensive and very meaningful work a lot of people are doing,” New Mexico state climatologist Dave DuBois told El Paso Matters.

The sites are among a wave of data centers under construction across the country, driven by the rapidly escalating demand for artificial intelligence services like Claude and ChatGPT. Such projects have drawn intense scrutiny in recent months, as residents and elected officials have questioned their impact on communities’ water supplies, household electric bills and air quality. Texas alone has 596 data centers that are either in operation or planned across Texas as of early September, according to research by The Texas Tribune.

But the projects located in this population center of 1.2 million, which encompasses El Paso and parts of southern New Mexico, are particularly notable because of their combined scope. When fully built out, the three data centers, each with its own power plant, will emit millions of tons of greenhouse gas emissions, equivalent to the planet-warming emissions released by more than two million cars in a year.

They will also release air pollutants like particulate matter and nitrogen oxides, which directly affect local air quality and human health. The Meta and Project Jupiter data centers are expected to release these kinds of pollutants at relatively low levels, according to paperwork submitted to state regulators. But even a small increase in air pollution can still negatively impact communities close to and downwind of the data center sites, said Shaolei Ren, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at University of California, Riverside.

“The health impacts can be significant for local communities,” Ren said.

Because Project Jupiter, Meta, and the Fort Bliss data centers are in two different states, and because there is no single federal regulation governing climate change or emissions, regulators have largely considered the projects’ impacts separately.

“We’ve never had a national climate law passed by Congress,” said Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School.

“And so what we’ve had in this country are primarily state and local efforts.”

The result is that officials in one state have little say over a project happening minutes away from them.

Texas and New Mexico also take different approaches to dealing with climate change. New Mexico has codified greenhouse gas reduction targets into state law; Texas has not.

New Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva, a Democrat, represents the community of Chaparral, directly across the state line from Meta’s data center site in northeast El Paso. Her state has the power to regulate air quality and impose noise requirements, but only in New Mexico, not at a Texas construction site, even if it’s only a few hundred yards away.

Likewise, residents living in west El Paso across the state line from Project Jupiter have no say in the project despite sharing an aquifer that crosses the state boundary. Emissions do not remain within the state where they originate, Silva said.

“This is why we need federal regulation,” said Silva. “How do we knit something together that makes sense for our region when actually this is the job of the federal government?”

Though they profess a desire to mitigate the impacts of climate change, local governments in El Paso and Doña Ana counties green-lit these projects in a part of the country seeing rapidly rising temperatures. The counties offered Meta and Project Jupiter tax incentives in exchange for corporate investment in their communities, job creation and, hopefully, the ability to attract more technology companies to the region.

State officials have also provided incentives. More than a decade ago, Texas legislators approved a data center sales tax break, which exempts the facilities from paying sales tax on equipment they purchase, a decision that could now cost the state $3.2 billion in revenue over the next two years, according to The Texas Tribune.

New Mexico lawmakers declined to advance a bill creating a similar tax break for data centers in 2021. But in 2025, they passed an unrelated law allowing large facilities such as Project Jupiter to generate their own electricity using natural gas. The law exempts these private power systems, known as microgrids, from renewable energy requirements, even as New Mexico requires electric utilities to source 50% of the power they sell from clean energy by 2030.

The power plants that keep data centers running typically produce large amounts of emissions like carbon dioxide and methane that drive global climate change over time. Combined, the plants proposed for Project Jupiter and Meta’s data center could emit up to 10 million tons of planet-warming emissions annually. Comparatively, the region spanning El Paso County and neighboring Hudspeth County released 8.4 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2019. (The Army has shared scant information about the Fort Bliss data center, so it’s not clear what level of emissions the facility will produce.)

“This does add to our greenhouse gas emissions in a massive way,” said Gunnar Schade, an associate professor of atmospheric sciences at Texas A&M University.

“This is a huge source.”

An Unprecedented Amount of Energy

Silva, the New Mexico representative, was initially supportive of Project Jupiter, in part seeing it as an opportunity to create long-term jobs. Last year, she voted in favor of a bill that included an amendment — tacked on by state Sen. Michael Padilla, a Democrat from Albuquerque — that allows facilities like Project Jupiter, which aren’t connected to the local power grid, a 20-year exemption from clean energy laws, allowing them to generate all their electricity with fossil fuels.

“We worked this bill pretty much the entire session, but it did not quite get done. So, we found a piece of legislation that was very similar,” Padilla said in an interview last year.

“That’s the legislative process. You have to be very creative to get your work done.”

But Silva soon soured on the project out of concern that it won’t employ enough local workers and because it won’t rely on zero-emission renewable energy. Oracle has said the data center will have 750 full-time employees when it’s up and running. The company told Doña Ana County officials in early September that nearly 3,700 people had worked at the site during construction up to that point.

Silva and other state lawmakers have said they voted for Padilla’s bill without realizing the broader implications for a data center project in the southern part of the state.

“State regulators, state legislators, I think, were so caught off guard at the speed at which these hyperscale data centers showed up in all of our communities almost simultaneously,” Silva said.

“I would support a moratorium.”

The amount of energy Project Jupiter needs is unprecedented in the region: The data center will receive electricity from an on-site power plant made up of fuel cells built by a company called Bloom Energy. Bloom has said the plant will have the ability to produce up to 2.45 gigawatts of electricity — enough to power around 1.5 million homes and more than El Paso Electric has ever supplied to its 465,000 residential and commercial customers at one time, according to the utility’s corporate reports.

New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat, has specifically lauded Oracle’s promise to use fuel cells for electricity instead of natural gas turbines, which would have used more water and produced more air pollution. However, an air permit — a state-granted license that authorizes industrial facilities to emit a predetermined amount of pollution — would allow the fuel cells to produce up to 8.8 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions per year. Lujan Grisham didn’t address questions from El Paso Matters about the impact of these additional climate emissions.

The Meta power plant in El Paso could release up to 1.3 million tons of climate emissions every year, according to an estimate calculated by El Paso Matters based on El Paso Electric regulatory filings and the Environmental Protection Agency’s emissions factors.

Nancy L. Seidman, a senior adviser with the Regulatory Assistance Project, a nonpartisan nonprofit focused on energy policy, confirmed the emissions estimate is sound.

“Regulators should weigh all emissions and other impacts like water usage, noise and local air pollution, which can affect public health, when they make decisions about data center projects,” Seidman wrote in an email to El Paso Matters.

“This is particularly important when projects are phased over time, so that an accurate account can be made of the total, holistic impacts.”

The data center planned for Fort Bliss is expected to use 3 gigawatts of electricity that would likely be supplied by natural gas turbines, according to officials with the Department of Defense, who shared details with reporters during a briefing in April. The Army has issued few other details about the project because it is still in “exclusive negotiations” with the developer, Carlyle Group, a large publicly traded private equity firm.

Carlyle Group did not respond to a request for comment.

“These are cities in terms of their electricity consumption,” Peskoe, of Harvard Law School, said of AI hyperscale data center campuses such as Oracle’s and Meta’s. The facilities are cropping up so fast that “the pace of this and the scale of this — I think there’s no real parallel, at least for 50, 60, 70 years, but probably ever for the U.S. power industry.”

Facilities in New Mexico seeking a state air permit are required by law to disclose estimated amounts of air pollutants and greenhouse gas emissions the project will release. And the state Environment Department has spent months evaluating Project Jupiter’s air permit application, which was submitted in April. A spokesperson for the environmental department didn’t respond to emailed questions.

By contrast, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality only requires project developers to disclose information about pollutants that affect local air quality, and not about greenhouse gas emissions, which are what contribute to climate change.

So when El Paso Electric sought an air permit last fall for the Meta data center’s natural gas power plant, the utility didn’t have to share estimated greenhouse gas emissions. The Texas commission approved the permit 20 days after it was filed, following an expedited review.

Meta directed questions about its data center’s power plant to El Paso Electric. The electric company declined to share estimates of the plant’s greenhouse gas emissions but said in a statement that the Texas environmental commission had reviewed and authorized the Meta power plant “under a standard permit, which is specifically for projects with limited and well-controlled emissions.” The statement said the facility will “operate in compliance with state and federal standards.”

A spokesperson for the agency said, “All Standard Permits have gone through formal notice and comment procedures and have been adopted by the Commission in a public meeting.”

These plants will be releasing large amounts of greenhouse gases even as climate change has become increasingly evident in the El Paso metro area, which sits where Texas’ westernmost boundary meets New Mexico and northern Mexico.

El Paso’s temperatures have risen faster than those of almost any other city in the U.S. since 1970, according to Climate Central, a nonprofit that quantifies climate shifts throughout the United States.

Drought driven by climate change has amplified the impact of wind storms that fill the air in El Paso with hazardous dust in the spring and summertime.

This year has been the hottest on record in El Paso through the first nine months of 2026, according to the National Weather Service. Similar records have been set across the state line in New Mexico.

“If we started to do these kinds of things — having big data centers with natural-gas-fired turbines — it’s kind of like bringing back a lot of the retired plants that were more dirty, like coal,” said DuBois, the New Mexico state climatologist.

Fernando Berjano, El Paso’s climate coordinator, wouldn’t comment specifically on effects resulting from the data centers in the region, but he said the kinds of power plants tied to them produce greenhouse gases that will make it harder for the city to meet its climate goals, as well as produce air pollutants.

If emissions increase in the El Paso area, “that has an impact on air quality, that has an impact on pollution,” Berjano said, “which is something that we all know is not good.”

The Road Ahead for Data Centers

Although construction is already underway on the Project Jupiter and Meta data centers, regulatory hurdles remain for both facilities. The public hearing on the Project Jupiter air permit was scheduled to begin Sept. 14, but the New Mexico Supreme Court delayed it when opponents filed lawsuits challenging the state’s approval process and the facility’s use of groundwater.

The state Supreme Court last month lifted the stay. New Mexico more recently appointed an examiner to preside over the hearing that would authorize the facility’s emissions. Other legal challenges are making their way through the court system.

In Texas, El Paso Electric is still waiting for the state’s Public Utility Commission to approve construction of the power plant planned next to Meta’s data center, a decision that could come later this year.

Officials with both Project Jupiter and Meta have said they are taking steps to help mitigate the climate effects of their projects and plan to develop clean energy projects elsewhere to create new electricity sources and offset the greenhouse gases their data center power plants will release. Oracle also maintains that its emissions will be lower than what it sought in its air permit application and that it plans to get to net zero greenhouse emissions by 2031.

“Oracle is committed to building Project Jupiter responsibly and incorporating community feedback into our planning,” the company said in a statement.

The road ahead for data centers is unclear. Even once-supportive officials have softened or changed course: Last year, Lujan Grisham, New Mexico’s governor, said Project Jupiter “reaffirms New Mexico’s leadership in global trade, advanced manufacturing, and digital infrastructure.” In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott at one point called his state “the epicenter of AI development.”

Now, amid growing opposition to Project Jupiter, Lujan Grisham recently said she takes seriously residents’ concerns about the data center “and expects any data center operating in New Mexico to meet the state’s rigorous environmental standards and use water responsibly.”

This summer, Abbott called on the Texas Public Utility Commission to ensure the projects pay for their own infrastructure and don’t lead to higher electricity costs for residents. He also recommended the state Legislature pass a number of regulations related to data centers next year, many concerning water and electricity usage, and recently told the Texas Water Development Board to penalize data centers that do not report their water usage.

Abbott’s new edicts do not address air pollution or climate change, nor the effects that a data center project in one state can have on another.

Texas Democratic state Rep. Joe Moody, whose district includes much of west and northeast El Paso, near two of the data center projects, said Abbott’s proposals will likely shape the Texas Legislature’s debate over data-center-related policies next year but called them just a starting point.

“In the governor’s directives, we’re not talking about local control and local autonomy to make decisions on these projects,” he said. “And I do think that that’s a whole other lane of conversation that we’re going to get into next session.”

text:
The Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE) launched a grant program to replace diesel trucks with electric vehicles.

The new 2026 Michigan Clean Heavy-Duty Vehicle (CHDV) Program will provide funding to replace eligible Class 6 (19,501-26,000 pounds) and Class 7 (26,001-33,000 pounds) diesel refuse and recycling vehicles with new, zero-emission battery electric vehicles and associated charging equipment.

According to state officials, the program aims to reduce diesel emissions, improve air quality, protect public health, and help fleets modernize their operations with advanced heavy-duty vehicle technologies.

Local: FEMA grant of $131,000 to train firefighters across Berrien County and beyond

Since diesel refuse and recycling trucks operate daily in neighborhoods, often at low speeds, they are among the largest contributors of localized air pollution, according to a release from EGLE.

Trucks eligible for replacement include large, heavy-duty diesel trucks commonly used for trash collection, recycling, composting, and food waste recovery. Both private and public vehicles in the state are eligible to apply.

Roughly $4.29 million is expected to be made available through the grant program, according to EGLE. Awards are expected to range from $100,000 to $1 million, with a cap of $260,000 per vehicle.

State: Michigan DNR seeks bear den reports as black bears prepare to hibernate across the state

Recipients of the grant must provide a minimum 50% cost match of total project costs. Awards will be given on a reimbursement basis. The deadline for submitting payment requests is Dec. 15, 2028.

text:
Midstream companies are advancing new storage and pipeline projects along the Gulf Coast as a wave of LNG and power developments drives expectations for sharply higher natural gas demand over the coming decade, speakers said Oct. 14 at the Gulf Coast Energy Forum in New Orleans.

But analysts and some of the developers behind those projects said the industry’s infrastructure buildout may still struggle to keep pace with expected demand growth.

“We need more storage,” ConocoPhillips analyst James Pearson said, adding natural gas markets are becoming more volatile as demand growth continues to outpace development of the supporting infrastructure. “And we need more interstate pipelines.”

Gulf Coast LNG feedgas demand is expected to rise to about 35 Bcf/d by 2031, more than double 2025 levels, according to S&P Global Energy CERA’s latest North American gas outlook. LNG exports are expected to account for roughly 80% of the region’s projected demand growth over the period.

That growth is increasing the value of storage, which gives LNG exporters a place to temporarily hold gas when maintenance, operational problems, severe weather or other disruptions reduce feedgas demand.

Developers said the changing market is already reshaping investment decisions across the Gulf Coast.

“The need for storage has changed,” Enbridge’s Elizabeth Perez, director of business development, said. “It’s not a seasonal need anymore. It’s not just the marketers participating. You have LNG players participating in a big way.”

Enbridge is expanding storage capacity at its Tres Palacios, Moss Bluff and Egan facilities while also marketing the proposed Katy-to-Gillis Expansion Project, which could provide up to 2 Bcf/d of transportation capacity from the Katy Hub to growing demand centers in southwest Louisiana.

The project is being developed in coordination with the Mustang Express Pipeline, whose planned Cougar Lateral would connect Tres Palacios Gas Storage to Katy Hub.

It is among several intended to link growing Permian gas production and Gulf Coast storage capacity to downstream demand across the US Gulf Coast.

Fellow developer Gulf Coast Midstream Partners is also marketing capacity at its proposed Nash Storage Hub in Texas, targeting demand from power generators, LNG facilities and other consumers in the region. The project’s first phase would provide 23 Bcf of working gas capacity, along with 900 MMcf/d of injection capacity and 1.5 Bcf/d of withdrawal capacity.

The Nash hub would be the first new salt-cavern natural gas storage project developed on the Texas Gulf Coast in about two decades, Gulf Coast Midstream Partners CEO Edmund Knolle said.

“Salt cavern storage has been very slow to catch up to the growing market,” Knolle said. “And even with the expansions — the real expansions that are out there — we’re not going to be keeping up by 2030.”

East Daley Analytics analyst Jack Weixel said storage could become particularly valuable as LNG export volumes increase, pointing to the potential impact for a major Gulf Coast hurricane to knock LNG export terminals concentrated in the region offline.

name: Clean Energy
title: 6 threats to public lands in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act
description:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is presented as a false choice between building renewable energy and protecting public lands, cultural resources, and the public’s ability to engage on what impacts shared landscapes.
These tradeoffs are neither necessary nor acceptable—under this administration or any future administration.
The Wilderness Society has grave concerns about the provisions that threaten public lands listed below and calls on Congress to fix them: 1.
Participation in public lands management decisions ensures our shared lands serve the common good rather than private interests.
2215 is an unprecedented giveaway of public lands to the mining industry.
text:
The United States can and must reach a clean energy future as soon as possible. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is presented as a false choice between building renewable energy and protecting public lands, cultural resources, and the public’s ability to engage on what impacts shared landscapes. These tradeoffs are neither necessary nor acceptable—under this administration or any future administration. We can move toward a clean energy future while ensuring that America’s public lands, waters, and wildlife habitat are not sacrificed for future generations, and that is the standard elected officials should insist on as well.

This bill would:

Lock in drilling and mining projects making it impossible for future administrations to correct permits, even if they are unlawful;

Weaken public participation in decisions affecting shared lands;

Erode Tribal consultation and Tribal sovereignty while threatening sacred sites and cultural resources;

Limit judicial review and make unlawful projects harder to correct in court; and

Expand industry access to public lands without adequate safeguards.

It is necessary to view this bill in the broader context of escalating threats to public lands and waters, wildlife, Tribes and communities, and the agencies responsible for managing them:

The fossil fuel industry is already benefiting from the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and multiple recent rollbacks and revisions of common-sense reforms that better balanced public lands values with energy development, including the Public Lands Rule and Oil and Gas Leasing Rule.

Counter to the public’s wishes, the Administration has stripped protections from and already granted hardrock mining and fossil fuel industries the green light to mine and drill some of our most iconic public landscapes, including the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, the Arctic, Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument and Bears Ears National Monument and the Greater Chaco Region.

Federal agencies that would be responsible for meeting the deadlines in the bill are decimated – recent layoffs and forced early retirements mean there’s limited staff to review permits, consult with Tribes and communities, enforce safeguards, and follow through with the bill’s new requirements. And a provision in the bill would force the government to pay companies for missed deadlines, even if they missed them because of lack of staffing.

The Wilderness Society has grave concerns about the provisions that threaten public lands listed below and calls on Congress to fix them:

1. Sec. 1401 is the final nail in the coffin for threatened landscapes.

This section bans future administrations from taking any action on permitted projects on public lands, even when permits were approved unlawfully, except under extremely limited circumstances. This means permanently entrenching drilling and mining projects on public landscapes that are currently targeted for shortsighted, corporate control. This includes the Greater Chaco Canyon region, Bears Ears National Monument and Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument, the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, the Arctic, all national public lands in the lower 48 that are currently available to oil and gas leasing, and increasingly, data center construction. Simply put, the “project certainty” provision in this bill would wedge the door open for these cherished landscapes to be permanently developed and exploited.

While entrenching existing sell-outs of treasured landscapes, this section also further emboldens the current administration to make reckless, unlawful decisions over the next two-plus years that hand over even more public lands to drilling and mining, while also restricting access to the courts and limiting the ability of the public and public interest organizations like TWS to challenge unlawful project decisions.

2. Div. A, Title I enacts sweeping changes to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), harming the public interest and disregarding the voices and welfare of communities.

Participation in public lands management decisions ensures our shared lands serve the common good rather than private interests. Since 2025, the administration and Congress have weakened transparency and narrowed the ability of local communities and Tribes to raise concerns about projects that affect their lands, waters, cultural resources and health. Simply put: This bill’s proposed changes to NEPA effectively turn the bedrock environmental law into a dead letter.

The bill provides broad loopholes for actions that would no longer be subject to NEPA and eliminates meaningful judicial review (and therefore government accountability) for communities that seek to challenge agency decisions. If this bill becomes law, most public land management decisions will go under the radar, and communities will be severely limited in their ability to comment on or oppose them. New science and research that could have informed a project will not be considered after the publication of a notice of intent. And communities will have to conform to stricter standards to prove harm from a project and challenge decisions in court.

3. Sec. 2301 threatens cultural resources and historic sites by drastically undermining the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA).

This bill is not only an affront to Tribal sovereignty, but it would also directly threaten sacred sites and cultural resources across ancestral lands. Places of cultural significance like Chaco Canyon or Bears Ears National Monument would be at risk. For example, under these new standards, negative impacts from oil and gas rigs or mines on the border of protected areas would not be considered a direct harm.

This section proposes to rewrite the provision that is used to identify historic places, consult with Tribal Nations and affected communities, consider alternatives, and seek ways to avoid, minimize, or mitigate harm before federal undertakings move forward.

It would make consultation with Tribes and communities optional, arbitrarily restrict what is considered an important cultural site, allow more projects to skip review and require fewer environmental impacts to be taken into consideration.

Taken together, these changes would restrict the power of Tribal Nations and communities to define the places that matter to them, silencing those who should have a voice in decisions that impact their lands. Congress must heed the call of Tribes and Indigenous groups speaking out against these provisions.

4. Sec. 2215 is an unprecedented giveaway of public lands to the mining industry.

The bill closely reflects the Mining Regulatory and Clarity Act (MRCA) and would reverse over a century of public land law precedent and severely undermine the federal government’s ability to safeguard cultural, environmental, water, and economic resources. Similar to the MRCA, the bill would allow companies to occupy and industrialize vast areas of public land, including waste dumps and infrastructure, without holding valid mineral rights, paying royalties or undergoing rigorous environmental review. It would shut out competing uses such as recreation, renewable energy and cultural preservation.

The bill also would codify a dangerous loophole that prioritizes private mining interests over public good, threatens Indigenous lands and ecosystems and burdens underfunded federal agencies without providing resources or accountability. This bill opens the floodgates to unchecked exploitation of public lands.

5. Sec. 1402 bans the ability to pause projects such as data centers on public lands for better analysis of impacts to communities and natural and cultural resources.

This section gives a developer the ability to sue the administration if a project approval is taking too long. The provision could be weaponized against a future administration that might try to deprioritize harmful development like fossil fuel projects or data centers. It would also seemingly make it impossible to put forward a pause or moratorium on an activity, even if the pause would only be to allow time for closer review of potential impacts. For example, it would have prevented the pause on offshore drilling permits and development following the Deepwater Horizon oil spill and the coal leasing moratorium enacted by the Obama administration, and could block a future moratorium on data centers on public lands. At a time when the public and local officials are clamoring for transparency and input into the rapid buildout of data centers across the country, this provision runs counter to the moratorium TWS has called for from the administration.

6. Sec. 2211 eliminates landowner and public input opportunities for imminent drilling projects on split estate properties.

This section takes this assault to public input a step further by exempting hundreds of thousands potentially millions—of acres of split-estate lands from the federal permitting process, eliminating key public input opportunities that are currently often the only way neighbors and landowners know drilling is imminent. This also eliminates a key federal decision point where BLM can make sure an operator’s bond can fully cover the costs of reclaiming the well when production ends. In short, this provision could grow our national tally of orphaned and abandoned wells that leech into our rivers and streams and leak methane into our atmosphere.

Overall Takeaway: The irreversible destruction these provisions would cause to treasured places like the Arctic, the Boundary Waters, Bears Ears, and Chaco is simply not a reasonable or necessary tradeoff.

Congress must eliminate or significantly amend these provisions before advancing this legislation.

description: TORONTO - Tesla says it is pausing orders for its Chinese-made sedan Model 3 Premium in Canada, citing a high demand for the vehicle that used up its import quota
text:
EDMONTON - An online user claimed on social media that Alber…

EDMONTON - Supporters of Alberta's separatist movement have …



A Tesla Model 3 charges at a Tesla supercharging station situated in the parking lot of an outlet mall Wednesday, Sept. 25, 2024, in Lakewood, Colo. (AP Photo/David Zalubowski)

TORONTO - Tesla says it is pausing orders for its Chinese-made sedan Model 3 Premium in Canada, citing a high demand for the vehicle that used up its import quota from China. Statistics from the federal government show that the overall quota for 49,000 imported Chinese electrical vehicles during the 12 months beginning March 1 has not been used up.

A banner appearing on top of Tesla's website for its Model 3 claims that orders for the Premium version of the car are paused after "high demand exhausted Tesla's import quota," alluding to the government of Canada's partnership with China to import 49,000 electric vehicles a year at a lower tariff of 6.1 per cent from the previous 100 per cent.

The banner added: "Ordering resumes if Govt of Canada issues more quota, expected March 2027."

Its Model 3 Performance vehicles, which are more expensive than Premium, are still available to Canadians.

The federal government in January reached a deal with Beijing to slash tariffs on 49,000 Chinese EVs in exchange for China dropping duties on canola seeds.

That brought tariffs back down to single digits from 100 per cent duties on Chinese EVs imposed in late 2024 . Back then, former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s government had argued cheap, heavily subsidized EVs being sold in the North American market constituted a threat to the auto sector.

The quota for 49,000 EVs is split up in two six-month periods : March 1 to Aug. 31, 2026, and Sept. 1,  2026 to Feb. 28, 2027. The first period allotted 24,500 units, while the current period would allow 24,500 units plus any unused units from the previous period, according to the federal Department of Global Affairs.

During the first six months, Global Affairs Canada says 15,603 electric vehicles were imported from China. That means 8,897 units will roll over in the current period, increasing the quota for the second half to 33,397 units.

The quota was implemented on a first-come, first-served basis for an initial period of six months . It is not clear whether the program is still running on a first-come, first-served basis, and Global Affairs did not immediately respond to questions about the timeline.

For the month of September, only 328 Chinese EVs were imported, according to Global Affairs .

Global Affairs spokesperson Rachael Dolan said in an email the agency does not disclose the names of companies or details of any shipments, "including anticipated quota use, due to commercial confidentiality considerations."

But Prime Minister Mark Carney has said most Chinese EVs entering Canada are Teslas. "Historically, they're all Teslas. It looks like most of the ones that'll come in are Teslas as well in the short term," he said at the Economic Club of New York on May 28 .

Daniel Ross, director of strategic market insights at auto data tracking company Canadian Black Book, estimated 97 per cent of all Chinese vehicles that were imported this year were Teslas.

The company's data showed 259 Lincoln Nautilus Hybrids, 18 Lotus Eletres and an estimated 200 Polestar 2s were shipped between March and September 2026. The remainder were estimated to be Teslas, he said. It's unclear how many of those were Tesla Model 3 Premiums.

Tesla did not respond to questions about the pause.

Tesla already had a strong presence for its Chinese EVs, even before Ottawa allowed them in Canada — and before the federal government imposed the 100 per cent tariff.

A 2024 RBC report shows total EV imports from China amounted to $2.3 billion, or 13.3 per cent of total imports in 2023, a massive increase from $116 million in 2022 .

Tesla manufactures Model 3 and Model Y vehicles at its Gigafactory Shanghai plant, which has a capacity to produce about 950,000 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles a year, while its California plant produces about 550,000 vehicles, according to Tesla's second-quarter 2026 update .

In Canada, the starting price for the Chinese-made Model 3 Premium is close to $40,000, and many vehicles started arriving in full flow this summer, according to DesRosiers Automotive Consultants Inc.'s September auto sales report.

Prices are significantly lower compared to the $73,000 starting price for the Model 3 Performance, according to Tesla's website.

In the second year of the EV tariff deal, 10 per cent of the quota will be reserved for vehicles under $35,000. Tesla does not have EVs under $35,000 at the moment.

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

October 16, 2026

Environmental Rules Board & IDEM Act to Lift Fuel Restrictions, Reduce Red Tape for Indiana Fire Departments

INDIANAPOLIS – Indiana’s Environmental Rules Board voted this week to advance two actions aimed at lifting costly fuel restrictions on Hoosiers and cutting administrative hurdles for fire departments across the state. In the first action, the board voted to permanently suspend low Reid vapor pressure (LRVP) fuel requirements for residents in Clark and Floyd counties, who had been subject to the more stringent gasoline standard for decades.

Separately, the board voted to amend Indiana’s open burning rule to exempt certain state fire agencies and the Indiana Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from seeking prior authorization from IDEM for training related burn exercises.

“From the start of my administration, we looked for ways to remove unnecessary government burdens on Hoosiers and places we can cut the red tape,” said Gov. Mike Braun. “These steps strike the right balance between ensuring meaningful environmental protection and improving government efficiency.”

Low Reid Vapor pressure requirements

Existing requirements for LRVP gasoline are only in effect for Clark and Floyd counties in Indiana during the summer ozone season, a 1995 measure originally adopted to meet Clean Air Act requirements for the Louisville Metropolitan Area. However, advances in vehicle technologies and changes in engine and fuel standards have made the emissions benefits from LRVP negligible, while continuing to pass the added cost of non-conventional fuel onto consumers.

LRVP gasoline typically increases prices by 10 to 20 cents per gallon. Eliminating this requirement could save Indiana residents between $2.5 and $5.1 million during a single summer fuel season, according to an evaluation by IDEM’s Office of Air Quality.

Earlier this year, the U.S. EPA lifted LRVP requirements in Kentucky, effectively eliminating the special fuel standard used in the Louisville area. Because LRVP was embedded in Indiana’s rules and State Implementation Plan, IDEM was required to complete a formal rulemaking to repeal the requirement.

Open Burning for Fire Training Purposes

IDEM initiated rulemaking to add an exemption to Indiana’s open burning rule (326 IAC 4-1-3) allowing certain fire agencies to conduct open burning for fire training without obtaining prior authorization from IDEM. This update aligns Indiana’s rules with statutory changes enacted by the General Assembly in 2025.

The exemption enables fire departments and the Indiana Department of Homeland Security to carry out essential training burns without going through the one time approval process for each event or, in the case of DHS' mobile burn demonstration unit, seeking multi-year authorizations.

By reducing paperwork and clearing administrative delays, the rule gives firefighters greater flexibility to conduct the hands on training they need to keep communities safe.

Other Agency Updates

IDEM senior leadership also provided updates on recent agency activities, including numerous recent comments and engagement on federal environmental comment periods on rulemakings.

This week, IDEM provided direct correspondence to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin concerning Indiana’s progress in improving water quality and the importance of ensuring federal oversight aligns with what’s working in Indiana. Since 2008, Indiana has overseen a 71% reduction in untreated sewage releases from combined sewage overflow (CSO) utilities. The success is directly attributable to the sustained commitment of Indiana’s CSO communities, which have implemented long‑term control plans and infrastructure upgrades that continue to protect Hoosier waterways.

Since 2025, IDEM has provided more than 30 comments on the federal docket pertaining to various environmental actions on matters ranging from:

Definition of the "Waters of the United States" under the Clean Water Act

Public Participation Requirements in Air Permitting

Compliance Deadline for Safe Drinking Water Act PFAS Levels

Greenhouse Gas Emission Standards for Power Plants

Disposal of Coal Combustion Residuals from Electric Utilities

Chemical Risk Evaluations under the Toxic Substances Control Act

“IDEM oversees nearly all federal environmental laws and programs in Indiana, and decisions made in Washington have an enormous impact on Hoosiers,” said IDEM Commissioner Clint Woods. “I am proud that IDEM has stepped up as a national leader, more actively influencing in federal environmental policy over the last 18 months than any other state agency.”

This increased engagement follows Senate Enrolled Act 277, passed by the General Assembly earlier this year, which modernized Indiana’s environmental statutes for the first time in decades. Indiana is also now the only state in the country with environmental law that enshrines “cooperative federalism” in statute.

The law directs IDEM to “actively engage with its federal counterparts through comments, petitions, letters, advisory committees, rulemaking activities, and other means, to ensure federal environmental laws and their implementation serve the state of Indiana.”

text:
The developer of a proposed data centre in Cardiff has said it is also seeking permission to build a gas power plant to get it up and running.

Developer Curtis Hall said the plant, which could operate for up to five years, may be needed if the site cannot get on the national grid quick enough.

It also said the gas turbine plan was a "worst-case scenario", and the project - planned for the site of an existing park and ride near Llanrumney - would bring significant benefits.

Friends of the Earth called it "climate-wrecking" infrastructure, and almost all the area's Members of the Senedd (MSs), and a Welsh government minister, have now formally objected to the plans to build the data centre.

A senior Labour councillor from Cardiff council - which has an agreement to sell the site to the developer - had also objected.

The Welsh government is considering whether it will take over the planning process for the facility - meaning Cardiff Council is unable to grant planning permission in the meantime.

The government is also planning to publish its own policy on the wider issue by the end of the year.

Interest in building data centres has increased with the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies - but they have been controversial worldwide, in part for the amount of electricity they require.

Cardiff East Park and Ride currently serves staff and patients using Cardiff's University Hospital of Wales.

Some of those living in a new-build housing estate nearby are concerned about the project, including James George, 32, who said he was worried about the impact on the environment and his home.

"The main concern is the noise and the pollution, like they have to run a diesel generator in case of any power disruption," he said.

Alexander Grant, 51, said: "My main worry is the situation with the Heath hospital with regards to the staff and the patients."

"There's also other reasons as well, from the environmental side of things. I think it's an absolute travesty."

Dale Harvey said he was concerned it would add the noise from the A48 dual carriageway, saying the proposal was "not great".

"You buy a new build, and we're being told all of a sudden there's going to be generators run - all the fumes and all the noises," he said.

The developer said the site would not be audible locally, and air quality would not have a significant impact.

Planning documents for an outline planning application detail a "temporary ancillary energy centre" with gas turbines that have a maximum generating capacity of 49.9MW.

They say that the energy centre is "proposed to start in operation in July 2028 and last approximately for five years until the site has a full electricity connection [until July 2033]".

The centre, according to the documents, would include five gas turbines, a steam generator, and another two gas turbines on standby.

In the long-term the data centre would require a connection of 150MW from the national grid. This may not be delivered, however, until between 2030 and 2034.

Energy generation facilities of 50MW need planning permission from the Welsh government. Curtis Hall denied it was trying to avoid having to make such an application by limiting the plant to 49.9MW.

Another 40 diesel backup generators would also be needed after a connection is made to the grid to ensure "continuous power".

The use of fossil fuels to power the centre prompted criticism from environmental campaign group Friends of the Earth Cymru.

Its interim director Jenny Lloyd said: ​"After a summer of heat waves and drought and worries about flooding over the autumn and winter, it's completely irresponsible to give the green light to this climate-wrecking piece of infrastructure."

Plaid Cymru MS Nick Carter, who represents Cardiff's Caerdydd Fynnon Taf constituency, said: "There is no reason why a data centre needs to be sited in an urban area close to schools and care homes, when in fact underneath the headlines is a small gas-fired power station."

Senior Labour councillor Lee Bridgeman added his voice to those objecting this week.

The member of the Cardiff Council cabinet and Llanrumney ward councillor said in a letter it was "hard to reconcile" the centre's emissions "with Cardiff's climate emergency declaration and Planning Policy Wales".

As well as the data centre, the plans included a new bridge and link road for pedestrians and cyclists.

Curtis Hall previously had planning permission for a logistics centre. According to Cardiff Council the company had switched to a data centre because of "changing market demand".

The company said the gas generation was "not the data centre's permanent power supply, and once the grid connection is live it would no longer be needed".

"If the connection arrives in time, the energy centre will not be needed at all," it said.

"Gas turbines appear in the planning documents because they represent the worst case for emissions and noise, so assessing them tests the upper limit of any impact."

The company said the technology was "not confirmed" for the energy centre - suggesting fuel cells that convert gas or hydrogen to electricity could be used.

It said the air quality effects of gas and diesel generators were also "not significant".

In response to climate change concerns, Curtis Hall said south Wales' electricity grid was "decarbonising fast" with plans for floating offshore wind.

A spokesperson for the company said the development would bring "significant benefits", such as "the delivery of the new road bridge" and by helping "attract much-needed investment, create well-paid jobs and provide new training opportunities".

text:
The US Department of Energy is providing up to $4.4 billion in loans to restore operations at three shut-down nuclear power plants: Palisades in Michigan, the Crane Clean Energy Center at the Three Mile Island site in Pennsylvania, and the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa. According to The Independent, their restart is expected to restore a combined capacity of 2.25 gigawatts, which could be enough for approximately two million households and businesses.

All three plants were closed before their licenses expired, mainly because of the high cost of the electricity they produced. At the same time, demand for electricity is rising, including due to large data centers. President Donald Trump’s administration is promoting the use of nuclear energy for the development of artificial intelligence and industry, and is also funding upgrades at operating nuclear power plants.

Contracts with technology companies

NextEra Energy and Google are working together to restart Duane Arnold in early 2029. NextEra CEO John Ketchum said that a long-term agreement with a major data center operator makes it possible to avoid passing costs on to Iowa household consumers.

Microsoft has signed an agreement with Constellation Energy to purchase electricity after the Crane Clean Energy Center is restored. In 2024, Constellation said it planned to spend $1.6 billion to restart the reactor under a 20-year agreement with Microsoft and expected to put it into operation in 2027. The Department of Energy provided the project with a $1 billion loan.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Palisades is closest to restarting

The Palisades nuclear power plant, which operated from 1971 to 2022, has made the most progress toward restoration. Holtec International acquired the plant and began dismantling it, but the work carried out was not irreversible. In 2024, Joe Biden’s administration approved a $1.5 billion loan to restart the facility, and the current administration continued the disbursements.

In August, Holtec began loading nuclear fuel but suspended the process after one of the fuel assemblies tilted. The company must determine the cause. Power purchase agreements provide for Palisades to enter service by March 2027.

Nuclear engineering expert Todd Allen said that restoring a reactor could be faster and cheaper than building a new large reactor. At the same time, Edwin Lyman, director of nuclear power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists, stressed that, in his view, public funding should primarily be directed toward addressing safety risks, including those related to more frequent extreme weather events.

text:
A major investment aimed at strengthening Virginia’s power grid is coming to the Commonwealth.

U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright visited the Hill City alongside Congressman John McGuire and Appalachian Power President and CEO Brian Abraham to announce a $50 million federal grant to upgrade Virginia’s power grid.

The money comes from the U.S. Department of Energy through the deployment of the Defense Production Act (DPA).

Appalachian Power said it plans to match the federal funding, bringing the total investment to $100 million.

SEE ALSO: Google evaluating Wood Haven Technology Park for potential data center

The upgrades come as demand for electricity continues to grow, adding an estimated 290 megawatts of transmission capacity across Appalachian Power's Virginia system. But the goal goes beyond just power expansion.

“To drive down the price of energy for residents in this district and also to increase the supply of electricity so businesses can locate here, because as you create more jobs, that’s how you push up wages," Secretary Wright said.

ABC13's Allison Mullet asked when ratepayers can expect to see change from the upgrades.

Mullet: When exactly do you expect ratepayers to see a drop in their bills with this project, and how much do you expect that change to be?

“The building up something doesn’t turn it like a light switch,” Abraham said. “We’ve got to grow our generation. We’ve got to grow our transmission, our distribution. We’ve got to grow the demand in this area because as those large load customers come on, it reduces rates for our residential customers.”

Instead of relying only on new power lines, the project aims to upgrade existing infrastructure.

AEP said the improvements could be completed one to four years faster than conventional transmission upgrades. Appalachian Power said it expects the upgrades to start sometime within the next two years.

description:
The “patently false” statement in question was a corporate press release claiming algae biofuel was a viable solution to climate change that the company would soon be producing at scale.
These corporations are not just afraid of losing these lawsuits; they’re also afraid of the damning evidence the suits will uncover.
This is the skeleton key for understanding Suncor v. Boulder, the high-profile climate case the Supreme Court heard in early October.
Suncor began in 2018, when Boulder, Colorado, sued fossil fuel companies Suncor and ExxonMobil for damages from climate change and the companies’ lies about their role in fueling it.
We have likely seen just a sliver of the evidence they have that shows they’ve spent decades knowingly deceiving the public about climate science, climate harms, and their commitment to climate action.
text:
“Do you believe that statement’s misleading?”

“All the clauses in there are patently false. And I told them so.”

So reads an exchange from the deposition of Joseph Weissman, an ExxonMobil scientist with the company’s former algae biofuels program. The “patently false” statement in question was a corporate press release claiming algae biofuel was a viable solution to climate change that the company would soon be producing at scale. Extensive reporting has already uncovered how ExxonMobil spent nearly half as much advertising its algae research as it spent on the research itself. But testimony like Weissman’s shows just how clearly the company understood that this much-touted project was, in Weissman’s words, a “dead end.” The goal was not to create a viable alternative energy source, but simply, as one internal memo put it, to make consumers “[b]elieve ExxonMobil is committed to helping solve climate change.”

Weissman’s deposition was taken by the Massachusetts Attorney General’s Office as part of its lawsuit against ExxonMobil alleging consumer protection violations. In an under-the-radar filing in April, Massachusetts disclosed this deposition, as well as a range of other documents it had uncovered, to demonstrate the relevance of additional investigative targets that ExxonMobil had been furiously attempting to shield from discovery. These newly released materials cover a range of topics and time periods, from memos on the company’s more recent deceptive advertising campaigns to evidence of its decades-old climate knowledge.

One of the documents is a 1992 paper, “Climate Change Impacts on Northern Offshore Petroleum Operations,” which analyzes how Exxon’s operations in the Beaufort Sea would be affected by its predictions of a “much thinner ice sheet” and other anticipated effects of global warming caused by the use of its products. The upshot for Exxon: “[I]f ice conditions become less severe as predicted, then offshore petroleum operations will become easier and less costly.” Papers like this, demonstrating ExxonMobil’s sophisticated understanding of the realities of global warming, were produced at the same time the company was ramping up its public efforts to, in its own words, “emphasize the uncertainty in scientific conclusions” on climate change in order to prevent the “development of nonfossil fuel resources.”

Needless to say, the contrast between oil companies’ internal climate knowledge and external climate denial is profoundly damaging to the industry. This helps explain why it is going to such extraordinary lengths to attack these climate cases. These corporations are not just afraid of losing these lawsuits; they’re also afraid of the damning evidence the suits will uncover.

This is the skeleton key for understanding Suncor v. Boulder, the high-profile climate case the Supreme Court heard in early October.

Suncor began in 2018, when Boulder, Colorado, sued fossil fuel companies Suncor and ExxonMobil for damages from climate change and the companies’ lies about their role in fueling it. After the Colorado Supreme Court rejected the defendants’ motion to dismiss the case, Suncor and ExxonMobil — likely terrified of what would happen if Boulder were allowed to have its day in court — asked the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene, repeating a request the fossil fuel industry has made again and again in recent years, alongside parallel efforts to lobby Congress and state legislatures to grant it immunity from all climate-related liability.

There is a reason why oil and gas companies are so desperate to stop these cases by any means before they proceed any further. We have likely seen just a sliver of the evidence they have that shows they’ve spent decades knowingly deceiving the public about climate science, climate harms, and their commitment to climate action. How many more reports are they sitting on like the 1992 paper laying out ExxonMobil’s projected opportunities for profiting off a melting Arctic? How many more internal communications like Weissman’s saying that “all the clauses” in a 2018 press release about ExxonMobil’s signature climate solution were “patently false?” The current offensive isn’t just about defeating the cases. It’s also about preventing the public from learning the extent and severity of the industry’s wrongdoing. It’s about fossil fuel CEOs’ profound fear of sitting in front of a jury of 12 Americans and trying to defend their companies’ deceptive conduct — because they know it’s indefensible.

Regardless of how the Supreme Court rules in Suncor, it’s hard to imagine these companies can bury the evidence of their lies and escape accountability indefinitely. Whatever the onetime value of fossil fuels to the economy, their harms now massively outweigh their benefits, particularly since the vast majority of fossil fuel use can be replaced by cleaner, cheaper, safer forms of energy — and this has been true for a long time. Instead of adapting, the industry has clung tightly to a civilization-endangering business model and engaged in a massive deception campaign to do so. Along the way, its conduct has become some of the most harmful and culpable in human history. Eventually, it will be held to account.
