title: Oklahoma lawmakers consider the future of property tax exemptions for renewable energy ...
description:
Earlier this year, lawmakers passed Senate Bill 237, which would have excluded solar energy and related battery storage facilities from qualifying for property tax exemptions.
Findings show both states have better incentive policies that could push renewable energy companies away from Oklahoma.
Kansas offers a 10-year property tax exemption for renewable energy companies looking to build solar and wind production and the battery storage facilities they need.
Meanwhile, Texas allows certain local jurisdictions to grant temporary tax exemptions or reductions to companies looking to build renewable energy infrastructure nearby.
That means property tax exemptions for manufacturers can sometimes mean budget gaps for county public safety or education budgets.
text:
Earlier this year, lawmakers passed Senate Bill 237, which would have excluded solar energy and related battery storage facilities from qualifying for property tax exemptions.

Gov. Kevin Stitt pocket vetoed the measure by not acting on it before the session ended, but Representative Mike Dobrinski of Okeene says the bill raised the need for an important discussion amid a shifting energy environment. So, he requested an interim study by the House Appropriations and Budget Committee, which took place Thursday at the statehouse.

"As Oklahoma's economy and energy industry evolve over the last 40 years, the scale of proposed developments makes this discussion timely," Dobrinski said to open the meeting.

"Oklahoma has more than 100 applications for solar and battery storage projects, representing approximately 17.6 Gigawatts, or basically 43% of Oklahoma's proposed queue," he said. "While the application does not guarantee a project will be built, these numbers demonstrate the potential magnitude of future development and the importance of understanding its tax implications."

House Fiscal staff compared Oklahoma's tax incentive policies with those in neighboring Texas and Kansas. Findings show both states have better incentive policies that could push renewable energy companies away from Oklahoma.

House fiscal analyst Mariah Searock said policy in those states contributes. Kansas offers a 10-year property tax exemption for renewable energy companies looking to build solar and wind production and the battery storage facilities they need.

"Kansas, they really want wind, solar and all the things," Searock said. "They have a huge property tax advantage."

Meanwhile, Texas allows certain local jurisdictions to grant temporary tax exemptions or reductions to companies looking to build renewable energy infrastructure nearby. The structure allows local Texas jurisdictions to weigh their communities' interests and needs on a case-by-case basis.

Right now, Oklahoma offers a 5-year tax break for several types of manufacturing companies, mostly in the oil and gas sector, but also in solar and computer processing, except for AI data centers.

But the Oklahoma Constitution, unlike that of its neighboring states, also ties property taxes paid by private owners and companies to the state to essential funding streams for local county jurisdictions. That means property tax exemptions for manufacturers can sometimes mean budget gaps for county public safety or education budgets.

So, when the exemptions were devised in the 1980s, the state promised to reimburse local jurisdictions by establishing a revolving fund. Rep. Melodee Blancett, D-Tulsa, pointed out the original intention of that legislation.

"One of the difficulties of recruiting manufacturing, and they're very valuable from an economic development perspective, is the upfront cost to build," Blancett said. "And so that therein was the reason for doing the manufacturing exemption to begin with."But the policy environment has changed, she noted.

"It appears to me that the definition of what a manufacturer has morphed significantly over the last 25 years from when it was completed based on its original objective, because it seems like a lot of the people that may today qualify really are not manufacturers."

The legislature has allocated money every year for local county reimbursements. Searock said the state fund, which is also meant to reimburse school districts and disabled veterans for property tax breaks, is sitting at about $50 million as of last year. The baseline appropriation for the fund each year totals 1% of the state's annual income tax revenue.

But that's not enough to cover all the reimbursements, she said, and it hasn't been for more than 20 years.

"Back in about 2003 was the first year that the funding into the ad valorem reimbursement fund was not sufficient to cover the reimbursement claims that came in from counties, so that since that point, the legislature has had to appropriate money to make up for that," Searock said.

During the 2026 legislative session the extra appropriation to make schools and veterans whole amounted to over nearly $65 million, according to the House and Senate budget transparency portals.

Major changes to Oklahoma's manufacturing ad valorem exemptions laws would require constitutional reforms, Searock said.

And for his part, Dobrinski is up for the challenge of tweaking the relevant Oklahoma law.

"I think it's been very, very successful when it comes to actually encouraging manufacturing," he said. "But I do think it is time to give an overall review of it because at the end of the day, whether it be solar, wind, battery storage, or, you know, computer data processing facilities, whether those be Bitcoin or AI they're going to go where the market leads them."

name: EPA
title: NAM Calls for Clear, Predictable WOTUS Definition
description:
Manufacturers support efforts by the Environmental Protection Agency and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to give regulated entities greater certainty and predictability regarding the reach of the Clean Water Act’s jurisdiction, the NAM said recently.
What’s going on: In November 2025, the agencies proposed a rule to rightsize the definition of “waters of the United States” under the Clean Water Act to comply with a landmark 2023 Supreme Court ruling.
The NAM responded by calling for clear definitions of “relatively permanent” and “continuous surface connection” and urging caution about the concept of a “wet season.” Last month, following the NAM’s recommendations, the agencies released a narrower supplemental proposal seeking public feedback on the WOTUS definition.
Why it’s important: Manufacturers rely on dependable, consistent regulations that align with the 2023 NAM-supported Supreme Court decision in Sackett v. EPA, in which the justices determined that the EPA only had jurisdiction over wetlands with “continuous surface connection” to navigable waters.
What should be done: In response to the supplemental proposal, the NAM last week urged the agencies to adopt the updated definitions, including to: Define “‘relatively permanent’ based on perennial waters rather than the previously proposed ‘wet season’ approach”; Finalize the proposed definition of “perennial” to mean “having standing or continuously flowing water every day of the year during ordinary conditions”; Finalize the definition of “continuous surface connection” as requiring a wetland to be “indistinguishable from the jurisdictional water”; and Ensure the final WOTUS definition “provides the certainty and predictability manufacturers need to plan and invest in projects over significant periods of time.”

What’s going on: In November 2025, the agencies proposed a rule to rightsize the definition of “waters of the United States” under the Clean Water Act to comply with a landmark 2023 Supreme Court ruling.

The NAM responded by calling for clear definitions of “relatively permanent” and “continuous surface connection” and urging caution about the concept of a “wet season.”

Last month, following the NAM’s recommendations, the agencies released a narrower supplemental proposal seeking public feedback on the WOTUS definition.

Why it’s important: Manufacturers rely on dependable, consistent regulations that align with the 2023 NAM-supported Supreme Court decision in Sackett v. EPA, in which the justices determined that the EPA only had jurisdiction over wetlands with “continuous surface connection” to navigable waters.

What should be done: In response to the supplemental proposal, the NAM last week urged the agencies to adopt the updated definitions, including to:

Define “‘relatively permanent’ based on perennial waters rather than the previously proposed ‘wet season’ approach”;

Finalize the proposed definition of “perennial” to mean “having standing or continuously flowing water every day of the year during ordinary conditions”;

Finalize the definition of “continuous surface connection” as requiring a wetland to be “indistinguishable from the jurisdictional water”; and

Ensure the final WOTUS definition “provides the certainty and predictability manufacturers need to plan and invest in projects over significant periods of time.”

text:
Tonight’s developments have seen renewed tensions across the Middle East, with missiles striking near Aden airport in Yemen and Saudi Arabia reporting interceptions of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones.

Qatar’s prime minister has called for Israel to withdraw from occupied areas in southern Lebanon, while condemning attacks on peacekeeping forces and pledging continued support for the Lebanese armed forces.

In Lebanon, authorities have opened an investigation into the abduction of former Syrian militia commander Ali Kayali, who was detained by Syrian intelligence after allegedly attempting to cross the border.

Meanwhile, a UN aviation agency has flagged safety deficiencies at Beirut airport that could delay plans to restore direct flights between the US and Lebanon.

Elsewhere, the US has condemned violence in the occupied West Bank following an attack by Israeli settlers on veteran Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, while Italian prosecutors have expanded an investigation into Israeli officials over the treatment of Gaza flotilla activists.

In the US, police are assessing a social media post by the wife of National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell that appeared to express support for banned group Palestine Action.

The FIFA Appeal Committee has rejected a Spanish appeal against punishment for racist chants during a friendly against Egypt in March, the Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) announced on Friday.

During the match against Egypt played at the Cornella, home of Espanyol, on March 31, part of the crowd chanted "whoever doesn't jump is Muslim".

On August 4, three weeks after Spain won the World Cup, FIFA's disciplinary committee imposed a fine of $20,000 (17,800 euros) and closure of at least 15 per cent of the stadium for Spain's next home friendly.

The RFEF reiterated on Friday that this misconduct "was detected by the Federation's own monitoring mechanisms" and that announcements urged the crowd to stop the chanting at half-time, during the second half and on the stadium video screens.

The RFEF said it had cooperated fully to help identify those responsible. It said it would appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

One of Spain's starters during the match, forward Lamine Yamal who plays for Espanyol's local rivals Barcelona and was born in a suburb near the Cornella stadium, is Muslim. At the time he called the chants "a lack of respect and something intolerable".

Spain manager Luis de la Fuente also called the chants "intolerable".

"Violent individuals exploit football to carve out a space for themselves," he said after the match. "They must be removed from society, identified, and the further away the better."

The Egyptian Football Association issued a statement expressing its "total condemnation of the vile racist incident" by some spectators who "went beyond the limits".

Lebanese authorities were investigating how a former Syrian militia commander suspected of committing crimes during the government of ousted President Bashar Assad was abducted in Lebanon and taken to Syria, judicial and security officials said Friday.

Syria’s intelligence department said Thursday that it had detained Ali Kayali, also known as Mihrac Ural, as he was trying to flee from Syria across the border.

The intelligence department said that Kayali was responsible for killings in 2013 in the coastal town of Baniyas that left hundreds of people dead.

Lebanese judicial officials said that the country’s public prosecution had opened an investigation into the case.

Authorities asked army intelligence and police intelligence units to analyze telecommunication calls to determine whether Kayali was taken to the Syrian Embassy outside of Beirut or straight to Syria after he was picked up in the Lebanese mountain town of Mansouriyeh where he had been living.

The three judicial and two security officials spoke on condition of anonymity, because they weren't authorized to speak to the media about the case, which was still under investigation.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a notoriously tense relationship with US president Barack Obama. A decade on, and days ahead of a tight Israeli election, the two again are taking each other to task.

Netanyahu on Friday denounced remarks by Obama, without saying his name, after the former US president said Israel had "ceded moral high ground" in its treatment of the Palestinians.

"I said this directly to Netanyahu when I was president -- at some point, to break the cycle, the stronger party has a responsibility by virtue of its strength," Obama told an event Tuesday in Belfast, according to videos posted online.

"If the attitude of Israel is, now that we are the strongest army, most technologically advanced in the region, then our security is dependent on us simply doing whatever we please and taking whatever we want and not making any concessions to anyone -- that may work short term; it is a disaster for you," Obama said.

Obama also sharply criticised Hamas, which attacked Israel on October 7, 2023.

Israeli media heavily covered another part of the remarks in which Obama referred to the creation of the state of Israel in 1948 in the shadow of the Holocaust.

"The Jewish people for millennia were oppressed, discriminated against, killed. Europe was responsible for much of that," Obama said.

"They understandably sought a refuge in a place where they had historic ties. That is undeniable," Obama said.

"What is also undeniable is that they took the land of people. They were expelled," Obama said of the Palestinians.

"And those people understandably said, this is an injustice and I want my land back."

The United States on Friday condemned "criminal violence by any party" in the occupied West Bank, after Israeli settlers attacked an American photojournalist covering violence against Palestinian olive farmers for The Washington Post.

Veteran photographer Heidi Levine was taken to hospital in Ramallah following the attack, with photos showing her lying on a gurney with injuries to her leg and hand.

"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible," a State Department official said, on condition of anonymity, without directly criticizing the settlers.

"We are greatly concerned when any American is harmed overseas and stand ready to provide all appropriate consular assistance," the official said. "The Department has reached out to the Washington Post to offer consular assistance."

Speaking to journalists from her hospital bed, Levine said that "more than 50" masked settlers holding sticks suddenly attacked her while she was working near the Palestinian villages of Abu Falah and Turmus Ayya in the central West Bank.

"All of a sudden they jumped me and I luckily had my helmet and flak jacket on and I... kept my face to the ground to try to protect my face," she said.

"They just kept kicking me and kicking me," she added.

The State Department official said that Washington was in "regular dialogue with partners about improving stability and security in the West Bank."

Iran's foreign ministry on Friday rejected Saudi Arabia's accusation that Tehran was involved in Houthi attacks on the kingdom, offering to mediate between the two sides.

"The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a statement, reiterating Tehran's offer to act as a bridge between the Houthis and Riyadh.

Baqaei said Tehran "has always been ready to use its good offices to help end the hostilities" and remained prepared to use "all its capacities for this purpose at the request of both sides".

The Houthis are part of Iran's so-called "Axis of Resistance", which also includes Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq, all united in opposing Israel.

Tehran has repeatedly denied directing Houthi operations, saying the Yemeni group acts according to its own interests.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi targets in recent weeks, including vessels in the Red Sea, oil facilities and Riyadh's international airport, where 13 people were killed in a single attack last week.

British police said on Friday they were assessing a social media post after the wife of National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell appeared to express support for Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian group banned as a terrorist organisation.

Journalist and author Sarah Helm, who is married to Powell, responded on X to a post about the Irish novelist Sally Rooney, who this week announced her books would no longer be sold in Britain over her plans to use her royalties to support Palestine Action.

Helm said in the post: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action."

In response, a Metropolitan Police spokesperson said the post is "being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required".

Palestine Action was proscribed under terrorism laws last year, so expressing support for the group constitutes a criminal offence.

Asked for comment, a government spokeswoman said: "These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity."

Palestine Action has carried out protests including vandalism in support of Palestinian causes, and denies that this amounts to terrorism. Four members of the group were jailed in June over a 2024 raid on a factory ​operated by Israeli defence firm Elbit which caused more than £1 million of damage.

Amnesty International says more than 3,500 people have been arrested in Britain for alleged support of Palestine Action since it was banned last year, many of them for holding up placards.

Palestine Action challenged the government's decision to ban the group, but the Court of Appeal ruled in June that the proscription was lawful.

The United Nations aviation agency has found Lebanon's main airport lacks valid certification, according to a report summary, in a setback to US President Donald Trump's move to revive direct US-Beirut flights.

Trump made the announcement in July and signed an order last month for the US government to allow direct flights from the US to Lebanon, reversing a four-decade-long suspension after TWA Flight 847 was hijacked and forced to land in Beirut in 1985.

While the US Federal Aviation Administration and the Transportation Security Administration would still need to conduct safety reviews before flights could resume, the Lebanese embassy in Washington called Trump's order "a significant first step toward restoring direct air service between Lebanon and the United States."

However, the UN's International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) technical assistance mission to Lebanon in July identified shortcomings at Beirut-Rafic Hariri International Airport and in the aviation system.

The findings, which two senior industry officials familiar with the matter expect to delay the resumption of service, complicate efforts to follow up on an order Trump signed after meeting Lebanese President Joseph Aoun. Washington has backed Aoun as it pushes for Iran-backed Hezbollah to be disarmed.

The agency sent its internal report, made at the request of the Lebanese Civil Aviation Authority (LCAA), to Lebanon in September.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian denied Friday that Tehran sought nuclear weapons, expressed readiness for dialogue and condemned US sanctions during talks with Georgia's prime minister.

In his meeting with Georgian premier Irakli Kobakhidze, Pezeshkian also called for closer ties with Georgia, weeks after Tbilisi cut aviation links between the two countries following US sanctions targeting Iranian airlines.

The two met on the sidelines of a UN biodiversity summit in Armenia's capital Yerevan.

"Iran is not seeking nuclear weapons, and we consider the malicious propaganda against our country to be lies," Pezeshkian said, according to a statement from his office.

"We have always been ready for dialogue. They think they can force us to surrender, but we will not bow to coercion," he added, calling US sanctions against Tehran "unjustifiable and inhumane".

In his meeting with Kobakhidze, Pezeshkian also called for a clear timetable to expand cooperation between Tehran and Tbilisi, Iran's Tasnim news agency reported.

The report quoted Kobakhidze as saying he opposed foreign interference in neighbouring countries' internal affairs, but his office made no mention of those remarks in its own account of the meeting.

It said the leaders had discussed bilateral ties and regional security, with Kobakhidze stressing the "importance of dialogue and diplomacy to achieve de-escalation and lasting peace".

Yemen’s Saudi-backed forces, fighting on behalf of the internationally recognised government, say they have carried out air strikes against Houthi positions in al-Dhabab, west of Taiz governorate.

The city of Taiz is rapidly emerging as the most important battlefront in Yemen's reignited civil war, pitting the Iran-allied Houthis against the internationally recognised government, which is backed by a Saudi-led coalition.

Houthi forces have encircled Taiz in recent weeks by cutting its main road south to Aden, causing widespread displacement and worsening a humanitarian crisis.

Any Houthi victory in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, would mark one of the biggest turning points in the country's long civil war, which resumed this summer after a four-year truce.

Taiz has been on the frontline between the Houthis and the government since the first days of the conflict that started in early 2015 and has long been seen as a bastion of opposition to the Iran-allied group.

Israeli settlers on Friday beat an American photojournalist working for The Washington Post while she was covering ongoing violence against Palestinian olive farmers in the occupied West Bank.

Heidi Levine, a veteran photographer, was taken to hospital in Ramallah following the attack, with photos showing her lying on a gurney with injuries to her leg and hand.

The incident comes 10 days after settlers beat an AFP photographer covering the West Bank olive harvest, Jaafar Ashtiyeh, leaving him also requiring hospital treatment.

Speaking to journalists from her hospital bed, Levine said that "more than 50" masked settlers holding sticks suddenly attacked her while she was working near the Palestinian villages of Abu Falah and Turmus Ayya in the central West Bank.

"All of a sudden they jumped me and I luckily had my helmet and flak jacket on and I... kept my face to the ground to try to protect my face," she said.

"They just kept kicking me and kicking me," she added.

The Washington Post reported that Levine had been wearing a flak jacket with "Press" clearly marked on the front and back.

A spokesman for the US embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack, declining to comment further due to privacy laws.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and senior military, police and prison officials have been placed under investigation in Italy over the treatment of Gaza flotilla activists, Italian prosecutors said on Friday.

The move expands an investigation that was previously focused on Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir.

The case concerns suspected torture, kidnapping, personal injury, robbery and damage when Israeli forces intercepted small fleets of boats headed towards Gaza in 2025 and 2026, the Rome prosecutors' office said in a statement.

Investigators opened the probe after complaints from 50 Italian citizens who were detained by Israeli authorities following two Global Sumud Flotilla missions in September to October 2025 and April to May 2026.

Katz did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Ben-Gvir in June dismissed news that he was under investigation, saying he would "continue to stand proudly alongside our fighters".

text:
California drivers are paying more than $6 for regular gasoline, putting a pressure on household budgets and giving some people another reason to consider an electric vehicle.

But higher gas prices don’t necessarily mean drivers will rush to buy one.

California’s sales of zero-emission vehicles rebounded in the second quarter of 2026 even as the national market cooled following the expiration of federal tax credits.

Researchers say the recovery highlights a bigger challenge for the state’s transition away from gas-powered cars: Drivers need affordable electric vehicles to be available and the economics of owning them long-term needs to make sense.

Gil Tal, director of the Electric Vehicle Research Center at UC Davis, said California’s recent sales growth was concentrated in models that automakers had available to sell. The issue with that is many of them have stopped or slowed down production of their EVs in the U.S because of lost incentives and loosening of emissions standards that make gas-powered cars, including hybrids, better investments.

“We have no leverages on the car companies,” Tal said. “When gas prices are really high, people are looking for EVs, but there is not enough supply.”

UC Davis Electric Vehicle Research Center Director Gil Tal plugs in an EV Friday, Sept. 25, 2026, at UC Davis.(Gerardo Zavala/CapRadio)

Affordable EV models are scarce despite market re

bound

California sold nearly 87,000 new zero-emission vehicles in the second quarter of 2026, which accounts for about a fifth of new-car sales, according to the California Energy Commission.

That includes electric vehicles, plug-in hybrids and hydrogen-powered cars. Electric Vehicles represent the vast majority of those sales by themselves, accounting for roughly 17% of new-car sales in the state.

That’s nearly three times the national average of 6% of new-car sales being EVs during the same time period.

Tal’s research suggests that vehicle availability helped drive California’s rebound while the expiration of federal incentives contributed to a downturn in demand across the country as automakers pulled back on some electric models.

When gasoline prices climbed, Californians — and Americans in general — increasingly looked for electric vehicles but found that the supply of affordable options limited their choices.

“Our market is very limited on affordable cars — any affordable cars — in the U.S.,” Tal said. “If you drive one country to the north or one country to the south, you will find many affordable EVs that are not offered here.”

Tal said that means consumers showing up to dealerships looking for their ideal electric vehicle might not find any, which has led many to purchasing alternatives like hybrids instead.

“In California, I think that many people used to go to Tesla, but now there are other reasons for people not to like Tesla,” he said. “If you have a large family and you look for a seven-seater or if you are looking for a more affordable [vehicle], the number of models in these segments is very limited.”

His research found that most of the country is shifting towards hybrids in response to high gas prices — over $4 on average nationally. He said the share of new hybrid vehicle sales jumped from 13.3% to 16.9% between January and May — roughly 35,000 more hybrid buyers a month, dwarfing California’s “plug-in” rebound.

High electricity prices have also made convincing consumers to make that transition even more difficult. In response to that and the loss of federal incentives, the state recently launched its own incentive program to encourage Californians to ditch the pump for the plug.

California’s rebate program lowers upfront cost

California is trying to lower the upfront cost through MyFirstEV, a program offering qualifying first-time zero-emission vehicle buyers up to $3,500 toward a new vehicle and $1,750 toward a qualifying used one.

The program combines state funding with contributions from automakers for roughly $271 million in total incentives. It’s run by the California Air Resources Board, or CARB.

CARB communications director Lindsay Buckley said early demand has been strong.

“One early indicator of its success was Tesla, a California company that participated,” she said. “They actually sold out in a week.”

But rebates can only help people buy vehicles that are available. Tal’s research suggests that automakers’ supply decisions will remain a key factor in whether the state can sustain its recent sales growth.

Republican state Senator Tony Strickland argued that California’s own policies are also part of the problem. High electricity prices, limited charging infrastructure and concerns about energy capacity are three things he said makes transitioning to EVs difficult for most.

“There is no demand right now for the EV vehicle,” Strickland said. “If the technology gets better and more people move towards it, great, but that’s not what’s happening.

Strickland, who is vice chair of the Senate Transportation Committee, also said he’s against using taxpayer money to subsidize EV purchases.

Buckley said the state is monitoring electricity demand and encouraging EV owners to charge outside peak energy-consumption hours to avoid straining the power grid.

High gas prices might not be the only issue

Andrew Campbell, executive director of the UC Berkeley Haas Energy Institute, has cautioned against assuming a spike in gasoline prices will lead to widespread EV adoption.

“I suspect right now consumers understand that prices are high because of the Iran War and that the Iran War and the circumstances around that could change at some point,” he said. “My guess is consumers are not going to make major decisions based on the prices they’re seeing at the pump right now.”

Campbell said Europe’s EV market may offer some clues about what could help expand sales in the U.S.

“They have allowed in Chinese electric vehicles and those vehicles are lower cost than a lot of the other electric vehicles that are available,” he said.

California has limited control over the global vehicle market, including import policies and tariffs. But Campbell said policymakers do have some control over the costs associated with owning an EV.

One possibility is changing how electricity bills are structured. California’s electricity rates often rely heavily on charges for each kilowatt-hour used, but Cambell said a higher fixed monthly charge paired with a lower charge for each additional kilowatt-hour used could reduce the cost of charging.

He also suggested rethinking vehicle registration fees, which are largely based on a vehicle’s value. Campbell said a system that accounts for pollution could better reflect the environmental impact of older, less efficient vehicles.

“The idea of graduated charges would be to not so much set it based on age or value of the vehicle, but instead set the annual registration fees based on the environmental harms that those vehicles cause,” he said.

For renters, charging can be a hurdle

According to the Public Policy Institute of California, renters made up around 44% of Californianas in 2024. Many of them are locked out of purchasing an EV because they don't have access to an affordable place to charge.

Dahlia Garas, research program director for the UC Davis Electric Vehicle Research Center, said California has requirements for new buildings to be equipped for EV charging. The cost of using that infrastructure can vary though.

“If an apartment complex has chargers that are shared, there's no consistency of like a monthly permit or a per-kilowatt-hour charge, or a monthly fee plus a killowatt-per-hour-charge,” she said.

UC Davis Electric Vehicle Research Center Research Program Director Dahlia Garas Friday, Sept. 25, 2026, in Davis.(Gerardo Zavala/CapRadio)

Garas said the impact is even worse for people who live in apartments with no access to charging infrastructure.

“That pushes people out to public charging and particularly DC fast charging, which is the least economical way to charge a vehicle,” she added. “That puts EVs at a financial operation cost disadvantage.”

How are drivers reacting?

At a Sacramento gas station, drivers say they are feeling the pinch while at the pump, but not necessarily enough to consider an EV.

Mark Haw was filling up his Honda CR-V at Interstate Gasoline in East Sacramento. He commutes from Elk Grove and said he’s considering a hybrid rather than an EV because gas prices are going to come down eventually.

“It costs me about $20 a week more in gas for me to commute to and from my job,” he said. “And so it makes for smaller meals.”

Lillian Schmidt paid $70 to fill up her Volkswagen Golf at the same station.

title: Africa Rising – The Carbon Markets Africa Summit, 2026 - Climate 411 - News and stories
description:
For Africa, initiatives that can reduce emissions, protect ecosystems, and support livelihoods have not been well-financed.
Critically, carbon markets are tipped to also play a key role, through compliance mechanisms under the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanisms and Voluntary markets.
Yet African countries have demonstrated commitment and action in developing carbon markets.
The Carbon Markets Africa Summit offers a space to bring these efforts together with Africa in focus.
Two key first-of-a-kind initiatives were launched; the Africa Nature Impact Fund and the Africa Carbon Investment and Finance Alliance.
text:
Meeting the world’s collective climate targets demands significant finance. Countries have set out their climate ambitions in their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), but turning these into full scale action requires investment that is available, accessible and suited to their needs. For Africa, initiatives that can reduce emissions, protect ecosystems, and support livelihoods have not been well-financed. That needs to change.

The scale of the financing challenge is clear. Drawing on the UNFCCC Standing Committee on Finance’s assessment, the COP29 finance decision in Baku, Azerbaijan, recognised that developing countries’ costed needs in their NDCs amounted to between US$5.1 trillion and US$6.8 trillion through 2030. This is an estimate of needs, rather than the financing gap itself, but it shows the scale of investment required and the urgency of closing the gap between ambition and available finance.

This finance can be delivered through several instruments, including debt for nature swaps, sovereign green bonds and first loss capital that helps reduce risks for other investors. Critically, carbon markets are tipped to also play a key role, through compliance mechanisms under the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanisms and Voluntary markets.

Many countries have included both conditional and unconditional targets in their NDCs. The unconditional targets reflect commitments countries intend to deliver with their own resources albeit not always budgeted, while conditional targets depend on external support. In that space, Carbon markets offer a way to on-board private finance, including through blended financing arrangements, to support national commitments and further climate action, while delivering a path to net-zero for industry.

Countries in Africa are no exception. Although the continent has contributed relatively little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving climate change, it faces harsh changing climatic impacts. Droughts, flooding, and changing rainfall patterns are affecting agriculture, nature, energy, industry and ultimately people. These impacts are already placing pressure on livelihoods and national development.

Yet African countries have demonstrated commitment and action in developing carbon markets. Kenya has a long history of carbon market participation and has strengthened its legal framework to support investment. Ghana’s Article 6 pathway includes cooperation with a number of Countries and a pipeline spanning clean cooking, sustainable rice cultivation, waste management and electric mobility. Senegal have also authorized a programme supporting the transition to electric vehicles. These examples show that African countries are building practical pathways for climate finance and are supported through Cooperative Approaches with Switzerland, Singapore, Sweden and others, allowing them to engage in the carbon market to meet their climate goals.

The Carbon Markets Africa Summit offers a space to bring these efforts together with Africa in focus. Created by the VUKA Group, the maiden summit was in Johannesburg in 2025, bringing governments, investors, project developers and other partners into discussions on Africa’s carbon market opportunities. Although still young, it is creating an important platform to showcase initiatives, connect projects with finance and support the growth of viable investments.

This year’s summit was held from 13th to 15th October in Kigali, Rwanda, under the auspices of Rwanda’s Ministry of Environment, with the United Nations Development Programme and African Development Bank serving as host organisations. Opening the Conference, Dr. Bernadette Arakwiye, Minister for Environment of the Republic of Rwanda, mentioned three key priorities needed for Carbon Markets to work for Africa:

Accessible Methodologies

Project Preparation and Readiness Finance and

Long term demand at fair value

The three days featured high level discussions, investor and buyer roundtables, project showcases, technical workshops and deal rooms, including a Nature Deal Room hosted by the United Nations Environment Programme.

The platform was beyond presenting projects. It was also a space to understand how the infrastructure for Article 6 and voluntary carbon markets is being built, exchange knowledge and learn from practical experience, such as clear authorisation processes, reliable registries and credible measurement and verification. Two key first-of-a-kind initiatives were launched; the Africa Nature Impact Fund and the Africa Carbon Investment and Finance Alliance. Africa Nature is set up to raise and deploy USD100 million for nature-based climate projects, while ACIFA, which has EDF as a collaborating founding member, is to mobilize capital into high integrity African Carbon Markets. These can help turn promising initiatives into investments that buyers and financiers can trust and deploy at scale.

EDF connected with partners through bi-laterals, roundtable discussions and active panel discussions. These conversations offered an opportunity to strengthen partnerships around nature-based climate action, support transparent and bankable initiatives, and explore meaningful support for Indigenous Peoples, local communities and forest jurisdictions. Their participation, rights and benefits must remain central as these markets develop.

text:
Swedish Wind Centre 2.0 has secured funding from the Swedish Energy Agency and participating partners for five years of research into wind power. Chalmers University of Technology and Uppsala University will jointly lead the national competence centre, bringing researchers and industry together. The centre will focus on wind power in a range of environments, from forested landscapes on land to complex marine conditions in the Baltic Sea and off Sweden’s west coast.

Building on the existing Swedish Wind Centre, the new centre will receive more than SEK 100 million in total funding over five years. Uppsala University will host the centre, with leadership shared between the two universities. The centre will be led by Stefan Ivanell, Professor of Wind Energy at Uppsala University, and Sara Fogelström, Research Project Manager at the Department of Electrical Engineering at Chalmers University of Technology.

Swedish Wind Centre 2.0 brings together nine universities and 13 partners from industry, regional organisations and public authorities. Participants include Energiforsk, Fu-Gen, OX2, Rabbalshede Kraft, Region Gotland, RES, SR Energy, Statkraft, Svenska kraftnät, Vasa Vind, Vattenfall, Vestas and Västra Götaland Region.

Previously, funding from participating companies and Västra Götaland Region limited the centre’s ability to undertake longer-term research projects. Support from the Swedish Energy Agency is expected to provide greater scope for research over extended periods and for projects spanning multiple research fields.

Preparatory work will begin in autumn 2026, with the centre scheduled to launch on 1 January 2027. The first research projects are expected to start during 2027.

text:
Peter Hubbard (D)

Hubbard believes that the Public Service Commission’s decisions have historically been tilted toward utilities over ratepayers and wants to rebalance that relationship. He called for implementing “performance-based rate making,” which would, for example, reward Georgia Power for improvements to the grid or provide penalties for grid deterioration, instead of guaranteeing profits.

“A quick example would be to look at those reliability statistics of the last five years and set a baseline, and then give them a carrot if they can improve that over time, and a stick if they get worse, and that’s one way to redirect those incentives,” Hubbard said.

He also proposed ending automatic approvals for gas utilities rates and wants them to formally justify their rates in traditional rate case hearings.

“The gas utilities have not had to come in and justify their costs in a traditional rate case in years. They just drew up the numbers year after year,” Hubbard said.

Hubbard also supports strengthening the PSC consumer affairs department that helps with resolving complaints and can investigate violations, as well as educating consumers about their rights.

Peter Hubbard (D)

In the short term, Hubbard proposed tapping into the $25 million Universal Service Fund that is funded by natural gas companies to help lower income households with their monthly gas bills instead of funding further fossil fuel expansion.

“We can use it to expand natural gas infrastructure and lock more people into dirty pollution and fossil fuels in their homes, or we can use it to help pay down folks’ gas bills, low- to moderate-income customers. That’s an immediate thing that we can do,” Hubbard said.

In the long term, he proposed expanding access to residential and community solar energy to reduce monthly electric bills. He also proposed creating a bill calculator tool to help residents identify and switch to one of Georgia Power’s seven residential plans that might be cheaper.

“We need to be investing more in things like resiliency hubs. A church that would have solar panels on its roof and a battery in the basement, where the community can come to in a time of need to recharge their batteries or keep their medicine cold or whatever it may be,” Hubbard said.

Fitz Johnson (R)

Johnson pointed to the rule the PSC approved last year aimed at protecting residential ratepayers from paying for the infrastructure data centers require, which he said “is now helping drive energy bills down.” He said that there is more the commission can do, but also that costs, not just those related to energy, are going up across the board.

“My record of delivering affordability is proven,” Johnson said.

Johnson said that one of the key differences between him and Hubbard is their approach to the state’s energy mix, in which he said that he’d consider deploying all sources of energy to meet the state’s needs.

“I am an all-of-the-above believer, and he would drive Georgia to fulfill green energy mandates regardless of their impacts to Georgians’ monthly bills,” Johnson said.

Peter Hubbard (D)

Hubbard believes that Georgia Power is overreliant on fossil fuels and proposed a fast transition towards renewables, such as solar and battery storage, saying that Georgia is behind on transitioning from fossil fuel sources to clean energy. He said that the state should focus on deploying renewable energy as much as possible.

“There are real benefits to clean energy, and we’re oversubscribed on the fossil fuel side. The United States is building clean energy. 90% of the power plants are solar, wind and batteries, and somehow in Georgia we’re building mostly fossil fuel,” Hubbard said.

Hubbard also supports net metering, which is an electricity billing system that credits solar panel owners for the excess electricity they send back to the energy grid, saying that families could see their bills drop dramatically, especially in summer months when the sun shines the longest.

Peter Hubbard (D)

Hubbard said that data centers now need an unprecedented amount of energy because of the rise of artificial intelligence, pointing to the recent PSC decision to expand the energy infrastructure by up to 10 gigawatts, and he is concerned that they aren’t paying for the full cost of that infrastructure.

“We’re talking about the next five years doubling what Georgia Power has already built to meet peak load. That has real implications for us because we not only have to pay for these power plants and there’s open questions to whether or not the data centers are truly covering their costs, but also we have to live with these power plants,” Hubbard said.

He wants to ensure that data centers fully cover the cost of building that infrastructure instead of possibly passing that down to residential ratepayers in the long-term.

“I think about data centers as who’s really going to be paying those costs, and I’m trying to look holistically at all of the different costs and if there are benefits, who gets those benefits,” Hubbard said.

text:
U.S. Department of Energy Assistant Secretary for Electricity Katie Jereza on Oct. 14 joined Indiana Secretary of Energy and Natural Resources Suzanne Jaworowski and state energy representatives at the Indiana Municipal Power Agency's Carmel, Indiana, headquarters. The event brought together federal, state, and local partners to showcase a unified effort to deploy creative solutions for a more robust energy grid.

The visit put a spotlight on ongoing grid modernization and infrastructure resilience grant projects awarded to IMPA, Centerville, Indiana, and Middletown, Indiana. Together, these three grants represent more than $1.8 million in investments.

The three investments are actively transforming local utility infrastructure across the state:

Indiana Municipal Power Agency

IMPA is investing more than $255,000 to install two advanced software programs -- True Grid Reliability Analytics (TGRA) and Tantalus Transformer Analytics (TTA) -- to monitor the IMPA AMI system operated on behalf of participating members. This technology uses predictive data to fix grid vulnerabilities before they cause problems, leading to fewer outages and faster power restoration times when disruptions do happen.

Town of Centerville

Utilizing $1.1 million to upgrade aging, lower voltage distribution circuits into modern, higher voltage and more efficient distribution circuits. The work also includes replacing aged poles and clearing hazardous vegetation to reduce system interference and outages.

Town of Middletown

Deploying a $474,000 smart, advanced metering infrastructure to actively monitor the local distribution system, pinpoint outage locations and other electric issues, and enable faster response to power interruptions caused by severe weather, high winds, and storms common to central Indiana.

"These grants enable IMPA and our members to make intentional, impactful investments in communities across the state, strengthening the resilience of local electrical infrastructure and safeguarding it for the future," said Jack Alvey, IMPA President and CEO. "These investments will make a tangible, daily difference in the lives of everyday Hoosiers."

“Electricity powers more than homes and businesses. It powers opportunity,” said Jereza. “By modernizing Indiana’s electric grid today, we’re laying the groundwork for communities to attract new industries, create jobs, and power an economy ready for tomorrow.”

"Today’s visit recognizes and acknowledges the hard work Indiana is doing to ensure affordability and reliability for all Hoosiers," Jaworowski said. "These two crucial focal points of Governor Braun’s agenda go hand in hand. Projects like the ones we are recognizing today advance Governor Braun's affordability focus by implementing energy improvements to reduce recurring costs and improve quality of life."

As Indiana's economy demands more power, state and federal partnerships are driving smart grid strategies to match escalating needs, the Indiana Office of Energy Development noted.

The investments target three core objectives of Indiana's Grid Resilience Program: reducing the frequency and duration of power interruptions, fortifying the grid against natural disasters to protect critical community services, and investing in a highly skilled, well-paid workforce.

Jon Ford, Executive Director of the Indiana Office of Energy Development, emphasized that the funding translates into direct, visible benefits for local communities.

title: In Texas and New Mexico, AI data centers threaten to undo multimillion-dollar climate plans
description:

text:
New Mexico and El Paso each adopted climate plans to cut emissions sharply by 2050.

But near the Texas-New Mexico border, three huge data center projects linked to the AI boom could swamp those goals with pollution from the power plants expected to keep them running, according to El Paso Matters.

Here's what to know

Within about half an hour of one another are three major sites: Oracle's Project Jupiter in Doña Ana County, Meta's data center in northeast El Paso, and a proposed third campus at Fort Bliss.

Together, the three developments could add millions of tons of greenhouse gases and release other pollutants that will worsen air quality in the region.

The two projects with disclosed power plans — Oracle's and Meta's — could produce as much as 10 million tons of climate-heating pollution a year. That is more than the 8.4 million tons emitted in 2019 across El Paso and neighboring Hudspeth counties.

Dave DuBois, New Mexico's state climatologist, warned the projects are "going to undo a lot of the very expensive and very meaningful work a lot of people are doing."

Surging demand for AI tools such as Claude and ChatGPT is driving the rapid build-out.

That technology can help streamline operations and improve how systems are managed, including in the energy sector, but it also requires enormous amounts of electricity and water.

In El Paso and southern New Mexico, that has fueled concerns about more pollution, grid strain, and higher household energy costs.

More background

Their scale is massive, but the system overseeing them is patchwork.

With developments split between two states and no single federal rule that fully covers climate pollution, regulators mostly evaluate each project on its own.

Ari Peskoe of Harvard Law School, who directs the Electricity Law Initiative, addressed the underlying issue.

"We've never had a national climate law passed by Congress. And so what we've had in this country are primarily state and local efforts," Peskoe explained.

That means nearby communities have limited sway over projects just across a state line.

Sarah Silva, a Democratic New Mexico state representative, represents Chaparral across the border from Meta's site, but New Mexico's authority stops there.

West El Paso residents share an aquifer with Project Jupiter, but they have no formal say over the New Mexico project.

According to Climate Central, El Paso has warmed faster than nearly any other American city since 1970, and the National Weather Service said 2026 was the hottest year on record there through the first nine months.

Shaolei Ren, who teaches electrical and computer engineering at the University of California, Riverside, said even relatively modest increases in pollution are detrimental.

"The health impacts can be significant for local communities."

What's being done?

Major regulatory disputes continue to slow the projects.

Oracle filed Project Jupiter's air permit in April, and New Mexico officials have spent months reviewing it, while court challenges over the approval process and groundwater use have delayed a public hearing.

The state Supreme Court lifted that stay, and an examiner was appointed to run the hearing.

In Texas, El Paso Electric is still seeking approval from the Public Utility Commission to build the natural gas plant planned next to Meta's facility.

Gov. Greg Abbott has also said data centers should pay for their own infrastructure and has pushed lawmakers to consider new rules on water and electricity use, though those ideas do not directly address climate pollution.

After initially backing legislation that gave certain off-grid facilities a 20-year exemption from clean-energy rules, Silva later said she "would support a moratorium."

Oracle has claimed it aims for net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2031 and is "committed to building Project Jupiter responsibly and incorporating community feedback into our planning."

DuBois noted that the shift feels like a step backward in a border region already dealing with extreme heat.

"If we started to do these kinds of things — having big data centers with natural gas-fired turbines — it's kind of like bringing back a lot of the retired plants that were more dirty, like coal."

Where can I learn more?

These stories look at how AI's rapid expansion is colliding with energy, water, and climate pressures in Texas and New Mexico. They cover gas-backed data center power plans, local resistance, and the broader surge in electricity demand.

• Across the US, AI data centers hit a tipping point in electricity demand.

title: NC State University, Toyota power workforce of future | FOX8 WGHP
description:
North Carolina State University decided it was time to change.
“I’ve been at NC State for three years, and when I arrived here, we were embarking on an initiative known as Engineering North Carolina’s Future.
Toyota built its first lithium-ion battery plant just up the road in Liberty and is already collaborating with NC State.
Toyota has a product to produce, and so does NC State.
We have a lot of faculty here at NC State who are studying what comes next.” For NC State, this is about being as adaptable as a university as businesses have to be in the marketplace.
text:
(WGHP) — For a couple of generations, colleges and universities have done little to evolve the way they taught students. North Carolina State University decided it was time to change.

“I’ve been at NC State for three years, and when I arrived here, we were embarking on an initiative known as Engineering North Carolina’s Future. With support from the North Carolina General Assembly, we’ve been asked to grow our engineering workforce and our graduates to meet the growing demand here in North Carolina and beyond,” NC State Provost Jim Pfaendtner said.

To do that, they decided that they needed to blend the traditional classroom lecture with more of an apprentice style of education, and the result was the university’s first makerspace.

“A makerspace is a concept that’s evolved in the last two decades in higher education, designed to teach students at the same time as they’re doing,” Pfaendtner said. “So our motto here at NC State is Think and Do. Every opportunity we get to give students hands-on experiences while they’re learning, we take that opportunity because we know it makes better engineers and scientists.”

Corporations located in North Carolina want in on the idea. Toyota built its first lithium-ion battery plant just up the road in Liberty and is already collaborating with NC State. Toyota has a product to produce, and so does NC State.

“The product from a university is our students,” said Peter Fedkiw, an NC State professor who will work with students in the makerspace. “We are generating the workforce of tomorrow. So we’re running through the first cohort of students who are going through this laboratory experience here at NC State. Most of those students are undergraduates. So they’ll end up with a bachelor’s degree and enter the workforce. So if you want a time frame for … when they start looking for jobs, two to three years.”

As FOX8 looked at the space, we asked the NC State team running it if there were any chance lithium-ion batteries might go the way of the music compact disc, which had a brilliant 20-year career until streaming made them obsolete.

“The timeline of change in energy storage is pretty long,” said Shelby Pillai, a post-doctoral researcher at NC State who teaches the students in the makerspace. “From whenever the first Prius came out, I remember I was in high school, and my dad was talking about Priuses to now. That’s been a long time where we’re still adopting electric vehicles. And so for something like that, the adoption ramp is pretty long. And so there will continue to be need for knowledge of lithium-ion batteries because that’s now kind of like our base. We have a lot of faculty here at NC State who are studying what comes next.”

For NC State, this is about being as adaptable as a university as businesses have to be in the marketplace.

“We realized we can’t just become bigger. That doesn’t mean you’re better,” Pfaendtner said. “We need to adapt engineering curricula to where the jobs are going to be, where the highest technology, where the demand is going to be and, importantly, where the innovation is going to be.”

WASHINGTON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - California said on Friday nearly 12,000 residents bought electric vehicles using rebates under a new $270 million program funded by the state and automakers.

Still, overall EV sales have fallen both in California and nationwide as President Donald Trump's administration has removed federal incentives for EVs. EV sales are up globally.

text:
The NC Department of Environmental Quality’s Division of Air Quality is providing an additional week to submit public comments on the draft air quality permit for Carolina Lithium, a proposed lithium mine and processing facility in Gaston County.

Public comments must now be submitted by Oct. 23, 2026.

DEQ held a public hearing to receive comments on Oct. 13. The audio recording for that hearing is available online.

Carolina Lithium, owned and operated by Piedmont Lithium Carolinas Inc., applied for a major-source Title V air quality permit, a federal air quality permit required for facilities whose operations have the potential to emit air pollutants above certain thresholds. The proposed permit would allow emissions associated with mining, crushing and handling of spodumene ore, a key source of lithium for batteries, as well as processing and concentrating the ore into lithium hydroxide at on-site plants.

The facility’s potential emissions of particle pollution, nitrogen oxides and carbon monoxide are each above the threshold that triggers a Prevention of Significant Deterioration review to ensure that the emissions will not cause a violation of federal ambient air quality standards.

DEQ’s review found that the emissions, controlled by the best available control technology required in the draft permit, are expected to maintain the state’s compliance with federal air quality standards, including the more stringent fine particle pollution standard set by the Environmental Protection Agency in 2024. These federal standards are protective of public health, including the health of sensitive groups like children and older adults, as well as public welfare, including protection against decreased visibility and damage to animals, crops, vegetation, and buildings.

The facility’s emissions of hazardous air pollutants would be capped to minor source levels, meaning the facility must keep hazardous air pollutant emissions below 10 tons per year for any single pollutant and below 25 tons per year for all pollutants combined. Remaining below these limits triggers a different set of federal standards designed for lower-emitting facilities.

The facility would be subject to multiple federal performance standards. Air dispersion modeling determined that emissions of toxic air pollutants are not expected to violate health-based air quality levels.

Carolina Lithium received a mining permit from DEQ’s Division of Energy, Mineral, and Land Resources in 2024 to operate the 1,548-acre mine. The draft air quality permit would require the facility to comply with any applicable local zoning regulations before it could begin construction and operation.

Copies of the public notice, draft permit, draft permit review, permit application and a one-page fact sheet are available online.

The public is encouraged to review these materials and provide comments. Comments can be submitted by email to DAQ.publiccomments@deq.nc.gov with the subject line “CarolinaLithium.22A” or by leaving a voicemail at 919-707-8714.

Comments can also be mailed to:

NCDEQ Division of Air Quality

1628 Mail Service Center

Raleigh, North Carolina 27699-1628

The public comment period ends on Oct. 23, 2026. DAQ will consider all public comments before making a final decision on the proposed permit.

text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - A new report from Environment America found that 83% of water samples collected across the United States tested positive for PFAS, also known as forever chemicals.

A U.S. Geological Survey study found nearly half of tap water in the country contains forever chemicals. Bottled water also contains the chemicals.

Trey Sherard, Anacostia Riverkeeper, said, “Their solution? Bottled water may be just a different toxin.”

Where the chemicals come from

PFAS are used in many everyday products. The chemicals are what make non-stick cookware non-stick. Products branded as waterproof or stain-resistant are also likely to contain PFAS.

The chemicals are known carcinogens, specifically linked to ovarian and testicular cancer. They can also cause infertility, and in children, developmental delays.

The biggest sources of PFAS entering water supplies are industrial runoff and firefighting foam.

Calls for regulation

Environment America is calling attention to the issue.

Lisa Frank, who heads Environment America said, “When we allow the use of toxic chemicals and we allow those chemicals to get into our environment without considering the downstream consequences, the problem can get out of hand very quickly,” adding “Removing all those parts from our environment is going to be a very tall order. But stopping new people’s contamination can start right now.”

The organization is calling on lawmakers to take action. U.S. Rep. Paul Tonko, D-New York, is calling for an overhaul of the Safe Drinking Water Act to include forever chemicals.

Tonko said, “Americans deserve to have confidence and peace of mind that when they turn on the tap, they’re being delivered safe, safe drinking water.”

Some of the worst contamination can be found in the Northeast and along the northern Mississippi River.

text:
WASHINGTON — A record-breaking $3.3 billion loan from the U.S. Department of Agriculture to a power plant in Georgia‘s Monroe County could potentially benefit data centers in the state, the agency’s head of rural development said in an interview with Reuters.

The administration of President Donald Trump has supported the rapid expansion of data centers, despite their unpopularity with communities concerned about water use and utility costs. Democrats are attempting to capitalize on that discontent in November’s midterm elections.

Glen Smith, the USDA’s Under Secretary for Rural Development, said in the Thursday interview that he hopes to secure more funding for such projects.

Here are more details:

• The USDA announced on Tuesday the loan to Oglethorpe Power Corporation, the largest ever given under the agency’s Rural Utilities Service.

• Smith said the plant will serve 38 rural utility cooperatives and support growing industry in the state, including potentially data centers.

• Last year, Google purchased nearly 1,000 acres of land in Monroe County for a data center.

• Oglethorpe spokesperson Blair Romero said in an email, “This facility is not dedicated to serving a data center. The new facility will help our Member cooperatives meet growing electricity demand across their communities.”

• Smith said he plans to meet with congressional appropriators next week and request more money for such loans. “We have almost $8.6 billion in requests, and we’re only into our fiscal year one month,” he said.

• Smith said rural areas can benefit from data centers, “but you have to have the infrastructure in place. and that’s where rural utilies and rural development comes into play.”

• Data centers are driving US electricity use to record highs and in some regions, demanding more power than grids can supply.

• The Trump administration has not sought to regulate data center construction, instead asking tech companies to pledge not to pass on electricity costs to consumers.

title: What Does It Say That Elon Musk Finds It Easier To Build A Flying Car Than A Cheap EV?
description:
The Morning Dump is going to dip once more into the controversial world of Elon Musk, even though some of you may be sick of hearing about it.
Why not end with a low-mileage Ferrari F50 going up for auction then?
Musk is the richest man in the world and can use that money to impact politics in a way that should be unconstitutional.
Tesla was once planning to build a sub-$25,000 car, but then reversed course, with Musk saying that building a sub-$25,000 car would be “silly” and “pointless.” That a cheap EV is more silly and pointless than a car that maybe flies, says something about the present moment and Musk’s view of the world.
Ohhhh Low Mileage Ferrari F50 There’s something a little bothersome about buying a car like a Ferrari F50 and never driving it, especially when at least a few hundred were built.
text:
Last night, two major automakers revealed two maybe important cars. Porsche showed off a preview of its above-911 supercar, and Tesla showed a flying Roadster that, curiously, wasn’t a roadster at all. What’s notable here is that neither of these cars are going to be affordable to the vast majority of people reading this.

The Morning Dump is going to dip once more into the controversial world of Elon Musk, even though some of you may be sick of hearing about it. After that, I might as well talk about the price of steel, because the price of steel is going up, and that’ll probably impact cars. Lexus, too, has been consumed by fancy cars, and now it’s going to have to redirect some slightly-less-fancy cars from China and the Middle East to make up for the lack of normal cars on the lot.

This is a fancy car TMD, eh? Why not end with a low-mileage Ferrari F50 going up for auction then?

Maybe There Are More Customers For A $250,000 EV Sports Car Than A $25,000 Family EV

As I often have to do when Elon Musk appears, let me start by saying that there’s never been more of a gap between how interesting or impressive it is to write about a product and how annoying it is to write about its ostensible creator. It’s clear based on comments yesterday that many of you have strong feelings about Musk; in the interest of full disclosure, I have plenty of reasons to dislike him as well. (DOGE destroyed the work of good people I know, I was a big Twitter fan, his good buddy is the reason why my kid’s first college fund went to Hulk Hogan, blah blah blah).

Musk is the richest man in the world and can use that money to impact politics in a way that should be unconstitutional. That definitely gives him power, though — as much as anger towards Musk can be cathartic — part of me thinks there’s a danger in acting like anyone is some all-powerful being, because the illusion itself is where much of that power actually resides. Personally, I think he’s someone with little shame and bizarre ideas of how the world works, which sometimes allows him to create products others might not see the value in (like the initial, actually roadster-like Tesla Roadster and Model S). Maybe you view him as some sort of amazing anti-hero; I don’t really care either way.

As the man more responsible for the success of electric cars as a product than any other person alive, I think it’s interesting that his next move is not a sub-$25,000 car, but a flying one that’ll cost at least $200,000 and is targeted at a small percentage of the population. Why is that?

Tesla was once planning to build a sub-$25,000 car, but then reversed course, with Musk saying that building a sub-$25,000 car would be “silly” and “pointless.” That a cheap EV is more silly and pointless than a car that maybe flies, says something about the present moment and Musk’s view of the world.

Specifically, Musk sees the world as autonomous. From an investor call earlier this year:

So, I think we’ve made very clear that we’re — the future is autonomous. I mean, it’s going to be — I’ve actually said this many years ago, but that in my strong belief and I believe that is panning out to be true, very obvious retrospect is that the future is autonomous electric vehicles. And nonautonomous gasoline vehicles here will be like riding a horse and using a foot bone. It’s not that there are no horses.

Yes, there are some but they’re unusual. They’re niche. And so, everything is going to be electric autonomous. I think this is like it should be, frankly, blindingly obvious at this point, that is the future.

So, a lot of automotive companies, most of the companies have not internalized this, which is surprising because we’re shouting from the rooftops for such a long time.

The cheap self-driving Tesla EV became the Cybercab, and the idea is that it’s a car you’d own, and also allow to be used as an autonomous cab when you don’t need it. This means that your car can actually start generating revenue. Will this ever happen? Who knows, but it’s clear that a world in which a Roadster exists is also a world where cheap EVs are less important. To some degree, cheap EVs are less sexy and maybe better left to Chinese automakers.

If we extrapolate that a little further, though, there are two kinds of people in this future. If you’re not extremely wealthy, you don’t really get to enjoy driving. Instead, you’re getting driven around from place-to-place. If you want something super cool and fun the only way that works is if you’re extremely rich.

This is contrast to an automaker like Toyota or Ford, which offers a variety of fun to drive vehicles at various price points.

Steel Isn’t Exactly A Steal

Fun fact: Most cars are still made up of a lot of steel. As Bloomberg reports, steel is getting more expensive:

US steel prices climbed to the highest in more than four years as President Donald Trump’s tariffs restrict foreign supplies, boosting domestic producers while raising costs for American manufacturers.

Pricing for hot-rolled coil, a widely used form of steel that serves as a US benchmark, has been on a steady upward trajectory for the past year, rising 52% to $1,255 per short ton, according to Fasmarkets. The last time prices touched that level was May 2022.

Inflation poses a major challenge for Trump’s Republican Party heading into the midterm elections, and the steel rally underscores the impact of tariffs and his push to revive American steelmaking. What’s proven to be a boon for domestic mills and steelworkers has been a burden for manufacturers, builders and data-center developers.

Hot-rolled Coil is a great name for a band, just saying.

Lexus Will Shift Some Cars From China And The Middle East To The United States

Lexus has among the tightest inventories, second only to Toyota. With China and the Middle East seeing a tougher sales environment, it sounds like vehicles will be rerouted from those regions to the United States.

Per Automotive News:

About 10 percent of the windfall — roughly 3,500 vehicles — will consist of the high-demand GX off-roader, with the remainder spread across core nameplates including the RX, NX, and ES.

Ross noted that despite the lack of inventory, September was still the best in the brand’s history. However, its chances of achieving a third consecutive year of U.S. sales records will depend almost entirely on whether it can get enough vehicles to sell.

It’s a good problem to have.

Ohhhh Low Mileage Ferrari F50

There’s something a little bothersome about buying a car like a Ferrari F50 and never driving it, especially when at least a few hundred were built. It’s not my car, though, so the owner of this Ferrari F50 holding onto it and then selling it some years later at the Broad Arrow Auction in Las Vegas is his or her business.

Here are some details, though:

According to the research of Ferrari historian Marcel Massini, chassis 107165 began assembly in Maranello on 27 June 1997, and was completed and invoiced on 6 August. It was dispatched that December to Maranello Concessionaires, the official U.K. importer, and its factory warranty commenced on 31 December 1997. The F50 was later exported to Japan, where it spent many years as part of a significant private collection in Kashiwa, Chiba Prefecture, near Tokyo, and it was still recorded there in 2008. By 2015, it had joined the stable of a prominent Chinese supercar collector who stored his cars in Düsseldorf, Germany, and it was serviced that June by Rosso Scuderia. Eberlein Automobile GmbH of Kassel, Germany, serviced the car in March 2021 and again in February 2025. It was recently imported to the United States in preparation for the sale.

Ferrari built the F50 to be driven hard, and most surviving examples show at least some evidence of it, but this example has been entirely spared from the moment it was delivered. As a result, its paintwork, carbon-fiber cabin, leather upholstery, and switchgear are free of the fading, wear, and handling marks that even careful use brings. The car presents today much as it would have on the day Maranello Sales handed it over. Additionally, it has received a fresh service and a Ferrari Classiche inspection at Ferrari of Newport Beach.

If I had absolutely stupid money it would be great to buy this and put some real miles on it.

What I’m Listening To While Writing TMD

There’s a new Olivia Rodrigo video, featuring Chappell Roan and, uh, David Byrne as the host of a game show. Please enjoy “expectations.”

The Big Question

Which automaker has the most egalitarian lineup?
