AI data centers use water directly to cool their equipment, but also indirectly to create the power on which they run.
text:
The staggering rise of AI has become a political flashpoint, especially when it comes to the data centers needed to train and operate it.

As the industry booms, many people are increasingly worried about the environmental impacts of these hulking buildings, from their seemingly insatiable demand for water and energy, to the heat and noise they produce.

Nearly 90% of Americans say they’re more concerned than excited about the rise of AI data centers, according to a CNN poll conducted by SSRS in September.

Information and statistics are flying around, with some groups framing the AI data center boom as a potential environmental catastrophe, while others say concerns are overblown or even fake. It’s adding up to a confusing picture.

So, just how bad is AI for the environment?

Well, to be annoying, it’s complicated. The impacts of each data center depend on a slew of factors, including where it’s located, the kind of electricity that powers it and the technology it uses.

There is also a dearth of fully transparent and detailed data from AI providers, making it tricky to build an accurate picture of impacts. Instead, we rely on estimates.

To make the whole picture even more challenging, it’s difficult to project future impacts because there is so little certainty about how AI technology and demand will develop.

But here’s what we can say at the moment:

It has big energy demands…

Training and running AI models require large amounts of computing power, and that takes a ton of energy.

AI’s energy efficiency is improving at a fast clip, but more people are using the technology and there’s been a boom in particularly energy-intensive forms.

Simple text queries, for example, typically use less electricity than a TV would over the same time period, according an analysis by the International Energy Agency. But, more energy-intensive applications, such as video generation, sometimes require thousands of times more energy. The electricity consumption of AI data centers surged by 50% last year, the IEA found.

Around 0.5% of the world’s electricity was consumed by AI data centers in 2025, according to an analysis from Our World in Data, which projects that figure will reach 1.5% by 2030.

It might sound small, but data centers are very geographically concentrated. Nearly half of their global electricity consumption happens in the United States, where data centers could account for up to 12% of electricity consumption by 2028 as AI rapidly expands, according to an analysis from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

… and that means climate (and health) impacts

Because the world’s electricity is still dominated by fossil fuels, it adds up to more planet-heating pollution. There are big concerns that the AI boom is pushing climate targets even further out of reach.

Where a data center gets its power from is key; the more clean energy is on the grid, the lower its climate impact. Currently, global data centers are powered mostly by coal (30%), followed by renewables at 27% and natural gas at 26%.

As AI electricity demand soars, some is being met with clean energy, but there are also plenty of planet-warming fossil fuels in the mix.

Natural gas is emerging as a key data center power source in the US. The country has the most gas-fired power capacity in development globally, with more than a third intended to power AI, according to a January report from Global Energy Monitor.

Data centers are increasingly building their own energy infrastructure to avoid straining local grids and driving up people’s bills. This often takes the form of gas turbines, which are less efficient than big power plants and can not only bring hefty climate impacts but also health costs, due to harmful air pollution, including nitrogen oxides and fine particulate matter.

The public health burden of US data centers could reach $20 billion by 2028, according to one recent study.

It’s thirsty for water

There’s an oft-cited statistic that a 100-word email generated by an AI chatbot requires about one bottle of water — just over 2 cups — to produce.

But there’s another estimate, from Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, who says the average ChatGPT query uses about one fifteenth of a teaspoon of water.

So which is right? As with many data center impacts, it depends on context and on what people choose to measure.

AI data centers use water directly to cool their equipment, but also indirectly to create the power on which they run.

The water impacts of an individual data center will depend on its specific circumstances: the technology it uses, the kind of energy it relies on and the local water situation.

Some regions, for example, have plentiful water resources; others face high stress. Around two-thirds of data centers built or in construction in the US since 2022 are in areas of water stress, according to a 2025 Bloomberg analysis.

Tech companies say they are introducing measures to slash water use, including by developing new cooling technologies. Some analysts say water concerns have been vastly overestimated and that the burger you eat or cotton shirt you wear require much more water.

But AI’s water impacts are far from minimal. US data centers could consume up to 110 billion gallons a year by 2030, equivalent to 7% of total annual consumptive use in US public water systems, according to a March analysis by scientists from the University of California, Riverside and other institutions.

Indirect water use for electricity could push this figure much higher. A recent report from Ceres, a nonprofit advocacy organization, analyzed data centers across seven states and found they used around 3.4 trillion gallons of freshwater a year for electricity generation, equivalent to roughly 12 times the annual water use of Los Angeles, Phoenix and Washington, DC, combined.

It can be a noisy neighbor

Some of the key concerns people have about data centers revolve around quality of life impacts — including noise pollution.

Data centers can produce a cacophony of noises: the low thrum of cooling systems, the drone of gas turbines or diesel generators and the humming of equipment.

Some communities have filed noise pollution lawsuits, including residents near a huge data center in Vineland, New Jersey.

There are steps data centers can take to reduce their impact, including soundproofing equipment and the building itself. Some experts are urging state and local governments to beef up noise regulations.

It could increase temperatures

There are also fears the data centers could create “heat islands,” warming the air and land around them — a phenomenon that would add to the temperature rises already happening due to fossil fuel pollution.

A study by scientists at Arizona State University found data center heat pollution in Phoenix warmed downwind neighborhoods by as much as 4 degrees Fahrenheit.

“Even if these data centers only contribute to an additional heat island magnitude of 1 degree or 2 degrees, that can still have a very significant impact on our lives,” said lead author David Sailor, director of ASU’s School of Geographical Sciences and Urban Planning.

More research is needed, however, to really pin down these impacts, and some experts argue there is little difference between a data center and any other industrial facility when it comes to heat.

It’s hungry for critical minerals

One of the more overlooked aspects of AI are the minerals and metals it requires, including for semiconductors and data storage components.

Mining for these raw materials, often in the Global South, has been linked to air and water pollution, deforestation, human health risks and climate pollution.

And as AI scales and advances, it will generate electronic waste, a rapidly-growing waste stream that is toxic if not disposed of properly. Currently only about a fifth of e-waste is recycled.

There’s also concern that AI’s demand for these minerals put it in direct competition with sectors that are critical for reducing planet heating pollution, namely wind and solar energy.

Ultimately AI’s impacts depend on us

Experts say AI’s environmental harms are not locked in. Instead, its impacts will depend on the choices we make: Where data centers are located, how they are powered, how they are regulated, how transparent AI providers must be about impacts along their full supply chains.

Before a new AI data center is built, it needs to be clear “who benefits from it,” said Kaveh Madani, director of the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health. That includes asking questions like: Does it bring jobs? Will it improve the local economy? Will it take water from local users who need it more, like farmers?

“There are trade-offs like any other technology,” Madani said. “It has has downsides that need to be regulated, monitored, and mitigated.”

Keynote speaker Katharine Wilkinson speaks at Sun Valley Resort on Tuesday during the Mountain Towns 2030 annual Climate Summit.

Speakers addressing a crowd of hundreds of climate activists, public officials, sustainability experts and ski resort executives at Sun Valley Resort on Tuesday found unity in one message: The movement to halt climate change is facing substantial challenges, but action on the local level can keep it influential.

“There is hope in action in local communities,” said Benjamin Backer, founder and CEO of the nonprofit organization Nature is Nonpartisan, which works to establish—and expand—the environmental movement as politically neutral.

Backer was joined on stage by filmmaker and producer Nadia Gill for a moderated keynote panel discussion during the two-day Mountain Towns 2030 Climate Summit in Sun Valley this week. The discussion was followed by a keynote speech by Katharine Wilkinson, author of the book “Climate Wayfinding: Healing Ourselves and the Planet We Call Home.”

Mountain Towns 2030 is a nonprofit organization that works to assist a network of North American mountain towns to take action to reduce climate emissions and promote sustainability, thereby helping them to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2030. It holds an annual conference in one of its so-called “anchor communities,” which include Blaine County and the city of Ketchum. It also has affiliations with the city of Hailey and Sun Valley Resort.

In the panel discussion, Backer emphasized his work to bring conservatives into the environmental-protection movement in the U.S. A onetime solid conservative himself, Backer said he now identifies as a “politically homeless independent.”

Statistics indicate that 90% of Americans care about the environment but only 7% say they are involved in protecting nature, Backer said. He wants to mobilize the other 83%, he said.

“No one’s at the table when it comes to the environment,” he said.

A critical element of bringing more people to the table is taking the politics out of how Americans view nature and environmental issues. His goal is to have 5 million new Americans involved in environmental protection by 2035, to create “the most nature-connected generation” the country has seen.

A major problem, Backer said, is that politics can mislead people. He has met staunch conservatives who say they love nature but think climate change is a hoax, largely because of how it has been framed in the political realm. So, activists need to tap into people’s basic appreciation of nature, he said.

Most average Americans don’t really care about climate change, per se, he said, so leaders and activists need to get them involved in local environmental projects that they can benefit from—and possibly might have an associated positive impact on climate change.

“It’s local issues that really get people involved,” he said.

In addition, pro-environment Americans need to stop over-vilifying workers in industries they perceive as destructive. Miners are one example, he said.

“They don’t want to be pitted as the enemy,” he said. “… They’re just trying to make ends meet.”

Another reason Backer thinks environmentalists need to work from the local level up is that “the federal government is broken.”

In his work, he made efforts to work with the Trump administration on environmental issues, but those efforts—and those of others—were firmly stymied, something he called “despicable to watch.”

So, he has modified his approach to addressing the challenges facing the planet, Backer said, but he didn’t give up.

“You have to try. … You either try or you automatically lose,” he said.

The environmental movement is “down right now,” Backer said, but it has overcome major challenges in the past. Once, some of the country’s waterways were so polluted with chemicals that they caught on fire, he noted.

In the end, bringing more Americans into the pro-environment tent lies in basics and grassroots efforts, Backer said. Rather than chastising people for not taking deep dives into the climate-change movement or bombarding them with dire statistics, environmentalists should appeal to people’s appreciation for their own backyard, and what they can do to make it a better place.

“This is about the fate of our future,” Backer said.

In her keynote address, Wilkinson aimed to give the crowd inspiration to find happiness and peace in efforts to help the environment and slow climate change.

Many people feel stuck and some younger people feel “betrayed” amid the myriad setbacks and hurdles that the conservation and environmental movement has suffered, she said.

People looking to find their way toward positive action should think more about the places they love and where they go to feel joy, happiness and rejuvenation, recognizing that for many that those places are among nature. She said they should shift the question of “What can I do?” to “Who can I be?”

“Find the place where you feel thoroughly immersed and lead from there,” she said.

The environmental movement has had too much preaching and “fact touting,” Wilkinson said. Renewing Americans’ basic appreciation of nature and beautiful places can inspire motivation to action, she said. People can struggle emotionally when they try to confront climate change, she said, but connecting to nature can provide a platform for positive change.

The threat of the impacts of climate change is nonetheless real, Wilkinson said, and humans are approaching an “inevitable crossroads,” but it’s one they should greet, even if they stumble as they find their way forward.

“All of it hinges on people,” she said. “It hinges on us.” ￼ ￼

name: Clean Energy
title: Nottingham secures £20m to boost clean energy innovation and jobs
description:
The University of Nottingham will lead three new green projects following a £20 million funding grant from UK Research and Innovation.
These projects are said to be intended to help the region seize time-critical opportunities in clean energy and decarbonising propulsion – alongside partner universities, the programme is expected to add £325–340 million in gross value to the regional economy over its lifespan and will support up to 1,775 jobs.
It will be matched by at least £36 million of private sector investment.
The projects are the Advanced Manufacturing and Clean Energy Accelerator (supporting the commercialisation and development stage of the research-to-market pathway), the Next Generation Single-Aisle Hybrid-Electric Propulsion Challenge (responding to industry-led challenges and testing propulsion technologies) and the Connected Factories Programme (helping regional suppliers adopt digital, automated and low-carbon technologies).
Professor Tom Rodden, Pro-Vice-Chancellor for Research and Knowledge Exchange at the University of Nottingham, said: “We are bringing our strengths and expertise in advanced manufacturing, transport decarbonisation and industry-focused research and partnership to accelerate the development of technologies that can create growth, attract investment and deliver real-world impact.”

text:
LINYI, SHANDONG, CHINA, October 16, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ --

The global electric mobility industry continues to evolve as consumers, distributors, and commercial operators seek transportation options that combine practical design, operational efficiency, and flexible applications. Against this background, Linyi Lanshan Merco Electric Bicycle Factory is developing its presence in the electric vehicle manufacturing sector through a product portfolio that includes electric bicycles, electric motorcycles, and electric tricycles. Based in Linyi, Shandong Province, China, the company serves domestic and international customers and presents itself as a manufacturing partner for businesses seeking electric mobility products for different markets.

Electric vehicles have become an increasingly visible part of transportation planning in urban and rural areas. Rising interest in convenient short-distance travel, local delivery services, and lower-emission mobility has encouraged manufacturers to develop vehicles for a wider range of daily activities. Electric bicycles can support personal commuting, while electric motorcycles offer another option for motorized travel. Electric tricycles, meanwhile, can serve passenger transportation, leisure activities, and cargo movement. This variety has created opportunities for manufacturers to offer products suited to different customer requirements rather than relying on a single vehicle category.

For manufacturers, meeting these varied needs requires more than producing a vehicle that runs on electric power. Product design, frame structure, motor and battery configuration, riding comfort, braking systems, cargo capacity, and maintenance considerations all influence a vehicle’s suitability for its intended purpose. Companies supplying international markets must also consider differences in customer expectations, road conditions, regulations, and distribution channels.

Linyi Lanshan Merco Electric Bicycle Factory has established a product portfolio covering three principal categories: electric bicycles, electric motorcycles, and electric tricycles. Its official website organizes electric motorcycles into street motorcycle and scooter-style motorcycle categories, while its electric tricycle range includes leisure, cargo, and enclosed models. This range gives buyers several product directions to explore, from personal transportation to utility-focused vehicles and passenger-oriented designs.

Electric Motorcycles for Everyday Transportation

Electric motorcycles occupy an important position in the wider electric mobility market. Compared with conventional bicycles, they provide motorized transportation for journeys where riders may need additional speed or power, depending on the vehicle’s specifications and the regulations governing its use. Their potential applications include daily commuting, neighborhood travel, and short-distance transportation in areas where compact vehicles are practical.

Linyi Lanshan Merco Electric Bicycle Factory includes Electric Motorcycle among its product categories. Its website features street-style electric motorcycles and scooter-style electric motorcycles, offering buyers different design approaches within the same general vehicle segment. Street-style models may appeal to customers who prefer a motorcycle-inspired appearance, while scooter-style models can suit buyers looking for a familiar step-through or urban mobility design, depending on the configuration of the specific model.

Selecting an electric motorcycle involves several technical considerations. Motor output influences acceleration and the vehicle’s ability to handle different riding conditions. Battery capacity affects potential operating range, although actual distance depends on factors such as rider weight, terrain, speed, temperature, and load. Charging time, battery availability, tire dimensions, braking performance, lighting, and suspension also contribute to the overall ownership experience.

For wholesalers and distributors, the ability to compare specifications across different models is particularly important. A product intended for short urban trips may require a different configuration from one intended for longer daily journeys. Similarly, buyers in different countries may have different expectations regarding vehicle styling, power output, battery technology, and safety equipment.

Manufacturers and buyers therefore benefit from clear communication during product selection. Before placing a bulk order, distributors should confirm the exact motor and battery specifications, rated speed, charging requirements, braking configuration, warranty coverage, and any applicable market certifications. These details help ensure that the selected electric motorcycle is appropriate for its intended market and use.

Electric Tricycles for Cargo and Passenger Applications

Electric tricycles provide another important area of opportunity within the electric vehicle sector. Their three-wheel configuration allows manufacturers to develop designs for cargo transportation, leisure travel, and passenger mobility. Depending on the structure and specifications, these vehicles may be used by small businesses, delivery operators, families, older adults, and customers who require a practical alternative to two-wheel transportation.

Linyi Lanshan Merco Electric Bicycle Factory offers an Electric Tricycle product category with several configurations. Its published lineup includes leisure electric tricycles, cargo electric tricycles, and enclosed electric tricycles. Individual models listed on the company website include an Electric Weather-Proof Enclosed Trike, Electric Family Leisure Tricycle, Electric Senior Mobility Tricycle, Electric Heavy-Duty Cargo Tricycle, Electric Cargo Delivery Tricycle, and Full-Enclosed Passenger Tricycle.

This range reflects the different purposes electric tricycles can serve. Leisure models are designed around recreational or everyday personal travel. Cargo versions focus on transporting goods, making them potentially relevant to local retailers, small businesses, farms, and delivery operations. Enclosed tricycles introduce a different body design intended to provide additional shelter from weather conditions, depending on the model’s construction.

For commercial users, cargo capacity is one of the first factors to examine. The vehicle must be able to accommodate the intended goods while maintaining suitable handling and braking performance. Buyers should check the rated payload, cargo-box dimensions, frame construction, wheelbase, tire specifications, and the vehicle’s stability when loaded. Battery capacity and motor output should also be considered in relation to the expected routes and working hours.

Passenger-oriented tricycles involve a different set of requirements. Seating arrangement, ease of entry and exit, visibility, lighting, suspension, and protective bodywork may affect user comfort and convenience. Where enclosed models are concerned, buyers should verify the actual enclosure design, ventilation, weather protection, and available safety features rather than assuming that all models provide the same level of protection.

For distributors serving mixed customer groups, a product portfolio that includes leisure, cargo, and enclosed tricycles can create opportunities to address multiple market segments. However, each vehicle should be evaluated according to its own technical specifications, intended application, and local regulatory requirements.

Customization and Product Selection for Business Buyers

Customization is an important consideration for companies sourcing electric vehicles for resale or distribution. Retailers may need products that fit local consumer preferences, while importers may seek model variations that align with their existing product ranges. Differences in styling, colors, equipment, packaging, and branding can influence how a product is positioned in a particular market.

Linyi Lanshan Merco Electric Bicycle Factory presents itself as a supplier that supports customized services. Its website describes customer-oriented operations and highlights production, research and development, testing, quality standards, and service support as areas of focus. These capabilities are relevant to business buyers evaluating potential manufacturing partners, although the exact scope of customization should be confirmed for each model and order.

OEM and customized sourcing arrangements can involve several discussions before production begins. Buyers may need to identify the intended user group, target price range, preferred design, required motor and battery configuration, and expected order volume. They may also need to confirm the availability of branding options, color choices, accessories, manuals, packaging, and spare parts.

Sample approval and specification confirmation are important steps in this process. A detailed product specification helps both parties establish a shared understanding of the vehicle being supplied. It should identify the relevant components and technical parameters, as well as any agreed testing, packaging, labeling, or documentation requirements. For international orders, the destination market and its regulatory requirements should be discussed before the final configuration is approved.

The company’s electric vehicle categories give prospective buyers a starting point for these discussions. Rather than selecting solely by appearance, importers can compare available models according to the needs of their customers. A distributor specializing in urban transportation may focus on electric motorcycles and commuter-oriented vehicles, while a business serving agricultural or commercial users may give greater attention to cargo tricycles.

Manufacturing Quality and Product Testing

Quality management is central to electric vehicle manufacturing because a finished vehicle brings together mechanical, electrical, and structural components. Frame integrity, weld quality, fasteners, electrical connections, battery installation, motor operation, brakes, tires, and lighting all contribute to the final product. A problem in one area can affect reliability, maintenance needs, or user safety.

According to its official website, Linyi Lanshan Merco Electric Bicycle Factory operates a factory covering approximately 10,000 square meters and employs more than 50 people. The company also describes its research and development and testing capabilities, professional technical team, quality-control team, and testing laboratory as part of its manufacturing operations. These are company-reported details that prospective buyers can use as a starting point for further supplier evaluation.

For wholesale customers, it is useful to understand how quality is managed throughout production. Incoming component inspection can help identify inconsistencies before assembly begins. During assembly, checks may focus on mechanical connections, wiring, component installation, and conformity with the approved specifications. Final inspection can then verify the operation of key systems before packaging and dispatch.

Electric vehicle buyers should also ask how battery and charging components are sourced and tested. Battery compatibility, protection systems, charger specifications, and handling procedures are important considerations in electric vehicle supply chains. Clear documentation and suitable after-sales support can help distributors manage customer questions and reduce confusion when maintenance is required.

Quality evaluation should not be limited to a single pre-shipment check. Buyers placing repeat orders may want to establish consistent specifications, inspection criteria, and procedures for addressing defects or component changes. Maintaining these records can help both parties compare production batches and resolve issues more efficiently.

Linyi Lanshan Merco Electric Bicycle Factory states that it maintains strict quality standards and has international certifications. Buyers should request the relevant documents and confirm their scope, validity, and applicability to the specific models being purchased. Certification requirements can differ by destination and vehicle category, so verification is an important part of international procurement.

International Markets and Supply Chain Coordination

International distribution presents opportunities for electric vehicle manufacturers, but it also introduces additional operational requirements. Buyers need to coordinate product specifications, production schedules, shipping arrangements, import documentation, spare parts, and after-sales responsibilities. These factors can influence the total cost of sourcing and the ability to support customers after delivery.

Linyi Lanshan Merco Electric Bicycle Factory reports that its products are sold in more than 50 countries and regions and that it has maintained long-term relationships with hundreds of domestic and overseas bicycle wholesalers. The company also reports an annual output value of more than US$9 million. These figures are published by the company and provide context for its stated international business activities.

For importers, experience in overseas markets can be useful, but each new sourcing project still requires careful planning. Electric vehicles may be subject to different rules for road use, product safety, battery transport, labeling, and documentation. An electric motorcycle that is suitable for one market may require different approval or registration in another. Electric tricycles may also be classified differently depending on their design, speed, power, and intended use.

Logistics planning should account for vehicle dimensions, packaging, battery shipping requirements, order quantity, and delivery schedules. Buyers should clarify whether products will be supplied fully assembled or in another shipping configuration, what documents will accompany the shipment, and which party is responsible for specific transport and import arrangements.

After-sales support is another important factor. Distributors may need access to replacement components, technical instructions, warranty procedures, and guidance on common maintenance questions. Before entering a long-term supply relationship, buyers should establish how technical inquiries will be handled and how replacement parts can be obtained.

These considerations are particularly relevant for businesses building a product line rather than making a one-time purchase. A reliable sourcing process depends on a shared understanding of product requirements, clear communication, and realistic expectations regarding lead times and support.

The Role of Electric Vehicle Manufacturers in Changing Mobility Needs

The development of electric mobility is creating a more varied marketplace for two-wheel and three-wheel vehicles. Personal commuters, delivery businesses, small retailers, families, and other users may have different priorities, even when they are shopping within the same broad electric vehicle category. Some place greater emphasis on compact dimensions and everyday convenience, while others need cargo capacity, passenger space, weather protection, or a configuration suited to local roads.

Manufacturers that provide multiple vehicle categories can help buyers explore these different requirements through a broader product portfolio. Electric bicycles, electric motorcycles, and electric tricycles serve related but distinct purposes. Their suitability depends on design, technical specifications, operating conditions, and the regulations applicable to the market.

Linyi Lanshan Merco Electric Bicycle Factory brings these categories together through its published product range and states that it supports research and development, testing, production, and quality-control activities. Its electric motorcycle and electric tricycle offerings provide prospective distributors with options to investigate across personal mobility, cargo transportation, and passenger-oriented applications.

For buyers, the next step is to evaluate each model in practical terms: intended use, motor and battery specifications, safety equipment, payload where relevant, certification documentation, warranty, spare-parts availability, and total landed cost. Clear answers to these questions can help businesses select products that match their customers’ needs and establish more predictable supplier relationships.

As the electric mobility sector continues to develop, product variety and manufacturing coordination will remain important considerations for distributors and importers. Suppliers that communicate specifications clearly, support product evaluation, and provide appropriate technical and commercial information can help buyers navigate a market in which vehicle categories and customer expectations continue to diversify.

About Linyi Lanshan Merco Electric Bicycle Factory

According to its official website, the company operates a factory covering approximately 10,000 square meters, employs more than 50 people, and reports an annual output value exceeding US$9 million. It describes its business as incorporating production, research and development, testing, and quality-control activities, and states that its products reach more than 50 countries and regions.

The company’s product portfolio includes electric bicycles, electric motorcycles, and electric tricycles. Its listed electric bicycle categories include city commuter bikes, folding e-bikes, delivery bikes, and mountain bikes. For wholesalers, distributors, and international buyers seeking information about electric mobility products and manufacturing services, the company’s official website, www.mercoebike.com, provides further details about its product categories, available models, and contact information. text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 16. Baker Hughes, GE Vernova and Venture Global have signed a framework agreement to support the development of behind-the-meter power generation capacity in the United States, Baker Hughes said on October 15.

The agreement provides for the supply of gas turbines, steam turbines and related equipment and services for up to 16 new power island units. Baker Hughes will also supply control and electrical integration technologies for the units, including electrical houses (E-houses) and electrical control systems.

The power generation infrastructure is intended to support Venture Global’s LNG production and liquefaction operations, as well as potential future data center projects adjacent to its LNG facilities.

Under the framework, deliveries are scheduled for 2028–2034. Venture Global expects to place its first purchase order for a power island by the end of 2026, with additional orders anticipated from 2027.

The agreement builds on the LNG power island architecture Baker Hughes has previously deployed for Venture Global. The framework is intended to establish a repeatable model for supplying electricity directly to industrial facilities, with potential applications beyond LNG operations.

“Behind-the-meter power generation has emerged as a critical component to LNG operations as well as advancing the AI economy,” said Baker Hughes Chairman and CEO Lorenzo Simonelli.

“This framework will replicate what we have already built with Venture Global to develop more power – quickly, safely and at scale,” he added.

Baker Hughes (NASDAQ: BKR) is an energy technology company providing solutions to energy and industrial customers worldwide. The company operates in more than 120 countries.

U.S. electricity generation

The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) says that the country uses many different energy sources and technologies to generate electricity. These sources and technologies have changed over time, and some are used more than others.

The three major categories of energy for electricity generation are fossil fuels (coal, natural gas, and petroleum), nuclear energy, and renewable energy. Most electricity is generated with steam turbines that use fossil fuels, nuclear, biomass, geothermal, or solar thermal energy. Other major electricity generation technologies include gas turbines, hydro (water) turbines, wind turbines, and solar photovoltaics.

“Fossil fuels accounted for about 58% of U.S. electricity generation in 2025. Natural gas was the top source—about 41%—of U.S. utility-scale electricity generation in 2025. Natural gas is used in steam turbines and gas turbines to generate electricity. Coal was the third-highest source and accounted for about 17% of U.S. electricity generation in 2025. Nearly all coal-fired power plants use steam turbines. Some power plants convert coal to gas for gas turbines that generate electricity.

Petroleum was the source of about 0.7% of U.S. electricity generation in 2025. Residual fuel oil and petroleum coke are used in steam turbines. Distillate—or diesel—fuel oil is used in internal-combustion engines such as diesel-engine generators. Residual fuel oil and distillates can also be burned in steam turbines and gas turbines.

Other gases and other sources accounted for about 0.2% of U.S. utility-scale electricity generation in 2025. Other gases include blast furnace gas and other manufactured and waste gases derived from fossil fuels. Other sources include pumped-storage hydroelectric, non-biogenic municipal solid waste, batteries, hydrogen, purchased steam, sulfur, tire-derived fuel, and other miscellaneous energy sources,” says the EIA.

text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

Three regional transmission organizations (RTOs) set records for peak hourly load this past summer, according to data reported on Form EIA-930 and presented in the Hourly Electric Grid Monitor:

PJM peaked at 162.6 gigawatts (GW) on July 2, 2026, 1.3% higher than the pre-2026 peak of 160.6 GW on June 23, 2025.

The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) peaked at 91.1 GW on July 22, 2026, 6.5% higher than the pre-2026 record of 85.5 GW on August 20, 2024.

The Southwest Power Pool (SWPP) peaked at 58.0 GW on July 27, 2026, 3.5% higher than the pre-2026 peak of 56.0 GW on August 21, 2023.

Most of these peaks occurred during regional heat waves, amid the hottest summer on record nationally, which drove up cooling demand.

The California Independent System Operator (CAISO) and the Independent System Operator for New England (ISO-NE) came within 2% of their previous records. The New York Independent System Operator (NYISO) was within 3% of its previous record load, and the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) was within 4%, according to Form EIA-930:

CAISO reached 50.0 GW on September 9, 2026, below its record high of 51.1 GW reached on September 6, 2022.

ISO-NE reached 25.3 GW on July 2, 2026, below its record of 25.9 GW on June 24, 2025.

NYISO reached 31.1 GW on July 2, 2026, below its previous record of 31.9 GW on June 24, 2025 (NYISO reports a record of 34.0 GW set in 2013, before we collected hourly data).

MISO peaked at 121.5 gigawatts (GW) on June 30, 2026, the highest in our Hourly Electric Grid Monitor but below the previous peak of 127.1 GW on July 20, 2011, as reported by MISO.

Data from Form EIA-930 is reported to us by each balancing authority (BA) and is made available “as-is”. The data BAs report on the Form EIA-930 represent best values at the time of reporting, but various reporting issues may limit the quality of these data. Data published directly by BAs may differ from the data in Form EIA-930.

text:
The electric vehicles were splattered after a concrete spray incident, but repairable. Eager to recoup their costs, insurers sent the 40 BYD vehicles to an auction run by asset sales company Pickles in late March.

With fuel prices soaring in response to the US and Israel war on Iran, a bidding frenzy erupted.

“We had thousands of buyers trying to bid on about 40 cars, so just the prices we generated were incredible,” says Brendon Green, the general manager of automotive solutions at Pickles.

“The amount of views that we got on those cars, the bidders that registered and the amount of bids that we took were extraordinary compared to what we would typically see.”

It is a striking shift for an industry where sceptics have long warned that used EVs would rapidly depreciate in value and become worthless.

Instead, scenes like the Pickles auction are turning that anxiety on its head, forcing drivers grappling with high fuel prices to ask whether it could actually be petrol cars that pose the bigger secondhand valuation risk.

Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter

The shift is evident in written-off vehicles, too.

Salvage EVs, with pre-accident values of up to $40,000, fetched substantially higher auction prices than comparable combustion models, the auction house says.

Written-off EVs sold for spare parts and second-life batteries achieved 16% higher sale results than petrol equivalents, while repairable write-offs generated a huge 71% price premium.

‘The demand is there’

While EVs and hybrids have been gaining traction for years, the Iran conflict and associated enduring oil price rise accelerated demand in March, and it has continued largely unabated.

More EVs than petrol-only cars were sold in September, according to Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries data, supported by an influx of Chinese auto brands offering low-priced EVs.

Rob Chan, the managing director of car rental marketplace Turo Australia, says customer demand for EVs and hybrids has rocketed, with bookings growing at 28 times the pace of petrol and diesel over the past year.

In response, Turo “hosts” – those who list their vehicles for others to use – are meeting that demand by buying secondhand EVs.

“A lot of hosts are on auction sites or on sales sites looking for more inventory because they know that this rising tide is lifting all the boats,” says Chan.

“They’re looking for EVs because the demand is there.”

The secondhand demand for used EVs is supported by their better-than-expected battery life, according to Pickles, which has tested more than 2,750 used batteries.

It has found that five-year-old EVs tend to retain a battery life score of 93%, referring to their charge capacity. Even high-mileage former ride share vehicles with more than 230,000km on the odometer are rated at about 89%.

The results challenge earlier concerns that an EV would run out of battery power after about a decade, making them near worthless. Pickles is finding that even old batteries running at just 60% would have some value for people looking for a used car for regular short trips.

Cost-of-living over climate

While many early adopters purchased electric vehicles for environmental purposes, the falling sticker prices and cheaper running costs have made them mass market.

Aman Gaur, head of policy at the Electric Vehicle Council, says some of the suburbs with the highest EV uptake are in outer-suburban commuter hubs like Tarneit, 30km west of Melbourne’s city centre.

“For most buyers, it is no longer a climate issue, it is very much a cost-of-living issue because it is one of the best ways you can save money,” says Gaur.

“But it might be comforting for them to know that EVs also have a higher residual value based on the value of the battery, whereas a 15-year-old [internal combustion engine] vehicle is just scrap metal.”

That shifting economic landscape means the heavy secondhand price discounts once associated with early EVs are disappearing, replaced by robust resale values.

The broader transition is not without friction, with charging infrastructure lagging behind the surging buyer demand, according to the EV council. Australia’s nascent battery recycling and mineral processing industry also needs to advance.

Andrew Chadwick, a lithium battery repair specialist, says he suspects the demand for secondhand EVs is being mainly driven by their lower running costs.

“I’m a huge fan of EV adoption because the technology is so much more simple than an [internal combustion engine] vehicle,” says Chadwick.

“I’m a massive petrol head, and I love a little turbo, but in terms of practicality and reliability and running costs, ICE [internal combustion engine] is awful. An equivalent EV will be worth more over the long term because there are fewer parts to go wrong.”

name: North Carolina Environment
title: Maya Cruz: Turning Passion Into Environmental Action
description:
From the Cape Fear River, to Greenfield Lake, to Burnt Mill Creek, and our stunning intercoastal waterways.
This summer I was an intern for the nonprofit Cape Fear River Watch (CFRW).
The Cape Fear River Watch is led by Kemp Burdette, the Cape Fear Riverkeeper, and is dedicated to improving water quality through education, advocacy, and action.
One of the best parts about interning with Cape Fear River Watch was the opportunity to work on my intern project.
I love this kind of field work and was so excited to get to work with so many incredible people at the Cape Fear River Watch.
text:
Being born and raised in Wilmington I have always been around the water. From the Cape Fear River, to Greenfield Lake, to Burnt Mill Creek, and our stunning intercoastal waterways. However, the water where I call home has been and continues to be at risk of extreme pollution. The Cape Fear River and surrounding waterways have faced pollution from industrial sources, including PFAS chemicals such as GenX, which have affected water quality throughout the region. Cape Fear River Watch has worked with community and environmental partners to address these issues, including efforts to reduce PFAS pollution from the Chemours facility near Fayetteville and to hold polluters accountable for protecting the watershed. If polluters in North Carolina have their way, none of these waters would be healthy or even accessible to any nearby communities.

This summer I was an intern for the nonprofit Cape Fear River Watch (CFRW). The Cape Fear River Watch is led by Kemp Burdette, the Cape Fear Riverkeeper, and is dedicated to improving water quality through education, advocacy, and action. I was involved in all three of those missions this summer. As an intern, my work changed often, but it always had a focus on improving the waterways in Wilmington. A typical week involved a consistent day of lab work, outreach events around the community, and additional water quality projects.

Every week all of the interns assisted in monitoring the creeks of New Hanover county by conducting lab testing on samples collected by volunteers for the Creekwatchers program. We collected samples, processed them, and collected data about bacteria in the water around Wilmington. Oftentimes our days in the lab were spent processing these samples. One of the best parts about interning with Cape Fear River Watch was the opportunity to work on my intern project. Every intern got to pick a project to work on that suited their specific skills. I decided to use my passion for live music to put together a fundraising concert nearby our offices: Rock the River. I decided that by getting together a handful of talented musicians, we could raise awareness for many of the issues affecting the river, raise money for the projects we had been working on all summer, and engage a younger generation in local environmental causes. I began my project in May, reaching out to venues, putting together a list of bands, and seeing if there was interest from the community. The project turned out to be much bigger than I thought it would be. As I worked on it more and more, hoops to jump through continued to appear. A lot of problems popped up that I hadn’t considered. I needed to market the event, there had to be limits on how many people we could have in the building at one time, we needed wristbands and a food vendor to come cater the event. However, dealing with many of these problems revealed opportunities I hadn’t considered. People were very interested in the event, and I was able to invite a handful of local vendors to set up booths. Many of these vendors even decided to donate gifts, which I was able to turn into a raffle to raise even more money.

When the event finally came around in mid-August, it was one of the most nerve-racking experiences of my life. Despite all of the problems and setbacks I faced while organizing the event, on the day, I came in with a degree of confidence due to how many people ordered tickets ahead of time. I had no idea just how galvanized the community could become to support environmental causes. Hundreds of people came to the event, and we ended up raising over $5,000. It was a stressful, inspiring, and an honestly amazing time. I’ve learned that this kind of event can bring people together in a way that supports environmental causes nearly as much as the scientific studies and clean ups do. The people who came to Rock the River were not only willing to donate just to come to the event, but many of them donated more on top of the entry fee, and many of them brought their friends and family who now have a better idea of what the CFRW does.

This internship project has made me even more confident in my decision to work in the environmental field. I love doing field work, and love the position I was able to be in at a non-profit not stuck to working on monotonous, profit-driven projects. I love this kind of field work and was so excited to get to work with so many incredible people at the Cape Fear River Watch. What I’ve learned is that it’s a very tough field to work in. Oftentimes fundraising can be a very hard task. However, approaching problems like this in a creative and out of the box way can be more effective than I ever would have imagined. By using my passion for music, community, and the environment, I’ve managed to blend some of my biggest passions in a way that lets me accomplish things I couldn’t have otherwise.

My next step is to build on my time at the riverwatch through NC State’s accelerated masters program in Environmental Assessment. Gaining more knowledge and technical experience in my field will allow me to better understand the environmental issues I care about and prepare me for a career working to protect our waterways. I also want to carry forward what I learned from Rock the River: that scientific knowledge is most effective when it can be understood and supported by the communities it is meant to protect.

title: NextGen batteries could be transformational - Wood Mackenzie

text:
High fuel prices are good news for electric vehicle (EV) sales, a theme we’ve been monitoring closely since the start of the Iran war. France, UK, Sweden, Australia, Norway and China are among those reporting record EV penetration in September, while sales in Southeast Asia and Latin America are also surging.

But the global picture of switching from internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles to electric is far from uniform. I asked Milan Thakore, Principal Analyst in our Electric Vehicle and Battery Supply Chain team, how he sees things playing out.

Where have EV sales surged?

The global trend is up, with global EV (including battery electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle) sales increasing 14% year-on-year to end August. EVs now represent nearly one in three new car sales globally. However, at a regional level, the picture is patchy. In Europe and most emerging markets, Chinese EVs have set the benchmark in terms of affordability, and this is reflected in strong sales numbers in those markets.

The US has still not recovered from the withdrawal of supportive policy and EV penetration is down. Even ‘difficult-to-electrify’ markets like India are now overtaking the US in percentage terms. The surprise is China’s own domestic sales. Despite EV penetration approaching 70%, EV sales are down by nearly 1 million units from last year’s peak of 9 million.

What’s holding EVs back in China?

The entire vehicle market in China is tanking, with light vehicle sales across all power trains falling by 3.6 million units year-on-year. ICE vehicles account for the biggest share of the drop – more than double the hit to EVs – with the main factors high fuel costs, a shrinking pool of legacy replacement buyers and a weaker macroeconomic outlook. This twist has unexpectedly lifted EVs’ penetration rate almost to the country’s 2030 EV target four years ahead of time. High fuel costs are also changing consumer behaviour – owners with two vehicles are unsurprisingly favouring their EV and leaving the ICE car at home.

Will Chinese EVs manufacturers ramp up exports?

Big time, as they look to offset slowing growth domestically. More Chinese brands are coming to the market, with ever-improving vehicle designs and performance. Critically, they are priced very competitively to entice customers to often unheard-of brands. One such brand is Leapmotor, which has partnered with Stellantis, the world’s fifth-largest automaker.

Leapmotor’s B05 model sells at around €30,000 for which the buyer gets up to a 300-mile range and a wide array of features as standard, including ventilated seats, panoramic sunroof and the whole suite of safety features. A comparable German ICE model could cost up to €5,000 more once you’ve added on all the ‘extras’.

Could ‘NextGen’ batteries be transformational?

Yes. The latest LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries will hit international markets at the end of 2026. The largest battery makers, CATL and BYD, are amongst those pushing the technology, and others will follow. These will dramatically speed up charging from up to 30 minutes today to below 10 minutes. Charging infrastructure will have to move from kilowatts to the megawatt-level to achieve ‘flash’ charging. BYD doesn’t see this as a challenge.

Is Europe about to be swamped by Chinese exports?

Europe has the highest EV penetration outside China, with sales pushing towards 40%. Sustained subsidy support, abundant model availability, and high retail gasoline and diesel prices drove record September sales in most European countries.

Policymakers need to balance climate goals with defending European manufacturing and employment by supporting a local EV and battery manufacturing value chain. Chinese automative companies are already building manufacturing capacity and battery supply chains in Europe so European-made Chinese EVs will eventually replace imports. European OEMs are also investing heavily but will need to keep advancing to protect market share.

Where else are EVs flourishing?

Sales in South America and Southeast Asia have all but doubled, driven primarily by a flood of imports from China. As in Europe, these regions want to keep manufacturing local, and Chinese automakers are already building out that capacity. East Asian BEV growth has also doubled as South Korean manufacturer Hyundai-Kia attempts to offset the drop off in US EV demand with sales into its home market.

Are we at an inflection point for EVs? There’s a good chance we are for two reasons. First, the evolving attractiveness of EVs as a product, particularly the quality of vehicles on offer, longer battery range and speed of charging all of which will continue to improve into the future. Secondly, the soaring cost of gasoline and diesel fuel in 2026 has shifted running costs massively in favour of EVs in all markets.

Our sense is that the Iran war will be seen as an inflection point, accelerating a trend already well underway, with EVs eating into ICE vehicles’ market share in many markets. The duration of both the conflict and high pump prices will determine how soon it unfolds – and how much road fuel demand is eroded.

It’s possible that Wood Mackenzie’s base case assumption that global passenger EV penetration hits 50% by 2035 arrives a few years earlier.

title: US voters want action on global heating. So why are midterm candidates 'climate hushing'?
description:
Most Americans feel unease or alarm about the climate crisis and, in both red and blue states, want to know how political leaders are going to fix it.
Yet the unfolding climate crisis, and the imperative to transition to cleaner, less volatile forms of energy, has been starkly absent on campaign trails before the midterms in three weeks’ time.
This so-called “climate hushing”, however, is disconnected from what voters actually want, polling suggests.
Nixon has, unlike most other candidates from both parties, repeatedly mentioned her state’s vulnerability to the climate crisis during her campaign.
His party should instead actively raise and weaponize the climate crisis, Whitehouse insists, much like how Republicans do for far more niche topics, such as trans people playing sports.
text:
Most Americans feel unease or alarm about the climate crisis and, in both red and blue states, want to know how political leaders are going to fix it. But in midterm election campaigns across the US, candidates have responded to this desire with near silence.

People in the US have this year endured a record hot summer as well as soaring costs, equating to roughly $2,000 per household, in extra energy and mortgage payments, due to the country’s dependence on a fossil fuel supply scrambled by Donald Trump’s decision to attack Iran.

Yet the unfolding climate crisis, and the imperative to transition to cleaner, less volatile forms of energy, has been starkly absent on campaign trails before the midterms in three weeks’ time. Even among previously pro-green Democrats, 2026 has seen a widespread climate omerta.

“Look, I’m not going to defend the Green New Deal,” Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic US Senate candidate in Michigan, told Fox News in August, after previously campaigning for 100% renewable energy.

Jon Ossoff, seeking to retain his Senate seat in Georgia, has ditched mentions of the environment in favor of focusing on the Iran war and inflation. Meanwhile, James Talarico, another leading Democratic Senate hope who previously compared oil and gas to 1980s cassette tapes that are “not gonna last”, has struck a very different tone in this campaign.

“I support our oil and gas industry,” Talarico, aiming for a first Democratic win in Texas in decades, said last month. “I had family members who worked in the industry. I went to public schools here in Texas, funded by the oil and gas industry.”

Among all Democratic and Republican candidates in eight battleground states that will determine control of the US Senate – Alaska, Georgia, Maine, Iowa, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas – none mention “climate” on their campaign websites other than El-Sayed and Talarico.

This so-called “climate hushing”, however, is disconnected from what voters actually want, polling suggests. Three times as many voters in these eight swing states want politicians to spend more time talking about the climate crisis than those who want to hear less about it, a large survey from last month found, with thumping majorities in each state saying they are more likely to vote for a candidate who prioritizes a transition to clean energy.

“The climate hushers are dead wrong – voters want to hear more about climate change, not less, and they will reward politicians who are strong climate leaders,” said Nathaniel Stinnett, executive director of the Environmental Voter Project, which conducted the poll. “Politicians should always tailor their message to their district but it’s pure fiction to say that talking about climate change will lose you votes.”

“In fact, it’s a huge vote-winner, even with independents in red states who favor fairly aggressive climate action by a four-to-one margin,” Stinnett added. “There’s this idea that climate has become a curse word and you shouldn’t say it. That’s just wrong.”

Midterm candidates may have disparaged or ignored climate action in search of electability, but the data indicates a mainstream position among US voters is concern about climate change and support for a prompt switch away from fossil fuels. More Americans are starting to link their rising living costs with fossil fuels and climate-driven disasters, too, despite a dwindling interest in political and media circles to mention such connections.

“The norm has shifted, yet so many politicians seem stuck in a 1990s world where clean energy and climate change are radical, fringe things that only environmentalists think about,” said Anthony Leiserowitz, an expert in climate communication at Yale University.

“This climate-hushing strategy, which has been adopted by many politicians, is not a logical response to where voters are,” he added. Yale’s own polling has found a majority of Americans remain worried about global heating despite the electoral success of Donald Trump, who has called climate science “a hoax”.

This is the case even in major oil and gas producing states: in the Environmental Voter Project polling released last month, 54% of voters in Texas said they’d be more likely to vote for a pro-renewables candidate, compared with 19% who said they’d be less likely, with more Texans more favorable of solar and wind energy than oil.

Despite this, Republicans have sought to paint Talarico as an eco-extremist bent on shutting down the oil and gas industry, with Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued GOP candidate, calling his opponent “Tofu Talarico” and an enemy of the fossil fuel sector.

“In Texas, he talks about: ‘I’m a vaygan [sic], I’m a vaygan.’ He’s a vaygan meaning he likes lettuce,” Trump said about Talarico at a rally this month, with the president mis-pronouncing the word “vegan” (Talarico is not a vegan). “And now he goes to every barbecue available. He then throws up immediately after eating the steak. Throwing up all over the place.”

In Alaska, there is even stronger support for renewables, with 63% of voters saying they’d back a campaign that prioritizes the transition to clean energy. Mary Peltola, the Democratic US Senate candidate in Alaska who has run on a tagline of “fish, family, freedom”, has called for the return of tax credits for clean energy but also demands more oil be refined in the state and has pushed for the approval of a large oil project in the Alaskan Arctic.

“Increasing Alaska energy production is critical to addressing the affordability crisis, and Mary will aggressively advocate for every solution on the table – including increased oil and gas production, as well as restoring tax credits for solar, wind and hydropower projects that were cut by Dan Sullivan,” said a Peltola spokesperson, referencing her Republican opponent, who voted with other GOP lawmakers to gut Joe Biden-era legislation to boost renewables.

The Trump administration, which has moved to eliminate any limits on greenhouse gas pollution while bolstering the fossil fuel industry, considers the climate issue to be in full retreat. “You don’t hear the word ‘climate change’ as much as you did two years ago, because the legs have been knocked out from under that movement,” Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, claimed last week.

Media mentions of the climate crisis have dropped in the past year and the issue has slipped down the list of voters’ stated priorities as inflation has taken its toll and alarm over the Iran war and the state of US democracy has surged. Candidates faced with limited cash and fractured voter attention spans have found it expedient to focus on these headline topics, rather than global heating.

Attitudes towards the climate crisis also continue to differ sharply by party affiliation, with Democrats still overwhelmingly the most concerned about the issue and Republicans far more likely to see it as a trivial or even non-existent problem. This has spurred many Democrats running in states previously won by Trump to bury any mention of climate, although some have bucked this strategy.

“Voters are concerned about the climate. Sometimes people just don’t understand how it impacts the cost of things like insurance, which is unfortunate,” said Angie Nixon, a Democrat running a surprisingly competitive US Senate race in Florida, which has become a Republican stronghold in recent years.

Nixon has, unlike most other candidates from both parties, repeatedly mentioned her state’s vulnerability to the climate crisis during her campaign.

“A lot of Florida will be under water in the next few decades and I’m worried about that,” she said. “I want the world to be around for my kids. Young people really care about climate change because they know it will really affect them.”

Democrats have long had a “weak” message on the climate crisis because they simply repeat back to voters what polls tell them the most pressing issues are, the Democratic senator and climate advocate Sheldon Whitehouse has argued. His party should instead actively raise and weaponize the climate crisis, Whitehouse insists, much like how Republicans do for far more niche topics, such as trans people playing sports.

“This is a story with villains – the greedy fossil fuel companies wrecking the planet and sticking Americans with the bill for the damage,” Whitehouse said. “Frustrated voters are hungry to see politicians really fighting for them, and the climate fight presents a real opportunity to show them that we are.”

But for the growing cohort of Americans who have had their lives upended by extreme events such as storms, floods and wildfires – by one estimate, this includes about a third of all people in the US over the previous two years – there is scant evidence of a fight being waged on their behalf to stem the rising temperatures that worsen such calamities.

At a meeting of disaster survivors in Kerrville, Texas, last week, several people who endured deadly flash floods that swept through the region last year – killing 136 people, including 28 of whom were at a riverside Christian camp for girls – expressed frustration that politicians have tuned out of their plight.

“I think that a lot of politicians couldn’t be bothered, they couldn’t be bothered by it,” said Georgia Bishop, an 18-year-old whose best friend, Felicity Jarmon, died in the floods. “They see it, they know it, they’ve heard us scream to the rooftops about it. But it just seems to be: ‘Well, this is weather, this is life.’”

A developing El Niño climate event, already one of the strongest ever recorded, is set to further accelerate extreme heat and flooding risk in parts of the US in the coming months. Bishop said at this point she wouldn’t be surprised to see a snowstorm in Texas in July. The political indifference to this is, she added, “infuriating”.

The Republican and Democratic Senate candidates from the key eight battleground states – Alaska, Georgia, Maine, Iowa, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas – were all contacted for comment about their stance, or lack of it, on the climate crisis.

name: Clean Energy
title: The New Industrial Revolution Is Green — Here's Why That Matters - Global Citizen
description:
We started with the big question: Is the “new industrial revolution” the right way to describe the shift to clean energy?
“Given that the energy transition is requiring us to rebuild our energy system, I think the framing is appropriate,” she said.
One big idea is "green iron," iron made using clean energy instead of coal.
It’s locally owned, with 90% of shareholders living in Denmark, and it provides clean energy to the town.
Leave a positive comment encouraging Australia's leaders to make Perth a platform for bold clean energy action.
text:
Think about the phone in your pocket, the electric bus on your street, or the solar panels on your neighbor's roof. Every one of them depends on minerals from the ground and on energy to turn those minerals into something useful.

For more than two centuries, the world's factories ran on coal, oil, and gas. Now that's starting to change. A new wave of industry is taking shape, powered by the sun and wind, and it could decide where the next generation of jobs comes from.

It could also help reach the millions of people who still live without electricity, families who can't switch on a light at night or keep medicine cool.

Western Australia is right at the center of this story. It's also where leaders will meet at Global Citizen NOW: Perth from October 18 to 20, 2026, where the agenda for action is set ahead of COP31, the UN's next big climate summit.

Professor Peta Ashworth OAM, Director of the Curtin Institute for Energy Transition. Image: Courtesy of the Curtin Institute for Energy Transition

To understand what this moment means, we spoke with Professor Peta Ashworth OAM, Director of the Curtin Institute for Energy Transition, who has spent her career studying how people adopt new energy technologies.

We started with the big question: Is the “new industrial revolution” the right way to describe the shift to clean energy?

“Given that the energy transition is requiring us to rebuild our energy system, I think the framing is appropriate,” she said. What makes this moment different, she explained, is that the world needs more energy at the very time it’s trying to switch to cleaner sources.

“We live in an increasingly interconnected world and our reliance on data only continues to grow,” she said. “These factors are increasing energy demand at the time we are trying to transition to lower-carbon alternatives, making the shift increasingly complex.”

Building gigawatt-scale renewable energy also means new trading partners and new global supply chains, Ashworth added, at a time when shifting geopolitics is changing which partners countries can trust and rely on.

Ashworth pointed to what her US colleague Dr. Emily Grubert calls the “messy mid-transition,” when renewable and fossil fuel energy run side by side, but neither can fully meet demand alone. “As we transform our energy system, we can expect major challenges and disruptions if we don’t take on board lessons from the past and plan ahead to manage this period of such enormous change,” she said.

Related Stories

Why Is Western Australia at the Center of This Shift?

Western Australia (WA) supplies 38% of the world's iron ore, the main ingredient in steel. That matters, because making steel is one of the biggest sources of climate pollution, responsible for more than 7% of global carbon emissions.

The state is also rich in the minerals that go into batteries for phones, electric cars, and home solar systems, like lithium and nickel. Sales of these minerals more than tripled between 2019 and 2023, according to the WA government.

Now the state wants to do even more with them. Its plan for battery minerals aims to process more of them locally and make battery ingredients at home, bringing more jobs and benefits to WA.

One big idea is "green iron," iron made using clean energy instead of coal. One study cited by the OECD estimates that, with the right support, WA could produce at least 4.5 million tonnes a year by 2030.

For Ashworth, two priorities stand out. “We must urgently deploy renewable energy projects and transmission lines at scale, and we must recognize Traditional Owners as rights holders so that they can actively participate in projects with an equity share,” she said. “Our failure to do this has been the missing puzzle piece standing in the way of WA capturing more of the value chain.”

That goes for products WA already makes, like direct reduced iron, and for new industries, from magnets and chips to battery recycling.

“Without infrastructure to produce and transport renewable energy, it will be impossible for WA industry to power their operations with the clean, cheap energy that we have in abundance,” Ashworth explained.

Delays in building transmission and getting projects running, she warned, mean longer dependence on coal and gas, higher costs, and less certainty for businesses looking to invest in the state.

Related Stories

Who Gets the Jobs?

Every industrial shift is ultimately about people. The WA government has made creating quality jobs a core goal of its battery minerals plan. The clean energy boom will need electricians, engineers, technicians, and builders, many of them in regional towns where new projects are going up.

Getting the timing right matters. When training keeps pace with investment, projects move forward, local workers benefit, and people who worked in coal or gas can move into new, long-term careers.

Ashworth said it all comes down to how well WA scales up its energy infrastructure. “If we can do this well, new industries will emerge in the regions and create new opportunities for people living in those regions and attract new workers to the area,” she said.

That growth needs support, she added, including enough housing, health and childcare services, and education options in regional communities.

Australia will also need to stay an attractive place for skilled workers from overseas. Countries around the world are facing labor shortages as the transition ramps up, driving up demand for clean energy workers. “If we want people with the skills and expertise needed to advance the energy transition to work here in Australia, we need to make our country an attractive destination for them to settle,” Ashworth said.

Related Stories

Why Does Community Trust Matter?

A new wind farm or power line can change how a place looks and how people earn a living. Whether locals welcome it often comes down to something simple: Were they asked? Were they listened to? Do they share in the benefits?

That's exactly what Professor Ashworth studies at the Curtin Institute for Energy Transition: how people feel about new energy projects, and what builds their trust.

“People do not want to have projects happen to them — they want to have a say in the future of their local area,” Ashworth explained. “When communities are not consulted, information is not clear and benefits are inadequate, projects may be seen as a burden or even a hazard, creating opposition and division among host communities.”

She pointed to the Denmark Community Wind Farm in WA as a success story. Local residents proposed the wind farm themselves in 2003, and it began operating in 2013. It’s locally owned, with 90% of shareholders living in Denmark, and it provides clean energy to the town.

“The turbines are even a tourist attraction!” Ashworth said. “The positive sentiment in the community reflects what I have found through my research — genuine engagement, consultation and benefits are crucial to build community support.”

What Role Do First Nations Communities Play?

First Nations peoples hold recognized rights and interests across almost 60% of Australia, and nearly half of the clean energy projects the country needs will be built on First Nations lands and waters. That means First Nations communities aren't just neighbors to this shift. They're rightsholders, landowners, partners, and investors in it.

In WA's Pilbara region, the Yindjibarndi people are teaming up with renewable energy company ACEN to build large-scale solar and wind projects on their own land, with the community holding a 25–50% ownership stake.

For Ashworth, genuine partnership starts with consent. The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted in 2007, affirms the right of Indigenous peoples to free, prior and informed consent: the power to give or withhold consent to actions that affect them.

“It is important to ensure that First Nations communities have the opportunity to participate in engagement, co-design projects and negotiate benefits,” she said, ideally with equity in new energy projects. That work must also be grounded in an understanding of First Nations peoples’ deep and continuing connection to Country.

The stakes are high. Research by Net Zero Australia estimates that 43% of the renewable energy projects needed to reach net zero by 2060 will need to be sited on legally recognized Indigenous-owned land and waters.

“These communities must be included, engaged with respect and have the opportunity to benefit from projects taking place on their Country, otherwise we risk entrenching existing inequality as we saw with the mining and agriculture booms,” Ashworth said. “If our energy transition is to succeed, the first step is ensuring that First Nations communities have agency in the process.”

Related Stories

What Does This Mean Beyond Australia?

This isn't only an Australian story. Around the world, millions of people still live without electricity. Without reliable power, it's harder to run a health clinic, keep a small business open after dark, or study at night.

Australia is already helping its neighbors. Through a five-year, AU$75 million program called REnew Pacific, it funds local clean energy systems for remote communities across the Pacific and Timor-Leste, bringing light, clean water, and better health care and schools.

Ashworth recently attended the Pre-COP meeting in Fiji to better understand how Australia can support the energy transition across the Indo-Pacific. In the Pacific, she said, the urgent call was to move from priorities and plans to action.

Palau’s President Surangel S. Whipps Jr. spoke about closing the gap between ambition and action by deploying renewable energy to strengthen resilience and energy security and to create lasting economic opportunities. Priorities included funding and delivering projects under each country’s national plan, building local skills so every country can electrify, and innovative financing that gets money to the communities that need it without losing it to unnecessary overheads.

Cutting reliance on diesel came up as a win on several fronts, not least by freeing up money currently spent on fuel.

But Ashworth was clear that Australia has work to do at home, too. “WA and Australia need to clean up our own backyard,” she said. “For WA, this means the need for a clearly articulated plan that demonstrates how WA will transition away from fossil fuels to reach net zero.”

The first industrial revolution was powered by coal and steam. This one will be powered by sunshine, wind, and the people and partnerships that turn them into job opportunities and electricity.

That's why leaders from government, business, philanthropy, and First Nations communities are meeting at Global Citizen NOW: Perth, to align and advance commitments that bring clean, reliable power to more people across the Indo-Pacific.
