title: Harris County has 46 data centers and almost no power to regulate them - Click2Houston
description:
The officials said Harris County has 46 operating data centers, with at least six more in various stages of development.
RELATED: Texas data centers are booming.
County’s regulatory authority remains limited Despite the concerns, Harris County faces significant legal restrictions on its ability to regulate data centers.
Kamen said the county generally cannot use zoning to control where data centers are located.
She also pointed to unresolved legal questions about whether counties can impose a moratorium on data center development.
text:
Harris County officials are pushing for greater local control over data center development, citing concerns about electricity demand, water consumption, air quality and neighborhood safety as the industry expands across Texas.

County Attorney Abbie Kamen joined Commissioners Lesley Briones and Adrian Garcia at a press conference to outline the county’s limited regulatory authority and discuss potential legislative changes ahead of the Texas Legislature’s next session in January.

The officials said Harris County has 46 operating data centers, with at least six more in various stages of development. They emphasized that the rapid expansion presents immediate challenges for local infrastructure and communities.

RELATED: Texas data centers are booming. Who is watching out for homeowners?

“This is something that is here,” Briones said. “The county today wants to make sure that we are taking action to protect our communities, protect our environment, and make sure that we’re leaning in.”

Electricity demand raises concerns

Kamen pointed to projections from CenterPoint Energy indicating that the Houston area is expected to add eight gigawatts of new data center electricity demand by 2029, with approximately four additional gigawatts expected afterward.

That growth could increase peak electricity demand across the utility’s service area by roughly 50%, Kamen said.

Officials also raised concerns about the amount of water data centers consume, potential pollution and the effects of additional demand on local utility bills.

“The biggest question I get is how much power are these centers consuming? And what does that mean to local residents?” Garcia said.

The commissioners connected those concerns to the broader issue of affordability, noting that residents are already feeling pressure from rising electricity and water costs.

They said the impact of a data center depends largely on its location, design and the conditions under which it is approved.

County’s regulatory authority remains limited

Despite the concerns, Harris County faces significant legal restrictions on its ability to regulate data centers.

Kamen said the county generally cannot use zoning to control where data centers are located. Land-use regulation within incorporated cities falls primarily to municipal governments, while the county has limited authority over development in unincorporated areas.

She also pointed to unresolved legal questions about whether counties can impose a moratorium on data center development. Kamen said the county is monitoring the issue as it awaits a determination from Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.

“The short answer right now is the county has little to no authority to stop them,” Briones said.

County officials plan to seek legal guidance on what measures they can pursue under existing law and what additional powers might require state legislation.

The commissioners also want county departments, including the county engineer and fire marshal’s office, to notify them as early as possible when a data center seeks permitting. They said earlier notice would help officials evaluate potential community and environmental impacts and prepare for safety concerns.

Garcia noted that the county’s fire marshal is responsible for responding to fires at facilities within its jurisdiction, underscoring the need for adequate safety planning and resources.

He said officials also want legislation that could address existing facilities, rather than focusing exclusively on future developments.

Legislative push focuses on local control

Briones said Harris County is working with other Texas counties through the Conference of Urban Counties to develop a legislative agenda for the upcoming session.

The effort will focus on identifying what regulatory authority counties can seek from state lawmakers and examining approaches used in other cities and states.

Officials said they want to understand which policies have effectively addressed data center impacts, particularly those involving water resources, electricity demand, pollution and the distance between facilities and residential neighborhoods.

The commissioners also called on state representatives and senators from both parties to consider legislation that would give local governments more tools to respond to community concerns.

Briones said the goal is to balance the industry’s economic benefits with responsible development.

“How can we both protect the community and environment while bringing the economic impact?” she asked, pointing to potential benefits such as good-paying jobs, local hiring policies, infrastructure investments, parks and trails, and community benefit agreements.

She added that county officials want to establish a framework that accounts for long-term impacts over the next 10, 20 or even 50 years.

The balance between growth and safeguards

County leaders acknowledged that data centers can bring investment and employment opportunities to Texas, but argued that communities should not have to absorb the costs without adequate protections.

Briones said officials are examining how other jurisdictions have approached the issue while recognizing that technology and industry practices continue to evolve.

She also stressed that future development is a priority, even as officials consider how to address facilities that have already been approved.

“The ones that have been approved have been approved under the laws that state leaders have allowed,” Briones said, calling for a more deliberate approach to future projects.

The county’s immediate priorities include bringing residents together to hear their concerns, improving information-sharing about proposed projects, clarifying existing legal authority and preparing legislative proposals.

Questions about timing

When asked why the county was addressing the issue now, given that data centers have been operating in the area for years, Garcia said recent news coverage and growing public concern had pushed the issue to the forefront.

He said residents have increasingly raised questions about electricity bills, water costs and the broader effects of rapid development.

Garcia argued that the county needs more authority to respond meaningfully to those concerns rather than relying on state officials to make decisions for local communities.

He also urged state leaders to ensure that any proposed pause in data center development is accompanied by meaningful action to restore local control.

The press conference comes as officials prepare for the legislative session beginning in January, when county leaders hope to advance proposals addressing data center development.

For now, the commissioners said, Harris County’s options remain constrained by state law. Their stated goal is to secure additional authority to protect residents and natural resources while allowing responsible economic development to continue.

text:
The Environmental Protection Agency proposed to make larger refiners blend more biofuels into their products over the next two years, a move that will likely appeal to farm-state voters ahead of November's congressional elections.

The proposal would help offset concerns about lost demand for ethanol producers and farmers after the EPA announced in August it would waive renewable fuel volume obligations for 29 small refineries that argued the requirements would cause economic hardship.

The EPA proposed reallocating 100% of those waived fuel volume obligations and is seeking public comment after putting forward two approaches. One would split the additional 2025 small refinery exemption volume evenly between the 2026 and 2027 compliance years, while the other would allocate all of it to 2027.

Comments are due by December 4, 2026, the EPA said in a statement.

Key points in the EPA announcement:

Obligation reallocation proposal: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency proposed a 100% reallocation of waived biofuel blending obligations to larger refiners over the next two years to offset demand losses suffered by ethanol producers and agricultural feedstocks.

Reallocation mechanisms and timeline: The agency outlined two proposed options for public comment through December 4, 2026—either splitting the 1.76 billion Renewable Identification Number (RIN) exemption volume evenly between the 2026 and 2027 compliance years, or shifting the entire volume to 2027.

Background and compliance impact: The proposal responds to August exemptions granted to 29 small refineries facing economic hardship, with the agency noting the additional volume obligations may require extending the 2026 compliance deadline past March 31, 2027.

Renewable credit prices for biodiesel and ethanol fell slightly on the news, according to a refinery trader at the OPIS biofuels conference in Chicago.

The EPA in August decided to grant 1.76 billion RINs worth of small refinery exemptions for the 2025 compliance year, including full exemptions for 18 refineries and partial waivers for 11 others. At the time, the agency said it would seek to reallocate the exempted volumes to other refiners in future years to preserve overall biofuel blending requirements.

The exemptions, the largest ever issued under the Renewable Fuel Standard, drew sharp criticism from biofuel producers and farm groups, which argued they would reduce demand for ethanol and biodiesel and undermine markets for agricultural feedstocks.

Refiners said compliance costs and elevated RIN prices justified relief for facilities facing economic hardship.

"While we believe most of the exemptions were unjustified, EPA's reallocation plan, if finalized as proposed, will help offset the demand loss for ethanol producers and farmers," said Geoff Cooper, CEO of the Renewable Fuels Association, which represents ethanol producers.

The EPA also said reallocating the waived obligations could require extending the 2026 compliance year deadline of March 31, 2027.

When gasoline prices climbed, Californians — and Americans in general — increasingly looked for electric vehicles but found that the supply of affordable options limited their choices.

text:
Affordable EV models are scarce despite market rebound

California sold nearly 87,000 new zero-emission vehicles in the second quarter of 2026, which accounts for about a fifth of new-car sales, according to the California Energy Commission.

That includes electric vehicles, plug-in hybrids and hydrogen-powered cars. Electric Vehicles represent the vast majority of those sales by themselves, accounting for roughly 17% of new-car sales in the state.

That’s nearly three times the national average of 6% of new-car sales being EVs during the same time period.

Tal’s research suggests that vehicle availability helped drive California’s rebound while the expiration of federal incentives contributed to a downturn in demand across the country as automakers pulled back on some electric models.

When gasoline prices climbed, Californians — and Americans in general — increasingly looked for electric vehicles but found that the supply of affordable options limited their choices.

“Our market is very limited on affordable cars — any affordable cars — in the U.S.,” Tal said. “If you drive one country to the north or one country to the south, you will find many affordable EVs that are not offered here.”

Tal said that means consumers showing up to dealerships looking for their ideal electric vehicle might not find any, which has led many to purchasing alternatives like hybrids instead.

“In California, I think that many people used to go to Tesla, but now there are other reasons for people not to like Tesla,” he said. “If you have a large family and you look for a seven-seater or if you are looking for a more affordable [vehicle], the number of models in these segments is very limited.”

His research found that most of the country is shifting towards hybrids in response to high gas prices — over $4 on average nationally. He said the share of new hybrid vehicle sales jumped from 13.3% to 16.9% between January and May — roughly 35,000 more hybrid buyers a month, dwarfing California’s “plug-in” rebound.

High electricity prices have also made convincing consumers to make that transition even more difficult. In response to that and the loss of federal incentives, the state recently launched its own incentive program to encourage Californians to ditch the pump for the plug.

California’s rebate program lowers upfront cost

California is trying to lower the upfront cost through MyFirstEV, a program offering qualifying first-time zero-emission vehicle buyers up to $3,500 toward a new vehicle and $1,750 toward a qualifying used one.

The program combines state funding with contributions from automakers for roughly $271 million in total incentives. It’s run by the California Air Resources Board, or CARB.

CARB communications director Lindsay Buckley said early demand has been strong.

“One early indicator of its success was Tesla, a California company that participated,” she said. “They actually sold out in a week.”

But rebates can only help people buy vehicles that are available. Tal’s research suggests that automakers’ supply decisions will remain a key factor in whether the state can sustain its recent sales growth.

Republican state Senator Tony Strickland argued that California’s own policies are also part of the problem. High electricity prices, limited charging infrastructure and concerns about energy capacity are three things he said makes transitioning to EVs difficult for most.

“There is no demand right now for the EV vehicle,” Strickland said. “If the technology gets better and more people move towards it, great, but that’s not what’s happening.

Strickland, who is vice chair of the Senate Transportation Committee, also said he’s against using taxpayer money to subsidize EV purchases.

Buckley said the state is monitoring electricity demand and encouraging EV owners to charge outside peak energy-consumption hours to avoid straining the power grid.

High gas prices might not be the only issue

Andrew Campbell, executive director of the UC Berkeley Haas Energy Institute, has cautioned against assuming a spike in gasoline prices will lead to widespread EV adoption.

“I suspect right now consumers understand that prices are high because of the Iran War and that the Iran War and the circumstances around that could change at some point,” he said. “My guess is consumers are not going to make major decisions based on the prices they’re seeing at the pump right now.”

Campbell said Europe’s EV market may offer some clues about what could help expand sales in the U.S.

“They have allowed in Chinese electric vehicles and those vehicles are lower cost than a lot of the other electric vehicles that are available,” he said.

California has limited control over the global vehicle market, including import policies and tariffs. But Campbell said policymakers do have some control over the costs associated with owning an EV.

One possibility is changing how electricity bills are structured. California’s electricity rates often rely heavily on charges for each kilowatt-hour used, but Cambell said a higher fixed monthly charge paired with a lower charge for each additional kilowatt-hour used could reduce the cost of charging.

He also suggested rethinking vehicle registration fees, which are largely based on a vehicle’s value. Campbell said a system that accounts for pollution could better reflect the environmental impact of older, less efficient vehicles.

“The idea of graduated charges would be to not so much set it based on age or value of the vehicle, but instead set the annual registration fees based on the environmental harms that those vehicles cause,” he said.

For renters, charging can be a hurdle

According to the Public Policy Institute of California, renters made up around 44% of Californianas in 2024. Many of them are locked out of purchasing an EV because they don't have access to an affordable place to charge.

Dahlia Garas, research program director for the UC Davis Electric Vehicle Research Center, said California has requirements for new buildings to be equipped for EV charging. The cost of using that infrastructure can vary though.

“If an apartment complex has chargers that are shared, there's no consistency of like a monthly permit or a per-kilowatt-hour charge, or a monthly fee plus a killowatt-per-hour-charge,” she said.

(Gerardo Zavala/CapRadio)

Garas said the impact is even worse for people who live in apartments with no access to charging infrastructure.

“That pushes people out to public charging and particularly DC fast charging, which is the least economical way to charge a vehicle,” she added. “That puts EVs at a financial operation cost disadvantage.”

How are drivers reacting?

At a Sacramento gas station, drivers say they are feeling the pinch while at the pump, but not necessarily enough to consider an EV.

Mark Haw was filling up his Honda CR-V at Interstate Gasoline in East Sacramento. He commutes from Elk Grove and said he’s considering a hybrid rather than an EV because gas prices are going to come down eventually.

“It costs me about $20 a week more in gas for me to commute to and from my job,” he said. “And so it makes for smaller meals.”

Lillian Schmidt paid $70 to fill up her Volkswagen Golf at the same station.

“We’re going to run this thing into the ground and then if we need to decide that we do need a second vehicle or if we have to replace this one, that one will be some sort of hybrid or EV, solely,” she said.

(Gerardo Zavala/CapRadio)

text:
North Carolina State House District 96 covers Catawba County, including parts of the Hickory area.

Current representative Republican Jay Adams is facing Democrat Park Inglefield.

Jay Adams (R)

We will add a response once it is received.

Park Inglefield (D)

Why are you running?

The status quo isn’t working for North Carolinians. I’m running because my neighbors deserve a representative who shows up, listens, and delivers results. We are facing a cost of living emergency and the General Assembly isn’t doing enough to support working families. I want to bring Catawba County voices to Raleigh to fight for affordable housing, strong public schools, and a government residents can trust.

Are you in favor of the three constitutional amendments on North Carolina’s ballot? Why or why not?

I oppose all three amendments. The income tax amendment would lock a 3.5% cap into our Constitution, permanently favoring the wealthy and profitable corporations while limiting legislators ability to respond to emergencies, a recession, hurricanes, or school funding needs.

The property tax amendment is vaguely written, giving Raleigh power to limit the revenue counties and towns rely on most, risking cuts to schools, fire, and police. Permanent constitutional provisions shouldn’t be used to hamstring local governments power. Their own elections should take care of this.

I also oppose extending photo ID to mail-in ballots. It’s an unnecessary barrier that will make voting harder for seniors, disabled, and rural voters.

What should the state do about data centers?

I support a moratorium on new large-scale data centers until the state fully studies their impact on our electric grid, water supply, and environment. Several NC towns have already paused projects for this reason and Raleigh should follow their lead. I oppose all tax exemptions and subsidies for data centers.

I’ll push for strict penalties and clawbacks when a facility pollutes, overdraws local water, damages land and wildlife habitat, or exceeds its power allotment, with repayment of any benefits received.

Protecting our grid and natural resources must come before corporate giveaways.

CMS has faced numerous controversies over the past month, what, if anything, should state lawmakers do?

CMS families deserve transparency and stability, not more turmoil. With the State Auditor, SBI, and now the FBI investigating alleged financial irregularities, state lawmakers should let those investigations run their course without political interference, while demanding full transparency from the district. I would push for stronger financial oversight and reporting requirements for school districts statewide, so problems surface before federal and state investigations are needed. Most importantly, lawmakers must ensure the chaos in the central office doesn’t disrupt funding or instruction for CMS’s 148,000 students.

What legislation will you pursue to bring down costs?

I will push legislation to protect families from utility rate hikes tied to data center growth, expand access to affordable housing and childcare, and lower healthcare and prescription drug costs.

I support targeted tax relief for working families and small businesses rather than broad cuts that benefit large corporations. I’ll also fight for transparency in how utilities justify rate increases to the Utilities Commission, so North Carolinians aren’t stuck subsidizing costs they didn’t create.

What sets you apart from your opponent?

I am 32 years old. The decisions made in Raleigh over the next decade will shape the rest of my life, my career, and whether I can afford to raise a family. My campaign is powered by a large base of small-dollar donors from my community, not a handful of large checks. My campaign reflects the interests of thousands of people in my district. The question voters should ask is simple: is my opponent accountable to you, or to his donors?

At 77, Jay Adams has skipped candidate forums and made himself largely unavailable to constituents. Jay pursues special interest projects for his buddies and advocates for a “proper road racing circuit in North Carolina.” He’s out of touch, has gotten lazy, and the time has come to send him home. I show up and answer tough questions in front of the public. I’ll stay accessible once elected because this job belongs to the voters, not special interests or projects, and not to the people writing the biggest checks.

text:
By Patturaja Murugaboopathy Oct 15 (Reuters) - Private credi…

Oct 15 (Reuters) - Tesla's top energy executive, Mike Snyder…



Tesla electric vehicles are pictured at one of the company's delivery centers in Valenton, near Paris, France, April 24, 2025. REUTERS/Benoit Tessier/File Photo

By Amir Orusov

Oct 16 (Reuters) - Global demand for electric vehicles fell 2% in September, ending six consecutive months of growth, as record sales in Europe were not enough to offset sharp declines in North America and China, data from UK-based research firm Benchmark Mineral Intelligence showed on Friday.

The data highlights growing divergence across major EV markets. Europe is benefiting from strong consumer demand and policy support, while China's domestic market remains weak and North America continues to feel the impact of the expiration of US federal EV tax credits at the end of September 2025.

• Global EV sales slid to 2.15 million vehicles in September, while year-to-date volumes are up 3% at 15.5 million units

• "Europe had its strongest month on record, with almost 600,000 EVs sold in September, 10% above the previous high set in June," BMI data manager Charles Lester said

• North American sales fell 44%, the steepest monthly decline this year, reflecting the strong year-ago period when buyers rushed to dealerships before the tax credits expired

• From the fourth quarter, these comparisons will ease as they lap the post-tax-credit slump, Lester said

• Sales in China dropped 18% to 1.11 million vehicles, prompting carmakers to increasingly rely on exports

(Reporting by Amir Orusov in Gdansk, editing by Milla Nissi-Prussak)

text:
Canada is spending almost CA$5 million ($3.5 million USD) to bolster the industrial and manufacturing industry in Sarnia, Ont.

Parliament member Marilyn Gladu and Evan Solomon, Federal Economic Development Agency for Southern Ontario (FedDev Ontario) announced the federal investment for two Sarnia businesses.

AlumaPower Corp. will receive $4 million from FedDev Ontario and its Regional Defence Investment Initiative, to support the commercialization of its aluminum-fueled generator systems. The project will help improve productivity, strengthen operations and advance Canadian-developed clean energy technology, officials said. It will also help Canada integrate into global defense supply chains.

The government is contributing $900,000 to Promart Industrial Products Ltd. to modernize its operations and manufacturing capabilities. The funds come from the Regional Tariff Response Initiative, which is designed to help companies diversify its customer base and reduce the effects of U.S. tariffs. The money will be used to add equipment and to increase capacity and productivity.

In a statement, Gladu, who represents the region, said she was thankful for the federal funds.

“Sarnia–Lambton–Bkejwanong has a proud history of manufacturing, innovation and industrial excellence, supported by skilled workers and businesses that are ready to seize new opportunities,” Gladu said. “Today’s investments in AlumaPower and Promart Industrial Products will help local companies strengthen their capabilities and grow right here in our community. This is good news for local businesses, workers and the future of our regional economy.”

Rob Alexander, AlumaPower CEO, echoed Gladu in his statement.

“We are extremely grateful for this support, which will accelerate the commercialization of our technology,” he said. “National defense requires power generation that is safe, clean, reliable, and difficult to detect in the field. This investment will help us bring our products to market faster, strengthen Canada's defense innovation ecosystem, and create high-quality jobs as we scale. On behalf of the entire AlumaPower team, we thank FedDev Ontario for this support.”

text:
NJBIA is cautioning the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection in a hearing today that the state’s continued participation in the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI), as currently established, will only worsen energy affordability and increase greenhouse gas emissions for the Garden State.

The association is also greatly concerned about the DEP’s proposed mandate of a 90% reduction in allowances from natural gas plants over the next 10 years at a time of increased energy demand, which will cause more New Jersey energy plants to shut down and more in-state pollution.

The DEP is hosting a virtual meeting this morning to amend the New Jersey Carbon Dioxide (CO2) Budget Trading Program rules, which were published in the New Jersey Register on Sept. 8.

NJBIA’s warnings come after it launched a “Rethink RGGI” awareness campaign in June to promote a potential policy solution addressing the state’s current economic and environmental challenges of participating in RGGI, with auction rates now approaching $40 per ton.

NJBIA's solution would offer relief for New Jersey ratepayers, improve the state’s air quality, while also maintaining reinvestment dollars in state clean energy and environment programs.

“RGGI, despite its initial intent and presumed effectiveness in reducing carbon emissions, no longer works to achieve its goals,” said NJBIA Deputy Chief Government Affairs Officer Ray Cantor.

“Our natural gas power plants, many of which are highly efficient combined cycle units, cannot economically compete with dirtier power plants in other states, such as Pennsylvania and West Virginia, who are not part of RGGI.

“This results in ‘leakage’ to those states,” Cantor said.

Cantor said the state’s predicament was foreseeable, and the current rule proposal does not offer a solution.

“We knew that if the cost of allowances rose significantly, which they have, that our clean power plants could not compete with lower cost, dirtier plants in non-RGGI states,” Cantor said.

“The result now is that we produce less energy in-state, and we therefore must buy more electricity from the PJM grid. This leads to higher costs for consumers and, ironically, more greenhouse gas emissions for our residents.”

NJBIA’s recommendation during the Rethink RGGI campaign, based on industry analyses, is to eliminate the RGGI auction allowance price and replace it with a $7-per-ton allowance charge.

Cantor said this change could annually save New Jersey consumers $279 million, provide $135 million to the state for ratepayer relief or reinvestment, and reduce carbon emissions by 5 tons.

Assemblyman Wayne D’Angelo (D-14) has also proposed similar legislation.

“The DEP must seriously consider this change if it is serious about affordability and emission reductions,” Cantor said.

Regarding DEP’s proposal for a 90% reduction in allowance over 10 years, Cantor said it will cause more New Jersey plants to shut down, more leakage to other states and more pollution for New Jersey.

“We assume that this proposal was based on assumptions that there is a replacement of clean energy for this mandated reduction of electricity from natural gas plants in New Jersey,” Cantor said. “But there isn’t any viable replacement of clean energy and, as we all know, demand is rising.

“So the replacement energy will be from the PJM grid leading to even more pollution and higher costs for our residents. These changes to RGGI will also exacerbate the resource inadequacy issues now facing the entire PJM region."

Cantor questioned how the DEP could support an effective 90% reduction of generation from clean natural gas plants at a time of a capacity shortage.

“Governor Sherrill has called for the modernization of gas plants, but no investor will upgrade their plants to stay online when RGGI makes them non-competitive with other sources and is calling for them to reduce emissions to an extent where they can no longer operate,” Cantor said.

“RGGI can’t just operate in a vacuum. It must be reevaluated, re-thought, in the context of the region, the need for capacity, the competition from non-RGGI states, and growing demand for energy.”

description:

text:
US solid-state battery developer Factorial Energy is building a solid-state battery production line in Cheonan, South Korea, with local equipment suppliers playing key roles. PNT has been selected to supply dry electrode equipment, a critical component of mass production, while Philenergy will provide turnkey equipment for the assembly process.

According to industry sources on Oct. 15, Factorial issued purchase orders this week for equipment needed at its solid-state battery pilot line. Korean equipment manufacturers will participate across the battery production process, from electrode manufacturing and assembly to downstream processes. Factorial CEO Siyu Huang was also understood to have visited South Korea to inspect the company's Cheonan production facility.

Headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts, Factorial develops solid-state batteries and has attracted investments from global automakers including Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz and Hyundai Motor. The company listed on the US Nasdaq in June through a merger with a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC).

Factorial established its Korean subsidiary, Factorial Korea, in April 2022 and set up a production facility in Cheonan. The facility currently produces its FEST semi-solid-state batteries on a bench-scale production line to validate manufacturing processes and sample performance. Unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries, semi-solid-state batteries use electrolytes in gel or slurry form rather than liquid electrolytes.

Factorial decided to expand its Cheonan production line to meet customer letters of intent (LOIs) and order volumes. The new line will be used to verify productivity and secure manufacturing technologies needed for future mass production. Factorial has previously tested the performance of its FEST batteries in electric vehicles from Stellantis and Mercedes-Benz.

Factorial's battery manufacturing process is largely similar to that of conventional lithium-ion batteries. Cathodes and anodes are produced during electrode manufacturing, then processed and assembled into cells. The batteries are completed through downstream processes including formation and inspection. Factorial plans to introduce dry electrode technology for cathode production to improve battery performance and simplify manufacturing.

Dry electrode technology involves mixing cathode active materials, conductive additives and binders without liquid solvents, then compressing the mixture into electrodes. By reducing the need for drying equipment used in conventional wet processes, the technology can lower energy consumption and capital expenditure. It is particularly important for solid-state batteries, whose solid electrolytes are sensitive to moisture and solvents.

Factorial combines dry cathodes with ultrathin lithium-metal anodes, an approach that can significantly increase battery energy density.

However, manufacturing dry cathodes is more difficult than producing dry anodes because cathode materials are harder and more brittle, making it challenging to achieve uniform electrodes during compression. Factorial selected PNT for its competitiveness in technically demanding dry electrode equipment. PNT has developed roll-to-roll technology capable of processing electrodes up to 1,500 millimeters wide at high speeds. The company has also secured five orders for dry electrode equipment and two for solid-state battery equipment.

Philenergy will supply assembly equipment, including notching machines that cut electrodes into specified shapes and stacking systems that layer cathodes and anodes. The notching process will use a press method in which dies stamp out electrode shapes. Yujin Technology will supply the die components.

Philenergy disclosed on Oct. 15 that it had signed a new equipment supply contract with Factorial. The contract runs through the end of December 2027. Although the contract value was not disclosed, it is estimated at several billion won.

"Factorial selected equipment suppliers based on the capital expenditure required for its Cheonan pilot line," an industry official said. "It chose relatively large companies such as PNT and Philenergy for core processes including electrode manufacturing and assembly, while assigning other processes to smaller suppliers."

"Semi-solid-state and solid-state batteries still require further technological validation to achieve stable mass production," the official added. "Factorial plans to establish a mass production line in Boston after securing process stability and satisfactory yields in Cheonan. Existing equipment suppliers are also likely to participate in the US investment."

Factorial's batteries are expected to be commercialized in drones and robots before electric vehicles. In July, the company announced its first commercial order for drone batteries. Earlier, in May, it established a partnership with US-based KULR, Netherlands-based Tulip Tech and South Korea's JR Energy Solution to commercialize drone batteries.

KULR is responsible for battery thermal management and safety improvements, while Tulip Tech will develop battery packs. JR Energy Solution will oversee the Asia-Pacific market from its base in South Korea.

Factorial is also working with SK On. The companies signed a memorandum of understanding in July to cooperate on solid-state battery manufacturing. SK On will contribute manufacturing technology and production experience, while Factorial will provide battery cell design technology. They will also evaluate the feasibility of mass-producing solid-state batteries using existing production equipment.

In South Korea, Samsung SDI, LG Energy Solution and SK On have established solid-state battery production lines. Samsung SDI operates its S-Line pilot facility at its Suwon research and development center and aims to begin mass production of solid-state batteries for humanoid robots in the second half of next year.

LG Energy Solution produces solid-state battery samples at its Ochang mother line. At its Gwacheon research center, the company assembles the samples into battery packs to evaluate their performance for electric vehicle applications. SK On has established a solid-state battery pilot plant at its Daejeon research institute.

Michigan’s House, Senate and governor’s office are all up for grabs in November as Democrats and Republicans compete

Democrats say they’d prioritize affordability by pursuing policies to address prescription drug prices, price gouging

LANSING — Michigan Democrats and Republicans are already building legislative wishlists should they win full control of state government in November, when the governor’s office and all 148 seats in the Legislature are up for grabs.

Democrats say they want to control prescription drug costs. Republicans say they want to cut property taxes. And legislative leaders from both parties say they want to crack down on price gouging and rein in high healthcare costs.

Many of the ideas are holdovers from the current Legislature, in which a Republican-led House and Democratic-led Senate have been at odds during what is considered one of the least productive two-year sessions in state history.

While candidates from both parties are pushing affordability proposals on the campaign trail, the midterm election may ultimately come down to how voters feel about Republican President Donald Trump, said Matt Grossmann, director of Michigan State University’s Institute for Public Policy and Social Research.

“That has an almost perfect relationship for who they say they’re going to support in the state legislative race,” said Grossmann, who noted the significant national headwinds Republicans are facing due to Trump’s poor favorability ratings.

“If you believe the national, generic ballot numbers and the statewide polls, then you would expect a very large shift toward the Democrats,” he said.

That could be good news for Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson, who is up in polls and has spent significant time campaigning with legislative candidates she’d like to join her in Lansing.

But Republican nominee John James is claiming momentum for the GOP in the homestretch and has proposed a slew of conservative proposals he would need a cooperative Legislature to help pass.

Here’s a look at what current and prospective legislative leaders say state government could look like if their party wins full control on Nov. 3.

What Democrats want

Democrats last enjoyed full control of state government in the 2023-24 session, which began with a roar of sweeping new laws — gun reforms, clean energy laws, Right-to-Work repeal, protections for gay rights — but ended with a whimper amid political infighting.

Should Democrats get another chance, they’d focus on affordability issues from the outset, said Sen. Darrin Camilleri of Trenton, the party’s presumptive leader for the upper chamber next term.

In doing so, “it’s critical that we look to legislation that we’ve tried to address this year,” he said, referencing Democratic bills to create a prescription drug affordability board that could cap prices and crack down on algorithmically driven dynamic pricing.

Democrats who helped pass data center tax breaks in late 2024 have more recently proposed additional data center regulations that have not advanced in Lansing but could be revisited next year.

Under the bills, hyperscale data centers could not use more than 2 million gallons of water a day and would be required to pay laborers and contractors tasked with building these data centers an area’s prevailing wage. Notably, the package does not include a moratorium on building data centers, nor does it provide limits on how loud the facilities can be.

“We have a lot of ideas to pull from, which I do think will help set us up to be very productive starting in 2027,” Camilleri said.

House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri, D-Canton, is keeping potential policy priorities closer to the chest.

Speaking with Bridge Michigan on Monday, Puri agreed that “affordability is absolutely the need of this moment” but said he did not want to prescribe a policy agenda until he learns the makeup of the new Democratic caucus and the ideas these lawmakers could bring to Lansing.

But housing and healthcare access are going to continue to be prominent issues, he said, adding it was important Democrats “have a plan for community and economic development, and … ensuring that every kid has access to a great public education.”

What Republicans want

Republicans last had full control of state government from 2011 to 2018, when legislators worked with Gov. Rick Snyder to pass tax code reforms, expand Medicaid and create Right-to-Work and read-or-flunk laws that Democrats later repealed.

Whether or not Republicans retake control of state government, House Speaker Matt Hall told Bridge he will resume his fight to “dramatically lower property taxes,” which his chamber proposed this term.

“I’ve proven in the first term – whether it’s a trifecta, whether it’s one chamber (control) – we can pretty much accomplish the same things,” said Hall, R-Richland Township.

A proposal to eliminate the 6-mill state property tax rate passed the Republican-led House in June but did not include a plan to backfill state revenue losses for schools and local governments. Hall floated the possibility of a replacement tax on certain services at the time.

Hall also expressed interest in improving “the regulatory environment” for Michigan businesses, telling Bridge it is important not only to entice new companies to the state but also to keep and grow those already here.

Hall said he’d try again to repeal Michigan’s clean energy standards, a shared goal with James, the GOP gubernatorial nominee. A 2023 law passed by Democrats will require the state’s electric providers to have a 100% clean energy portfolio by 2040.

State Sen. Roger Hauck of Mount Pleasant, the presumptive Senate GOP leader next term, said he’s “open to looking at” the kind of property tax repeal plan Hall is pushing but said he hadn’t dug into the policy and noted that “property tax reform starts at the local level.”

Hauck told Bridge he’d like to see the Senate — and, by extension, its 17 standing committees — meet more regularly with Republicans back at the helm.

In doing so, Hauck said he’d like there to be a focus on state department accountability, which he defined as requiring agencies to respond to taxpayer inquiries in a more timely manner.

Hauck also said he was interested in addressing chronic absenteeism in Michigan. Hall said legislators need to “hold the schools accountable and continue to improve them” when it comes to childhood literacy scores.

“We’re bringing back phonics,” Hall said, referencing a newly adopted literacy training requirement for teachers, “but there’s more we have to do.”

text:
Chinese storage system provider Mova has introduced the LumeGret S5000, a residential energy storage system designed to integrate rooftop solar generation, battery storage, household electricity consumption, and electric vehicle charging.

The system features an integrated inverter with four maximum power point trackers (MPPTs), supporting a combined solar input of up to 4.8 kW. The PV input operates across a voltage range of 13 V to 48 V, with a maximum input voltage of 60 V and a startup voltage of 15 V.

The S5000 can be combined with Mova’s LumeGret B3000G and B5000G lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery modules, which offer storage capacities of 3 kWh and 5 kWh, respectively. According to the manufacturer’s specifications, the systems can be expanded to 15 kWh and 25 kWh.

The battery modules are rated for at least 10,000 cycles under specified test conditions and feature self-heating and aerosol fire-extinguishing functions. Mova specifies an operating temperature range of -20 C to 55 C, IP65 protection, a 10-year warranty, and a design lifespan of 20 years.

The S5000 supports grid-connected AC output of 800 W by default, with a maximum configurable output of 3 kW. It also provides up to 3 kW of off-grid output, with a bypass rating of 3.6 kW.

For electric vehicle owners, the system can be paired with Mova’s optional LumeGret E7000 charger, which supports charging at up to 7 kW when sufficient power is available. The manufacturer specifies an EV charging output of up to 3 kW in off-grid operation and a bypass capacity of up to 6.6 kW in grid-connected operation.

EV charging can be managed through the Movahome app, which allows users to configure charging schedules, power levels, and energy priorities. The system offers manual and automated charging modes.

In smart charging mode, the S5000 uses electricity price information, solar generation, and available surplus PV power to optimize charging schedules. Mova says the system can access electricity pricing information from approximately 860 electricity providers.

Users can configure price thresholds to pause charging during periods of high electricity prices or prioritize charging when grid electricity becomes cheaper. The system also supports charging during periods of negative electricity prices.

A solar-surplus charging function can automatically initiate EV charging when excess PV generation exceeds 500 W, according to the company.

The S5000 measures 480 mm × 290 mm × 168.4 mm and weighs 14.8 kg. It uses natural cooling and supports Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and RS485 communication. Optional accessories include smart meters, EV chargers, and smart plugs.

Mova has not disclosed pricing or commercial availability details in the supplied product information.

text:
Three county leaders called for local data center development oversight and protections for Harris County residents during a press conference Oct. 15.

The overview

Harris County Attorney Abbie Kamin, alongside county commissioners Adrian Garcia and Lesley Briones, held a press conference to ask the state legislature to expand the county’s authority to oversee data center development. The three Democratic officials are seeking reelection in November.

Currently, counties have “little to no authority” to stop data centers from developing in the county, Briones said.

“We need to be informed so we can be leaning in to do everything we can to protect our community and environment,” Briones said.

During its Oct. 15 meeting, the Harris County Commissioners Court passed a motion to increase information on oversight. The court’s action will require:

County departments to notify the court when major data centers apply for permits

The County Attorney’s Office to report on the county’s existing authority and oversight over data center development

The county’s Office of Intergovernmental and Global Affairs to identify and advocate for statutory changes to strengthen county oversight in unincorporated areas during the next legislative session

Harris County has 55 operating, under construction or planned data centers, according to agenda documents. In Texas, Harris County is second to Dallas County in the number of data centers, per a press release.

The background

In September, Gov. Greg Abbott directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to halt all data center permits until the state can complete an audit, per previous Community Impact reporting. The decision bars state agencies from advancing regulatory approvals on data center development until the audit is complete. Kamin said the findings are expected in December.

“We know data centers place a significant demand on our electrical grid, our water supply, air quality and impact the neighborhoods around them,” Kamin said. “Whether a project is a net benefit depends largely on where it’s located, how it’s designed and in terms under which they’re approved. The question is, ‘What can Harris County do about this?’”

Harris County is not permitted to regulate data center locations through zoning because the county does not have zoning laws, Kamin said.

According to agenda documents, residents near existing and proposed data center sites have raised concerns about:

Environmental impacts

Grid reliability

Noise

Property values

Public safety

Utility costs

Water and energy use

Kamin said CenterPoint Energy, the county’s primary utility provider, expects to connect eight gigawatts of new data center load in the Houston area by 2029, with about four additional gigawatts to follow. That would increase “peak demand” in the region by about half, she said.

Large data centers can generate significant tax revenue, but they require substantial land, electricity, water and supporting infrastructure while creating relatively few permanent jobs, agenda documents state.

Kamin said state law offers sales tax exemptions of 10-20 years to qualifying data centers.

“This isn’t about being against technology or new technology, but growth has to go hand in hand with accountability,” Kamin said. “And any facility that comes to our county should follow the rules, be a good neighbor and be transparent with the community that they are joining.”

What’s next

Garcia said the upcoming legislative session, which begins in January, will be an opportunity to regain some local control.

“We need real authority and the opportunity to have a real voice,” Garcia said.

Garcia, a board member of the Texas Conference of Urban Counties, said the group is working to bring “meaningful legislation” to obtain local control and “make sure that we are protecting the quality of life of our neighbors.”

“We are working to understand what opportunities the county has in terms of legal authority,” Garcia said. “But the reality is that there’s very little. That’s the bottom line. There’s very little that the county can do. However, we have to work toward legislation to make sure that local officials have an actual seat at the table.”

text:
A proposed expansion at the Juniper Ridge landfill has left Old Town, Maine, residents pressing for more information. The plan would reach into three acres of wetlands even as the facility already manages PFAS-related waste streams.

Here's what to know

At a Juniper Ridge Advisory meeting in Old Town, public concern focused on two connected issues: the wetlands included in the proposal and how the facility handles PFAS-related leachate. WABI reported that the expansion would affect three acres of wetlands, a detail residents said raised the stakes for runoff and water-quality risks.

When officials explained where PFAS at the landfill comes from, they said construction and demolition debris accounts for the largest share, about 35 percent. They also pointed to incinerator ash, special waste including fuel-truck discharge, and asbestos.

The larger question is whether a project framed as a public benefit justifies putting more strain on the host community and the surrounding waters.

More background

Heavy rain was a major part of the objection. Because Old Town already takes in around 52% of Maine's trash, neighbors said adding wetland acreage to the landfill footprint increases the chance that stronger storms could push runoff past the site and into local waterways.

Neighbors also tied those worries to the kinds of waste handled there. PFAS—often called "forever chemicals" because they persist in the environment—came up alongside construction debris, incinerator ash, and other special waste streams, reinforcing residents' view that the proposal carries environmental and public health implications beyond a routine land-use decision.

Another unresolved point was where treatment would occur. Officials said Maine's public benefit determination does not require PFAS treatment to happen in any particular place, which residents took as a sign that a key piece of the plan remains unsettled even as the community is asked to accept further impacts.

What's being done?

Officials say PFAS treatment at Juniper Ridge focuses on leachate rather than other contaminants, and the current plan is to send that leachate 20 miles away to a separate wastewater treatment facility.

An official said, "After it's been treated, it will either be taken by pipeline to a wastewater treatment facility or be trucked to its further destination of a wastewater treatment facility. So they have to say, they have to get the phone up and say to us, okay, we're putting this on bypass, something that we started doing in 2000."

Project officials said the transport of leachate and other cancer-causing materials would be handled with an emphasis on regulatory compliance and public safety. Even with those assurances, residents continued to object as officials said the same standards would guide the project going forward.

Where can I learn more?

The concerns raised in Old Town echo fights elsewhere over landfill expansion, PFAS, and who gets a say in how waste is managed. Coverage from North Carolina, Tennessee, and California shows how those battles play out around approvals, contamination concerns, and hazardous waste handling.

• In North Carolina, residents sued after a landfill was linked to the state's highest PFAS in tap water.

• In Tennessee, residents warned rural towns were outgunned as lawmakers weighed changes to landfill control.

• In North Carolina, an audit warned that hundreds still haven't been checked at old landfill sites.

• In Napa Valley, landfill workers threatened suit over a toxic waste disposal practice they called deliberate pollution.

Harris County saw a nearly 20% increase in voter registrations in four years.

text:
James Talarico’s chance to flip a U.S. seat in Texas has been a decade in the making.

Surging voter registrations along the urbanizing Interstate 35 corridor and in previously Republican Harris County have created a one-two punch for Democrats to run up the score on election night – if they have an energizing candidate. .

As Beto O’Rourke showed in 2018, a Democrat who can create the right energy can use turnout in those areas to offset GOP dominance in the Texas Panhandle, deep East Texas and deep-red Montgomery County.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

FLIP-FLOP TRACKER: How Texas’ top candidates are changing their tune on key issues

O’Rourke came within 219,000 votes of defeating U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz that year. His surprisingly close run set the playbook for Talarico, who now hopes to carry the baton across the finish line.

Houston Chronicle Logo

Want more Houston Chronicle?

Make us a Preferred Source on Google to see more of us when you search.

Add Preferred Source

Here’s a look at four key areas Talarico will need to win on Nov. 3.

Harris County

Before 2018, Republicans regularly won Harris County, becoming one of the rare massive urban counties in America that the GOP could rely on during almost any election cycle.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Republicans held the county judge seat for 44 years, carried the county in seven of the eight previous gubernatorial races and both U.S. Sens. Ted Cruz and John Cornyn easily carried it. That all changed when President Donald Trump assumed office.

By 2018, Trump’s approval ratings were slumping and voter registrations were surging thanks to aggressive Democratic-leaning groups who had learned how to navigate the state’s complicated voter registration laws. Harris County saw a nearly 20% increase in voter registrations in four years. Coupled with O’Rourke’s frequent campaigning in the largest county in Texas, he won the county by 200,000 votes.

For Talarico’s camp, the good news is Harris County has continued to grow, adding another 400,000 voters over the past six years. If turnout is even just a few percentage points higher than 2018 and he were to win closer to 60% of the county versus O’Rourke’s 56%, that alone would generate close to 100,000 more votes, bridging half the gap that kept O’Rourke from winning in 2018.

Inching that turnout up seems plausible for Talarico, given that Paxton doesn’t have the same Houston roots as Cruz.

State Rep. Ann Johnson, D-Houston, said Texans are still paying the price for a missed opportunity in 2018 and hopes Harris County can serve as a model for the rest of the state.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“Harris County has been a community that has elected Democrats, when you look at 2018 at Beto and the enthusiasm (he had),” Johnson said. “Life would be different if we’d gotten that right.”

Johnson, who is running for reelection in state House District 134, gave a pep talk to about a half dozen volunteer blockwalkers on a Saturday morning this month in Houston.

Kien Tom and Nathan Thokala, both high school seniors, were assigned a roster of about 40 doors to knock in Rice Military. The narrow streets and garage-entry townhomes that define the neighborhood are not particularly conducive to blockwalking, but the two teenagers found themselves speaking to a friendly audience when they did get people to answer their doors.

Most homeowners signaled that they were already on board with Talarico, so Tom and Thokala’s primary goal became to provide them with information on how and when they could cast their ballots.

“A lot of people have very strong opinions of who they’re voting for but not a strong voting plan, and that’s a problem especially in Texas where there’s a lot of rules that are pretty predatory toward voters,” Tom said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Rio Grande Valley

For most of the last 50 years, the Rio Grande Valley has been a blue beacon for Democrats. President Donald Trump shattered all of that in 2024 when he won Hidalgo County, the largest county along the Texas border with Mexico. He was the first Republican presidential candidate to carry the county since Richard Nixon in 1972.

Talarico desperately needs that outcome to be a one-off. If Hidalgo doesn’t flip back to blue, there is no way Talarico will win, said Richard Gonzales, the Hidalgo County Democratic Party chairman.

“There’s no way,” he said. “I don’t see the math.”

After launching his Senate bid in September 2025, Talarico went straight to McAllen for his first rally. He’s made at least another dozen stops in the Valley or further west along the border, into Laredo.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Talarico has outspent Paxton and his allies on Spanish-language television in the Valley by more than a million dollars through September and has built a get-out-the-vote operation that needs to outperform O’Rourke’s in 2018. O’Rourke won Hidalgo County in 2018, but his margin of victory was less than Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton’s two years earlier.

While Trump carried the county in 2024, races down ballot stayed blue, and in the last two midterm elections with the governor’s race on the ballot, Democrats dominated.

Trump may be unintentionally helping Talarico. Polls show Hispanic voters shifting heavily away from the president as affordability issues, immigration roundups and the Iran war have taken over the national conversation.

But Hidalgo County Republican Party chairman Robert Cantu said more and more people in the Valley see Republicans in line with their politics.

“I do think we can keep it up,” Cantu said about 2026. “The Republican turnout keeps growing and growing, and I think that it’s going to be more permanent because we’ve been working to make that happen on the ground for a long time now.”

Williamson County

Talarico needs to run up the score in his home region around Austin.

He can’t just win cobalt blue Travis County; he needs neighboring suburban counties like Williamson and Hays to break even harder for him than they did for O’Rourke in 2018.

Williamson and Hays broke for Ted Cruz in 2012 during his first campaign for the Senate. O’Rourke narrowly won both in 2018. And there’s reason to think the trend away from Republicans can happen again for Talarico.

The evolution really started in 2014, said State Rep. John Bucy. Bucy lost his first statehouse run that year, but he said local Democrats have been steadily building a grassroots infrastructure that has helped move the county from red to purple.

“I really think he’s going to run up the score here,” the Williamson County Democrat said of Talarico.

One reason for his optimism: Talarico grew up in Round Rock and kicked off his campaign in the now burgeoning suburb. Talarico and Bucy both flipped Republican-held seats in the Texas House in 2018.

Voter registrations in Hays and Williamson have also jumped off the charts in recent years, growing at twice the state average.

Tarrant County

The state’s largest purple county, Tarrant is now one of the biggest potential prizes for any Democrat. Ahead of the election, Talarico has especially tried to appeal to moderate Republicans and independents, and both have strong presences in the Fort Worth region. That was evidenced by the region’s willingness to back Trump in 2016, Joe Biden in 2020, and then Trump again in 2024.

Trump’s margin of victory was about 40,000 in Tarrant in 2024. O’Rourke won it by just over 4,000 votes in 2018. That’s a 45,000-vote swing from Democrats back to Republicans that Talarico cannot allow to happen.

But Paxton has a strong track record in Tarrant County, carrying it in every statewide election for Texas attorney general since 2014.

“The energy this time is different,” said Crystal Gayden, the former chair of the Tarrant County Democratic Party.

Democrats have blasted Tarrant County leaders this cycle for voting to close down several polling locations. Gayden said that, along with a full slate of local candidates, including a high-interest county judge race, will drive voters to the polls.

“We have really given voters a reason to get out and vote,” Gayden said ahead of a recent blockwalking event in Fort Worth. “I also believe that we're going to see some swing votes – those voters who may have traditionally always voted Republican – from the blockwalks and the interactions that we're having with voters. Their base is tired.”

Like Williamson and Hays counties, Tarrant sits along Interstate 35, which runs north from Laredo and has become a kind of blue spine for Democrats.

Before 2018, Cruz and Cornyn would routinely win the 21 urbanizing counties along I-35. But that year, O’Rourke won the stretch by more than 440,000 votes – an almost 800,000 vote swing for Democrats compared to 2014.

For Democrats, the good news is those counties are also growing faster than the rest of the state.

text:
DARTMOUTH — On Oct. 15, Tim Hodgson, Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, committed $100 million to advance offshore wind development in Nova Scotia.

This commitment intends to help secure the private investment needed to move projects like the province’s Wind West clean energy initiative from concept to development.

Wind West, a Nova Scotia–led project to develop offshore wind farms and connect their electricity to customers, aims to generate enough zero-emissions electricity to power Nova Scotia’s entire population and export additional power beyond Nova Scotia via new transmission infrastructure.

Per an Oct. 15 press release, $5 million of this $100-million commitment will go to the deployment of floating light detection and ranging (FLiDAR)–mounted buoys. By measuring offshore wind speeds and ocean conditions, these buoys will provide data to help proponents prepare for the upcoming project’s Call for Bids, which will be launched by the Canada–Nova Scotia Offshore Energy Regulator in winter 2027.

Natural Resources Canada says it is also providing nearly $3 million to Net Zero Atlantic to expand existing modelling to include the transmission of offshore wind power from Nova Scotia to Quebec, Ontario and beyond and conduct marine survey work to support transmission cable routing.

“Nova Scotia’s world-class wind and highly skilled offshore workforce, developed through the legacy of offshore oil and gas, give Canada a competitive advantage in the potentially $1-trillion global offshore wind market — an advantage we are determined to seize. We will unlock Atlantic Canada’s massive potential by accelerating offshore wind development and strengthening Nova Scotia’s position as a supplier of reliable, affordable and clean energy to customers in the province and across Canada,” Minister Hodgson said in a press release.

High gas prices have prompted many car shoppers to reconsider electric cars this year, and sales so far show Tesla is still by far the most dominant player in the U.S. plug-in vehicle market.

Electric vehicles accounted for 6.4% of all U.S. new car sales in the third quarter of 2026, up from 5.8% in the second quarter, according to Cox Automotive. This comes as the price of gas in the U.S. averaged $4.33 on Oct. 15, according to AAA. That's up from $3.06 one year ago on Oct. 15, 2025.

The most popular electric car so far this year is the Tesla Model Y, which the Austin, Texas-based company sold over 262,000 units of this year, more than the next 24 best-selling models combined, according to Cox.

“What we’re seeing now is a market finding its footing again,” Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of Industry Insights at Cox Automotive, said in a statement. “And high pump prices are likely helping as well. With gas prices well above $4 a gallon, electric vehicles look better than ever.”

With that in mind, USA TODAY Cars took a look at which cars are the top-selling EVs so far this year and what that list says about the current market.

What do the top EV sellers say about the market?

The electric market entered 2026 in one of its biggest-ever periods of uncertainty. President Donald Trump ended a popular $7,500 tax credit for EVs that had existed since the end of former President George W. Bush's administration, meaning plug-in models would have to sink or swim on their own for the first time in decades. California state leaders stepped in to offer $3,750 in tax rebates to first-time EV buyers in a bid to bridge at least some of the gap, but those discounts only go to Golden State residents.

EV makers received an unexpected boost, however, when gas prices spiked over $4 per gallon this year after the launch of the U.S-Iran war. Drivers flocked to fuel-efficient models like hybrids and EVs, giving plug-in makers a second chance to make a first impression in some cases.

Valdez Streaty, Cox's director of Industry Insights, said the numbers show the EV industry is stabilizing after taking a big hit when Trump pulled the plug on the federal tax credits.

"The third quarter was the highest EV sales volume in a year, and improvement through 2026 suggests the reset phase is largely behind us," she said. "The next stage of growth will be driven by great products, competitive pricing, and automakers that continue to give consumers compelling reasons to make the switch."

There are many more manufacturers entering into the EV market now than there were several years ago, as evidenced by the fact that there are 10 models this year that have sold more than 10,000 units. But the numbers also show that despite all the controversies causes by its CEO Elon Musk taking very public political stances, Tesla is still far and away the most dominant player in the U.S. EV market. The Model Y and Model 3 have accounted for more than 35% of all EV sales this year, according to Cox's data.

"Nearly every automaker posted lower year-over-year EV volume in Q3, although a handful stood out," Cox said, singling out brands like Toyota, Lexus, Rivian and Subaru for continuing to gain momentum with increased 2026 EV sales.

"At the same time, the brand with the market’s most mature product line continues to drive industry growth," Cox continued. "Despite a 20% year-over-year decline, market leader Tesla remained dominant, accounting for more than half of all EV sales in the United States during the quarter."
