title: The Political Beat Candidate Guide: North Carolina State Senate District 41 - WSOC TV
description:
That means being able to afford a home, raise a family, find a good job, and send their children to a strong public school.
My focus is on lowering everyday costs, strengthening public education, improving public safety, and making government more responsive.
North Carolina should help build the next generation of technology, but residents should share in the benefits.
My opponent supports all three constitutional amendments and legislation allowing the state to dissolve an elected school board.
North Carolina needs the power to dissolve a board that fails its students, parents, and taxpayers, through more reconstitution authority.
text:
Senate District 41 includes areas from central and west Mecklenburg County to Plaza Midwood.

Incumbent Democrat Caleb Theodros and Republican Kevin Gray are vying for the seat.

Caleb Theodros (D)

Why are you running?

I’m running for reelection because people should be able to build a good life in the community they call home. That means being able to afford a home, raise a family, find a good job, and send their children to a strong public school.

I grew up in Charlotte as the son of immigrants and attended Harding High School. My family’s experience helped shape my belief that hard work matters, but so does having access to opportunity.

I want our growth to work for the people who already live here, not just those who can afford to move here. My focus is on lowering everyday costs, strengthening public education, improving public safety, and making government more responsive. I’m running to continue that work and make sure the concerns people bring to me become priorities in Raleigh.

Are you in favor of the three constitutional amendments on North Carolina’s ballot? Why or why not?

No. I support responsible tax relief and secure elections, but I do not support these amendments.

The income-tax amendment would lower the constitutional cap to 3.5%. I oppose locking that limit into the Constitution because future lawmakers need the ability to respond to recessions, natural disasters, and the needs of our schools and communities. We should debate tax policy based on what families need, not permanently restrict the choices available to future voters.

The property-tax amendment requires the legislature to impose limits but leaves the actual limits and exceptions to future legislation. Voters deserve to know those details before changing the Constitution. I support targeted relief that helps people stay in their homes, rather than an undefined restriction that could put local services at risk.

The voter-ID amendment expands the constitutional requirement to all voting methods. State law already requires photo identification for in-person and mail voting, with an exception process. I do not see a need for this additional constitutional change. My priority is secure elections that remain accessible to every eligible voter.

What should the state do about data centers?

North Carolina should help build the next generation of technology, but residents should share in the benefits. I support artificial intelligence and the opportunities it can create. I also take seriously the concerns about electricity, water, and what host communities receive in return.

The state should establish clear rules that protect households from paying for infrastructure built primarily to serve these facilities. Data-center companies should cover the costs they create, including necessary electric-grid and water-system upgrades. We should require transparent reporting on resource use, enforceable environmental standards, and meaningful local input.

Any public incentive should be tied to measurable public benefits, such as workforce training, local investment, and lasting revenue for the community.

I do not support a blanket ban, and I do not support a blank check. The question should be whether a project makes life better for the people who will live alongside it.

CMS has faced numerous controversies over the past month. What, if anything, should state lawmakers do?

Parents and taxpayers deserve answers, and students need stability. I support the independent investigations and financial reviews underway. CMS should cooperate fully, and any findings of misconduct should lead to accountability, regardless of someone’s position or political affiliation.

State lawmakers should focus on the safeguards that protect public money: stronger disclosure of consulting contracts and payments, clear conflict-of-interest rules, protection for employees who report wrongdoing, and corrective-action plans with firm deadlines when audits identify failures.

We also need to distinguish allegations from proven facts. Accountability requires an honest investigation, not a political rush to judgment.

I would not support using this situation as an excuse to cut classroom funding or take away the voice of local voters. Our responsibility is to protect students, restore trust, and make sure education dollars serve their intended purpose.

What legislation will you pursue to bring down costs?

I will focus on the expenses that determine whether a family can get ahead: housing, utilities, child care, and unexpected fees.

I introduced the Secure Home, Secure Future Act to help longtime homeowners remain in their homes. For qualifying residents who have owned and occupied their home for at least 15 years, it would generally limit annual property-tax payment increases to 2% by allowing larger increases to be deferred. This is a deferral, not blanket tax cancellation, and repayment rules would apply. I will continue pushing for that protection.

I also helped introduce the Affordable Housing Efficiency Grant Program, which would support upgrades that reduce energy costs in affordable multifamily housing. My Working Hearts, Empowered Homes Act would expand and better coordinate support for working families, including child care and health services.

I will also continue working with Representative Laura Budd on legislation to address predatory towing. We need clear pricing, enforceable consumer protections, and a fair process for disputing improper charges.

Affordability should be measured by what families have left at the end of the month.

What sets you apart from your opponent?

What sets me apart is my approach to solving problems and a record that voters can evaluate.

Before entering the Senate, I chaired Charlotte’s Equitable Development Commission and the Black Political Caucus. My background also includes banking, technology, and small business. Those experiences shape how I approach public service: understand the problem, bring the right people together, and follow through.

The Coaches Care initiative is one example. After introducing legislation on mental-health training for school coaches, I worked with advocates and education leaders to advance the proposal through the North Carolina High School Athletic Association. Its board adopted the requirement for high school head coaches unanimously. I did not treat a stalled bill as the end of the work.

There are also clear policy differences. My opponent supports all three constitutional amendments and legislation allowing the state to dissolve an elected school board. I favor targeted affordability measures and strong financial accountability while preserving local voters’ voice.

I want people to judge me by whether I listen, show up, and turn their concerns into action.

Kevin Gray (R)

Why are you running?

I am running to represent the common sense citizen, to let them know they have a voice in Charlotte. In my 42 years of living in major cities and working on both sides of the political aisle, I’ve seen how what policies corrode communities over time, up close. Growing up in a Black conservative household and tight-knit community, I lived out the formula that took working class families like my own, to the middle and upper-middle class, without the help of government. That formula is what I want to inject into our politics. At that same time, Democrats proved to me that their leadership leads to a rise in crime, substandard education, children being harmed, homelessness rising, cost of living rising, and overall quality of life declining. Charlotte is too amazing of a city for me to sit back and watch this predicted decline without stepping up and being a canary in the coal mine with the lived experience to be a voice for what our communities truly need.

Are you in favor of the three constitutional amendments on North Carolina’s ballot? Why or why not?

Voting YES for all three amendments is the common sense way to go! Working and middle class North Carolinians should definitely want to KEEP TAXES LOW! That 3% doesn’t sound high, until you realize that’s the percentage of your income that goes to your phone bill. Why give that to Uncle Sam? Protecting our elections through voter ID is a no-brainer as well. An 85/15 issue. I will not let common senses policies go the way of the asterisk of an issue because special interests groups are paid to make a fuss about them.

What should the state do about data centers?

The state should educate the public on data centers, and leave it to local jurisdictions to decide. They aren’t for every community, but they will benefit some. However, as I talk one-on-one to voters, data centers are not a personal priority. It’s a news headline. They’re way more concerned with the decline in safety in our streets. When I ride the light rail, the potential nuisance of data center noise is not on my mind. The lack of security in our city and rise in the mental health crisis, is. We should be talking about what the state should do about safety in our big cities.

CMS has faced numerous controversies over the past month. What, if anything, should state lawmakers do?

It’s time to clean house, for our children’s sake! CMS is under investigation by the State Auditor, SBI, and FBI. I’m not prejudging the outcome, but if the allegations prove true, the General Assembly must step in. Current law lets the State Board seize the district’s finances, but it wouldn’t be able to remove the elected school board. North Carolina needs the power to dissolve a board that fails its students, parents, and taxpayers, through more reconstitution authority. I would sponsor that legislation.

What legislation will you pursue to bring down costs?

Bring down taxes! When taxes increase, your bank account shrinks. When your bank account shrinks, prices don’t shrink…and everyday purchases become more costly to you. Lawmakers can easily lower costs by lowering taxes. Mecklenburg just experienced an increase in taxes, which made our trips to the grocery store more expensive! Plus, with the amount of local corruption we’ve seen in recent years, giving even more money to this government would personally make me feel complicit in lining the pockets of fraudsters and scammers. Don’t get fleeced by politicians who say they want to make things more affordable, by taking more of your money. It literally makes no sense!

What sets you apart from your opponent?

”Woven into the American fabric” is what comes to mind. And undoubtedly, I come from a long line of American weavers. My (Harris/McWhirter) roots in the piedmont region date back to the early 1700s. We’ve helped make this area the beautiful and unique place that it is today through business and land ownership, conservative Godly values, civil service, and understanding how fortunate we are to add value to American society in any capacity we see fit…because we know it gives back in return. In my mid 20s, I didn’t honor that legacy. I succumbed to left wing propaganda and revisionist history, and saw socialist policies I pushed for degrade the Black community in particular. Thankfully, I had a history to look to and see better outcomes. My opponent doesn’t have the legacy and wisdom to fall back on to see how Democrats and leftist policies have stagnated and hurt the Black community in every era of history when everything around him is blaming White people and republicans for holding us back. I see right through it. TLDR: I’ve lived the American dream, and I’ve seen what turns America into a nightmare. My opponent hasn’t.

title: 6 Policy Levers Local Governments Can Use to Shape Data Center Energy Impacts
description:
How Data Centers Impact Local and Regional Energy Systems The first step for setting local policy is to understand the energy impacts of potential data center development.
Local Governments Have More Influence Than They Realize Local governments have three primary pathways for influencing data center energy use and impacts: Mitigate facility-level impacts through local policies, zoning, permitting and development requirements that shape data center design and operations.
Policy Levers for Mitigating Facility-Level Data Center Energy Impacts Few local regulations were designed with data centers in mind.
A major challenge for local governments is understanding the energy and water demands and broader system impacts of proposed data center developments.
Ensuring Data Center Growth Delivers Community Benefits Without clear policy frameworks, data center development can quickly outpace the energy, economic and climate goals of the communities that host it.
text:
As local governments across the United States make progress toward their clean energy goals, a new challenge is emerging: rising electricity demand from data centers.

Data centers are not new, nor are they the only driver of growing electricity demand. However, the speed and scale of recent development have placed them at the center of conversations about land use, infrastructure investment, siting and economic development. Communities are increasingly concerned about the impacts of data centers on local energy and water systems, noise and air pollution, as well as the broader implications of the growth of artificial intelligence (AI) on economies and society.

Local officials are now grappling with how to enable responsible data center development while delivering tangible community benefits and minimizing potential harms. In most cases, existing local zoning and regulatory frameworks were not designed for today's large-scale data centers, prompting jurisdictions across the country to reevaluate their rules and processes. More than 500 local governments have passed data center-related ordinances or moratoria.

Many of the most consequential decisions affecting data center energy demand occur at the state and regional levels, including utility regulation, transmission planning and wholesale market rules. But local governments retain significant influence over facility-level energy impacts through zoning, permitting, disclosure requirements, design standards and community benefits frameworks.

This article explores these policy levers, highlights emerging practices from communities across the U.S. and offers practical considerations based on WRI’s ongoing technical assistance to local governments. Together, these levers can shape where data centers are built, how they operate and whether their energy demand supports or undermines broader community goals.

How Data Centers Impact Local and Regional Energy Systems

The first step for setting local policy is to understand the energy impacts of potential data center development. Not all data centers are alike. A data center operated by a local business, hospital or university may have very different energy needs and community impacts than a much larger hyperscale facility used to support cloud computing or train AI models. Similarly, local and regional energy systems vary significantly. Factors such as facility size, computing workload, project design and operations, location and grid conditions all influence how much electricity a data center uses and how it affects the regional grid.

Historically, data centers have been sited in or near metropolitan areas to be close to end users and support digital services that rely on fast data processing. Today, the rapid growth of AI and cloud computing is resulting in larger facilities that can require enormous amounts of electricity. Some facilities are adding hundreds of megawatts of new electricity load, equivalent to the energy use of a small city. As a result, these facilities are increasingly being sited in rural or exurban areas where land, power, water, and other infrastructure may be more readily available and where larger projects can be more easily accommodated.

Mid-scale (facilities over 10 MW) and hyperscale data centers (generally 50 MW to over 1 GW) can place significant pressure on local and regional energy systems. Concentrated electricity demand can strain aging grid infrastructure, increase electricity costs and complicate efforts to meet state and local climate goals if this new demand is primarily met with fossil fuels. To accommodate growing demand, including from data centers, some utilities are delaying planned coal plant retirements and proposing gigawatts of new natural gas generation. Some data centers are planning to build new power plants behind the meter.

In addition, data centers use back-up power generation on-site to maintain operations during grid outages. Today, diesel generators are the most common form of backup power, though some facilities are beginning to use natural gas generators, battery storage or hybrid systems. Depending on the technology used, these backup systems can contribute significantly to local air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.

Local Governments Have More Influence Than They Realize

Local governments have three primary pathways for influencing data center energy use and impacts:

Mitigate facility-level impacts through local policies, zoning, permitting and development requirements that shape data center design and operations.

Catalyze community-scale energy investments that lower energy costs, reduce emissions, strengthen resilience and increase grid flexibility.

Influence utility, regulatory, legislative and wholesale market decisions to address regional grid impacts and ensure existing customers are not burdened with undue costs.

This article focuses on the first pathway: the policy levers local governments can use to shape data center development and operations at the facility level, from siting and permitting through decommissioning. Future articles will cover the other two pathways.

Policy Levers for Mitigating Facility-Level Data Center Energy Impacts

Few local regulations were designed with data centers in mind. However, local governments can draw on decades of experience managing other forms of large-scale industrial and infrastructure development. Crafting effective policy requires transparent processes for evaluating proposed projects, engaging residents, assessing risks and benefits and monitoring outcomes over time. It also requires clear rules and guardrails for project approval, operations, enforcement and decommissioning to help protect communities throughout a facility's life cycle.

The six policy levers below can help jurisdictions put these principles into practice. Many local governments combine these levers into a comprehensive data center ordinance, but they can also be tailored to reflect local authority and community priorities.

Lever 1: Use Zoning to Guide Where Data Centers Are Built

Zoning is one of the most powerful tools local governments have to influence where and how data centers are developed. While cities and counties typically have limited authority over utility planning and electricity policy, they retain significant control over local land use and project approvals. As a result, zoning, comprehensive planning and other land use authorities can help address concerns about locating data centers near homes, schools and other sensitive uses while shaping facility design and potential energy impacts.

To better manage growth, jurisdictions are increasingly defining data center types as distinct land-use categories within comprehensive plans and zoning codes and creating dedicated overlay districts. These tools allow jurisdictions to direct development to preferred locations and apply additional requirements to certain types of projects, such as hyperscale developments. Overlay districts can steer data centers toward locations with available transmission capacity, areas where clean energy is accessible, sites collocated near potential end uses for heat recovery and reuse or areas that avoid further clustering in grid-constrained regions. For example, Prince William County, Virginia created Data Center Opportunity Zone Overlay Districts to direct development toward areas with existing infrastructure capable of supporting it. Local governments can further strengthen these efforts by coordinating with neighboring jurisdictions to promote a more consistent regional approach.

Lever 2: Establish Clear Requirements Through Permitting

Permitting is a critical mechanism for translating community priorities into project requirements. Cities and counties can influence project design and operations through site plan approvals and conditional or special-use permits, as is done in Atlanta, Georgia. Project approval can be conditioned on requirements such as energy and impact assessments, disclosure of anticipated electricity use, energy-efficient design features, clean energy procurement or specified community benefits. Permitting can also be used to limit the use of fossil fuel backup generators. To be effective, these requirements should be backed by monitoring, enforcement mechanisms and clear penalties for noncompliance. For facilities already in operation, permit renewals can be used to introduce new requirements.

A major challenge for local governments is understanding the energy and water demands and broader system impacts of proposed data center developments. Without this information, it is difficult to evaluate community impacts, negotiate project design or benefits or establish operating guidelines. To address this gap, some jurisdictions require energy- and water-related disclosures during the permitting process. For example, Phoenix, Arizona adopted a zoning text amendment requiring data centers to report estimated annual “Power Consumption (MW)” and demonstrate utility service or capacity before obtaining a permit.

These disclosures can help jurisdictions assess a facility's operational characteristics before approving a project. Local governments can use tools such as the Great Plains Institute's development review checklist to guide evaluation of proposed facilities.

Lever 3: Increase Transparency Through Energy Disclosure and Monitoring

Jurisdictions cannot manage what they do not measure. Beyond initial assessments conducted during permit review, local governments can require ongoing reporting from data center operators to monitor whether facilities are operating as anticipated and assess cumulative impacts on local infrastructure, utility systems and climate goals. Many jurisdictions already collect and report building performance data through benchmarking ordinances and building performance standards. Similar approaches could be adapted for data centers by requiring ongoing disclosure of electricity use, peak demand, backup generation capacity, water use and other operational characteristics. Chicago, Illinois is considering such an approach. Some jurisdictions are also experimenting with disclosure requirements for other energy-intensive land uses, such as cryptocurrency mining and marijuana cultivation, as is being done in Boulder, Colorado.

Reporting requirements may also be linked to permit renewals, operating agreements or decommissioning processes to ensure accountability throughout a facility’s lifecycle, similar to practices used for utility-scale energy projects and other industrial developments. Public-facing dashboards can further increase transparency, strengthen accountability and build community trust. To ensure disclosures are meaningful, municipalities should clearly define required metrics, reporting timelines, data formats and verification procedures, as well as legally enforceable mechanisms and fees for noncompliance.

Lever 4: Shape How Facilities Are Designed and Powered

Data center design is a primary determinant of energy use and environmental impact. Key considerations include building and IT equipment efficiency, cooling systems, backup power and opportunities for heat recovery and reuse.

Local governments can encourage more sustainable design through permitting requirements, development incentives and sustainability standards. Some jurisdictions, like Lake County, Indiana, require an energy efficiency plan demonstrating how facilities will conserve energy and use renewable energy resources for permit approval. Jurisdictions can also require or incentivize certification under recognized sustainability programs such as LEED for data centers, Green Globes for Data Centers and BREEAM. Minnesota recently enacted legislation requiring just this.

Policies can also shape key operational choices, including backup power sources. Diesel backup generators, in particular, can contribute to local air pollution, greenhouse gas emissions and noise impacts, especially when deployed at large scale or operated for extended periods. Battery energy storage can reduce emissions and air pollution while improving system flexibility and resilience. Local governments can further encourage innovative approaches such as waste heat reuse through district energy systems or industrial applications.

While most large-scale data centers cannot meet all of their electricity needs through on-site renewable energy alone, jurisdictions can encourage clean energy adoption through on-site generation and storage, as well as off-site clean energy procurement. Solar and battery can improve resilience, reduce reliance on the grid, provide grid-support services and lower emissions and local air pollution if used instead of fossil fuel generators. Aurora, Illinois, for example, requires data centers to either use on-site renewables for at least 25% of peak load or provide battery storage equal to at least 50% of peak load for 15 minutes, with alternative compliance available. Clear compliance pathways should identify allowable procurement mechanisms (such as power purchase agreements, renewable energy credits or utility green tariffs) or other requirements.

Lever 5: Remove Barriers to Clean Energy and Storage

Local governments can remove barriers to clean energy deployment and facilitate the installation and scaling of distributed and utility-scale clean energy resources, including solar, wind, battery storage and microgrids. Streamlining permitting and modernizing municipal regulations can make it easier for residents, businesses, data center developers and renewable energy developers to install and scale clean energy technologies.

Local governments can update zoning ordinances to clarify what can be installed where and establish simple, transparent permitting pathways for clean energy projects. Organizations like WRI support jurisdictions in identifying and addressing these barriers through programs such as the U.S. Department of Energy’s SolSmart program, which provides free technical assistance and resources to improve local zoning and permitting for solar development.

Battery energy storage systems deserve particular attention from local governments. Expanded battery storage can help maximize use of existing grid infrastructure, increase system flexibility and reduce the need for new fossil fuel generation. However, many jurisdictions lack clear rules governing the siting and deployment of battery energy storage systems, creating uncertainty for developers and slowing project deployment. Clarifying local requirements can dramatically accelerate battery adoption by data centers, businesses and residents alike. For example, New York State has developed model laws and guidance documents to help municipalities standardize local battery storage regulations.

Lever 6: Align Private Investment with Public Priorities

Local governments can use community benefits ordinances, development agreements and other approval requirements to ensure data center projects deliver tangible value to residents. These policies establish expectations for community investments and create a formal mechanism for aligning private development with public priorities.

Detroit, Michigan, provides one example. The city’s Community Benefits Ordinance applies to qualifying development projects and creates a structured process for negotiating benefits between developers and residents. Similar approaches are emerging for data center development. In November 2025, Lancaster, Pennsylvania signed a community benefits agreement with a data center developer that included a $20 million community investment and commitments related to clean energy procurement. Communities can use these agreements to secure investments in priorities such as energy efficiency, clean energy deployment, workforce development, utility bill assistance, virtual power plants or other locally defined priorities.

Local governments can also tie tax incentives, tax increment financing, expedited permitting or other development incentives to measurable public outcomes. Incentives may be conditioned on commitments related to clean energy use, sustainable design, workforce training, community investment or other policy goals. To protect public interests, these agreements should include clear performance metrics, reporting requirements and clawback provisions if commitments are not met. Climate Mayors provides resources for elected officials interested in negotiating with data center developers.

Ensuring Data Center Growth Delivers Community Benefits

Without clear policy frameworks, data center development can quickly outpace the energy, economic and climate goals of the communities that host it. Yet local governments are far from powerless. Through policy levers like zoning, permitting, disclosure requirements, enforcement mechanisms, incentives and community benefits frameworks, local governments have significant authority to shape how data centers are developed and operated, what impacts they have on communities and energy systems and whether and how communities benefit.

Energy is only one part of the story. Communities are also grappling with issues such as land use, water consumption, economic development, housing pressures and community engagement. Many of the same policy levers discussed above can help local governments address these challenges, making proactive planning essential to ensuring data center growth aligns with community priorities and delivers shared benefits.

At the same time, local governments do not operate in a vacuum. Many of the most significant impacts of data center growth, particularly those related to electricity infrastructure, regional grid planning and electricity costs, extend far beyond municipal boundaries. Addressing these challenges will require coordination among neighboring jurisdictions, utilities, regulators, legislators and regional grid operators. The effect of data centers on electricity bills varies based on factors such as supply constraints, tariff design, and how infrastructure costs are allocated across customer classes. In some regions, including PJM, rapid data center-driven load growth is already contributing to higher electricity prices, while the urgency to bring new capacity online is increasing costs across the energy supply chain. As policymakers debate how to allocate the costs and benefits of data center growth, local governments can play an important role in advocating for policies that support responsible development, protect residents and ratepayers and ensure communities share in the economic opportunities these investments create.

text:
High gas prices have led to an increase in electric vehicle sales in the U.S.

Tesla remains the dominant brand in the EV market, with the Model Y being the top-selling model.

EVs accounted for 6.4% of all new car sales in the third quarter of 2026.

High gas prices have prompted many car shoppers to reconsider electric cars this year, and sales so far show Tesla is still by far the most dominant player in the U.S. plug-in vehicle market.

Electric vehicles accounted for 6.4% of all U.S. new car sales in the third quarter of 2026, up from 5.8% in the second quarter, according to Cox Automotive. This comes as the price of gas in the U.S. averaged $4.33 on Oct. 15, according to AAA. That's up from $3.06 one year ago on Oct. 15, 2025.

The most popular electric car so far this year is the Tesla Model Y, which the Austin, Texas-based company sold over 262,000 units of this year, more than the next 24 best-selling models combined, according to Cox.

“What we’re seeing now is a market finding its footing again,” Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of Industry Insights at Cox Automotive, said in a statement. “And high pump prices are likely helping as well. With gas prices well above $4 a gallon, electric vehicles look better than ever.”

With that in mind, USA TODAY Cars took a look at which cars are the top-selling EVs so far this year and what that list says about the current market.

What do the top EV sellers say about the market?

The electric market entered 2026 in one of its biggest-ever periods of uncertainty. President Donald Trump ended a popular $7,500 tax credit for EVs that had existed since the end of former President George W. Bush's administration, meaning plug-in models would have to sink or swim on their own for the first time in decades. California state leaders stepped in to offer $3,750 in tax rebates to first-time EV buyers in a bid to bridge at least some of the gap, but those discounts only go to Golden State residents.

EV makers received an unexpected boost, however, when gas prices spiked over $4 per gallon this year after the launch of the U.S-Iran war. Drivers flocked to fuel-efficient models like hybrids and EVs, giving plug-in makers a second chance to make a first impression in some cases.

Valdez Streaty, Cox's director of Industry Insights, said the numbers show the EV industry is stabilizing after taking a big hit when Trump pulled the plug on the federal tax credits.

"The third quarter was the highest EV sales volume in a year, and improvement through 2026 suggests the reset phase is largely behind us," she said. "The next stage of growth will be driven by great products, competitive pricing, and automakers that continue to give consumers compelling reasons to make the switch."

There are many more manufacturers entering into the EV market now than there were several years ago, as evidenced by the fact that there are 10 models this year that have sold more than 10,000 units. But the numbers also show that despite all the controversies causes by its CEO Elon Musk taking very public political stances, Tesla is still far and away the most dominant player in the U.S. EV market. The Model Y and Model 3 have accounted for more than 35% of all EV sales this year, according to Cox's data.

"Nearly every automaker posted lower year-over-year EV volume in Q3, although a handful stood out," Cox said, singling out brands like Toyota, Lexus, Rivian and Subaru for continuing to gain momentum with increased 2026 EV sales.

"At the same time, the brand with the market’s most mature product line continues to drive industry growth," Cox continued. "Despite a 20% year-over-year decline, market leader Tesla remained dominant, accounting for more than half of all EV sales in the United States during the quarter."

text:
An aerial view of the Pennsylvania Digital 1, known as Pax-1, data center project in Middlesex Township, Cumberland County, Pennsylvania. Photo: Courtesy of Kyle Gerber / Used with Permission

(The Center Square) – A group of Democratic lawmakers is demanding answers from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency about its recent guidance exempting data center power generation facilities from certain Clean Air Act rules.

The EPA “misapprehends its own mission” to protect human health and the environment, the group wrote in a letter to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, by its decision to exclude data center power generation facilities that are unconnected to the public electricity grid from the Acid Rain Program – no matter how large or pollutive those facilities are.

“EPA is specifically exempting new, highly-polluting sources owned by companies with near unlimited capital from any obligation to adopt the basic, long-established control standards that apply to existing facilities,” the lawmakers, led by U.S. Sen. Sheldon WhiteHouse, D-R.I., and Rep. Jennifer McClellan, D-Va., wrote.

The Acid Rain Program limits power plant emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, the primary causes of acid rain. Among other conditions, sulfur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOx) are associated with respiratory system damage, adverse pregnancy and birth outcomes, kidney damage, autoimmune disorders, and cancer.

“Bizarrely, under EPA’s new guidance, massive new gas-fired power plants large enough to power cities would be exempt from NOx and SO2 caps under the ARP only as long as they do not serve the public electricity grid and instead exclusively power a privately-owned data center,” the lawmakers commented.

“This is a perverse outcome, and it is contrary to Congress’s design for the Clean Air Act, which creates specific and comprehensive regulatory requirements for significant pollution sources like these.”

Though the group originally sent the letter in September, the EPA still hasn’t responded to its questions about who and what influenced the agency’s guidance, Merkley said Thursday.

Pollution and other concerns surrounding data centers have dominated midterm election campaigns, with many Democrats using those concerns as a political cudgel against Republicans.

Communities with data centers often shoulder higher energy costs due to electricity demand soaring, grid upgrade costs getting passed on to ratepayers, and American taxpayers often funding the discounted rates enjoyed by data centers , according to studies by Harvard Law School and other organizations.

Despite that, the second Trump administration has focused on stimulating AI development and also pushed for national cohesion on regulations. Weeks after being sworn in, President Donald Trump reversed former President Joe Biden’s executive order that took a more cautious approach to AI development.

Trump also signed an executive order last July to expedite data center infrastructure development by allowing projects to be built on publicly owned lands and making taxpayer-funded loans and grants available to financially support “qualifying projects.”

Additionally, he signed an executive order in December withholding broadband funding from states with AI regulations deemed to “harm innovation.” With Trump’s approval, congressional Republicans’ “One Big, Beautiful Bill” also funneled billions of dollars to AI-related initiatives.

Trump has said the U.S. needs to beat China in the AI race.

text:
Washington, D.C. – Congresswoman Jennifer McClellan (VA-04) and U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works (EPW), last month launched a bicameral investigation into the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) guidance exempting data center power plants from the Acid Rain Program (ARP).

By EPA’s own admission, the decision to issue new guidance came at the behest of data center companies. And according to the EPA press release issuing the new guidance, the agency took this action to “further President Trump’s agenda promoting data centers.”

“EPA’s new ARP guidance is a handout to the richest and most powerful companies in the world. And this handout comes at the expense of Americans’ health and the safety of our ecosystems and communities that were, prior to the inception of the ARP, regularly drenched in dangerous acidic rainfall,” the lawmakers wrote in their letter to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin.

The ARP regulates the emission of sulfur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOx) from power plants. SO2 and NOx are both harmful to human health, damaging the respiratory system and worsening heart disease. They are also linked to adverse pregnancy and birth outcomes, kidney damage, autoimmune disorders, and cancer.

The pollutants are also the primary causes of acid rain. Prior to the ARP, acid rain poisoned rivers, lakes, and streams; damaged forests; killed and sickened aquatic animals; and corroded buildings, monuments, and statues.

“EPA explicitly bills its new guidance as a means to facilitate data center development. In so doing, EPA misapprehends its own mission, which is to ‘protect human health and the environment,’ as stated in black and white on the agency’s own website,” continued the lawmakers.

“Bizarrely, under EPA’s new guidance, massive new gas-fired power plants large enough to power cities would be exempt from NOx and SO2 caps under the ARP only as long as they do not serve the public electricity grid and instead exclusively power a privately-owned data center. This is a perverse outcome, and it is contrary to Congress’s design for the Clean Air Act, which creates specific and comprehensive regulatory requirements for significant pollution sources like these,” added the lawmakers.

The lawmakers, together with Senators Ed Markey (D-MA) and Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), requested answers from EPA by October 7th about the agency’s decision-making process while crafting this new guidance, as well as any information regarding the agency’s communications with data center companies. Senators Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Cory Booker (D-NJ), and 24 Members of the House of Representatives also signed the letter. EPA has not yet responded to the lawmakers’ letter.

Paxton announced that his office sent letters to 156 data center developments requiring them to provide accurate, up-to-date information about their water usage.

Data centers support the computing and storage needs of digital services, including artificial intelligence. Their rapid expansion has drawn attention to the resources needed to operate them, including electricity and water.

“Data center developers must follow the law and respect the Texans and communities affected by their operations,” Paxton said. “I am actively investigating data centers across Texas to make sure that Texans and our natural resources are protected.”

Paxton said his office is working to ensure data center companies comply with state law and that their operations do not place unlawful burdens on taxpayers or threaten critical resources.

The announcement did not identify individual developments that received letters in the Houston area or specify whether any companies had violated the law.

The investigation is ongoing.

text:
Ohio-based electric utility American Electric Power (AEP) announced a $4 billion investment to develop a 702 MW fuel cell power generation facility near Cheyenne, Wyoming, under a 20-year power purchase agreement (PPA) with Google, aimed at supporting the technology company’s growing energy needs in the region.

Under the agreement, Google will purchase electricity from fuel cell power generation company Cheyenne Fuel Cell, which is approximately 92% owned and controlled by AEP.

The companies said that they plan to start construction of the new facility in 2026, which the project scheduled to be fully operational by the end of 2028.

The new facility will use fuel cell technology developed by Bloom Energy, designed to provide reliable, on-demand electricity to large-scale customers. According to AEP, the technology generates electricity without combustion of natural gas, and the project includes plans to integrate carbon capture technology to enable near-zero-emissions power generation.

The announcement follows agreements reached between Google and South Dakota-based electric and natural gas utility Black Hills to provide electricity to Google’s planned data center in Cheyenne.

AEP President and CEO Bill Fehrman said:

“As power demand continues to grow, AEP is bringing together new technologies and strong partnerships to deliver reliable, innovative energy solutions quickly and at scale. This project demonstrates how we are creating new opportunities to meet evolving energy needs for customers both within and beyond our traditional service territory.”

title: More Than 71 Million People Still Breathe Unhealthy Air as EPA Delays Soot Protections

text:
Since we published our blog post and white paper concerning the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) failure to implement the 2024 particulate matter, also referred to as PM2.5 or soot, National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS), there have been several updates.

As anticipated, the EPA missed its February 2026 deadline to issue designations. Those designations identify as “nonattainment” the areas that violate the 2024 standard and as “attainment” the areas that comply with the standard, and are a key step in bringing communities around the country into compliance with the standard. In response, we sued on behalf of our clients to compel EPA to act. While that case was working its way through the court, the D.C. Circuit, in a separate proceeding, upheld the 2024 soot standard. Not long after, the Northern District of California court ruled overwhelmingly in our favor that the EPA is overdue in its duties and gave the agency until Feb. 6, 2027, to issue final designations. Areas in nonattainment will then need to follow concrete steps to bring PM2.5 pollution down.

Then, in October 2026, the EPA doubled down on its stance that these life-saving measures should not move forward and announced it would be completing additional analysis for states, tribes, and territories before making the final court-ordered designations. The EPA opened a comment period on the designations, which runs through Nov. 5, 2026. It is vital that the EPA follow the Clean Air Act and designate as nonattainment the areas that violate the 2024 soot standard, including those nearby areas that contribute to violations, just as it historically has done and said it intended to do in February 2024. Anything else would be illegal and arbitrary.

Most states — 45 out of 50, plus Washington, D.C., Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, and three tribes — took the opportunity last year to inform the EPA how the state thinks its areas should be designated. EPA is not required to adhere to the states’ recommendations, but if it intends to deviate from one, it must notify the state at least 120 days before making final designations to give the state an opportunity to disagree with the agency’s decision. Such letters notifying states of the EPA’s planned changes are known as 120-day letters and were due by Oct. 9, 2026, under the deadline set by the Northern District of California ruling. As noted above, the EPA publicly released the letters on Oct. 2.

In the midst of those events, on June 9, the EPA released additional data that incorporated air monitoring done in 2025. These data are referred to as the 2025 PM2.5 design values (DVs) and consist of the three-year averages of annual ambient PM2.5 concentrations at monitors across the country from 2023 through 2025. Then, on Sept. 16, EPA re-released the same design values with a few changes incorporating the agency’s approvals of several exceptional event demonstrations, which moved some counties from nonattainment to attainment. The 2025 DVs are important because they are what the EPA will rely on in the now ongoing designations process. We accordingly updated the analysis in our original blog post and white paper with these new data to determine how many people live in counties with air violating the standard of 9.0 µg/m3. The most current information confirms that soot pollution remains a serious concern for tens of millions of people across the country.

The 2025 PM2.5 design values show 68 counties across 20 states (Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, New Mexico, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, and Texas)[1] reporting a design value greater than the 9.0 µ/m3 standard. The total population of counties not meeting the standard, distributed over 52 metro areas, is over 71 million.[2] DuPage (930,000 people) and Will (701,000 people) in Illinois; Dakota, Minnesota (446,000 people); and Stark, Ohio (374,000 people) are among the counties that previously met the standard, but no longer do.[3] These counties join other areas with long-standing PM2.5 pollution problems on the list of counties where monitoring shows unhealthy air.

Counties violating PM2.5 standard (2025 DVs) Number of counties 68 Population 71,682,747

The subset of U.S. counties with 2025 DVs violating the standard is home to far more people of color, percentage-wise, than the U.S as a whole: counties with unhealthy air are 56% people of color, compared with 39% nationwide.[4] This subset of counties is also 15% Black and 35% Hispanic/Latino, whereas the U.S. overall is 12.5% Black and 20% Hispanic/Latino, making PM2.5 pollution a problem of health inequity.[5]

Now that the EPA has requested additional information from states, tribes and territories, it’s unclear how the agency will use the 2025 design values to set the designations. According to the EPA’s own analysis, implementing the updated soot standard could prevent up to 4,500 premature deaths each year, reduce hundreds of thousands of asthma cases, and deliver up to $46 billion in net benefits. Hopefully communities soon will see meaningful relief if the EPA abides by the law and rightfully implements the court-ordered designations and upholds the life-saving national soot standard.

Sources

[1] In contrast to the 2024 DVs, Minnesota, New Mexico, and Oklahoma now have one county each with a 2025 DV above the standard; and Idaho, Tennessee, and Washington no longer have any counties with a 2025 DV above the standard.

[2] See 2025 Design Value Reports – PM2.5 Design Values, 2025 (xlsx), available at https://www.epa.gov/air-trends/air-quality-design-values#report.

[3] Demographic data obtained from the United States Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-Year Data (2009-2024) (Jan. 29, 2026), available at https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/acs-5year.html.

[4] People of color totals found by subtracting numbers of non-Hispanic white people from the total population of a given area.

Editor's note: This story was produced for the ear and designed to be heard. If you're able, WCMU encourages you to listen to the audio version of this story by clicking the LISTEN button above. This transcript was edited for clarity and length.

WCMU has reached out to Republican Jack Bergman's campaign for an interview and have not heard back. The invitation remains open.

Kenadie Mlujeak: You’re listening to WCMU, I’m Kenadie Mlujeak. Seven candidates are on the ballot this election season in Michigan's 1st Congressional District.

The district includes the entire Upper Peninsula and most of the northern Lower Peninsula. WCMU reached out to all seven candidates several weeks ago to schedule individual interviews with the same questions to give them an equal chance to speak to voters directly.

Today, David Nicholas speaks with Democrat Callie Barr.

David Nicholas: Callie Barr, thank you very much for joining us.

Callie Barr: Thank you so much for having me.

DN: First question is, how would you define yourself politically?

CB: You know, I'm a patriot. I believe in representing the people of upper and northern Michigan to deliver what we need here. I often say this isn't a seat for Republicans or Democrats, it's a seat for the people of upper and northern Michigan, and being a fifth-generation Michigander from Cheboygan, Michigan, I'm deeply, deeply rooted here. And so right now to me, it's about returning this seat to the people who live and work here and just want a shot to be able to afford life.

DN: And what specific ideas or plans do you have to address affordability?

CB: Yeah, well, right now I'm running against an incumbent, Jack Bergman, who's done nothing but increase our costs while actually costing the taxpayer. I mean, he's the number one spender, number one out of 435 members of Congress, the number one spending on lodging. I mean, even during COVID, when members were getting reimbursed like $600, he was reimbursed over $61,000. And along with that, he's done things like vote to cut Medicaid. I would not do that, right? Medicaid funds our rural hospitals.

He didn't extend the ACA subsidies. I would not have done that, right? Because that is something that has increased our insurance premiums across this district. He supports the war in Iran. That has increased the cost of gas and diesel, which has increased the cost of our food and our groceries and the things that we buy at the store. He supports the tariffs, which has increased our costs for our small businesses and also for us, the consumer, and damaged our relationship with Canada.

So, when we think about decreasing costs, what we need to do is get someone out of Congress right now who is at every point increasing our cost of living here, while also at the same time using our taxpayer dollars to live a pretty lavish lifestyle. And so, enough's enough. And so, I support policies that will decrease our costs, which means tackling insurance, making sure we can negotiate every drug price, making sure our rural hospitals are fully funded, not supporting a war right now that is driving up the cost of gas and everything else.

DN: And what is your position on US foreign policy specifically in Iran?

CB: Yeah so, no one's crying, because, you know, that, we fight terrorism, right? And I want to be clear about that. The problem is though, is when you go into a country and you have no plan, and when you are, like I said, increasing, the cost for us, right? We're spending billions of dollars there. We don't have a plan. It's increasing our gas prices.

The other thing is, we're not at full military readiness. You know, I come a military family. My husband is a Marine for 15 years. He served in Iraq and Afghanistan. And what concerns me is that we fired inspector generals. We fired JAG officers. We fired military leaders and commanders who had decades of knowledge and experience in the Middle East because they weren't yes men and yes women.

And so, that is also very concerning that we don't have a military that's at its full capacity and full military readiness to do the job that they're over there being asked to do. And frankly, I don't even know that they know what the plan is because there isn't a plan. And so, all of that, we need leaders in Congress right now, leaders in Congress that are going to have to take a look at this and figure out how we work to negotiate so that we're not in an endless conflict in the Middle East again, like my family was a part of for 20 years.

DN: We are speaking with Callie Barr, Democratic candidate for Michigan's 1st Congressional District. And the next question, what is your position then on tariffs and trade wars, specifically with Canada?

CB: Ugh, I mean, this is... this is ridiculous. Canada is a friend of ours and has been. We have been so damaged, not just with our friendships, but economically as well. When we look at our Canadian friends coming across and sue Canada, they're not coming anymore. We've seen just significant declines, and it has resulted in the loss of millions and millions of dollars of economic benefit to us.

These tariffs have not… these were not thoughtful. They’re chaotic. They've damaged our relationship with Canada. They've damaged our own economy. They were thoughtless and stupid. And we should not be supporting something that not only hurts one of our closest relationships, but also just hurts us too.

DN: And what is your position specifically on the construction of data centers in Michigan?

CB: We are the Great Lakes State, and we have to do everything we can to protect our water. And we need regulation to protect our water. We also need to make sure that there is strong local control that means something, that local communities can make decisions and have voice to actually realize that.

And that also means that we need absolute transparency. We need to know what risks are. We need to know what the impact on the environment is. And the other thing is that our local communities in no way are paying for any kind of energy infrastructure upgrades or costs associated with data centers.

DN: And finally, how would you address the ongoing debate over the Line 5 pipeline running under the Straits of Mackinac?

CB: Yeah, as a congressional representative, I think about what are the things that you can actually do as a congressional representative? Because of course, a representative is not gonna... cannot, by law, overturn a federal permit, a state permit, a state court decision, which is where that line is right now. But what you can do is help to advance towards a clean energy future.

You know, we had tax incentives and subsidies to do exactly that, to help us have the jobs of the future when it comes to working towards a cleaner energy future. And this was supported by, you know, environmentalists. It was supported by our businesses. It was supported by labor, because it was a way to have jobs and training and to start thinking about how we can diversify our energy sources, because we want to have reliable and affordable energy.

And of course, we want to continue to move towards energy sources that help protect this wonderful environment that we live in and that we are stewards over of. And so, to me, that's really important, that we revitalize that effort, which this administration has pulled us back years in that kind of progress.

DN: Callie Barr, Democratic candidate, we want to thank you for your time with us and your time to speak to the voters in the 1st District. We wish you all the best luck with the remainder of your campaign.

title: Tech giants want clean energy in N.C. Is Duke finally ready to help? - Canary Media
description:
For the better part of this decade, Google and other companies have been pushing for a ​“clean transition tariff” as a solution.
In a statement to Canary Media, Duke said it would start negotiations on a clean transition tariff early next year.
Allowing companies to pay for their own clean energy goes a long way in protecting consumers against risk, he said.
Duke’s statement to Canary Media committing to negotiations on a clean transition tariff goes one step further.
​“I find it hard to get excited” about a promise for negotiations over a clean transition tariff, he said.
text:
In North Carolina, tech giants and other large corporations that want their own 24/7 carbon-free electricity have a problem. Across most of the state, only Duke Energy, the state’s vertically integrated utility, can sell them power, and the company’s grid isn’t required to be 100% clean until mid-century.

For the better part of this decade, Google and other companies have been pushing for a ​“clean transition tariff” as a solution. The scheme would allow the large customers to pay a premium for new, zero-carbon energy, using Duke as a go-between.

The idea has virtually no opponents, yet Duke has done little to make it a reality. Now, the company says, that’s about to change.

In a statement to Canary Media, Duke said it would start negotiations on a clean transition tariff early next year. The company said the tariff should build on an existing suite of Duke programs called Green Source Advantage that lets large energy users chip in for already-underway renewable energy projects.

“We continue to be open to a clean transition tariff, over and above our current Green Source Advantage offerings,” Duke spokesperson Bill Norton said. ​“We will seek to engage stakeholders in early 2027 to explore gaps in the current offerings and potential new features and options.”

Norton said that the plans for a stakeholder discussion were ​“definite.” While the statement doesn’t carry the weight of a state policy, it marks the most concrete progress toward a clean transition tariff in North Carolina in years.

In the spring of 2024, Duke announced its intention to pursue such a plan with major tech firms and steel company Nucor but never followed through. Earlier this year, the company said it would evaluate the tariff ​“in good faith,” but made no promises.

Today the need for a clean transition tariff is more acute than ever. Like many utilities around the country, Duke projects surging energy demand from voracious data centers, and wants to raise electric rates and build a spate of new fossil-fuel plants in part to serve the facilities.

Large load tariffs are gaining traction across the U.S. as a way to protect consumers against this massive buildout. In general, they require data centers and other large energy users to commit to paying for a minimum amount of power, and some include bring-your-own-clean-energy provisions.

Such provisions don’t just advance climate goals, advocates say. They also help ensure household customers don’t end up footing the bill for expensive fossil fuel infrastructure for data centers that don’t pan out or that leave the state early.

“So much of the talk around a large load tariff is, rightly, ​‘how do we protect customers from stranded-asset risk?’” said David Neal, a senior attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center and a key proponent of a clean transition tariff.

Allowing companies to pay for their own clean energy goes a long way in protecting consumers against risk, he said. ​“Making it easy for those customers to both fulfill their corporate clean energy and climate goals and help protect ratepayers: It’s just a win-win for everybody.”

That’s in part why clean energy advocates objected to a large load tariff agreement Duke and tech companies unveiled last week: It lacks a clean transition tariff. ​“It’s very frustrating that it keeps getting punted,” Neal said. ​“It should really be front and center.”

That agreement needs approval from the North Carolina Utilities Commission. When Duke presented it to the regulators, the utility said it would support a separate proceeding to advance the clean tariff concept, ​“to the extent stakeholders wish to pursue” one. Duke’s statement to Canary Media committing to negotiations on a clean transition tariff goes one step further.

Some of the most vocal stakeholders pushing for a clean tariff are hyperscalers. Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon all told utility commissioners this summer they backed the concept. Google, which helped enact a clean transition tariff in Nevada and is pursuing ones in Indiana and Minnesota, has frequently promoted the mechanism to North Carolina regulators, including in March testimony.

“Google remains committed to advancing the Clean Transition Tariff in North Carolina,” even though it was left out of the Oct. 6 agreement on a large load tariff, Rachel Wilson, Southeast energy lead for the company, told Canary Media in a written statement.

In September, the Corporate Energy Buyers Association, whose 300 business members run the gamut from hospitality to manufacturing, told regulators that Duke should propose such a tariff for commercial and industrial customers within six months.

“Data centers are an important focus of the current discussion,” the trade association testified, ​“but they are not the only customers creating significant electricity demand or seeking new clean energy resources.”

Clean energy advocates contacted by Canary Media about Duke’s planned talks stressed that regulators need to follow through to make sure the clean tariff comes to fruition.

“This is a long overdue commitment to allowing new customers like data centers to choose their own new, clean, cheap power,” said Will Scott, North Carolina policy director with the Environmental Defense Fund. ​“But we need enforceable direction from the Utilities Commission to make sure this leads to a real, on-the-books outcome that saves North Carolina households money.”

Neal won’t be celebrating unless and until that happens. ​“I find it hard to get excited” about a promise for negotiations over a clean transition tariff, he said. ​“A commitment from Duke to talk about it is insufficient. A commission ordering a date certain by which parameters will be worked out — that’s different.”

title: Blackburn promotes coal, nuclear while Green vows to protect rivers, forest and farmland
description:

text:
Photos Courtesy Marsha Blackburn and Jerri Green

Share:

Tennessee’s next governor will have the power to help shape the policies and priorities for the state’s land, air, climate and water.

Governors can veto state legislation that favors highly polluting energy sources, challenge federal rollbacks on environmental regulations and direct state agencies to fund programs designed to improve air quality or reduce heat risks.

While the state is likely to elect its first female governor this fall, the two leading candidates represent vastly different perspectives on energy and environmental priorities.

Republican candidate and U.S. Senator Marsha Blackburn has aligned her campaign with President Donald Trump’s agenda. The Trump administration has taken at least 570 actions that directly threaten the environment, climate and human health since January 2025.

Blackburn plans to support Tennessee’s nuclear buildout

Blackburn has consistently voted “anti-environment” throughout her career in Congress, according to the advocacy group League of Conservation Voters, which gave her a lifetime voting score of just 3% on environmental issues.

If elected governor, Blackburn promises to focus on expanding the state’s nuclear energy supply and support projects like the Tennessee Valley Authority’s planned small modular reactors in Oak Ridge.

“Tennessee has always been a leader in advanced energy and clean coal technologies, and the road to America’s nuclear renaissance runs right through Oak Ridge,” Blackburn said in a statement to WPLN News. “With ever-growing electricity needs, nuclear power provides a sustainable, efficient, and reliable source of power that won’t let Tennesseans down when they need it most.”

Last year, Blackburn became vocal about expanding Tennessee’s nuclear industry to support data centers for artificial intelligence. She penned an editorial with Sen. Bill Hagerty, R-TN in Power Magazine asking TVA to hire an interim CEO and search for external leadership to lead a nuclear buildout.

“The 21st century will be America’s next Golden Age only if we can supply the vast amounts of power required to run artificial intelligence, quantum computers, and advanced manufacturing,” the senators wrote.

They argued that nuclear energy was the “only viable” solution, and the U.S. was falling behind the world’s energy leader China in expanding nuclear capacity — the U.S. has the largest nuclear fleet but has added little new capacity while China has nearly doubled its nuclear footprint in the past decade. The senators also argued that TVA was preventing a large buildout of nuclear reactors due to a “paralysis of analysis.”

“TVA could be to the nuclear race what NASA was to the space race,” they wrote.

As a senator, just in the past two years, Blackburn has also denied funding for veterans exposed to toxic chemicals, repealed the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s rule under the Clean Air Act that places pollution control requirements on facilities emitting hazardous air pollutants, and allowed Congress to use the proceeds from public land sales to reduce the federal deficit — which can benefit real estate developers and extractive industries like oil and gas. She also voted against bills designed to protect federal funding to support clean energy manufacturing, at times Tennessee’s largest economic driver of new investments, and federal funding for residential clean energy tax credits.

In 2020, Blackburn voted against a bipartisan bill called the “Great American Outdoors Act,” which provides funding to public lands and Tennessee’s Great Smoky Mountains National Park.

Throughout her career, Blackburn has voiced misinformation on climate change. She argued with Bill Nye “The Science Guy” in 2014 about the scientific consensus on planetary warming and claimed “Earth is no longer warming” in 2016. The planet is, in fact, facing warming at an increasingly accelerated rate due mostly to the burning of fossil fuels, deforestation and animal agriculture.

WPLN asked Blackburn about her current position on taking climate action, including whether she supports phasing out fossil fuels, and TVA’s recent announcement to reinvest in its coal plants.

“I fully support the use of fossil fuels,” she said in a written statement.

She had received the ninth-highest amount of donations from fossil fuel interests of any member in Congress as of December 2025, according to an analysis by the liberal think tank Center for American Progress.

Jerri Green plans an AI data center moratorium, climate resiliency efforts

The Democratic nominee Jerri Green is a lawyer and city council member in Memphis.

If elected, Green plans to introduce a statewide moratorium on data centers aimed at “stopping AI companies from running polluting, unpermitted power plants in our neighborhoods and rural communities,” she told WPLN News.

Last week, Green unsuccessfully voted not to delay a vote on a 12-month moratorium on new data centers in Memphis. (City lawmakers are next expected to take up that matter on Oct. 20.)

Green also plans to enforce clean air and water regulations in rural and urban communities that face the most industrial pollution, invest in renewable energy and hold utilities accountable for how they respond to energy demand, which has largely come from data centers in recent years.

“We must aggressively protect Tennessee’s rivers, forests, farmland, and public lands from pollution and overdevelopment to preserve them for future generations of Tennesseans,” Green told WPLN.

On her campaign website, Green lists plans to implement AI literacy in schools, fine large corporations that replace 25 or more workers with AI to pay for local job retraining, require data centers to use recycled water and take back tax breaks from companies that replace “promised Tennessee jobs with robots.”

The Democratic nominee also promises to ensure state-level emergency protections for farmers affected by drought and market swings, invest in rural water systems and prepare communities for climate resilience and disaster recovery.

“Tennesseans deserve a governor who values clean air, safe water, and protecting our land for the next generation, rather than rubber-stamping corporate pollution for short-term profit,” Green said.
