text:
Understanding how city and subnational climate mitigation efforts contribute to global pathways toward meeting the Paris Agreement goals is a persistent challenge. Most global mitigation scenarios are generated by integrated assessment models (IAMs)1,2,3, which represent coupled energy, land, economic, and climate systems over long time horizons and at large scales such as world regions or, in some cases, individual countries4. As a result, these scenarios provide limited guidance at the scale at which a substantial share of mitigation planning and implementation occurs. This mismatch has become increasingly consequential as cities and subnational governments have assumed a more central role in climate governance5,6,7,8, and are often expected to align their emission reduction targets and climate plans with global temperature goals9,10. Here, subnational governments refer to both local governments, including cities and municipalities (defined as below admin-1), and to regional governments such as states and provinces, defined as the administrative tier immediately below the national government (admin-1)11.

Although thousands of cities and subnational governments have developed climate action plans and adopted emission reduction targets12,13,14,15, existing modeling frameworks and climate scenario tools are too coarsely resolved to assess how these actions contribute to or can alter emission trajectories over time9,16. IAMs provide the dominant benchmarks for global mitigation, but their broad resolution makes it difficult to gauge urban commitments within those pathways or to evaluate the cumulative contribution of city action at scale. At the same time, the empirical basis to bridge these models with urban-scale analysis has improved dramatically, with city-level socioeconomic, energy and greenhouse gas (GHG) data rapidly expanding due to the availability of high spatio-temporal data products and emerging machine learning approaches that can predict or harmonize emissions data across large numbers of subnational governments17,18. These developments provide an increasingly strong empirical basis for connecting global mitigation scenarios into spatially-explicit pathways relevant for subnational governance.

Statistical downscaling offers a means of bridging these scales by disaggregating coarse-scale emission totals to finer spatial units19,20. The need for such approaches is increasingly recognized in scenario research, which has emphasized that Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) and related global scenario frameworks require adaptation or downscaling to support both national and local analysis21. Previous studies have demonstrated the feasibility and importance of translating coarse-scale scenarios to finer spatial units, whether for socio-economic trajectories22,23,24,25,26,27, urban land expansion28, or emissions29,30,31. However, downscaling is not only sensitive to the choice of allocation rules and proxy variables, but also to the spatial units through which “urban” areas are defined17. Morphology or pixel-based definitions are well suited to identifying dense urban settlements and the physical location of emissions, but they do not correspond to the jurisdictions through which climate policy and action, budgeting and regulatory authority are exercised32. Analyzing subnational climate action through the lens of administrative boundaries can encompass urban settlements, peri-urban areas where large industrial facilities are located (Figure S1), as well as rural areas within urban jurisdictions. For the purposes of urban climate planning and evaluating responsibility and policy ambition, this broader lens of administrative boundaries allows emissions, and subsequently future pathways, to be associated with political units governing them, although still imperfect and heterogeneous across countries33. Therefore, any statistical downscaling exercise is inherently sensitive to these methodological choices and assumptions.

In this article, we develop a novel framework that integrates downscaled global mitigation pathways from the IMAGE IAM with a dynamic boundary approach to derive urban policy-compatible mitigation pathways. The analysis is based on the SSP2 baseline, a middle-of-the-road socioeconomic pathway characterized by intermediate trends in population growth, economic development and technological change2,34. We downscale macro-regional emissions using a Kaya-based statistical downscaling approach that applies appropriate socio-economic factors most relevant to urban emissions. We further test the robustness of the resulting urban pathway using alternative models and socioeconomic assumptions from the newly developed ScenarioMIP-CMIP7 ensemble35, alternative sources for gridded socio-economic projections, and different model parameters.

Our framework is designed to provide consistent urban administrative pathways across countries rather than detailed projections for individual cities, which would require additional information on infrastructure, sectoral composition, and other drivers of local emissions. We then apply the framework to a unique dataset of emissions mitigation targets (pledges) from 1363 subnational governments from 48 countries12, enabling urban mitigation commitments to be benchmarked against urban-specific climate policy pathways. We focus on territorial emissions and therefore do not capture the full consumption-based footprint of subnational governments36. Subnational governments’ targets also vary in their sectoral inclusion, accounting scope and implementation status. The resulting pathways should therefore be interpreted as scenario-based benchmarks rather than forecasts of future emissions for individual cities or subnational governments.

Our results show that global decarbonization is predominantly urban and that this urban concentration is both prevalent and intensifying across regions and scenarios when using a dynamic administrative-boundary approach. We also find that, if fully achieved, subnational pledges could deliver additional mitigation to up to 16% of the global Medium scenario beyond reductions projected under national policies.

Urban areas are central to future mitigation pathways

Urban emissions trajectories closely follow global pathways under both the Medium and Low SSP2 scenarios, indicating that a large share of long-term decarbonization occurs within urban administrative areas (Fig. 1). The Medium scenario represents the trajectory resulting from national climate policies across both urban and rural areas, whereas the Low scenario represents a pathway that aims to keep warming likely below 2 °C35. Our central estimates use the dynamic urban boundary classification based on a 70% probability threshold, with alternative thresholds included in the sensitivity analysis. Under the Medium scenario, urban gross CO2 emissions (excluding negative, AFOLU and aviation and shipping emissions) increase from 27.3 GtCO2 in 2020 to 29.5 GtCO2 in 2030, and then decrease to 22.2 GtCO2 by 2100. Under the Low scenario, urban gross emissions fall to 10.8 GtCO2 by 2050 and then to 1.93 GtCO2 in 2100. These results illustrate the persistent and increasing concentration of emissions in urban administrative areas and their central role in shaping global emissions trajectories (Fig. 1a).

Urban net CO2 emissions (excluding AFOLU, aviation and shipping emissions) (Fig. 1b) follow a similar trajectory as gross emissions. The net emissions in the Medium scenario begin at 27.3 GtCO2 in 2020, decrease to 24.9 GtCO2 in 2050, then decrease at a slower pace to 22.8 GtCO2 by 2100. The Low scenario follows a similar evolution with a steep decline to 9.2 GtCO2 in 2050, reaching negative values of -0.98 GtCO2 by 2080 then continuing to decrease to -2.5 GtCO2 by 2100.

The downscaled urban emissions pathways are broadly robust across alternative model configurations and methodological assumptions, although the choice of socioeconomic pathway produces larger differences. Figure 2 compares downscaled net emissions across nine sensitivity runs (see Methods). These runs vary the convergence year (2120 and 2180), use alternative gridded datasets for gridded population37,38, GDP37,38, and emissions39, apply a different model (REMIND-MAgPIE), or adopt a different baseline (SSP1). We also include the range of urbanization (50–90%) from the dynamic urban approach as part of the sensitivity. For the main IMAGE-SSP2 scenarios, results are highly consistent across alternative convergence years and gridded datasets, with an average range of 9.9% around the central estimate for both the Medium and Low scenarios over 2020–2100. Results using the REMIND-MAgPIE model for both the Medium and Low scenarios are similar, differing from IMAGE by 3.2 GtCO2 by 2050 and 4.2 GtCO2 by 2100 for the Medium scenario, and by 1.8 GtCO2 in 2050 and 0.8 GtCO2 in 2100 for the Low Scenario. Changing the socioeconomic baseline from SSP2 (Middle of the Road) to SSP1 (Sustainability) produces larger differences. Under the Medium scenario, SSP1 shifts emissions lower by approximately 8.1 GtCO₂ in 2050 and 12.1 GtCO₂ in 2100. Under the Low scenario, emissions are 2.4 GtCO₂ higher in 2050 but 0.9 GtCO₂ lower by 2100. Full results are described in Tables S1 and S2.

Future urbanization concentrates emissions in cities and peri-urban areas

Emissions become increasingly concentrated in urban administrative areas. The share of global emissions associated with urban administrative areas increases substantially over time under both scenarios. Based on gross CO2 emissions, the urban share of global emissions is estimated as 81.2% (78.2–83.0%) in 2020, rising to 90% (85.3–91.7%) by 2100 under the Medium scenario and to 89.0% (83.2–90.9%) in 2100 for the Low Scenario. These estimates are higher than many previously published estimates for the urban share of emissions16,40 because they reflect an administrative boundary perspective, which is more aligned for comparison with trajectories from subnational reduction pledges, and are intentionally more inclusive than morphology or pixel-based definitions of urban areas17. Additionally, similar aggregate urban shares can arise from different spatial dynamics. Our population- and GDP-based downscaling approach captures how emissions shift across urban and non-urban administrative areas over time without prescribing the precise location of individual emission sources or low-carbon technologies. National or regional trajectories may therefore reflect emissions remaining concentrated in established urban areas, shifting toward newly urbanizing and peri-urban jurisdictions, or remaining in areas classified as non-urban.

This global trend masks substantial regional variation in the pace and extent of urbanization (Fig. 3). Some geographic regions already have highly urbanized emissions profiles and experience relatively limited further change, including Eastern Asia (96% in 2020 to 98% in 2100), North America (84% in 2020 to 91% in 2100) and Australia, Japan and New Zealand (85% in 2020 to 88% in 2100) under the Medium scenario. Other regions show more moderate increases in the urban share of emissions, including Latin America and the Caribbean (70% in 2020 to 84% in 2100) and Eastern Europe (73% in 2020 to 80% in 2100). The largest increases occur in Africa (55% in 2020 to 85% in 2100) and Southern Asia (59% in 2020 to 99% in 2100), where ongoing urbanization and economic development will gradually shift emissions to urban and peri-urban administrative areas. The Low scenario shows a similar pattern.

Importantly, relative stability in the urban share should not be interpreted as evidence of a static urban landscape. In several regions, relatively flat trajectories reflect the interaction between population- and GDP-based downscaling and the dynamic reclassification of administrative areas as they urbanize over time. Eastern Asia, for example, already has a highly urbanized emissions profile, while additional growth increasingly occurs in administrative areas that subsequently enter the urban category. By contrast, in rapidly urbanizing regions such as Africa and Southern Asia, development and population growth produce much larger increases in the urban share of emissions. These patterns show that similar aggregate urban shares can mask substantially different underlying urbanization dynamics across regions (Figure S6).

These regional differences are also evident at the subnational level (Fig. 4). Between 2020 and 2050, 51% of first-order administrative entities (admin-1) are projected to experience changes of less than 5% in their urban emissions share, particularly in already highly urbanized regions such as Europe, China and the United States. By contrast, large changes are projected for a smaller set of subnational entities, especially in South America, Africa, and South Asia.

Urban areas drive most modeled mitigation, but subnational ambition varies across countries

We next assess whether existing subnational climate pledges are consistent with the level of mitigation implied by the downscaled urban pathways. We compare the aggregated urban-pledge trajectories of 1363 subnational governments across 48 countries12, with the corresponding downscaled Medium and Low pathways to the same administrative areas. The Medium pathway represents emissions expected under implementation of national policies, whereas the pledged pathway assumes that each participating subnational government fully achieves its reported CO2 reduction target (see Methods). We define mitigation potential as the additional emissions reduction delivered by these subnational pledges beyond the reductions already represented in the Medium pathway. We then compare the resulting pledge trajectories with both the Medium and Low pathways to assess how collective voluntary subnational action relates to the level of mitigation implied by current national policies and a below 2 °C pathway.

If all recorded subnational CO2 reduction pledges were fully achieved, they would deliver an additional 3727.5 MtCO2 of mitigation in 2050 beyond the reductions already represented by national policies (Fig. 5). For the countries with pledging subnational entities, this additional mitigation would reduce emissions by approximately 62% relative to their original Medium pathway in 2050 (5955.1 MtCO2), resulting in collective emissions of 2227.6 MtCO2. This level is only 3% above the corresponding 2050 Low scenario for those entities, indicating that full implementation of existing subnational pledges could bring their collective emissions close to a pathway consistent with keeping warming likely below 2 °C. When only G20 countries are considered, the results are similar to the global results, with a mitigation potential of 3643.4 MtCO2 in 2050, which is 62% of the original Medium pathway (5847.7 MtCO2). The similarity is mainly explained by the high share of pledges located in G20 countries (1352 out of 1363) due to data availability and the fact that the majority of subnational pledges are located there.

A country-level breakdown reveals substantial variation in both the scale and distribution of subnational mitigation potential. China accounts for the largest contribution: if achieved, 26 subnational pledges would collectively mitigate 2346.1 MtCO2 in 2050, equivalent to approximately 61% of their collective Medium pathway (3810.5 MtCO2), and reaching emissions levels only 7% above its estimated emissions in the Low Scenario (1464.4 MtCO2). Other substantial contributions come from Japan (271.1 MtCO2 in 2050 across 125 entities), the US (244.0 MtCO2 in 2050 across 106 entities), and Brazil (227.9 MtCO2 in 2050 across 20 entities). By contrast, the EU contains 935 subnational pledging entities but would only reduce emissionss of around 40.9 MtCO2 in 2050 if all pledges were achieved, likely due to the fact that these entities tend to be smaller in population size (median population of 24,267 for EU pledging cities and 1604,795 for pledging admin-1 regions).

The number of pledges therefore does not translate directly into greater mitigation potential. Instead, the level of government making the pledge appears to be more consequential. Globally, states, provinces and other first-order administrative entities account for 2872.6 MtCO2 (77% of the total urban mitigation potential), compared with 854.9 MtCO2 (23% of the total urban mitigation potential) from cities. This pattern is present in most countries, where region-level governments account for particularly large shares in China (87.5%), the United States (59.2%), Japan (77.6%) and Brazil (86%), whereas cities contribute a larger share in the EU (55%) and South Africa (77%).

Finally, we assess how subnational pledges could alter the aggregated emissions trajectories represented in the Medium (current policies) scenario at the global, G20 and EU levels. A pledge is considered “additional” if the ambition is higher compared to the trend of the Medium emissions pathway7. Figure 6 combines the pledged trajectories of participating subnational entities with the Medium trajectories of non-pledging entities to estimate the aggregate effect of subnational action. Globally, the combined additional mitigation pledged by urban subnational entities is between 14.6 and 15.9% of emissions under the Medium scenario. For the G20, the mitigation potential is between 17.5 and 18.4% of the Medium scenario, and for the EU the mitigation potential is between 5.1 and 5.3% of the Medium scenario. The magnitude of this additional mitigation varies substantially across countries. Relative to their respective Medium pathways, the largest estimated contributions include Japan (60%), Côte d’Ivoire (44%), Brazil (44%), Canada (40%), China (36%) and Kenya (21%). By contrast, the additional contribution is small in Argentina (6%) and India (1%), while in Poland (-2%) and France (-5%) the collective pledge trajectory is slightly higher than the corresponding Medium pathway, indicating no additional mitigation relative to current national policies.

By linking global mitigation pathways from IAMs to dynamically shifting administrative urban units, and using these pathways to benchmark subnational reduction commitments, this study provides a framework for assessing how city and subnational climate action relates to global climate policy pathways. In doing so, we make global decarbonization pathways that have long remained too coarse for urban decision-making more relevant to the scale of subnational governance. Our results show that emissions and mitigation remain strongly concentrated in urban administrative areas across geographic regions and scenarios, that existing subnational commitments could make a substantial additional contribution beyond national policies, and that this mitigation potential varies considerably across countries and levels of government. These findings, together with the downscaling methods and framework established here, provide a policy-compatible framework for interpreting urban climate ambition within broader decarbonization pathways and support the development of more urban-relevant scenario analysis for assessments. Below we discuss three key implications of this work as well as its limitations.

First, deep decarbonization is, to a large extent, an urban process when excluding the AFOLU sector. Urban emissions trajectories closely follow global pathways under both Medium and Low scenarios, but their divergence becomes more pronounced after 2030. Under the Low pathway, urban gross emissions decline substantially through mid-century and approach very low residual levels by the end of the century, whereas considerably higher emissions persist under the Medium pathway. These results reinforce the importance of urban areas and systems to deep decarbonization41, not simply because cities concentrate population and economic activity but because achieving low-warming pathways requires sustained reductions associated with urban infrastructure, energy demand and economic development42. The Low pathway also becomes net-negative later in the century, but should be understood as a feature of the modeled pathway rather than a prediction of where future carbon removals will physically occur.

We also find that existing voluntary subnational commitments are large enough to materially alter future emissions trajectories, but not to close the global mitigation gap on their own. If all pledging subnational jurisdictions in our dataset fulfilled their commitments, they would reduce those jurisdictions’ collective 2050 emissions by approximately 62% compared to the Medium pathway beyond national pledges alone. At the global level, these commitments could reduce emissions by 14.6–15.9% of the urban Medium scenario in the year 2050 and 17.5–18.4% when considering subnational entities in G20 countries, which are the source of nearly 80% of global emissions43. These results demonstrate the potential significance of voluntary subnational action, while also showing that its contribution depends on both the implementation of existing commitments and the capacity of subnational governments to influence the emissions within their jurisdictions.

Realizing this mitigation potential is not guaranteed. Our pathways assume full implementation of existing commitments, whereas implementation can lag behind target-setting because subnational governments face financial and administrative capacity constraints44,45,46, uneven multilevel governance support47,48, and limited authority over major emission sources within their administrative boundaries49. The estimated trajectories are also shaped by the time horizon of current pledges. Where no subsequent target is specified, we assume that emissions remain constant once an entity reaches its target year. Future strengthening, weakening or replacement of these commitments could therefore increase or decrease the contribution of subnational action relative to the pathways estimated here.

The ability of subnational governments to deliver mitigation also depends strongly on the scale and authority of the pledging jurisdiction. As our results demonstrate, first-order administrative governments, including states and provinces, account for over 77% of the estimated mitigation potential, compared with 23% attributable to city-level (below admin-1) governments. This finding suggests that city-level governments may need to align their mitigation efforts with regional jurisdictions, who tend to exercise greater authority over energy systems and transportation infrastructure that extends beyond municipal control, whereas cities may possess greater control over sectors such as buildings, local transport and waste49. Our results reinforce the need for multi-level governance of urban mitigation, where cities, regions and national governments must coordinate to support local decarbonization47,48,50.

Limitations

Our framework prioritizes global consistency and comparability across jurisdictions, which necessarily limits the level of local and sectoral detail it can capture. Several considerations are therefore important when interpreting the results. First, we built our framework around territorial CO2 pathways, which is appropriate for linking subnational targets to IAM-derived mitigation scenarios and to governance units with formal policy authority. But territorial accounting captures only part of urban climate responsibility36. Prior research comparing urban and peri-urban areas’ territorial emissions compared to consumption-based emissions shows that a city’s consumption-based emissions frequently exceed its territorial emissions, particularly in wealthier cities in developed countries where major emission sources (e.g., industry and electric utility) relocate outside of an urban center but a larger share of emissions is embodied in imported goods and services32,36. Benchmarking solely from a territorial-emission lens could make a city appear aligned with a deep decarbonization pathway while in reality its emissions are being displaced through consumption. Similarly urban pledges can also be limited to specific sectors and coverage due to policy responsibility or limited purview. Therefore, future studies should seek to explicitly integrate consumption-based accounting and sectoral disaggregation to help address this issue51.

Second, since we primarily focus on CO2, we are likely undercounting mitigation opportunities for cities and urban areas to reduce non-CO2 gases, such as methane, which is a byproduct of waste and landfills. Recent observational work suggests that landfill methane emissions are substantial for urban areas, particularly in developing countries, but poorly captured in reported or modeled inventories52. Third, our findings on net-negative urban pathways should not be interpreted as forecasts of where CO2 removal will physically occur, but rather as an indication of where responsibility for balancing residual emissions lies within an administrative-boundary approach. This distinction is important because we do not know where future CO2 capture will take place. It may depend on land availability, geological storage potential, and energy infrastructure that are likely located outside of city centers, even when policy responsibility and financing occur within an urban boundary. However, cities also have capture potential such as Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) and carbon storage in buildings53. Fourth, our analysis considers only a global cost-effective implementation of the temperature goal underlying the Low scenario. Although this does not necessarily imply that cities where mitigation occurs also bear the associated costs, effort sharing approaches accounting for a fair distribution of mitigation actions could yield a different picture10. Fifth, although urban emissions can be estimated using population and GDP, additional factors could also influence these emissions18,32. While this study assesses urban pledges at the aggregated country level for which population and GDP are appropriate drivers, future work can explore additional factors relevant to urban emissions and might be able to report consistent and sound results at lower resolutions. Finally, although the urban share is substantial in our analysis, actors beyond subnational governments such as businesses and financial institutions, play a crucial role in achieving the Paris goals, often operating within urban boundaries54.

Global and macro-region scenarios

The scenarios for macro-regions in this study were implemented in the Integrated Model to Assess the Global Environment version 3.4 (IMAGE 3.4) model, which is an assessment model that represents the interaction between the human and earth system and has a focus on global environmental problems such as climate change35,55,56. The model includes 26 macro-regions across the globe, which include some representative large countries such as the US, China, and India. For an IAM, IMAGE has a detailed representation of economic sectors and activities.

In this study, global and macro-regional emissions were downscaled to urban areas under two distinct climate policy scenarios. Both scenarios are grounded in the SSP2 (Middle of the Road) framework, which serves as a reference socioeconomic background where social, economic, and technological trends persist along historical patterns2,34. Using SSP2 as a consistent baseline allows for a direct comparison of urban emission trajectories under different policy interventions. Using this baseline, the Medium and Low scenarios were developed with the IMAGE model as part of the ScenarioMIP-CMIP7 project35,56. The Medium scenario represents the implementation of current policies, assuming national governments implement only domestic climate, energy, and land-use measures already secured by law or executive orders3,57,58. In contrast, the Low scenario represents keeping temperature increase below 2 °C this century with a > 66% probability, and assumes a cost-effective global implementation. This cost-effective approach prioritizes mitigation where it is least expensive, independent of equity-based effort-sharing principles or the actual source of funding for these reductions. Finally, the Very Low emissions scenario, which represents keeping the temperature as low as plausible given feasibility constraints was also included for reference (Figure S8).

Downscaling using Kaya

Downscaling is the process of transforming low-resolution data into finer spatial detail20. In the context of IAMs, downscaling has mainly involved disaggregating macro-regional data into individual country-level estimates29,30. This study advanced this process by developing a two-step approach to estimate future urban emissions. We first downscaled IMAGE-projected macro-regional emissions to gridded emissions at 6 arc-minute resolution, then aggregated them to urban emissions using projected shifting urban boundaries over time. This approach is feasible because emerging studies have estimated diverse gridded data products from 2020 to 2100 aligned with SSP storylines for population22,24,25,26,59,60,61 and GDP in Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) terms23,25,27. However, to our knowledge, spatially downscaled high-resolution CO2 projections until 2050 and beyond are currently unavailable, leaving a knowledge gap between high-resolution historical records and future scenarios39,62,63.

To estimate territorial CO2 emissions for urban areas, we downscaled IMAGE emission projections from macro-regions to urban areas by taking three key steps: (1) downscaling CO2 emissions from the IMAGE model for the 26 macro-regions to the high-resolution grid level35,56; (2) projecting future urbanized pixels based on a rural-urban classification (see below) at the grid level; (3) consolidating the gridded CO2 emissions data for urban administrative areas.

The emissions downscaling was achieved by using a Kaya downscaling approach. The Kaya approach assumes that population and GDP per capita are the primary drivers of territorial CO2 emissions, as described by the Kaya identity64 (Eq. 1). We applied a method based on van Vuuren29, which uses the Kaya identity to downscale CO2 emissions from macro-regional scenario projections to the country level. In this study, we advanced this approach by proceeding to the grid-cell level, which enabled aggregation to urban areas based on spatially downscaled high-resolution gridded emissions (Eq. 2). First, population and GDP (PPP) per capita were calculated for each grid cell on gridded population22,61 and GDP (PPP)23 projections. For this purpose, we selected projections consistent with the SSP2 scenario and compiled a dataset covering the period from 2020 to 2100 at ten-year intervals. Second, CO2 intensity per grid cell was calculated for the last available historical year from EDGAR65, which further excludes AFOLU, waste, aviation, and shipping sectors because of lack of representation in urban areas. In addition to net CO2 emissions, we calculated gross emissions by excluding negative emissions from Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) in the energy supply and industry sectors. The CO2 intensity of each grid cell was estimated under the assumption that it converges toward the value of its corresponding macro-region (see Eq. 3). While this convergence reaches completion in 2150, the values for 2100 represent a state of partial convergence. To this end, it was assumed that emissions and GDP (PPP) values would remain constant between 2100 and 2150. Third, the aggregated regional values for population and GDP (PPP) per capita were then harmonized with the IAM regional projections. Fourth, the Kaya identity is applied to estimate annual CO2 emissions for each grid cell, resulting in a dataset with a spatial resolution of 6 arc-minutes. To ensure consistency with the IAM scenarios, CO2 emissions were scaled using a harmonization factor defined as the ratio between the sum of gridded emissions per year for each region and the corresponding maro-regional emissions from the model. Figure S9 shows the relative difference between unharmonized and harmonized dowscaling results.

The gridded results of the downscaling are aggregated using the Global Administrative Database (GADM v4.1)11, which describes administrative boundaries for all countries. The aggregation was performed through pixel based aggregation considering a proportional share of each pixel to the corresponding administrative unit. The results of each administrative entity are then aggregated at the country level, regional and global level. See Table S5 for aggregation definitions.

Dynamic administrative-boundary approach for projecting urbanization trends

For the identification of each urban area, we use administrative boundaries, the spatial delineation of the subnational jurisdiction defined by each national government, to align emissions estimates with the governance units responsible for pledged mitigation32. To account for increasing urbanization over time, we developed a dynamic administrative-boundary approach that updates the classification of administrative entities as urban or rural across selected time steps. To our knowledge, this is the first explicit future-scenario framework to incorporate dynamically changing administrative boundaries in urban mitigation pathways. Our method builds on the classification proposed by Yu et al.32, which categorizes administrative entities in the GADM 4.1 dataset as urban (urban center + peri-urban) or rural using indicators that capture human settlement activities, and includes population density, GDP per capita, electricity consumption, and built-up proportion and trend over a 40-year period.

We calculated 10 variables used for prediction based onpopulation66, GDP23 and built-up area66 extracted from gridded databases compatible with SSP2 pathways for every decade from 2020 to 2100, as well as spatial characteristics such as each administrative boundary centroid and area (Figure S5). Using the classification results from Yu et al.32 we trained and validated a binary classification machine learning model (XGBoost)67 to predict whether each administrative entity should be classified as urban or rural. For each year, the model estimates the probability that an administrative entity should be classified as urban. We then use these predictions to assign entities to urban or rural categories under a range of probability thresholds (50% to 90%) to represent different urbanization conditions through 2100. For example, under the 70% threshold, entities with a predicted probability of at least 0.7 or higher are classified as urban.

The machine learning model (XGBoost) achieved 97.0% accuracy, 96.1% precision (proportion of predicted target items that are actually target items), and 94.5% recall (proportion of actual target items that are correctly predicted as target items), indicating strong performance in distinguishing urban from rural areas while maintaining low rates of false positives and false negatives. Figure S5 presents how much each input variable contributes to the predictions (feature importance), showing that built-up proportion, population density, and GDP per capita are the three most important predictors. As a final adjustment, we imposed a no-regression rule under which entities classified as urban would not revert to rural status in later years, aligning with the typical persistence of built-up land even where population or economic productivity declines. In other words, once an entity was classified as urban, it remained urban in all subsequent years. A summary of the classification results are available in Table S4.

Based on the assumption of a 70% probability threshold, our results indicate that by 2050, 78.8% of the people globally, or 7.24 billion people, will live within urban administrative boundaries, rising to 91.5% or 8.3 billion people by 2100. These shares are similar to the latest United Nations World Urbanization Prospects projection68 that estimates an 82.9% urban (Cities + Towns) population share in 2050. Under the SSP2 baseline scenario, Asia and Latin America account for most urbanization until 2060, after which Africa will see the majority of urbanization through 2100. Europe and North America see smaller increases due to their already high urbanization levels in 2020 (Fig. 7).

Sensitivity analysis

To assess the robustness of our results, we developed nine additional pathways to the two main scenarios. Each pathway changes one of the key assumptions relative to the main scenarios, while all others are kept the same (see Fig. 2). These sensitivity pathways were: (1) Sensitivity to baseline: we used SSP1 instead of SSP2 as the starting baseline for both the Medium and Low scenarios, together with the SSP1 versions of the gridded population22,61 and GDP data23; (2) Sensitivity to model: instead of IMAGE, we used the Medium and Low scenarios from the REMIND-MagPIE, which were also developed within ScenarioMIP-CMIP7. Both models have a high responsiveness (fast implementation of mitigation potential) but differ in the choice of implemented technologies (lower/higher share of renewables); (3) Sensitivity to gridded emissions: instead of EDGAR69, we used CO2 emissions from the same sectors based on CEDS/CMIP735,39; (4) Sensitivity to gridded population: instead of 2UP22,61, we used CO2 emissions from the same sectors based on COMPASS37,38; (5) Sensitivity to gridded GDP (PPP): instead of Murakami, we used CO2 emissions from the same sectors based on COMPASS; (6/7) Sensitivity to convergence year used for downscaling emissions per GDP (PPP): instead of 2150, we used the convergence years 2120 and 2180 to extrapolate IAM projections; 8/9) Sensitivity to urban-rural classification: instead of 70%, we used 50% and 90% to identify the probability that an admistrative entity would be classified as urban by the model for each year.

Emissions levels based on city reduction targets

To benchmark and evaluate city-level mitigation targets, we implemented a two-step process to compare subnational governments’ climate commitments to the downscaled scenarios. We utilized the ClimActor dataset, which contains self-reported emissions data and mitigation commitments from subnational governments (i.e., cities, states, and regions) reported to public disclosure platforms like CDP, the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy, and other sources12. These commitments specify target years and percentage emission reductions relative to historical baseline, enabling the modeling of emission trajectories for each subnational entity. Each entity is represented by one of the Global Administrative Areas (GADM)11 geometries, enabling the identification of urban areas that have pledged a quantifiable climate mitigation target.

To estimate emissions trajectories for urban entities, we intentionally use only the urban administrative areas. For subnational pledges we consider two groups of entities. The first group represents the subnational entities below the first administrative level (e.g., cities and municipalities) that are considered urban. The urban classification is determined by the proportion of urban area within each entity, based on an urban-rural layer derived from the XGBoost model described above. Specifically, an administrative entity is classified as urban if at least 91% of its pixels are identified as urban for the 70% probability threshold. This cutoff was identified using the first and second derivative to identify inflection points and preserves over 95% of the total emissions and population from the total sample. The second group are the administrative 1 subnational entities (e.g., federated states or provinces) and for these entities their total emissions was adjusted to consider only their urban share based on the same classification used before. To prevent double counting and to ensure global spatial coverage, overlapping entities were excluded. After classifying the urban and rural ADMs, total emissions were aggregated at the country (ISO) level for 2020, 2030, 2040, and 2050. This process allows us to have a complete coverage of subnational pledges and trajectories specifically adjusted to urban areas.

We constructed emission trajectories for urban subnational entities using self-reported mitigation targets from the ClimActor dataset. For each entity, target-year emissions were calculated based on the pledge percentage reduction relative to baseline emissions. Linear interpolation was then applied between base-year emissions, intermediate self-reported emissions, and target-year emissions, with emissions assumed to remain constant after the target year. This approach resulted in emissions projections for each entity, for the years 2020, 2030, 2040, and 2050. We then calculated the resulting rates of change relative to 2020 and applied these rates to the corresponding downscaled Medium and Low emissions pathways for each entity. The resulting pledge-adjusted trajectories are then aggregated at the country or state level by combining the original downscaled scenario for the non-pledging entities and the modified pathway for the pledging entities. The results produced specific urban pathways for 1363 subnational entities using 1718 reported climate mitigation targets. Additional mitigation potential was estimated as the difference between the Medium pathway and the pledge-adjusted Medium pathway, while the Low pathway served as a benchmark for assessing alignment with a below-2 °C trajectory.

title: Environmental activist raises concerns about proposed Galveston LNG facility
authors: Julianna Washburn, Galveston County Bureau, www.houstonpublicmedia.org, julianna-washburn
description:
The Galveston Wharves Board of Trustees approved a lease and development agreement with Power LNG on Oct. 8.
The Galveston Wharves port director and CEO Rodger Rees previously said the project will create jobs and contribute to improved air quality.
The 30-acre development will be located on the east side of an approximately 82-acre tract on the deep-water Galveston Harbor, according to Galveston Wharves officials.
Power LNG and Galveston Wharves officials did not immediately respond for comment about potential environmental concerns at the plant.
Production at the Power LNG facility is expected to begin near the end of 2028 following required approvals and agreements.
text:
An environmental activist is expressing concerns about plans for a liquefied natural gas (LNG) company on Pelican Island.

Power LNG plans to develop a $250 million facility that would be capable of producing about 400,000 gallons of liquefied natural gas per day, which would primarily fuel cruise ships coming in and out of the region. The Galveston Wharves Board of Trustees approved a lease and development agreement with Power LNG on Oct. 8.

Joanie Steinhaus, environmental activist and ocean program director with Turtle Island Restoration Network, said she's worried about the impact the facility could have on the nearby environment, especially when it comes to the release of methane.

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

"If you are working with a project that releases methane and the methane leaks and there’s also methane from the unburned ships and the engines, the methane slips. It’s not cleaner air. This is a fossil methane-producing project, and there are going to be impacts," Steinhaus said.

Steinhaus also expressed concerns about the risk of vapor cloud explosions. She referenced a vapor cloud explosion at a Freeport LNG facility in 2022 that led to excess emissions of carbon monoxide, nitrous oxides, particulate matter, sulfur dioxide and volatile organic compounds, according to the Associated Press.

Methane making contact with open and damaged electrical conduits and circuitry led to the vapor cloud explosion, according to a case study by IFO Group on the incident.

"What risk-based safety areas is this LNG facility going to have? They’re next to a major university. They’re directly across from the community in town," Steinhaus said.

The Galveston Wharves port director and CEO Rodger Rees previously said the project will create jobs and contribute to improved air quality.

"This agreement paves the way for the Port of Galveston to play a leading role in providing cleaner marine fuels to the region. The project will create jobs, bring more LNG-powered ships and contribute to improved air quality. Pelican Island, with its deep-water harbor, industrial operations and available acreage, is the ideal location for an LNG facility," Rees said in an Oct. 8 news release.

The 30-acre development will be located on the east side of an approximately 82-acre tract on the deep-water Galveston Harbor, according to Galveston Wharves officials. Texas A&M University at Galveston is also located on Pelican Island.

Officials with Texas A&M University at Galveston did not immediately respond to a request for comment about whether they have any concerns with the proximity of the facility.

Galveston Wharves officials talked about environmental initiatives and the benefits of LNG earlier this year in a May 27 news release. In the release, Rees said he believed building a small-scale LNG facility on Pelican Island would bring "newer, environmentally beneficial ships," to the Port of Galveston.

LNG cuts sulfur oxide, nitrous oxide and particulate matter by more than 90 percent, according to Rees. He also said Galveston Wharves is making efforts to provide electricity for docked ships so they don't have to use their engines and emissions can be further reduced.

Steinhaus said while liquefied natural gas might be a cleaner-burning fuel than others, it is still linked to health problems.

"I hope people will investigate and understand that they don’t clean the air; they’re adding pollution, it’s still harming our health, and it’s still harming our environment, Steinhaus said.

Power LNG and Galveston Wharves officials did not immediately respond for comment about potential environmental concerns at the plant.

Steinhaus said she plans to attend an upcoming Galveston Wharves board meeting on Oct. 27, in which discussion about the Power LNG facility is on the agenda.

Production at the Power LNG facility is expected to begin near the end of 2028 following required approvals and agreements.

name: Clean Energy
title: What's not to love about big businesses funding local climate resilience? | Letter to the editor
authors: Letters to the Editor, Ashli Blow, William L. Sullivan, Owen Murray, Jaime Adame, Mike McInally, Tyson Alger, Alex Baumhardt, Oregon Capital Chronicle
description:
Eugene voters’ November election ballot includes a gem of a measure, Measure 20-388, the Eugene Clean Energy Fund.
A yes vote will result in millions of dollars a year dedicated to help Eugene build clean energy projects and create clean energy jobs.
It was inspired by a similar program, the Portland Clean Energy Fund, which has been going since 2018 and has invested $1.7 billion dollars for clean energy projects.
The Eugene Clean Energy Fund offers a way for Eugene to reduce emissions and increase climate resilience, especially for our most vulnerable communities.
I urge a yes vote on Eugene Measure 20-388!
text:
Eugene voters’ November election ballot includes a gem of a measure, Measure 20-388, the Eugene Clean Energy Fund. A yes vote will result in millions of dollars a year dedicated to help Eugene build clean energy projects and create clean energy jobs.

It is the brainchild of a local coalition representing Eugene-based organizations, including Beyond Toxics and 350Eugene. It was inspired by a similar program, the Portland Clean Energy Fund, which has been going since 2018 and has invested $1.7 billion dollars for clean energy projects.

The fund will be managed by a panel of experts appointed by the Eugene City Council. Council will also make final decisions about where the money goes. The measure’s popularity with Eugene folks was clear when over 14,000 signatures were gathered in only a few months — an effort I proudly took part in.

How do millions of dollars come into Eugene you ask? The project is based on the concept of license fee that the city would impose on businesses that operate in Eugene. To qualify for the fee, a business would have to make over $1 billion a year nationally and $500,000 a year here in Eugene. Small businesses in Eugene are exempt. A number of other business types are also exempted from the fee including groceries, credit unions, construction firms and a number of others.

These are times of rapidly worsening climate dangers. Heat domes in Europe this summer likely are responsible for 35,000 heat-related deaths. Heat has fueled the “super” El Niño this year, causing extreme weather events and disasters.

Meanwhile, Eugene has only managed a 10% reduction in emissions since 2010, way behind its promise of a 50% reduction by 2030. The Eugene Clean Energy Fund offers a way for Eugene to reduce emissions and increase climate resilience, especially for our most vulnerable communities. I urge a yes vote on Eugene Measure 20-388!

name: American Energy
title: A new class of batteries helps data centers play nicely with the grid - Canary Media
description:
Lithium-ion batteries could do so much for AI data centers and the power grid.
And they’re much cleaner than the diesel backup generators almost all data centers rely on.
Data centers have in fact relied for decades on a type of battery known as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system.
Now data centers have become large enough to represent similar trip-off risks.
But the most recent building under construction has set aside land to one side where the AI UPS batteries will be installed.
text:
Lithium-ion batteries could do so much for AI data centers and the power grid. They’re cheaper than the fossil-gas turbines that tech giants are building at gigawatt scale for their ​“AI factories.” They can cushion the cost of building out grid infrastructure and power plants just to serve data centers’ peak energy demands. And they’re much cleaner than the diesel backup generators almost all data centers rely on.

So why haven’t on-site batteries taken off yet with the computing crowd? It comes down to costs and benefits. Data center developers and operators often see fossil fuels as more reliable for 24/7 power. And industry watchers say the companies are leery of adding batteries unless they see a clear payback — or if they simply can’t do without them.

Data centers have in fact relied for decades on a type of battery known as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) system. It’s essentially a bank of batteries — most of them old-fashioned lead-acid chemistries — that connects to servers and other computing gear to keep them running smoothly in case utility power flickers or fails. Much like backup generators, they don’t do anything useful except during emergencies.

With the right technological fixes, however, lithium-ion batteries that sit between the grid and the data center complex could perform this task, and solve a host of other problems. Specifically, they could serve as shock absorbers to prevent the kind of power disruptions, caused by data centers dropping off the grid unexpectedly, that are emerging as a major threat to grid stability.

That’s the idea behind startup ON.Energy’s new AI UPS. According to CEO and cofounder Alan Cooper, it’s the result of roughly a half-decade of technology development, aimed at delivering what he described as ​“the new standard for connecting the data center to the grid.”

The trick has been to prove that these centralized systems are capable of performing the critical tasks they need to. Earlier this year, ON.Energy concluded trials at the nation’s premiere grid testing facility showing that its technology works.

Now, with a 5-gigawatt order from major AI data center developer Crusoe, ON.Energy is preparing to put this centralized UPS system to the test at commercial scale.

“The grid sees a battery that’s always charging, and the load sees a battery that’s always outputting perfect quality power,” Cooper said. ​“In an oversimplified way, it smashes together BESS” — the industry term of art for grid-scale battery energy storage systems — ​“and UPS into a single asset.”

ON.Energy isn’t the only company building batteries for this purpose, said Shahil Shah, chief engineer at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, formerly known as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. Shah is in charge of the grid simulator lab that tested the AI UPS system at multi-megawatt configurations. He’s also overseeing tests of a similar battery system from Prevalon Energy, and some others he said he can’t name yet.

Besides providing UPS services, these technologies aim to solve a growing problem created by the rapid buildout of data centers, Shah said. ​“Many power system operators are coming up with requirements to make sure that the data center loads — the large loads — don’t negatively impact the reliability of the grid.”

Data centers are uniquely challenging for utilities and grid operators to manage for a couple of reasons. First, their appetite for power can rise and fall dramatically, depending on how much computing they’re doing at any moment. And those changes can happen really fast, Shah said — ​“say, from 5% to 100% in a few milliseconds. You’re hammering the grid if you do that.”

Second, data centers’ sensitivity to fluctuations in grid power quality can trigger them to disconnect from the grid and switch to UPS and backup generators at a moment’s notice, leading to massive unexpected drops in power demand that threaten to throw grid balances out of whack. Grid operator PJM Interconnection has recorded a handful of such multi-gigawatt drop-offs in recent years, including one in July where nearly 4 gigawatts of data center load in Virginia disconnected.

Utilities and grid operators like PJM need to carefully balance supply and demand to avoid voltage and frequency fluctuations that can, in the worst case, lead to region-wide grid collapses. Many grid operators require big solar and wind farms to configure their systems to avoid tripping offline in response to grid voltage disturbances. Now data centers have become large enough to represent similar trip-off risks.

The North American Electric Reliability Corp., which oversees the U.S. and Canadian electric systems, has targeted large ​“computational loads” for new requirements on this front, and Texas utility regulators instituted similar requirements this year.

ON.Energy’s AI UPS is designed to handle those kinds of power isolation services, Cooper said. ​“Our double-conversion technology, which we’ve patented, is basically the process of fully electrically decoupling the load from the power generation source,” he said. ​“We’re using the fastest-response, best-in-class inverters in the market.”

That technological sophistication adds up to a relatively simple solution for the utilities and grid operators, he said. ​“We’re basically a really predictable utility-scale battery that just sits and takes power from the grid.”

To be clear, data centers need to be designed ahead of time to use ON.Energy’s AI UPS system, Cooper said. To illustrate the point, he showed me aerial photos of a Crusoe data center campus under construction. The parts of the campus built first include a central building that will house traditional UPS systems, he said. But the most recent building under construction has set aside land to one side where the AI UPS batteries will be installed.

Once a data center commits to a centralized UPS system like ON.Energy’s, it could look to use it for other purposes, he said.

Data center operators are under a lot of pressure to find ways to reduce the costs they’re imposing on utilities — and by extension, utility customers — by bringing their own technologies to avoid the need for costly grid expansions or new power plants.

It’s a lot easier to justify a standalone battery for reducing a data center’s peak power demand, or to soak up excess solar and wind power for use later, when it’s already paid its way as a UPS and grid-stabilization tool.

“The main thing is, you have a battery on site that’s multi-hour duration, and you’re able to curtail the data center from the grid whenever you need,” Cooper said. ​“It’s kind of a natural way to get data center flexibility — and there are a bunch of ways to back into that.”

text:
Puget Sound Energy announced a groundbreaking for a 130-megawatt solar array near Rapelje in southcentral Montana.

Called the “Battle Butte Solar Project,” it’s expected to provide enough energy for 20,000 homes as the company looks to comply with Washington state law, which reduces the amount of power generated from fossil fuels and increases renewables. Puget Sound Energy provides electricity and energy services for a broad swath of northwestern Washington. The company has worked in Montana since the 1970s and this project is expected to add about 250 construction jobs.

PSE also has another facility nearby, the recently completed 248 MW Beaver Creek Wind Project.

“Battle Butte solar represents a critical component of our clean energy strategy,” Craig Pospisil, Senior Vice President and Chief Development Officer for PSE said in a press release. “This project will give us the opportunity to build upon the positive relationships we’ve forged with our neighbors in Stillwater County through the development of the Beaver Creek Wind facility and it positions PSE to meet our customers’ growing clean energy needs.”

PSE said that since 2019 they’ve added 22 long-term clean energy projects totalling about 4,000MW.

Local leaders also hailed the project.

“We look forward to Battle Butte bringing construction jobs, tax revenue and new economic activity to Stillwater County while adding another important piece to Montana’s all-of-the-above energy portfolio,” said Roger Webb, Stillwater County Commissioner. “Throughout the process of developing both Beaver Creek and Battle Butte, PSE has shown a commitment to working with our county and investing in Montana while being a good neighbor – we look forward to the ongoing partnership.”

The project will sit in the high plains near Rapelje on 1,400 acres of flat, open ranch land with full site control. PSE hosted an open house sharing information and answering questions about the Battle Butte Solar Project in Rapelje at the end of January. Construction is expected to start this fall with an anticipated completion date in mid-2028.

As part of Montana’s “all-of-the-above” energy economy, PSE continues to build energy projects and partner with energy producers throughout the state. PSE has power purchase agreements with Energy Keepers, Inc., the tribally owned corporation of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes for hydroelectric power, and an agreement with NextEra for power from Montana’s largest wind farm, Clearwater Wind, based in Rosebud, Custer and Garfield Counties as well as a long-term contract with Clearway Energy Group for wind from Haymaker Wind Farm in Wheatland and Meagher counties.

PSE has already eliminated coal from its energy portfolio at the end of 2025 and added 22 long-term clean energy resources totaling more than 4,000 MW since 2019, when the Clean Energy Transformation Act was passed.

title: Why India's critical minerals push could echo its refining rise - ET Chemical News
description:

Refining critical minerals requires specialised equipment, environmental safeguards, waste management systems and reliable utilities.
Partnerships will decide how fast the sector matures The article argues that industry partnerships will be crucial to making domestic refining viable.

Critical minerals refining will need to balance competitiveness with sustainability, because processing can be energy-intensive and environmentally sensitive.
text:
India’s race to secure the materials behind batteries, electric vehicles and clean energy is moving beyond mining licences and overseas deals. The more consequential prize may lie closer to home: turning the country into a refining hub for critical minerals, much as crude oil refining once reshaped its energy economy. According to ORF Online, the debate is no longer only about whether India can find lithium, cobalt or nickel. The harder and more valuable question is whether it can process those inputs domestically, create industrial depth and capture more of the value chain before imported ores are converted into battery-grade materials elsewhere.

From mineral access to industrial capability Critical minerals have become central to the energy transition because they are essential for battery manufacturing, grid storage and a range of advanced technologies. Lithium, cobalt and nickel are among the most sought-after inputs, and countries that can refine them to usable grades hold a strategic advantage over those that merely extract or import raw material.

For India, that distinction matters. The country has already recognised that supply security in energy and manufacturing cannot rely only on overseas shipments. In minerals, as in petroleum, the bigger opportunity is not just in sourcing the raw feedstock but in building domestic processing capacity that anchors jobs, technology and downstream industry.

That shift also reflects a wider industrial logic. Refining and processing are where technical know-how, environmental controls, logistics and long-term contracts intersect. A country that develops this layer can become harder to sideline in global supply chains, even if it remains dependent on imports for part of its raw material needs.Why processing parks could change the economics

One of the ideas highlighted by the ORF Online piece is the creation of processing parks. The concept is straightforward: cluster refining, testing, handling and allied services in dedicated industrial zones so that companies can share infrastructure and reduce the cost of entry.

For capital-intensive sectors, that kind of shared ecosystem can be decisive. Refining critical minerals requires specialised equipment, environmental safeguards, waste management systems and reliable utilities. If each investor has to build those systems from scratch, project costs rise and timelines stretch. A well-designed park can lower friction, attract new entrants and encourage smaller firms to participate alongside larger industrial groups.

Such parks could also help India address a familiar weakness in industrial policy: fragmentation. When processing capacity is dispersed and approvals are slow, firms struggle to scale. By contrast, a cluster approach can speed up permitting, improve compliance oversight and create a single node for infrastructure, training and logistics.

Partnerships will decide how fast the sector matures The article argues that industry partnerships will be crucial to making domestic refining viable. That is not surprising. Critical minerals are part of a global market shaped by concentrated supply, technical barriers and strategic competition, which means no single player is likely to solve the challenge alone. Joint ventures, technology tie-ups and long-term supply agreements can help Indian firms access process expertise and reduce execution risk. They can also connect domestic refiners to overseas sources of feedstock, which is essential because India is unlikely to become self-sufficient in every critical mineral in the near term.

There is also a commercial reason for collaboration. Battery supply chains are moving quickly, and refiners need offtake visibility before they commit large sums to plant and equipment. Partnerships with downstream users such as battery makers, auto companies and energy storage developers can provide that demand certainty and make domestic refining bankable. In practice, this means India’s critical minerals strategy will have to be built as an ecosystem, not as a stand-alone mining policy. The winners are likely to be those who can connect resource access, conversion technology, industrial land and end-user demand into one operating model.The petroleum parallel is strategic, not literal The comparison with petroleum is useful because it captures a familiar Indian policy lesson. India expanded its oil refining capacity over time and turned that segment into a major industrial strength. Critical minerals may not follow the same market dynamics, but the underlying principle is similar: value rises sharply once raw inputs are processed domestically rather than exported in low-value form. That parallel also underscores the strategic implications. Petroleum refining reduced dependence on imported finished fuels and built a globally competitive industry. Domestic mineral refining could do something analogous for the next generation of energy technologies, especially as electric mobility and storage move from niche to mainstream. There is, however, an important difference. Critical minerals refining will need to balance competitiveness with sustainability, because processing can be energy-intensive and environmentally sensitive. That means India will need clear standards, efficient regulation and infrastructure that supports both industrial scale and responsible operations.What India must do next The policy task ahead is therefore broader than simply encouraging more mineral imports. India will need to identify which minerals offer the strongest strategic and commercial case for domestic refining, where processing parks can be located, and how public policy can de-risk early investment without creating bottlenecks. It will also need to align mining, trade, industry and energy policy. Refining capacity cannot be built in isolation from ports, rail links, power supply and skilled manpower. Nor can it succeed without a predictable regulatory framework that reassures investors while maintaining environmental safeguards. If India gets this right, the gains could be significant. Domestic refining would deepen industrial capability, improve supply-chain resilience and create a platform for battery manufacturing and other clean-tech sectors. It would also help India move from being a buyer of strategic inputs to a more influential participant in the global minerals economy. The next big energy story, in other words, may not be written in oilfields or solar farms alone. It may be written in the refineries, processing parks and industrial corridors that determine who controls the materials powering the low-carbon economy.

title: Interconnection Crossfire: PJM Grid Constraint Prompts DOE Emergency Order as FERC ...
description:
For commercial energy users, the DOE order allows PJM to tap into more than 35 GW of unused backup generation that remains available nationwide.
The U.S. grid is currently facing a critical moment to fast-track third-party power suppliers for data centers.
However, in the very same ruling, FERC rejected PJM’s "Bring Your Own Capacity" (BYOC) rules and broader Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS) framework.
Voltus will aggregate this energy from local businesses and homes into a Google-funded VPP in the PJM grid to help offset data center load growth.
It also establishes additional power capacity for Google's AI and data center infrastructure over the next two years.
text:
To maintain grid reliability, PJM Interconnection was granted authority under a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) emergency order on Monday to manage tight electricity supply conditions across 13 states and Washington, D.C.

The directive arrived just as the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) rejected a PJM proposal that aimed to allow data centers to forgo matching new capacity if they agreed to be curtailed in the lead-up to grid emergencies.

The DOE emergency federal order, in effect Oct. 13 through Oct. 16, authorizes the largest U.S. grid operator to dictate exactly how much electricity power operators must produce and when to run units to prevent potential widespread blackouts during this period. For commercial energy users, the DOE order allows PJM to tap into more than 35 GW of unused backup generation that remains available nationwide.

This would be done as a last resort before declaring an Energy Emergency Alert 3—the highest and most critical level of a power grid emergency, triggered when electricity supply and demand can no longer be balanced.

“This order will help ensure millions of American families and businesses across the mid-Atlantic have access to affordable, reliable and secure electricity by making additional power generation, including backup power, available to use as needed,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright in a statement.

The U.S. grid is currently facing a critical moment to fast-track third-party power suppliers for data centers. At the same time, balancing paths to strengthen reliability while managing affordability has become a severe challenge.

FERC greenlights data center registry, blocks PJM’s broader grid framework

FERC approved a PJM proposal this month to create a registry for large electricity users like data centers to better define large loads as facilities demanding 50 MW or more. However, in the very same ruling, FERC rejected PJM’s "Bring Your Own Capacity" (BYOC) rules and broader Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS) framework.

Under the rejected IRAS proposal, PJM had included provisions that would allow large loads to connect to the grid without matching new capacity if they agreed to be curtailed in the lead-up to grid emergencies. But ultimately, FERC determined that this curtailment proposal would “intrude on state jurisdiction over retail rates and appear to discriminate against large loads.”

“We find that several provisions of the proposed tariff appear to place obligations directly on eligible new large loads, which are, for the most part, retail customers; that certain other provisions appear to dictate which retail customers taking retail service will be curtailed; and that the proposed compensation framework appears to establish a retail rate,” FERC said in its IRAS framework rejection filing.

Hyperscalers tap on-site generation to counter load growth

Because the nation’s long and winding grid interconnection queue has slowed and entangled both utility and distributed energy power generation projects since at least 2020, support for the“speed to power” movement has become a core objective for microgrid developers and industrial customers.

An example of this strategy is Google's grid optimization strategy within PJM's territory. Virtual Power Plant (VPP) aggregator Voltus plans to deploy up to 100 MW of distributed energy resources (DERs) under a three-year BYOC agreement.

Voltus will aggregate this energy from local businesses and homes into a Google-funded VPP in the PJM grid to help offset data center load growth. It also establishes additional power capacity for Google's AI and data center infrastructure over the next two years.

However, scaling these private-capacity solutions faces steep regulatory hesitation, as highlighted in FERC’s rejection ruling over PJM’s proposed BYOC framework. This included suspension over PJM’s permission to hold private auctions as a third party for data centers to negotiate and purchase power generation from suppliers for distribution and transmission onto PJM’s grid.

These regulatory dilemmas add grid pressure as PJM forecasts new large load requests are expected to increase by an estimated 70 GW by 2038, even as 15 GW of existing electricity generating resources have been retired since 2022. Highlighting this supply crunch, PJM’s recent capacity auction for the 2028/2029 delivery year left a 6.8 GW shortfall below its strict reliability requirement.

In June, FERC issued show-cause orders toall six regional grid and independent system operators to try and revolutionize timelines under which “speed to power” projects are achieved for the nation’s amassing new GWs of digital and industrial infrastructure capacity.

Attorney Eric Runge of law firm Day Pitney LLP previously toldMicrogrid Knowledge that these reforms should positively impact development of microgrids, co-located “energy parks” and behind-the-meter projects built and paid for in large part by the data center or manufacturing site customer.

PJM’s 13-state region includes 67 million residential, commercial and industrial customers across Virginia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Michigan, North Carolina, West Virginia, six other states and the District of Columbia.
