title: The Offshore Wind Innovation Hub Announces 2026 Selections For Its Innovator Program
description:
Newswise — The Offshore Wind Innovation Hub has announced the selection of five companies for its 2026 Innovator Program.
The applicant pool underscores New York's pull as a destination for offshore wind innovation worldwide.
SAIL GTX (New York, US) - Platform for smarter customs workflows for offshore wind components.
“Programs like the Offshore Wind Innovation Hub help emerging businesses develop technologies and services that create domestic jobs and support American energy infrastructure,” said Robert Fenton, Orsted’s Head of Americas Generation Procurement.
Corporate partners Equinor, Ørsted, and Vestas round out the network, mentoring cohort companies and leveraging their ongoing offshore projects for solution validation and commercialization feedback.
text:
Newswise — The Offshore Wind Innovation Hub has announced the selection of five companies for its 2026 Innovator Program.

The Hub is led by Urban Future Lab at NYU Tandon School of Engineering and the National Offshore Wind Research and Development Consortium (NOWRDC) in collaboration with New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) and New York City Economic Development Corporation (NYCEDC). The Innovator Program is also supported by Equinor, Ørsted and Vestas.

This year’s cohort was selected from a record-breaking pool of applications, the program’s highest total to date and a 123% increase over last year’s. These were reviewed by 40 evaluators and subject matter experts, including program partners, Tier 1 supply chain companies, industry NGOs, and research institutions. The 2026 applicant pool well reflects where New York’s offshore wind projects and partners stand today:

Operations, maintenance, and asset performance: 42%

Installation, construction, and commissioning: 12%

Environmental monitoring and coexistence: 12%

Supply chain, ports, and maritime: 11%

That shift toward operations technology tracks the industry's own maturation. As it moves from construction into operation, the innovation needed moves with it: from solutions that get projects through planning to ones that keep projects operating. This year's Call for Innovators built that shift directly into its scope, prioritizing technologies that can maximize the performance and value of existing and near-term projects. In addition to this, 56% of applicants submitted technology combining hardware and software, consistent with prior years and considered a key feature for industry startups.

The applicant pool underscores New York's pull as a destination for offshore wind innovation worldwide. While 54% of applicants were U.S.-based, the program drew submissions from 26 countries in total, reflecting the Hub's standing as a program that brings global innovators into direct contact with New York's offshore wind ecosystem, and New York's ecosystem into contact with the world's best offshore wind technology.

Join the 2026 cohort in person at the Wind-Win Startup Showdown on November 17, 2026, where they’ll pitch to industry leaders, and attendees can connect directly alongside program partners.

Bubble Robotics (California, US) - Resident fleet of autonomous underwater robots monitoring offshore infrastructure.

Hefring Marine (Iceland) - Intelligence platform combining onboard hardware with software to optimize marine operations.

SAIL GTX (New York, US) - Platform for smarter customs workflows for offshore wind components.

TMA The Hazardous Goods Companion (Germany) - RFID and AIoT inventory visibility and predictive inventory management solution.

Vital Ocean (Oregon, US) - Intelligence platform combining ocean data, marine environment, and decision interface.

Selected companies will receive individualized technical mentorship from corporate partners, along with seed innovation grants ranging from $10,000 - $20,000 to catalyze validation and demonstration opportunities in New York. The program will also provide bespoke entrepreneurial support, including strategic advising, hiring assistance, pro bono legal and accounting office hours, and commercialization guidance, alongside a tailored curriculum of expert talks, workshops, and peer-to-peer sessions. Cohort companies gain visibility through a flagship event and program mentions, exclusive introductions to industry stakeholders, investors, and public entities, and office access at BATWorks, New York's climate innovation hub at the Brooklyn Army Terminal.

“The strength and diversity of this year’s cohort demonstrates the impact of prioritizing innovation in the New York’s offshore wind industry across the entire supply chain,” said Doreen M. Harris, President and CEO, NYSERDA. “From procurement, to manufacturing, to operations and more, each of these companies will play an essential role in advancing the state’s domestic production of clean, reliable and affordable energy and we look forward to seeing their progress.”

“We are proud that New York City is shaping the future of the offshore wind industry, and the record number of applications to this year's Innovator Program underscores the city's position as a global destination for climate and offshore wind innovation," said New York City Economic Development Corporation (NYCEDC) President and CEO Anthony Shorris. "This cohort reflects both the strength of New York's innovation ecosystem and the growing global demand for solutions that can improve operations, strengthen supply chains, and advance clean energy technologies for a more resilient and competitive green economy.

"This year's applicant pool shows the industry moving from getting projects built to keeping them running well, and that's a challenging operational problem for a startup to solve alone," said Linda Ng Boyle, NYU Tandon Vice Dean for Research. "NYU Tandon offers these entrepreneurs a collaborative environment where they can work through that problem alongside our academic researchers who study it, and we're glad to be part of getting these technologies into the field."

"This cohort represents some of the most promising technologies in offshore renewable energy today," said Lyndie Hice-Dunton, Executive Director of NOWRDC. "Led by exceptional founders and technical teams, these companies are developing creative solutions that deliver real value across the project lifecycle. We look forward to working closely with them to help their innovations make a lasting impact on the U.S. industry. Together, we're helping build the technologies that will power a cleaner, more resilient energy future."

“Programs like the Offshore Wind Innovation Hub help emerging businesses develop technologies and services that create domestic jobs and support American energy infrastructure,” said Robert Fenton, Orsted’s Head of Americas Generation Procurement. “We congratulate the companies selected for the 2026 Innovator Program and look forward to seeing how their innovations can strengthen U.S. supply chains, support American jobs, and help improve the safe and efficient operation of offshore energy projects.”

“The enthusiasm we’ve seen for the 2026 Innovator Program is a powerful reminder of the opportunities created by offshore wind for innovators, entrepreneurs, and suppliers,” said Amy McGinty, VP Offshore Construction, Vestas. “Offshore wind reflects where American energy stands today, full of challenges but even bigger opportunities, and the companies selected for this year’s cohort represent the creativity and ambition needed to tackle that. We are proud to help foster an environment where new ideas can scale into real-world solutions that deliver economic growth, energy independence, and lasting impact."

“Bubble Robotics is building the ocean's autonomous workforce of autonomous surface and subsea robots,” said Jean Crosetti, Co-founder & CEO, Bubble Robotics. “We’re excited to join the Offshore Wind Innovation Hub to work closely with developers and industry partners, validate our solution against real operational needs, and accelerate our path to commercial deployments in the U.S.”

“Offshore wind is an enormous industrial opportunity, operating in an increasingly complex tariff and trade landscape,” said Ali Raza, Co-Founder & CEO, SAIL “We're excited to join the Offshore Wind Innovation Hub to work alongside the industry and help teams understand their full duty exposure, stay ahead of regulatory change, and keep critical components moving.”

Rather than a one-size-fits-all approach, cohort companies receive introductions curated to their specific needs across the Hub's full partner network. The Urban Future Lab and NYU Tandon contribute hands-on startup support, a network of fellow climate founders, and venture capital relationships, alongside access to the university’s engineering intern and capstone programs. NOWRDC offers industry-specific R&D guidance and an exclusive opportunity to pitch its R&D committee and present at the National Offshore Wind R&D Symposium, while NYSERDA provides solution-specific market and regulatory insight, and NYCEDC connects companies to its full suite of business support. Corporate partners Equinor, Ørsted, and Vestas round out the network, mentoring cohort companies and leveraging their ongoing offshore projects for solution validation and commercialization feedback.

text:
EPA proposal brings biofuel discussion to Iowa

October 15, 2026 | Kriss Nelson

A proposal to restore renewable fuel volumes lost to small refinery exemptions could provide greater certainty for Iowa soybean farmers seeking stronger domestic markets.

The Environmental Protection Agency announced Oct. 13 a proposal to fully reallocate renewable fuel volumes lost to 2025 small refinery exemptions under the Renewable Fuel Standard.

The announcement followed an agricultural stakeholder roundtable Oct. 12 in Monticello, where Iowa Soybean Association District 6 Director Joe Sperfslage, a farmer from Coggon, met with EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and other agricultural stakeholders.

Zeldin indicated during the meeting that EPA intended to restore 100% of the waived volumes.

The proposal is significant for soybean farmers because renewable diesel and biodiesel provide important domestic markets for soybean oil, says Grant Kimberley, ISA senior director of market development. Restoring waived fuel volumes could help preserve demand as farmers navigate tighter margins and market uncertainty.

Farmers at the table

Sperfslage says he appreciated meeting directly with Zeldin to discuss farmers' concerns, including mixed messages from federal agencies about agricultural production and conservation priorities.

“It's great if we can get farmers in front of administrators, especially ones like the EPA and the USDA,” he says. “Great to see them outside of D.C.”

While farmers may not always agree with federal policy decisions, Sperfslage says direct conversations help ensure their perspectives are considered.

“It was nice to sit down with an EPA administrator who seemed to at least be taking the farmer's opinion and experiences into account,” he says.

Looking beyond reallocation

Kimberley says the discussion extended beyond small refinery exemptions to EPA's work on the next Renewable Fuel Standard proposal, often referred to as Set 3.

Zeldin indicated that EPA is considering the half-RIN proposal as part of that work, making domestic feedstock availability an important consideration.

Kimberley says demonstrating sufficient domestic feedstock supplies will be important as the agency develops the next rule.

According to Kimberley, Zeldin also emphasized EPA's willingness to consider agricultural priorities supported by science and within the agency's legal authority.

The discussion highlighted the competing interests EPA must consider within the renewable fuels and petroleum refining sectors.

Market certainty

ISA President Lee Brooke, a soybean farmer from Clarinda, welcomed the proposed reallocation.

“We thank Administrator Zeldin and the Trump administration for signaling their commitment to farmers by proposing to restore 100% of biofuel demand lost to 2025 small refinery exemptions,” Brooke said. The proposal could provide greater certainty and additional domestic soybean demand, he says.

“Iowa farmers are navigating a challenging farm economy while bringing in this year’s crop,” Brooke says. “This proposal offers the potential for greater certainty and much-needed domestic demand for soybeans if finalized later this year.”

Written by Kriss Nelson.

description:
Today the UpgradeNY collaboration and allies from across the environmental movement and renewable energy industry applaud the approval of two utility-led thermal energy network (TEN) pilots by the New York Public Service Commission.
“…a gas utility’s transition into thermal energy service in a Disadvantaged community.” National Fuel Gas, Buffalo: This project will demonstrate a gas utility’s transition into thermal energy service in a Disadvantaged community.

We are building the next generation of energy infrastructure, with strong labor standards that the Utility Thermal Energy Network and Jobs Act guarantees.

text:
Today the UpgradeNY collaboration and allies from across the environmental movement and renewable energy industry applaud the approval of two utility-led thermal energy network (TEN) pilots by the New York Public Service Commission.

These projects, authorized under the Utility Thermal Energy Network and Jobs Act, will allow utilities to build TENs that will use less energy, save ratepayers money, and build more resilient communities while creating hundreds of family-sustaining union jobs.

Orange & Rockland, Haverstraw West: This project will use an ambient temperature loop supported by both geothermal borefields and wastewater heat recovery from a sewer main to serve a mix of residential, commercial, and municipal buildings in downtown Haverstraw. This innovative, replicable model for future TENs will utilize one of the most abundant and cost-effective thermal resources available: wastewater. In addition, two geothermal borefields on municipal land will use the steady temperature of the earth to serve the loop. It is designed to connect up to 30 buildings, including single- and multi-family residential, commercial, government buildings, and an elementary school.

“…a gas utility’s transition into thermal energy service in a Disadvantaged community.”

National Fuel Gas, Buffalo: This project will demonstrate a gas utility’s transition into thermal energy service in a Disadvantaged community. It includes a central plant and wastewater heat recovery from a storm/sanitary main, and strategic connection to an existing district heating system. Decarbonizing a legacy district energy system and serving low-income multifamily housing with clean thermal energy will provide real benefit to residents by significantly reducing greenhouse gas emissions and air pollutants. This is an important interim step in the evolution from legacy district energy systems to clean thermal energy networks.

There are nine more projects that the Public Service Commission did not advance, including proposals on the East Side of Haverstraw, in Syracuse, New York City, and other communities across the state. We are disappointed the Commission didn’t recognize all of the benefits of those projects, missing the opportunity to bring this exciting technology to more communities and provide more union jobs. We applaud Governor Hochul for her leadership and the Public Service Commission for giving these two innovative projects the green light and demonstrating that New York is ready to lead on the next generation of clean energy solutions.”

Allison Considine, NY Director of the Building Decarbonization Coalition said, “This is a breakthrough moment for thermal energy networks in New York. Jessica Azulay, Executive Director for Alliance for a Green Economy (AGREE) said, “We thank the Public Service Commission and the Governor for making this investment in the next generation of heating and cooling infrastructure in New York. Gary LaBarbera, President of the New York State Building Trades said, “The approval of these projects not only represents a key milestone for advancing the state’s thermal energy networks, but also for creating thousands of family-sustaining union careers for hardworking people. Jenille Scott, ALIGN Climate Director said, “New York is ready to build! We’re proud to see the Public Service Commission commit to clean energy technology that is proven to provide safer, cheaper, and more efficient heating and cooling for families while creating good union jobs. As nationwide cuts ignore the growing devastation of our intersecting climate and affordability crises, New York is taking a meaningful step forward, investing in clean air, family-sustaining careers, and our green, affordable future.”

Oct. 15, 2026

By Ryan LaFontaine

AUSTIN – The electric vehicle charging network in Texas is expanding with hundreds coming over the next couple years.

As a part of Phase II of the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Program, TxDOT has awarded $226 million in federal funds for 321 electric vehicle charging stations across the state. This includes 264 in metropolitan planning organization areas and 57 in county seats.

Meanwhile, Phase I continues to bring charging stations online along Texas highways. There are 22 stations open with five more expected to by the end of 2026, and another 30 are planned to open in 2027.

TxDOT Data Management Director Michael Chamberlain recently traveled more than 2,000 miles across Texas to inspect newly opened stations in Wichita Falls, Mount Pleasant, Van, Selma, Natalia, Encinal, Three Rivers and Kerrville. He also visited stations under construction in Corsicana and Mission.

“The number of alternatively fueled vehicles on our roads continues to rise,” Chamberlain said. “The demand for charging stations has never been higher, and these new stations will help strengthen TxDOT’s effort to keep pace.”

text:
Why It Matters

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) would determine whether federal permitting authority can override state objections to high-voltage transmission lines. Energy developers, state regulators and utility ratepayers are watching the impact of these these developments closely, according to a new Congressional Research Service report. ​

FERC's backstop siting power allows the federal government to approve transmission projects in designated corridors when states fail to act or deny permits. That authority has been contested in courts and revisited by Congress repeatedly since it was first established, making the current bill another chapter in a long-running dispute over the boundary between federal energy policy and state land-use control.

The Big Picture

The CRS report examines the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 and its provisions affecting FERC's backstop siting authority. Under current law, FERC holds conditional authority to site transmission facilities in federally designated National Interest Electric Transmission Corridors when states fail to act or deny permits. That authority traces to the Energy Policy Act of 2005, which first granted it.

Courts subsequently narrowed FERC's backstop siting powers, finding that the agency could not exercise jurisdiction when a state had already denied a permit application. Congress has revisited the scope of that authority in legislation since then, and the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 represents the latest effort to clarify or expand it.

The bill's title signals bipartisan support, which is notable given that transmission siting has historically divided lawmakers along regional and jurisdictional lines. States have resisted federal preemption of their land-use and permitting decisions, and that tension has slowed or blocked numerous transmission projects over the years.

FERC backstop siting authority sits at the intersection of federal energy policy and state sovereignty. Grid planners have identified transmission buildout as necessary to integrate renewable generation and meet growing electricity demand, but siting disputes have repeatedly delayed or blocked projects before they reach construction.

The bill's provisions would, if enacted, give FERC a stronger legal basis to approve projects over state objections, shifting the balance of authority in a way that transmission developers and state utility commissions would need to account for in project planning and regulatory strategy.

The Bottom Line

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 is before Congress, and its fate will determine whether FERC gains stronger legal footing to approve transmission projects over state objections. If the bill advances, state utility commissions and transmission developers would face a materially different federal permitting landscape for high-voltage infrastructure.

North America Green Hydrogen Market Report Scope & Overview:

The North America Green Hydrogen Market size was valued at USD 0.33 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 3.30 billion by 2035, growing at a CAGR of roughly 25.89% from 2026 to 2035.

The North America Green Hydrogen Market continues to expand as the United States and Canada scale federal and provincial clean-hydrogen funding programs supporting electrolyzer manufacturing and large-scale hub development. Growing industrial decarbonization mandates and expanding refinery and ammonia-producer offtake interest continue to support sustained regional project investment. Established industrial gas distribution infrastructure across the region continues lowering the integration cost of new green hydrogen supply for existing customers.

Rising renewable power generation capacity, particularly wind across the Midwest and Gulf Coast and solar across the Southwest, continues improving regional green hydrogen project economics. Growing collaboration between electrolyzer manufacturers and industrial gas distributors is further widening the domestic supply chain supporting large-scale hydrogen hub development. Continued federal loan-guarantee and tax-credit support is additionally reinforcing developer confidence in long-term project bankability.

⮞Air Products and Chemicals continued progress on its large-scale North American green hydrogen production and liquefaction project through 2025-2026, reinforcing sustained originator investment in regional clean-hydrogen infrastructure.

Market Context:

Global Green Hydrogen Market size was valued at USD 10.02 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 201.07 billion by 2035, growing at a CAGR of 35.0% from 2026 to 2035, driven by rising investments in clean energy infrastructure, increasing industrial decarbonization initiatives, and growing demand for low-carbon hydrogen across refining, chemicals, and transportation industries.

North America Green Hydrogen Market Segment Analysis:

By Technology, Alkaline Electrolysis led with 53.72% share in 2025; PEM Electrolysis is the fastest-growing technology, projected to expand at an estimated CAGR of 47.2% through 2035.

By Source, Wind led with 44.95% share in 2025; Solar is the fastest-growing source, projected to expand at an estimated CAGR of 50.4% through 2035.

By End-User Industry, Refining led with 36.18% share in 2025; Chemicals is the fastest-growing end-user industry, projected to expand at an estimated CAGR of 46.5% through 2035.

By Technology, Alkaline Electrolysis Dominates the North America Green Hydrogen Market, PEM Electrolysis Grows Fastest

Alkaline Electrolysis retained the largest technology share across North America, reflecting its proven reliability and lower upfront capital costs for gigawatt-scale hydrogen hub projects. Large U.S. developers continue favoring alkaline systems for baseload industrial offtake where capital efficiency outweighs rapid load-following requirements. Established supply chains for balance-of-plant components further reinforce alkaline technology's cost advantage across the region. Decades of accumulated operating experience across adjacent chemical-manufacturing industries continue lowering the perceived technical risk of large-scale alkaline deployments. Extensive field-proven stack lifetimes further reduce total cost of ownership for operators.

PEM Electrolysis is forecast to grow fastest owing to its compact footprint and superior load-flexibility, which make it well suited to pairing with variable wind and solar generation across the region. Falling iridium-catalyst loading requirements and expanding domestic manufacturing scale are steadily narrowing the capital-cost gap with alkaline systems. Growing developer preference for PEM in projects requiring rapid response to renewable variability is reinforcing this above-average growth trajectory. Several U.S. suppliers have further announced new PEM stack manufacturing capacity to meet anticipated hub-scale demand. Growing standardization of balance-of-plant components is further compressing installed costs for PEM systems.

⮞In January 2025, Nel Hydrogen US received an approximately USD 7 million purchase order for two 2.5 MW containerized PEM electrolyzers from an undisclosed U.S. steel producer, extending the customer’s existing use of Nel systems for on-site hydrogen production.

By Source, Wind Dominates the North America Green Hydrogen Market, Solar Grows Fastest

Wind retained the largest source share across North America, reflecting higher and more consistent capacity factors across the Midwest and Gulf Coast relative to solar in many leading project geographies. Developers continue favoring dedicated onshore wind power purchase agreements to secure stable, high-utilization electrolyzer operation. Established wind-development supply chains across the Midwest further reinforce wind's dominant position for large-scale regional project financing. Grid-interconnection precedent built up over years of wind development also shortens permitting timelines for co-located electrolyzer projects. Rising capacity-factor data from operating wind-paired projects is reinforcing long-term financier confidence.

Solar is forecast to grow fastest as steadily falling photovoltaic module costs make solar-paired electrolysis increasingly competitive across the high-irradiance U.S. Southwest. Growing hybrid wind-solar project configurations are also widening the addressable resource base for regional developers seeking higher overall capacity factors. Expanding battery-storage integration alongside solar-paired electrolyzers is further smoothing production profiles and improving project bankability across the region. Several developers have additionally begun co-locating large solar arrays directly with electrolyzer sites to reduce transmission costs. Continued improvements in bifacial panel efficiency are widening the range of commercially viable solar sites.

⮞In 2024, the U.S. Department of Energy selected Exergy Labs for USD 3 million in funding to develop a modular solar-thermal dish reactor for lower-cost clean hydrogen production, with prototype testing planned in North Carolina and Arizona.

By End-User Industry, Refining Dominates the North America Green Hydrogen Market, Chemicals Grows Fastest

Refining accounted for the largest end-user share across North America, as Gulf Coast and Midwest refiners increasingly replace grey hydrogen used in desulfurization and hydrocracking with green hydrogen to meet tightening carbon-intensity regulations. Established hydrogen offtake infrastructure at existing refinery sites continues lowering integration costs relative to greenfield industrial users. Large-scale refiners also benefit from existing hydrogen storage and distribution infrastructure that shortens project lead times. Several state-level fuel-quality standards are further accelerating refiner adoption of lower-carbon hydrogen feedstock. Growing regulatory pressure on refinery carbon intensity is reinforcing sustained offtake commitments across the segment.

Chemicals is forecast to grow fastest as ammonia and methanol producers across the Gulf Coast increasingly pursue green hydrogen feedstock to decarbonize energy-intensive production and access premium low-carbon product markets. Growing export demand for green ammonia as a hydrogen carrier is reinforcing this above-average growth trajectory across the regional chemicals segment. Expanding green methanol offtake agreements with the shipping industry are further widening chemical producers' feedstock requirements. Rising customer willingness to pay premiums for certified low-carbon chemical products is additionally reinforcing this segment's growth. Expanding carbon-border adjustment mechanisms are incentivizing chemical producers to secure low-carbon hydrogen feedstock early.

⮞In April 2026, Plug Power received a front-end engineering design contract to supply a 275 MW PEM electrolyzer system for Hy2gen Canada’s Courant project in Québec, which is being developed to produce decarbonized ammonium nitrate for mining markets.

U.S. Green Hydrogen Market Insights

The U.S. dominated the North America Green Hydrogen Market with the highest revenue share of about 80.30% in 2025, supported by large-scale federal clean-hydrogen hub funding, expanding industrial decarbonization mandates, and sustained refinery and ammonia-producer offtake interest across multiple states. Expanding hydrogen hub project announcements across multiple states are further accelerating federal and private capacity-investment momentum nationwide. Rising industrial customer commitments are additionally reinforcing long-term investor confidence in sustained American production growth.

Continued federal loan-guarantee and tax-credit support, growing originator-developer collaboration, and sustained interest in domestic electrolyzer manufacturing reinforce U.S. dominance within North America. Rising investment in hydrogen hub infrastructure is expected to keep the United States the region's primary revenue engine through the remainder of the decade, with several states competing directly for new greenfield project investment through tax incentives. Growing collaboration between U.S. developers and global off-takers is further widening export-market access for domestically produced green hydrogen. Canada Green Hydrogen Market Insights

Canada is expected to grow at the fastest CAGR of about 38.47% from 2026-2035, facilitated by growing hydroelectric-paired electrolyzer development and rising federal clean-fuel-standard support for low-carbon hydrogen production. Federal research and manufacturing-incentive funding is reinforcing Canada's above-regional growth trajectory as domestic developers expand export-oriented production capacity. Expanding provincial clean-fuel-standard support is further accelerating electrolyzer project permitting and renewable power procurement across Canada. Rising interest from international off-takers is additionally reinforcing long-term investment confidence in Canadian export-oriented production capacity.

Continued investment by regional developers in Canadian distribution and export infrastructure, combined with growing interest from European off-takers, is supporting faster-than-average volume growth across the country through the forecast period. Expanding cross-border supply-chain coordination is expected to reinforce this pattern through the remainder of the decade as Canadian manufacturers continue aligning quality and certification practices with export-market requirements. Growing hydroelectric-paired project announcements across Quebec and British Columbia are further widening Canada's addressable renewable-resource base. Continued federal research funding is additionally supporting early-stage domestic electrolyzer manufacturing ventures across multiple provinces.

⮞In September 2026, Natural Resources Canada announced CAD 2 million in funding for Next Hydrogen to develop scalable manufacturing processes for advanced third-generation electrolyzer modules, supporting higher-efficiency equipment and the development of Canada's domestic electrolyzer supply chain.

Market Dynamics:

Growth Drivers: Federal Hub Funding and Sustained Industrial Decarbonization Demand

The North American industry is driven by growing federal and provincial clean-hydrogen hub funding, sustained refinery, chemicals and transportation decarbonization demand, and rising originator interest in diversifying hydrogen supply after fossil-based production faced tightening carbon-intensity regulation. As industrial customers prioritize both cost containment and compliance, demand for domestic green hydrogen production capacity continues rising across the United States and Canada.

Growing electrolyzer manufacturing investment, reinforced by Plug Power's and Cummins's continued capacity expansion, is reinforcing this driver by giving developers flexible access to domestic manufacturing capacity. Expanding collaboration between developers and industrial gas distributors is further widening the addressable customer base able to justify early capacity investment across the region.

⮞In January 2025, the U.S. Department of Energy awarded the Heartland Hydrogen Hub USD 20 million to begin its first phase, advancing plans for commercial-scale clean hydrogen production to supply low-carbon nitrogen fertilizer manufacturers across the agricultural region.

Restraints: High Capital Costs and Renewable Power Intermittency

High per-project capital costs continue restraining faster capacity expansion across North America, as gigawatt-scale hydrogen hub projects can require hundreds of millions of dollars in upfront investment before production revenue is realized. Renewable power intermittency further complicates electrolyzer utilization rates and project financing assumptions for developers across the region.

Limited long-duration storage and pipeline infrastructure also complicate capacity expansion decisions for manufacturers across the United States and Canada. Because new facility permitting and interconnection cycles can take several years, some developers continue favoring modular electrolyzer deployments over gigawatt-scale greenfield investment.

Opportunities: Industrial Hub Development and Export-Oriented Capacity Growth

The growing federal interest in dedicated hydrogen hubs is an important trend in North America, where industrial consumers and policy makers are putting more emphasis on supply chain stability, in addition to cost savings. Early developers of hub-scale projects will have important shares of this market in the forecast period.

Expansion into export-oriented green ammonia production offers a second opportunity for North American developers able to differentiate on reliability and certified low-carbon credentials. Continued collaboration between domestic developers and European off-takers is expected to further accelerate this opportunity through the remainder of the forecast period.

KCRW’s Press Play with Madeleine Brand invited both nominees to be California’s next governor to join us for wide-ranging conversations.

Democrat Xavier Becerra declined the invitation.

Republican Steve Hilton, the British-born former advisor to Prime Minister David Cameron and former Fox News host and commentator accepted, and spoke with Madeleine Brand at length Wednesday afternoon.

The interview text below has been edited for length and clarity.

Interview Highlights

On pushing back against Trump administration policies he doesn’t agree with

I'll fight any policy that I think harms Californians… Top of the list for me were cuts to the UC system from federal funding, which I strongly oppose and disagree with, and would want to reverse. There's a suggestion of removing Customs and Border Protection from our airports as some kind of retribution for California's sanctuary state policy. I strongly disagree with that. That's a ridiculous idea.

On reducing California’s high cost of living and eliminating the state income tax for people who make less than $150,000 per year

It's actually the quickest way we can really get money into people's pockets, is through changes to the tax system. If we did that, if we eliminated state income tax for people earning under $150,000, that will put thousands of dollars in their pocket. We've done a calculation for the typical household: it would save $11,047 a year. People can actually look up how much they would benefit, and that's a really direct way of helping people while the longer-term reforms take effect.

On his proposal for an 8 percent flat tax on income above $150,000

It's pro-worker. It's, let's call it the working-class tax cut—regular working people, more money directly to them. We also need to create jobs in California. We've got the highest unemployment rate of all 50 states. We've got the highest poverty rate in America. And one major reason for that is that we've got a very uncompetitive tax climate, which is driving business and entrepreneurs to other states, especially Texas. A lot of these states that people and businesses are moving to don't have any state income tax. So we've got to do something to stem the flow of jobs and opportunity going to other states. And yes, so that's exactly why we need a pro-growth component of the tax changes that I want to make as well.

On cutting the gas tax and his promise of $3-per-gallon gasoline

We've got the highest gas prices in the country, higher even than Hawaii in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, even though we have abundant oil reserves right here in California. Prior to the Iran war, there were 40 states with gas prices at $3 or below; most of them don't have any oil reserves. There's no reason that we have to be paying these high prices. Most of the increase, the extra that we pay here, is actually not the direct gas tax; the main part, what you might think of as hidden gas taxes, this is a combination of the Low Carbon Fuel Standard and the Cap-and-Invest program. That actually adds more to the gas price than the direct gas tax does.

And then on top of that, you've got outdated regulations that make it twice as expensive to refine gasoline here compared to other states. And then the big one, really, is the insanity of what we're doing with our oil imports. We are importing now nearly 80 percent of the oil that we use in California, including refined gasoline, which is increasing carbon emissions as well as increasing the cost. So my plan would involve replacing costly imports with domestic California production… mainly [in] Kern County.

On transitioning to electric vehicles, and President Trump ending EV tax credits

We have an electric vehicle at home, and I'm very supportive of the industry… and if people want to do that, that's great. But I don't think we should be subsidizing it. The idea of taxing working-class people in order to give subsidies to the higher-income groups who typically buy EVs just isn't fair. So sure, if people want to do the transition, but I don't think that it's something that should be subsidized by taxpayers.

On how to make homebuying more affordable when the median home price in California is around $750,000

First of all, we've got to reduce the fees and charges that are put onto new homes. Right now, the estimate is that about $200,000 of the cost of a new home is directly attributable to government fees and charges. Things like, they call them impact fees. They're not paid directly by the home buyer, but they go indirectly into the price. That's something that's just got completely out of control, and we need to cap that. My proposal is capping that at $50,000, and that would take immediately, on average for an average home, about $150,000 off the price.

Secondly, we need to simplify and streamline the regulations around construction that have, again, got disproportionate. A lot of these things start with good intentions, but they've ended up creating a situation where it costs two or three times as much to build the exact same building—whether that's an apartment building, or single-family home, or office, or whatever it may be—costs two or three times as much in California as in any other state.

The third thing we need to do is open up more land for development… I'm not against densification, but I don't think that can be the only answer, because not everyone wants to live in an apartment. And just the fact that that's been the only focus of policy in recent years has really held things up. That's why I think Gavin Newsom's pledge of building 3 million homes, which he made in 2018 when he first ran for governor, has just wildly been missed, because it's been such a narrow focus on a particular type of housing. I think we need choice in housing; we need to have diversity in the kind of homes that are built and in the places.

I've got a plan which I've laid out for how we can get 10 new cities built in California from the bottom-up perspective, where counties would bid for the right to build new towns and cities, and they would get more of the financial incentives for doing so.

On addressing homelessness

The number one priority is to get people the help that they need. And it's usually a combination of two things: drug rehabilitation and mental healthcare, often they go together. But nobody is going to be helped or help get their life back on track living on the streets. So we have to make sure that people are taken off the streets and placed in a safe, secure environment where they can be given the help that they need.

So one part of that is a plan that I'm actually going to be announcing on Saturday, after we're having this conversation, which is a proposal to use unused military space, a base near San Diego for a triage center—what I'm calling the Homeless Recovery Centers—with plenty of space for secure shelter where people can get the care that they need, and their needs identified so we can then get them into the next step, whatever that may be.

One of the reasons that people are resistant to go into shelters is that they're often just not designed well. They lump everybody together, whatever their circumstances, whatever their needs. For example, you may find a veteran with serious mental health problems, even psychosis, placed in a setting right next to a single parent who's just there with a couple of kids, they’ve fallen on hard times and are desperate for somewhere to stay.

Another barrier that a lot of people who are homeless have towards going into these shelters is that they can't bring their pets, and so on. I think we've got to look at it from a very human point of view and say: Well, what do people need? Their needs are not all the same. Homeless people have very—you know, some have been there just six months because they’ve fallen on hard times and actually can get pretty quickly back on track. Others have been out on the streets for 20 years and need incredibly intensive help to get their lives in order.

So we can't be treating people the same, and we do need space for that initial triage function. I think that's very important; that's what's missing at the moment.

On his call for mayors to clear encampments within a year, and what would happen if they don’t (or can’t)

I'd ask them what help they need, but I just think, again, what's the alternative? This is an unacceptable situation. We do not see this in other states on this scale, in other countries. We are the richest state in the richest country on Earth, and for people to be living in these numbers, in these conditions, I just think is completely unacceptable.

And so we have to take urgent action. My plan would involve sitting down right away with the mayors of the cities where this is the biggest problem and say, "Right, what do you need from me as governor? How can I help you? But let's agree [on] a timeline, and it needs to be measured in months, not years. We've had years, and we can't go on like this; we've got to sort this out."

Then during that period, by the way, I would be making sure we got the triage centers that I've just described up and running as much as we can, as quickly as we can, so that by, I don't know, six months, nine months, this would be a conversation between me and the local leaders.

On if he would arrest people who don’t accept services

My instinctive approach is ‘carrot’ rather than ‘stick,’ to design facilities that people want to go to because they meet their needs. But in the end, you have to have some kind of backstop. What we've got is unacceptable. And so I think that, yes, I'm very prepared to say that in the end, if that's the only way we can get people the help they need, then we shouldn't take that off the table.

But the starting point would be to make this a positive incentive. We've really got somewhere for you to go that is safe and clean, away from all this toxic, dangerous situation that you're in in the middle of a city, and we're going to help you. And you can bring your pet if that's what you want to bring, and you're going to be with people like yourself, and you're not going to be treated poorly with terrible food and dangerous conditions. I think that that is what—in the end, I've spoken to so many people, that is what they want.

On his sexually suggestive campaign ad, its intended audience, and pushback he received

It's part of a campaign called "Just Try It." There's been a few other ads in the series, and there's going to be a few more as well. And the simple point is this: We've been doing things the same way in California for 16 years now—one-party rule, Democrats running the state legislature with a two-thirds majority, all the statewide offices, every big city, every big county, the state Supreme Court with a 6-1 majority. We've been doing the same thing for 16 years, and the basic argument—especially in a state where we now have a clear majority, whichever poll you look at, that thinks the state's going in the wrong direction and needs change—is just to say to those people especially, "Look, just try something different. Just try it."

It was just a creative expression of an overall argument, and there'll be other ones… In a way, they play on caricatures and stereotypes, and there's an element of misdirection in that. That's the whole point. That's the joke in the ads, and there's been a few others, and there'll be more.

I was taken aback by the strength of [the pushback and denouncement by many, including his fellow Republicans], but I had good conversations with many of those people, and they understand what we're trying to do. We probably don't agree on it, but the most important point is that we speak for the majority of Californians who want something different. And really something's got to change, because millions of people are leaving this beautiful state of ours for places that they think offer them the kinds of things we used to offer here in California: the opportunity to buy your own home, to start a business, to make a life. Now people are moving to Texas for that, or Nashville or whatever, and no, it's California! There's nowhere better than California. It's the greatest place on Earth, and yet we're making it impossible for people to live here, and that's what I want to change.

title: Global Energy Scenarios 2026: Pathways to resilience
description:
Rystad Energy’s fifth edition of its flagship annual report, Global Energy Scenarios (GES) 2026, finds that global reliance on imported energy is projected to peak by 2034 as energy security concerns accelerate the shift towards electrification.
Against the backdrop of two major energy crises in five years, the report highlights how a broader range of rapidly deployable technologies is helping the energy system withstand major disruptions to energy flows.
Under Pragmatism, primary energy demand reaches 702 exajoules (EJ) by 2050, equivalent to adding another India to global energy demand in less than 25 years.
The report notes that several emerging clean-technology supply chains are more concentrated than the current fossil energy system.
Contacts Jon Ødegård Hansen Senior Vice President, Head of Energy Systems jon.hansen@rystadenergy.com Lars Nitter Havro Vice President, Head of Energy Macro Solution lars.nitter.havro@rystadenergy.com Katie Keenan Senior Communications Manager Phone: +1 713-301-9300 katie.keenan@rystadenergy.com About Rystad Energy Rystad Energy is a leading global independent research and energy intelligence company dedicated to helping clients navigate the future of energy.
text:
Rystad Energy’s fifth edition of its flagship annual report, Global Energy Scenarios (GES) 2026, finds that global reliance on imported energy is projected to peak by 2034 as energy security concerns accelerate the shift towards electrification. Against the backdrop of two major energy crises in five years, the report highlights how a broader range of rapidly deployable technologies is helping the energy system withstand major disruptions to energy flows. It explores how energy import dependency could evolve under three possible future scenarios, each reflecting a different pace of change.

Russia’s war in Ukraine and the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has severely affected flows through the Strait of Hormuz, are among the most severe tests of the energy system since the oil crises of the 1970s. Both had long been considered major risks, but they played out differently than anticipated.

Much of the system’s resilience thus far comes from energy capacity built after the first shock. In 2021, Russia supplied around 36% of Europe’s gas imports and the US around 6%. By 2025, Russia was down to around 7.5% while US LNG supplied around 21%. That infrastructure is now helping buffer the system, although Europe and Asia are competing for the same LNG cargoes, which risks leaving Europe short of winter stocks and Asia short of supply. For oil, pipelines, crude on water, storage and demand response have done much of the work, most visibly in China. The two conflicts also overlap in diesel: Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have pushed Moscow to ban diesel exports just as Hormuz has reduced Middle East supply. With diesel stocks around 14% below their five-year average, US diesel cracks have climbed above a record $100 per barrel, raising costs for trucking, shipping and freight.

Governments protect consumers first, then turn to structural change

Since February 2026, nearly 100 countries have cut fuel taxes, paid subsidies or capped prices to shield consumers, 60 have introduced demand-reduction measures and 34 have pursued structural changes. Of those, 26 adopted electrification policies, 22 of them in Europe and Asia. Energy security is making electrification more politically durable, including in countries such as Italy and Japan that had placed relatively less emphasis on sustainability. Most countries are electrifying with domestic energy: renewables and nuclear where available, and coal where reserves exist. Little new coal capacity is being built, but plant life extensions, restarts and delayed phaseouts, including Italy to 2038 and Thailand’s Mae Moh, add years of emissions.

The system has absorbed the current crisis remarkably well so far, much of it through capacity built after the previous shock. Decades of investment, innovation and diversification created this optionality and, with ample buffers at the onset of the crisis, this has bought the system valuable time. How much remains depends on how long the Strait of Hormuz stays constricted and how fast new options can materialize. The longer the conflict lasts, the harder it will affect interlinked systems like food, logistics and manufacturing,

Jarand Rystad, Founder & Executive Chairman, Rystad Energy

Pragmatism: a new reference pathway to 2050

The report introduces Pragmatism as a new reference scenario to 2050. It assumes a gradual strengthening of current policies, with affordability, energy security and technology costs setting the pace. It reflects a shift away from a transition driven mainly by stringent climate policy toward one that balances reliable, affordable and clean energy. Climate first, which assumes rapid and coordinated global action, and Fossil first, which assumes weaker policy support and slower clean-technology progress, bracket the range.

Learn more with Rystad Energy’s Energy Macro solution.

Under Pragmatism, primary energy demand reaches 702 exajoules (EJ) by 2050, equivalent to adding another India to global energy demand in less than 25 years. Liquids demand declines about 2.2% per year to 102 million bpd in 2026, and gas demand about 0.9% per year to 4,150 billion cubic meters. Oil and gas trade grows into the mid-2030s and stays above today’s level until 2043. Middle East exports hold near current levels through 2050, and Europe and Asia still import around 76% and 49% of their gas, respectively. Import dependence among importing countries falls from around 40% today to 26% by 2050 in Pragmatism, compared with 33% in Fossil first and 14% in Climate first.

Each pathway involves trade-offs. Fossil first costs less upfront because it avoids the capital needed for electrification, while Climate first front-loads investment, at an average of $3.8 trillion per year from 2026 to 2050, compared with $2.9 trillion in Pragmatism and $2.3 trillion in Fossil first. For net importers, Climate first capex peaks at $3.1 trillion in 2037 and then falls to $1.1 trillion by 2050, below Fossil first. The cost gap narrows after 2040 as fuel bills fall and clean technologies scale.

Electricity moves to the center of the system

Electricity overtook oil in 2025 as the largest carrier of useful energy for direct fuel use, and its share is projected to rise from around 28% today to 41% by 2050 under Pragmatism. By midcentury, electricity supplies more useful energy than coal, oil and gas combined. Primary energy demand among importers peaks in 2038 at 421 EJ, yet the energy they put to work grows 22% through 2050 because electric end uses lose less energy than combustion. Electricity is now linked to about 47% of global gross domestic product (GDP), up from 38% in 2000, with China’s share up 28 percentage points to 48%.

Artificial intelligence adds a different kind of pressure. It is felt most in local power markets and grids, where data centers outbid existing customers, strain the supply of gas-fired generation equipment and fill order books for gas turbines and fuel cells. In the US, data centers lean largely on gas for the firm power they need first. Nuclear has returned to the agenda, with Asia moving fastest and data centers contracting it directly.

Whichever mix countries choose, the common denominator is electricity. Established technologies continue to get cheaper, while newer ones, from long-duration heat storage to new battery chemistries, approach commercialization.

China's clean-technology exports grow as importers look beyond oil and gas

The Hormuz crisis is the first major energy shock with a real electric alternative, and Chinese manufacturers are supplying much of it. Chinese battery electric vehicle exports are on track to reach 12% of global car sales outside China in 2026. Between January and July, exports to Europe reached nearly 1 million vehicles, about double the level of the same period in 2025, while exports to South America rose to around half a million from approximately 170,000. Global EV sales reached 33% in the middle of the year as diesel prices hit records across Europe, South America and Southeast Asia. Battery storage is set to grow around 56% this year, ahead of solar at 18%, and electric trucks are on track to reach over 40% of heavy-truck sales in China, four years ahead of its 2030 target.

This also concentrates supply in a few places. China holds 96% of solar wafer capacity, 95% of cathode materials, 91% of rare earth refining, 88% of solar cells and 78% of battery cells, and its smallest share among the segments shown, wind nacelles, is about two-thirds. Importers in Europe and India are replacing oil and gas from the Persian Gulf with Chinese batteries, minerals and EVs, which deepens that dependence. The report notes that several emerging clean-technology supply chains are more concentrated than the current fossil energy system. It frames this as a shift in the nature of risk: energy security moves from a flow of fuels to a stock of assets, and an imported solar panel or battery can produce for decades, while an imported barrel of oil must be replaced tomorrow. How quickly the dependency eases depends on how fast other countries build their own manufacturing capacity, in the way Japanese automakers rose out of the 1970s efficiency drive.

Emissions plateau near 40 gigatonnes, with the pace of decline still open

Global fossil CO₂ emissions are plateauing at around 40 Gt. Under the Pragmatism scenario they fall to about 20 Gt by 2050. Cumulative emissions of 800 Gt from 2026 to 2050 correspond to around 0.35 degrees Celsius of additional warming, based on the IPCC estimate of about 0.1 degrees per 220 Gt of CO₂. That is above the goal of the Paris Agreement, which requires net zero emissions by 2050, but well below the trajectories once seen as business as usual. In the Climate first scenario, emissions fall to about 2 Gt by 2050 and add around 0.25 degrees. In Fossil first, emissions stay near today’s level for longer and add around 0.45 degrees.

Cleaner power has delivered most of the progress so far. Rystad Energy’s Decarbonization Index, which tracks the Three Tasks of the energy transition, rises from the low 20% range in the mid-2020s to above 60% by 2050 under Pragmatism. Clean power reaches about 85% and electrification about 50%. Policy targets are following the same order. The EU has set an indicative electrification target of 46% by 2040, and the COP31 presidency has proposed raising electricity’s share of global final energy demand to 35% by 2035, after COP28 focused on tripling renewable capacity.

description:

This blog post focuses specifically on BAAJA’s impact on federal transmission development, arguably the backbone of the bill.

Points to Watch: Downstream State Permitting Effects: At a high level, the possibility of FERC taking over transmission permitting from state regulators could serve as an incentive to timely grant permits with reasonable conditions.
OSW Transmission Permitting: Offshore wind lines from the Outer Continental Shelf are expressly covered by FERC’s permitting authority and eligible for cost allocation.
text:
Preface

This is the first post in a four-part “BAAJA Blast” series covering the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026—a Senate bill proposing significant reforms to federal permitting and environmental review processes. Released in late September, the 417-page bill reaches well beyond its permitting heading, with provisions addressing broader questions of national energy policy.

In this series, we will take a sector-by-sector look at how the bill’s provisions would affect specific technologies and industries—and what they could mean in practice for developers, investors, large energy users, and other market participants. The series is organized around four areas: (1) transmission; (2) offshore wind; (3) data centers and large loads; and (4) distributed energy resources and virtual power plants. Throughout the series, we will also highlight the bill’s cross-cutting changes to environmental and historic preservation review where they bear on each sector.

The bill still faces significant hurdles. It must pass both chambers and be signed by the President, and it is not expected to be taken up until after the midterm elections, by which point its text—and the political landscape—could look quite different. Even so, the bill’s introduction is a major development in its own right. Federal permitting reform has been debated in Congress for years without enactment, and this bipartisan package offers the most concrete picture to date of what a durable compromise could look like. We hope this series will serve as a practical resource, and we will continue to track the bill’s progress through Congress.

Background

On September 30, 2026, Senate leaders released the “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026” or “BAAJA.” BAAJA is a broad federal permitting reform bill that shortens review timelines, narrows judicial remedies, and protects permits once they are issued, across nearly every type of energy and natural resource project.

This blog post focuses specifically on BAAJA’s impact on federal transmission development, arguably the backbone of the bill. As we have previously noted, transmission bottlenecks are keeping hundreds of gigawatts of solar, wind, and battery projects off the grid. These constraints result in higher electricity bills: C2ES/Greenline modeling projects about $7 billion in net delivery-cost savings by 2035 (after about $1.9 billion in new transmission investment) and about $1.1 billion in residential bill savings. The same modeling projects nearly 40 GW of added interregional transmission capacity.

FERC’s Beefed-Up Backstop Siting Authority (Section 2101)

Under the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), states have historically retained authority over transmission-line siting, permitting, and construction. One exception to this general rule are certain National Interest Electric Transmission Corridors (“NIETCs”) designated by the U.S. Department of Energy (“DOE”). Under current law, within NIETCs, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) may issue permits to construct or modify electricity transmission facilities under specified conditions (e.g., when a state has failed to act or denied an application).

BAAJA significantly expands FERC’s siting authority, removing the requirement that a line sit in a NIETC. DOE no longer plays an intermediary role, and instead conducts a congestion study under new FPA § 224, based on which DOE may identify “geographic areas” experiencing (or expected to experience) constraints or congestion. These geographic areas replace NIETCs as the reference point for certain DOE financing programs, but are not a prerequisite for a FERC permit.

The bill requires FERC to issue a permit if it finds that the transmission project is necessary in the national interest, that one of the state-failure triggers has been met (e.g., if a state denies the permit or fails to issue a permit within one year), and that certain other criteria are satisfied. A line qualifies if it carries power in interstate commerce (expressly including transmission from the Outer Continental Shelf to a state) and is capable of 230 kV or more; lines with advanced conductors can qualify at voltages FERC sets.

For lines of 345 kV or more, FERC review runs simultaneously with state review so as to avoid any delay if FERC has to take over the permitting process, but FERC cannot issue a permit until one of the state-failure findings in § 216(b)(1) is made.

BAAJA sets forth a cost allocation methodology for transmission lines that FERC finds meet the § 216(b) permitting criteria, under which costs follow beneficiaries. Customers that receive no benefit, or only a trivial one, cannot be involuntarily charged for a line, although a transmitting utility may still recover those costs through a voluntary agreement with its customers.

Points to Watch:

Downstream State Permitting Effects: At a high level, the possibility of FERC taking over transmission permitting from state regulators could serve as an incentive to timely grant permits with reasonable conditions. This could indirectly impact state permitting processes even where FERC does not issue permits directly.

OSW Transmission Permitting: Offshore wind lines from the Outer Continental Shelf are expressly covered by FERC’s permitting authority and eligible for cost allocation. This could significantly derisk permitting of those lines, allow for transmission-first development to lease areas, and when combined with FERC’s backstop protection for non-beneficiaries, allow for streamlined development for projects impacting multiple states.

Jurisdiction Over In-State Lines: FERC’s jurisdiction may reach lines located entirely within one state provided such projects meet the 230 kV threshold and are used for the transmission of electric energy in interstate commerce. Though high-voltage lines typically fall under federal jurisdiction, this could raise jurisdictional questions over in-state lines depending on how aggressively FERC exercises this authority.

Trump v. Slaughter and Increased Executive Control over FERC: In the wake of the U.S. Supreme Court’s recent ruling in Trump v. Slaughter, which held that for-cause removal protections for independent agency commissioners exercising executive power violate the separation of powers, a pro-transmission President could appoint commissioners to make full use of FERC’s expanded authority, potentially heightening the import of these provisions.

Regional and interregional planning (new FPA § 225)

All planning regions must use a common set of input assumptions and models and a common list of benefits. Regional and joint interregional plans are due within 2 years of enactment and must be updated at least every 4 years. ERCOT is excluded.

Point to Watch: A project selected in a regional or interregional plan is deemed to satisfy most of the § 216(b) findings, creating a fast route from planning to permit.

Interconnection

Regions must plan generation and transmission together over a 20-year horizon and publish interconnection locations, each with an upfront, fixed, zonal per-MW cost. Cluster studies get a single decision point, nonrefundable security, and withdrawal penalties.

FERC must begin a rulemaking within one year requiring public utility transmission providers to share and employ, as appropriate, queue management practices that use AI, machine learning, and automation to speed interconnection studies, and must reopen the rule at least every four years.

Point to Watch: By legally mandating that neighboring regional grid operators proactively plan together, the bill aims to fix a broken regulatory system that has resulted in few, if any, major interregional transmission lines actually being built over the last 15 years.

Grid-enhancing technologies and reconductoring

The bill requires public utilities to deploy advanced transmission technologies where the benefit-cost ratio exceeds one or face a FERC-determined penalty, which may include a reduced return on equity. Reconductoring within existing rights-of-way is excluded from NEPA review and is not an undertaking under NHPA Section 106.

text:
New episode of Making the Case available now on Spotify, Apple, and YouTube

Washington, DC – U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Courts Subcommittee and Ranking Member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, released the eleventh episode of season two of his podcast, Making the Case. In the new episode, Whitehouse is joined by Jay Inslee, former Governor of Washington and a leading advocate for climate action.

Governance in America is done by legislation, regulation, and litigation. The Supreme Court struck a fatal blow to climate legislation by unleashing dark money through its Citizens United decision. The Court later struck down EPA’s Clean Power Plan and concocted the “major questions doctrine” to kill climate regulation efforts. Whitehouse and Inslee dive into what’s next for the captured Court and how a landmark climate liability case – Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County – could upend the future of climate litigation and with this trifecta, create a governance-free zone for the industry. They discuss how the nation’s highest court assumed a star role in stopping climate action and how the American people, from coast to coast, are experiencing a climate upheaval that’s already roiling insurance markets.

“After blowing up both congressional efforts to legislate on climate and prior administrations’ climate pollution standards, immunizing the fossil fuel industry from litigation is the final target for the Captured Court. It’s why Suncor is such an important case, and why Governor Inslee and I are watching this one closely,” said Whitehouse. “Remember this episode when the dangers of an ungovernable, free-to-pollute industry start landing hard at home.”

The episode is now available on Spotify, Apple Podcasts, and other podcast platforms.

Whitehouse recently led 90 members of Congress on an amicus brief to the Supreme Court in the Suncor case, explaining that nothing in the Clean Air Act, the Constitution, and federal foreign policy prevents states and localities from holding oil and gas companies accountable for climate-related harms.

title: Changan And CATL Are Developing Solid-State Batteries With Nearly 1,000 Miles Of Range
description:
Together, Changan and CATL are preparing to strengthen their supply chain while developing technologies that could shape future electric vehicles.
Solid-State Batteries Could Deliver 932 Miles Of Range According to Libattery, Changan is continuing development of its Golden Bell solid-state battery technology, first announced in 2023.
Changan And CATL Expand Battery Production The two companies plan to establish a combined battery production capacity of 75 GWh through their joint venture.
Their collaboration also extends to sodium-ion batteries, battery swapping, and solid-state technology.
Achieving those goals will depend on overcoming the manufacturing and durability challenges associated with solid-state batteries.
text:
Electric vehicles capable of traveling nearly 1,000 miles on a single charge could eventually become a reality if Chinese automaker Changan achieves its latest battery ambitions. The company is expanding its partnership with battery giant CATL while continuing development of next-generation solid-state technology.

Changan has outlined plans for batteries capable of delivering over 1,500 kilometers (932 miles) of driving range, which is much farther than the range offered by most electric vehicles currently on sale.

The technology promises improvements in energy density, charging performance, and battery durability. However, the impressive figures are just manufacturer targets, not independently verified results from production vehicles.

The announcement also includes a major expansion of battery manufacturing capacity in China. Together, Changan and CATL are preparing to strengthen their supply chain while developing technologies that could shape future electric vehicles.

Solid-State Batteries Could Deliver 932 Miles Of Range

According to Libattery, Changan is continuing development of its Golden Bell solid-state battery technology, first announced in 2023. The automaker is targeting an energy density of up to 400 Wh/kg, potentially enabling electric vehicles to travel over 1,500 kilometers on a full charge.

Changan also claims its battery technology could deliver improved safety through AI-assisted monitoring. The company has previously suggested a 70 percent safety improvement compared with conventional liquid-electrolyte batteries, although the precise testing conditions are unclear.

Durability is another major focus, with Changan targeting a lifespan exceeding 5,000 charging cycles. Its Golden Bell battery technology also includes a claimed 30-to-80-percent charging time of just nine minutes using 6C fast charging.

Changan And CATL Expand Battery Production

The two companies plan to establish a combined battery production capacity of 75 GWh through their joint venture. Their collaboration also extends to sodium-ion batteries, battery swapping, and solid-state technology.

A new 25 GWh manufacturing facility is planned for the Sichuan-Chongqing region, with production expected to begin during the second half of 2027. The project involves an investment of approximately 5.5 billion yuan ($770 million) and is expected to create around 2,500 jobs.

The facility will supply batteries to Changan's electric vehicle brands, including Avatr, Deepal, and Nevo. Full production capacity is expected to be reached within three years of operations beginning.

Production Could Begin In 2027

Changan previously outlined plans to begin testing its all-solid-state batteries in vehicles during 2026. The automaker is targeting a gradual transition toward commercial production starting in 2027.

Achieving those goals will depend on overcoming the manufacturing and durability challenges associated with solid-state batteries. For now, the nearly 1,000-mile range represents an ambitious projection rather than a capability available to customers.

If Changan succeeds, the technology could significantly reduce the frequency of charging stops and help make long-distance electric driving far more convenient.

title: Fuel Costs are Crushing Family Farmers. It's Time for Serious Solutions
description:

Ad-hoc diesel relief: In the last decade, Congress has authorized over $100 billion in ad-hoc financial assistance for farmers.
