text:
By Charlie Decker, NFU Advocacy Coordinator

With the fall harvest fully underway, America’s family farmers are feeling the squeeze of high input costs. The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) Economic Research Service projects that farm production expenses will climb by 4.5 percent in 2026, with fuel and oil costs accounting for up to 30 percent of the projected increase, and diesel leading the way.

Diesel is a vital fuel source for farmers and the entire U.S. economy, as it powers heavy-duty farm equipment and most commercial freight. In September 2026, the nationwide average cost of diesel reached a record high of $6.53 per gallon, up nearly $3 (or 77 percent) from the beginning of 2026, and a 25-percent increase from the previous three months.

Diesel prices have steadily risen dating back to the beginning of 2021, and various forecasts suggest they are likely to remain elevated in 2027. This is an economic time bomb that many farmers will not be able to withstand.

Over the last month, lawmakers and candidates for elected office have urged the Trump administration to act immediately to lower fuel prices. Among the proposals floated were a ban on diesel exports, suspending state and federal fuel taxes, and creating an ad-hoc diesel relief program.

Let’s dissect each of these a bit further:

Banning diesel exports: While this move might ease diesel prices in select regions of the country, strong evidence suggests it would do the opposite in other regions and would eventually backfire altogether. The U.S. is the world’s largest diesel supplier, and an export ban would push refiners to cut production of all fuels once their reserves reach capacity, reducing the overall global supply and pushing fuel prices higher in the long run. An export ban may bring about some short-term relief for harvest season but would generate sharp increases on the horizon as farmers get ready for the spring planting season.

Suspending fuel taxes: On October 5, President Trump signed an executive order that seeks to allow red-dyed, off-road diesel to be used on public roadways. Red-dyed diesel powers off-road vehicles like tractors, combines, and other heavy farm equipment, and it is exempt from the 24.4-cent-per-gallon federal highway tax. It is chemically identical to regular diesel, with the lone distinction being an added red dye to indicate its tax status, and it cannot be used in vehicles that use public roadways.

The president’s order has been advertised as an alternative mechanism to bypass the federal diesel tax, but there’s a catch: it provides only a deferral on these taxes through the end of the year, not a guaranteed elimination. That means the bill could ultimately come due for any diesel driver who took advantage of the waiver. And while farmers use on-highway diesel for hauling grain and livestock, suspending these taxes will provide only marginal relief given the large wholesale price increases that have occurred. The varying state laws on the use and tax of red-dyed diesel further complicate the ability of this order to provide meaningful savings.

Furthermore, in whatever form it takes, a suspension of federal fuel taxes will increase demand while supply is tight, putting upward pressure on pre-tax fuel prices. Suspending these taxes also undermine the Highway Trust Fund, which is the primary funding source for the construction and maintenance of U.S. transportation infrastructure – a high price to pay for relatively small benefits.

Ad-hoc diesel relief: In the last decade, Congress has authorized over $100 billion in ad-hoc financial assistance for farmers. In July 2026, the Trump administration and Congress introduced another $11 billion in farm relief; however, this relief is tucked within a larger supplemental package that authorizes over $70 billion in funding for the Iran war, the very conflict that is driving up the costs of fuel and fertilizer, stoking global market chaos, and exacerbating the economic pressures weighing down farm operations. Farmers shouldn’t have to sacrifice their short-term economic health for long-term policy choices that further erode their bottom lines.

The above actions represent band aid solutions to challenges stemming from deeper, underlying wounds, and they are certainly no substitute for enacting reforms to lower fuel costs. Congress must take bold action to deliver commonsense policies that tackle the affordability crisis head-on and put American family farmers first.

Protect and promote biodiesel and renewable diesel under the RFS

Currently, the only alternatives to petroleum-based fuels available to American farmers and consumers are biodiesel and renewable diesel. The Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) supports the growth of renewably produced fuels in the United States. It establishes the number of gallons of renewably produced fuel that must be blended into the nation’s total fuel supply each year. When properly implemented, the RFS opens transportation fuels markets to competition, drives investments in domestic fuel production, and helps increase the overall fuel supply, all of which help lower the costs of transportation fuel.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) sets renewable volumes each year for total renewable fuel, including biomass-based diesel. For 2026 and 2027, EPA established historic blending volumes for biodiesel and renewable diesel, an action NFU applauded.

However, the RFS has been threatened over the last decade by an influx of small refinery exemption (SRE) petitions, which exempt certain oil refineries from part or all of the RFS renewable volumes. While SREs were intended to be a temporary measure to provide truly small and independent refiners with additional time to come into RFS compliance, regulatory actions have allowed large refiners to exploit them and effectively bypass their blending obligations, with biodiesel and renewable diesel taking the biggest hits.

Between 2017 and 2020, EPA exempted nearly 1.75 billion gallons of bio- and renewable diesel, costing producers $6.7 billion in lost revenue. Meanwhile, consumers saw practically zero savings from these SREs at the pump.

In recent years, EPA has begun to rectify this issue by reallocating previously exempted volumes from SREs. NFU has consistently urged EPA to treat SREs as the exception, as opposed to the rule when considering petitions. The EPA must also ensure previously exempted gallons are fully reallocated into future RFS volume obligations for bio- and renewable diesel.

Robust investment in renewable, low-carbon fuels

NFU supports the pursuit of balanced national energy policy that recognizes the contributions of America’s agricultural sector. Homegrown renewables, with the proper investments, are best positioned to lead the way in reducing our reliance on foreign oil and lowering overall fuel costs while providing greater demand for U.S. agricultural products.

The Next Generation Fuels Act (last introduced in the 118th Congress) would expedite the transition of the U.S. fuel supply to renewables by establishing higher octane standards for new vehicles, requiring reduced lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions, and advancing towards higher-level blends of ethanol, such as E25 and E30 (gasoline with a 25% and 30% ethanol blend, respectively). The Flex Fuel Fairness Act (introduced in July 2025) would provide regulatory credits for automakers that produce flexible-fuel vehicles that run on lower-carbon liquid fuels to legally recognize the emissions’ savings that can be achieved through higher-level blends of ethanol and expanded use of biofuels.

There are also opportunities to support advanced biofuels for diesel by reinstating the Section 40A biodiesel blenders tax credit and extending the small agri-biodiesel producer credit. The biodiesel blenders tax credit (before it expired in 2024) provided a $1 credit for every gallon of biodiesel, agri-biodiesel, or renewable diesel blended with petroleum diesel. The small agri-biodiesel producer credit provides an additional tax credit of 20 cents per gallon for the first 15 million gallons produced by small agricultural biodiesel manufacturers.

Authorize year-round E15

NFU is pushing for a permanent authorization of the year-round, nationwide sale of E15. Currently, E15 can only be sold in a handful of states during the summer months. While the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has issued annual waivers in recent years to allow summer E15 sales, year-to-year uncertainty creates challenges for corn growers and hinders investment and growth in renewable fuel infrastructure.

A permanent authorization will significantly boost demand for domestically grown corn and provide immediate and meaningful relief for drivers at the gas pump. The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) recently found that E15 has been selling for $0.47 less per gallon than conventional gasoline on average, an 11.5 percent discount.

In May 2026, the House of Representatives passed year-round E15 legislation (H.R.1346, the Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act), and the Senate farm bill includes similar provisions that authorize year-round E15. Congress must get this done before the end of the year, as farmers cannot afford any more delays.

There are plenty of opportunities for lawmakers to work in a bipartisan fashion to make meaningful reforms that promote stability and affordability in fuel markets. It’s time for Congress to get serious about enacting them.

text:
THE ISLAND—The Maine Department of Energy Resources recently announced a new grant program to help small businesses cut energy costs by improving energy efficiency.

The grants are available to businesses in manufacturing, forest products, life sciences, marine/aquaculture, food/agriculture, outdoor recreation and clean energy.

The money is offered through the state’s Affordable and Clean Energy for Rural Enterprises (ACRES) program. The state is issuing $950,000 in grants through the program.

As communities across the state brace for what looks to be a hard winter, with heating oil costs up more than 75 percent from last year, the grant program aims to help small businesses cut energy costs.

According to the program’s request for applications (RFA), projects fall into two basic categories: technical assistance and implementation.

Technical Assistance grants range from $5,000 to $10,000 per award, have no match requirement, and fund pre-implementation and planning work: energy assessments, project scoping, and funding navigation support.

Implementation funds may be upwards of $100,000 per award and include a 20 percent match requirement. These funds are designed to cover the cost of installing energy-efficient equipment and infrastructure.

Potential projects include behind-the-meter solar, battery energy storage, EV charging ports, weatherization, and efficient wood pellet or wood-burning technology, among others. The smaller technical assistance grants may cover, among other things, identifying energy efficiency opportunities within a specific business or providing guidance on return-on-investment projections.

Applications are available through the vendor self-service system on the Department of Energy Resources website. A link to the application is also posted to the town of Deer Isle website. The application deadline is 4 p.m. on Tuesday, November 3.

Town officials in Deer Isle and Stonington have been encouraging local business to apply for the grant online. Stonington Economic Development Director Linda Nelson said she already has a local business interested.

But even for professionals like Nelson and Deer Isle Town Manager Jim Fisher, navigating the complicated application process for federal and state grants can be a challenge. Nelson and Fisher are offering their assistance to any local businesses as they go through the application process.

“All our small businesses, including our marine businesses, are struggling with inflation—especially energy inflation,” Nelson said. “The Town of Stonington wants our small businesses to thrive into an uncertain future, and using less energy will always be an important part of that. This grant program offers an opportunity to determine how best to reduce their load and costs.”

text:
Rivian has expanded its partnership with energy technology company Redwood Materials to recycle production scrap and end-of-life EV batteries, according to a Rivian press release. Redwood will also provide stationary battery storage at its manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois.

Redwood collects Rivian EV battery packs through Rivian’s nationwide network of service centers when they are no longer suitable for in-vehicle use. Redwood then evaluates each battery pack for energy storage at Rivian’s manufacturing facilities or other locations, or for recycling. Redwood will now also recycle battery scrap generated at Rivian’s manufacturing operations.

Rivian says the partnership expansion builds on existing work, announced in April, that provides 10 megawatt-hours (MWh) of battery energy storage from repurposed Rivian battery packs at the automaker’s Illinois manufacturing plant.

“Giving Rivian battery packs a second life in stationary storage is a massive unlock for the energy transition,” said RJ Scaringe, Rivian founder and CEO, in the release. “By partnering with JB and the Redwood team, we’re turning retired EV batteries into a powerful tool to make the grid more reliable and lower energy costs for everyone.”

JB Straubel, Redwood Materials founder and CEO, added that every Rivian battery pack can potentially provide domestic grid energy storage and critical materials.

“Redwood’s unique ability to integrate and redeploy Rivian batteries with our technology is an opportunity to enable fast, flexible, and more cost-efficient energy storage,” he said. “As the demand and cost for energy keep rising, working with companies like Rivian is how we help meet these challenges.”

Energy storage applications with repurposed batteries can ease grid stress during periods of high electricity demand, improving grid reliability while reducing energy costs for users and the grid at large, the release states.

During periods of low demand or when low-cost renewable energy is most productive, the packs can store electricity for easy dispatch during periods of higher demand. When paired with EV battery packs from Rivian and others, the release states that Redwood’s proprietary technology architecture offers an integrated system that can respond intelligently to the needs of the facility it is serving.

Then, when batteries are no longer useful in energy storage applications, or when manufacturing generates scrap, they can be recycled.

Redwood’s process can recycle and recover critical minerals, such as lithium, nickel, cobalt, and copper, at rates exceeding 95%, encouraging circular, domestic supply chain development for battery materials in the U.S., according to the release.

“This expanded partnership reflects a broader shift underway in how American manufacturers source power,” the release states. “As grid connections take years to secure and conventional infrastructure remains supply-constrained, companies increasingly need partners who can solve more than one piece of the problem — recovering materials, managing recycling, and deploying storage as a single system rather than separate vendors.”

BMW and General Motors have also previously announced partnerships with Redwood. BMW’s was to recycle lithium-ion batteries, similar to recycling partnerships Redwood signed with Toyota, Ford, Volvo, and Volkswagen.

GM launched a program to accelerate the deployment of energy storage systems using new and second-life battery packs from the automaker’s EVs.

text:
For nearly two decades, the Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) has helped agricultural producers and rural small businesses lower energy costs and strengthen their operations. A new rule from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), however, could make REAP increasingly difficult to access for those it intended to serve.

Through grants and guaranteed loans, the program supports projects that increase energy efficiency, such as improvements to heating and cooling systems, grain dryers, and refrigeration systems. In addition, REAP supports behind-the-meter, small-scale renewable energy systems (such as solar or wind) that offset on-site energy usage.

In an attempt to protect farmland from large-scale development, USDA’s Oct. 1 final rule restricts the sizing and siting of projects that could help farmers reduce operating expenses, even though these projects generally occupy only a small portion of the land, with minimal impact on agricultural production.

The rule also shifts the Rural Energy for America Program to a post-completion, performance based program. Rather than applying for a grant before starting a project and minimizing financial risk up-front, applicants will build the project, operate it for 12 months, then apply using energy production or savings data — with no guarantee of receiving an award.

For large businesses with ready access to capital, the change may be manageable, but for a small farm or rural business operating in tight margins, the ruling could prevent many worthwhile projects.

While the rule is set to go into effect on Oct. 16, USDA has opened a comment period, giving former award recipients, farmers, rural business owners, and others an opportunity to share their feedback. Comments can be submitted through regulations.gov under Docket RBS-26-Business-0529 until Nov. 2.

A strong REAP should continue helping rural Americans invest in their businesses and communities, while remaining accessible to the small operations that stand to benefit most.

text:
A newly filed proposal would hold electric base rates steady during 2027 and 2028, but the plan requires state regulatory approval and would not necessarily freeze every charge on customers' bills.

ST. PAUL, MN (October 15, 2026). Xcel Energy has proposed an alternative to a conventional Minnesota electricity rate case, offering to freeze customer base rates for calendar years 2027 and 2028 in exchange for accelerated recognition of federal tax benefits associated with five battery storage projects.

The proposal was submitted October 9 by Northern States Power Company, Xcel Energy's Minnesota utility subsidiary, to the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission.

Xcel disclosed the filing in a report to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

The plan could provide a period of greater rate stability for Minnesota electricity customers, but its financial structure and long-term implications require regulatory review.

The company has requested a commission decision by January 2027.

If the proposal is not approved, Xcel expects to file a conventional electric rate case in early 2027.

What the Company Is Proposing

The proposal is called the Electric Customer Rate Stability Plan.

According to the SEC filing, it contains three principal elements.

First, customer base rates would remain frozen during 2027 and 2028.

Second, Xcel would accelerate the recognition of federal investment tax credits related to five battery energy storage projects.

Third, the company would continue certain existing regulatory adjustment mechanisms, including previously approved true-up and tracker arrangements.

The third provision is particularly important.

A base-rate freeze does not necessarily mean that every amount appearing on an electricity bill would remain unchanged.

Customers may encounter charges or adjustments governed by mechanisms outside the base-rate component.

The plan therefore should not be described as a guarantee that every customer's total monthly bill will remain identical for two years.

Why Battery Storage Tax Credits Matter

Federal investment tax credits can reduce the financial cost of qualifying energy projects.

Battery storage systems are designed to store electricity for use at another time, helping utilities manage variations in supply and demand.

Depending on their design and operation, storage projects can support reliability and help integrate electricity generated from variable sources.

Xcel's proposal would recognize the financial benefits of certain federal tax credits earlier than originally scheduled.

The company says those benefits could offset the additional revenue it would otherwise seek to recover from customers for necessary capital investments.

The proposed arrangement is therefore based on the timing of tax benefits rather than a promise that utility operating expenses will stop increasing.

What the Regulatory Commission Must Determine

The Minnesota Public Utilities Commission must evaluate whether the proposed arrangement is consistent with applicable utility law and reasonable for customers.

Regulators will need to examine the timing and value of the tax credits, the costs being offset and the consequences for future rate proceedings.

One question is whether using benefits earlier reduces the amount available to offset costs later.

Another is whether the proposed freeze adequately protects customers if other approved adjustment mechanisms continue changing charges.

A third concerns the treatment of investments that Xcel makes during the two-year period.

The company has indicated that the accelerated tax credits would help offset the revenue requirement associated with ongoing capital improvements.

Regulators must assess whether the arrangement produces an appropriate balance between customer affordability and the utility's financial obligations.

What It Could Mean for Households

For households managing tight budgets, greater predictability in electricity base rates could be valuable.

Electricity is an essential expense, and changes in utility costs affect residents regardless of whether they own or rent their homes.

However, the exact savings from the proposal have not been independently established for a typical residential customer.

Without a verified customer bill comparison, it would be misleading to assign a specific monthly or annual savings figure.

The impact may also vary depending on customer usage, rate class and the components of a bill that remain subject to adjustment.

Business and Community Implications

Electricity costs also affect businesses, nonprofit organizations, schools and other institutions.

A period of base-rate stability could help some organizations plan their operating expenses.

For businesses with substantial electricity consumption, even modest changes in rates can affect budgets.

But the proposal's effect on different customer classes must be evaluated through the regulatory filing.

The public should not assume that every residential, commercial and industrial customer would receive an identical financial benefit.

What Happens After 2028?

The proposed freeze would apply to calendar years 2027 and 2028.

It would not establish a permanent prohibition on future rate increases.

The treatment of costs and tax benefits after the proposed period is therefore a central question.

Regulators and consumer advocates must examine whether the plan provides a durable financial advantage or primarily changes the timing of rate recovery.

That analysis requires access to the underlying financial calculations, not simply the headline promise of a freeze.

A Decision Requested by January

Xcel has asked the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission to act by January 2027.

If regulators decline to approve the plan, the utility expects to pursue a conventional rate case.

That would place the company's proposed revenue requirements before the commission through the ordinary rate-setting process.

For Minnesota customers, the immediate development is an offer of two years of base-rate stability.

Whether the arrangement is approved, and whether it produces the financial benefits the company anticipates, remain open questions.

text:
Benefiting from these changes often requires specialised skills and access to the latest technologies, putting disadvantaged groups at risk of being left behind.

Women, young people, older persons, persons with disabilities, migrants, Indigenous Peoples and low-income communities are particularly vulnerable, the report stresses, outlining recommendations for governments to ensure these transformations benefit everyone.

Inclusion is a priority

Social inclusion is a moral imperative, but it is also an economic necessity, the report from the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA) underlined.

It found that expanding opportunities to marginalised groups enlarges the productive workforce, strengthens human capital, increases innovation and entrepreneurship, improves labour allocation and spreads productivity gains more widely.

“Inclusive societies are more productive, resilient, and prosperous,” Secretary-General António Guterres summarised in a video message for the launch of the report.

Measures towards social inclusion should also be taken urgently, as those left outside key systems face steeper barriers to catching up later, the report emphasised.

What to do

As artificial intelligence transforms labour markets, the report urges governments to invest in continuous training and reskilling for workers whose jobs may be replaced or transformed, rather than focusing solely on creating new jobs.

Similarly, the shift to renewable energy must include support for workers and communities reliant on fossil fuels, through retraining, alternative employment opportunities and social assistance.

To bridge the digital divide, governments should also expand affordable access to the internet, digital infrastructure and technology training – particularly in disadvantaged communities.

One last major recommendation is to stop relying mainly on GDP to evaluate growth, and to also assess progress through poverty reduction, access to education and healthcare, employment security, inequality and environmental protection.

Economic growth that benefits only a small share of the population, it argues, cannot be considered genuinely inclusive.

Funding these investments

Importantly, these investments require resources and many developing countries are facing financial constraints that could hamper the transition.

Nearly half of the world’s poorest countries are either in or at high risk of debt distress, with interest payments relative to revenue at their highest levels in a generation, the UN Secretary-General warned.

He called on leaders to live up to the commitments made through last year’s Doha Political Declaration on Social Development and the Sevilla Commitment on financing for development.

He also pushed for reform of international financial institutions to better represent and serve developing countries.

“Transformations are inevitable. Inequality and exclusion are not,” the UN Secretary-General said.

“Let’s work together to ensure that the profound transformations reshaping our world help build societies rooted in justice, dignity and opportunity for all.”

Its customers range from start-ups to high-volume manufacturers, all using Oxford Instruments’ technology to advance augmented reality, power devices, three-dimensional sensing, and the optoelectronic transceivers that support hyperscale data centers.

A notable example of Oxford Instruments’ global impact is the role that the company is playing in the success of Singapore’s gallium nitride (GaN) initiative.

The GaN initiative was announced in June 2025 by A*STAR (Agency for Science, Technology, and Research). This initiative forms part of the National Semiconductor Translation and Innovation Center (NSTIC)’s wider efforts.

A*STAR – Agency for Science, Technology, and Research, brings together R&D and infrastructure to accelerate innovation in the semiconductor space. Image Credit: Oxford Instruments Plasma Technology

This program seeks to position Singapore as a global leader in advanced semiconductor technologies, focusing on the development and adoption of silicon carbide (SiC) and GaN-based semiconductors, which are widely recognized for their high efficiency and performance.

NSTIC supports the development and production of GaN and GaN-on-SiC-based semiconductors, supported by Oxford Instruments’ cutting-edge compound semiconductor equipment and expertise.

These semiconductors are critical for high-performance applications in electric vehicles, 5G, renewable energy, and more. They can also help increase Singapore’s manufacturing output in advanced technologies.

Oxford Instruments supports the NSTIC initiative in several key ways.

Providing Cutting-Edge Semiconductor Tools

Oxford Instruments supplies advanced equipment and tools that underpin the research, development, and manufacturing of wide bandgap semiconductors.

The company’s considerable expertise in atomic layer etching (ALE), atomic layer deposition (ALD) technologies, plasma etching, and deposition are key to ensuring precise and scalable semiconductor fabrication.

These tools help address challenges in material interfaces while allowing material properties to be tailored for high-performance applications.

Enabling Innovation in GaN and SiC Device Development

Oxford Instruments’ state-of-the-art solutions, products, and expertise empower researchers and industry partners to effectively prototype and refine GaN / SiC devices with improved speed, energy efficiency, and reliability.

The company’s technologies are integral to the center’s goal of expanding performance boundaries for applications such as 5G, electric vehicles, power electronics, and renewable energy systems.

Image Credit: Oxford Instruments Plasma Technology

Supporting R&D, Regional Collaborations, and Singapore’s Semiconductor Ecosystem

Oxford Instruments’ core aim throughout this project is to collaborate closely with A*STAR, local research institutions, and industry partners to advance R&D efforts in GaN/SiC technology.

Providing advanced manufacturing tools and sharing technical expertise is key to enabling the rapid innovation and commercialization of GaN and GaN-on-SiC-based solutions.

Oxford Instruments also contributes to strengthening Singapore’s semiconductor ecosystem by enabling the broader adoption of advanced GaN and SiC manufacturing processes.

The program aims to position Singapore as a key player in the global wide bandgap (WGB) supply chain, simultaneously supporting the country's overarching goals of economic growth and technological innovation.

Powering Innovation in GaN / SiC Device Development

Oxford Instruments is also contributing to the scalability of GaN/SiC technology, enabling the implementation of high-precision, efficient production processes.

The company’s tools, like those used at the new NSTIC, support the transition of GaN / SiC devices from their research and prototyping stages through to pilot production and high-volume manufacturing. In turn, this ensures the technology can accommodate increasing global demand.

Image Credit: Oxford Instruments Plasma Technology

The company’s expertise in plasma etching, deposition, ALD, and ALE technologies is also key to enabling precise and scalable fabrication of semiconductor devices, with these tools proving essential in meeting the challenges in material interfaces and better tailoring material properties to high-performance application requirements.

Mr. Cheong Chee Hoo, Chairman of the NSTIC (GaN) Steering Committee, has stated that the NSTIC (GaN) is more than a facility. It’s a national platform for innovation and a catalyst for future technologies.

Strategic Goals and Developments

The partnership between NSTIC (GaN) and Oxford Instruments underscores Singapore’s commitment to remaining at the forefront of global semiconductor technology innovation, bringing societal and economic benefits and significant technological advances to Singapore.

Dignitaries visiting the National Semiconductor Translation and Innovation Centre for Gallium Nitride – NSTIC (GaN) facility. Image Credit: Oxford Instruments Plasma Technology

Global Leadership in Advanced Semiconductors

Focusing on pioneering GaN technology will enable Singapore to position itself as a global leader in semiconductor innovation, improving its competitiveness and strengthening its position in the global market.

Advancing GaN Technology

GaN and GaN-on-SiC semiconductors are key to the semiconductor industry’s future due to their advanced properties, including faster performance, higher energy efficiency, and reduced size versus traditional silicon-based solutions.

Collaborative Effort and an Improved R&D Ecosystem

The initiative will encourage collaboration among research institutions, industry partners, and government agencies to expedite the innovation, prototyping, and commercialization of GaN/SiC technologies.

Long-Term Goals

The NSTIC (GaN) is working to reinforce Singapore’s semiconductor ecosystem by driving R&D, fostering the development of local talent, and attracting global partnerships.

Economic Impact

Semiconductors continue to be a cornerstone of Singapore's economy, accounting for 6 % of GDP and supporting approximately 35,000 skilled jobs across design, R&D, and advanced manufacturing.

It is expected that the GaN Centre will contribute to the country's ongoing growth in high-value manufacturing and innovation in rapidly growing markets such as the automotive, telecommunications, and clean energy sectors.

New Job Opportunities

The initiative will create jobs in engineering, manufacturing, R&D, and other high-skill areas. This will also include workforce development programs to upskill local talent, ensuring that Singapore remains globally competitive in its semiconductor workforce.

Attracting Investment

The GaN Centre is expected to draw start-ups, multinational corporations, and research institutions to Singapore by fostering a strong research and development ecosystem. This will further strengthen the country’s status as a semiconductor hub.

Applications Across Industries

The superior efficiency, speed, and compact size of GaN/SiC technology will drive technological advancements across multiple sectors, enabling innovations in industries such as healthcare, clean energy, telecommunications, and automotive applications.

Enabling Greener Technologies

GaN / SiC semiconductors are extremely energy-efficient, meaning that they are ideally suited to use in electric vehicles, renewable energy applications, and power electronics. These capabilities align with Singapore's sustainability goals and worldwide efforts to lower carbon emissions.

Supporting a Low-Carbon Economy

Adopting GaN/SiC technology for energy-efficient applications will support industries’ efforts to reduce energy consumption, thereby furthering Singapore’s green transformation agenda.

Integration Into the Global Supply Chain

Singapore strengthens its role in the global semiconductor supply chain by advancing GaN / SiC technologies, helping to ensure the country’s resilience and leadership in a rapidly evolving industry.

Expanding Market Reach

The GaN Center initiative will allow Singapore-based companies to access high-growth global markets for GaN / SiC applications, including autonomous vehicles, 5G infrastructure, and advanced medical devices.

Summary

Oxford Instruments is proud to have undertaken a key role in this transformative project, which will deliver technological leadership, energy efficiency, economic growth, job creation, and sustainability benefits to Singapore.

text:
NJBIA has joined with the National Association of Manufacturers and a coalition of energy producers and aligned manufacturing and business organizations in support of a bipartisan permitting reform legislation that was recently introduced in the U.S. Senate.

Senate Bill 5653 aims to accelerate federal approvals for major energy, infrastructure, transmission, mining, and manufacturing projects by modernizing the federal permitting process. The goal is to address the regulatory gridlock that causes extensive delays and inflates project costs, driving up utility bills for businesses and consumers.

On Tuesday, the National Association of Manufacturers and over 100 business organizations, including NJBIA, signed a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) urging a speedy vote on the bill, also known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

“Our nation’s broken permitting system affects projects in every industry and of every energy source, directly contributing to the rising cost of electricity to homeowners and businesses,” the letter stated. “Right now, in the United States, it takes 80% longer to get a permit authorized for a manufacturing facility than it does in any other free market economy.”

Permitting reform will help to remove infrastructure barriers to investment, expansion, and job creation, wrote the trade organizations, which represent employers who collectively provide jobs for millions of U.S. workers.

“Permitting delays cost manufacturers at least $8 billion every year,” the letter said. “That’s money not being spent on hiring new workers, expanding shop floors, or going back into the local economy. Manufacturers are ready to build in America; we just need the certainty and a modernized permitting process to make it happen.”

To modernize the permitting process, the 417-page bill would amend multiple federal environmental statutes, including the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Clean Water Act (CWA), and the Endangered Species Act (ESA), by establishing strict, enforceable timelines for permit decisions and setting tighter deadlines for litigation challenging approvals.

The bill would also modernize and facilitate energy and electric-grid development to accelerate construction and investment in power generation.

text:
October 15, 2026 Dartmouth, Nova Scotia Natural Resources Canada

Canada’s east coast has some of the strongest winds in the world, and developing that natural advantage presents a transformative economic opportunity for Nova Scotia, Atlantic Canada, and our entire nation. As a source of clean, abundant energy, offshore wind can secure generational prosperity for the entire Atlantic region by making clean electricity a major new export for Nova Scotia, powering Canadian homes and businesses, securing major investment and creating thousands of jobs.

The Government of Canada will make sure we seize this opportunity. That is why today, the Honourable Tim Hodgson, Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, committed $100 million to advance offshore wind development in Nova Scotia. This will help secure the private investment needed to move projects like the province’s Wind West clean energy initiative from concept to development.

Referred to the federal Major Projects Office in September 2025, the Atlantic Energy Strategy focuses on leveraging on- and offshore wind, nuclear and hydro power across Atlantic Canada to build a stronger, more connected grid. Wind West, a Nova Scotia–led project to develop offshore wind farms and connect their electricity to customers, is a key component of this Strategy. Wind West aims to generate enough zero-emissions electricity to power Nova Scotia’s entire population and export additional power beyond Nova Scotia via new transmission infrastructure.

Before wind turbines can be built, companies need reliable information about the ocean and wind conditions. That is why $5 million of this $100-million commitment will go to the deployment of floating light detection and ranging (FLiDAR)–mounted buoys. By measuring offshore wind speeds and ocean conditions, these buoys will provide data to help proponents prepare for the upcoming project’s Call for Bids, which will be launched by the Canada–Nova Scotia Offshore Energy Regulator in winter 2027.

Natural Resources Canada is also providing nearly $3 million to Net Zero Atlantic to expand existing modelling to include the transmission of offshore wind power from Nova Scotia to Quebec, Ontario and beyond and conduct marine survey work to support transmission cable routing.

Today’s announcement builds on the Atlantic Economic Panel’s call to develop the region’s energy resources and strengthen electricity connections between provinces. Alongside the historic new Churchill Falls agreement, which represented the largest clean energy investment in North American history, it demonstrates the federal government’s commitment to unlocking Atlantic Canada’s potential as a clean energy superpower. Building out new clean electricity will bring economic prosperity, energy security, thousands of job opportunities, and a cleaner future to Canadians on the east coast and beyond.

Right now, 83% of energy projects stuck in the interconnection queue are clean energy projects.
Heinrich’s legislation will get those projects up and running to address rising demand, while creating greater certainty for energy projects approved and financed across presidential administrations by prohibiting any administration from improperly delaying or blocking clean energy projects without facing legal action or fines.
Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) Meets with Manufacturers to Discuss His Landmark Legislation that Will Create More Jobs and Spark a Manufacturing Renaissance in New Mexico, October 12, 2026.
text:
PHOTOS

ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. — This week, U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, met with New Mexicans to discuss his newly introduced Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, legislation that will lower utility bills, create good-paying jobs, and force data centers to fully pay for their grid upgrades, as well as their share of the existing grid — resulting in savings for New Mexico families.

Heinrich hosted a roundtable discussion with members of UA Local 412, LiUNA Local 16, Painters and Allied Trades District Council 36, and New Mexico Building and Construction Trades Council to underscore how his Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will create more high-quality jobs New Mexicans can build their families around, lower electricity bills, and require data centers to fully pay for the costs they create.

PHOTO: U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) Meets with New Mexicans to Discuss His Landmark Legislation to Create More Jobs, Lower Electricity Bills, and Require Data Centers to Fully Pay for Costs They Create, October 12, 2026.

“We want to build the jobs in New Mexico that you can build a family around, and that's what unions are all about. That's the way I grew up with my dad,” said Heinrich. “My Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is going to generate benefits for our skilled workers in the state of New Mexico for a very long time to come. This bill is about building the infrastructure and manufacturing capacity we need with union labor for the future of our country — and making sure that those jobs are right here in New Mexico.”

Heinrich hosted a second roundtable discussion with Pattern Energy, Grid United, Black Forest Partners, RioSol New Mexico, and NM Renewable Energy Industries Association to highlight how his Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will bring more energy projects online faster and lower utility bills for New Mexico families by speeding up the federal process for reviewing and approving energy projects. Right now, 83% of energy projects stuck in the interconnection queue are clean energy projects.

Heinrich’s legislation will get those projects up and running to address rising demand, while creating greater certainty for energy projects approved and financed across presidential administrations by prohibiting any administration from improperly delaying or blocking clean energy projects without facing legal action or fines.

PHOTO: U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) Hosts a Roundtable with Clean Energy Companies on How His Landmark Legislation Will Bring More Energy Projects Online Faster and Lower Utility Bills for New Mexico Families, October 12, 2026.

“Our whole premise as we approached this permitting bill was: How do we create a faster process, not lower the bar on standards,” said Heinrich. “My Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will help us create more certainty and predictability for projects permitted and financed across administrations – so that energy companies can get projects from idea to go, faster. That means more clean energy projects can get off the ground, more good-paying jobs, and more investments in New Mexico communities.”

Additionally, Heinrich joined a roundtable discussion hosted by ABB and the National Association of Manufacturers to highlight how his Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will create more jobs and spark a manufacturing renaissance in New Mexico and nationwide by creating a construction boom and increasing demand for American-made machinery and equipment.

PHOTO: U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) Meets with Manufacturers to Discuss His Landmark Legislation that Will Create More Jobs and Spark a Manufacturing Renaissance in New Mexico, October 12, 2026.

“We need permitting reform to put more electrons on the grid. It results in more jobs, and it's the one thing that can bring down the pressure on the cost of electricity and energy right now,” said Heinrich. “The folks at ABB make the components that really build out the grid across the country, and so they're supplying the individual components that connect from the grid, through the utility, to the neighborhood. The more of these projects move forward, the more demand there is for the things that they manufacture right here in Albuquerque, New Mexico.”

Kathleen OKeefe, Ringwood, NJ asks in a callout question: How will the rising interest rates affect an already challenging housing market?

double quotation markLauren: Interest rates have a direct impact on mortgage rates and other loans as it defines how much it costs to borrow money. At the beginning of the pandemic, the US Federal Reserve set interest rates to zero, bringing mortgage rates down to historic lows.This is why we saw a surge of activity in the housing market from 2020 to 2022. At the end of that period, the Fed started to bring interest rates up, bringing mortgage rates to the averages that we see today (over 7% for a 30-year mortgage). This has brought the housing market to a standstill, and even though interest rates are still lower than its most recent peak in 2023, mortgage rates haven’t really come down all that much. It was only this past February that the rate for a 30-year mortgage went below 6% for the first time since September 2022, and it’s only kept climbing.

This tends to mean that elections are decided by the floaters. Is there any indication of how these voters have been impacted by the first two years of Trump 2?

By April 2026, that support declined to 26%. A September 2026 YouGov survey found that 23% of independents approve of Trump, compared with 79% of Republicans and 2% of Democrats. A September poll conducted by Fox News found 73% saying Trump has made the economy worse, compared to 95% of Democrats and 26% of Republicans.

double quotation markGaya: Our polling with Harris earlier this summer captured the angst and frustration that rural American voters are feeling in today’s economy, often more so than their urban and suburban counterparts. Here’s what we found about rural voters :

- 70% say that the federal government has made the affordability crisis either significantly or somewhat worse in 2026

- 64% believe that the national economy is getting worse; 57% believe that their local economy is getting worse

- Nearly half believe that their financial security is getting worse

- 46% say they are just getting by, while 29% say they are struggling to make ends meet

Politicians say the US economy is growing - is it actually?

Clifford Weiler, San Diego, CA asks in a callout question: Politicians cite how the economy is improving, but how is the rising rate of inflation taken into account?

double quotation markLauren: What growth in the economy means really depends on who you’re talking to. For economists, economic growth is measured by gross domestic product (GDP), which is an equation adding together consumption, investment, government spending and net exports. A little inflation can actually stimulate further growth, as long as it doesn’t lead to a pullback in spending. That’s why the US Federal Reserve’s target inflation rate is 2% (something that hasn’t been seen since January 2021 – for context, it was 3.7% in September).

For both economists and politicians, inflation really only becomes a bad thing when it starts to impact consumer spending. When prices get too high and consumers start spending less money, the wheels of the economy can start to slow. Even though inflation has been high, and consumers are anxious about the economy, we haven’t yet seen a large pullback in spending that would cause alarm over growth.

double quotation markLauren continues: For many goods and services, economists actually think prices going down as a bad thing for the overall economy that can trigger a downtown. There are some major exceptions, energy prices being a big one. If the US and Iran ever reach a peace deal, and oil transportation and reduction goes back to normal, gas prices will go down. This is what we saw in 2022, once the energy market recalibrated for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. After high periods of inflation, certain food prices can also go down. The cost of eggs is about 20% lower than they were a year ago, when prices were high because of avian-flu related shortages.

For both economists and politicians, inflation really only becomes a bad thing when it starts to impact consumer spending. When prices get too high and consumers start spending less money, the wheels of the economy can start to slow. text:
(Washington, DC) - On Tuesday, Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren (D-CA) sent a letter to Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin demanding that he comply with outstanding congressional oversight requests from the Committee.

“Since January 2025, I have sent a number of formal oversight letters to EPA requesting agency records, documents, and communications regarding various policies and activities,” writes Ranking Member Lofgren in her letter. “However, rather than providing the requested information in a comprehensive and timely manner, EPA has failed to produce a single responsive document, communication, or record.”

In closing, she writes: “EPA’s non-responsiveness to Committee oversight during the 119th Congress has been unacceptable. The agency must respect congressional prerogatives. We remain determined to obtain the information we need to perform our duties on behalf of the American people. EPA should understand that a lack of cooperation will not frustrate the Committee’s oversight permanently. It will merely strengthen our commitment to employing all the tools at our disposal to hold the agency accountable.”

In her letter, Ranking Member Lofgren requires a response from EPA to the Committee’s outstanding oversight requests by no later than 5:00 pm Friday, November 6th, 2026.

Access the letter here and below.

Dear Administrator Zeldin,

Agencies are required to comply with congressional oversight. It is an obligation, not a choice. But under your leadership, the EPA appears to have forgotten that basic principle. Since President Trump took office in January 2025, I have made multiple requests to the agency for internal records, documents, and communications related to various topics. These oversight requests are crucial to my ability to properly carry out my oversight duties as the Ranking Member of the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, which possesses jurisdiction over environmental research and development programs at EPA. However, rather than providing the requested information in a comprehensive and timely manner, EPA has failed to produce a single responsive document, communication, or record. Instead, the agency has merely responded with letters that deflect questions rather than answering them. That was never acceptable. It becomes less tolerable with each passing month. I am writing to you to reaffirm my prior oversight requests from the 119th Congress, and to formally notify the agency that they remain outstanding. I expect EPA to promptly comply.

Since your confirmation as the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) on January 29th, 2025, roughly 20% of the agency’s workforce has quit, retired, or been fired. Irreplaceable laboratory facilities have been shut down. The independent Office of Research and Development (ORD) has been wiped out. Scientific capacity has been gutted, scientific integrity is compromised, industry capture is widespread, and climate denialism is ascendant. In short, EPA’s basic mission to use the best available science to protect human health and the environment has been damaged under your leadership.

To take just one of countless examples, I have learned that the Office of Air and Radiation (OAR), acting under direct orders from former Assistant Administrator Aaron Szabo, has refused to grant the Office of Applied Sciences and Environmental Solutions (OASES) permission to conduct or publish virtually any air pollution research without prior approval from OAR political leadership. OASES is the ostensible successor to ORD, which was a global scientific leader in air quality and air pollution research. It is my understanding that OAR has categorically denied OASES the authority to conduct and publish its own air-related research without OAR political approval, except for narrow circumstances in which technical support from OASES cannot be avoided for OAR to meet certain statutory obligations. Indeed, OASES cannot even independently initiate air-related research without approval from OAR political appointees. OAR can only assert this control because of the agency’s new “no surprises” policy for OASES, which appallingly requires that OASES research “must be supported by appropriate political leadership” before it can proceed. The policy is a clear violation of scientific integrity, and the notion that EPA’s primary science office cannot even study air pollution without getting permission from the political appointees of a different office would be laughable if it was not so dangerous.

In my role as the Ranking Member of the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology (“the Committee”), I have attempted to conduct oversight of these types of actions. There are many reasons for this oversight: to document the damage done to the agency and its workforce; to understand the scientific capabilities that have been lost and the implications of those losses for human health and the American people; to identify violations of scientific integrity and administrative procedure; and to comprehend why all of this happened in order to inform legislative efforts to reverse it and prevent it from ever happening again. Since January 2025, I have sent a number of formal oversight letters to EPA requesting agency records, documents, and communications regarding various policies and activities. The agency has been non-responsive to my requests and has utterly failed to comply. I am now reaffirming these oversight requests to provide the agency with a second opportunity to demonstrate the appropriate degree of deference and respect for congressional prerogatives. I expect EPA’s full and prompt responsiveness to each of the requests detailed below, which are long overdue:

1. Agency RIF and Reorganization Plans (ARRPs)

On March 26th, 2025, I sent a letter to EPA along with several other Democratic Committee Members requesting that the agency “provide the Committee with your Agency RIF and Reorganization Plan immediately upon transmitting it to OMB and the Office of Personnel Management (OPM).” The context for this request was the revelation that EPA’s ARRP proposed to “eliminate the Office of Research and Development as an EPA National Program Office” while pushing “a majority (50-75%)” of ORD’s employees out of the agency. Of course, that is exactly what happened. But EPA never provided its Phase One and Phase Two ARRPs to the Committee, which has hindered the Committee’s ability to understand the motivations and decisions that led to the elimination of ORD. For instance, information revealed last year in a lawsuit related to agency ARRPs appeared to suggest that disagreements may have existed between EPA and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) regarding the elimination of ORD. Without reviewing the ARRPs themselves, the Committee cannot properly assess the agency’s position towards ORD and the bureaucratic actions that contributed to its demise.

2. Laboratory Budget and Staffing Levels

On May 27th, 2025, I sent a letter to EPA along with Environment Subcommittee Ranking Member Gabe Amo requesting that the agency “share the projected post-reorganization budget and staffing levels for each of the facilities that will remain open.” The “facilities” in this case referred specifically to the ten field laboratory and research facilities managed by ORD. These research laboratories are a crown jewel of EPA science, and the agency’s intention to eliminate ORD had raised the alarming prospect that the laboratories might be shut down as well. EPA has not subsequently acted to do so, and the laboratories appear to be continuing under the management of different program offices. But while I am relieved that they continue to operate, I remain concerned that staffing shortages and reduced scientific capabilities at the former ORD laboratories could undermine their ability to appropriately study environmental hazards. EPA’s unwillingness to provide basic budgetary and personnel information for its research laboratories impedes the Committee’s ability to evaluate whether they remain capable of supporting core agency activities.

3. Endangerment Finding Repeal Documents and Communications

On August 18th, 2025, I sent a letter to EPA along with Environment Subcommittee Ranking Member Amo requesting that the agency provide “all documents and communications” exchanged between EPA and OMB, the Department of Energy (DOE), and the Trump Vance 2025 Transition Team, regarding “the repeal of the Endangerment Finding.” I also requested “all documents and communications” exchanged between EPA and DOE regarding the report developed by DOE’s Climate Working Group, and “all documents and communications” within EPA regarding “the agency’s review of the scientific basis for the proposal to repeal the Endangerment Finding.” These oversight requests relate to the repeal of the 2009 Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding, which the agency proposed in July 2025 and finalized in February 2026. I continue to have concerns about potential violations of administrative law in the agency’s rulemaking process to repeal the Endangerment Finding. The documents and communications that I requested are central to the Committee’s ability to conduct oversight of the agency’s actions. EPA’s refusal to provide them only strengthens my belief that these records remain highly material to my review and must be disclosed without delay.

4. Status of PFNA IRIS Assessment

Dr. Maureen Gwinn, the EPA Deputy Associate Administrator for Science, testified before the Science Committee’s Subcommittee on Environment on June 4th, 2026. The subject of her testimony was OASES and the general status of environmental research and development at the agency after the elimination of ORD. During that hearing, I questioned Dr. Gwinn about the agency’s decision earlier in 2026 to disavow chemical assessments conducted by the Integrated Risk Information System (IRIS). In particular, I asked about the status of the IRIS assessment for PFNA, which press reports indicate has been fully completed for more than a year but which the agency refuses to finalize and publish. In response, Dr. Gwinn told me that she was “not sure of the details on that” and said that she would “have to get back to you.” She also stated that she would “go back and confirm” the status of the PFNA assessment. While that hearing took place over four months ago, the agency has not provided any subsequent information regarding the PFNA assessment and whether it ever intends to finalize and publish the assessment, nor has it offered any scientific justification for refusing to do so. I continue to seek clarity on whether the IRIS assessment for PFNA, a dangerous and highly toxic PFAS chemical, will ever see the light of day under this administration.

5. Administration Delays of Environmental Research

At the same June 4th Environment Subcommittee hearing with Dr. Gwinn, one of my colleagues, Representative Suzanne Bonamici, questioned Dr. Gwinn about whether the agency under its current leadership had sought to delay or suppress any environmental research due to its perceived lack of alignment with administration priorities. Specifically, Representative Bonamici asked whether “any proposed research products, even one, [had] been delayed, modified, or declined because they did not align with the priorities set by political appointees?” In response, Dr. Gwinn acknowledged that “there have been delays” due to the agency’s review of whether certain research products complied with President Trump’s various Executive Orders. But when Representative Bonamici followed up and directly asked “what was the topic of the research,” pertaining to research that had been halted, Dr. Gwinn could only respond that she would “have to get back to you on that.” The agency has not provided any further information regarding which specific research topics were “delayed, modified, or declined” due to the political directives of agency leadership. This information is highly material to the Committee’s ability to understand the current state of scientific integrity at EPA, as well as the role played by political appointees in influencing the environmental research being conducted by the agency.

In summary, the following oversight requests remain outstanding and require compliance on the part of the agency. Please produce the requested records no later than 5:00 PM on Friday, November 6th, 2026:

1. Please provide to the Committee the EPA’s Agency RIF and Reorganization Plans (ARRPs) transmitted to OMB and OPM pursuant to OMB Director Russ Vought’s February 2025 memo.

2. Please provide to the Committee the post-reorganization budget and staffing levels for each of the agency’s field laboratory and research facilities that remain open.

3. Please provide to the Committee all documents and communications (including, but not limited to, emails, text messages, instant messages, comments, notes, analyses, legal and other memoranda, letters, telephone logs, Signal messages, meeting minutes, calendar entries, PowerPoint slides, and presentation materials) exchanged between EPA and OMB regarding the repeal of the Endangerment Finding.

4. Please provide to the Committee all documents and communications (including, but not limited to, emails, text messages, instant messages, comments, notes, analyses, legal and other memoranda, letters, telephone logs, Signal messages, meeting minutes, calendar entries, PowerPoint slides, and presentation materials) exchanged between EPA and DOE regarding the repeal of the Endangerment Finding.

5. Please provide to the Committee all documents and communications (including, but not limited to, emails, text messages, instant messages, comments, notes, analyses, legal and other memoranda, letters, telephone logs, Signal messages, meeting minutes, calendar entries, PowerPoint slides, and presentation materials) exchanged between EPA and the Trump Vance 2025 Transition Team regarding the repeal of the Endangerment Finding.

6. Please provide to the Committee all documents and communications (including, but not limited to, emails, text messages, instant messages, comments, notes, analyses, legal and other memoranda, letters, telephone logs, Signal messages, meeting minutes, calendar entries, PowerPoint slides, and presentation materials) exchanged between EPA and DOE regarding the report titled, “A Critical Review of Impacts of Greenhouse Gas Emissions on the U.S. Climate.”

7. Please provide to the Committee all documents and communications (including, but not limited to, emails, text messages, instant messages, comments, notes, analyses, legal and other memoranda, letters, telephone logs, Signal messages, meeting minutes, calendar entries, PowerPoint slides, and presentation materials) within EPA regarding the agency’s review of the scientific basis for the proposal to repeal the Endangerment Finding.

8. Please provide to the Committee a written update regarding the status of the IRIS assessment for PFNA, including whether any scientific work remains ongoing for the assessment and the date by which the agency intends to finalize and publish the assessment.

9. Please provide to the Committee a list of all research products that have been delayed, modified, or declined since January 20th, 2025, due to the agency’s review or conclusions regarding the alignment of scientific research with administration priorities, including the topics of the research products.

EPA’s non-responsiveness to Committee oversight during the 119th Congress has been unacceptable. The agency must respect congressional prerogatives. We remain determined to obtain the information we need to perform our duties on behalf of the American people. EPA should understand that a lack of cooperation will not frustrate the Committee’s oversight permanently. It will merely strengthen our commitment to employing all the tools at our disposal to hold the agency accountable.

Pursuant to Rule X of the House of Representatives, the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology “shall review and study on a continuing basis laws, programs, and Government activities relating to nonmilitary research and development.” The Committee possesses jurisdiction over environmental research and development.

text:
EPA adopted new policy in response to lobbying from data center companies and in furtherance of Trump’s data center-over-people agenda

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works (EPW), and Representative Jennifer McClellan (D-VA-04), last month launched a bicameral investigation into the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) guidance exempting data center power plants from the Acid Rain Program (ARP).

By EPA’s own admission, the decision to issue new guidance came at the behest of data center companies. And according to the EPA press release issuing the new guidance, the agency took this action to “further President Trump’s agenda promoting data centers.”

“EPA’s new ARP guidance is a handout to the richest and most powerful companies in the world. And this handout comes at the expense of Americans’ health and the safety of our ecosystems and communities that were, prior to the inception of the ARP, regularly drenched in dangerous acidic rainfall,” the lawmakers wrote in their letter to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin.

The ARP regulates the emission of sulfur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOx) from power plants. SO2 and NOx are both harmful to human health, damaging the respiratory system and worsening heart disease. They are also linked to adverse pregnancy and birth outcomes, kidney damage, autoimmune disorders, and cancer.

The pollutants are also the primary causes of acid rain. Prior to the ARP, acid rain poisoned rivers, lakes, and streams; damaged forests; killed and sickened aquatic animals; and corroded buildings, monuments, and statues.

“EPA explicitly bills its new guidance as a means to facilitate data center development. In so doing, EPA misapprehends its own mission, which is to ‘protect human health and the environment,’ as stated in black and white on the agency’s own website,” continued the lawmakers.

“Bizarrely, under EPA’s new guidance, massive new gas-fired power plants large enough to power cities would be exempt from NOx and SO2 caps under the ARP only as long as they do not serve the public electricity grid and instead exclusively power a privately-owned data center. This is a perverse outcome, and it is contrary to Congress’s design for the Clean Air Act, which creates specific and comprehensive regulatory requirements for significant pollution sources like these,” added the lawmakers.

The lawmakers, together with Senators Ed Markey (D-MA) and Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), requested answers from EPA by October 7th about the agency’s decision-making process while crafting this new guidance, as well as any information regarding the agency’s communications with data center companies. Senators Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Cory Booker (D-NJ), and 24 Members of the House of Representatives also signed the letter. EPA has not yet responded to the lawmakers’ letter.

Ranking Member Whitehouse also requested information and documents from the following companies by October 7th: Meta, Microsoft, Google, OpenAI, xAI, Amazon Web Services, Anthropic, Fermi America, and Joule.

In March 2026, Ranking Member Whitehouse, Senator Van Hollen, and Senator Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, launched an investigation into eight technology and related companies, including Meta, xAI, and OpenAI, regarding twelve planned data center projects that would be powered by massive new gas plants. The gas plants—many of which are ten or more times the size of the average gas plant currently powering the U.S. electric grid—would emit millions of tons of greenhouse gases and tens of thousands of tons of health-harming pollutants every year.

title: Utilities can use AI to solve grid backlogs: AWS energy lead | Utility Dive
description:
With energy demand projected to grow more than 50% by 2050, utilities are under growing pressure to keep up.
New AI-powered grid tools can help shorten the time to approval by completing these studies in hours instead of months.
Utilities that have invested in AI grid tools are already seeing results.
This summer, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission brought together utilities, tech companies, government agencies and others to discuss how AI can speed up grid planning.
The utilities moving first on AI-powered grid planning are delivering real results — faster approvals, fewer outages and lower costs.
text:
Joseph Santamaria is general manager of energy and utilities at Amazon Web Services.

The U.S. economy is facing a looming shortage of electricity on the grid. With energy demand projected to grow more than 50% by 2050, utilities are under growing pressure to keep up.

The problem isn’t a lack of new energy projects. In the United States, more than 2,000 GW of potential power projects are waiting to be reviewed — enough to power every home in the country more than twice over. The challenge is bringing those projects from planning to execution.

Before utilities can bring new sources online, they must complete interconnection studies. These technical reviews determine how and where new power sources can safely plug into the existing grid. Each study takes months to complete, and projects can wait years just to reach the front of the line. In the early 2000s, the average project waited about two years. Today, surging power demand has more than doubled the wait to five years and counting.

New AI-powered grid tools can help shorten the time to approval by completing these studies in hours instead of months. With power demand growing rapidly, using new technology to speed up the approval process is critical to fueling economic growth, meeting demand from essential industries, and keeping electricity affordable and reliable for everyone.

Where a traditional study might test a handful of what-if scenarios one at a time, AI tools can model thousands of them at once by testing how new projects interact with the existing grid, including its power lines, substations and generators, across multiple scenarios. These systems run thousands of simulations to generate recommendations while human engineers make the final decision. With machines performing the legwork, operators can evaluate new projects much more quickly.

Utilities that have invested in AI grid tools are already seeing results.

Duke Energy, the largest utility in the country, has used AI-powered grid planning to reduce study time while doubling the number of projects evaluated in a year.

On the West Coast, Pacific Gas & Electric pulled together data from more than 80 sources across 20 different systems into a single planning tool, helping prioritize more than 17,000 upgrades across the grid. The program cut costs by 20% within a $100 million pilot program and eliminated millions of customer outage minutes.

Regulators are paying attention, too. This summer, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission brought together utilities, tech companies, government agencies and others to discuss how AI can speed up grid planning. It’s a clear sign that regulators see AI as a potential solution to grid backlog.

The urgency is clear. Increased demand from across the electric grid, from electrification to renewable energy projects to AI data centers, is adding pressure to an already backlogged system. Critics have raised questions about whether new facilities will drive up costs for existing customers or worsen the approval bottleneck.

The answer depends on how these projects are structured. When large energy users cover the cost of new infrastructure and utilities use modern planning tools, everyone benefits. In Indiana, an agreement between Amazon and Northern Indiana Public Service Co. is expected to deliver approximately $1 billion in savings to existing customers over 15 years, with Amazon covering all costs associated with building new data centers. Research from the Electric Power Research Institute confirms that with the right planning and pricing rules, new demand can help keep electricity prices in check.

These deals work best when utilities can evaluate and approve projects quickly enough to meet demand. That’s where AI becomes a key player not just as a driver of new demand, but as the tool that makes it possible to bring new power demand onto the grid while shortening the time that everyone waits in line.

The utilities moving first on AI-powered grid planning are delivering real results — faster approvals, fewer outages and lower costs. For the communities where this new energy infrastructure is being built, that means reliable power and stable electric bills. The longer utilities stick with outdated planning processes, the longer families and businesses wait for the energy they need.

text:
A child relying on a home ventilator. A northern Michigan restaurant gearing up for the dinner rush. A family’s refrigerator keeping a week of groceries fresh. A neighbor staying comfortable through a summer heat wave.

These are the everyday moments Michigan’s grid is built to protect, and why continued investment matters.

The case for investment

Electricity powers nearly every part of modern life. When the grid fails, whether for minutes or days, the consequences ripple quickly: spoiled food and medications, disrupted services, lost productivity and real safety risks for vulnerable populations. During the 2025 northern Michigan ice storm, businesses across the region lost an estimated $6.2 million in revenue from closures alone.

That’s why Michigan’s utilities have been making significant, measurable investments to strengthen the grid, and why those investments are beginning to show results.

Michigan is leading the nation in reliability improvement

According to the Michigan Public Service Commission’s 2025 annual report and federal energy data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Michigan leads the nation in power reliability improvement since 2019. Total outage times dropped 88.5 minutes from 2019 to 2024, the greatest weather-adjusted improvement of any state in the country.

That progress didn’t happen by accident. Across Michigan’s utilities:

DTE Energy installed nearly 700 smart devices in 2025, rebuilding key sections of the grid and trimming nearly 6,600 miles of trees.

Smart grid technology prevented more than 16,000 outages at DTE in 2025 alone.

Consumers Energy completed nearly 2,700 low and high-voltage reliability improvement projects and restored power to nearly 90% of customers within 24 hours of major events.

These aren’t marketing statistics. They’re tracked, verified and reported to state and federal regulators.

Deferring investment is more expensive, not less

The conversation about grid investment often gets framed as a cost question: upgrades carry expenses, and those expenses can show up in rates over time. That’s true. But the alternative has costs as well. They just show up differently.

Aging infrastructure fails more often and more severely. Emergency repairs after major outages cost far more than planned maintenance. Prolonged outages damage businesses, spoil groceries and impose indirect costs on communities that are difficult to calculate in real time. The most expensive energy decision a state can make is to defer necessary investment and absorb the consequences later.

Michigan’s approach takes the long view: modernize the grid, expand automation and strengthen infrastructure against the weather extremes Michigan increasingly faces, from ice storms and derechos to summer thunderstorm systems that roll off Lake Michigan with serious force.

Affordability and reliability aren’t opposites

Families facing stretched budgets deserve honesty about both sides of this equation. Michigan’s home electric bills already rank 15th-lowest nationally, at $23 below the U.S. average, $16 below Ohio and $13 below Indiana, according to the Michigan Public Service Commission. And since 2021, Michigan’s electric bill increases have totaled just 7.8% compared to a national average of 25.5%.

Keeping bills affordable over the long term requires a grid that doesn’t fail. Powering Michigan Forward, the campaign behind PoweringMIForward.org, exists to connect those dots. The goal is a Michigan energy system that is affordable, reliable and built for the decades ahead. That balance isn’t achieved by avoiding investment. It’s achieved by making smart, regulated investments that deliver real results.
