text:
Here is how the Democratic Senate candidates are campaigning on climate and energy issues in competitive states this year, and their stance on the Green New Deal.

GEORGIA

Jon Ossoff

Campaign priorities: Sen. Jon Ossoff’s (D-GA) reelection campaign has focused on energy affordability.

He has said that rising electricity and other household costs have been a concern for those in Georgia. Ossoff has also focused on ensuring that the growth of data centers does not raise energy costs for households.

“Groceries, rent, power, a meal out at a restaurant, all of these things hit their all-time record high this year,” Ossoff said in April. “The power bill is skyrocketing. We’re in the middle right now of a global energy crisis.”

Does he support the Green New Deal? Ossoff opposed the Green New Deal in 2020.

However, he has expressed concerns about the impact of climate change. In 2021, Ossoff spoke in favor of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, which contained some clean energy provisions, stating that “we’re making a national decision about the future of our planet and the future of our society.”

Ossoff last year also pressed Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin for canceling public health and environmental grants.

NORTH CAROLINA

Roy Cooper

Campaign priorities: Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper’s priorities, as listed on his website, are lowering costs related to household utilities, energy, and groceries.

He has previously called for limiting carbon emissions.

In 2024, Cooper spoke at the New York Times Climate Forward conference, where he noted that “most everyday people understand that we need to move to renewable clean energy, we need to take steps to become more sustainable, energy efficient. And we need to have leaders who will do that.”

Cooper said at the conference that climate change isn’t necessarily the top issue for candidates, but environmental groups know which candidates will help in the fight against climate change.

“You have to meet people where they are, and not change your message. But you only have so much time in order to try to communicate with people,” Cooper said.

Does he support the Green New Deal? He has not endorsed the Green New Deal.

Cooper has been a strong proponent of measures to limit climate change in the past, but has not vocally supported the Green New Deal.

His opponent, Republican Michael Whatley, has recently tried to connect Cooper with the Green New Deal, stating that “Roy Cooper has always been a fan of the Green New Deal and the policies that Joe Biden put in place.”

A campaign spokesperson for Cooper told the Duke Chronicle that Whatley’s claim was “false.”

ALASKA

Mary Peltola

Campaign priorities: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s energy priorities have focused on lowering electricity and fuel prices, including by expanding oil and gas production in the state. Peltola, as stated on her website, said she would also work to restore federal tax credits for solar, wind, and hydropower projects.

Peltola has also promised to expand the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, which help low-income households pay for their energy bills.

Does she support the Green New Deal? Peltola has not endorsed the Green New Deal but has drawn attacks from Republicans for receiving endorsements from high-profile Democrats who back it, such as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA), who introduced the initiative in 2019.

Peltola’s campaign rejected the idea that endorsements define her candidacy.

“Mary’s record is clear: She will always put Alaska First, and no one from the Lower 48 will ever tell her how to vote or how to think,” a campaign spokesperson told the Washington Examiner in a statement.

“That’s why she took on her own party to secure the Willow project [an oil drilling project] after years of delays, and why she has been a strong advocate of the Alaska LNG pipeline project,” the spokesperson added.

Peltola has also said she “likes the concepts” contained in the Green New Deal framework, even as she argues oil and gas will remain central to Alaska’s future.

IOWA

Josh Turek

Campaign priorities: Iowa Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek has campaigned on energy affordability, focusing on the cost of living for families and farmers.

“The thing I hear the most, ‘I am struggling to keep food on the table, a roof over my head, pay my electric bill; and now with this stupid war in Iran, struggling just to keep gas in my tank,’” Turek said at a tailgate at Iowa State University.

Turek has supported the state’s wind and solar energy resources. He has also supported expanding renewable fuels, visiting ethanol plants and calling for higher blends of ethanol in gasoline year-round.

Does he support the Green New Deal? He has not endorsed or campaigned on the Green New Deal.

Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-IA), the GOP candidate in Iowa, has accused Turek of supporting climate and environmental policies that harm farmers.

Earlier this year, Turek hosted a roundtable with Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) to talk to farmers, business owners, and homeowners about how climate change has affected insurance prices. Turek noted that Iowa has seen significant increases in insurance rates because of extreme weather events.

MAINE

Troy Jackson

Campaign priorities: Senate Democratic candidate Troy Jackson has made heating and energy costs a focal point of his campaign. Maine has seen record-high heating oil prices. Jackson supports expanding the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, which helps certain homeowners and renters with energy costs.

Jackson worked as a state senator, including as Senate president from 2018 to 2024. He also worked as a logger and has sponsored a bill to ban aerial spraying of glyphosate, which is used by logging companies and some large landowners.

He also sponsored several unsuccessful bond measures and other bills that supported research into the use of woody biomass. Jackson led the effort to pass legislation in 2021 to build onshore wind power in Aroostook County and a transmission line to carry the power south to Maine and New England.

Does he support the Green New Deal? He has not endorsed or campaigned on the Green New Deal.

Jackson received a lifetime score of 81% for his legislative tenure from the green group Maine Conservation Voters.

NEW HAMPSHIRE

Chris Pappas

Campaign priorities: Rep. Chris Pappas (D-NH) has focused on energy affordability but as a lawmaker and candidate continues to push for environmental protections and clean energy.

On his website, one of his priorities is listed as “Lowering Energy Costs and Protecting the Environment.” He says he is supporting an all-of-the-above energy strategy.

But he also noted that he aims to protect the environment and “address the existential threat of climate change” by investing in clean energy solutions.

Does he support the Green New Deal? In 2018, he supported to create a select committee to examine the Green New Deal.

As a congressman, he has supported legislation like the Inflation Reduction Act, which was signed into law in August 2022. It was deemed Biden’s signature climate law, providing hundreds of billions of dollars for tax credits and programs to bolster the clean energy sector (much of that funding was repealed by the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act). He also supported the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law.

Pappas has also supported strict limits on perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, which are synthetic chemicals found in a range of consumer products, including clothing, shampoo, electronics, and cleaning products. PFAS have been referred to as “forever chemicals.”

Pappas received a 97% lifetime score on the League of Conservation Voters for his legislative record. He was also endorsed by the green group the Sierra Club.

OHIO

Sherrod Brown

Campaign priorities: Former Sen. Sherrod Brown has focused on lowering electricity bills and has sought to hold utility companies accountable for high prices.

“Our utility bills are higher than ever because no one is holding the utility companies accountable,” Brown wrote on X last month. “It’s time we cap how much these companies can increase electricity rates and lower costs for working families.”

Does he support the Green New Deal? In 2019, Brown decided not to sign on as co-sponsor of the Green New Deal. But, at the time, he said he did support “aggressively addressing climate change.”

As a senator, he voted for the Inflation Reduction Act, but in 2024, he began to take positions contrary to Democrats’ agenda on matters like electric vehicles and power plant regulations. His efforts to distance himself from the Biden administration came as he ran for reelection. He lost that race, but is now seeking to return to the Senate.

TEXAS

James Talarico

Campaign priorities: Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico supports an all-of-the-above energy agenda but has noted the importance of combating climate change.

According to his website, one of Talarico’s priorities is to reinstate federal tax credits for clean energy. He also wants to streamline permitting processes for energy projects and make gas more affordable.

Talarico has called for the expansion of LIHEAP to help low-income households afford their utility bills. He also supports expanding the Department of Energy’s Weatherization Assistance Program and eligibility for FEMA’s Pre-Disaster Mitigation Program.

He also wants to dedicate greater federal resources to strengthening the grid.

Does he support the Green New Deal? He has not endorsed or campaigned on the Green New Deal.

In 2021, while serving as a state lawmaker, he authored the Texas Climate Action Act, which aimed to reduce the state’s emissions by 90% by 2050.

In an interview with CBS News, Talarico was asked about the bill and whether it could have hurt Texas’s oil and gas industry.

“I support our oil and gas industry. I had family members who worked in the industry. I went to public schools here in Texas, funded by the oil and gas industry,” Talarico said. “What I’m opposing is greenhouse emissions. There are ways that we can support our oil and gas industry while limiting those emissions.”

“In fact, ExxonMobil has been a leader in carbon capture, ensuring that our oil and gas industry can continue to grow while capturing these harmful emissions so we can both grow our Texas energy industry and protect our planet,” he added.

MICHIGAN

Abdul el Sayed

Campaign priorities: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul el Sayed has been campaigning on energy and environmental priorities.

Like many other Democratic candidates, el Sayed has focused on the high energy costs that many people are facing. According to his website, el Sayed said he will focus on a pathway to 100% renewable energy, including massive investments in solar, wind, battery storage, and modernizing the grid.

El Sayed has also promised to ensure that households in Michigan have access to clean water. He said he will look to accelerate federal infrastructure funding to remove every lead pipe in the state’s water system by 2030.

He also plans to hold polluters accountable for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances contamination, also known as “forever chemicals.”

Does he support the Green New Deal? He has previously backed the Green New Deal, but has since distanced himself from the initiative.

While serving as a public health official, el Sayed wrote a 2019 op-ed strongly supporting the Green New Deal, arguing that reducing greenhouse gas emissions will help improve public health.

El Sayed in August joined Fox News, where he faced the assertion that he wants to phase out internal combustion car engines due to his past support for the Green New Deal.

“Look, I’m not going to defend the Green New Deal,” el Sayed said.

Green groups like Clean Water Action and the Sierra Club have endorsed el Sayed.

MINNESOTA

Peggy Flanagan

Campaign priorities: Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D-MN) has focused her campaign on energy affordability, emphasizing the cost of gas and food.

“It took 216 days for Michele Tafoya [her opponent] to say that the war in Iran was wrong,” Flanagan told CBS News. “Up until that point she had been lockstep with Donald Trump, and in particular when asked about the high cost of fuel and diesel prices, she said people should keep a stiff upper lip and take one less trip to Starbucks. That is not an economic plan.”

Does she support the Green New Deal? Flanagan has not endorsed or campaigned on the Green New Deal.

As lieutenant governor, Flanagan has supported the One Minnesota Path to Clean Energy, a set of policies to help Minnesota reach 100% renewable energy by 2050.

She has opposed the Trump administration’s rollback of clean energy. Flanagan also promised to protect Minnesota’s water from pollution.

KANSAS

Adam Hamilton

Campaign priorities: Adam Hamilton has centered his campaign on energy costs.

Hamilton’s website reads: “Congress has failed to act to bring costs down for Kansas families, and the White House has made things worse. We need a comprehensive, all of the above strategy that creates jobs and increases energy independence while bringing down costs for consumers today.”

He said he plans to restore tax credits for clean energy. Hamilton has also said he would require competitive bidding processes for transmission projects.

Does he support the Green New Deal? Hamilton told the Washington Examiner in a statement that he does not support the Green New Deal. He noted that he supports all-of-the-above energy policy.

“As I travel across Kansas, I hear from voters of all political stripes who are frustrated with their sitting Senator for not being focused on the issues impacting them, whether it’s the war in Iran driving up fuel costs and crushing farmers, the tariffs are making life more expensive, or the federal cuts to healthcare leaving 1 in 50 Kansans without the care they had a year and half ago,” he said.

“[Roger] Marshall supports every single one of these policies. As Kansas’s next senator, I will listen to Kansans and fight for lower costs and expanded access to healthcare,” he added.

LIST: WHERE ALL THE CANDIDATES IN COMPETITIVE SENATE RACES STAND ON DATA CENTERS

NEBRASKA

Dan Osborn

Campaign priorities: Independent Senate candidate Dan Osborn has focused his campaign on energy affordability.

Osborn has promised to focus on “energy independence,” which includes prioritizing nuclear, wind, and solar energy to lower fuel and electricity costs in Nebraska.

Osborn, who is a Navy veteran, would also push to end the war in Iran, which has increased global energy prices.

He has also promised to ensure that Nebraskans have clean air, water, and land.

Does he support the Green New Deal? He has not endorsed the Green New Deal or developed much of a climate platform.

SOUTH CAROLINA

Annie Andrews

Campaign priorities: South Carolina Senate Democratic candidate Annie Andrews has focused her campaign on energy affordability.

At the end of August, she launched the “Gas, Grits, and Groceries Tour,” where she traveled across the state to unveil her plans to tackle affordability issues.

As part of that plan, she would prioritize ending the Trump administration’s sweeping tariffs, suspending the gas tax, stopping the war in Iran, and supporting the clean energy transition.

text:
TerraPower's in-house report for the third quarter of 2025 showed $160,000 in lobbying expenditures.

In the second quarter of 2026, Venture Government Strategies LLC and Kountoupes Denham Carr & Reid LLC each filed at $80,000, bringing that quarter's client total to $360,000.

The filing names one lobbyist: Andrew Richards, TerraPower's vice president of government affairs, with no prior congressional staff experience on record.

Broader Context

The IIJA includes funding for nuclear energy infrastructure and advanced reactor programs.

The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) creates a tax credit for qualifying zero-emission nuclear electricity produced and sold.

The filing lists implementation of S. 870, which it describes as the Fire Grants and Safety Act of 2023, while the bill record is titled the Native ELDER Act.

The filing lists implementation of H.R. 1042, the Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act.

The filing also covers fiscal 2026 appropriations and identifies the One Big Beautiful Act as H.R. 1.

In March 2026, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approved TerraPower's construction permit for the Kemmerer Power Station. Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-WY) called reliable baseload power key to energy independence.

On May 15, Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) and Lummis, along with Rep. Byron Donalds (R-FL-19), introduced the Build Nuclear with Local Materials Act, which would direct the NRC to allow commercial-grade concrete and steel in non-safety structures of nuclear plants. Lummis's release cited the NRC's precedent set for TerraPower's Natrium reactor as the basis for the bill; supporters including Americans for Prosperity, the Breakthrough Institute, and C3 Solutions Action backed it as a way to reduce construction costs without compromising safety.

At a May 20 Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) subcommittee hearing on nuclear legislation, Lummis cited TerraPower's Kemmerer project as a model for the RECHARGE Act discussion draft and stressed the need to build domestic uranium conversion and enrichment capacity ahead of the 2028 end of Russian uranium import reliance.

The Bottom Line

TerraPower's in-house spend has held steady across the first three quarters of 2026, while the outside-firm roster contracted from the multi-firm structure seen through 2025.

“Energy storage has become so mature now that it’s acceptable for a CFO or a board to approve it,” he said.

text:
More building owners appear to see the value of on-site energy as the technology and cost for power generation and storage has improved, says an attorney who works at the crossroads of energy and real estate.

“I’ve seen more [of these projects] in the last few years,” David Streier, a shareholder at Fredrikson & Byron, said in an interview.

The bids that building operators get from contractors to add power or storage have dropped from when he first started working in the field 15 years ago, said Streier, who mainly works on the power side of deals but has represented the facilities side as well.

“Costs have come down so far that this is more attractive to a company,” he said. “If [building owners] are doing a new construction or some sort of renovation or expansion, [adding on-site power or storage] is an incremental cost in the budget — a line item — but it’s not just an expense; it’s going to help with energy savings and eventually it’ll have a payback, a return on investment. So, you pay a little bit more or you borrow a little more while you’re doing your project, but you get some energy savings over time and you might get some … goodwill out of it.”

Streier credits state and federal incentives for helping to bring renewable energy technology costs down by accelerating the manufacturing of renewables and energy storage — but even with some federal tax credits sunsetting, the long-term trajectory of the technology is solid, he said.

Independent power producers and others on the generating side will continue to build projects, which will help building operators on the facilities side looking for partners to reduce their grid exposure. “They might not be growing their pipelines as much as they had been, but they’re executing on the projects they have and pivoting to new ways … to adapt,” he said.

Streier says he’s seeing more facilities treat on-site generation or storage as part of their business strategy. “Energy storage has become so mature now that it’s acceptable for a CFO or a board to approve it,” he said. “They see their competitors doing it. Even without [federal incentives], they just want to do it because it’s part of their sustainability goals.”

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Facilities Dive free daily newsletter

Lithium-ion remains the most common technology for battery storage, but with innovations in other technologies, including long-duration iron-air batteries and thermal storage like graphite blocks, building operators could have more storage options to consider going forward, he said.

Iron-air batteries show promise because of their long duration — as much as 100 hours, according to Form Energy, which signed a deal with Google and Xcel Energy in August to provide 30 gigawatt-hours of battery energy to one of Google’s data centers. Graphite blocks are a thermal technology that stores excess electricity, from solar arrays or other sources, as extreme heat that can be deployed later.

“The battery technology that’s coming to market is pretty exciting,” he said.

Whatever happens with the federal investment tax credits and production tax credits that are being phased out — whether they’re brought back in some form — the long-term trajectory of solar and other renewable projects appears solid, he said. For that reason, building operators looking to partner with power companies to bring generation on site, or to add storage, should continue to benefit from the maturing technology, according to Streier.

text:
Around the corner from one of Cameron LaPoint’s favorite sushi restaurants is a parking lot that looks much like any other. But LaPoint recently learned that a portion of this particular parking lot in New Haven is classified by the Environmental Protection Agency as a brownfield, a property thought to contain a hazardous substance, pollutant, or contaminant.

Right now, the lot “probably isn’t suitable to be used for other things, because if you dig up what’s underneath, it could create a bigger problem,” says LaPoint, an assistant professor of finance at Yale SOM. But he suspects the land could be put to better use with the help of some TLC: “There’s not that much need for parking there.”

Around the United States, up to 15 million acres of land sit similarly vacant or underused. “These sites are everywhere, and you may not know it,” LaPoint says. “It’s something that’s really under our noses.”

Brownfields are usually contaminated because they were previously the site of illegal dumping or home to businesses that work with toxic substances, such as automotive repair facilities, dry cleaners, gas stations, and manufacturing plants. But compared to Superfund sites, their better-known and more dangerous cousins, brownfields are easier to clean up and return to productive use.

In fact, it turns out that relatively modest federal grants for brownfield remediation can significantly boost the economy near a previously contaminated site by creating jobs, boosting entrepreneurship, and increasing home values, among other benefits. That’s one of the findings of a new working paper co-authored by LaPoint, Aymeric Bellon of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, and Jason Chen of Auburn University.

The research also provides evidence for a phenomenon economists call the flypaper effect—the idea that federal government funding within a municipality attracts additional investment, whether from other federal agencies, state and local governments, or private sources. And because the EPA’s grants for brownfield cleanup rarely cover the full cost of the project, these additional funds are essential.

To study the economic effects of brownfield remediation, LaPoint and his co-authors took advantage of several aspects of how the EPA funds and administers the brownfield cleanup program.

For instance, the passage of the Better Utilization of Investments Leading to Development (BUILD) Act more than doubled the size of the maximum EPA cleanup grant, which jumped from $200,000 in 2018 to $500,000 in 2019. That allowed the researchers to compare employment near sites that received grants in 2018 to employment near sites that received much bigger grants just a year later, in 2019.

There’s no reason to think anything was fundamentally different about the sites that applied in 2018 versus 2019, so this comparison was a tidy way to “isolate the incremental value of the funding expansion,” LaPoint says. “If I give you more dollars, conditional on getting funding, what is that going to do in terms of job growth?”

In another part of their analysis, the researchers looked at the grant proposals submitted to the EPA. These proposals describe particular brownfield sites and what they need, including factors such as the severity of contamination and the potential for future use. The agency scores each proposal and sets a minimum score for funding that varies from year to year; proposals above the cutoff receive grants. In their statistical analysis, the researchers zoomed in on proposals that scored just above and below the cutoff, which are otherwise very similar.

“Those are good treatment and control groups,” LaPoint explains, “because otherwise you might just be comparing two sites where one was on a really strong growth trajectory and one was not.”

Then, within each grant cohort in their sample, the researchers compared job growth, new firm entry, and home prices near sites that barely missed out on funding to sites that barely scored high enough to receive it. They also examined the non-EPA sources of funding received by these two groups of sites.

Together, these analyses told several compelling stories. The researchers found that cleanup grants meaningfully benefit local economies, increasing employment within three miles of a funded site by approximately 5-6%. These effects lasted well beyond the active cleanup period, suggesting that the increase isn’t simply the result of jobs being created during the work. What’s more, the benefits accrued mainly to people living near funded sites, rather than commuters coming from elsewhere. Grant funding also increased new firm entry—the number of new businesses created—by 1.6 percentage points.

In addition, home prices within a half mile of funded sites increased—by about 5% 7 years after the grant was received and about 10% 10 years after.

LaPoint highlights a possible relationship between these two sets of findings. Economists have long known that home values influence entrepreneurship. “If you’re fixing the unemployment problem in the area and people’s home values are going up, they can leverage their home values to take out home equity lines of credit,” he says. “That can be the seed money for starting a new business.”

Finally, the researchers found, receiving EPA grant funding increases the overall amount of non-EPA money flowing to a site by between $3 and $5 million. In other words, “giving grants to these sites seems to help them accumulate millions more on top of that,” LaPoint says.

Notably, LaPoint says, the economic benefits of brownfield remediation are similar to those stemming from more conventional government subsidies to municipalities. Typically, these place-based subsidies aim to encourage a large employer to set up shop in a particular town through tax breaks. Often, however, multiple areas end up competing for the same manufacturing plant or warehouse, offering sweeter and sweeter deals. The result is that taxpayers lose out on a significant amount of money in exchange for a relatively small number of jobs.

Brownfield remediation, the researchers suggest, may offer more bang for the public buck—and provide an environmental benefit along the way. The cost per job created by EPA funding ranged from $7,500 to $19,700, depending on how the researchers calculated it, a figure that is in line with or lower than conventional place-based subsidies.

By unlocking land in places that need it, LaPoint says, “you’re not subsidizing firms directly—you’re really subsidizing the area.”

title: AEP in deal to buy up to 1.6 GW of Mainspring linear generators | Utility Dive
description:
American Electric Power has agreed to buy up to 1.6 GW of Mainspring Energy’s linear generators over the next eight years, with an initial 190-MW delivery set for next year, the Menlo Park, California-based company said Tuesday.
Mainspring’s investors include AEP, NextEra Energy, Gates Frontiers Fund, Khosla Ventures and others.
AEP plans to use Bloom Energy fuel cells for the project.
Bloom’s fuel cells produce electricity without burning natural gas, and the project includes plans for carbon capture technology for near-zero-emissions power, AEP said.
The Wyoming project shows how AEP is expanding beyond its traditional utility service territory, he said.

American Electric Power has agreed to buy up to 1.6 GW of Mainspring Energy’s linear generators over the next eight years, with an initial 190-MW delivery set for next year, the Menlo Park, California-based company said Tuesday.

Under the agreement, which could be worth up to $4 billion, AEP will be able to buy about 200 MW a year, with the linear generating units expected to be online within 12 months, Tom Linebarger, Mainspring chairman and CEO, said Tuesday in an interview with Bloomberg Tech.

The dispatchable generating units, which can use different fuel sources, such as natural gas, biogas and hydrogen, offer AEP flexibility, including by potentially firming renewable energy, according to Linebarger.

“Having the ability to both react to the customers’ needs and the grid’s needs at the same time gives them incredible flexibility,” Linebarger said. “Of course, the speed to power means [AEP] can deploy them quickly where they need them to serve customers better.”

The transaction is Mainspring’s largest purchase order to date, and marks a shift into the investor-owned utility market beyond commercial, industrial and data center markets, the company said.

Mainspring’s linear generators come in standard 2.5-MW configurations. They convert fuel into electricity through a low-temperature, flameless reaction that produces close to zero nitrogen oxide emissions, according to the company.

Mainspring, founded in 2010, recently closed on a $242 million Series G round led by private equity firm Valiant Peregrine, with participation from all existing company investors and a new strategic backer, according to a company spokeswoman. The company has raised a little more than $1 billion through all its funding rounds, she said in an email to Utility Dive.

Mainspring’s investors include AEP, NextEra Energy, Gates Frontiers Fund, Khosla Ventures and others.

AEP advances Wyoming fuel cell project

Meanwhile, AEP on Wednesday said it plans to spend about $4 billion building a 702-MW fuel cell generation project near Cheyenne, Wyoming, under a 20-year power purchase agreement with Google. AEP plans to use Bloom Energy fuel cells for the project.

AEP expects to start building the project this year and bring it online in 2028.

Bloom’s fuel cells produce electricity without burning natural gas, and the project includes plans for carbon capture technology for near-zero-emissions power, AEP said. The project follows agreements reached between Google and Black Hills Corp., which owns a utility serving the Cheyenne area, effective Sept. 30, according to AEP.

Under the PPA, Google will buy power from Cheyenne Fuel Cell, which is about 92% owned by AEP, with funds advised by Basalt Infrastructure Partners owning the remaining share, the utility company said.

“As power demand continues to grow, AEP is bringing together new technologies and strong partnerships to deliver reliable, innovative energy solutions quickly and at scale,” Bill Fehrman, AEP chairman, president and CEO, said in the press release.

The Wyoming project shows how AEP is expanding beyond its traditional utility service territory, he said.

text:
In a move being praised by farm and biofuel groups, a new draft rule from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) calls for reallocating 100% of renewable fuel volumes lost through small refinery exemptions.

EPA waived renewable fuel production requirements for 29 small refineries for the 2025 renewable volume obligations (RVOs), which set the number of gallons of biofuels that the nation’s oil refiners must blend into the nation’s fuel supply each year under the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS).

That decision threatened to take those volumes out of the historic 2026-27 RVOs if the fuel levels weren’t reallocated, but EPA pledged to fully account for any lost demand from those exemptions.

On Tuesday, EPA made good on that promise, with the proposed rule ensuring the original renewable fuel volumes set by the EPA will be made — all with North American feedstocks.

Ensuring steady demand

American Farm Bureau Federation Economist Faith Parum said EPA’s reallocations are a big benefit for farmers.

“This is great for the farm economy because it keeps demand for our feedstock strong,” Parum said. “So, our corn, our soybeans, canola — all of that is used for these renewable fuels. And by making sure that these volumes are reallocated, it'll make sure that demand is steady for U.S. farmers and ranchers.”

Michigan corn farmer and National Corn Growers Association President Matt Frostic said his organization is pleased to see that the Trump administration kept its pledge to protect farmers and biofuel producers.

“Biofuels provide essential energy supplies for our nation, and corn farmers are proud to contribute to our nation’s energy security,” Frostic wrote in a statement. “We hope that the Renewable Fuel Standard and the small refinery exemption program are managed with certainty in the years to come.”

American Soybean Association Vice President Dave Walton applauded EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and the Trump administration for keeping their commitment to farmers.

“Soybean farmers are navigating a tough farm economy, and the administration’s strong domestic biofuel policies will continue to drive much-needed market demand in the U.S. We are encouraged by today’s proposal and urge EPA to get it across the finish line quickly,” Walton said.

Growth Energy, the nation’s largest biofuels trade organization, also commended EPA’s action, noting that RFS is one of America’s most vital energy programs, providing stability and growth to rural communities and biofuel producers across the U.S.

“With this proposal, EPA would deliver on the full potential of historic RVOs and fulfill its promise to make American farmers and biofuel producers whole,” said Growth Energy CEO Emily Skor.

“Reallocating lost gallons would strengthen the rural economy and provide relief to farmers looking for reliable new markets that won’t be destroyed by costly exemptions.”

Biofuels group calls for SRE reform

EPA’s exemptions represented a total of 1.76 billion renewable fuel blending credits, which the Renewable Fuels Association (RFA) said represented the second-highest annual volume of exemptions ever granted.

In a statement, RFA continued to call for “reform of the broken SRE program.”

“These exemptions were always meant to be a temporary measure to give truly small, independent refiners a little more time to come into compliance with the RFS program,” said RFA President and CEO Geoff Cooper, who noted that refiners are seeing record-high profit margins while gasoline supplies are tightening.

“Unfortunately, many so-called small refiners have viewed SREs as an entitlement program and have exploited this loophole for two decades, putting American consumers, farmers, and biofuel producers on the losing end.”

Creating additional demand

EPA estimates the final rule will generate over $10 billion for rural economies and create over 100,000 new jobs in the agricultural and manufacturing sectors, building a larger, more stable and more reliable domestic market for U.S. crops.

“As soon as we got into office, American farmers asked the Trump EPA not to give them handouts but create avenues for them to enter additional markets,” Zeldin said.

“As our farmers continue to harvest their crops, today’s proposal is working to maintain a strong and durable market for them to sell to.”

Ag Secretary Brooke Rollins said she’s thrilled to see Zeldin act on the growing momentum for biofuels and provide a path forward to 100% reallocation by 2027.

“American biofuel producers have stepped up to the plate to provide record production, helping to fuel our nation and provide more market opportunities for our farmers,” Rollins said.

“The American biofuel industry provides over $100 billion in economic activity and supports over 100,000 American jobs while helping to deliver on President Trump’s energy dominance agenda. The Trump Administration will continue to stand by and deliver results for our farmers.”

text:
Up to $4.29 million available to help communities replace aging diesel refuse trucks with modern, zero-emission battery electric refuse vehicles

LANSING, Michigan — The Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE) is announcing the launch of the 2026 Michigan Clean Heavy-Duty Vehicle (CHDV) Program, a new grant opportunity that will provide funding to replace eligible Class 6 (19,501-26,000 pounds) and Class 7 (26,001-33,000 pounds) diesel refuse vehicles with new, zero-emission battery electric refuse vehicles and associated charging equipment.

The program is designed to reduce diesel emissions, improve air quality, protect public health, and support the deployment of advanced heavy-duty vehicle technologies while helping fleets modernize their operations.

Diesel refuse and recycling trucks are among the largest contributors of localized air pollution because they operate daily in neighborhoods, often at low speeds and close to homes, schools, and businesses. Replacing these vehicles with newer all-electric models can significantly reduce harmful exhaust emissions, lower noise, and improve quality of life for Michigan residents.

The program will provide funding to replace large, heavy-duty diesel trucks commonly used for trash collection, recycling, composting, and food waste recovery with zero-emission certified vehicles. The program also supports workforce development and training needed for the successful deployment and operation of the new vehicles. Both public and private entities physically located in Michigan are eligible to apply.

“This program is an important step toward cleaner air and healthier communities,” said EGLE Director Phillip D. Roos. “By reducing diesel exhaust from vehicles that operate directly in our neighborhoods, we can deliver meaningful public health benefits to communities that need it most while advancing Michigan’s clean energy future.”

Program focus and priorities

The CHDV Program prioritizes projects operating in designated ozone nonattainment or maintenance areas across the state that struggle to meet federal air quality standards, as well as in counties with a high asthma burden. Additional priority will be given to refuse truck replacements operating in Macomb, Oakland, and Wayne counties, within the Detroit Metropolitan Area, where long-standing environmental and public health challenges are most acute.

All funded projects must replace existing diesel vehicles with zero-emission alternatives and demonstrate long-term operational use at open and actively operating facilities.

Funding details

EGLE expects up to $4.29 million in funding will be made available through this competitive grant program. Individual awards are anticipated to range from $100,000 to $1 million, with funding capped at $260,000 per vehicle. Eligible costs include vehicle purchase, charging infrastructure, and workforce development and training.

Grant recipients must provide a minimum 50% cost match of total project costs for new battery electric refuse vehicles. All grant awards will be issued on a reimbursement basis, requiring grantees to pay project costs upfront and submit proper documentation for reimbursement.

All funds must be expended by Dec. 31, 2028. Projects should demonstrate readiness to complete vehicle replacement and charging infrastructure installation within the grant period.

Application timeline and requirements

Applications will be accepted and reviewed on a rolling, competitive basis until all funding is exhausted. Project start dates will be tied to the effective date of the grant agreement, and the deadline for submitting payment requests is Dec. 15, 2028.

Applicants are encouraged to begin preparing their application as early as possible by verifying project eligibility, securing vehicle and infrastructure quotes, assembling project teams, and developing site layouts, schedules, and budgets.

In a related move, EGLE launched the Michigan Electric Fleet Network in September to bring together fleets operating electric vehicles with fleets considering the technology. Members will meet regularly to compare notes and provide input on state programs, policies, and infrastructure planning that affect fleet electrification.

Supporting Michigan’s climate goals

The 2026 Michigan CHDV Program supports the MI Healthy Climate Plan and Michigan’s broader decarbonization goals by reducing diesel emissions, lowering greenhouse gas output, and accelerating the transition to clean transportation technologies.

Program materials, including the CHDV Request for Proposals, Online Application Form, and Eligibility Statement, are available on the CHDV Program webpage.

text:
Hyundai donates electric vehicle to Southeastern Community College for hands-on training

WHITEVILLE, NC (WWAY) — Students at Southeastern Community College now have a new opportunity to train on electric vehicle technology thanks to a donation from Hyundai Motor America.

The college’s Automotive Systems Technology program recently received a 2022 Hyundai Ioniq 5, along with a diagnostic scan tool, manufacturer service information and access to specialized training resources.

The fully electric vehicle arrived Aug. 9 and will be used in the college’s Electric Vehicle Certificate program to give students hands-on experience with maintenance, repairs, charging and vehicle operation.

According to Automotive Systems Technology instructor Johnny O’Connell, the donation grew out of a partnership between SCC and Hyundai that began several years ago.

O’Connell said the college started using Hyundai’s online learning management system about three years ago, allowing students to complete the same training and certifications offered to Hyundai dealership technicians.

“Students can complete all 54 modules, each having its own certification, to earn the overall Hyundai Service Technician Certification,” O’Connell explained. “Because we have regularly used the training over the past three years, we were chosen by Hyundai to receive a vehicle donation.”

The donation also gives SCC direct access to Hyundai’s manufacturer-specific service database for the first time, allowing students to work with the same technical information used in professional automotive service settings.

Michel Poirier, vice president of After Sales & Customer Experience at Hyundai Motor America, said the donation is intended to help prepare students for careers in the automotive industry.

“Hyundai Motor America is proud to support Southeastern Community College and its Automotive Systems Technology program through resources that bring today’s vehicle technology directly into the classroom and provide students with hands-on experience using the latest automotive and electric vehicle technologies,” said Poirier.

The Ioniq 5 is currently the only drivable electric vehicle available in SCC’s automotive program, according to O’Connell.

“This vehicle will be used in all of our electric vehicle program offerings,” O’Connell said. “Students will gain hands-on experience from using the vehicle in the lab to perform repairs and maintenance, and will learn how to charge the vehicle, along with how to operate the vehicle.”

Students will also have access to additional Hyundai training focused specifically on the Ioniq 5.

Those who complete SCC’s electric vehicle coursework will earn the college’s Electric Vehicle Certificate while gaining practical experience with current automotive technology.

text:
Indiana lawmakers are divided over the question of whether to give tax breaks to large corporations and data centers.

An interim study committee meeting became heated Wednesday as lawmakers sparred over the effectiveness of tax abatements.

The debate kicked off after Indiana’s Office of Fiscal and Management Analysis presented a report that found little evidence that abatements incentivize businesses to move to an area on their own.

Indiana leaders have long touted the state as a business-friendly environment. Tax abatements are often used to suspend or reduce the amount of property taxes a new business needs to pay in order to incentivize that company to build in a region. The argument for those abatements has been that the economic benefits, including new jobs, make sense for local governments.

Lauren Tanselle with the fiscal office explained to lawmakers that abatements have had mixed success, even as local governments are increasingly utilizing them.

“These are the most used local economic development incentives in Indiana,” she said. “Tax savings have increased over the past several years. We can see that in [2017] the total tax savings were about 182 million, and in 2026 they rose to 322 million.”

Tanselle’s comments immediately received pushback from Sen. Scott Baldwin (R-Noblesville).

“That’s an incredible thing to hear,” he said. “What informed that statement that these abatements have no impact on the decision a company might make as to whether to invest?”

As the report presentation continued, Baldwin repeatedly pushed back on the idea that abatements didn’t work – eventually saying he simply disagreed with Tanselle’s findings.

“To say that if they [businesses] were going to do it anyway, this was just reducing income for taxpayers is a but for conversation,” Baldwin said. “I’m not sure that’s a qualified statement.”

Under the state’s analysis, the “but for” question is defined as whether an investment would have been made “but for” the underlying incentives.

During the meeting, Sen. Fady Qaddoura (D-Indianapolis) pivoted to ask why Indiana is giving out so many abatements to data centers, noting that it was his understanding the total abatements offered to data centers in Indiana were roughly $694 million as of June.

“I’m completely perplexed by the idea that Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos need tax incentives from Hoosiers,” Qaddoura said. “I think we really need a comprehensive review, regardless of economic theory of what these data centers bring, regardless of the environmental impact, water, electricity, utilities.”

Sen. Chris Garten (R-Charlestown) immediately pushed back.

“Those decisions [tax abatements] are made at the local level,” he told Qaddoura. “If we want to make changes, that has to be done during session, which would be in January of 2027.”

Garten added that the idea that tax incentives to businesses haven’t benefitted the state ignores other factors.

“In the last five years, 200,000 people from all across the nation uprooted their family and said, ‘I want to raise my family in Indiana.’ No other state in the Midwest can say that,” he told the committee.

The question of abatements – and their efficacy – could come up during the next legislative session.

description:

text:
Only weeks after Premier Doug Ford threatened to cut off electricity exports to the United States as retaliation in the ongoing trade war, Ontario has signed a contract to import electricity from New York state through the winter.

The 600-megawatt contract starting Nov. 1 will provide power to compensate for “facility maintenance,” the Independent Electricity System Operator said in its announcement of the deal, without being more specific.

The Pickering nuclear plant was shut down in September for a multi-year refurbishment and this contract will partially replace its emissions-free electricity with carbon-intensive power from oil- and gas-fired plants.

There was no price mentioned in the announcement.

“This deal just increases our dependency on Donald Trump’s America to keep our lights on,” said Jack Gibbons, chair of the Ontario Clean Air Alliance and a former Toronto Hydro commissioner. “It’s absolutely the wrong way to go because it means more pollution, higher electricity bills and it means that we’re more vulnerable to attack.”

Ford imposed tax on power exports

In March 2024, Ford imposed a 25 per cent tax on power exports to the U.S. before backtracking and lifting them the next day. In August of this year, he threatened to reimpose the surcharges, saying “everything is on the table.”

Just over a month later, the province’s power grid operator, the IESO, announced a contract with Alpha Generation, a company that runs fossil-fuel power plants in the U.S. northeast and California, including the Oswego oil-fired generator north of Syracuse, N.Y.

Energy Minister Stephen Lecce’s office referred the Star to the IESO for comment as decisions around energy supply and import contracts are made without input from the ministry.

“Ontario’s electricity system remains reliable, and securing additional short-term capacity provides greater flexibility,” wrote IESO spokesperson Michael Dodsworth. “This also provides additional safeguards through the winter months, as the IESO prepares for higher winter peak demand.”

Last year, U.S. power imports made up only one per cent of electricity demand and the province exported nearly seven times more, Dodsworth said.

Ontario previously signed a much smaller deal with Oswego for the winter of 2024-25, providing one-quarter of power secured by the current contract. The province also has an existing contract with Quebec that imports and exports up to 600 megawatts of power when either province needs it.

Alpha Generation is partly owned by the Canadian Pension Plan, which announced a $1.4-billion investment in the company last year.

“In a weird twist, not only are Ontarians paying an American fuel oil plant to pollute, that same money is being used to generate returns for the CPP,” said Patrick DeRochie, senior manager of Shift Action for Pension Wealth and Planet Health, a non-profit that works to protect pensions and the climate.

Energy analysts say this new deal represents a departure from the past 18 years when Ontario did not import much power from the U.S. Prior to 2008, Ontario imported significant amounts of electricity, far more than this contract represents.

“The era of long-term capacity surpluses in Ontario is officially over,” wrote Brendan Callery and Brady Yauch, analysts with Power Advisory, in a report on Ontario’s power procurement. This import contract “is the latest sign of an increasingly tight supply/demand balance.”

Pickering, Darlington reactors offline

In addition to the Pickering nuclear plant going offline, the Darlington reactors, which completed their own years-long refurbishment in February, are being taken back offline for additional maintenance next spring, creating more power shortfalls, they wrote.

Ontario was unable to procure all the electricity it wanted for this winter in its most recent capacity auction, which drove up the wholesale price paid to generators to $725 per megawatt per business day, which is the “the highest ever capacity price in Ontario,” the Power Advisory analysts wrote.

Mike Marcolongo, associate director of Environmental Defence, says the import contract is likely the result of a hard lesson learned last winter: that Ontario’s gas plants can’t be relied upon during big winter storms.

“In January 2026’s winter storm Fern, 2,400 megawatts of natural gas went offline. That’s not just one or two, it’s multiple gas plants across the province that couldn’t produce power because the gas was routed away from Canada and to the U.S,” he said.

In a public presentation from last spring, the IESO said multiple gas plants “had issues securing gas,” during last winter’s coldest months. Fortunately, Ontario’s 800 megawatts of battery storage “performed really well,” allowing the province to avoid blackouts.

Push for nuclear power leaves province short of electricity

Gibbons says Ontario’s push to increase nuclear generation by building new reactors and repairing old ones has been carried out at the expense of cheaper options like renewables and battery storage and has left the province short on power.

“Six hundred megawatts is a substantial amount of power. It’s larger than one of the Pickering nuclear station’s reactors,” he said. “And we need it to keep the lights on this winter.”

“This problem has arisen because we’re too dependent on high-cost and slow-to-deploy nuclear power and we’re not investing enough in energy efficiency and load shifting and battery storage.”

The Ford government has introduced a suite of energy efficiency programs that offer rebates for home renovations, payments to households for the ability to remotely turn down air conditioning and to industry for curbing demand during peak periods. The Energy Ministry says these programs collectively represent the biggest investment in energy efficiency in the country, and are projected to save ratepayers $12.2 billion over the next 24 years.

A national poll conducted for the Canadian Renewable Energy Association found affordability was Canadians’ top priority for new generation, with solar power the most popular choice, ahead of hydro, nuclear, wind and natural gas.

“The most affordable energy in the world right now is renewables,” said Vittoria Bellissimo, president and CEO of CanREA. “Ontario should be building as much solar, wind and storage as possible.”

The Ford government, which was elected on a platform overtly hostile to renewable energy, and spent $231 million to cancel more than 700 renewable projects. In recent years, faced with increasing demand for power, the government has held several rounds of procurements, contracting new solar and wind projects at significantly lower prices than the ones that were cancelled and making the province a leader in battery storage.

“Ontario is still moving forward with wind, solar and storage,” Bellissimo said. “It would serve customers better if it did more.”

Editor’s note - Oct. 15, 2026

This article was updated from a previous version to include additional information from the Energy Ministry.

title: Sakuu produces 100 dry-printed carbon fiber battery cell on Kavian manufacturing platform
description:
“Our dry-printed carbon fiber PCC test cell demonstrates how to produce innovative batteries that can safely power—and also conform to and strengthen—new structural designs in transportation and energy storage systems.” Sakuu’s carbon fiber test cell is a fully functional lithium-ion 0.5 Ahr battery cell.
Dry-processed PCC cells possess several advantages over the standard wet-processed lithium-ion battery cells, Sakuu explains.
PCC cells are still made layer by layer, but each layer is individually sealed and connected directly, one on top of the other.
Carbon fiber doesn’t wrinkle.
It has unique properties that add strength and electrical conductivity to the composite in a PCC cell.
text:
Sakuu, a provider of commercial-scale equipment and technologies to the battery and supercapacitor manufacturing industries, has printed a 100% dry anode and dry cathode metal-free battery cell using carbon composite and polymeric current collector (PCC) technology on its Kavian manufacturing platform. This fully functional metal-free cell delivers the safety benefits of PCC architecture and the structural integrity of carbon fiber while remaining flexible and extremely lightweight, the company says.

“The ability to manufacture safer batteries at scale is essential to meeting surging demand across industries, yet battery manufacturing technology has been stuck in a rut for 30 years,” said Arwed Niestroj, President and COO of Sakuu. “Our dry-printed carbon fiber PCC test cell demonstrates how to produce innovative batteries that can safely power—and also conform to and strengthen—new structural designs in transportation and energy storage systems.”

Sakuu’s carbon fiber test cell is a fully functional lithium-ion 0.5 Ahr battery cell. The company says it’s immune to thermal runaway, and is made with lightweight, inexpensive and globally readily available materials.

Dry-processed PCC cells possess several advantages over the standard wet-processed lithium-ion battery cells, Sakuu explains. “A PCC cell is a series-connected battery, not parallel-connected. PCC cells are still made layer by layer, but each layer is individually sealed and connected directly, one on top of the other. The layers use a thin conductive polymer film and current flows vertically up through a stack of sealed layers, moving from one layer to the next over the entire surface of contact. Any short, defect, or puncture in the cell results in a slow dissipation of energy that does not produce excessive heat and thesrefore cannot produce fire.”

These cells are not yet widely available because they cannot be made with standard wet-process manufacturing equipment—but Sakuu says they can be mass-produced cost-effectively with the company’s dry-process manufacturing technology.

Thin polymer films are flimsy and subject to wrinkling, Sakuu CTO Karl Littau tells us. “Wrinkles are defects that could make good electrical contact difficult or impossible. Carbon fiber doesn’t wrinkle. It has unique properties that add strength and electrical conductivity to the composite in a PCC cell. Using carbon fiber veils allows us to make strong yet conformable and flexible electrode layers and current collector layers: The fibers not only penetrate the current collector, but are also embedded within the dry powder anode and cathode. This ensures intimate contact of the adjacent layers in a cell and provides a robust reinforcing network, which also conducts electricity quite well.”

The partnership brings together Rivian’s electric vehicle operations and Redwood Materials’ battery recycling and energy storage technology, offering a potential solution to two growing challenges for American manufacturers: rising electricity demand and the need for a reliable domestic supply of battery materials.

text:
Rivian is expanding its partnership with Redwood Materials to create a more comprehensive battery lifecycle system that combines EV battery recycling, second-life energy storage, and manufacturing waste recovery. The expanded agreement will help Rivian recover valuable materials from used batteries while deploying repurposed battery packs to support electricity demand at its manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois.

The partnership brings together Rivian’s electric vehicle operations and Redwood Materials’ battery recycling and energy storage technology, offering a potential solution to two growing challenges for American manufacturers: rising electricity demand and the need for a reliable domestic supply of battery materials.

Under the expanded agreement, Redwood Materials will collect Rivian battery packs that are no longer suitable for use in electric vehicles through Rivian’s nationwide service center network.

Each battery pack will be evaluated to determine whether it can be reused in stationary energy storage systems or should be recycled to recover valuable materials.

Battery packs that retain sufficient capacity can be repurposed for stationary storage at Rivian’s manufacturing facilities or other locations. Batteries that are no longer suitable for energy storage will be sent for recycling.

The agreement also expands Redwood’s responsibilities to include battery manufacturing scrap generated at Rivian’s production operations. This will allow more battery materials to be recovered and returned to the supply chain instead of being wasted.

The expanded partnership builds on an energy storage agreement announced in April 2026, which involves deploying 10 megawatt-hours (MWh) of energy storage using repurposed Rivian battery packs at the automaker’s Normal, Illinois, manufacturing plant.

Instead of immediately recycling batteries removed from vehicles, the companies will give suitable packs a second life by using them to store electricity.

These systems can charge during periods of lower electricity demand or when renewable energy is readily available, then release stored power when demand increases. This approach can help reduce electricity costs, ease pressure on the grid, and improve energy reliability for industrial facilities.

Stationary storage also offers a way to extract additional value from EV batteries before they reach the end of their useful lives.

Rivian Founder and CEO RJ Scaringe said that giving retired battery packs a second life in stationary storage could help make the electricity grid more reliable while lowering energy costs.

When batteries can no longer support energy storage applications, recycling becomes the next step in the process.

Redwood Materials says its advanced recycling technology can recover more than 95% of critical minerals, including lithium, nickel, cobalt, and copper.

Recovering these materials can help reduce dependence on newly mined resources and strengthen the domestic supply chain for EV battery production in the United States.

The process also creates a more circular battery economy. Materials recovered from retired EV batteries and manufacturing scrap can potentially be returned to the supply chain for use in new batteries and other applications.

text:
It’s been two weeks since a bipartisan team of senators unveiled a proposal to reshape the future of energy and infrastructure projects in America — and some of the biggest environmental groups still haven’t come out with a full-throated position on it.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act — the ambitious proposal from Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia) and Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico) — pits two core tenets of the environmental movement against one another: the urgency for a clean energy transition and the decades-long fight for stronger federal protections for air, water, animals and nature.

That tension has created a minefield for large environmental groups and their allies on the left.

Major green groups — the League of Conservation Voters, the Sierra Club, the Environmental Defense Fund, the Natural Resources Defense Council — have hedged. They’ve shown modest support for certain provisions, brought up concerns about others and largely strayed away from endorsement or opposition.

Trending

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), longtime adversaries of the fossil fuel industry and proponents of a “Green New Deal,” have not made any statements about their positions. Ocasio-Cortez’s office said it had nothing to share, while Sanders’s office did not respond to The Washington Sun’s request for comment.

A lobbyist familiar with where environmental organizations stand called the permitting reform bill a “Sophie’s Choice” for the major green groups.

“They’re legitimately struggling,” they said. “Imagine you’re an environmental group, and you have a climate team and an environment side. And the environment side includes environmental justice and clean air and clean water — how do you balance that?”

The past two years have created a unique moment for infrastructure and energy policy. Energy got more expensive. President Donald Trump sharply halted federal investments in clean energy and climate projects. Democrats have “hushed” their climate rhetoric just as a new crop of bipartisan groups, spurred by the “abundance” movement, amplified calls to ease regulations and build big. Meanwhile, the backlash to data center development catalyzed support around local water and land protections and cast blame on AI infrastructure for increasing electricity costs.

These conditions have scrambled political alliances around Congress’ newest permitting reform bill — a sweeping, 400-page document that includes changes to environmental laws that haven’t been touched by Congress in years and provisions that could accelerate the build-out of transmission and clean energy, as well as fossil fuel infrastructure.

“What this bill evidences is a contested fight over different theories of change,” said Erik Schlenker-Goodrich, the executive director of the Western Environmental Law Center, which opposes the bill.

The debate, he said, boils down to whether you believe that the arc of capitalism will bend toward renewable energy.

“Down one path, what this bill reflects is, ‘Let the market rip, let tech, energy and finance capital rip, and then through the magic wand of the market this will lead to decarbonization and robust energy supply,’” he said. “We think that’s problematic because it essentially cedes control over our energy future to capital and takes that power away from the public.”

Environmental groups, including Food and Water Watch, the Center for Biological Diversity and Bill McKibben’s Third Act, are organizing efforts to block the bill over concerns about the loss of environmental protections and benefits to the fossil fuel industry. On Tuesday, a group of 185 organizations sent a letter to House Democratic leadership calling the legislation a backdoor deal and a “massive power grab by Big Tech and the fossil fuel industry.”

On the other side, there’s an unsteady coalition of climate hawks, clean energy groups, AI infrastructure associations and fossil fuel companies who see a new path forward for the kinds of massive projects long stalled by red tape.

Citizens’ Climate Lobby endorsed the bill, saying it would make “remarkable, rapid progress” toward reducing emissions and addressing climate change. The Solar Energy Industries Association said it was “exactly the kind of bipartisan action America needs.” Incompas, an AI infrastructure association, said the bill could “accelerate the energy and infrastructure projects needed to support America’s AI future.” And the American Petroleum Institute called the bill a “generational opportunity.”

Clean energy groups are highlighting the bill’s potential to reduce emissions.Modeling from the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions suggests transmission and interconnection reforms alone could lead to deep reductions in climate-warming pollution, though there isn’t yet a comprehensive report on the net impact of the bill as a whole.

Major environmental groups seem to largely be dealing with these tensions by slow-walking their responses. In several statements, groups say that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is too long to quickly formulate a response.

“This is significant and complex legislation and we will be taking the time to analyze and understand its full impacts,” Sara Chieffo, the senior vice president of government affairs at the League of Conservation Voters, said in a statement.

In a blog post last week, the Sierra Club’s chief program officer, Holly Bender, made the climate case for a version of permitting reform but stopped short of endorsing the bipartisan compromise.

“America’s energy demands are higher than ever and it’s never been more critical that we build as much clean energy as possible, as quickly as possible,” she wrote, adding that supporting clean energy infrastructure is work that “literally saves lives.”

Bender noted some “green flags” in the bill: requirements for regional grid operators to work together on transmission planning; a federal “backstop” that would allow the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to approve transmission lines if states drag out their processes beyond one year; and protections against power-hungry data centers spiking electric costs.

But her “red flags” — limiting courts’ powers to stop projects, weakening Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act protections, permitting certain provisions that could “lock-in” fossil fuel projects — outnumbered the green ones.

Add to that the Trump administration, which has targeted precisely the energy projects the Sierra Club wants to see succeed, and the bill as written becomes a hard sell.

Still, the organization’s response is a marked departure from its critique of permitting reform efforts from two years ago, which it dubbed a “dirty deal.”

This time, Bender wrote, “the stakes couldn’t be higher.”

“If Congress fails to get this right, it could mean continued reliance on fossil fuels, higher costs for families, and ever-worsening extreme weather events,” she wrote.

Other major green groups have taken similar middle-of-the-road stances.

The Natural Resources Defense Council called permitting reform a “necessity” but said it was still trying to understand the trade-offs — major changes to the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act and National Environmental Policy Act that could accelerate fossil fuel development.

Kameran Onley, a managing director at The Nature Conservancy, said in a statement that the organization believes modernizing permitting can hold both: moving faster to build infrastructure and protecting people and nature.

“While we are still analyzing the many details of the bill, we see some promising improvements and hard compromises,” she said, adding that the organization would advocate for community and conservation interests as the legislative process moves forward.

Onley also said the group would advocate for tribal sovereignty in the process. Provisions that would limit the National Historic Preservation Act have emerged as a major issue for tribal preservation leaders. The National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers has opposed the permitting bill, saying it would cut tribes out of the planning process for federal projects.

Valerie Grussing, the executive director for legislative affairs and strategic partnerships at the association, said in a statement that the bill was a “legislative assault on the sovereignty of Tribal Nations” and would be a violation of the federal government’s treaty responsibilities if enacted.

A major critique that has emerged is how the bill was written behind closed doors in negotiations among Senate leaders. The Trump administration’s interference with renewable energy projects threatened to kill the deal several times.

The senators responsible for the deal may be hesitant to accept too many changes. But Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) told The Sun he would work on amendments that are important to tribal preservation offices, as well as “relatively technical” amendments that conservation groups have pushed for.

“But, you know, it’s a planetary emergency,” he said on The Washington Sun Cast. “I’m, generally speaking, hawkish on taking big steps in the direction of clean energy, even if it’s a mixed bag.”

Todd Tucker, the industrial policy and trade director at the Roosevelt Institute, said he anticipates that green groups taking a middle road on the bill will ultimately help the permitting reform deal move forward.

“I think there’s a big difference here between opposing and staying neutral,” he said. “I think most of the larger groups are going to stay neutral or somewhat positive. And I think that is likely to give this bill the support that it needs,” he said.

text:
With the US midterm elections less than three weeks away, is it any surprise that corruption has emerged as voters’ top concern? “Corrupt” was the adjective most often chosen when registered voters were asked for a single word to describe President Donald Trump, according to a survey conducted in September by The Economist and the market research firm YouGov, with 53 percent of respondents calling Trump corrupt and only 23 percent saying he is “honest.” A Pew Research Center poll in early October found that nearly seven in 10, or 69 percent, of Americans are “not confident” that Trump keeps his business interests separate from his presidential decisions.

1/1Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE

Americans can thank diligent investigative reporting for alerting them to much of Trump, his family, and aides’ self-dealings. For example, The Washington Post has reported that Trump’s sons, Don Jr. and Eric, were investors in 15 companies that “collectively generated at least $3.2 billion in direct government business since the sons invested and an additional $3.1 billion in future contract options.” And on Tuesday, in a rare retreat, the White House asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign as US ambassador to Greece after a Wall Street Journal investigation revealed that Guilfoyle promised political favors to a Trump donor if he would quietly pay off her $100,000 American Express credit card bill.

Throughout the history of modern polling, voters have usually ranked the economy (or its proxies, such as “the cost of living”) as their top issue. Now, linking corruption with the cost of living, “Democrats Are Making Corruption Messaging a Pocketbook Issue,” a recent Politico headline declared. The Democrats’ claim, The New York Times reported, “that rampant corruption in Congress and the administration is directly costing average citizens who are paying more for necessities like groceries, gas, and medicin.”

Both Democrats and the press however are so far overlooking one of the most overt and consequential examples of Trump’s pay-to-play behavior. On May 24, 2024, Josh Hawley and Maxine Joselow of The Washington Post published a blockbuster exposé, reporting that Trump privately told a group of oil company CEOs they should donate $1 billion to his 2024 presidential campaign: It would be a good “deal” for the industry, Trump reportedly said, because of the tax and regulation benefits they would receive if he returned to the Oval Office.

Specifically, Trump reportedly said he would reverse the Biden administration’s pause on new liquified natural gas export permits, approve more drilling for oil in the Gulf of Mexico and Alaska, and roll back environmental regulations that the industry didn’t like, including electric vehicle purchasing mandates and vehicle emissions limits. Hawley and Joselow then published a follow-up, reporting that Trump also promised to soften Federal Trade Commission scrutiny of industry mergers and acquisitions.

Two and a half years later, his administration has delivered on each of these promises and then some. The Brennan Center has published a well-documented summary of Trump’s assault on climate policy—including his administration’s repeal of the “endangerment finding” that has granted the federal government the authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions—that connects the dots between Trump’s actions and the many billions of dollars the oil industry has reaped as a result, including the millions of dollars that benefit oil executives individually.

What makes all this relevant to the midterm elections—beyond the fact that the leader of the Republican Party is directly implicated—is that many of Trump’s accomplishments were only possible because of rubber-stamp support from Republicans in Congress. Now, those same Republicans must face the voters. How will they explain themselves?

To be clear, Democrats don’t get a pass here; corruption has been part of politics forever, and one of the press’s central obligations is to expose and hold its perpetrators to account, whoever they may be. That requires following the facts where they lead. But it also requires challenging the practice, still common among old-school newsrooms, of false equivalence—or of portraying both sides as equally culpable for a given transgression for fear that an accurate portrayal would look like “taking sides.” If most of the facts point in one direction, our reporting should have the integrity and courage to say so.

Most voters don’t have access to directly question candidates seeking their votes. It’s our job as journalists to ask questions on their behalf so they can make informed decisions about their leaders.
