LOS ANGELES, CA, UNITED STATES, October 15, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Becker Transactions today announced the availability of MagTrac’s patent portfolio for acquisition, licensing, or strategic partnership. The portfolio includes eight issued U.S. patents, with additional patent applications pending, addressing technologies intended to improve the safety, reliability, and operational capabilities of autonomous and electric vehicles.

The growing MagTrac patent portfolio will soon include a ninth issued US patent, as well as a further pending application, covering magnetic, RFID, conductive, and other roadway-based technologies designed to improve autonomous vehicle perception and navigation. The MagTrac patents have been cited more than 170 times by companies and organizations across the automotive, technology, robotics, and transportation industries. For a list of such companies, please refer to Google Patents using as a search term, US Pat. No. 12,248,839, and see, Info: "Cited By", including Toyota, Aichi Steel, Hyundai, Uber, Honda, Ford Global Technologies, Volkswagen, Baidu, Waymo, Mobileye, Hitatchi, Mircon, AT&T, LG Electronics, Robert Bosch, 3M, State Farm, MIT, Volvo, IBM and Bombardier.

Addressing a Critical Challenge in Autonomous Driving

Autonomous vehicles depend on perception systems to detect roadway conditions, lane markings, vehicles, pedestrians, and other objects. Snow, ice, rain, dirt, and reduced visibility can significantly degrade camera- and vision-based sensing systems.

These limitations remain a major obstacle to the widespread deployment of highly automated and Level 5 autonomous vehicles, which must be capable of operating safely under diverse environmental conditions.

MagTrac’s technology is designed to provide additional, weather-resilient sources of roadway and object information, supporting vehicle localization, lane recognition, steering, collision avoidance, and situational awareness.

The MagTrac Technology

The patent portfolio covers systems and methods involving specialized roadway markings and recognition features that may incorporate:

- Magnetic materials and magnetic markers

- RFID and radio-frequency identification technologies

- Conductive and thin-film materials

- Visible, infrared, ultraviolet, and other detectable elements

- Encoded information embedded in roadway markers

- Vehicle-based systems for detecting and interpreting roadway signals

- Recognition features for pedestrians, bicyclists, vehicles, and other roadway users

In certain embodiments, detectable elements may be embedded in painted or prefabricated pavement markings. These technologies are intended to provide redundant sensor feedback even when visible roadway features are obscured by snow, ice, rain, dirt, sand, or other conditions.

The technology may also support temporary roadway configurations, including construction zones, work zones, and detours, by enabling detectable markers to define alternate travel paths.

Broad Commercial and Strategic Applications

MagTrac’s portfolio may provide opportunities for:

- Autonomous vehicle manufacturers seeking enhanced all-weather perception

- Electric vehicle companies developing advanced driver-assistance systems

- Roadway and infrastructure operators deploying intelligent pavement systems

- Technology companies** developing vehicle localization and navigation platforms

- Joint ventures and strategic partnerships combining roadway and vehicle technologies

- Licensing programs for automotive, infrastructure, robotics, and transportation markets

Because the portfolio includes early priority dates and broad technical disclosures, an acquirer or licensee may be able to develop additional claims and applications tailored to emerging competitive and commercial requirements.

About the Inventor

The lead inventor of the patent portfolio is James J. Kovarik, who, during his over 30 years of experience with non-destructive inspection technologies, is familiar with systems that employ one or more of Ultrasonic, Radiographic, Magnetic Particle, and Optical inspections. Among his many inventions, he developed an innovative technology used to inspect utility boom trucks to prevent previous electrical fatalities. See, e.g., U.S. Pat. Nos. 8,750,594 and 8,280,145, “System and Method for Non-destructively Examining Degradation of an Interior of a Device; and U.S. Pat. No. ; 8023722, “Radiography Test System and Method”. Such technologies involved examining non-visible degradation in vehicle-mounted systems, and detecting corrosion and wear where metal and composite layers are present.

His latest focus has been on autonomous vehicle systems and methods that address a long-felt but unsolved need: the ability of autonomous vehicles to safely traverse roads in bad weather conditions. Snow and ice can obscure lane markings, interfere with sensor performance (like lidar and cameras), and make it difficult to detect and avoid obstacles. Snow can cause confidence issues in perception algorithms, leading to failures in detecting objects or false detections. And snow affects different sensor types differently, making it harder to achieve consensus on what the sensors "see," which is crucial for safe autonomous driving.

Opportunity for Acquisition or Licensing

MagTrac owns the issued patents and pending applications outright and is seeking qualified parties interested in acquiring, licensing, or partnering around the portfolio.

The portfolio represents an opportunity to participate in the development of infrastructure-supported autonomous driving—a model that supplements onboard vehicle sensors with intelligent, detectable roadway and user-based technologies.

title: Institutional, Not Neutronic: Why Advanced Reactors Actually Get Built, or Don't
description:
More Paper Reactors Than this Industry has Ever Had Gibboney Nuclear maintains a dataset of advanced reactor developers built from public announcements and my own meetings with developer teams.
It is the industrial system that makes advanced reactor deployment real.
Advanced reactor commercialization is institutional, not neutronic.
“Commercial” is a Defined Term, not a Marketing Term “Commercialization” is an abused word in advanced nuclear.
Personal communication, Plant Hatch operator present since Unit 1 initial criticality, Edwin I. Hatch Nuclear Plant, Baxley, Georgia, 2005–2006.
text:
Guest Column to Neutron Bytes

by: Sarah Gibboney, P.E., Founder & CEO Gibboney Nuclear, PLLC.

Adapted from the forthcoming book ~ Due Diligence: How to Design, License, and Deploy Advanced Reactors ~ Rocky Flats Books

There is an old management parable about primates in an enclosure and a pole with a bunch of bananas.1 Every animal that climbs up the pole to score of the bananas gets shocked. Eventually the power is cut and new animals are introduced, ones who have never felt the current. The veterans pull them down anyway even though the banana pole is no longer carrying live electricity, because the fear is still alive among them due to prior experience.

The commercial nuclear industry spent four decades on that pole. In the last few years, between the ADVANCE Act, NRC modernization, and a market that suddenly wants firm, clean power, much of the current has been switched off.

A lot of very smart people are still pulling newcomers back down out of habit. And a lot of newcomers are climbing without asking why the pole was electrified in the first place. This column is about that second group, and the people funding, hiring into, and partnering with them.

More Paper Reactors Than this Industry has Ever Had

Gibboney Nuclear maintains a dataset of advanced reactor developers built from public announcements and my own meetings with developer teams. It currently tracks 125 developer companies and 178 unique reactor designs.2 The industry has never had more entrants, more ideas, or more people willing to try.

The reactor count gets the headlines, but the fuel cycle is scaling in parallel. The same dataset tracks two new more expanding mining companies, two new or expanding conversion companies, eight new or expanding enrichment companies, 13 new or expanding fuel fabrication companies, seven new fuel recycling companies, and two new radioactive waste repository companies.2 The fuel cycle is not background infrastructure. It is the industrial system that makes advanced reactor deployment real.

So, the constraint is not ideation. It is conversion: turning a design into a licensed, financed, built, and operating power plant. This is the thesis of the book in one line. Advanced reactor commercialization is institutional, not neutronic. Neutronics makes a reactor possible. Institutions make it licensable, financeable, buildable, and operable.

“Commercial” is a Defined Term, not a Marketing Term

“Commercialization” is an abused word in advanced nuclear. In venture finance it can mean a company raised money past the seed funding stage. In policy it can mean a government authorized and cost-shared funded a demonstration project. In NRC licensing, it has a number attached to it.

Under 10 CFR 50.22(c), as amended in April 2026 to implement NEIMA and the ADVANCE Act, a utilization facility operating under a Section 104 research and development license cannot devote more than 50 percent of its annual operating costs to the sale of energy. Cross that line and the facility is deemed to be for industrial or commercial purposes, and it needs a Section 103 commercial license instead.3 Until a reactor crosses that number under its own NRC-issued license, calling it “commercial” is aspirational, but it is not accurate.

The Four Forces that Decide Whether a Reactor Gets Built

The book organizes commercialization into four forces. All four are active at the same time, and most programs fail because they optimize one while neglecting the others.

Force One: Regulatory Credibility

Licensing does not create the safety case. It translates one. Neutronics, thermal hydraulics, materials performance, fuel qualification, and code validation are the raw inputs this force runs on. Licensing takes what the technical organization has already established and turns it into a coherent, bounded licensing basis a regulator can evaluate. I have watched this relationship break in two directions.

Design-centered organizations let engineers chase whatever is technically interesting. It feels like progress until a licensing engineer explains that a meaningful fraction of the work has to be redone, not because it is wrong, but because it was never aimed at a licensing basis.

Licensing-centered organizations fail the opposite way: they treat licensing as an independent workstream, and either starve the technical program of direction or discover too late that the analysis underneath the licensing tip of the iceberg was never built.

Force Two: Capital and Supply Chain constraints

After Vogtle 3 and 4, financial readiness and industrial readiness are hard to pull apart. Westinghouse filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy status on March 29, 2017, driven primarily by schedule delays and cost overruns on the AP1000 builds at Vogtle and V.C. Summer.4 These projects did not just run late and over budget. The took down the company that built them.

Firms involved in building reactors in the U.S., and globally, absorbed that lesson the way any market absorbs a bankruptcy caused by an underpriced risk. Recently, in my own work with developers, requests for proposal to EPCs have come back with no-bids more often than shared-risk term sheets.5 A firm that watched a competitor go bankrupt on a first-of-a-kind nuclear build does not need a risk-sharing slide deck. It has its pick of projects, and it will choose the ones that look buildable.

Force Three: Organizational Maturity

You do not need inside information to evaluate a developer. You need to know what to look for. The failures that sink a nuclear company are usually visible long before the bankruptcy filing or the leadership exit. Three signs I watch closely:

Vendor and payroll timelines slip

Hiring outruns confirmed funding

Promotions reward loyalty over skill

Those patterns showed up in public before Ultra Safe Nuclear Corporation’s Chapter 11 filings and before the abrupt departures of Fermi America’s CEO and CFO this spring.6, 7 The book breaks down about a dozen more cases.

I learned to trust these signals the hard way. I watched the pattern once during the layoffs at the MOX Fuel Fabrication Facility.8 When I started seeing the same signs at X-energy in 2023, I told coworkers to expect layoffs within about a year. I was wrong about the timing. The reduction came in November 2023, while I was still there, already on my two weeks’ notice and handing off my work. Some of the people I was training to take over were let go in the same round.9

Organizational maturity cuts both ways. Where is falls short, it looks like a strong design team that has never worked under a controlled QA program, with institutional knowledge living in people’s heads until they leave. With over reach, it looks like a ten-person startup adopted a 300-procedure program written for a company a hundred times its size, which nobody follows because nobody can. In my opinion, a startup needs 25-to-30 procedures that actually get followed and can scale with the headcount.

Force Four: Operations and Maintenance

“Walk-away safe” is a claim about physics. Capacity factor, achieved efficiency, and cost-per- kilowatt-hour are claims about operations, and none of them are knowable until a unit is running.

Early in my career, I shadowed an operator at Plant Hatch who had been there since Unit 1 first went critical in September 1974. As he told it, a commissioning scram test, the test that drives the control rods in hard enough to prove the plant can stop the chain reaction on demand, tore the anchors holding the 36-inch main steam lines clean out of the wall.10 In my view, episodes like that one, and worse ones like TMI-2, are why NQA-1 exists. The standard did not come from a committee anticipating problems. It came from problems actually happening.11

Efficiency claims deserve the same skepticism. New designs routinely publish thermal efficiency numbers straight from a thermodynamic analysis. That figure is real, but it is not what you get once the plant is built, commissioned, and operating.

In the mid-2000s at Hatch, Southern Nuclear ran a dedicated effort to squeeze every megawatt it could out of the plant, and we landed at about 30 percent.12 That is what it took just to move the number.

For context, the EIA’s average operating heat rate for the U.S. nuclear fleet has held near 10,450 Btu per kilowatt-hour for the past decade, which works out to roughly 32 to 33 percent thermal efficiency.13

If a design’s efficiency claim outperforms fifty years of light water reactor operating history before a single unit has run, it is not a physics result yet. It is a slide deck pitch, until operation proves it.

Hatch also shows what happens when an industry metabolizes its mistakes. The plant had a slogan, “Leave it better than you found it,” which workers sang at all-hands meetings to the tune of the Battle Hymn of the Republic.14

It sounds ridiculous written down. It also worked. In June 2026, the NRC approved subsequent license renewal for both Hatch units, Unit 1 through 2054 and Unit 2 through 2058.15 The same plant that could not pass its own commissioning test without damaging itself is now licensed for roughly 80 years.

The Question I Cannot Stop Circling

At a National Academies event where I presented this summer, an associate professor asked me where the nuclear industry would be in five, ten, and twenty years.16 My honest answer: I think we are about to repeat the buildout of the 1970s and 1980s. Not because physics has changed, but because people and institutions have not, and neither has the pipeline that trains them.

In October 2024, I sat in an NRC stakeholder listening session for its University Nuclear Leadership Program, including the traineeship subprogram created by the ADVANCE Act. When the idea of requiring students to work at an operating plant came up, the pushback from engineering deans was immediate, and it was mostly about money.17

“Some of our students won’t be able to afford to travel for this.” The students would be engaged in paid work. “Is there a remote option?” There is no remote option for standing in a plant.

My read is that the incentives point the wrong way. A university that produces job-ready graduates with bachelor’s degrees loses the tuition for master’s degrees those students no longer need. The economics of higher education and the economics of a ready workforce pull in opposite directions, and so far, higher education is winning.

Not Short on Entrants. Short on Conversions

If you are evaluating one of these 125 companies list in my database as either a partner, supplier, customer, investor, or a future employer, these four forces are on your due diligence checklist:

Regulatory credibility: Is the safety case built by the technical organization, or invented by licensing?

Capital and supply chain: Will a constructor actually bid on this project?

Organizational maturity: Is leadership a good steward of money and employees’ time, not just technically charismatic?

Operations and maintenance: Does the plan for keeping it running look as serious as the plan for building it?

Investors and future employees deserve more than a sense of whether they like a founder. Every dollar and every working hour given to a program optimizing for a story instead of megawatts on the grid is a dollar and an hour not given to a team that will actually get reactors built. That is why I wrote ‘Due Diligence’.18

Physics makes a reactor feasible. Governance makes it licensable. Institutional discipline makes it deployable.

I will be presenting this framework at the ANS Winter Conference in Phoenix, AZ, on Wednesday, November 18th, in the Nuclear Energy Markets, Financing, and Economics ~ Session II 10:00–11:45 AM MST . If you will be there, come argue with me.

About the Author

Sarah Gibboney, P.E., is Founder and CEO of Gibboney Nuclear, PLLC, a licensing and quality assurance consultancy that helps advanced reactor developers become licensable, financeable, buildable, and deployable.

Over more than seventeen years on the applicant and developer side, she has designed or licensed eight reactor designs, including reload design for operating light water reactors, and has worked across nearly every link of the fuel cycle, from enrichment and MOX construction and startup to spent fuel and waste disposal. She co-authored construction permit applications work for both of the firms that that are receiving cost-shared funding through the DOE Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program.

title: Worldwide Boom In Solar Power Might Just Bring Hope To Your Coal-Black Heart - Jalopnik
description:
In particular, a worldwide boom in solar power is rapidly shifting the economics of making a green transition on the power grid, which in turn aids a shift to electric vehicles.
Think of it this way: the entire world hit a combined 100 gigawatts of solar power in 2012.
And the world is picking, as over 75% of all new power capacity worldwide has been renewable since 2020.
In fact, in just the last five years, China alone built enough solar storage to power California and Texas for an entire day.
Southeast Asia is swinging hard towards renewable energy as a direct response, focusing on building out solar power in particular.
text:
There's a tendency to treat climate change like it's a lost cause, that inevitable doom is just around the corner, and that the Earth will be a wasteland in a generation or two (or sooner). It's true that ice caps are melting, sea levels are rising, extreme weather events keep getting worse, and even our roads and bridges are cracking in the heat. Quietly, though, some reasons for hope have started to emerge, like a green shoot somehow finding its way through cement. In particular, a worldwide boom in solar power is rapidly shifting the economics of making a green transition on the power grid, which in turn aids a shift to electric vehicles. A tipping point is coming when photons from the Sun move more electrons on Earth than burning old dinosaur bones, and it's sooner than you think. Let's not say we're saved just yet, but you can be optimistic without sounding crazy.

The solar boom took the world a bit by surprise, largely because it happened so quickly. Think of it this way: the entire world hit a combined 100 gigawatts of solar power in 2012. To get all the way up to 1 terawatt took a further 10 years. But getting to 2 terawatts happened just three years later, and getting to 3 terawatts took under two years. That is exponential growth in the amount of electricity coming from solar, and it hasn't slowed down. Current projections put the world at 9 terawatts of solar power by 2036.

Ah, but what about the United States, where the Trump administration has killed or delayed $83 billion in clean energy investments? Well, in the face of unrelenting headwinds from the federal government, solar power and storage only managed to be... 91% of all new grid capacity in the first quarter of 2026. In fact, over the last five years, more solar capacity has been built than any other type of power. Just in May, solar eclipsed coal in terms of total power output for the month, a first in the nation. If you're thinking this must be a blue state thing, think again. On March 14, Texas got 79% of its power from renewable energy. In fact, in 2026 Texas overtook California in utility-scale solar output.

Solar's superpower is simple: it's cheap. That wasn't always true, but at this point, it's usually less expensive to build a solar farm than a whole new fossil fuel plant. Beyond money, solar farms go up quickly, whereas fossil fuel plants take years to construct. Basically, if you want more power, there's an option that is quicker, cheaper, and greener (solar), and another that is the opposite. Which would you pick? And the world is picking, as over 75% of all new power capacity worldwide has been renewable since 2020. In fact, the fastest-growing energy technologies, ever, have been solar and wind in the last few years.

The results have been pretty striking. In June, the European Union – the entire EU! – got 25% of all its power from solar. That's pretty great! You know what's better? Making so much power from solar that your government just starts giving it to you for free. Last year, three Australian states just gave everyone electricity at no charge in midday, every day. It's worth noting that this excess electricity isn't even coming from utility-scale solar farms, but from privately owned rooftop solar just pushing that many electrons to the grid.

No matter how hard America tries to use Daylight Savings Time, the Sun sets anyway. Once upon a time, this was solar power's Achilles heel: it reached peak generation at noon, slowly faded throughout the afternoon, and dropped to zero at night. And of course there would be less light during winter or cloudy days, making for unreliable power. Better to just choke the planet with pollution instead.

But hey, did you know there's this thing called a "battery"? It's really neat, you can put electricity in it and then use it later. Battery storage at utility scale, which look a bit like shipping containers, has been one of the quiet triumphs of the last decade. In fact, in just the last five years, China alone built enough solar storage to power California and Texas for an entire day. Economies of scale mean that the more such batteries are made, the cheaper they get, leading to more batteries, which makes solar power a more reliable proposition, which leads to more solar, which leads to more batteries...

On July 9, California solar batteries discharged 13 gigawatts of power, or enough to power New York City on a hot day. Once a state famous for its rolling blackouts, this new storage capacity has allowed California to get through its hottest August on record without turning off anybody's lights.

The war in Iran has surged oil prices all over the world, which is having long-term ripple consequences. Southeast Asia is swinging hard towards renewable energy as a direct response, focusing on building out solar power in particular. Meanwhile, having 25% of its power come from solar has saved the EU about $42 billion in gas surcharges. Other countries are likely to start making strategic investments into green energy, where solar plus storage remains the cheapest option; individuals, aghast at the numbers on gas station display boards, are more likely to start considering electric cars.

All combined, this one conflict may bring up the year when global oil consumption peaks by three whole years, from 2029 to 2026. As in, it is just possible that we are living through the peak of fossil fuels right now, this very year. This is the most that fossil fuels will ever be burned. It's all downhill from here. That void is most likely to be filled by the Sun. Already, global emissions are down by 0.5% because the Strait of Hormuz is closed. The longer the war lasts, the faster the transition will come.

None of this is to say that all is well or that you should stop putting pressure on your elected officials to prioritize the environment. But the "all is lost" discourse hasn't kept pace with the rapid advances in solar and storage, which are on track to generate a significant percentage of all power worldwide in the not too distant future. And that's while there's a renewable-hostile administration in the White House. So maybe, just maybe, there's a little room for some optimism. You know, see the sunny side of things.

text:
North Carolina State House District 82 covers parts of the Concord and Harrisburg areas.

Republican Brian Echevarria will face Democratic candidate Chris Bishopp in the midterms.

Echevarria has not responded to our candidate guide questionnaire.

If we receive his response, we will publish it here.

Chris Bishopp (D)

Why are you running?

I am running to represent NC House District 82 because I believe the people of our district deserve a true choice and a representative who will put their needs ahead of party politics, special interests, and powerful corporations. Public office should be about service, accountability, and ensuring that every person has a meaningful voice in the decisions that affect their family and community.

I strongly believe in protecting free and fair elections, expanding opportunity, and making sure our government works for everyone — not just those with the most influence or resources. Our communities deserve leadership that listens, brings people together, and addresses issues that affect their everyday lives, including quality public education, good-paying jobs, affordable housing and healthcare, safe communities, and economic opportunity.

Are you in favor of the three constitutional amendments on North Carolina’s ballot? Why or why not?

Property tax amendment: I am against this amendment. Decisions about property taxes are best made by the local governments that understand the local economy and needs. There are 100 counties in this state, and they are very different. This amendment could require lawmakers in Raleigh to limit increases in local property tax levies, without telling voters what those limits would be. Depending on how those limits are written, this amendment could force cuts to services such as police, fire, and EMS, as well as funding for public schools and infrastructure. Local governments could face pressure to make up for the shortfalls through other means, such as user fees and sales tax. A statewide restriction risks overlooking the differences each municipality faces. Some are facing tremendous growth, while others are struggling with a shrinking economy, and some are somewhere in between. Voters deserve to know the actual limits and safeguards before being asked to put this requirement in the Constitution. “Trust us” is not a policy anyone should be comfortable voting for. The big winners, if this amendment passes, would be large corporations that already are getting a windfall from the decreasing corporate income tax.

3.5% cap on income tax: I am against this amendment. First, it could restrict future funding if the need arises due to a recession, another natural disaster, population growth, or the need for increased funding for schools, infrastructure, healthcare, or public safety. Second, it could shift the tax burden to other revenue sources, such as sales tax and fees, or force service cuts. Sales tax in particular takes a larger share of lower-income households’ earnings, in turn making the overall tax system more regressive. We should preserve the flexibility to respond to future needs, rather than lock a tax-rate ceiling into our Constitution.

Expanded voter ID: I am against this amendment. North Carolina already has a voter ID requirement for both in-person and absentee voting, with exceptions for eligible voters who cannot reasonably provide an acceptable ID. This amendment would extend the Constitution’s existing in-person requirement to all voting methods, making it more difficult to change in the future without constitutionally protecting those exceptions. I am concerned that narrowing those safeguards could create additional barriers for seniors, students, voters with disabilities, and military personnel serving away from home. The data shows that voter fraud is practically non-existent. This is a solution looking for a problem and just another attempt at voter suppression.

What should the state do about data centers?

First, we should institute a temporary moratorium on any new data center construction until we fully understand the impact on the environment, water resources, electric grid, and local communities. Second, we need legislation with explicit standards to ensure that the environment and resources are protected and that the local community is not forced to shoulder the burden with higher electricity rates and adverse effects to their local environment. Attorney General Jeff Jackson has proposed a separate rate schedule for these facilities, which I fully support. Once these regulations are in place, the ultimate decision should rest with the local governments.

CMS has faced numerous controversies over the past month, what, if anything, should state lawmakers do?

I am not a resident of Mecklenburg County, nor are CMS schools in NC House District 82, so I will not make a judgment on this issue.

What legislation will you pursue to bring down costs?

The North Carolina House Democratic Caucus has put forward an affordability agenda — introducing multiple bills that Republican leadership has not advanced — because families can no longer wait for the legislature to act on the cost-of-living crisis. Current General Assembly leadership refuses to adequately fund education, healthcare, mental health, public safety, and basic infrastructure. Democratic-proposed legislation such as HB 1063, the Ratepayer and Resource Protection Act; HB 1057, the Affordable Food Act; HB 1059, the Fair Minimum Wage Act; and HB 1175, the Affordability in Healthcare Act are just a few of the bills that have been submitted as part of this agenda. I will fight for these proposals and work to build the support needed to pass them, regardless of which party holds the majority.

What sets you apart from your opponent?

My approach is to always have the best interest of the people of this county guiding my decision-making. I believe big business in general, and Duke Energy in particular, have too much sway over the decisions being made by the GOP-controlled General Assembly, and my opponent is too willing to go along with that agenda. I also believe we need a nonpartisan redistricting committee to end gerrymandering and develop fair maps that do not violate citizens’ rights to have their vote count and manipulate our political system to keep one party or group in power. My opponent is on the House Select Committee on Redistricting that has approved all of this gerrymandering.

text:
Residents and businesses in the Metro Detroit area can compost their food scraps easily through the Scrap Soils pickup service. Scrap Soils is a nonprofit dedicated to making Detroit more sustainable by transforming food scraps and waste into soil.

Scrap Soils team members bring bins to homes and businesses for them to put their kitchen scraps into. The crew then comes by once a week to pick up the waste and bring it to Sanctuary Farms, which composts the scraps and turns it into nutrient-rich soil.

Food waste in landfills contributes to greenhouse gas emissions, as when it decomposes, it creates methane. Emily Cassidy, a research associate with the climate solutions nonprofit Project Drawdown, says composting can cut those emissions and help put nutrients back into the soil. She noted that cutting down on methane emissions may help slow climate change, according to the World Economic Forum.

Ricky Blanding, Scrap Soils co-founder and CEO, started the company in 2020. He grew up in Detroit and saw a need for a pickup composting business. Today, the company picks up kitchen scraps weekly from more than 70 homes and businesses.

The Grand Porter, a restaurant in southwest Detroit, is one customer. Executive chef Lou Hammer says the kitchen fills its compost bin with eggshells, cardboard, stale bread, tomato tops, and avocado skins. He notes that composting doesn't add extra work to his kitchen staff, as the pieces are already cut and ready to dispose of.

On Blanding's and his crew's weekly routes, which cover over 100 miles, they pick up a variety of food scraps, from old pumpkins to apple cores, corn husks, and coffee grounds. Farmers and gardeners can then visit the composting sites, like Sanctuary Farm, and buy nutrient-rich soil made from the local food scraps.

For Blanding, one of the challenges Scrap Soils faces is trying to grow the operation and encouraging residents and businesses to use the food scrap pickup service. In addition, people who use the service need to be aware of what can and what can't go into the bins for composting, such as peeling stickers on fruit.

Last year, Detroit launched its first city food scrap drop-off program, the City of Detroit's Office of Sustainability Compost Pilot Program, and hundreds of residents signed up for the program. Scrap Soils helped educate people about the food scrap-to-compost process. Detroit plans to open more drop-off sites.

Those steps fit into a climate strategy that aims to keep 15% of waste out of landfills through a three-year effort. The long-term plan also calls for ending municipal greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. The more people receive education on composting, and the easier it is for them to access composting bins, drop-off sites, and use pickup services, the more residents will help fill Detroit's environmental goals.

Other cities are creating and offering food scrap pickup and composting services, including Denver, Nashville, Atlanta, Raleigh, Durham, and Asheville. A 2023 report from BioCycle, a publication focused on composting and recycling, counted 400 residential food scrap programs with support from city officials.

Explore Scraps Soils' residential and commercial membership plans to help make Detroit more sustainable.

name: North Carolina American Energy
title: AI data centers' energy needs spur natural gas, solar growth, challenge power grids
authors: Mike Sunnucks, Adams MultiMedia, Sandra Costello
description: Artificial intelligence data centers demand vastly more power than traditional centers, with racks consuming up to 100 kW, driven by the surge in AI computing and machine learning needs. Energy consumption is a critical factor in the rapid deployment of new AI infrastructure globally.
text:
MADISON, Wis. (AP) — A coalition of Wisconsin school distric…

The botched execution of Christa Gail Pike in Tennessee on W…



Artificial intelligence (AI) data centers are a power play — literally.

The technical backbone to power AI’s computers and machine learning algorithms need significantly more electricity than existing data centers that have fueled the internet age.

A server rack in an existing, conventional data center consumes 5 to 10 kilowatts of electricity compared to AI data center racks, which require 40 to 100 kW, according to Hanwha Data Centers.

A single AI query or prompt uses 10 to 15 times more electricity than a traditional web search.

A data center uses 10 to 50 times more energy per square foot than a commercial office building.

The need for power is in tandem with the need for speed to market with new data centers. Hyperscalers and developers are projected to spend $7.6 trillion on AI data centers through 2031, according to Goldman Sachs.

That “force of capital” is the AI bus driving the search for consistent electricity flows, said Brandon Michalski, chief economist at MOCA Systems Inc., a Boston-based infrastructure technology firm.

“It’s all about available power,” Michalski said.

Data center developers and users are looking at various energy options for planned and proposed AI projects.

Some energy sources are more doable than others, at least for the first phases of the AI wave.

Natural gas is a top power source for new electricity-hungry data centers, according to Parag Nathaney, a Washington-based energy and electricity markets analyst.

Nathaney said right now data center builders’ preference is to be on the grid with close connections to natural gas pipelines. That helps get projects to the AI marketplace quicker.

Brandon Michalski

“Large gas-powered generators are what most data centers are using,” he said.

GE Vernova, Siemens, Mitsubishi, Generac and Caterpillar have seen upswings in orders for generators, turbines and energy equipment orders related to data centers.

Some data center builders are facing supply chain backlogs.

Britt Burt, senior vice president for power industry research at Texas-based Industrial Info Resources, said some data center builders and users are looking at using repurposed aerospace and engines as well as hydrogen fuel cells to power AI’s computers and machines.

Natural gas demand from data centers could increase by close to 20% by 2030, according to an analysis by Christopher Louney, a commodity strategist for RBC Capital Markets.

“U.S. natural gas offers strategic advantages due to insularity from geopolitical volatility, abundant domestic supply, and fully utilized LNG (liquefied natural gas) capacity,” Louney said.

Some data centers are looking to locate near natural gas pipelines with some new connections being built.

Natural gas supplied 40% of energy needed for data centers in the U.S. in 2024, according to a report by the International Energy Agency (IEA).

Renewable energy accounted for 24% followed by nuclear and coal with 20% and 15% respectively.

The agency said natural gas and renewables have the supplies and growth trajectories to offer additional energy for the expected data center surge.

Louney agrees.

"On-site gas generation is being increasingly viewed as a permanent fixture of the digital infrastructure landscape through decade's end at least, and potentially beyond,” he said in his analysis.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration projects data centers growth to help increase U.S. solar generation by 21% in 2026 and 18% in 2027.

U.S. President Donald Trump is a strong advocate for the AI wave and the data centers to power them.

The Trump administration wants to allow data center developers and users to build their own off-meter power plants for their AI projects.

Trump has also eased regulations and encouraged more natural gas and other domestic energy production such as oil and coal. Some coal-fired power plants are being given new life by the data center wave, to the chagrin of those concerns about emissions.

In August, the U.S. Energy Information Administration projected the highest domestic natural gas production since 2016.

The U.S. agency said developers plan to bring 44.9 billion cubic feet per day of new pipeline capacity in the U.S. in 2026 and 2027. Sixty-six percent of that new capacity is in Texas, which is seeing significant data center growth, and Louisiana, which is seeing data center interest.

In Texas, Chevron and Microsoft announced in June a 20-year deal for the energy conglomerate to provide off-meter natural gas for a 2.67 gigawatt power plant and AI data center near Pecos, Texas.

The project is off-grid from the local utility.

Kim Lundgren, CEO of sustainability consulting firm Kim Lundgren Associates (KLA), said the global energy surge raises concerns about emissions linked to climate change.

“This is all coming to the local level,” she said.

While natural gas does not have the emissions of coal-fired power plants, methane leaks from transport and pipelines are a significant driver of climate change, according to the Climate & Clean Air Coalition.

Kim Lundgren

Some developers and users have talked about nuclear energy, via leveraging nuclear plants or installing small micro-reactors, to power AI data centers.

Constellation Energy is pumping $1.6 billion into reopening a reactor at the Three Mile Island Nuclear Generating Station in Pennsylvania as part of a 20-year deal to provide power for Microsoft’s new AI data centers.

NextEra Energy and Alphabet/Google are partnering to reopen the 615-megawatt Duane Arnold Energy Center nuclear plant in Iowa. The facility closed in 2020 after weather damage and is slated to reopen in 2029.

TerraPower, a Bill Gates-backed energy company, is building a nuclear reactor in Wyoming, adjacent to a coal plant, to help offer energy to large users, including data centers.

But nuclear power has its own set of worries over safety, Lundgren said.

Nuclear energy also has high startup costs and long approval processes, according to Arif Gasilov, a partner with the Gasilov Group, an Arizona-based energy and infrastructure consulting firm.

“It just requires a lot of upfront investment,” he said.

Gasilov said he does not expect nuclear energy options to be ready for AI data centers until 2030-2035.

That could result in new data centers relying on natural gas going forward.

“Some might stay on gas,” Gasilov said.

New data centers also face potential supply chain backlogs and delays for energy and technology equipment.

Demand is high for generators, turbines and other equipment.

The U.S. power grid and local energy infrastructure also needs to be ready for a potential doubling or tripling of electricity consumption driven by AI data centers.

“The nation is vastly underbuilt in transmission lines,” Michalski said.

Much of the country’s electricity infrastructure is also older. Seventy percent of transformers and transmission lines are 25 years or older and 60% of circuit breakers are 30 years or older, according to the American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE) and Georgia-based utility MEAG Power.

On Sept. 24, the Trump administration announced it was dispensing $1.9 billion to utilities across the country for transmission lines and power grid improvements.

Utilities, including ones in Washington state, North Carolina, Tennessee, Florida and Ohio, will put $3.35 billion towards the efforts to rebuild more than 1,500 miles of transmission lines and upgrade another 21,000 miles of lines, according to the U.S. Department of Energy.

Energy use and the potential for higher utility bills for ratepayers are some of the concerns cited by AI data center opponents in their pushes for development moratoriums, as well as codifying cost assurances and protections for other ratepayers.

“Data centers must pay their own way to lower our electricity costs,” said North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein, a Democrat, in a statement, calling for state regulators to codify utilities’ rate pledges.

Survival for European OEMs will depend on a shift in strategy.
text:
Natixis CIB Thematic Research is launching an Electric Vehicle Quarterly series to track the transformation of the automotive industry and its implications for growth, trade, investment and corporate profitability.

Authored by Valentin Mory, Gary Ng, and Jiayu Huang, each edition combines market, technology and regulatory updates, as well as a chartbook of demand and production data.

The inaugural issue examines Chinese carmakers’ rapid overseas expansion and Europe’s subsequent response. Interview.

The surge in Chinese EV penetration in Europe is driven by key domestic pressures in China combined with favorable market conditions in Europe. Characterized by dwindling first-time buyers and a halving of tax relief in 2025, China's weak domestic demand no longer absorbs production capacity as fast as it is built. This has left Chinese manufacturers grappling with a low domestic capacity utilization rate of just 71%. The resulting persistent overcapacity has forced an accelerated overseas export push to keep factories running.

Conversely, European EV adoption continues to accelerate, with battery electric vehicle (BEVs) and hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) accounting for 32% of new car registrations in the first half of the year. This demand is fueled by newly introduced purchase incentives across the continent, rising fuel costs, and rapid charging infrastructure rollouts - for instance, ultra-fast chargers now make up 11.8% of the network.

On the other hand, China's alternative export markets have narrowed. With the US eliminating federal tax credits and nations like Brazil (35%) and Mexico (50%) imposing prohibitive tariffs, Europe remains the most open and lucrative major market. Consequently, Chinese OEMs successfully absorbed much of Europe’s BEV growth.

The scale of China's dominance is unprecedented. By mid-2025, China displaced Japan as the world's largest vehicle producer. Chinese brands (including acquisitions) now produce 28% of all cars globally - surpassing Japan (26%) and Europe (22%) - while manufacturing nearly three-quarters of the world's EVs and controlling the battery supply chain.

However, the nature of the competition has evolved. Chinese brands are used to gaining market share overseas through lower prices, faster product cycles and increasingly competitive technology. Realizing that relentless domestic price wars and razor-thin margins are unsustainable, Chinese brands are moving beyond entry-level models.

In addition, Chinese regulators recently issued guidelines urging overseas-bound OEMs to adopt fair trade practices and ensure export pricing reflects actual production costs. This aligns with ongoing EU discussions aimed at tightening import conditions.

Indeed, the five-year agreement signed last Friday - by which China has agreed to cap its hybrid vehicle exports to the EU at 350,000 units annually - is a significant tactical development in a long-standing negotiation process. Starting this December, it will effectively limit Chinese OEMs to capturing no more than 3% of the EU market through their hybrid vehicle offerings. As part of the deal, China has also agreed to ease restrictions on rare earths licensing, drop some tariffs on car parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU.

In our opinion, by agreeing to this cap, China has bought valuable time while providing immediate relief to European automakers and suppliers. In a technology segment that Chinese manufacturers have strongly favored, since it was previously exempt from tariffs, unlike Chinese BEV imports. It also enables Chinese OEMs to continue selling their BEVs without being subject to stricter trade tariffs.

Crucially, however, the quota does not apply to Chinese vehicles assembled within the EU, leaving a strategic gateway open for Chinese technology to remain highly competitive on European soil.

Chinese OEMs are now positioning themselves on high-end, premium vehicles (priced above RMB 300,000) packed with advanced technology. By offering feature-rich premium models at highly competitive prices, they are directly challenging the historically resilient pricing power and margins of European premium brands.

This adds pressure on European legacy brands, but they are not down for the count. While the rapid influx of Chinese competitors has compressed margins, triggered painful restructurings, and placed credit outlooks under negative watch, profitability remains an uphill battle for Chinese OEMs as well. The Chinese EV sector has largely operated at a loss, heavily reliant on state subsidies, with only a select few players actually breaking even.

Survival for European OEMs will depend on a shift in strategy. The years 2026–2027 look like an inflection point, as European manufacturers are currently exiting a heavy capital expenditure cycle. From 2026 onward, lower spending on software and manufacturing should provide meaningful support to free cash flow. Operating margins, however, will depend more on restructuring efforts delivering results and on BEV offerings reaching critical scale from 2027 onward.

title: Morgan Stanley Cuts Lucid's Target to Lowest Among Wall Street Peers | EV
description:
Morgan Stanley cut its price target on Lucid to $3 from $5 on Thursday and kept its ‘Underweight’ rating, extending five years of mostly bearish coverage of the EV manufacturer.
Morgan Stanley has rated Lucid ‘Underweight’ for all but about nine months since it began covering the company in September 2021, and its analysts have never recommended buying the shares.
An Underweight Start Jonas initiated coverage on September 14, 2021, with an ‘Underweight’ rating and a $12 target, about 40% below the previous day’s close of $20.06.
On May 6, 2026, after Lucid’s first-quarter results, Percoco halved the target to $5 and kept the ‘Underweight’ rating.
Morgan Stanley kept the ‘Underweight’ rating and $5 target through the summer, including after Lucid’s second-quarter results in August, before Thursday’s cut.
text:
Morgan Stanley cut its price target on Lucid to $3 from $5 on Thursday and kept its ‘Underweight’ rating, extending five years of mostly bearish coverage of the EV manufacturer.

The new target from analyst Andrew Percoco, which was first reported by StreetInsider, is about 9% below the Wednesday’s closing price of $3.29.

Morgan Stanley’s cut is the firm’s third since December, when it downgraded the stock and lowered the target to $10 from $30.

The cut comes ten days after Lucid reported third-quarter deliveries of 3,806 vehicles, down 6.7% from a year earlier, and less than a week after the company disclosed a further $400 million draw on its credit line from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF).

Earlier this week, RBC Capital Markets cut its target to $4.

Lucid is due to report third-quarter results on November 9.

Morgan Stanley has rated Lucid ‘Underweight’ for all but about nine months since it began covering the company in September 2021, and its analysts have never recommended buying the shares.

Over five years, the bank’s view has moved from an outright bearish start through a brief neutral period in 2025, when Adam Jonas, then the bank’s Lucid analyst, argued Lucid could become a “socket” for AI, and back to ‘Underweight’ on concerns about losses and dilution.

An Underweight Start

Jonas initiated coverage on September 14, 2021, with an ‘Underweight’ rating and a $12 target, about 40% below the previous day’s close of $20.06.

“Lucid is a highly vertically integrated BEV company that addresses the premium market at Tesla and above,” he wrote.

“However, we find ourselves asking how big is the market for this level of premium EVs and what are reasonable levels of risks that investors should shoulder in order to take what may eventually be only a modest slice of a crowded premium BEV market.”

“At a $31bn valuation, the stock market appears to be ascribing an unusually high probability of scenarios where LCID achieves very high market share, margins or both,” he wrote.

“We think LCID can occupy a sustainable niche place in a difficult market,” he added, while saying the road ahead would likely bring “many obstacles.”

He raised the target to $16 on November 17, 2021, after Lucid’s third-quarter results, while keeping the ‘Underweight’ rating.

On March 3, 2022, he cut the target back to $12 after Lucid lowered its 2022 production outlook to 12,000 to 14,000 vehicles from 20,000.

After the first-quarter results in May 2022, Jonas wrote, “We forecast 9.9k deliveries for FY22 which we believe may be on the aggressive side.”

He described Lucid as “not fully funded” in the same note.

In October 2022, he wrote that “the relationship between the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA) and Lucid could extend beyond a controlling shareholder status.”

‘Really Nice Car’

In January 2023, after Tesla cut prices by up to 20% in the US and Europe, Jonas halved his target to $5 from $10, calling the cuts “just the latest sign the EV market may be entering the ‘shake-out’ phase.”

He wrote that Lucid “builds cars for more than they sell them for.”

“As other EV manufacturers grind car prices lower, we think Lucid would need to react by lowering ATPs alongside them (making their loss-making vehicles even more loss-making), and/or brace for lower unit sale volumes,” he wrote, referring to average transaction prices.

On January 31, 2023, he summed up his view as “Really nice car, large cap valuation, niche market, continued cash needs.”

“In the wake of Tesla’s price cuts, we would be prepared for potentially further declines in reservations, assuming they are still reported,” he wrote.

“Taken together with SBC impact, we have forecasted a further 25% increase in LCID diluted shares outstanding through FY26,” he added, referring to stock-based compensation.

He also wrote that “forthcoming manufacturing innovation at rival Tesla could drive a step-change in EV deflation.”

After the fourth-quarter results in February 2023, he said, “We remain fans of LCID’s innovative technologies and talented management team.”

“Unlike many other startups, the company has shown an ability to deliver a compelling product to the end customer,” he said, while warning that “the high price point of most of the Lucid Air vehicle line is proving to attract a more limited addressable audience.”

He reiterated the ‘Underweight’ rating and $5 target in July 2023.

The target stood at $4 in February 2024, according to TipRanks, and at $3 by late 2024, when Jonas wrote that Lucid’s third-quarter results “did not materially change the narrative or our assessment of risk/reward for LCID shares.”

The ‘Socket’ for the AI ‘Brain’

In March 2025, Jonas upgraded Lucid to ‘Equal-weight‘, kept the $3 target and set a $10 bull case, and the shares rose more than 14% in early trading on March 18.

“More than an ‘EV 1.0’ automaker?” he wrote.

“Following the announced/ongoing changes in leadership, we believe Lucid has opportunity to execute an AI strategy leveraging strategic/sovereign partnerships within the context of the urgency to develop onshore manufacturing capacity for BEVs as the ‘socket’ for the AI ‘brain’.”

“We believe that at this stage, the risks to upside are more equilibrated with the risks to downside for Lucid shares,” he wrote.

“It’s difficult for us to see how near term quarterly results introduce new negative information that a bearish consensus doesn’t already expect.”

He also wrote that Lucid’s access to capital and strategic relationships could “uniquely position Lucid to straddle geopolitical hurdles in potentially partnering with both China and the West.”

When Lucid announced a robotaxi partnership with Nuro and Uber in July 2025, Jonas reiterated his ‘Equal-weight’ rating and called it a possible first of many strategic deals.

“Electric machines are the corporeal ‘sockets’ for AI brain,” he wrote.

“While $300mn in new equity funding from Uber equates to <1 quarter of cash burn for LCID, the investment may help to better align incentives between the two companies while providing modest financial cushion as Lucid ramps production of Gravity,” he wrote.

The bank moved its target to $30 on September 2, 2025, the day Lucid’s shares began trading after a one-for-10 reverse split, leaving the rating unchanged.

Back to Underweight

By December, coverage had passed to Percoco, who downgraded Lucid back to ‘Underweight’ on December 8, 2025, and cut the target to $10 from $30.

The downgrade came with an outlook in which Morgan Stanley described the US EV as heading into an “EV winter” in 2026, according to Barchart.

“Lucid’s premium positioning and higher ASPs help buffer near-term volatility from the loss of EV tax credits relative to other mass-market EV OEMs,” Percoco wrote.

He said Lucid’s “path to profitability hinges on successfully scaling its more affordable midsize platform,” with production due to start in late 2026 and ramp in 2027.

He wrote that “we do not forecast Lucid to reach gross profitability until 2028,” adding that EBIT losses per vehicle would improve “from $216k/vehicle in 2025 to $126k in 2026” but “persist until 2031.”

“In the interim, we see significant dilution risk for shareholders as we estimate it will need to raise ~$2bn of equity by 2H26 (relative to its $4.6bn market cap),” he wrote.

On May 6, 2026, after Lucid’s first-quarter results, Percoco halved the target to $5 and kept the ‘Underweight’ rating.

On that quarter’s earnings call, he had pressed management on free cash flow and liquidity through at least the second half of 2027.

Then-Chief Financial Officer Taoufiq Boussaid replied, “You need to recall that there is a typical seasonality in the company,” linking the first-quarter cash burn to a stop-sale on the Gravity SUV.

Morgan Stanley kept the ‘Underweight’ rating and $5 target through the summer, including after Lucid’s second-quarter results in August, before Thursday’s cut.

How the Calls Played Out

At $3.29, Lucid’s shares are worth the equivalent of about $0.33 before the reverse split, about 98% below their close the day before Morgan Stanley’s initiation.

They are about 85% below their level before the March 2025 upgrade, based on the 39% upside that Jonas’s $3 target implied at the time.

The shares have fallen 68.7% year to date based on the $3.32 price the stock was trading at as of publication time.

### About Silicon Valley Clean Energy Silicon Valley Clean Energy is a not-for-profit, community-owned agency providing electricity from renewable and clean sources to more than 280,000 residential and commercial customers in 13 Santa Clara County jurisdictions.
Silicon Valley Clean Energy customers receive clean power, competitive rates, and unique offers and services that reduce fossil fuel use, helping create a safer, healthier region.
text:
Menlo Park, Calif. – Silicon Valley Clean Energy (SVCE) recognized two organizations with the Building a Healthier Bay Area Award at the Best of Silicon Valley hosted by Modern Luxury Magazine in late September. Reuben Veek, Executive Director of SunWork, a Bay Area-based non-profit, and Bronwyn Barry, founder of Passive House BB, received this award for their leadership in helping Bay Area residents and businesses understand the benefits of electric equipment and increasing access to technologies that support healthier, safer, more comfortable living.

“In the Bay Area, we are actually out of federal clean air standards, and this pollution is known to increase risks of lung disease, heart disease and even dementia,” said Zoe Elizabeth, Director of Decarbonization Policy and Community Strategies at SVCE. “Gas-powered water and space heating alone accounts for nearly 40% of local emissions in Silicon Valley. Replacing those appliances with efficient, electric versions has an immediate and long-term impact.”

The Building a Healthier Bay Area Award recognizes the recipients’ efforts to address two significant barriers to building electrification: access to affordable pathways for making upgrades and lack of awareness about the benefits of modern electric technologies.

Electric appliances such as heat pump water heaters, heat pump heating and cooling systems, and induction cooktops reduce exposure to outdoor and indoor air pollutants associated with fossil fuel combustion, while improving comfort, safety and efficiency. Even with these benefits, many residents remain unfamiliar with available equipment or are uncertain about the cost of making upgrades.

SunWork is focused on making clean energy upgrades more accessible. Through education, hands-on support, and a commitment to serving residents, SunWork has helped countless homeowners take practical steps toward healthier, more efficient homes and is ensuring that the contractors making these upgrades possible are prepared to support this market transition. SunWork also provides subject matter expertise to policymakers on some of the most complex buildings to electrify. Their work demonstrates that the transition to clean energy can benefit every corner of the community.

“I’m grateful for the ongoing opportunity that I have to contribute alongside the smart, passionate, imaginative, thoughtful people all around the Bay Are who are working to make hot water and comfortable indoor air temperatures available without air pollution. It’s a real honor to have that work recognized in this way.” Said Reuben Veek, Executive Director of SunWork.

Both honorees have played important roles in expanding awareness of electric living and helping communities overcome practical barriers to adoption.

“Technology alone does not transform communities,” Elizabeth said. “The clean energy transition succeeds because of people who educate, inspire, and guide others toward solutions that improve daily life. SunWork and Bronwyn Barry exemplify that leadership.”

SVCE works with local governments, contractors, community organizations, and industry leaders throughout Santa Clara County to increase access to healthy, safe electric equipment. Rebates and resources to help customers go electric can be found at svcleanenergy.org.

text:
Although there has been a lot of turbulence in the wind power markets, land-based and offshore wind remain a powerful and resilient force for powering communities across America. ACP’s Research team has compiled and analyzed data from its members, producing a report that seeks to orient industry professionals to current market conditions, the state of policy, and the evolving technological landscape.

Overall, the outlook on wind power is strong. Presenting a balanced analysis of land-based and offshore wind’s current contributions to the U.S. grid, the report also dives into what the future of wind power holds; most notably, land-based wind capacity is expected to reach 202 GW by 2030, or enough power to supply 58 million homes.

Report Highlights:

Current land-based and offshore wind capacity is 166 GW as of Q2 2026, generating enough electricity to power 48 million homes.

Eleven percent of total U.S. electricity was generated by wind in the last 12 months, and 13% of new grid-connected capacity additions through 2030 will be land-based and offshore wind.

Forty-three states have at least one operational land-based wind project, and 22 states have at least one land-based wind project in the pipeline.

Iowa led the country in wind power generation, creating 57% of its electricity from land-based wind facilities, while South Dakota closely followed at nearly 56%. Regionally, the Great Plains has the largest share of generation from wind resources with 43%. Texas, as a region, ranks second with 22%, while the Midwest, Mountain West, and Northwest rounded out the top five at 16%, 15%, and 12%, respectively.

Year-over-year, the land-based wind pipeline dropped 4%, as the pause on federal permits from the U.S. Department of Defense obstructed 310 pre-construction projects from advancing to active construction.

title: What's up with Pennsylvania's hydrogen hubs? - Canary Media
description:
During a 2023 speech at Philadelphia’s Tioga Terminal, President Joe Biden assured the crowd that Pennsylvania’s two hubs — the Mid-Atlantic Clean Hydrogen Hub and the Appalachian Regional Clean Hydrogen Hub, commonly known as MACH2 and ARCH2 — would be transformational.
Oil and gas proponents wanted more carve-outs for blue hydrogen hubs, like ARCH2; environmentalists wanted to ensure that the subsidies went to hubs running solely off of clean energy, rather than pulling from Pennsylvania’s gas-heavy grid.
To complicate matters, green hydrogen, which involves using clean energy to produce a different kind of clean energy, is notoriously difficult to produce cost effectively.
Producers need to both find customers for their hydrogen and meet the deadlines to claim the 45V green-hydrogen tax credit and the 45Q carbon-capture credit, in the case of blue hydrogen hubs.
As a green hydrogen hub, MACH2 was dependent on the development of solar and offshore wind in order to operate.
text:
This article was originally published by Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, nonpartisan news organization that covers climate, energy, and the environment. Sign up for its newsletter.

Three years ago, hydrogen seemed poised for a long-awaited breakthrough. The Biden administration announced $7 billion in federal funding for seven hubs to produce the fuel across the country, and Pennsylvania was set to be a major player in the emerging industry.

Hydrogen has long been heralded as a potential skeleton key to emission reductions: able to power commuter vehicles and mass transportation, as well as hard-to-decarbonize industries like shipping and steel production.

During a 2023 speech at Philadelphia’s Tioga Terminal, President Joe Biden assured the crowd that Pennsylvania’s two hubs — the Mid-Atlantic Clean Hydrogen Hub and the Appalachian Regional Clean Hydrogen Hub, commonly known as MACH2 and ARCH2 — would be transformational. The hubs would connect a vast network of hydrogen producers, users, and researchers across Pennsylvania, Delaware, New Jersey, West Virginia, and Ohio. They were backed by a bipartisan coalition and designed to bring economic opportunity to red states, with support in Pennsylvania from both Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) and Sen. Dave McCormick (R). In 2023, Shapiro’s office said the hubs would ​“ensure Pennsylvania continues to be an energy leader for decades to come.”

MACH2 promised to bring over 20,000 jobs to the Delaware Valley region alone and lead the way in green hydrogen, produced entirely from clean energy, with a $750 million award from the Department of Energy. ARCH2 would receive $925 million to manufacture blue hydrogen, produced via fossil fuels, with emissions sequestered by carbon-capture technology. ARCH2 would be centered on Western Pennsylvania’s steel industry.

Today, that momentum has all but disappeared, one of many clean energy investments facing an uncertain future under the Trump administration. ARCH2 has gone totally dark, with former partners denying involvement or stonewalling media requests, and MACH2 has entered a holding pattern. Experts with knowledge of the hubs say that the federal government has been playing a game of ​“will they, won’t they” — changing their minds from week to week.

Community groups that initially opposed the hubs say they’ve heard nothing about the projects for months, although Manny Cintron, CEO of MACH2, told Inside Climate News via email that the hub’s ​“award is active,” but partners ​“continue to proceed cautiously in light of the current budget uncertainty.” In other words, no one wants to move forward with investment until they have a sense of whether the federal government will continue to fund the hub. As of late September, MACH2 was still circulating a request from January for potential partners to join the hub. The Department of Energy did not respond to repeated requests for comment.

“Until I see significant evidence to the contrary, I just don’t think the hubs are happening,” said Tom Torres, chief of staff at the Ohio River Valley Institute, a think tank focused on Appalachia.

This outcome is exactly what the hydrogen industry feared in the wake of the 2024 election. Losing the funding is going to ​“harm Pennsylvania,” Shapiro told Axios last year. ​“It’s going to mean we’re producing less energy. I have no idea why the president of the United States would want to do that.”

Even before Donald Trump took office, the hubs were facing an uphill battle, held up by a long lobbying fight over who would qualify for the 45V tax credits, which offered producers up to $3 per kilogram of hydrogen produced. Oil and gas proponents wanted more carve-outs for blue hydrogen hubs, like ARCH2; environmentalists wanted to ensure that the subsidies went to hubs running solely off of clean energy, rather than pulling from Pennsylvania’s gas-heavy grid. The debate dragged on nearly until Biden left office, delaying investment and leaving the projects in limbo.

To complicate matters, green hydrogen, which involves using clean energy to produce a different kind of clean energy, is notoriously difficult to produce cost effectively. The fuel is created through a process called electrolysis — essentially, running an electrical current through water, which separates the hydrogen and the oxygen. If you hook a solar panel up to an electrolyzer, about 30 percent of the energy from that panel will be lost just in the process of isolating the hydrogen. By the time you compress it into a fuel cell or liquefy it for transport, then convert it back into electricity, about 70 percent of the energy generated by that original solar panel is gone. And even once you’ve managed to produce it, hydrogen is exceedingly leaky — the smallest element in the periodic table, able to escape even from sealed steel vats.

This is part of why the hubs drew so much pushback from environmental groups, who decried the fuel as a false solution when Biden’s plans were first announced. The United States currently produces about 10 million metric tons of hydrogen per year, almost all of which are made using oil and gas. Clean hydrogen is significantly more expensive, and even with subsidies, experts have warned that it will never be a practical or cost-competitive fuel for public transit, personal vehicles, or commercial and residential heating.

But it is critical when it comes to replacing carbon-intensive chemical feedstocks that create products like ammonia, which is used to make fertilizer. Ammonia production alone accounts for roughly 2 percent of global energy consumption and 1.5 percent of greenhouse gas emissions. Green ammonia could also aid in decarbonizing global shipping, which produces another 3 percent of global emissions.

Under the Biden administration, MACH2 made a show of partnering with SEPTA, Philadelphia’s public transit system, to test hydrogen-powered buses. In the hub’s application, though, it was made clear that the main offtakers for MACH2 would, at least initially, be area oil refineries — a tough sell for community and environmental-justice groups, which were already concerned about hydrogen’s high flammability and its potential to serve as an indirect greenhouse gas, magnifying the effects of methane, ozone, and water vapor.

The second Trump administration gutted the Inflation Reduction Act, which invested billions in clean energy and incentives, but most of the hydrogen hubs were spared, at least on paper. Two hubs slated for California and the Pacific Northwest lost funding early on and remain mired in a legal battle, but the generous 45V hydrogen tax credit survived, albeit on a truncated timeline. Although it was initially reported that MACH2 was on the chopping block, Energy Secretary Chris Wright announced in April that the hydrogen hubs would retain their funding — but to what end is entirely unclear.

“What matters in the U.S. more than hub status is whether individual projects are going ahead,” Martin Tengler, head of hydrogen research at BloombergNEF, told Inside Climate News in an email. Producers need to both find customers for their hydrogen and meet the deadlines to claim the 45V green-hydrogen tax credit and the 45Q carbon-capture credit, in the case of blue hydrogen hubs. ​“All these have been a challenge, except 45Q,” said Tengler.

Producers now have until December 31, 2027 to begin work before the tax credits expire, rather than the original deadline of 2032. That deadline seems all but impossible to meet, especially given the fact that the DOE does not plan to spend any more on the hubs this year, according to its July apportionment plan. ARCH2 could choose to take advantage of the 45Q tax credits for carbon capture, which don’t expire until 2033, but like MACH2, it’s only drawn about one-fifth of its total Phase One award money, ​“a drop in the bucket of the overall award,” said Torres.

Despite their funding reprieve, it’s not clear that the hubs will be able to hold on to that money over the next few years. The 2027 President’s Budget Request released in April calls for ​“permanently cancelling” unobligated funding for clean hydrogen programs and repurposing ​“Green New Scam funding” in favor of baseload power upgrades and spending $1.2 billion on the construction of seven AI supercomputers at Argonne and Oak Ridge National Laboratories.

As a green hydrogen hub, MACH2 was dependent on the development of solar and offshore wind in order to operate. Although some solar projects are still moving forward, the American offshore wind industry has been effectively kneecapped over the last two years by the Trump administration.

Atlantic Shores Offshore Wind and Invenergy backed out of their contracts in 2025 amid delays and regulatory uncertainty, and early-stage products were abandoned after the Trump administration began paying companies out of their offshore-wind leases. In April, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities announced that it would no longer be building infrastructure to connect offshore wind to the grid. As a blue hydrogen hub, ARCH2 existed largely as a way for oil and gas to continue operating under stricter emissions regulations — somewhat redundant now that the Trump administration has moved to scrap emissions regulations for power plants entirely.

This was always part of the problem with the Biden administration’s initial plans, said Anika Juhn, an energy data analyst at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. Even if the government is willing to temporarily subsidize the production of clean hydrogen, that support won’t be enough unless there are complementary incentives on the demand side.

“The hydrogen story is really an ammonia story, in the U.S. at least,” said Juhn. Without subsidies to offset the increased cost of buying clean fertilizer for farmers, it’s difficult to build up a domestic market — meaning any green ammonia that is produced in the United States will ultimately be shipped overseas.

For the green steel industry, it’s a major setback, said Hilary Lewis, steel director at Industrious Labs. ​“I think it’s kind of surprising to folks that we still make steel the way that you imagine in your head — big, hot furnaces, with hot metal flying everywhere, dirty coal going in, and lots of pollution,” said Lewis. ​“That’s still how we do it. It’s how we’ve been doing it for centuries.”

Some indirect progress has been made toward cleaner steel, although not in Pennsylvania. Those old-fashioned furnaces Lewis described are known as blast furnaces: aging, inefficient, and impossible to run in an emissions-friendly way. The more modern furnaces, which are known as direct-reduced-iron furnaces, are also significantly cleaner. At the moment they run on methane, but a facility like the $5.8 billion steel mill being built by Hyundai in Louisiana could eventually be converted to green hydrogen. ​“There are two steps to modernizing Pennsylvania’s iron and steel industry: one is getting clean hydrogen available,” said Lewis. ​“And the other is building these new furnaces to replace the existing coal-based furnaces.”

In the meantime, Torres said, many former hydrogen hub partners are pivoting to the energy cause du jour — data centers. He pointed to the Adams Fork Energy Project in West Virginia, which was initially conceived as a coal-to-gas facility. In 2023 it joined the ARCH2 hub as a partner with plans to build a massive ammonia hub, but was later dropped from the project. This year, the same company pivoted to constructing gas plants to power a data center. At least four other former ARCH2 partners — Hog Lick Aggregates, EQT, Fidelis New Energy, and CNX Resources — have joined them.
