text:
Vulcan to commercialize technology enabled by multi-year contract to expand the frontier of magnetic performance

DURHAM, N.C., Oct. 15, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Vulcan Elements, an American rare earth magnet manufacturer, today announced that the company's Co-Founder and Chief Technology Officer, Dr. Piotr Kulik, will lead a multi-year research effort competitively selected for funding by the U.S. Department of Energy's Advanced Research Projects Agency–Energy (ARPA-E) to develop novel magnetic materials potentially more powerful than rare earth magnets. As the project progresses, Vulcan will explore opportunities to commercialize this new technology to deliver unprecedented magnetic performance. Dr. Kulik also serves as an Assistant Professor at the University of Central Florida (UCF).

The three-year project will enable novel research on the discovery, modeling, synthesis, and validation of new high-performance magnetic materials. This research has the potential to pave the way for magnets that exceed the current limits on magnetic performance, while reducing requirements for rare earth inputs.

Dr. Kulik will lead the research effort in collaboration with scientists at UCF and the Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), leveraging the laboratory's Frontier exascale supercomputer to accelerate the discovery and design of next-generation magnetic materials.

This unique capacity will leverage advanced computational modeling to explore non-rare earth inputs for magnets, with the goal of identifying materials capable of exceptional magnetic performance. As promising candidates are identified, Vulcan Elements will help develop pathways toward commercialization and manufacturing, drawing on its expertise in materials science, advanced manufacturing, and production scale-up.

"Through the combined efforts of government, industry, and academia, this research has the potential to drive a generational leap in magnetic materials development," said Dr. Kulik. "I look forward to continuing our collaboration with the world-class researchers at Oak Ridge National Laboratory to advance discoveries that could transform our energy infrastructure, strengthen national security, and reinforce American technological leadership. At Vulcan, we believe the future of magnet manufacturing lies not simply in replicating existing technologies, but in developing fundamentally new materials and processes that move the industry forward. ARPA-E is helping make that vision possible."

Vulcan Elements CEO John Maslin added: "This partnership is a model for how the United States can bend the curve for the magnetics industry and the entire advanced economy. By leveraging the nation's most sophisticated research talent, most advanced computational capability, and fastest growing magnetics manufacturing infrastructure, Dr. Kulik, ARPA-E, and Vulcan will drive tectonic change for our supply chains for years to come."

ARPA-E is the Department of Energy's "disruption wing" whose mission is to enhance the economic and energy security and technological leadership of the United States through the development of advanced energy technologies. The organization has a demonstrated record of funding groundbreaking technologies since its establishment in 2009.

Vulcan has developed a proven solution to one of the country's most critical economic vulnerabilities, and to its knowledge is the world's only rare earth magnet company that is decoupled from China—down to the material, technology, software, IP, and ownership. Vulcan Elements' Benson, North Carolina, manufacturing facility currently under construction will be the cornerstone of a domestic rare earth magnet supply chain and the largest rare earth magnet factory outside of China. The 1.1 million square foot facility will have an annual capacity of 10,000 metric tons of magnet production and will supply magnets for critical defense systems, semiconductor fabrication, robotics, drones, AI infrastructure, automobiles, and other strategic technologies and sectors of the American economy.

Vulcan Elements is an American rare earth magnet manufacturer driven by a core mission: to rebuild a secure, resilient rare earth magnet supply chain for America and its allies, and enable the technologies that will define the 21st century. Vulcan's world-class engineering, scientific rigor, and uncompromising work ethic are onshoring a fundamental capability to the United States and setting a new standard for advanced rare earth magnet production. title: House-Passed SPEED Act Would Narrow Federal Environmental Reviews | Legis1
description:
The bill would amend the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the foundational statute governing federal environmental reviews of major projects.
The bill would also restrict certain judicial challenges to environmental reviews.
Under current NEPA, federal agencies must conduct environmental reviews for certain proposed actions, with the most intensive review, an EIS, generally required for actions with reasonably foreseeable significant environmental effects.
The SPEED Act would modify the standards governing when environmental documents are required and narrow the scope of effects agencies must consider, which could reduce the number of projects subject to extensive environmental review.
The bill also modifies requirements governing coordination among federal agencies and limits the scope of environmental effects that agencies may consider.
text:
Why It Matters

Federal environmental reviews for energy infrastructure and other projects could become faster but less comprehensive if the Senate acts on a House-passed bill, according to a new Congressional Research Service (CRS) report. ​

The SPEED Act, short for the Standardizing Permitting and Expediting Economic Development Act, passed the House and was referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works. The bill would amend the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the foundational statute governing federal environmental reviews of major projects.

The CRS report identifies several categories of changes the bill would make: expanding circumstances in which environmental assessments (EAs) or environmental impact statements (EISs) are not required, modifying the thresholds for determining the appropriate level of review, establishing new deadlines for agency actions, limiting the scope of environmental analysis and allowing agencies to rely on prior environmental reviews to satisfy NEPA requirements for new projects. The bill would also restrict certain judicial challenges to environmental reviews.

The Big Picture

The bill reflects broader congressional efforts to streamline federal permitting, particularly for energy infrastructure. The Trump administration has prioritized permitting reform and energy dominance, and the bill's approach is broadly consistent with those executive priorities.

Under current NEPA, federal agencies must conduct environmental reviews for certain proposed actions, with the most intensive review, an EIS, generally required for actions with reasonably foreseeable significant environmental effects. The SPEED Act would modify the standards governing when environmental documents are required and narrow the scope of effects agencies must consider, which could reduce the number of projects subject to extensive environmental review.

The bill would expand the availability and application of categorical exclusions, which allow qualifying projects to proceed without preparation of an EA or EIS. New deadlines for agency actions, restrictions on considering newly available scientific research and provisions allowing greater reliance on prior environmental analyses are also among the bill's mechanisms for accelerating the process.

The bill also modifies requirements governing coordination among federal agencies and limits the scope of environmental effects that agencies may consider. CRS notes that these changes could reduce duplication and expedite reviews but could also limit opportunities to identify gaps, errors or environmental effects that extend beyond individual agencies' responsibilities.

The report notes that NEPA reviews have historically been a focal point of debate over federal permitting, with supporters of streamlining arguing that lengthy reviews delay critical infrastructure and opponents contending that robust review protects communities and the environment. Opponents have also raised concerns that the bill could restrict consideration of scientific evidence and limit judicial oversight of federal permitting decisions.

The Bottom Line

H.R. 4776 has been referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, and no Senate floor vote was scheduled as of Oct. 14. The committee could consider advancing the bill, potentially with amendments, before any floor consideration, although committee approval is not an absolute prerequisite for Senate action. How the Senate weighs the bill's permitting changes against existing NEPA protections could shape the scope of environmental review for energy infrastructure and other federally regulated projects going forward.

title: Fact check: What's true and what's not in Michigan's data center debate - Bridge Michigan
description:

text:
Michigan’s data center boom has brought with it some exaggerated claims from supporters and critics

Bridge spoke with experts to get their take on everything from economic benefits to local control

Among the takeaways, data centers indeed pose environmental concerns, but they aren’t raising electricity rates — at least not yet

Few issues are as controversial today as data centers, which polls show are overwhelmingly opposed by Michigan residents. Amid the debates, there are plenty of exaggerated claims from both opponents and supporters.

Bridge spoke with some of the leading experts in the field to separate fact from fiction.

Despite assurances from state leaders that Michigan is a fitting destination to build warehouse-scale server farms across hundreds of acres, projects have been met with considerable pushback from a public worried about everything from their potential environmental impact to the unpredictable nature of artificial intelligence itself.

Claim: Data centers are a new thing for Michigan

What the experts say: No, but their scale is much, much bigger.

“A data center is the most fantastic economic development opportunity in the last 150 years,” said business leader and former US ambassador John Rakolta Jr. before the Detroit Policy Conference this year.

His company, Walbridge, is leading construction of one of the state’s largest projects: Oracle’s 1.4-gigawatt data center complex in the farmlands of Saline Township. It’s also a partner in the proposed 282-acre Google data center in Van Buren Township.

Data centers have been in Michigan for decades — tucked inside office parks, university buildings and industrial parks. They’ve generally gone unnoticed as they’ve powered our email, streaming services and websites.

By some estimates, there are upward of 70 commercial data centers operating in Michigan powering our digital information ecosystem.

Rakolta was referring to a new class of “hyperscale” data centers that are far bigger, more powerful and more expensive. Tech companies like Meta and Amazon plan to spend trillions of dollars on AI infrastructure through 2030 with thousands of projects underway, saying the technology will usher in a new era of cost savings, increased productivity and domestic industrial development.

A new generation

While a standard data center facility used for cloud computing may draw around 50 megawatts of energy, the increasingly sophisticated AI systems powering large language models and neural networks require magnitudes more power.

Related:

Township vote paves way for Michigan’s second hyperscale data center

Where Michigan governor candidates stand on data centers, the environment

Survey: Michigan local leaders sour on data centers, want more regulations

Ypsilanti Township eyes moratorium on power transmission to slow U-M data center

“The technology is turning data centers into a new class of industrial infrastructure,” said Hengguang Li, director of the Institute for AI and Data Science at Wayne State University. “It’s nothing like the data centers we built 30 years ago.”

Near Grand Rapids, Switch, a Las Vegas company, operates what is likely Michigan’s biggest functioning data center. Appearing as a modern pyramid jutting up from the freeway, the sprawling data center in Gaines Township has expanded for AI in recent years, with a planned electrical capacity of 237 megawatts.

With the growth of AI, the US and Michigan are promoting data center development to buoy the economy.

In 2024, the Michigan Legislature exempted qualifying data centers from Michigan’s 6% sales and use tax. Several proposals for what the state views as “enterprise” data centers have since materialized, while communities are debating the tax breaks.

Claim: Data centers move in with little regard to nearby communities

What the experts say: Developers have overridden local decisions in the past, but communities can be proactive about regulation.

Companies wanting to build data centers are looking for large parcels of land and access to electricity, fiber connectivity and water, said Jean Hardy, an MSU associate professor who researches digital development in rural communities. Often, that means farmland.

Communities are pushing back. No fewer than 30 have enacted moratoriums on data center development.

Critics say their communities are being singled out because they’re perceived as less regulated, Hardy said. Some worry that massive tech companies are able to steamroll rural locales as they scramble to effectively control data center development.

Many communities in the state had not given industrial development “any serious consideration” in a long time, according to Sarah Mills, director of the Center for EmPowering Communities at the University of Michigan’s Graham Sustainability Institute.

“I don’t suggest to communities that they make a data center ordinance. I think instead they should update what they expect out of industrial development,” Mills told Bridge.

In Saline Township, some residents felt data center developers were able to “bully their way in.” After the township officials denied zoning for the project, developers sued, and the board settled citing expensive legal fees in fighting the lawsuit.

Attorney General Dana Nessel and several environmentalists are challenging the Michigan Public Service Commission and DTE over its decisions to permit the project, saying the process was “fast-tracked” despite apparent “red flags.”

Claim: Data centers are raising electricity rates

What the experts say: Not true, at least for now.

In promoting a responsible growth pledge for data centers, Whitmer said families “have been protected from any rate increases due to data center development.”

Michigan’s residential electric rates are higher than the US average and lead the midwest.

But that trend is “not related to data centers,” according to Erik Nordman, director of the Institute of Public Utilities at Michigan State University. He said decarbonization efforts, grid reliability improvements and increasing costs for equipment are all impacting what you pay now.

As utilities rise to meet data center-driven energy demands, Nordman said Michigan will have to build its grid both cleaner and faster. But the state faces a dilemma: Energy demands are increasing at the same time the state is working to comply with a law requiring it to adopt 100% clean energy by 2040.

“It’s going to be a really challenging time,” Nordman said.

Future energy demands

If there’s excess energy in a system ahead of construction, he said a data center may lower rates for customers by covering the utility’s fixed costs, citing recent rate reductions proposed by Indiana Michigan Power, which has some 130,000 customers in the southwest corner of the state.

Michigan’s biggest energy utilities have promised similar cuts.

Consumers Energy president and CEO Garrick Rochow said in a July report that the utility’s average residential electric customer could see about “$7.50 per month of bill benefit with every gigawatt of new large load.”

Still, Nordman said there are conditions where “rates could rise,” as data centers and ratepayers share costs for grid improvements that benefit both groups.

Regulators can directly assign upgrades like substations and high-voltage transmission lines to industrial customers in Michigan, Nordman said, while the addition of a data center’s onsite generators and batteries can improve reliability throughout the utility.

The Michigan Public Service Commission has approved two data center contracts — the Oracle site in Saline Township and the Google project in Van Buren Township — requiring both to pay for infrastructure upgrades. Data centers are unable to qualify for the state’s 2024 sales and use tax exemption if their power needs require residential customers to pay.

The Saline Township data center is expected to increase DTE Energy’s energy load by 25%. In addition to its agreements with OpenAI and Google, the utility says it has about 6 gigawatts in the pipeline for other data center development. One gigawatt is enough electricity to power about 1.2 million Michigan homes.

Data centers could account for 11.8% of total US electricity usage by 2030, according to the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The rate was 4.4% in 2023.

Claim: Data centers harm the environment

What the experts say: High energy demands are likely to increase greenhouse gas emissions. Water usage is a low risk, but noise pollution is a concern.

In response to a proposed $1.2 billion data center collaboration between the University of Michigan and Los Alamos National Laboratory, Ypsilanti City Council passed a resolution to oppose the effort.

The city cited its rejection of nuclear weapons research and cited media reports that data centers “pose significant environmental threats, including excessive water consumption and potential PFAS ‘forever chemical’ contamination that could endanger local water resources and public health.”

Hyperscale data centers need water for cooling, and some can consume millions of gallons of it per day. But how much the centers need can vary widely.

Some operate closed-loop systems designed to recirculate water, often mixed with glycol and other chemical additives, and use more power to keep servers cool. Open-loop systems consume more water as it evaporates into the atmosphere, but draw less energy.

“What’s really tricky is that some data centers use a lot of water to cool, and some data centers use practically none,” U-M’s Sarah Mills said.

Google’s Van Buren Township site could use up to 3.6 million gallons of water every day using both techniques, paying local authorities directly for usage. By comparison, the state reported the total industrial sector in Michigan used about 595 million gallons per day in 2025.

Most of a data center’s water usage would happen miles away. Michigan’s biggest consumer of water is electric power generation — Michigan utilities draw more than 5 billion gallons of water per day to cool energy production facilities.

Water in, water out

Michigan doesn’t require data centers to report all water usage, putting the onus on municipal systems. In Saline Township, developers have pledged to establish monitoring wells to track groundwater levels.

Data centers periodically discharge water into sewers and waterways under terms managed by local wastewater authorities. The Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy issues permits for large volume withdrawals and wastewater blowdowns, stepping in where municipal water authorities are non-existent.

Greenhouse gases

While data centers powered by nuclear and renewable energy sources offer low-carbon alternatives, natural gas and coal generation remains the leading source of energy in Michigan.

“We’re already using all the electricity from our wind and our solar plants,” said Michael Craig, associate professor at the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability and Industrial & Operations Engineering.

Leading up to Michigan’s 2040 clean energy rule, DTE and Consumers plan to use fossil fuel-burning power plants as they ramp up production to meet the demand of data centers, storing excess energy at battery storage facilities.

Craig said data center development in the state is expected to contribute to “more pollution in the air” from greenhouse gas emissions used for energy production unless they develop their own clean energy sources.

“Michigan is dirtier than most other grids in the United States, so a data center here is going to have more emissions than in California, which is one of the cleaner grids.”

Diesel backup generators also carry pollution risks, with concern they may run more frequently to meet demand.

Noise pollution

Data centers carry noise through their cooling equipment, battery energy storage systems and backup diesel generators.

Some studies show facilities with internal noise levels reaching up to 96 A-weighted decibels, or dBA — about the same noise level as a hairdryer. The noises can vary, too — low steady hums and high pitch alarms that can happen at all hours of the day or night.

How much that sound penetrates the environment is determined by how the center is designed.

Acoustical engineers say high frequency noise is more easily dampened by barriers and buildings. High pitch sounds are more easily absorbed through the ground and by foliage than low frequency sound, which experiences less loss due to atmospheric effects.

Prolonged exposure to loud sound has been linked to several adverse health outcomes, including hearing loss.

In Dowagiac, a recently idled 30-megawatt cryptomining operation next to a residential neighborhood is being sued in federal court over its noise. Residents claim industrial sounds have been recorded higher than 60 dBA outside the facility, causing them headaches and depriving them of enjoying the outdoors. The site closed in September and is converting to an AI data center — with an expected tenfold increase in energy usage.

Claim: Data centers are good for the economy

What the experts say: While the broad effects of AI in the workplace remain to be seen, local communities should see more tax revenue.

Consultants for the Michigan Chamber have called data centers a “once-in-a-generation opportunity” to create thousands of jobs and boost revenue for local communities.

Municipalities with major data center projects are expected to receive a boon in property taxes, even accounting for local exemptions and equipment depreciation.

For example, Van Buren Township is projected to earn more than $23 million from the Google project in 13 years.

That revenue picture gets complicated as estimates meet reality, according to Dennis of the Citizens Research Council. “I think it’s going to be really hard to figure out exactly how these things are going to be taxed and how much they’re going to benefit.”

Major job growth is limited to construction and site development, Dennis said.

“This is a huge investment that does not create a lot of jobs,” he told Bridge, estimating some sites will employ primarily in maintenance and security.

name: EVs
title: Clean Investment Monitor: The State of US Clean Energy Supply Chains in 2026
description:
As of Q3 2026, capacity for domestically produced battery modules, battery cells, and solar cells, as tracked by the Clean Investment Monitor (CIM), has roughly doubled from Q1 2025 levels.
We also summarize trends from our tracking of US clean energy manufacturing investment, updated through Q3 2026.
As of Q3 2026, storage and multi-use production lines account for roughly 23% of operational cell manufacturing capacity and 31% of operational module manufacturing capacity.
Overview of manufacturing investment in Q3 2026 In addition to assessing the current state of US clean energy supply chains, this report provides a summary of the Clean Investment Monitor’s updated Q3 2026 tracking of US clean energy manufacturing investment.
The electric vehicle (EV) supply chain—critical minerals, batteries, vehicle assembly, and charging equipment—continued to dominate manufacturing investment in Q3 2026, accounting for 79% of total manufacturing investment at around $5 billion.
text:
US clean energy manufacturing capacity has expanded notably since the spring of 2025, when Congress was debating whether to repeal key incentives enacted by the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). As of Q3 2026, capacity for domestically produced battery modules, battery cells, and solar cells, as tracked by the Clean Investment Monitor (CIM), has roughly doubled from Q1 2025 levels. Domestic manufacturing capacity for solar modules, wind blades, and nacelles has expanded by roughly 50% from Q1 2025, reflecting new facilities that have come online. The growth occurred as long-term projected demand for those clean technologies was dragged down by policy changes, such as the repeal of federal greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions standards for vehicles, and regulatory headwinds, such as permitting constraints on renewable energy. In this analysis, we assess the state of supply chains for solar, wind, batteries, and electric vehicles (EVs) as of Q3 2026 by comparing announced domestic manufacturing capacity from the CIM database with annual deployment of those technologies in 2025, and the range of projected annual deployment of those technologies from 2030 to 2035 as modeled in Rhodium Group’s Taking Stock 2026 report. We also summarize trends from our tracking of US clean energy manufacturing investment, updated through Q3 2026.

Assessing the domestic supply chain’s current capacity against projected demand

Since our 2025 supply chain assessment, the US clean energy manufacturing base has expanded considerably. In Q1 2025, 305 solar, wind, battery, and EV manufacturing facilities were operating. As of Q3 2026, we track 418 projects in operations. Meanwhile, the long-term domestic demand outlook for electric vehicles and renewable electricity generation has weakened as federal policies supporting their deployment have been phased down or eliminated.

In this update, we explore how announced domestic manufacturing capacity compares to 2025 deployment and the range of projected average annual deployment from 2030 through 2035 in Taking Stock 2026. Those projections incorporate US policies at the state and federal level as of June 2026, including the accelerated phaseout of the 45Y and 48E wind and solar deployment tax credits, the expiration of 30D and 45W EV tax credits, the repeal of federal greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions standards for vehicles and the revocation of the waiver enabling California to establish the Advanced Clean Cars II and Advanced Clean Trucks programs, as well as permitting constraints for solar and wind.

We evaluate current production from operating facilities and anticipated capacity tied to these operating facilities that have yet to come online. We separately identify capacity levels for under-construction facilities and those that are announced but have not yet broken ground.

For some clean energy supply chains, such as wind, current domestic capacity is much closer to projected deployment than the outlook in Q1 2025. We found substantial gaps in our 2025 outlook across solar upstream components, wind, and EVs, with batteries the closest to meeting forecasted deployment with domestic capacity. As of Q3 2026, operational manufacturing capacity now appears sufficient, or much closer to sufficient, to supply projected deployment under at least some scenarios from Rhodium Group’s 2026 Taking Stock report.

Solar supply chain

In 2025, the US added close to 48 gigawatts-direct current (GWdc) of solar capacity to the grid, spanning commercial, industrial, residential, and utility-scale installations. As of Q3 2026, CIM tracks 131 operational solar manufacturing projects across the US, compared to the 110 operational inQ1 2025. These facilities have the capacity to produce 10 GWdc of polysilicon, 3 GWdc of wafers, 20 GWdc of cells, and 65 GWdc of modules, including thin-film technology. Domestic module manufacturing is sufficient to fulfill 2025 deployment, while upstream components fall short: polysilicon capacity is equivalent to 22% of deployment, wafers to 5%, and cells to 41% (Figure 1).

Rhodium Group projects that the US is poised to see record levels of solar deployment in 2026 and 2027, as developers rush to claim expiring tax credits and electricity demand surges, driven by data centers, EVs, and increased manufacturing activity. Solar deployment remains high through 2030. After that, the range of possible outcomes widens, reflecting uncertainty around future natural gas prices and clean technology costs. From 2030 through 2035, Rhodium Group projects that the US will add 8 to 52 GWdc of solar capacity annually.

Current domestic module manufacturing capacity already exceeds the upper end of that range, with an additional 54 GWdc of module capacity expected to come online by 2035. Current domestic cell manufacturing capacity is equivalent to about 38% of projected deployment at the upper end of the range, but additional capacity already ramping, under construction, or announced would exceed projected deployment if those projects materialize. Further upstream, larger gaps remain. Domestic polysilicon manufacturing capacity is expected to reach 19 GWdc by 2035 if announced projects proceed, equivalent to just 36% of projected deployment at the upper end of the range, while wafer capacity, including projects in the pipeline, totals around 13 GWdc, equivalent to 26%.

New Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) restrictions added to the 45X manufacturing tax credit have led to corporate restructurings by solar manufacturers seeking to comply with the regulations on specified foreign entities and foreign-influenced entities. Limits on material assistance from prohibited foreign entities (particularly China) may incentivize greater onshoring of upstream component manufacturing. We’ll continue to monitor the evolution of the Treasury guidance on material assistance cost ratios as it phases in over the next few years.

Wind supply chain

In 2025, we estimate around 6 GW of utility-scale wind was deployed in the US, primarily from onshore wind projects. Current operational production capacity across blades, nacelles, and towers meets this level of deployment. As of Q3 2026, the Clean Investment Monitor tracks 33 operational wind component manufacturing projects across the US, compared to 30 in Q1 2025, with the capacity to annually produce 7 GW of blades, 12 GW of towers, and 27 GW of nacelles.

In the near term, we anticipate less than 1 GW of additional capacity to come online for each component, as operational projects ramp up production. No wind manufacturing projects were under construction as of Q3 2026. A negligible amount of announced capacity that has not yet started construction remains in the pipeline (Figure 2).

The headwinds for wind deployment and manufacturing include stop-work orders affecting offshore wind projects, permitting and interconnection delays, rising construction costs, and the early expiration of 45X tax credits for finished wind components enacted under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). Still, Rhodium Group projects the US will see several gigawatts of new onshore wind capacity come online this year, as developers rush to claim expiring tax credits and as growth in electricity demand accelerates.

From 2030 through 2035, Rhodium projects the US will deploy 2-13 GW of wind annually, depending on its cost competitiveness with natural gas. Current operational capacity across each wind subcomponent is sufficient to fulfill projected deployment at the lower end of that range. At the upper end, if all announced projects proceed as expected, blade capacity falls 51% short of domestic demand, tower capacity exceeds projected demand by 2%, and nacelle capacity significantly surpasses anticipated demand.

Battery supply chain

Battery deployment in 2025 totaled nearly 181 gigawatt-hours (GWh),comprising both utility-scale battery storage deployments and domestic demand for EV batteries derived from vehicle sales data. As of Q3 2026, we track 172 operational battery projects in the US, compared to 123 in Q1 2025, with around 440 GWh of module capacity and 392 GWh of cell capacity—more than double 2025 deployment. Notably, company-reported capacity often exceeds the actual output. Facilities frequently operate well below stated capacity because of demand, labor, or supply chain constraints.

In the near term, domestic demand for EV batteries—the dominant consumer of this technology—is slowing, while battery storage installations appear to be headed for record levels, deploying alongside renewables to capture variable generation that would otherwise be curtailed. US homeowners are also installing residential batteries at a historic level as electricity bills increase. Demand growth from data centers adds another source of uncertainty, since batteries can play a role in managing both grid-connected and behind-the-meter power needs.

From 2030 through 2035, we estimate domestic battery demand could range from 249 to 613 GWh, combining projected EV demand with a feasible estimate of strong stationary storage deployment. Current operational capacity alone is sufficient to fulfill forecasted deployment at the lower end of the 2030-2035 demand range. At the upper end, however, current module capacity is equivalent to 72% of projected deployment, and cell capacity to 64% (Figure 3). When including the remaining capacity ramp associated with operational projects, capacity appears sufficient to meet anticipated demand across the range.

Our analysis finds a substantial pipeline of projects that have not yet started or are currently under construction, representing 352 GWh of module capacity and 443 GWh of cell capacity. That additional capacity goes beyond the EV and stationary storage demand captured in our projections, increasing uncertainty around the execution of those outstanding projects. Battery manufacturers are already responding to shifting market and policy dynamics, such as the expiration of consumer EV credits in Q3 2025 and rising electricity demand, including from off-grid data center applications where storage is particularly useful. As of Q3 2026, storage and multi-use production lines account for roughly 23% of operational cell manufacturing capacity and 31% of operational module manufacturing capacity. Considering yet-to-come-online capacity at these facilities, storage and multi-use lines account for 63% of cell capacity and 73% of module capacity.

The combination of slower EV sales growth, a large existing manufacturing base, and a substantial pipeline of outstanding capacity increases the risk of factory downsizing and further cancellations. However, faster growth in grid storage and data center infrastructure demand, and the development of additional end markets such as defense, could expand demand for domestically manufactured batteries.

EV manufacturing supply chain

As of Q3 2026, we track 82 operational EV manufacturing projects, compared to 79 in Q1 2025, including new facilities as well as expansions and retrofits of existing facilities. Current capacity tied to these facilities represents around 2.5 million EVs annually, with the ability to ramp up production to an additional 300,000 EVs. Roughly 1.5 million EVs were sold in the US in calendar year 2025, including both battery electric (BEV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) models (Figure 4).

Looking ahead, Rhodium Group projects annual sales of 3 to 5 million EVs from 2030 through 2035. Current operational capacity falls 9-44% below that range, even after expected production ramps at existing facilities. An additional 21 projects currently under construction would add capacity to produce 2 million more vehicles annually, bringing capacity to 96% of projected demand at the upper end of the range. If announced projects come to fruition, those would add 300,000 EVs to annual domestic manufacturing capacity, sufficient to meet projected 2030-2035 sales across the range. Similar to battery manufacturing, vehicle assembly plants are subject to drastic changes in utilization rates and vehicle output, often operating at only a fraction of their reported capacity. This adds further uncertainty to the total production capacity estimates in our pipeline.

The EV sales outlook weakened significantly in the wake of the OBBBA, which phased out consumer and commercial EV tax credits, 30D and45W, in Q3 2025. CIM tracked a record $31 billion of EV purchases that quarter, followed by a substantial 43% decline in Q4 2025. Changes to regulation have also contributed to lower sales forecasts, down 6-7 million vehicles per year from our previous assessment. A February 2026 ruling by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) repealed the previously enacted federal greenhouse gas emissions standards that regulate emissions from vehicle manufacturers.

Legacy automakers have responded by revisiting and revising their previous electrification strategies. Since Q3 2025, CIM has tracked $6 billion in canceled EV manufacturing investment, as some automakers have pivoted toward established market ecosystems for traditional gas-powered vehicles, as well as cost-competitive, flexible hybrids and extended-range vehicles. With projected EV sales much closer to already operating or under-construction production capacity, automakers may have less incentive to proceed with previously announced projects at their originally planned scale.

Overview of manufacturing investment in Q3 2026

In addition to assessing the current state of US clean energy supply chains, this report provides a summary of the Clean Investment Monitor’s updated Q3 2026 tracking of US clean energy manufacturing investment. In the third quarter of 2026, actual investment in US clean technology manufacturing decreased 11% quarter-on-quarter to $7 billion, the lowest quarter of investment since Q1 2023. This followed a slight Q2 2026 uptick in investment, after six consecutive quarters of declines. New project announcements stalled in Q3 2026, totaling just $2 billion, compared to $11 billion last quarter. Developers canceled around $450 million of announced investment in Q3 2026, all tied to a single critical minerals project.

The electric vehicle (EV) supply chain—critical minerals, batteries, vehicle assembly, and charging equipment—continued to dominate manufacturing investment in Q3 2026, accounting for 79% of total manufacturing investment at around $5 billion. EV assembly investment rose 15% quarter-on-quarter to $2 billion, and is up 7% from this same period last year. Meanwhile, battery investment experienced notable declines both quarter-on-quarter and year-on-year, down 32% and 43%, respectively. This is the lowest quarter of battery investments since Q4 2022. EV investments this quarter reached the highest level on record. Investment in critical minerals projects decreased 16% from the previous quarter to roughly $250 million, down 32% from Q3 2025. Investment in charging equipment declined 9% quarter-on-quarter and 92% compared to Q3 2025.

Outside the EV supply chain, investment in solar manufacturing increased notably, up 52% relative to Q2 2026 and 26% relative to Q3 2025 levels. Investment in wind manufacturing dropped sharply, down 76% quarter-on-quarter and 93% compared to Q3 2025.

Announced investment across all manufacturing technologies totaled around $2 billion in Q3 2026. Battery manufacturing projects accounted for more than half (52%) of announcements this quarter at $1 billion. The rest came from new solar manufacturing and critical mineral projects, totaling around $600 million each. No new wind manufacturing or EV assembly projects were announced during this quarter.

Canceled investment in Q3 2026 came from one $450 million critical minerals project. That reflects a 73% decline from the previous quarter's $1.7 billion of canceled investment.

text:
US carmaker Rivian has expanded a partnership with battery recycling and reuse firm Redwood Materials to work together on “end-to-end energy solutions”.

The agreement will see Redwood recycle Rivian’s battery production scrap. It already repurposes its end-of-life EV batteries and is providing a stationary battery energy storage system (BESS) at its manufacturing plant in Normal, Illinois.

The Normal BESS will be a 10MWh system, employing “more than” 100 second-life battery packs from Rivian.

Initially launched as a battery recycling business and operating as the largest North American recycler of lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries, Redwood launched Redwood Energy, its energy storage division, in June 2025.

It uses batteries that are out of commission from EVs, which typically happens after between five and seven years. Despite being considered beyond use in an EV, those batteries are suitable to continue cycling in stationary storage applications.

It uses its Redwood Pack Manager technology to integrate battery packs across different chemistries, capacities and voltage classes by communicating with each pack’s onboard battery management system. Its scalability means that the companies will be able to increase its size as demand grows.

The additional scrap recycling process will recover the critical minerals used in EV batteries. According to the companies, grid constraints mean that manufacturers are looking to alternative power sourcing solutions and “increasingly need partners who can solve more than one piece of the problem,” which is what Redwood promises to do.

According to JB Straubel, Redwood Materials founder and CEO: "Redwood’s unique ability to integrate and redeploy Rivian batteries with our technology is an opportunity to enable fast, flexible and more cost-efficient energy storage. As the demand and cost for energy keeps rising, working with companies like Rivian is how we help meet these challenges.”

Straubel, an ex-Tesla CTO, identified EVs as a “massive amount of domestic battery assets already in the US market”, also noting the support for manufacturing that the 10MWh facility will provide.

text:
Rethinking Home Scores

Listening to the City Council’s public meeting on home energy scores was strangely upsetting and, on reflection, I realized that it sounded as though the proponents haven’t listened to opposing viewpoints of any kind and are stuck in their echo chambers. On reviewing the proposal, I could find no data on how well the process is going in those high-cost real estate areas already using it. Many questions surfaced: Who really is paying for this and benefiting from it? Lots of contractors, for sure. (Did you know that there are currently nine — just nine — qualified home score assessors for the entire South Willamette Valley? Can you say, “Backlog”?)

And why wouldn’t the seller just provide past usage and upgrade info instead of being demonized for installing high-efficiency gas upgrades? It’s as though they don’t know where the electricity can come from. The entire effort smacks of classism. Not only accountability is needed, but other supports: for low-income folks, for real estate agents, plus real data on the cost — and responsibilities — of ownership.

Candice Kramer

Eugene

More Political Doggerel

The pain, it’s plain, would mainly come from DeSpain.

Corruption will be brazen, and prices will be raisin’, if we elect Drazan.

John Brobst

Eugene

Clean Energy on the Ballot

The city of Eugene passed the Climate Recovery Ordinance in 2014 and committed to cutting fossil fuel use 50 percent below 2010 levels by 2030. To date, fossil fuel use has gone down only 11 percent. We must move faster to meet our climate commitments. Fortunately, the Eugene Clean Energy Fund (ECEF) is on the ballot in November.

ECEF, Measure 20-388, places a two percent license fee on the gross profits of large national chain stores that make more than $1 billion nationally and $500,000 locally, excluding basic groceries, medicines, garbage, recycling, and health care. Local businesses would not be affected because they do not meet the two profit criteria. Also, big chains wouldn’t pass the cost of the fee on to customers with higher prices because their prices are set nationally.

ECEF would invest an estimated $15 million per year directly back into our community through four grant areas: 60 percent renewable energy and efficiency programs for households, 25 percent creating clean energy jobs, 10 percent green infrastructure projects, and 5 percent future innovations.

Homeowners and renters would benefit through weatherization improvements, window replacements and heating / cooling upgrades, making energy bills more affordable. ECEF will provide training for electricians, HVAC and heat pump installers, building energy auditors, and solar, battery and EV infrastructure maintenance technicians.

Voting yes on the Eugene Clean Energy Fund may be the easiest single thing voters can do to lower energy bills and build the thriving green economy we all need.

Linda Kelley

Eugene

Let em’ Drive

When it comes to driving, age alone should not determine whether someone is safe to be on the road. I am writing in response to Kim Kelly’s letter, “Driving Older,” published on Sept. 24. I disagree with the idea that older drivers should generally be pushed off the road just because some of them may have slower reactions or physical limitations.

I believe the solution for improving safety is to require regular tests every few years that check reaction time and cognitive function for elderly drivers, as well as an evaluation by a physician with a mandatory report to the DMV.

Public transportation is also not a realistic alternative for every older driver in Oregon because many areas do not have reliable public transportation. In response to Kelly’s letter, Eugene Weekly reader Karl Keith Beyer pointed out in his Oct. 1. letter that the No. 33 bus route he used for years was reduced and now runs only rarely. Older drivers should be judged by their ability to drive safely, not simply by their age.

Dzmitry Fedarako

Eugene

A Message from District 3

I have known both Val Hoyle and Tina Kotek for decades, long before any of us were elected to public service. In 1999, Kotek and I were both working for regional food banks. Together, we advocated for policies ensuring basic needs for tens of thousands of Oregonians, helped streamline application processes for families needing food assistance, and ensured that the statewide network of local food pantries had the resources and training they needed to support the households that relied on them. A few years later, I met Hoyle, also through our shared work in nonprofits. This time it was working on vital initiatives creating innovative models for delivering community health care.

And none of us have slowed down since. Over the last 20 plus years, I’ve stood shoulder to shoulder with these hard working, effective, smart women leaders. From rallies and events to protect reproductive freedoms; to launching apprenticeship programs for union workers; from passing Paid Family and Medical Leave to securing funding for wildfire recovery; from pushing back on Trump’s harmful anti-immigrant agenda to sounding the alarm about threats to our vibrant environment. I know I can count on them both to lead with the same values we’ve held all these years.

That’s why I’m proud to cast my ballot for Gov. Tina Kotek and Congresswoman Val Hoyle. I hope you will too.

Laurie Trieger

Lane County Commissioner, District 3

Eugene

Vote for Aguiar

I’m supporting Athena Aguiar for the Eugene City Council Ward 5 seat. She’s a progressive running against the conservative incumbent Mike Clark.

Athena is young, bright, high energy, outspoken and articulate. Most importantly, she is struggling with the same employment and housing issues that afflict other young and working-class people. She gets it, on a gut level, unlike present middle-class councilors who are moving so slowly on affordable housing and homeless shelters, while obstinately harassing the homeless. Clark has been a council leader on that persecution.

Presently the council is split 50-50 progressive-conservative. If Athena is elected she will tip the balance on critical votes to 5-3.

The council desperately needs new blood. Let’s give Gen Z a chance to be heard.

Lynn Porter

Eugene

DeSpain x Mannix

On her website, Oct. 6, Monique DeSpain says, “Career politicians are all talk with no results…” Then after many lovely words about what a fine person she is, we learn that after her retirement in 2019, DeSpain joined the Kevin Mannix Law Firm.

Mannix is a lawyer/politician who began his political career in Oregon in 1988 and is currently a state representative. To think that his law office is not influenced by politics, and does not influence politics, is at best naive. He is certainly a career politician.

Is this the kind of double-talk we can expect from DeSpain as an elected representative? I’m voting for Val Hoyle, and encourage you to do the same.

Doug Curry

Eugene

Time for a Change

The letters to the editor have over and over again complained how the city and the county have failed to address the problems and the needs of this community.

The time is over for letters to the editor, it is time to take steps to change this, this election you have the vote that will address the problems and needs of this community.

Stop voting the way you have been voting, step outside of the box as I call it, try a different approach, try something new, the old ways are not working.

Vote not for the incumbent but a new person who, like you, is not satisfied with the way our local government is working, what have you to lose, nothing.

This is not about the Republicans, the Democrats, this is about getting the city and the county to listen to the people.

Vote, nothing will change if you do not vote, and most of all, vote how you feel, not what others tell you.

Steven E. Hunnicutt

Eugene

Election Extra Letters

Expect a Blitz of Corporate Misinformation Against 20-388

Those who fail to learn history’s lessons will repeat them. Given recent history, the November referendum on the Eugene Clean Energy Fund (ECEF) means our mail and local media will be flooded by slickly produced corporate propaganda and misinformation.

In May, opponents of the Lane County Watershed Bill of Rights, including Big Timber and corporate PACs spent record amounts, about $400,000, to defeat the initiative. Another lesson can be learned from the fate of the Oregon Climate Resilience Superfund Bill (SB1541) that was killed by a handful of petroleum and chemical industry lobbyists, despite overwhelmingly positive public testimony.

Expect similar heavy hitters to line up against the ECEF, which would levy a 2 percent city tax on billion dollar-a-year corporations with $500,000 in local revenue. ECEF would exempt profits on sales of food, medicines and prescription drugs, healthcare services and waste removal. Contractors, utilities, co-ops and credit unions are also exempt. The law decrees that revenue will be overseen by a nine-member community committee and the city council and distributed, by law, 60 percent to renewable energy and energy efficiency, 25 percent to clean energy jobs and workforce development, 10 percent to green infrastructure and 5 percent to future innovation. No more than 10 percent can be carved out to pay administrative costs.

This will be obscured by the affected corporations, which include multinational banks, big tech and retailers. Learn history lessons. Read the measure before you vote. Make greedy corporations pay their fair share of the damage they incur. Vote yes on 20-388!

Bernard Cowen

Eugene

A Thank You to last week’s Submitter

Dear Jojo Breslin,

Thank you for your letter endorsing Measure 20-388, which would establish the Eugene Clean Energy Fund. The fund would allocate 40–60 percent of revenue to renewable energy and energy efficiency, 25–30 percent to clean-energy job training, 5–10 percent to green infrastructure and 5 percent to future innovation.

The measure proposes an annual 2 percent fee on gross profits for corporations and big-box retailers earning at least $1 billion nationally, and $500,000 in Eugene. Basic groceries, medicines, healthcare, garbage and recycling services and credit unions would be exempt.

Research from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation indicates that every $1 invested in pre-disaster mitigation can yield approximately $13 in combined savings and avoided physical damage.

According to the Center for Sustainable Economy, Oregon’s 2018 wildfire season caused an estimated $6.8 billion in societal costs, equivalent to an indirect burden of approximately $3,900 per Oregon household.

Opponents, including out-of-state super PACs, warn that corporations will pass the fee on to consumers. Estimates suggest this could cost Eugene households $195.26–$520.68 annually if the entire fee were passed along.

Let’s do the math. Even if Measure 20-388 only saved each household $3,000 annually while costing $600 per year, the net savings would still be $2,400 per household.

Let’s vote yes on Measure 20-388 and invest in Eugene’s clean-energy future!

Darin Henry

Eugene

No Siphoning from Our Community

Supporters of Ballot Initiative 20-388, the Eugene Clean Energy Fund, often say that “corporations should pay their fair share.” While true, this sounds too much like friends splitting a dinner bill. The situation is more like if one diner ordered far more expensive items, expecting everyone else to split their outsized tab — while leaving a mess and secretly pocketing the restaurant’s sugar packets!

The reality is that billion-dollar corporations are doing just that — not only contributing less than their share, but additionally siphoning public resources and damaging the water, air and climate, leaving us to clean up after.

Local communities fund the infrastructure that corporations rely on for their construction, shipping and waste disposal, as well as the public services their underpaid workers need to survive. Meanwhile, mega-corporations pay little in taxes and actually move money out of our communities; national retailers recirculate only 14 cents per dollar back into the local community, in contrast with 53 cents at locally owned stores.

While corporate profits skyrocket, we see longer fire seasons, drier droughts, hotter heatwaves, public services cut and working families struggling to get by.

Ballot Initiative 20-388 would address these inequities by placing a fee on outsized corporate profits, and reinvesting the money to fund clean energy infrastructure and green jobs, reducing housing costs and building climate resilience here in Eugene.

A “Yes” on 20-388 is a vote to hold billion-dollar corporations more accountable for over-serving themselves from our community table.

Rose Comadurán

Eugene

Ambulance Levy

Last week’s (Oct. 1) Siuslaw News article on Tax Measure 20-389 is a case in point. Public agencies are a form of business with the same desire to grow. They extract profit in the form of salaries, benefits and influence. They grow by increasing responsibilities that need more regulations, supported by more fees and taxes. The main cost here is labor compensation with several being six figures; the highest is $1,000 plus compensation per day at work. Some of these compensation packages may be justified, only the public should be aware of what it’s voting on.

If a department, division, program etc. is costing more than it is generating; businesses will offload or shut them down. Lane County is required to provide ambulance service throughout the county unless covered by a political sub-division like our Western Lane Ambulance District (WLAD). Lane County convinced WLAD to assume the responsibility for an additional 22 percent coverage area from 564 to 686 square miles.

During a recorded public meeting, it was exposed that the 122 square mile area was a financial loss to Lane County, who were covering the subsidy in its 2026-27 $1.23 million adopted budget. Choosing to be philanthropic with other people’s money, WLAD agreed to assume the subsidy in its 26-27 almost $6 million adopted budget. It needs to be mentioned WLAD along with the smaller Siuslaw Valley Fire & Rescue District share administrative costs via an Intergovernmental Agreement named Western Lane Fire & EMS Authority (WLFEA).

Keith Stanton

Florence

ONLINE EXTRA LETTERS

Health Care in America

I read this morning that more than a quarter of Americans are saddled with oppressive medical debt. When are we going to come to grips with this giant problem of healthcare? Obamacare was a breakthrough but unfortunately just a patch work with lots of holes. Medicare for seniors is also full of holes.

Yes, we need to get rid of the maniac who is currently running the country, but are the Democrats prepared to push for a universal national healthcare system that other developed nations have? We endlessly hear our politicians spout how great our country is, but still, Americans cannot afford to get sick. How great does that make America? Mexico inaugurates a universal healthcare system in 2027. Why can’t we?

Russ Desaulnier

Eugene

Anti-Trans in Washington?

Exciting news has come out of Washington State: Washington Initiative 638 would ban biological males from competing in girls’ sports in K-12. Polls show strong bipartisan support for the measure in keeping with national polls, which indicate that this is an 80-20 issue political elites on the left ignore.

Following court rulings that allowed states to implement such measures, 27 states have done so. The deep blue West Coast states are not among them. That may soon change.

Republicans sponsored House Bill 2037 in the 2025 Oregon legislative session which would have implemented the same common sense directive. The Democrat majority killed it. Democrats in Congress killed House Resolution 28, the “Protect Women & Girls In Sports Act.”

If Washington voters pass I-638 it will put Oregon Democrats in an untenable position. But given their record on other high profile issues (e.g., the 2026 Transportation Package), they are unlikely to care what voters think and to get this done would probably require an initiative.

Jerry Ritter

Springfield

Hogsbreath’s Wet Dream?

Anyone who calls for, approves of or views a public execution is a sick, sadistic and soulless monster. “Republichristian” viewership of this event will get Super Bowl ratings. No Christian will watch it.

Remember: Public lynchings drew hundreds or even thousands of cheering viewers (and there was at least one occasion where tickets were sold).

I have said before that the Rose Bowl would sell out if ICE staged public hangings there and that the stands would be a sea of “MAGATs” wearing red hats, and I would be willing to bet that thousands, perhaps tens of thousands of viewers of the execution will time it so that their “guns” go off in perfect timing with the firing squads’ volley.

I also wonder how many MAGATs would have been willing to pay fifty dollars a “shot” to buy a ticket for a drawing for the opportunity of a lifetime, the chance to shoot a human being all proceeds going to the Trump 2028 Fund).

Am I against the execution? No, although I would have preferred that the murderer serve a life sentence. I am however totally against making it a public festival.

The cultist zombies keep repeating their glorious leader’s line that we are living in a “golden era.” It sure is, but not for us. Rather it is for racists, white supremacists, haters, self-haters, liars, sadists, pedophiles, rapists, bullies and incredibly stupid people who think their evil and desperately moronic Dunning-Kruger-exemplar cult leader is a genius sent by God.

Jamie Selko

Eugene

The Next Disaster

Oct. 5, another misguided missile launched by Donald Trump which landed directly on the poor people of the U.S. Failing to consider the ripple effect of his executive order, allowing heating oil meant for furnaces to be used as fuel for vehicles (throwing a very small bone to the trucking industry by lowering their cost by a measly 25 cents a gallon after rising over $2 because of his war), will cause already unsustainable home heating oil prices to skyrocket and result in thousands of poor people freezing this winter. The pending crisis for homeowners brought on by seven months of Trump’s ego-fueled insanity is now a full-fledged disaster, just for a few lousy votes in a desperate attempt to try to keep the sinking GOP ship of fools afloat in the upcoming congressional elections. There’s an easier solution — stop the war with Iran now.

John Tietjen

Corvallis

Pet Medications across Borders

U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has a dangerous new rule beginning Oct. 22 that will threaten the health care of millions of Americans. The rule, “Indefinite Suspension of the De Minimis Exemption for Mail Shipments,” will effectively end Americans’ ability to personally import their prescription medicines.

Importing prescription drugs from licensed international pharmacies is the only lifeline for seniors on limited incomes, people with high-deductible health plans and the uninsured. That’s why CBP and the FDA have allowed it for decades. Due to the much lower cost of medications in Canada and other countries, imported medicine is their only option.

Many imported drugs can be less than half the U.S. price. These necessary medicines prevent blood clots, treat diabetes and much more. This CBP rule will cut off access to the only affordable prescription drugs for millions, and that will lead to unnecessary harm and preventable deaths.

I rescue cats. I get a large dose of dog medication and split it between the 30-some-odd cats I care for. Fleas have become resistant to Advantage [flea medication] and it doesn’t work well — Revolution does work and also is an effective treatment for ear mites. I can’t take every single one of my cats to the vet to get a prescription for Revolution, which costs about 10 times the price it does with a prescription here anyway. This is all to help the drug companies and the private equity firms that own most of the vets in the U.S. now. This will break the rescuers trying to clean up after irresponsible people’s messes.

The people influenced by the orange disease in charge of this country, who doesn’t believe in vaccinating or spaying and neutering. The kids that can’t afford rent and groceries, let alone a few rounds of vaccines and a low cost spay and neuter. They have to be able to afford vehicles to take them to appointments also. Please reverse this when “Don the Con” is gone.

I ask readers to immediately call or write our senators and U.S. representatives and demand they stop CBP from implementing any rule-making that restricts Americans from importing personal-use prescription drugs from licensed pharmacies in Canada or other countries.

Susan Day

Eugene

Prose on the U.S. Secretary of War

Pete Hegseth: Would God help this man? Never. We know what he’s done and what he’s promising to do, following the cold-blooded murders of innocent Americans and those fictional “drug boat” crews, blown to bits by million-dollar missiles. Fun! Just not enough. He now proffers us his televised sine-qua-non, a bloody killing ripped from the worst aspects of human nature. And we’re all invited.

Popcorn!

Of all the unspeakable acts this hideous creature has gifted us, this latest should test the lily guts of any soul with one remaining atom of humanity. Will a single politician stand and demand this creature’s arrest? Can any law apply when all laws have been vomited into our faces? Or has a remaining spark of humanity vanished like the souls of Alex Pretti and Renee Good?

Calling all Republicans! Got a map?

I’d take it to The Hague, Democrats. Toothless gesture it is, but nothing vanishes quicker than a deafening silence.

Not that nervous Democrats will risk their precious careers. Hardly, as they’ve never shown the real spine to fiercely defend — at any cost — what tattered bits of civil law remain. Too much trouble and such a risky loss of income. Yes, a tough job — with great benefits! We’ve heard a weak squeak or two. Well, squeaks aren’t screams, but hey — thanks! Might take much more.

America —the greatest country in the bowels of Hell. My fellow citizens! Stand up and be shot.

Tom Erwin
