text:
Tesla’s Senior Manager of Cybercab General Assembly at Gigafactory Texas, Jody Kerns, is leaving the company to become Rivian’s Director of General Assembly for the R2 in Normal, Illinois.

He’s the second Cybercab launch leader to leave Tesla this year. The head of Cybercab new product introduction walked out in April, before the vehicle ever carried a paying passenger.

From Cybercab to R2

Kerns announced the move in a LinkedIn post this week, thanking his Tesla team for everything “from the WEOL project to the launch of the Cyber Cab.”

His profile shows he joined Tesla in January 2024 as an end-of-line manager and took over Cybercab general assembly in Austin in February 2026. That’s the same month Tesla rolled the first steering-wheel-less Cybercab off the line, so he ran final assembly through the entire ramp to commercial service.

Advertisement - scroll for more content

At Rivian, he’ll do the same job on the R2. He described the goal as making the R2 “the best electric SUV in the market.”

Kerns isn’t a Silicon Valley hire. He spent 14 years at Volkswagen of America, ending as Director of Assembly from 2021 to 2024, where his profile says he managed about 1,200 people and integrated the ID.4 into a line already building two other models. That’s the Chattanooga plant. Before that, he spent four years in Toyota’s paint shops.

So Rivian is getting someone who has slotted a new EV into a running factory and launched a brand new vehicle from scratch. That’s exactly the R2 problem.

The second Cybercab leader out the door

Kerns’ departure follows Michael So, who was Tesla’s Head of Cybercab NPI from September 2024 to April 2026. So was Giga Texas employee #1 in 2021, helped launch the Model Y and Cybertruck there, and lists the Cybercab’s “unboxed” manufacturing process, brake-by-wire, and butterfly doors among the things he launched.

He left in May to become VP of Product Engineering at Aalo Atomics, a nuclear reactor startup also based in Austin. Under Kerns’ post, So wrote that he “wouldn’t want to launch Cybercab with anyone else.”

The timing isn’t great for Tesla. Commercial Cybercab rides started in Austin on September 3, and NHTSA hit Tesla with a Special Order a week later demanding proof, under oath, that a car with no steering wheel or brake pedal meets federal safety standards. NHTSA now estimates the 2026 Robotaxi fleet, Model Y and Cybercab combined, at about 1,000 vehicles.

Rivian, on the other hand, is in the middle of the ramp that decides its future. R2 deliveries started June 9 from Normal, and Rivian produced 19,751 vehicles in Q3 while keeping its 2026 delivery guidance at 65,000 to 70,000. Rivian has already raised $1.5 billion partly to de-risk that ramp.

name: Clean Energy
title: Germany and China in the cleantech sector: Between opportunities, competition and location policy
description:
Germany and the EU must act immediately to safeguard industry, jobs, technology and energy security.
Through consistent technological support and industrial policy, China has overtaken Germany as a pioneer in green technologies.
The leading cleantech companies in Germany are generally closely linked to China as a supplier.
In principle, decarbonization with the help of Chinese technology still has the potential to become a stabilizing cornerstone of relations.
This is a challenge to German companies, and China is already competing with former German market leaders in almost all product categories.
text:
The so-called China Shock 2.0 – a wave of high-tech exports – has put traditional German industrial sectors like automotive and mechanical engineering under pressure. In addition, innovation, cost advantages and supply chain dominance are giving Chinese industry inroads into core areas of the German economy. The consequences are far-reaching: Germany’s industrial base and technological independence are at risk. Even the ”clean technology” sector – known as cleantech – is increasingly shifting into crisis mode. Chinese dominance in this area is affecting German and European efforts to secure energy supplies and transition to a decarbonized, climate-friendly economy.

European companies find themselves in a double bind of cut-throat competition. While they are losing market share in China, they are also facing massive competitive pressure from Chinese players in their home markets. This is particularly true for cleantech, where China is catching up in electric mobility, wind power, batteries, hydrogen and other segments. The business-driven priority for German firms to maintain a presence in the Chinese market is increasingly coming into conflict with macroeconomic risks in EU markets, like industrial decline and job losses.1

This report concludes a pilot study that surveyed German perspectives on China’s role in decarbonization – the reduction CO2 emissions – and cleantech.2 It analyzes public statements, press releases and background discussions with representatives from industry, politics, research and interest groups with the aim of mapping the various interests and positions and contrasting them with Chinese ambitions. Positions on China vary depending on the interests of the stakeholders and are in some cases even at odds with one another.

By presenting the various positions in a structured manner, this report aims to help identify common interests and put forward proposals for a policy based on a broader consensus. In light of Beijing’s growing dominance in the cleantech sector, the options outlined in the report emphasize the urgency of Germany taking swift and coordinated action.

This requires a more resolute policy that unites as many stakeholders as possible. Economic interdependence between the EU and China is becoming unsustainably tilted in Beijing’s favor: China’s trade surplus with the EU stood at EUR 360 billion in 2025.3 The political will of European member states to reduce strategic dependencies as part of a de-risking strategy – for example, in critical infrastructure and energy security – is currently at odds with geo-economic realities. The lack of (affordable) European alternatives, as well as high and complex supply chain dependencies, make diversification difficult in the short and medium term, particularly due to the significant costs involved.

In this time of geopolitical change, Beijing also faces the challenge of maintaining economic sovereignty and independence. It has clearly stated its intention to achieve global technological leadership and to promote its own industries. Through far-sighted policies and the deployment of substantial resources, China has succeeded in establishing dominant positions in technologies and global markets that, just a few years ago, were firmly in European hands.

Beijing is taking a systematic approach to implementing its innovation goals and has also strategically addressed its own dependencies. Europe, and Germany in particular, are now feeling the consequences. China has adopted the German, export-oriented economic model and combined it with centralized control. Germany and the EU must act immediately to safeguard industry, jobs, technology and energy security.

In addition, advocates of a greater focus on European security, particularly in the energy and technology sectors, warn that the shift away from fossil fuels – accelerated by the wars in Ukraine and Iran – may lead to a growing dependence on China’s technology without the development of locally sourced alternatives. Risks are also rising in the areas of cyber security, the protection of critical infrastructure, and the control and security of energy networks.

Yet, the conditions for decarbonization in Europe have never been more favorable than they are today, given the availability of cheap and innovative technology from China. Beijing recognized cleantech and the global energy transition as an economic opportunity at an early stage. Through consistent technological support and industrial policy, China has overtaken Germany as a pioneer in green technologies. It now dominates global value chains for photovoltaics, batteries, and electric mobility, among others, and supplies high-quality, innovative cleantech at the most competitive prices.

For Germany and the EU, this results in a complex strategic trilemma in which security, economic and climate interests come into conflict. The aim of protecting critical infrastructure and domestic industry conflicts with the need to implement the planned expansion of renewable energies swiftly and affordably through the import of low-cost technology.

To date, there is no agreement on a good balance for the use of domestic and Chinese products and technologies to achieve CO2 reduction targets. Without these Chinese goods, Germany’s national targets will be virtually unattainable in the short and medium term. They are therefore linked to Beijing’s geo-economic interests.

German stakeholder positions on China’s role in the cleantech sector are situated among three opposing poles that form a triangle of economic interests, security requirements and climate targets. These interests and objectives are not necessarily mutually exclusive and may overlap, but they may just as easily conflict.

Economic interests: China is particularly significant for major players as a market and technology partner

For decades, the Chinese market was a major sales market for German companies. German technology was developed at home, produced cheaply in China, and then sold worldwide. This division of labor was a recipe for economic success. With manufacturing facilities in China since the 1980s, German firms played a key role in making Germany one of the world’s largest exporting nations.

Today, trade relations between Germany and China have changed fundamentally. Germany’s decades-long trade surplus with China shifted to a deficit of EUR 89 billion in 2025, and China is now competing with German firms in the very same market segments that Germany previously dominated.4 Many of the driving forces behind the German economy remain firmly rooted in China. This also applies to companies in the cleantech sector. Today, however, German firms are represented in China not only by production facilities but also by research and development centers, and they maintain essential technology partnerships with Chinese companies.

Although the economic future of these firms in China now appears more tenuous, and even the view of large corporations regarding China is shifting, many continue to invest in the People’s Republic to maintain their position within the Chinese network of suppliers, and to benefit from the local innovation ecosystem. German firms also consider it important to maintain a presence in the Chinese market in the future, particularly in view of competition in third markets.

Industry representatives do not necessarily interpret the term de-risking as diversification of suppliers, but primarily as a strategic shift of production to alternative locations to mitigate the negative effects of trade barriers and boost their own competitiveness. A few selected quotes from the interviews conducted for this report illustrate this:

For automotive companies, de-risking means being less dependent on geopolitical measures. — Paraphrased from a confidential expert discussion5

“In China for China. That’s the only way to make headway in the current pricing landscape.” — Ola Källenius, CEO, Mercedes-Benz6

“We are deeply rooted in China and understand customer needs and market dynamics. The combination of German engineering, China’s extensive supplier network and local innovation creates a unique global advantage.” — Oliver Zipse, CEO, BMW7

“China is no longer just a manufacturing hub, but a global powerhouse for innovation. […] We are investing heavily and will continue to do so, […] and Bosch will optimize its presence to maintain its competitive edge.” — Stefan Hartung, CEO, Bosch8

However, even among companies that have been active in China for a long time, the mood is shifting in the face of shrinking market shares, particularly in the cleantech sector. German car manufacturers are being squeezed out of the electric vehicle sector by domestic manufacturers, and in the green energy sector, Chinese manufacturers generally have the upper hand for reasons of cost and procurement. This cut-throat competition is reflected equally in quarterly results in both China and Germany. While, for example, Mercedes’ latest electric vehicle sold only a few hundred units in China in the first half of 2026, Xiaomi – a company that only entered the market two years ago – delivered tens of thousands of models per month.9

German SMEs in particular feel under threat, as they are often unable to manufacture in China and benefit from low production costs. This is where the most critical voices on China are found.

Due to the comprehensive subsidy regime, we cannot compete with Chinese rivals. Even if we were to manufacture in China, we would not be able to benefit from the same level of capital subsidies and export support. So, does EU industry need protection from Chinese competition? Yes, because we are not competing with a single company, but with an entire economy. — Paraphrased from a confidential expert discussion

Security concerns: China’s investment and export strategy poses risks to Europe’s sustainable energy supply

Since at least the start of Russia’s full-scale war on Ukraine in 2022, many stakeholders in Germany have also become acutely aware of the risks of one-sided supply chain dependencies, particularly in the energy sector. The disruption to global oil supply chains due to the Iran war have once again highlighted this risk.

Reducing the share of fossil fuel sources in Germany’s energy mix – as the acting Federal Minister for the Environment, Carsten Schneider (SPD), has also stated10 – would make Germany less dependent on foreign energy suppliers. At the same time, however, there are complex security concerns regarding Chinese involvement in the European economy in general, and in Germany’s energy supply in particular. These include, for example, cyber-security risks arising from the use of Chinese technology for critical infrastructure, like wind farms.11

Competition from heavily subsidized Chinese companies is another cause for concern among German suppliers, as domestic firms are unable to match low Chinese prices. They fear being squeezed out of their home market. Furthermore, Germany and the EU face the threat of a gradual loss of manufacturing expertise and technological sovereignty in certain sectors – and thus of industrial independence from China.

There is also a dependence within cleantech supply chains, particularly when it comes to rare earths. The consequences of this became very apparent when China imposed export controls on rare earths in April and September 2024.12 Germany imports 47 percent of its rare earths needs from China, and this figure is rising.13 Further job losses are to be expected in industry. German industry is estimated to be losing 15,000 jobs per month – a trend that could continue if cut-throat competition persists.14

Various organizations and companies take a security-critical approach to China. These have often never had a presence in China or they have been squeezed out of the Chinese market due to Beijing’s support for domestic firms. Critical voices are also coming from trade associations and trade unions, whose members are already feeling the full force of competitive pressure from China.

In politics and policy-related research, security aspects of doing business with China have been the subject of more intensive debate for several years – yet there is still a lack of uniform and binding approaches to this challenge. A general strategy of de-risking – selectively reducing dependencies on China without fully decoupling – has been advocated, for example, by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU).15 In most cases, this approach is not clearly defined, although there have been some specific decisions to reject Chinese technology in favor of German suppliers. Following sharp criticism from political and security circles, for example, the offshore wind farm operator Luxcara awarded a contract to Siemens Gamesa instead of the preferred Chinese supplier Ming Yang.16

The line between acceptable risk and strategic vulnerability in the energy sector has not yet been definitively established and remains a matter of debate. It is becoming apparent that even a partial exclusion of Chinese components and products is likely to significantly increase the costs of Germany’s energy transition to renewables. Industry representatives are calling for systematic political support so they can compete with Chinese rivals:

“Following the solar sector, we are now exposing another future-oriented technology [wind energy] to the risk of falling victim to unfair competition. That cannot happen. If Germany aspires to be a frontrunner in green technologies, then we must back this up with clear political will.” — Jürgen Kramer, Deputy Chairman, IG Metall17

“Any project that receives even a single euro from European funding schemes should be obliged to purchase the technology in Europe as well. [...] As European companies, we cannot participate in China. We are denied this. On the other hand, we are still too naïve in Europe.” — Nils Aldag, CEO, Sunfire18

“Europe is the only continent that invites manufacturers from all over the world to offload their excess capacity here – and even subsidizes them to do so. […] Support should explicitly be given to companies that generate the bulk of their value added in Europe. France and Poland have already clearly aligned their funding regulations accordingly.” — Thomas Heim, Manager – Climate Solutions, Carrier (manufacturer of heat pumps, among other things)19

Climate targets: Decarbonization will be more expensive without affordable Chinese technologies

As part of its climate protection program adopted in the spring, Germany’s center-right and center-left government coalition (CDU/SPD) set itself the target of reducing CO2 emissions by 25 million tonnes by 2030. In order to achieve this and its other climate targets, Germany will need to make considerable societal and economic efforts. This is because simply reducing fossil fuel usage in the power supply is not enough – passenger and freight transport, as well as industry, must also decarbonize.

In this context, China’s range of renewables, batteries and electric vehicles (EVs) is unbeatable on price. Technologically, depending on the sector, the quality is comparable to Germany and therefore very attractive. It is thus crucial that policymakers also provide regulatory support and create effective incentives for the domestic economy. Among other things, the framework conditions for expanding renewable energy must be optimized. Take, for example, Germany’s current auction design for wind farms. In this process, sites are allocated through competitive bidding. This means that the developer who offers the highest sum may develop the site. The developer will therefore seek to reduce construction costs and tend to purchase cheaper Chinese turbines.

“Governments wish to maximize revenue through auctions. This auction design exerts price pressure on wind farm developers, who consequently switch to Chinese suppliers or pass the pressure on to European manufacturers, who in turn offset the higher prices by importing Chinese components. — Paraphrased from a confidential expert discussion

Partly because development cycles are often shorter, innovative solutions reach the commercial market more quickly in China than in Germany. Representatives at one research institute consider cooperation with China to be essential given the rapid pace of innovation in cleantech:

It is no longer possible to work without Chinese institutes. Innovation and research have reached a pace that is hard to imagine outside China. The scale achieved in China can be seen as an opportunity: technologies and production techniques can reach Germany more quickly and cheaply, thereby driving forward the energy transition. — Paraphrase from a confidential expert discussion

Climate research organizations and companies in the renewable energy sector also regard failing to decarbonize as a significantly greater risk than collaborating with Chinese suppliers. These stakeholders often view security risks a manageable – such as grid outages caused by Chinese components that have been tampered with. The following quotes illustrate the tension between risk awareness and competitiveness:

“By opting for the world’s most powerful offshore wind turbine [MingYang], we will be able to accelerate Germany’s energy transition while fostering much-needed competition in the industry. In any case, the management, operation and control of the Waterkant wind farm will remain entirely in the hands of an independent German company.” — Holger Matthiesen, Project Manager at Luxcara July 2, 202420

“The target of 15 million electric vehicles by 2030 can only be achieved with the involvement of Chinese manufacturers. An increase in import duties on Chinese vehicles would lead to significantly higher financing requirements for the roll-out of electric mobility.” — Study by Agora Verkehrswende21

The stance of German cleantech companies toward China is largely influenced by their level of integration in the Chinese market. Companies with years of collaboration and strong roots in the Chinese ecosystem often advocate a China-based production strategy referred to as “in China for the world.” A large proportion of their suppliers, technology partners and research centers are based in China and develop innovative products. These companies rely on China for sales, competitive production and fast development.

Many companies without sales to China also rely on Chinese suppliers for components, either for cost reasons, due to Chinese dominance in the supply chain, or simply because of a lack of alternatives. The degree of dependence varies from company to company. Companies that are entirely independent of China are rare in this sector. The leading cleantech companies in Germany are generally closely linked to China as a supplier.

In principle, decarbonization with the help of Chinese technology still has the potential to become a stabilizing cornerstone of relations. In 2025, the total value of (largely fossil-fuel-based) EU energy imports stood at EUR 337 billion. The EU’s enormous trade deficit with China also means that the continent is of central importance to China’s export industry. Beijing is therefore sensitive to justifiable efforts by the EU to restrict market access or impose stricter conditions.22 Tensions in this area should be identified early on by both sides and managed diplomatically, as the risk of supply-chain dependency is growing as a potent disruptive factor in Sino-German relations.

China has elevated cleantech to the status of a strategic industry. Beijing has been successful with its strategic development plans for industries and technologies and will continue to rely on these instruments in the future. The dominance it has achieved in the solar sector and other areas through industrial policy is set to be replicated in an ever-increasing number of sectors. For the cleantech sector, this means that China will strategically strengthen the entire value chain and drive forward the development of new clean technologies, both for domestic decarbonization and for the global market.

China views industrial policy as a systemic advantage. In particular, the successes achieved in green technologies such as solar power are to be replicated in other sectors. Green hydrogen, battery storage, drones and AI-supported energy technology are key markets in which a surge in activity is expected in the near future. Systemically oriented industrial policy and politically guided market development are core instruments that China is currently consolidating. They operate across sectors and combine politically stimulated demand with the promotion of industrial ramp-up.

China is striving for autonomy in supply chains, the domestic market and future technologies. This is a challenge to German companies, and China is already competing with former German market leaders in almost all product categories. From Beijing’s perspective, there has never been a level playing field. As an exporting nation, Germany has long enjoyed a dominant position in technology, which China now seeks to attain. Now, through consistent policy and long-term investment, these dependencies are simply being reversed.

As a technological superpower, China aims to dominate the technologies and industries of the future. Any dependencies on Western countries that still exist are to be eliminated or reversed. In chips, AI, robotics, and aerospace, for example, Beijing is pursuing a generational project designed to propel China to the forefront in these sectors. China has learned from Germany’s approach to developing a largely automated ‘Industry 4.0’ and has developed networked, partly AI-supported industrial clusters.

German manufacturers are taking China’s ambitions seriously, even in areas where European technology still leads the way:

We have a cost gap of 40 to 60 percent compared with Chinese products. But if you calculate over a project lifespan of 15 to 20 years, this evens out, as Chinese equipment currently needs to be replaced more often and is less efficient. OPEX costs [operating expenses] bring Chinese offers into line with ours in terms of price; sometimes Chinese offers are actually more expensive in the end. But we cannot rest on our laurels; the Chinese will catch up quickly. We cannot assume that we will remain technological pioneers if the ramp-up here is so slow. — Paraphrase from a confidential expert discussion

Cleantech is the key market of the future for China. More than 11 percent of its growth comes from this sector,23 and since the oil crisis sparked by the Iran War, exports of green technology have been rising rapidly. Growing global demand is expected in this area, and Beijing already has a head start.

In third-party markets, we are not necessarily competing with Chinese producers solely on a technological level, but also when it comes to financial and insurance packages. In a tender that we lost, we had the technologically more suitable bid, but the Chinese had a better financing offer. — Paraphrase from a confidential expert discussion

German firms are not only competing with similar companies in China, they are up against a strategically positioned industrial ecosystem that can draw on the resources of a politically directed economy. Consequently, competitive pressure from China is no longer an isolated problem for individual firms, but an economic challenge for Germany as a business location more broadly.

While the triangle organizes stakeholders according to their opposing positions on security, the economy and climate/decarbonization, this Venn diagram highlights where they overlap. Where two or three circles overlap, there is an interest shared by several stakeholders. These areas can be regarded as the starting points for a coherent and consensus-based policy. Measures that address these areas can strengthen Germany and bring together several different stakeholders into one camp.

It is difficult for Germany to serve the sometimes conflicting goals of reducing dependence, maintaining competitiveness and achieving rapid decarbonization optimally and at the same time. Those who reduce macroeconomic dependence pay more in the short term. Those who prioritize corporate profits and the cheapest possible procurement of cleantech deepen dependence. Those who protect local manufacturers across the board make the energy transition more expensive and hinder access to innovation from China.

A coherent policy toward China that takes the entire spectrum of interests into account cannot satisfy all stakeholders equally. It can, however, focus on the areas of overlap between the three key areas: economic interests, security concerns and decarbonization. Crucial to this is a cost-benefit analysis that balances both the socio-economic interests of society and the profit-driven logic of the private sector and industry. Cleantech should be seen as an opportunity to reconcile interests relating to security, economic viability and sustainability, while keeping cooperative relations with China.

Compromises will be necessary. Listed companies are obliged to adhere to principles of economic viability, while policymakers must ensure long-term job security and a reliable supply of public goods. Climate targets are enshrined in law, and decarbonization is therefore binding for all stakeholders. Accordingly, it is essential to find ways to bring corporate interests and political concerns closer together again. The positions outlined above identify four areas that should be the focus of strategic considerations:

Resilient supply chains: Raw materials diversification and recycling

There is broad support among stakeholders surveyed for diversifying supply chains for critical raw materials. Establishing alternative sources of supply for non-Chinese materials or components, building up strategic reserves, and recycling magnets and rare earths are possible avenues. Promoting local innovation and (re)building capacity along the entire supply chain for essential goods ensures security of supply in the event of external bottlenecks. Such measures can support the development of resilient supply chains and would at least limit Beijing’s ability to use export controls as a means of exerting pressure.

However, the investment costs are high, and the measures will only take effect in the medium term, as production outside Chinese supply chains and recycling are more expensive than Chinese imports and require years to set up. German companies that recycle rare earths, for example, are struggling to find markets for their products and are operating well below capacity.24 In May 2026, Heraeus Remloy, Europe’s largest recycling center for rare earths, was sold to a Canadian firm, although keeping it under European ownership would have enabled greater strategic independence for Germany as a cleantech hub.25 Diversification is akin to an insurance policy in which Germany must invest today in order to build long-term resilience and avert continued deindustrialization.

Green flagship markets: Securing investment and demand

Public investment in infrastructure, linked to CO₂ and resilience standards and incorporating localization criteria (procurement exclusively from the EU), can help to significantly boost demand for cleantech and upstream products such as green steel produced with low CO2 emissions.26

Such lead markets, supported by public procurement funds, can help to strengthen demand for European cleantech. Companies gain longer-term planning certainty and the opportunity to scale up their production. The higher costs of decarbonization using European technologies are borne, at least in part, by public sector actors. Compared with import duties, this generates demand for European-produced cleantech, rather than simply making competing products more expensive.

The Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA)27, currently under discussion in the EU, is an attempt to establish CO2 standards and localization criteria for such lead markets. Various factors are currently hampering the effectiveness of the IAA. Among other things, the vague definition of ”made with Europe” is problematic – it refers to the EU and all countries with which trade agreements are in place. Furthermore, for some industries, the IAA might not come into effect until 2029, which could be too late given the urgency of the situation. The Act’s effectiveness could also be limited if the idea gains traction to suspend localization criteria in public procurement, if there is a “disproportionate price increase” of more than 25 percent (and thus also cheaper offers from China).28 To create a reliable domestic market for clean technology manufactured in the EU, bolder and more rapidly deployable instruments are needed.

A sovereign energy transition: De-risking with a sense of proportion and a focus on critical infrastructure

Consistent steps toward de-risking are particularly justified when technology imports pose a security risk. This applies above all to critical infrastructure, such as energy (grids). One example is the planned removal of Huawei and ZTE technology from 5G core networks. However, a clearly differentiated, technology-specific approach is crucial. For many basic components and simpler technologies, such as solar panels or batteries, using Chinese manufacturers will remain the most cost-effective solution without posing serious security risks.29

Successful de-risking builds security where supply bottlenecks and cyber security risks could cause real damage. This will incur additional costs and slow down expansion in some critical areas. The EU cannot afford not to establish its own supply chains or, at the very least, to diversify its procurement in these key technologies. To this end, a strategically coordinated policy – particularly within the EU – is indispensable.

The hard core: European value creation in key components

At the heart of all three areas of interest mentioned above lies the ambitious goal of achieving domestic value creation in strategic bottleneck sectors, such as permanent magnets, green hydrogen and critical raw materials, which are currently sourced mainly from China. This requires a targeted industrial policy through the establishment of so-called IPCEI schemes (Important Projects of Common European Interest: transnational large-scale projects in strategic sectors jointly funded by several EU member states), start-up funding and support for green energy.

Such measures are costly in the short term but offer the greatest benefits for German industry and European independence in the medium term. The benefit achieved would be genuine, albeit limited, technological sovereignty. However, the upfront costs would require a high fiscal outlay initially, and its success would be difficult to measure within a single parliamentary term, making it politically challenging to communicate. Therefore, Germany should focus on a few truly critical bottlenecks such as rare earths and key components of critical infrastructure, rather than on broad-based investment. A European-coordinated policy is also essential in this regard.

The afternoon fireside chat was Newsom’s second appearance Wednesday at the California Economic Summit.
Earlier in the day, he also spoke about California’s economic successes over the years.
text:
Policies that are good for the environment and the economy aren’t mutually exclusive — and California is proof that advancing such goals doesn’t have to be a red or blue issue.

That seemed to be the message that former California Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, and current Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, shared during a joint appearance at the California Economic Summit in Long Beach on Wednesday, Oct. 14.

Related: Gov. Gavin Newsom paints optimistic picture of California’s economy

During a fireside chat recognizing the 20th anniversary of the Global Warming Solutions Act, landmark legislation that Schwarzenegger signed in 2006 to reduce California’s greenhouse gas emissions, both the former and current governors of the world’s fourth-largest economy touted the state’s role as a climate leader.

“We have shown to the world what a subnational … state can do,” said Schwarzenegger.

But getting Assembly Bill 32 implemented was no walk in the park — and not just because of pushback from the oil industry.

Schwarzenegger recounted the struggles California faced in getting the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, then under the administration of President George W. Bush, to grant the state the waivers it needed to adopt stricter environmental standards.

The state sued the EPA in 2007, and ultimately won.

Fast forward to today.

Newsom, sitting next to Schwarzenegger during the conversation at the Long Beach Convention Center, credited the former governor’s signing of AB 32 for the creation of the state’s cap-and-trade program, now known as the cap-and-invest program.

Under the program, companies must reduce how much carbon emissions they produce, purchase allowances from the state or other businesses, or pay into projects to offset the pollution they produce. Money the state receives pays for climate-change mitigation, affordable housing and transportation projects, along with utility bill credits for residents.

Since the AB 32 bill signing, Newsom said, $16 billion has been reinvested to offset the cost of Californians’ electric bills, and the state expects to receive another $8 billion over the next four years.

Newsom also said that the state’s cap-and-invest program has brought about market predictability, which is critical when companies are deciding whether to set up shop in California. Newsom last year signed legislation extending the cap-and-invest program through 2045.

He suggested that the cap-and-invest program is beneficial to the state and credited Schwarzenegger for helping advance the idea.

“There’s no Elon Musk without what Gov. Schwarzenegger did because there would be no Tesla,” Newsom said. “There would not be the predictability that created the incentives for him (Musk) to take the big risks and make the big bet in the state of California.”

Now, Newsom continued, “we’re on the other side of the debate as it relates to whether or not this is good for the economy.”

Some Republicans objected when Newsom extended the cap-and-invest program, raising concerns that it would increase gas prices.

Schwarzenegger, meanwhile, agreed that the market predictability is “why everyone is coming to California” and doubled down on the idea of California as a climate leader.

“What happens in California will happen worldwide,” he said.

The afternoon fireside chat was Newsom’s second appearance Wednesday at the California Economic Summit. Earlier in the day, he also spoke about California’s economic successes over the years.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

text:
Nova Scotia and Canada are investing to seize one of the largest economic development opportunities in generations.

A federal-provincial partnership worth $100 million announced today, October 15, will support the research, data collection and analysis required to advance offshore wind development and help position Nova Scotia as a global clean energy leader.

“Nova Scotia is no longer at the end of the energy transmission line – we are the starting point. Today’s announcement is another important step toward making Nova Scotia a global leader in offshore wind. By working together with the federal government, we are unlocking a generational economic opportunity that will attract investment, create good-paying jobs and strengthen our economy,” said Premier Tim Houston, who is also Minister of Energy. “We aren’t just protecting our own grid, we are powering Canada. This partnership positions Nova Scotia to compete on the world stage while building a cleaner, more prosperous future for our province and future generations.”

Nova Scotia's offshore winds are among the strongest and most consistent in the world. With growing international demand for clean energy, the province is uniquely positioned to attract billions of dollars in private-sector investment, create thousands of good-paying jobs and build a new renewable energy industry that will generate prosperity for communities from Sydney to Yarmouth.

The federal funding will support collection of critical meteorological, oceanographic and wind-resource information needed to inform future development and reduce risk for investors. The data will strengthen resource assessments, support financial planning, improve project design and help governments, regulators, Indigenous communities and industry make informed decisions as offshore wind development advances.

This work will help lay the foundation for Wind West and support Nova Scotia’s goal of licensing up to five gigawatts of offshore wind energy by 2030. The first phase of offshore wind development has the potential to attract $60 billion in private-sector investment while creating significant opportunities in construction, marine services, ports, manufacturing, engineering, technology and skilled trades.

Offshore wind represents an opportunity to transform Nova Scotia’s economy, strengthen communities, create careers for future generations and establish the province as a clean-energy powerhouse.

“History teaches us that Nova Scotia has always prospered when it has embraced its maritime advantages. The Age of Sail transformed a small Atlantic province into a globally connected trading hub. Today, offshore wind offers the chance to build a similarly transformative industry, creating jobs, attracting investment, strengthening communities and supporting long-term economic growth,” said Premier Houston.

Quotes:

“Nova Scotia’s world-class wind and highly skilled offshore workforce, developed through the legacy of offshore oil and gas, give Canada a competitive advantage in the potentially $1-trillion global offshore wind market – an advantage we are determined to seize. We will unlock Atlantic Canada’s massive potential by accelerating offshore wind development and strengthening Nova Scotia’s position as a supplier of reliable, affordable and clean energy to customers in the province and across Canada.”

— Tim Hodgson, federal Minister of Energy and Natural Resources

$5 million will support the deployment of floating light and detection ranging (FLiDAR) buoys to collect offshore wind, weather and ocean condition data

title: Examining arguments on both sides of Eugene's proposed clean energy fee
authors: Ashli Blow, Lucas Hellberg, Leo Heffron, Grace Chinowsky, Letters to the Editor, William L. Sullivan, Owen Murray

The proposed ordinance would require proceeds from the license fee to be placed in a “Eugene Clean Energy Fund” dedicated to funding renewable energy and energy efficiency programs; clean energy job training, apprenticeships, and contractor support; green infrastructure programs; future innovation; and fund administration (not to exceed 10% starting in 2030).

text:
QuickTake:

Measure 20-388 would charge large retailers a 2% fee on gross profits from Eugene sales to fund clean energy programs. Lookout Eugene-Springfield checked key claims from both campaigns, including whether the fee would raise prices and how retail plays into the city's climate pollution issues.

Inside the city of Eugene’s voter pamphlet are nearly 25 pages of ballot language, endorsements and arguments for and against Measure 20-388: a proposed ordinance that would enact a fee on large corporations to create a city fund for clean energy projects.

Local environmental justice organizers launched a campaign in February to promote their initiative, which qualified for the Nov. 3 election in August with about 14,000 signatures.

Since then, an opposition campaign representing industry groups has emerged to challenge the measure.

To help voters sort through the claims, Lookout Eugene-Springfield reviewed statements from both campaigns using the measure’s text, public records and interviews. But first, here’s what the measure would do and who is behind each campaign.

What is Measure 20-388?

Measure 20-388 would place a 2% fee on large retailers, defined as corporations earning more than $1 billion in gross profits annually in the United States and more than $500,000 in gross profits in Eugene. It exempts gross profits on basic groceries, medicine, and garbage and recycling services.

Here’s how it would work:

The fee would go into a fund designated for energy-efficiency projects and clean jobs that support communities in Eugene experiencing the harshest effects of climate change — for instance, low-income families living through extreme heat without air conditioning.

The measure would establish a nine-member committee with four-year terms that includes appointees from the City Council, the Eugene Water & Electric Board, and two city commissions, plus five members of the public who must have experience in fields such as renewable energy or workforce development.

The committee would make funding recommendations to the mayor and City Council for projects typically managed by nonprofit organizations.

If the measure passes, large retailers would need a license from the city in order to operate starting Jan. 1, 2029. According to the ballot summary, administrative costs are capped at 10% of the fund starting in 2030.

Read the measure’s official ballot summary.

The proposed ordinance would amend the Eugene code to, beginning January 1, 2029, require large retailers to obtain a license and pay an annual 2% license fee on gross profits from retail sales within the City. The ordinance defines “large retailer” as one engaged in retail sales in Eugene with gross profits exceeding $1,000,000,000 nationally and $500,000 in Eugene, excluding contractors, utilities, cooperatives, and credit unions. Gross profits from retail sales upon which the 2% is calculated would not include sales of most groceries, medicines, residential garbage and recycling services, and health care services. The proposed ordinance would require proceeds from the license fee to be placed in a “Eugene Clean Energy Fund” dedicated to funding renewable energy and energy efficiency programs; clean energy job training, apprenticeships, and contractor support; green infrastructure programs; future innovation; and fund administration (not to exceed 10% starting in 2030). The ordinance would require an expert committee to recommend use of funds, evaluate effectiveness of fund, and ensure work funded is performed by historically disadvantaged groups.

Read the full measure here.

The coalition behind the Eugene Clean Energy Fund, including chief petitioners, wrote the measure and based it on the Portland Clean Energy Fund. The Portland fund was enacted in 2019. Its revenue had reached $1 billion by June of this year.

Who’s involved in the campaigns?

Proponents

The local coalition supporting Measure 20-388 includes environmental groups such as Beyond Toxics, Breach Collective, Oregon Just Transition Alliance and Sierra Club of Oregon. The campaign filing name is listed as “Yes for Clean Energy Fund Eugene.”

Spokespeople and advisers include:

Aya Cockram, a chief petitioner, who is raising her family in Eugene and was a teacher before she started working for nonprofit organizations. She works as the Oregon energy transition organizer with the Breach Collective.

Joel Iboa, another chief petitioner, who lives in Eugene and has organized climate policy for years with Oregon Just Transition Alliance, where he is the executive director.

Dylan Plummer, a campaign adviser, who lives in Eugene and graduated from University of Oregon. He works on a national clean heat campaign for the Sierra Club.

Funding and endorsements:

The campaign has raised $292,695 as of Oct. 13. Contributions have come from chapters of labor unions including the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers and Smart Local; the Portland-based Northwest Health Foundation; and out-of-state groups including the Jane Fonda Climate PAC and Accelerator for America Action.

The measure has received about 100 endorsements, including U.S. Sen. Jeff Merkley, Eugene Education Association and Eugene councilmembers Jennifer Yeh, Matt Keating and Lyndsie Leech.

Opponents

The local opposition campaign represents the Eugene Chamber of Commerce, industry groups including the Oregon Bankers Association, the Northwest Grocery Retail Association and Oregon Business and Industry. The campaign filing name is listed as Stop the Hidden Tax on Eugene.

Spokespeople and advisers include:

Laura Sedwick, a spokesperson, is raising her family in Eugene and worked in the Oregon Legislature for elected officials including state Sen. Richard Devlin and U.S. Rep. Peter DeFazio. She served as the director of business and advocacy for the Eugene Chamber of Commerce for about four years. She now works in project management for a tech company.

PNW Strategies is a political consulting firm, which is listed as funding coordinating opposition arguments submitted to the voters pamphlet. This firm also managed a campaign against a watershed-rights measure earlier this year that raised 16 times the money as the supporters raised.

Funding and arguments:

The campaign has raised $38,360, as of Oct. 13. Contributions have come from Oregon Business & Industry’s political action committee and the Eugene Chamber of Commerce’s political action committee, called LIFT Lane.

People who have made a public argument against the measure in the voters’ pamphlet include Rusty Rexius, co-president of landscape company Rexius; Jason Williams, founder of Taxpayers Association of Oregon; former state Sen. Chris Edwards, D-Eugene; and former Eugene city councilors Chris Pryor and George Poling.

Examining the claims

Lookout checked the following claims and statements from both campaigns. Under state law, government employees can’t advocate for or against ballot measures, and so city officials could not take questions about the measure’s potential effects.

Claim: “Large retailers are a significant contributor to greenhouse gas emissions.”

Who said it: The measure’s findings, Section 1.

What Lookout found: The city’s 2021 greenhouse gas inventory, the most recent available, found that goods produced outside Eugene and delivered to the city, such as furniture and toys, make up the largest category of the community’s “imported” emissions.

“Community demand for these goods and services are the cause of the imported emissions. Consumption-based imported emissions are more difficult to measure and track, but when included in the accounting, make up a significant portion of the community’s emissions,” the report states.

The report looks at “consumption-based emissions” collectively, meaning pollution from what people consume, both imported and locally generated, such as from landfill waste. In total, the report found, the climate-warming pollution in the city comes to 2,461,883 metric tons of carbon equivalent. According to the report, to sequester that much carbon would take a natural area roughly 14 times the size of Crater Lake National Park.

Claim: “It will create good-paying jobs”

Who said it: Merkley, as part of his endorsement for the Eugene Clean Energy Fund.

What Lookout found: According to the measure, 25% to 30% of the fund would go to clean energy jobs training, apprenticeships and contractor support.

Contractors awarded the clean energy projects must meet wage and benefit standards according to Oregon law. They must either have a workforce with apprenticeships, sign project labor agreements, or qualify as a “high-road contractor” — which requires employer-paid retirement and full-family medical benefits to workers on their projects.

SEIU 503, Oregon’s largest labor union, has also endorsed the measure.

Claim: “We will see increased costs.”

Who said it: Sedwick, the opposition campaign spokesperson, during a City Club of Eugene forum.

What Lookout found: The opposition’s website, stopthehiddentax.com, argues that the 2% fee will be passed down to consumers. It shows a receipt of bills including cable, school supplies and a Costco trip, adding about $20 a month to “everyday” costs.

In an interview with Lookout, Sedwick said that the receipt is a “best guess.”

“It is just to give the consumer the visual that this isn’t just a licensing fee that Walmart is going to quietly pay,” said Sedwick, who caveats she is not an economist or business owner but someone worried about affordability and budget appropriations.

The opposition campaign did not reach out to Costco and other big businesses to ask whether the corporation had intentions about passing the cost onto consumers. Costco did not respond to Lookout by time of publication.

Sedwick pointed to a report analyzed by a nonpartisan committee out of the Oregon Legislature in 2016 and again in 2024 about corporate tax measures and consumer pricing.

Both projected that the taxes would raise consumer prices. However, the analyses were economic forecasts rather than a measure of actual price change. The estimates also considered a statewide tax on gross sales, which apply at every stage of production, not a local fee on gross profits from retail sales.

Sedwick and the opposition campaign refer to the measure as a tax, because they believe people will experience it like a sales tax. However, the measure itself describes it as a “license fee” that large businesses pay as a condition of doing business. Unlike a sales tax, the license fee is not assessed to customers at the register.

Claim: “There is no evidence to show this would be passed onto customers. In fact, there is evidence that says the opposite when we look at Portland.”

Who said it: Cockram in conversation with Sedwick on Oregon Public Broadcasting’s “Think Out Loud.”

What Lookout found: Under Portland’s rules, retailers are allowed to list the surcharge on receipts. (This is not a provision stated in the Eugene measure.)

However, when some large stores tried to do so in Portland, they faced lawsuits. In 2024, WinCo agreed to pay $3.6 million to settle a class action lawsuit that “alleged the company misled thousands of customers into paying hidden surcharges on certain non-grocery goods,” according to a 2024 report from The Oregonian. Safeway settled a similar lawsuit for up to $8.75 million.

Sedwick has asked the campaign why the Eugene measure exempts items like groceries if there isn’t a concern about prices being raised. (The Portland fund also exempts groceries.)

In a follow-up statement to Lookout, Plummer said: “We wanted to eliminate any doubt in the minds of voters reading the initiative for the first time that the costs of basic goods and services would increase by making them exempt from the fee. Whatever else voters believe about the measure, they can be 100% certain that the costs of essential goods and services wouldn’t be affected.”

In a follow-up statement to Lookout, Cockram added, “The bottom-line is PCEF (the Portland Clean Energy Fund) has been operating for eight years now. If there were direct evidence of this leading to increased prices, the opposition would have provided it.”

City of Portland staff who work on the fund told Lookout they do not track how businesses itemize surcharges on receipts or bills, because it is outside the scope of their program.

When asked what businesses in Portland have paid into the fund, the city said it could not disclose names due to tax confidentiality.

At a glance: Eugene’s progress on climate goals

Under its Climate Recovery Ordinance, adopted in 2014, the city of Eugene set a goal to cut communitywide fossil fuel use, such as gasoline, 50% by 2030 — with 2010 as its baseline.

To meet that goal, the city adopted a Climate Action Plan. About 67% of the plan’s actions, including investments in sustainable transportation, are complete, according to its 2025 annual report.

“We’re actually not on track to meet our goals even though we’ve implemented a majority of the plan,” Danielle Klinkebiel, climate policy analyst for the city of Eugene, told KEZI in August 2025.

“We’re in a really hard moment right now with some changes at the federal level and even at the state level,” Klinkebiel said. “We face a lot of new challenges in terms of funding to support this work.”

Those challenges still apply, alongside a strained city budget, spokesperson Marion Suitor told Lookout Wednesday, Oct. 15. In an email, Suitor said the city has not identified funding for the additional actions needed to meet its 2030 targets, and current work on the plan relies on partners.

text:
There is an enormous amount of money to be made for energy companies at the moment, considering the ongoing clean energy transition. One of the key elements for companies to become successful in the energy sector is ensuring that they capitalize on certain moments and generate as much revenue as possible while they still can, because of how quickly the energy sector evolves. There have been a lot of external companies that are reaching groundbreaking deals with energy companies with the aim of ensuring that they have a consistent energy supply for many years. On that note, Zelestra locked in $350 million for a 203 MW Indiana solar project, with Meta standing behind the power demand.

How influential has Zelestra been to the solar energy sector transformation?

There are many companies that are actively competing to be the sole pioneer in the energy sector, but this will be difficult to achieve given the abundance of companies that exist. However, there is a group of entities that have solidified themselves as leaders in the energy sector, and among those is Zelestra.

Zelestra is a global, multi-technology renewable energy company that was formerly known as Solarpack before rebranding in June 2024 to focus on customer-centric decarbonization solutions. The company was founded in 2005 and is headquartered in Madrid, Spain. It is backed by EQT Infrastructure V, which is part of EQT, one of the world’s largest private equity funds.

Zelestra operates as a vertically integrated independent power producer (IPP) providing tailored decarbonization options that combine solar PV and Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). In the modern era, companies that offer a wider range of services are more likely to be appointed in captivating projects.

Zelestra locks in $350 million for a 203 MW Indiana solar project, with Meta

A recent press release from Zelestra revealed that the company has closed $350 million in green financing credit facilities for the 203 MW Reclamation Solar project in Gibson County, Indiana. The finalization of the agreement takes Zelestra past $1 billion ($1.14bn) in project financing raised in the US in 2026, which is putting more than 800 MW of new solar into construction for its customers across the country. The company is enjoying a record-breaking year but is still not showing any signs of slowing down as it seeks to finish off the year on an incredibly high note.

The credit facilities were provided by Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC), BBVA and Societe Generale. Reclamation is underpinned by a long-term Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with Meta and is due to come online by the end of 2027. Zelestra is active in a variety of markets, including Spain, Italy, Germany, and the United States, which means it has a high chance of being involved in high-profile projects internationally and simultaneously.

An overview of Meta’s continued involvement in the energy sector

Meta has been involved in a number of projects in 2026, which is a testament to the company’s willingness to eliminate carbon emissions and possess reliable clean electricity for its data centers for many years to come. Meta is an American multinational technology conglomerate that is headquartered in Menlo Park, California.

Looking ahead: What does Zelestra’s collaboration with Meta signify?

Zelestra has a tremendous opportunity to create a blueprint that any other companies can latch on to as they pursue projects. Sybil Milo Cioffi, who is Zelestra’s US CFO, stated the following after the project’s announcement:

“Passing $1 billion in US project financing this year is a milestone we are pleased to share with our lenders and our customers. Reclamation is a major project that will deliver many benefits to our customer, and to the wider community. We are pleased that CIBC, BBVA and Societe Generale are backing our ambition.”

text:
US investment firm Pacolet Milliken has acquired Georgia Renewable Power (GRP), adding 116 MW of biomass generating capacity across two woody biomass power plants in northeast Georgia.

The deal, financed by Manulife, roughly triples the size of Pacolet's biomass platform. The family-owned firm entered the sector in 2024 with the acquisition of Piedmont Green Power, a 55 MW biomass plant in Barnesville, Georgia, and now operates three biomass facilities in the state. Financial terms were not disclosed.

The two GRP plants, in Franklin County and Madison County, sell their output to Georgia Power under long-term power purchase agreements. Both facilities are fuelled by woody biomass, qualify as renewable power sources under federal and state standards, and sell renewable energy credits on the open market.

William Crawford, chief executive of Pacolet, said: "Franklin and Madison are modern, efficient facilities that complement PGP well. We look forward to working with our partners and regulatory authorities to continue the plants' success, as well as ensuring the plants have a positive impact on their respective communities."

Lance Jordan, co-head and chief investment officer of Pacolet Power and Infrastructure, said the acquisition created "meaningful operational synergies" from running three facilities in the same state.

He added: "Going forward, we continue to see compelling opportunities to acquire high-quality assets that meet our sustainability and financial goals. We remain focused on pursuing additional renewables investments throughout the US."

text:
Manila, Philippines | 14 October 2026 — The ASEAN Energy Transition and Investment Roadmap (ETIR) was launched at the ASEAN Energy Business Forum (AEBF-26), providing a new regional analysis of how Southeast Asia’s energy system could evolve to meet rising energy demand while advancing the region’s long-term carbon neutrality ambitions.

ASEAN represents one of the largest and fastest growing economic regions of the world. At GBP 3 trillion, ASEAN is the world’s fifth-largest economy globally, accounting for about 3.5% of total global output. The ASEAN Strategy for Carbon Neutrality (CNS) was developed to support the region’s green transition, at the same time the ASEAN's climate ambitions are underpinned by a well-established regional energy policy architecture. The region is therefore poised to accelerate an inclusive transition towards a green economy, fostering sustainable growth and lasting climate action.

Supported by the UK Mission to ASEAN through ASEAN-UK Green Transition Fund and developed by Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) in close collaboration with the ASEAN Centre for Energy (ACE) and ASEAN Member States, the ETIR examines alternative pathways for ASEAN’s energy system through 2050.

The roadmap assesses pathways for ASEAN’s energy system through to 2050, focusing on the power, transport, buildings, industry and agriculture sectors, and identifying the investments, technologies, policies and regional cooperation required to deliver an inclusive and resilient energy transition.

The analysis highlights the scale of transformation that could accompany a net-zero pathway. By 2050, fossil-fuel supply under the modelled NZE pathway is around 57% lower than under BAU, while renewables could account for around 44% of total primary energy supply.

Electrification emerges as an important transition option across the economy, particularly in transport, buildings and suitable industrial processes. For harder-to-abate activities, the modelling explores more targeted roles for hydrogen, bioenergy and carbon management technologies.

The analysis also underscores the scale of investment associated with the transition. Under the modelled NZE pathway, average annual investment reaches approximately GBP 520 billion through 2050, with power and transport representing the largest shares.

Regional cooperation is another important theme emerging from the analysis. ETIR modelling indicates that greater cross-border electricity trade and interconnection could support access to diverse renewable resources, improve system flexibility and strengthen regional energy security.

These findings reinforce the potential value of continued cooperation on power-system integration alongside national transition efforts.

“The Report answers the question of how ASEAN can unlock investment and mobilise capital necessary to enhance ASEAN’s energy security, resilience, and connectivity, while facilitating the region’s energy transition. It demonstrates ACE’s ongoing commitment to supporting ASEAN Member States (AMS) in pursuing the region’s energy priorities and energy security, aligned with our regional energy blueprint, the ASEAN Plan of Action on Energy Cooperation 2026–2030 targets,” said Dato’ Ir. Ts. Razib Dawood, Executive Director of the ASEAN Centre for Energy (ACE)

At the same time, the ETIR proposes targeted just-transition measures to support workers, communities and economies affected by declining fossil-fuel activity.

“This roadmap is an important step in translating ASEAN's energy transition ambitions into practical action. Delivering the transition will require significant investment, supportive policy environments and close collaboration between governments, industry and investors. The UK is proud to support this work through the ASEAN-UK Green Transition Fund, which reflects our shared commitment under the new ASEAN-UK Plan of Action to support practical, ASEAN-led solutions to the region's energy transition challenges,” said UK Ambassador to ASEAN, Helen Fazey.

ASEAN has an extraordinary opportunity to meet its growing energy needs while building a more competitive, secure and sustainable economy. The ETIR provides a shared evidence base to help governments, investors and partners understand the choices ahead and where greater cooperation and investment can make the greatest difference. SEforALL is proud to have worked with ACE, ASEAN Member States and the UK to support this important regional conversation and help translate ambition into action,” said Damilola Ogunbiyi, the CEO and Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL).

As ASEAN’s energy demand continues to grow, the ETIR underscores the importance of acting early to build the infrastructure, markets and enabling policy environment needed for a secure, inclusive, resilient and net-zero energy future.

text:
Ford Motor Co. opened an online interest list for its new electric pickup, the Fathom, on October 14, 2026, according to Electrek. The move does not count as a preorder. It is a names-and-emails sign-up sheet meant to gauge demand ahead of an actual ordering window that Ford says will open in early 2027, more than a year before the first truck reaches a driveway.

The timing matters. Ford has spent the better part of two years promising a cheaper, smaller electric truck after the F-150 Lightning struggled to find buyers at its original price point. Fathom is that answer, and the automaker is now testing the market’s appetite for it a full year before anyone can actually place a deposit.
