What Ford Announced on the Fathom EV Pickup

Ford confirmed the production name of its midsize electric pickup as Fathom, according to reports covering the announcement. The truck carries a starting MSRP of $28,350 for the standard-range-battery model. Add Ford’s $1,595 destination charge and the reported starting price lands at $29,945, which Ford and multiple outlets are framing as “under $30,000 including destination.”

That positioning is deliberate. Ford’s support documentation confirms the Fathom will be “BlueCruise-capable,” tying the truck to the automaker’s existing hands-free highway driving system rather than launching a brand-new driver-assistance stack from scratch. Beyond that confirmed detail, Ford has not published a full specification sheet. Battery capacity, range, horsepower, payload, towing numbers, exterior dimensions, and the trim lineup all remain unconfirmed as of this writing, and readers should treat any number circulating online for those specs as speculation until Ford publishes an official sheet.

Production is reported to be planned for Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky. Customer deliveries are reported to begin in autumn or late 2027, roughly a year after the preorder window opens. No named Ford executive has an on-record quote in the available reporting, so this article avoids attributing any statement to a specific Ford spokesperson.

The Interest List Is Not a Preorder

The most important nuance in this story is also the one most likely to get flattened in headlines: signing up for Ford’s interest list does not reserve a truck, lock in a price, or guarantee any incentive. Reports describing the sign-up process are explicit that it functions as an interest form, sometimes described as a “preorder invite” list, rather than a binding order.

That distinction echoes a pattern Ford, Tesla, and other automakers have used repeatedly over the past decade: build a waiting list years before a vehicle ships, generate headlines and social proof, then convert a fraction of that list into actual orders once pricing, specs, and production timing are locked, a dynamic InsideEVs noted in its coverage of the Fathom invite list. Reservation lists do not obligate the manufacturer to honor original pricing, and they rarely come with legal protections for the person signing up. Readers who registered interest in the Fathom should not assume their spot on the list converts automatically into a 2027 delivery slot.

The gap between “interest registration opens” and “preorders open” is about a year by Ford’s own reported timeline, and the gap between preorders and actual deliveries is roughly another year, a sequence Car and Driver described as a pre-order list for a pre-order list. That’s a long runway for a company to revise pricing, trim configurations, or even delay the launch outright, something that has happened to other buzzy EV trucks before (see the historical context section below).

Why Ford Needs a Cheaper Truck

Ford’s F-150 Lightning launched with strong initial demand and then cooled as the EV truck market matured and buyers balked at price tags that climbed well past $50,000 for configurations with real-world range and towing capability. The broader EV truck segment has struggled to hit mainstream price points: Rivian’s R1T and Tesla’s Cybertruck both launched well north of $60,000 for their initial configurations, putting them out of reach for buyers who simply want a work truck replacement rather than a technology showcase.

That affordability gap is exactly where Ford is aiming the Fathom, as Edmunds noted in its pricing writeup. A reported sub-$30,000 starting price, even before any federal or state incentives, would put the Fathom closer to the price of a well-equipped gas-powered compact truck than to its electric-truck rivals. Whether Ford can actually hit that price at scale, with real factory margins and in a market where battery and component costs have been volatile, is the open question analysts will be watching over the next year.

Ford’s broader EV strategy has shifted more than once since 2022. The company has pulled back on some electric vehicle investments, delayed other programs, and repeatedly emphasized that profitability, not market share, is the priority for its EV lineup going forward. The Fathom appears to be the clearest expression yet of that profitability-first posture applied to trucks specifically: a smaller, cheaper vehicle built at a dedicated plant, rather than a larger, more expensive flagship competing directly with Cybertruck and R1T on raw capability.

Louisville Assembly Plant’s Role

Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky is reported as the planned production site for the Fathom. The plant has a long manufacturing history for Ford, and dedicating it to a new, lower-cost electric truck signals the company’s intent to build the Fathom at volume rather than treat it as a low-volume halo vehicle. Unconfirmed reporting details around plant retooling costs and timelines should be treated cautiously until Ford files or discloses specifics through official channels.

A Kentucky-built, sub-$30,000 electric truck also plays into a broader domestic-manufacturing narrative that automakers have leaned on heavily since 2022, particularly around potential eligibility for federal EV tax credits tied to North American assembly and battery sourcing requirements. Ford has not detailed the Fathom’s eligibility for any current incentive programs, and this article makes no claim about tax credit eligibility given the fact sheet does not confirm that detail.

Competitive Landscape: Where Fathom Fits

The electric truck market has gotten more crowded and more price-stratified since the Cybertruck and R1T first launched. Chevrolet has pushed the Silverado EV toward broader buyers. Startups have chased the budget end of the market directly, with Slate Truck positioning itself as a stripped-down, low-cost alternative built around simplicity rather than feature density.

Ford’s reported sub-$30,000 Fathom pricing, if it holds through 2027, would undercut most of that field by a wide margin. The table below lays out what’s publicly confirmed about the Fathom alongside general positioning of other electric trucks already on the market, without inventing specs Ford hasn’t disclosed.

Several figures in that table are intentionally left as “not covered” rather than filled with a number pulled from memory. Readers comparing exact prices and specs across these vehicles should check each manufacturer’s current configurator, since EV truck pricing has shifted multiple times across the industry since 2023 as automakers adjusted for battery costs, incentive eligibility, and demand.

Timeline: From Interest List to Delivery

Ford’s reported rollout plan for the Fathom stretches across roughly 18 months from this week’s interest-list opening to the first customer deliveries. Here is what’s confirmed about that sequence.

Historical Context: Ford’s Rocky EV Truck Road

Ford’s path to the Fathom has not been a straight line. The F-150 Lightning launched in 2022 to strong early reservations, then saw Ford cut production targets and pause the assembly line more than once as demand softened and the company absorbed losses on its EV division. Ford has disclosed billions of dollars in EV-related losses across its Model e division in successive annual reports, a figure that pushed the company to rethink its electric vehicle roadmap rather than keep chasing larger, pricier trucks.

That rethink produced reports of a canceled three-row electric SUV, a scaled-back electric van program, and a pivot toward what Ford has internally called a more affordable EV platform. The Fathom is the clearest public output of that pivot applied to trucks specifically. It is worth remembering that Tesla’s own Cybertruck took roughly four years from its 2019 unveiling to actual customer deliveries in late 2023, and arrived with a final price well above its original announced figure. Ford’s current one-year gap between interest list and preorders, and second year to delivery, gives the company a comparable runway to adjust before the Fathom reaches real customers. Readers who remember the Cybertruck’s price drift should treat Fathom’s current $28,350 figure as a stated intention rather than a locked-in guarantee, since Ford itself has not confirmed final trim and equipment details.

Market Impact: Suppliers, Dealers, and Rivals

A sub-$30,000 electric truck built at meaningful volume would ripple beyond Ford’s own balance sheet. Battery suppliers, dealers carrying competing EV trucks, and rival automakers chasing the same affordability tier all have reason to watch how the Fathom’s interest list performs over the coming weeks.

For dealers, an affordable electric truck solves a problem gas-powered compact trucks have faced for years: shrinking margins on low-cost vehicles. If Ford can build the Fathom profitably at its reported starting price, it gives dealers a volume electric product to sell without the showroom hesitation that has dogged pricier EV trucks. For rivals chasing the same budget tier, including Slate Truck’s stripped-down approach, a well-known brand entering the sub-$30,000 segment raises the competitive bar and could pressure smaller players to either cut prices further or differentiate on features Ford hasn’t matched.

Battery and component suppliers tied to Ford’s Kentucky manufacturing footprint also stand to benefit if the Louisville Assembly Plant ramps the Fathom to meaningful volume, though Ford has not disclosed specific sourcing or supply-chain details for this truck beyond the Louisville production reports already covered above.

What’s Still Unconfirmed

It’s worth being explicit about what Ford has not yet said, because a lot of chatter online fills those gaps with guesses. Ford has not confirmed battery capacity or chemistry, EPA-estimated range, horsepower or torque figures, payload or towing capacity, exterior and bed dimensions, or the final trim and equipment structure for the Fathom. Ford also has not confirmed whether registering on the current interest list carries any benefit, such as priority ordering or a locked-in price, once preorders actually open in early 2027.

That gap matters for a different reason too: it means the $28,350 starting figure circulating now describes a standard-range-battery configuration, likely the base trim. Buyers interested in higher-range or dual-motor configurations, which Ford is expected to offer, should expect a higher price than the headline figure once Ford discloses the full trim lineup.

Predictions: Where This Goes Next

Based on Ford’s reported timeline and the pattern of prior EV truck launches across the industry, here’s how the next 18 months are likely to unfold.

Ford will likely publish fuller Fathom specifications, including range and towing figures, in the months leading up to the early-2027 preorder window rather than all at once this fall.

The interest list will generate a large initial sign-up number in its first weeks, mirroring how EV reservation lists have historically spiked on launch before leveling off.

Expect at least one pricing or trim adjustment between now and the 2027 preorder opening, consistent with how Ford and other automakers have revised EV pricing in response to battery costs and incentive changes over the past three years.

Rival automakers chasing the sub-$30,000 EV truck tier, including smaller players like Slate Truck, will face pressure to clarify their own pricing and timelines in response to Ford’s move.

Louisville Assembly Plant hiring and retooling activity will likely become a recurring local news story in Kentucky through 2027 as the autumn/late-2027 delivery target approaches.

None of these are guarantees. They’re reasonable expectations based on Ford’s own stated timeline and how comparable EV launches, including Ford’s own F-150 Lightning rollout and Tesla’s Cybertruck rollout, have played out in the past. Anyone tracking the Fathom closely should expect official updates to arrive in stages over the next year rather than as one comprehensive reveal.

Should You Sign Up for the Fathom Interest List?

For anyone curious about the Fathom, signing up for Ford’s interest list costs nothing and carries no obligation, based on current reporting describing it as a non-binding form rather than an actual order. The practical upside is modest: it likely puts a prospective buyer on Ford’s communication list for updates as the truck’s specs and preorder process firm up over the next year.

The practical downside is also modest, but worth naming: nothing about the current list guarantees a 2027 delivery slot, a locked price, or priority over someone who signs up later. Buyers who want a sub-$30,000 electric truck today, rather than in late 2027, still have the Slate Truck’s reservation process and the existing lineup of pricier EV trucks from Rivian, Tesla, and Chevrolet to consider in the meantime.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Ford Fathom interest list an actual preorder?

No. Reports describe it as an online interest form, sometimes called a preorder invite list, rather than a binding order. Public preorders are expected to open in early 2027.

How much does the Ford Fathom cost?

Ford’s reported starting MSRP for the standard-range-battery model is $28,350. Including Ford’s $1,595 destination charge, the reported starting price is $29,945.

Where will the Ford Fathom be built?

Reports indicate Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky is the planned production site.

When will the Ford Fathom actually ship to customers?

Reports project customer deliveries beginning in autumn or late 2027, roughly a year after public preorders are expected to open.

Does the Ford Fathom have self-driving features?

Ford’s support documentation confirms the Fathom is “BlueCruise-capable,” referring to Ford’s existing hands-free highway driving system. Full details on how BlueCruise will be packaged or priced on this specific model have not been disclosed.

What are the Ford Fathom’s range and towing specs?

Ford has not confirmed final battery capacity, range, horsepower, payload, or towing figures. Treat any specific numbers circulating online as unconfirmed until Ford publishes an official specification sheet.

How does the Fathom compare to the Tesla Cybertruck or Rivian R1T?

The Fathom’s reported sub-$30,000 starting price targets a far lower price tier than either the Cybertruck or R1T, which both launched well above $60,000. Ford appears to be positioning the Fathom as an affordable truck replacement rather than a direct capability competitor to those vehicles.

Does signing up for the interest list guarantee a lower price or delivery priority?

No. Available reporting says registering does not lock in an order, guarantee a production vehicle, or confirm delivery timing or incentives.

text:
There’s an old line about nuclear power being a very expensive way to boil water. It’s a little unfair, but it’s basically accurate. A reactor makes heat, the heat turns water into steam, and the steam spins a turbine hooked up to a generator.

Terrestrial Energy, a North Carolina company developing molten salt reactors, would like the steam-and-electricity half of its plant treated like a regular industrial project. On October 8, the company said it had asked the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to confirm that building that half isn’t nuclear construction.

If the NRC agrees, the company says that half could go up first and start selling power and heat with an auxiliary heat source like natural gas. That could all happen before the reactors have a construction permit or an operating license.

The plant comes in two pieces

The design is called the Integral Molten Salt Reactor, or IMSR, and every plant is split into two parts. The Nuclear Facility holds the standardized, modular reactor systems. The Thermal and Electric Facility, or TEF, holds the turbines, the generators and the steam systems, which is pretty much the kind of gear you’d find at a coal or gas plant.

The filing itself is a topical report. If that term’s new to you, it’s basically a piece of a future license application that a company asks the NRC to review on its own, ahead of time. Once it’s approved, the company can point to it in later applications, and the NRC doesn’t have to go back over that part.

One IMSR Plant is rated at 390 megawatts of electricity from two reactors. Those reactors are built as replaceable core-units, and the company plans to swap them out every seven years.

The molten salt part means the IMSR’s fuel is dissolved in the salt that also carries the heat away, so there aren’t any solid fuel rods. We’ve covered how that works with a liquid-fuel research reactor going into a science building in Abilene, and the short version is that it runs hot at low pressure. The IMSR also uses standard low-enriched uranium, under 5% U-235, which is the same kind of fuel the existing US fleet uses.

So what counts as nuclear construction?

Less than you’d think. The NRC’s definition lives in a section of the federal rulebook called 10 CFR 50.10, and it doesn’t treat every bulldozer on a reactor site as nuclear work. Clearing and digging the site, putting up fences and warehouses, and building roads, parking lots and transmission lines are all on its list of things that don’t count.

The rule saves the word for driving piles, pouring foundations and installing equipment for the parts of a plant that matter for safety. It spells those out. They include safety-related equipment, anything the plant relies on to handle accidents, and anything whose failure could trip the reactor or keep safety systems from doing their job. Security, fire protection and onsite emergency facilities are on the list too. If a contractor’s working on any of that, it’s construction, and it needs the NRC’s permission first.

That reactor-trip clause matters here. At a lot of conventional plants, a turbine trip can automatically shut the reactor down too. According to the report, a failure that starts on the turbine side of an IMSR Plant stays isolated from the reactors, and the reactors don’t depend on the TEF to stay safe.

The report also leans on the company’s method for analyzing postulated initiating events, which the NRC has already approved. That’s regulator-speak for the things that could go wrong in a plant and kick off an accident.

If you’ve been following TerraPower’s Natrium project in Wyoming, some of this might sound familiar. TerraPower needed an NRC exemption to start driving piles and pouring foundations for the plant’s non-nuclear “energy island” in Kemmerer while its construction permit was still under review, and the NRC approved that permit in March.

Terrestrial’s CEO, Simon Irish, is pitching the TEF report as something more permanent. He called it “a fleet-wide advantage, not a one-off exemption,” since the same pathway would cover every IMSR Plant once the NRC signs off.

The gas is supposed to be a bridge

So why would a reactor developer want to burn natural gas?

Money, mostly. Licensing a reactor can take years, and a turbine side that’s already up and running can bring in revenue while you wait. In Irish’s telling, customers would get electricity and heat sooner, and the banks financing a plant would get a construction phase they can actually lend against, since only the reactor side would be stuck on the nuclear licensing clock.

Frankly, I think that’s a pretty smart way to sell a first-of-a-kind reactor to customers and lenders who’d otherwise be nervous about one. If the nuclear side runs late, whoever owns the site still has a working power plant, and that seems like a much easier conversation to have with a bank.

There’s a fair bit we don’t know yet. The company hasn’t said what the gas setup would look like, how big it’d be, or how long a plant could run on it before the reactors take over. Since every TEF is supposed to be customized for its site, I’d guess those answers change from project to project. The NRC hasn’t posted a review schedule for the report either, at least not one I could find.

And yes, burning gas at a plant built around nuclear reactors is arguably going to sound a little backwards to some of nuclear power’s biggest fans. The gas is described as a stopgap until the nuclear side is ready, so presumably it gets turned off once the reactors come online.

An Army project in Maryland starts with gas

The filing doesn’t name a specific site. But on September 18, the Army conditionally picked Ameresco, a Massachusetts energy company, to develop a power project at Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland, with Terrestrial lined up as the nuclear supplier.

The deal announcement describes a phased project combining natural gas and nuclear generation. Ameresco told POWER magazine that the gas comes first, and that the IMSR would be a potential second phase that won’t be available before 2030 and still depends on lease negotiations with the Army.

Neither company has connected Aberdeen to the TEF report. Still, a project that starts on gas and adds a reactor later sounds like a pretty natural fit for what the filing wants the NRC to sign off on, and I’d be a little surprised if that hadn’t crossed anyone’s mind in Charlotte. The Army, for its part, says nothing gets built until the environmental and regulatory reviews are done, and that development at its sites could start as early as 2027.

Terrestrial also has a plant planned for Texas A&M’s RELLIS campus in Bryan, Texas, where Last Energy has its own pilot reactor.

The NRC has already approved two of Terrestrial’s earlier topical reports. The TEF report, filed October 8, is the company’s third submission of 2026, and it’s still aiming to have its first IMSR plants running at multiple US sites in the early 2030s.

text:
Historically, U.S. mine tailings have been treated as waste to be disposed of, not as a potential resource. That view is changing. The U.S. Department of the Interior now considers mine waste “one promising domestic source of critical minerals,” and federal agencies are moving to ease recovery of critical minerals from tailings while encouraging remediation.

This post examines the federal framework for recovering critical minerals from mine waste, the regulatory and financial barriers that have historically inhibited the sector, and the funding opportunities available to companies seeking to turn tailings into profit.

Domestic Potential

The United States imports essentially 100% of 13 critical minerals and more than 50% of another 20 critical mineral commodities essential to national defense, advanced manufacturing, energy infrastructure, and emerging technologies. China dominates extraction and processing of many of these materials.

Domestic tailings could help close that gap. A preliminary analysis by the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) National Energy Technology Laboratory and the Idaho National Laboratory estimates that approximately 13,904 million metric tons of tailings across 189 major sites contain significant concentrations of rare earth elements, cobalt, gallium, germanium, indium, and platinum-group elements. For example, abandoned lead and zinc mines in Oklahoma have left behind waste rich in zinc and germanium. Researchers have also identified tellurium, which is vital for defense applications, in copper tailings at a Utah mine. Industry is already pursuing these opportunities: some mining companies estimate they could produce up to 800 million pounds of copper annually as soon as 2027 by leaching the metal from waste piles once considered worthless.

Reprocessing also offers environmental benefits. Legacy tailings sites can be sources of acid mine drainage, heavy-metal leaching, and dust. Reprocessing can remediate those conditions while recovering minerals.

The Current Political and Regulatory Framework

Fragmented regulation of domestic mining has historically impeded the expansion of the processing capacity needed to extract critical minerals from tailings. In recent years, Congress and the Executive Branch have taken a series of steps to address those barriers.

The Energy Act of 2020 created the first comprehensive statutory framework for federal critical minerals programs, including research on recovery from secondary and unconventional sources. The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021 then funded several programs explicitly targeting mine waste sites.

The Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 amended the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) to impose presumptive deadlines of one year for environmental assessments (EAs) and two years for environmental impact statements (EISs). The Act also allows agencies to rely on existing EAs and categorical exclusions for certain projects, which may include tailings recovery at previously permitted or remediation sites. That same year, the Federal Permitting Improvement Steering Council proposed prioritizing critical mineral projects for FAST-41 coordinated review, which offers a single coordinating agency, a predictable timetable, and a public permit tracking dashboard.

On March 20, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order (EO) 14241, which directs federal agencies to expedite permitting for domestic mineral projects and prioritize federal lands for mining and processing, delegates Defense Production Act (DPA) authorities to support domestic mineral production, and broadens the definition of “minerals” to include copper, zinc, uranium, potash, and gold.

In July 2025, Congress enacted the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), which made some of the most sweeping changes to federal mineral-resource policy in more than a generation.

Later that month, the Department of the Interior (DOI) issued Secretarial Order (SO) 3436, which defines mine waste broadly to include waste piles, coal refuse, tailings, and discharges on federal, state, tribal, and private lands. The Order directs DOI bureaus and offices to review and, where appropriate, amend regulations and streamline processes to encourage private-sector recovery of critical minerals from mine waste. Implementation will determine how much these reforms benefit the domestic mining industry.

Regulatory and Market Barriers

Tailings reprocessing does not fit neatly into existing regulatory categories. Depending on the site, regulators may treat a project as mining, waste management, remediation, or a hybrid, creating uncertainty about which rules apply and which agencies have jurisdiction.

The legal status of minerals in tailings under the General Mining Law of 1872 is also uncertain, including whether developers can claim tailings as minerals or whether tailings are waste governed by other frameworks, and what royalties apply on federal land. Some sites also face title disputes among surface owners, mineral estate holders, and the federal government.

Environmental liability has been a significant barrier to private investment in legacy tailings recovery. Because the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA or Superfund) imposes strict, joint, and several liability, a party that disturbs contamination can become a potentially responsible party even if it did not cause the original pollution and its work improves site conditions. In some cases, cleanup liability could exceed recovery revenue by orders of magnitude.

State permits for water discharges, air emissions, and residual tailings add further layers of review. Permitting a new mine in the U.S. typically takes seven to ten years, compared with two to three years in Canada and one to two years in Australia. The practical effect of recent NEPA reforms on complex mining projects remains to be seen.

Funding and Government Program Opportunities

Several federal funding streams support these projects. A 2022 presidential determination under Title III of the Defense Production Act (DPA) made “by-product and co-product production at existing mining, mine waste reclamation, and other industrial facilities” eligible for support, and the Department of War has since made several hundred million dollars in DPA funding available, including for recovery from secondary sources. DOE’s new Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation has also announced plans to issue nearly $1 billion in funding opportunities, including $275 million for “Mines and Metals Capacity Expansion,” $80 million for “Mine of the Future,” and $134 million for a “Rare Earth Elements Demonstration Facility.” On September 30, 2026, DOE announced $29.5 million in awards to 17 U.S. National Laboratory projects to accelerate the development of innovative technologies that expand and improve domestic mining capabilities.

Tax incentives are less certain. Inflation Reduction Act production tax credits mainly target primary production and recycling. The OBBBA phases out parts of the tax credit framework for critical minerals processing and advanced manufacturing and eliminates or accelerates the phase-out of key demand-side incentives, including under Sections 45X and 30D. Some policy proposals would extend Section 45X credits to minerals recovered from secondary sources.

Certain projects may qualify for Superfund cost recovery or brownfield redevelopment funding if they demonstrably improve site conditions. Several states also offer tax credits, infrastructure investment, workforce training support, or expedited review for critical mineral projects. Layering these incentives with federal support could make some otherwise marginal projects viable.

Looking Ahead

Ultimately, the main obstacles to recovering critical minerals from mine tailings are regulatory uncertainty, economic risk, and institutional frameworks designed for conventional mining. Federal policy has rarely been more favorable to these projects, but success will still turn on site-specific economics, careful management of environmental and mineral-title risks, and strategic use of the reclamation, defense, and energy funding now available.

Our team is tracking regulatory developments in this space and can help stakeholders navigate federal funding opportunities, regulatory challenges, and the evolving permitting landscape for critical minerals projects.

VAN BUREN TOWNSHIP, Mich. (WXYZ) — Despite months of opposition from residents, Van Buren Township officials approved plans Wednesday for a controversial Google data center campus, clearing the way for a project that is already under construction and expected to bring years of development activity to the area.

The hyperscale data center campus will span 282 acres north of I-94 between Haggerty Road and I-275.

See the full story in the video below

Van Buren approves Google data center, other communities move to slow similar projects

Residents packed public meetings leading up to the decision, raising concerns about everything from noise and dust to environmental impacts, property values and water usage.

"I have repeatedly expressed concern about the potential effects of continuous low frequency humming and total noise," one resident told officials.

Another resident argued that "noise and nuisance do not belong in residential neighborhoods."

Many residents said they felt their concerns were being ignored throughout the approval process.

Developers, however, said the project has been significantly modified in response to community feedback.

"We've worked hard over the last three years to take as much community feedback into the site plan and the design," said Adam Kramer, president of Panattoni Data Centers.

Kramer said the company has invested tens of millions of dollars into changes aimed at reducing impacts on nearby neighborhoods.

"Most residents won't even know that the data center is there just because visually you're not going to see it. Out of sight, out of mind. But you will feel the benefits from this," Kramer said.

Developers say the development will create jobs and generate substantial tax revenue. Township officials said that state law limits their ability to reject projects that meet zoning requirements.

"The planning commission, per Michigan state law, is required to approve site plans that satisfy the ordinance standards," one township official said during the meeting.

Construction Timeline

While debate over the project continues, construction activity is already underway.

According to project documents, underground utility work associated with the development will be completed in eight phases. Most of the work will require temporary road closures near the I-94 Service Drive, Van Buren Street and Old Haggerty Road.

The early phases of construction are expected to continue through the end of 2026, with additional work planned into early 2027.

The final phases are scheduled for March 2027 and will affect Haggerty Road traffic. Rather than full closures, drivers can expect alternating one-way traffic controlled by flaggers while work is underway.

A Growing Statewide Debate

According to reporting by GovTech, Springfield Township in Oakland County approved a 180-day moratorium on new data center applications while officials rewrite zoning regulations and study potential impacts on utilities, public safety and natural resources. Township leaders said they were not prepared to evaluate a large-scale data center proposal without additional rules in place.

Detroit is also weighing restrictions. According to Planet Detroit, the Detroit City Council approved a resolution urging a two-year pause on new data center permits while the city studies issues including power demand, water usage, noise and land-use impacts.

Oxford Township has gone a step further. According to Hoodline, township officials enacted a one-year moratorium while developing regulations related to noise, cooling systems, power demand, generators, water usage and eventual decommissioning requirements. Public interest has been high, with hundreds of residents attending meetings on the issue.

Similar conversations have also taken place in Washington Township and Wixom. According to DataCenterBans.com, Wixom previously adopted a temporary moratorium before implementing stricter zoning requirements, including setbacks from homes, sound studies and water protection measures.

The trend suggests local governments are no longer debating only whether to allow data centers. Instead, many communities are focusing on whether they have regulations in place before major proposals arrive.

For some Van Buren Township residents, that conversation is happening after the fact.

Township officials have maintained that the Google data center met existing zoning requirements, leaving them with no legal basis to deny the project. As construction moves forward, the development is expected to remain a focal point in the broader discussion over how Michigan communities should prepare for future data center proposals.

text:
Acciona has been appointed by the Western Australian government to deliver a significant component of the Clean Energy Link – East (CEL–East) electricity transmission project, a scheme valued at A$655m ($455m) and intended to support the region’s transition to renewable energy.

The announcement follows the selection of Acciona, in partnership with GenusPlus and UGL Engineering, to undertake key aspects of the project.

Under the contract, Acciona will construct a new electricity transmission terminal south of Darkan, around 200km from Perth.

This facility is designed to connect forthcoming renewable energy developments to the state’s existing power networks.

CEL–East will include new transmission lines, a new terminal at Cordering, expansions to the Shotts and Muja terminals, and upgrades to parts of the network.

Planned works will include 38km of new 330kV transmission lines between Shotts and Cordering, along with 54km of 330kV lines from Muja to Cordering.

Once operational, the infrastructure is expected to enable approximately 2.3GW of renewable energy capacity, estimated to be sufficient to power around one million households.

Stage one will focus on new and upgraded lines between Collie and Darkan to support additional energy delivery from renewable energy zones in the east and south-east.

Project organisers anticipate an initial creation of 300 jobs, with the number rising to 600 at the peak of construction.

Acciona has stated its intention to work closely with local communities and landowners, to use regional contractors, and to support technical training and inclusion of the Aboriginal workforce.

Western Australia (WA) Premier Roger Cook said: “Affordable, reliable, and lower carbon energy will power jobs in defence, advanced manufacturing, and the downstream processing of our minerals, including in green iron.

“That includes investing in Clean Energy Link – East to secure local jobs and opportunities for WA businesses while building a stronger energy system.

“Having granted it Priority Project status, we are fast-tracking its delivery, supporting up to 600 local jobs and ensuring our grid is ready for when we get out of State-owned coal by 2030.”

This contract builds on Acciona’s existing commitments in the region, where it is also involved in the Clean Energy Link North project and the HumeLink transmission line in New South Wales.

Acciona says these efforts will enhance the reliability and capacity of WA’s power network, supporting the gradual shift away from coal-fired generation.

text:
U.S. ESS Installations Rise About 37% to 70GWh This Year, Projected Over 110GWh by 2030 While LG, Samsung SDI and SK On Scale North American Production Backed by IRA Credits and Tariff Gap Favoring Korean Batteries

As the North American Energy Storage System (ESS) market rapidly grows due to the surge in power demand following the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, the domestic battery industry is accelerating the transition of its business structure.

According to energy research institutes such as Wood Mackenzie on Oct. 15, the U.S. ESS installation volume is expected to increase by about 37% from 51GWh last year to 70GWh this year.

It is expected to expand to more than 110 to 120GWh in 2030.

ESS is a device that stores electricity when power demand is low and supplies it when demand surges.

As facilities that consume a large amount of power and require a stable power supply, such as AI data centers, increase, the demand for ESS is also increasing.

Nvidia is also strengthening the connection between data center power infrastructure and ESS.

Battery energy storage systems (BESS) were included as the first certification category in the ‘DSX Ready’ certification program, which Nvidia launched last month to standardize the design of power infrastructure and cooling systems for AI factories.

The non-China supply chain policy and tariff system of the United States are also cited as opportunity factors for the domestic battery industry.

This is because the relative price competitiveness of Korean companies can increase if the tariff burden on Chinese batteries grows, in addition to tax support such as the Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit (AMPC) and the Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA).

In the United States, a 40.9% tariff rate has been applied to Chinese lithium-ion batteries since last July, while a 12.5% rate is applied to Korean batteries, resulting in a tariff rate difference reaching 28.4% points.

Under these circumstances, the three major domestic battery companies are expanding their ESS business by utilizing their North American production bases.

LG Energy Solution plans to expand its North American ESS production capacity from about 57GWh this year to 73GWh next year.

The plan is to strengthen its ESS supply capabilities by utilizing existing North American production bases, including the Holland and Lansing plants in Michigan, the Ultium Cells joint venture, and the Honda joint venture business in the United States.

LG Energy Solution is the only domestic company to have been selected as a BESS partner company for Nvidia’s DSX Ready.

Samsung SDI is also pushing for a plan to expand its North American production capacity to 32GWh in 2027 by utilizing production lines such as its Indiana plant in the United States and the Stellantis joint venture (SPE).

SK On aims to start mass production of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries at its Georgia plant in the United States from the second half of this year.

LFP batteries are highly utilized in the ESS market where price competitiveness is important, making them a product that can diversify the North American business portfolio.

An industry official said, “The battery industry is expected to strengthen its strategy of securing ESS as a new demand source to increase the utilization of production capacity,” adding, “If the non-China supply chain policy, tax benefits, and production line conversion effects are combined, the North American business competitiveness of domestic battery companies can be further strengthened.”

text:
The state of Michigan has awarded $65-million in grants, spread across 15 counties, to expand public transit.

Many of the grants are for rural counties. Roscommon County will receive a three-year, $3,371,763 grant to extend its on-demand, door-to-door system to neighboring Oscoda County, which has no public transit option of its own.

Steve Dubois is head of the Roscommon County Transportation Authority. He says the system also will pick people up from hospitals in Traverse City, which is more than an hour away from most places in the two counties.

"We have no hospitals in the counties whatsoever," Dubois said. "For emergent medical, everyone is transported out of county. If you don't have someone living with you or nearby or a neighbor you can rely on, how are you going to get home after that happens? So when they need medical attention in the middle of the night, and they get released at 1 a.m. from Traverse City, because that's where they ended up ultimately, we can go pick them up and bring them back home."

Other grants include:

$10 million to replace nine aging rail cars used by the Detroit People Mover

$5,986,000 for the U.P's Delta County to expand the Delta Area Transit Authority into a countywide public transportation network serving all of Delta County

$6,371,000 to unify Berrien County's public transit system, bringing the county’s four fragmented urban and rural transit systems into a coordinated regional network.

$6,600,000 to establish a high-capacity transit connection along one of the heaviest used routes between Ypsilanti and Ann Arbor

$9,980,000 to expand Genesee County's public transit system with a technology-enabled, on demand microtransit service, using smaller vehicles and a mobile app to provide rides within designated areas.

$571,000 to create a four-county regional transit network connecting the Mass Transportation Authority (MTA), Saginaw Transit Authority Regional Services (STARS), Greater Lapeer Transportation Authority (GLTA) and Shiawassee Area Transportation Agency (SATA)

$94,750 to study a redesign of Benzie County's public transportation system to include microtransit, enhanced demand response, and scheduled connections, as well as assess possible connections to neighboring counties and transit systems across the northwest Lower Peninsula

$1,069,000 for an an app-based, shared on-demand microtransit service designed to provide reliable and safe transportation across Michigan State University’s campus when fixed-route service is reduced or unavailable

$1,110,000 to add three accessible vehicles and two new weekday routes to Ionia County’s countywide microtransit service

$621,047 to support proposed service enhancements in northwest Ottawa County, extending hours to help residents who have difficulty finding transportation in the evening

$587,478 to Saginaw Transit Authority Regional Services to support a four a day, Monday through Thursday regional transit connection linking Midland, Delta College, Saginaw Valley State University (SVSU) and MBS International Airport.

$2 million for the Regional Transit Authority of Southeast Michigan's to plan and engineer potential transit improvements in downtown Detroit.

$6 million for The Rapid to add transit service during major events in downtown Grand Rapids, addressing spikes in travel demand associated with the Acrisure Amphitheater, the planned Amway Soccer Stadium, Van Andel Arena, DeVos Place and DeVos Performance Hall.

$678,366 for Thunder Bay Transportation Authority to establish on-demand service in Montmorency County, basing vehicles and drivers locally to address travel distances associated with dispatching vehicles from Alpena, and shorten response times and reduce miles traveled without passengers.
